Here is the story of “The Fall of the Muni Startup That Wanted to Upend Wall Street,” Neighborly Corp., which was trying to get into the business of selling municipal bonds in small-dollar increments directly to individuals: Neighborly sought to bring the crowdfunding approach popularized by Kickstarter to the $3.8 trillion municipal-securities market. Instead of selling bonds in minimum lots of $5,000, it would sell them in tiny amounts so local residents could buy them, expanding the market beyond the wealthy buyers and big investment firms who currently dominate it. To do that, Neighborly would help advertise the sale, hold town halls to answer questions and manage brokerage accounts. “If people knew they could invest in a street or school down the street, they would do that in a heartbeat,” Wilson told MIT News in 2016. “They don’t because the market has been made very, very complicated by a handful of global banks who make a profit off making it as complicated as it can be.” Anyway, right, it fell, or at least got out of the muni bonds business and into, uh, this: The Cambridge bond deal was one of just a handful the company won before shifting to other trendy businesses, including efforts to start a social-impact investing arm and allow cities to float a kind of cryptocurrency. It’s now planning to focus on extending high-speed Internet service to communities without it. Jase Wilson, who founded Neighborly, said the company chose to leave the municipal-bond market after deciding it was “solving the wrong problem.” “Even if we made it as efficient as it could possibly be, it’d be still structurally incapable of delivering information infrastructure, which is what our nation’s communities need more than anything,” Wilson said in a Sept. 25 interview. Ah. The story has some classic signifiers of startup hubris—“millions of dollars in venture-capital money, big-name hires, talented engineers and flashy marketing,” “profligate spending, an unclear route to turning a profit and erratic leadership”—and of financial industry entrenchment—“Neighborly still couldn’t overcome the obstacles of a more than century-old market built on ties between public officials and the bankers handling taxpayer money.” But without knowing any of the details, really, let me propose an alternative explanation for Neighborly’s failure to make a dent in the muni market. One absolute article of faith in modern fintech seems to be that people want to invest in every single random thing, but are thwarted by regulation or archaic technology or high minimum investment amounts. I distrust this assumption. I, for instance, could buy individual municipal bonds for $5,000, but I don’t, because I can buy muni-bond mutual funds, which are, and I don’t generally give investment advice around here but will put this out there anyway, better. Lots of smart people are working very hard on ways for me to buy $50 increments of local office buildings, and lots of other smart people worked very hard and have already cracked the code on ways for me to buy $50 increments of unsecured online loans to individual borrowers whom I select from a web page, but I will not do these things because they strike me as so, so dumb. Why would I want to pick individual office buildings or consumer borrowers or municipal projects to invest in when I could buy an index fund? Here I am certainly not giving investment advice, and obviously some people have different preferences, but my general sense is that most people are not desperate for vastly more fine-grained and complicated investing choices. The continuing long-term rise of passive investing suggests that for a lot of people, the ideal level of investing choice is, like, you give them a bucket called “investing,” they put money in the bucket, and it grows at the market rate of return and comes out of the bucket at retirement. That is certainly what I want! If you like things called “municipal bonds,” you probably like them as a category. Probably you vaguely assume that they’re safe and you’re vaguely aware of the tax benefits; I suppose there’s some chance that you vaguely think it is morally good to invest in municipal infrastructure, but it’s really very unlikely that you’ve been to a lot of town planning meetings and want to buy a bond that specifically funds a local project that you’re enthused about. There is a certain sort of tech person who has the opposite preferences, who wants to connect the entire world to a set of data structures and let everyone access and hack those data structures. “Why would I invest in other streets when I could invest in my street,” some tech founders probably do think. It just does not strike me as a universal, or even common, impulse. A lot of tech people love opening up computers and hacking them, but most normal people prefer the smooth surface and one-size-fits-all choices of the iPhone. If you spend your whole day building an elegant interface to let people choose exactly which municipal projects to finance, you can lose sight of the possibility that they might not want to do that at all. It seems to me that a lot of the drive to tokenization and customization and disintermediation in the world of fintech reflects the interests of tech founders, not of customers, and that most investment markets that do not currently exist will not be called into being if you just tokenize them.

Ahahaha super: [On September 10,] in the last 10 minutes of trading, someone bought 82,000 S&P e-minis when the index was trading at 2969. That was nearly 4 a.m. on September 11 in Beijing, where a few hours later, the Chinese government announced that it would lift tariffs on a range of American-made products. As has been the typical reaction in the U.S. stock markets as the trade war with China chugs on without any perceptible logic, when the news about a potential resolution of it seems positive, stock markets go up, and when the news about the trade war appears negative, they go down. The news was viewed positively. The S&P index moved swiftly on September 11 to 2996, up nearly 30 points. That same day, President Donald Trump said he would postpone tariffs on some Chinese goods, and the S&P index moved to 3016, or up 47 points since the fortunate person bought the 82,000 e-minis just before the market closed on September 10. Since a one-point movement, up or down, in an e-mini contract is worth $50, a 47-point movement up in a day was worth $2,350 per contract. If you were the lucky one who bought the 82,000 e-mini contracts, well, then you were sitting on a one-day profit of roughly $190 million. ... Traders in the Chicago pits have been watching these kinds of wagers with an increasing mixture of shock and awe since the start of the Trump presidency. They are used to rapid fluctuations in the S&P 500 index; volatility is common, of course. But the precision and timing of these trades, and the vast amount of money being made as a result of them, make the traders wonder if all this is on the level. Are the people behind these trades incredibly lucky, or do they have access to information that other people don’t have about, say, Trump’s or Beijing’s latest thinking on the trade war or any other of a number of ways that Trump is able to move the markets through his tweeting or slips of the tongue? Essentially, do they have inside information? I am torn here. On the one hand I am generally skeptical of conspiracy theories, particularly, like, pit-trader conspiracy theories, and really there is no evidence at all for this one. The evidence is “people sometimes trade a lot of S&P futures in the minutes, hours or days before some crazy news involving Donald Trump comes out,” but that just reduces to “people sometimes trade a lot of S&P futures.” Crazy news involving Donald Trump is everywhere dense; in the time it has taken you to read this sentence Donald Trump has done something crazy. I say that not because I have any privileged inside knowledge of whatever it is, but because it is a fundamental constant of the universe. “Trump picks Colorado Springs author of Illuminati books for education board,” is a thing I saw on Twitter just now, but some entirely different crazy thing is happening now. And now. Now. Now. So if you buy a lot of S&P futures, any time at all, Donald Trump will do something crazy shortly afterwards. Either the crazy thing will make stocks go up and you will look like you had inside information, or the crazy thing will make stocks go down and the people who sold you the futures will look like they had inside information (two sides to every trade!), or investors will be so resigned to the craziness that stocks won’t move. But every time stocks move after some crazy Donald Trump news—which, again, is every time stocks move —half the people who traded futures ahead of the move will look smart (and the other half will look dumb), and you can, if you want, build a conspiracy theory out of that. On the other hand the basic elements of this conspiracy are like “Donald Trump’s administration is not particularly good about information security, and at least one person in the administration, or at least one of their friends, is corrupt and wants to make a lot of money using government information,” and I’d sound like an idiot doubting that theory. So, sure, fine, maybe the Illuminati are making vast insider trades in S&P futures on advance knowledge of geopolitical events, why not. Also here is a passage that surprised me! One longtime CME trader who has been watching with disgust says he’s never seen anything quite like these trades, not at least since al-Qaida cashed in before initiating the September 11 attacks. “There is definite hanky-panky going on, to the world’s financial markets’ detriment,” he says. “This is abysmal.” Excuse me? Is that a thing? Is that common knowledge? Like … al-Qaeda made a lot of money on S&P futures right before 9/11, and then called up their broker and were like “hey wire us the proceeds to our cave in Afghanistan”? Who was the broker? Ugh Wikipedia tells me that this is a theory with some support, though “the 9/11 Commission Report concluded that ‘Exhaustive investigations by the Securities and Exchange Commission, FBI, and other agencies have uncovered no evidence that anyone with advance knowledge of the attacks profited through securities transactions.’” But that’s just what the Illuminati would want them to conclude.

Here’s a story about the r/WallStreetBets subreddit: The chat does have Eddie Choi, however. Choi said WallStreetBets taught him how to trade options -- contracts that offer the right to buy or sell a security by a specific date. Choi became a rock star on the forum last month after sharing details of his own big short -- playing Roku Inc. options. … When the stock of Roku, a streaming-service provider whose shares tend to fluctuate, cratered 19% on Sept. 20, Choi’s initial $766 investment in Roku puts -- a bet that the stock would decline -- ballooned to $50,553 overnight, a 6,500% gain. The profit was so meaty because the puts Choi bought were close to expiration and far out of the money. Bloomberg confirmed Choi’s account via screen shots of his Robinhood Financial trading history. A few days later, lightning struck again. Choi doubled his Roku winnings by buying more puts, this time on the S&P 500 exchange-traded fund. When the SPY fell to $295.87 on Sept. 24 -- the first time it closed below $297 in more than two weeks -- his $297 puts that were set to expire on Sept. 25 went ka-ching. Do you think he was getting fed inside information from the Trump administration? From the Chinese government? From Roku? To be clear, I do not. I think there are a lot of people reading r/WallStreetBets and trading options with Robinhood, and my guess is that most of them shouldn’t be, but their profits will be roughly normally distributed and somebody is going to be way over on the right tail making a lot of money. I am happy for Eddie Choi that it’s him. I mention this story here mostly so that I remember it next time someone gets in trouble for insider trading after buying short-dated out-of-the-money options just before a merger announcement. Often people do that because they have inside information, and the short-dated options are what tips the SEC off to their crimes. But somebody has to be trading short-dated options without inside information, and the fact that those options trade for a positive price means that sometimes they have to pay off. In a big enough sample, somebody is going to get wildly lucky. It is nice to match a name with that luck.

There was a minute when We Co., which is rapidly running out of cash after its aborted initial public offering, was going to be rescued by a multibillion-dollar equity infusion from SoftBank Group Corp., its biggest investor, but then it moved on to being rescued by a multibillion-dollar package of debt. Now it seems we’re back to SoftBank: SoftBank Group Corp. is in discussions to provide WeWork with roughly $5 billion of rescue financing in an effort to salvage one of the Japanese conglomerate’s biggest investments. The funds will come directly from SoftBank, rather than its Vision Fund, according to a person familiar with the matter who asked not to be named because the talks are private. SoftBank, which already owns about one-third of WeWork, would not amass a majority of voting rights, though its stake would increase, the person said. Part of the package may include non-voting preferred stock. The last time it was SoftBank, the talk was of it getting majority control, so this seems like a concession. That’s why you run parallel processes: If it seems like the debt is coming together that gives you leverage to talk down SoftBank’s demand for control, and if it seems like SoftBank will come through that gives you leverage to talk down the coupon on the debt. So, uh, great work by WeWork I guess, they are really playing this perfectly? Ignoring everything before last week I mean. By the way, “SoftBank has already plowed more than $10 billion into WeWork,” and this could be $5 billion more, and there was talk last month that the IPO couldn’t clear even at a $15 billion valuation. That means that there is some possibility that, after this deal, (1) SoftBank will have put more cash into WeWork than WeWork is currently worth, and (2) it won’t even have a majority of the stock. Oops!

The Wall Street Journal has a fun account of how Facebook Inc. launched its Libra cryptocurrency without being prepared for the negative reactions it got from regulators and politicians who do not like the idea of a world currency run by Facebook. The weirdest thing to me about Libra is that Facebook announced it with so little detail. This seems to have annoyed regulators: When Facebook went public with thinly sketched plans for libra in June, it hoped to delegate the details to a coalition of partners, the Libra Association, and position the effort as more of a public utility than a corporate land grab. It was envisioned as a digital alternative to government-backed currency, widely accepted by merchants world-wide and capable of being sent instantaneously across borders at low cost. … When Facebook executives met with officials of the U.S. Treasury, they responded to many questions by saying details would be ironed out later, concerning officials. Mr. Marcus said that Facebook was taking a consultative approach with regulators and wanted to hear any “profound concerns” they had early on. He added that answers to some questions could only be provided after the Libra Association had been formed and members agreed on an approach. “In early meetings we didn’t have all the answers, but that was by design,” Mr. Marcus said. “For something that at that point in time was a white paper with an idea to launch in 2020, I think that’s fairly normal.” That’s David Marcus, the Facebook executive in charge of Libra, and “we didn’t have all the answers, but that was by design” does not seem to me to show particularly great insight into the regulatory process. (“How will you prevent this thing from being used for terrorist financing?” “Great question, that is definitely on our list of things to think about!” Etc.) But even aside from the regulatory stuff, I just feel like, if I were launching a world-changing global currency and getting ready to sell it to potential users and partners, I might … want … to know … what it was? So much of the fun of cryptocurrency is in figuring out the mechanics and governance mechanisms, the baked-in automated methods for making sure that it works as intended. Also, you know, if you’re a for-profit business starting a crypto project, so much of the profit is in that stuff too. Facebook just punted all of it to a committee-to-be-named-later, and I’m sure it seemed like a good idea at the time (it’s not a Facebook currency, etc.), but it managed to both make the currency more controversial externally and make it harder to see what the benefits are to Facebook. Elsewhere, here is a speech by Federal Reserve Board Governor Lael Brainard on “Digital Currencies, Stablecoins, and the Evolving Payments Landscape.”

There isn’t really any new news in the WeWork saga, but there are a lot of people who have waited patiently in a long line to say something mean about WeWork, so we might as well give a few of them their shot. Here you go John McClain: Lending to WeWork is so potentially dicey that one junk-bond investor, Diamond Hill Capital Management’s John McClain, said anybody brave enough to do it would “be taking on substantial career risk.” Good good. Vicki Bryan do you have anything to add? “WeWork’s credit metrics remain off-the-chart ugly,” Vicki Bryan, chief executive officer of Bond Angle, a high-yield credit research company, said in a note Tuesday. Thanks guys! I will not be able to get to everyone but there’s more at that link, and this one. WeWork is considering raising several billion dollars of debt financing now that it has called off its initial public offering; potential equity investors have had a few months to trash WeWork, and now it is the potential bondholders’ turn. They are rising to the occasion. Actually the meanest thing might be from a Bloomberg story about the potential structure of a WeWork debt financing, which could involve “$1 billion of secured and $2 billion of unsecured debt with maturities ranging from four to five years,” with the secured paying 9 to 11% interest and the unsecured paying about 15% (partly in kind). “Investors have expressed concern about lack of assets that could back the proposed secured bonds,” reports Bloomberg, and, oops, right? Ordinarily you might think that the secured bonds of a real-estate company would be pretty safe, secured as they are by buildings, but then you have to remember that WeWork is an unusual real-estate company in that it doesn’t own its buildings. I suppose the asset-light approach was helpful in pitching WeWork as a tech company in happier times, but now: “WeWork has said it could secure debt against items including accounts receivable, intellectual property and equipment.” Imagine being a secured debt investor, having to foreclose, and getting paid in a trademark on the word “We” and a bunch of kombucha taps. Your collateral is basically the concentrated essence of WeWork, which is maybe not what you want. That’s mean. What is the bull case here?[1] I think there are two good ones. One is—look, I realize that I have spent what feels like every day for the past two months making fun of WeWork, but I do want to say that it seems to me like a perfectly reasonable business. WeWork clearly provides a product that people want: cool office space in smaller temporal and spatial increments than you’d typically get from a normal landlord. The thesis “we can rent raw space from landlords for long terms, gussy it up and subdivide it, and then sublet bits of it for short terms to businesses for more than our costs” is not crazy witchcraft, or even MoviePass. Why not? Layered on top of that plausible business model is much more guff than you’d ordinarily get in a public real estate company, and that guff (and its associated costs and governance problems) seems to have killed the IPO, but if you are a bondholder—particularly a secured bondholder—you can kind of tune out the guff. If WeWork ends up sinking beneath the historical costs of its expansion and general craziness, then the bondholders will end up owning the business. Buying the bonds is a bet that, in the downside case, WeWork’s brand and operational abilities and basic business model can be redirected to actually make money. (This is what I once wrote about WeWork’s vanity financial metric “community adjusted EBITDA”: If you adjust out the weird community-building stuff, WeWork arguably makes money, and in the downside case bondholders would adjust out that stuff.) That doesn’t seem like an insane bet? It seems like the sort of bet a distressed credit investor might be used to making. And of course in the upside case you get your money back and 9 or 11 or 15% or whatever interest. The other bull case is what you might call the “equity cushion” case, or what I have called “Netflix theory.” This is the theory that a company that achieves a $47 billion equity valuation can’t have that value go below zero for at least, you know, four to five years, or whatever the term of the debt is. It is not especially scientific. It is essentially a behavioral theory,[2] the idea being that if some incredibly deep-pocketed investor was to oh say I don’t know invest more than $10 billion in a company at ever-increasing valuations, that investor is not going to walk away at the first sign of trouble, but is instead going to continue pumping in billions of dollars to keep the company afloat, at ever-decreasing valuations if necessary. If you are a creditor, you are senior to that equity investor, so its continued willingness to float the company is what keeps you safe. And so WeWork is choosing between (1) this horrific bond package and (2) an equity investment from SoftBank Group Corp., its biggest investor, which would give SoftBank voting control of the company. That actually seems bullish for the bonds, no? SoftBank’s interest is a sign that the equity cushion is real, that SoftBank is not willing to give up on WeWork yet, and that it has both the money and the willingness to keep the company alive for a while. The first bull case was “if you have to foreclose it should work out”; the second is “SoftBank will make sure you don’t foreclose.” Neither is a slam-dunk, but neither relies on the WeWork hype of a few months ago either.

Given WeWork’s recent run of truly eerie bad news, I asked yesterday: “Did WeWork founder Adam Neumann disturb a mummy and trigger an ancient curse? Was a WeWork built on a haunted graveyard, unleashing powerful dark energies and also elevated levels of formaldehyde?” You probably thought I was joking! I probably thought I was joking! But no it turns out that Adam Neumann really was harnessing occult energies, because it is absolutely impossible to make up anything about this company that is stranger than the truth: WeWork’s senior executives would gather weekly in Adam Neumann’s office during a number of the company’s early years to study with a teacher from the Kabbalah Centre, a spiritual organization that promotes a brand of Jewish mysticism. … Mr. Neumann’s relationship with the Centre helped build the company from its early days. The Centre’s leaders connected Mr. Neumann to its network of wealthy people. At least two students were sources of early funding while several senior employees were Centre students, according to people familiar with the matter. Its tenets influenced WeWork’s community-centric philosophy, and its teachers were a regular presence in the company’s offices and on company retreats, according to other people familiar with the matter. … Kabbalah, which describes many divine forces powering the universe, aims to uncover the secret meaning of the Torah. The number 18, an auspicious number in Judaism and emphasized in Jewish mystical circles, often made an appearance in WeWork business decisions, according to people familiar with the matter. While in a hot tub on his 39th birthday in 2018 and talking on a conference call with WeWork executives, Mr. Neumann decided WeWork would sell $702 million in its first bond offering, according to a person who witnessed the scene. Mr. Neumann came to that figure by multiplying his age by 18, boosting the planned borrowing amount by $2 million, people familiar with the matter said. Do you think he raised a golem? “WeWork Warns Tenants About Rampaging Man of Clay in Midtown Office,” tomorrow’s headlines will read. You might think that dabbling in mystical arts can only help your startup’s bottom line, but the moral of the WeWork story is that powerful ancient energies are not to be taken lightly or watered down for an IPO prospectus. Though, never mind the Kabbalah stuff, I have to say that there are few things more cursed than taking a conference call about a bond offering from a hot tub. That is really the sort of thing that might cause a vengeful God to smite you.

Meanwhile, while one part of Goldman Sachs Group Inc. was trying to sell WeWork shares, another part of Goldman was … trying to sell WeWork shares: Goldman Sachs, one of the top underwriters on WeWork's aborted initial public offering last month, sold down its stake in the coworking company in the run-up to its planned IPO, according to a person with knowledge of the Wall Street bank's actions. That means that as Goldman was touting its services to WeWork and asking investors to buy newly minted public shares in a company most recently valued at $47 billion, the bank had already reduced its own exposure. The investment bankers sit in a different division than those who make investments for Goldman, and the WeWork investment was made by the merchant banking division. Regulations require so-called Chinese walls between such business units to prevent the sharing of privileged information. … Goldman also assigned a "much more modest" value to the company than WeWork's $47 billion valuation, the person said on Tuesday. There are two theories of underwriting. Theory 1 is that underwriters are in the business of picking the best companies, choosing a fair valuation for them, and vouching for them to investors. Theory 2 is that underwriters are middlemen, service providers; if companies want to sell stock and investors want to buy, then an underwriter will facilitate the trade without expressing any view on whether the stock is any good. Theory 1 is the sort of old-style traditional view, and there is clearly some truth to it. Underwriters really do, for instance, vouch for the accuracy of the company’s prospectus; it definitely is part of the underwriter’s job to make sure that the company doesn’t lie to investors while selling its stock. As a former underwriter myself—disclosure, at Goldman—I tend to take an even broader view that the underwriter’s job is to push issuers to agree to market-standard terms and avoid unpleasant surprises for investors, though that view is controversial. And the fact that, when a bank underwrites an IPO, its research analysts usually come out with a Buy recommendation on the stock suggests that those analysts and their customers believe at least to some extent in the bank-vouching-for-issuers theory. But for the most part I think Theory 2 is probably the dominant modern view of underwriting, and of most other things that an investment bank does for that matter. There are buyers and sellers, and the bank is in the business of connecting them and allowing them to transact, and if the buyers want to pay a price that the sellers are willing to accept, then that’s good enough. If you like weird tech companies, you’ll get weird tech companies, and the bank will keep its feelings about weird tech companies to itself. The bank is not in the business of independently blessing the price or promising that it’s a good investment; certainly it is not in the business of blessing the price on a firmwide, unanimous basis. If JPMorgan Chase & Co. underwrites an IPO, the lead banker doesn’t have to go to Jamie Dimon and ask “hey Jamie would you put some of your personal money into this company at this price?” And if Goldman’s investment bankers want to pitch an IPO at a $60+ billion valuation, that doesn’t stop its merchant bankers from unloading the same company’s shares at half that price.

Students of finance, law and economics sometimes email me asking me for suggestions for paper topics, and I have got a great one for you, though you’ll have to wait a few years to actually write it: Major League Baseball is now allowing investment funds to take minority stakes in multiple clubs, a move that lets the league capitalize on sky-high team valuations. Traditionally, baseball owners have been wealthy individuals, but the new policy could bring in cash from Wall Street firms and college endowments, according to the people familiar with the change, which was made earlier this year. … One sports banker is already taking advantage of the change. Galatioto Sports Partners has created a $500 million vehicle -- the GSP Baseball Fund -- to invest in teams, said the people, who asked not to be identified because the plans haven’t been announced. Something similar is happening in basketball, and we talked about it last month. I mean, GSP will have to launch and buy some stakes in some teams, and then competitors will need to start and buy stakes in some other teams, and then a Baseball Index Fund will need to start and buy stakes in all the teams, and then indexing will need to become standard practice, and then every baseball team will need to have a large shareholder base of diversified institutional investors with like 20% in indexed hands, and then you can write your paper. But what a good paper it will be! It is fairly clear what is in each baseball team’s individual best interest: Each team would like to win the World Series as often as possible while collecting a lot of popular players whose jerseys sell well; also it would like to make a lot of carefully considered pitching changes to maximize its odds of winning important games. It is fairly clear what is in the collective best interest of all the baseball teams: If games are all competitive and popular players are widely dispersed, if there’s a new champion every year but they always come from major media markets, if the important games move along without too many pitching changes, then that is good for the overall popularity and economics of the sport. Most companies in most industries are mostly supposed to maximize their individual best interests rather than colluding with their competitors to maximize the overall profits of the industry. Baseball (like other sports) is weird in that it requires collaboration between competitors—You need to agree on the rules! Both teams need to show up to every game!—and there is quite a lot of explicit collusion, revenue sharing, collective bargaining, salary caps, entry-level hiring by draft, and so forth. Individual teams frequently act against their own competitive interests for the good of the sport (uh, the business) as a whole. Baseball is famously exempt from U.S. antitrust laws. And of course it is in some general sense in every team’s individual self-interest to subscribe to some level of this sort of collusion; if one team won the World Series every year then the game would get boring and even that team would lose revenue. Still everything happens at the margin, and you could imagine teams seeking to be more or less competitive than they currently are. And there are few better generators of statistics than Major League Baseball. If you want to answer a question like “are baseball teams trying to be more or less competitive than they used to be,” or “are some teams trying to be more or less competitive than other teams,” you will have a million different data series to look at to try to answer it. Of course the question I want you to answer is: Does common minority ownership of multiple baseball teams by diversified (including indexed) institutional investors cause them to become less competitive and focus more on maximizing the overall profits of the baseball industry? You have a good shot at answering that question—once there is enough common ownership—because there is so much data, but also because of baseball’s antitrust exemption. You can call up the presidents of baseball teams and ask them questions like “do you care less about competition now that you have so many indexed investors” or “do you talk to your institutional shareholders about competitive strategy,” and you can call up the investors and ask questions like “do you encourage the small-market teams you own to make disadvantageous trades with the big-market teams so that your overall revenue can grow,” and if the answer is yes they can say “yes” without worrying about antitrust liability. If you asked CEOs of regular companies, or their investors, questions like that, you’d make them nervous. Obviously we talk about these questions all the time in the context of regular companies, airlines or banks or whatever, and the answers are fiercely disputed. Answering these questions for baseball doesn’t really tell you the answer for normal companies, because baseball really is a special case, but the answers still might be interesting. If minority passive common ownership can change the competitive dynamics of sports , which are played by hyper-competitive athletes who at least in theory ignore financial concerns to focus on winning, surely they can change the competitive dynamics of airline pricing.

One of the weirdest things in recent financial/criminal history is that for a while people really believed that Bitcoin, an electronic payments method that creates a permanent, traceable, public record of all transactions and links them to identifiable accounts, was somehow a good way to pay for crime. “It’s completely anonymous,” people thought, “like digital cash, but you can send it anywhere and no one will be able to trace you.” Not really! I suppose it was even true for a little while, but eventually law enforcement agencies figured out how to trace Bitcoin transactions, and then the fact that years’ worth of criminal financial transactions were just forever openly available to them on the Bitcoin blockchain was … bad for criminals. Here’s a story about a big child-pornography bust: Agents from the Internal Revenue Service’s Criminal Investigation Division determined the location of the Darknet server in South Korea, identified Son and found the physical location of the website, according to Don Fort, chief of the division. They also unmasked users hiding behind Bitcoin transactions, Fort said. “Our agency’s ability to analyze the blockchain and de-anonymize Bitcoin transactions allowed for the identification of hundreds of predators around the world,” Fort said. Oops, bad job predators. Do you think maybe Satoshi Nakamoto works for the FBI, and invented Bitcoin as a way to get criminals to make a convenient permanent record of their transactions?

It blows my mind that it’s not even two months since We Co. filed for an initial public offering targeting a valuation as high as $65 billion, and now here’s this: WeWork’s bankers are pitching investors on what would be one of the riskiest junk-debt offerings in recent years -- potentially giving the venture’s top private shareholders a final chance to avoid having their stakes severely diluted. A roughly $5 billion financing package led by JPMorgan Chase & Co. is the company’s preferred option, rather than selling a controlling stake in itself to SoftBank Group Corp., according to people with knowledge of the matter. The structure and terms under discussion may change depending on investor appetite. Notably, the financing may include at least $2 billion of unsecured payment-in-kind notes with an unusually hefty 15% coupon, one person said. … The $2 billion of proposed unsecured debt may carry an additional sweetener for investors: equity warrants designed so that investors could boost their return to around 30% if the company gets to a $20 billion valuation, according to the person who described the structure. WeWork would pay only a third of the coupon in cash, while the rest of the interest would accumulate and become due at maturity, the person said. The financing package may also include around $1 billion of secured debt that would be sold to investors, as well as about $1.7 billion in letters of credit that would be split among participating banks, according to the people. Fifteen percent PIK debt! In better times, really not that long ago at all, we talked about WeWork as a clever financial arbitrage, segmenting the market so that it could appeal to debt investors as a boring stable real-estate company while appealing to equity investors as a fast-growing high-multiple tech company. Now, in worse times, it is the opposite: If you invest now, you can get some terrifying debt that lenders don’t want combined with some cursed equity that the stock market doesn’t want. Here, debt investors, take a 15% coupon, why not, also have a bunch of warrants, whatever you like, here, come into our offices, look around, if you see anything that strikes your fancy you can just take that too. Oh wait not the phone booths, don’t take those: The beleaguered co-working company is removing 2,300 phone booths from some of its offices in the U.S. and Canada, “due to potentially elevated levels of formaldehyde caused by the manufacturer,” according to an email sent Monday to WeWork customers. The booths are small, enclosed spaces where members can talk on their cell phones or work in privacy. A WeWork member told staff about a smell in the booths and eye irritation, which prompted the company to hire an outside consultant and test a sampling of phone booths, the email said. After getting the results back, WeWork started shutting down 1,600 booths that may have high levels of the carcinogen. It’s shuttering 700 more “out of an abundance of caution.” I don’t understand what is happening here. Did WeWork founder Adam Neumann disturb a mummy and trigger an ancient curse? Was a WeWork built on a haunted graveyard, unleashing powerful dark energies and also elevated levels of formaldehyde? How do you have such a relentless parade of negative financial news and then find out that your phone booths cause cancer? “Our phone booths might cause cancer” was not an IPO risk factor.[1] Nobody had “phone booths cause cancer” on their WeWork Disaster Bingo cards. Anyway right that debt offering. We talked yesterday about the other financing option that WeWork is apparently considering, which involves taking billions more dollars from SoftBank Group Corp. in exchange for control of the business. I rather hopefully spun that as an effort to pivot to quiet profitability: You raise equity, staunch the bleeding, start running your locations at a profit, and—you hope!—end up a midsize office landlord generating a steady profit for your accidental owners at SoftBank. The dream of a $65 billion IPO is deferred, probably forever, but at least it is, you know, a business that covers its costs or whatever. What is this? Is it a path back to an IPO? This deal seems like it could add something like $500 million of annual interest expense[2]; by contrast, WeWork’s super-duper-adjusted favorite presentation of its positive unit economics, “contribution margin excluding non-cash GAAP straight-line lease cost,” was $467 million in 2018. This debt deal will eat up all the profits WeWork makes even in the alternate universe in which it makes profits. If WeWork does this deal and comes back to the equity market in six months, it will probably be with even bigger losses, more debt, and slower growth than it promised this time around, and it’s not like anyone liked it this time around. I am not sure I have ever seen anything like this. In general, an IPO is a negotiation between a company that would like to go public and the investors who might want to buy its shares. I like to think of every high-profile tech IPO as providing a precedent, a data point, a set of arguments for the next negotiation. For the past few years, it has generally seemed like companies tend to have the upper hand in these negotiations: Investors’ fear of missing out is strong, and the companies, with ready access to private capital, tend not to be in any rush to go public. And every time a tech startup with no earnings and questionable corporate governance easily went public, it became harder for investors to push back on the next deal: “Everyone bought the last one, so what makes you think they won’t buy this one?” WeWork is undoubtedly a special case, but in any case it is a striking one: It came to market with a high valuation, a questionable business model and embarrassing corporate governance; investors said “absolutely not” and meant it; and within weeks the company was reduced to a severe cash crunch, a humiliating rescue financing, and somehow carcinogenic phone booths. It’s not quite a win for investors, but it sure is a loss for the company, and it might have an impact on future negotiations in other IPOs. If you’re a big public investor who wants to push back on valuation or governance in the next high-profile IPO, now you have a bloody severed unicorn head to bring to the roadshow as a warning.

The New York Times has a story about how Deutsche Bank AG allegedly bribed Chinese officials to try to win business in China, and the answer is just, uh, the regular way? The bank gave a Chinese president a crystal tiger and a Bang & Olufsen sound system, together worth $18,000. A premier received a $15,000 crystal horse, his Chinese zodiac animal, and his son got $10,000 in golf outings and a trip to Las Vegas. A top state banking official, a son of one of China’s founding fathers, accepted a $4,254 bottle of French wine — Château Lafite Rothschild, vintage 1945, the year he was born. Millions of dollars were paid out to Chinese consultants, including a business partner of the premier’s family and a firm that secured a meeting for the bank’s chief executive with the president. And more than 100 relatives of the Communist Party’s ruling elite were hired for jobs at the bank, even though it had deemed many unqualified. “Inside a Brazen Scheme to Woo China: Gifts, Golf and a $4,254 Wine,” is the Times headline, and I kept waiting for the brazen scheme. Golf? Of all the forms of corporate bribery surely golf is the most acceptable one. The way that you convey to a corporate executive “I want to give you personal benefits in exchange for your company’s business, but not in a bribe-y way” is by taking her out for a round of golf. Goldman Sachs Group Inc. bankers allegedly helped corrupt sovereign wealth fund officials steal $6 billion, and kept several hundred million dollars of the proceeds for themselves. That’s a brazen scheme! Credit Suisse AG bankers allegedly helped finance Mozambican infrastructure projects that were awarded through multimillion-dollar bribes that the conspirators referred to as “chickens,” and again kept tens of millions of dollars for themselves. That’s a brazen scheme! This was, like, you wanna win some business, you play a little golf, you give a guy a nice bottle of wine. Really I would love to see an annual league table of Highest Wine Tabs at Business Dinners; I doubt $4,254 would crack the top 20. Oh yeah also you hire a bunch of children of potential clients but that was also pretty normal practice among global investment banks in China. Really it’s not unheard-of everywhere else; it gets more focus in China in part because it was so pervasive and so blatant, but also in part because winning business in China requires hiring the children of government officials. Bribe-hiring of government officials’ children probably violates the U.S. Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, while bribe-hiring of corporate executives’ children might not; you sometimes meet important clients’ relatives wandering around investment banks in the U.S. and Europe too, but they tend not to be the subject of enforcement actions. The Times even got a quote from Josef Ackermann, Deutsche Bank’s chief executive officer during much of this alleged bribery, being like “wait what is the big deal”: Some of the gifts, like the crystal tiger for Mr. Jiang, who was born in 1926, the year of the tiger, were “provided” by Mr. Ackermann, according to the internal investigation. Mr. Ackermann said that while he didn’t recall personally giving the items, he was aware that the bank’s staff thought it a good idea. He has not been accused of wrongdoing in China. “They said that’s what Goldman and JPMorgan are doing, so we should do it,” Mr. Ackermann said in the interview. “I don’t think Wen Jiabao would be somehow influenced by a gift of a few thousand.” This is true! Wen Jiabao was the premier of China from 2003 through 2013, and “the Wens’ enormous accumulation of wealth was the focus of a 2012 investigation by The Times that found family members had controlled assets worth at least $2.7 billion.” Ackermann allegedly gave Wen Jiabao “a $15,000 crystal horse, his Chinese zodiac animal,” and I’m sure it was a lovely horse, but honestly if you have racked up billions of dollars during your time as a head of state you can probably buy your own trinkets. A nice crystal horse is not really going to move the needle! Corporate bribery is interesting because it exists entirely on a continuum. Everyone pretty much agrees that taking a person out to coffee to try to win business from her company is acceptable business relationship-building, even if you pay for the coffee. Taking her out to dinner is also pretty widely accepted, though some companies will have strict policies that forbid it, or at least limit the quality of the wine at the dinner. Taking her out to play golf, or to good seats at a big sporting event, is also absolutely standard practice in investment banking, though it might raise more eyebrows; it did here. Giving her a paper bag stuffed with cash is pretty much unacceptable everywhere. But between a game of golf and a sack of cash there is a wide range of ambiguity, and much depends on cultural and financial context. If you give someone a fancy crystal horse and he turns around and sells it for cash then that was probably a bribe. If you give him a crystal horse and he casually chucks it into his crystal horse cabinet with all of the other crystal horses that people keep giving him, then he at least took it as just a polite gesture.

I assume you can hear me giggling as I type this, but the Libra Association, the independent body that will control the digital currency dreamed up by Facebook Inc., had its inaugural meeting and chose a board of directors this week. That was somewhat overshadowed by all the big payments companies dropping out of their extremely vague commitments to join Libra, but, whatever, you know, progress. “Our commitment is that the project will not launch until such time as it has met all the necessary regulatory approvals on both sides of the Atlantic,” says its deputy chairman, which is both a pretty low bar (“we won’t launch until we are legally allowed to”!?) and, for Libra, a daunting one. Ben Thompson writes at Stratechery that the vision of Libra as an independent currency originally looked like “an easier sale” to regulators and the public than a currency entirely controlled by Facebook, but: It turns out it was not an easier sale at all, which then raises the question as to why Facebook would want all of the significant downsides of not simply controlling the entire platform. The company has to move slower, have less control, offer a worse user experience, all for arguably more regulator oversight given that Libra is far more easily framed as a currency replacement than would be Facebook Credits 2.0. In the early days of Libra, I contrasted it to the blockchain-based “JPM Coin” that JPMorgan Chase & Co. is building for its banking clients: JPMorgan is trying to build a JPM Coin for JPMorgan, while Facebook is trying to build a stablecoin for the world. JPMorgan sees itself as an actor in a system, and is trying to accomplish its goals within the rules of that system. Facebook sees itself as the system ; it has decided that the world needs a new currency, and so it sets up its own new worldwide governance body to solicit input from others about how to build that currency. Of course the other governance bodies—like Congress—will be annoyed. Arguably the idea of Libra as a universal currency backed by every big payments company was more hubristic, and more sort of threateningly Facebook-y, than the idea of just building an internal payments mechanism on Facebook. And now, as many of Facebook’s payment partners drop out and it looks increasingly like a Facebook coin, it is kind of the worst of all worlds: It has upset regulators and politicians with its claims to universality, it has the unwieldy governance of a coin-by-committee, and still it might only be usable on Facebook.

Marc Benioff, the chief executive officer of Salesforce.com Inc., apparently really wanted to buy Twitter Inc. a few years ago but then his investors told him not to, and also he sliced his leg open, which is somehow connected to the story? He had a vision that Twitter could integrate well into Salesforce’s business, becoming a great way for his customers to reach their consumers. A lot of his advisors were against the idea, saying it would be too complicated and risky. He kept pushing forward anyway. Then, as he was heading to a meeting to begin to secure financing for the deal, Benioff slipped on a curb and sliced his leg open. He took it as a sign that he should think twice. He recounted the circumstances in a recent phone interview: “I slipped on the sidewalk and split my leg, and had other problems with my knee,” Benioff said. “As I had blood dripping down my leg as I was pitching the bond-rating firms, [I was] thinking to myself, ‘Is this a sign?’ Maybe I shouldn’t be moving in this direction. But I so strongly loved my vision of what it could become. Eventually our investors, who are a key stakeholder of mine, they said no, we don’t really want you to move in this direction.” I do not really understand anything about this story, but I just want to say he should be glad he wasn’t on his way to buy WeWork! A piano filled with formaldehyde would probably have fallen on him while he contemplated his bloody leg; that mummy’s curse is no joke.

A thing that serious people worried about, not all that long ago, was that regular everyday investors did not have the opportunity to invest in fast-growing technology unicorns like Uber Technologies Inc. and WeWork Cos. An important historical basis of American prosperity, the worry went, was that regular people were able to invest their money in our most dynamic businesses, and thereby participate in economic growth. But in a world in which the innovative growing businesses were all private, while the big public companies mostly sat around returning cash to shareholders, ordinary people would not share the gains from innovation, which would all accrue to rich founders and venture capitalists. The counterargument was, to exaggerate slightly, that those big fast-growing tech businesses were all scams and that ordinary investors were better off not being exposed to them. Well, I don’t know, here we are. The unicorn bubble looks a bit deflated. If you invested in Uber in its later private funding rounds, you are sad, because Uber went public this year and trades well below its private valuation. If you invested in WeWork (now the We Co.) in its later private rounds, you are also sad, because WeWork couldn’t go public at a price anywhere near its private valuation and is now in a weird and embarrassing limbo. Other once-hot tech unicorns have also struggled in the public markets. Some number of ordinary investors who would have loved to buy unicorn shares a few years ago basically dodged a bullet. Another, quite different counterargument, though, was: Actually ordinary people can invest in unicorns. One reason that the big tech unicorns were able to stay public so long and at such high valuations was that they were able to raise lots of money from institutions that did not traditionally invest in private companies, including mutual funds. Ordinary people who invested in mutual funds from Vanguard, BlackRock, Fidelity, T. Rowe Price, Wellington, etc. all had a little bit of Uber in their portfolios. Retail investors couldn’t buy Uber directly, but professional mutual fund managers could buy it on their behalf. Anyway here’s a story about how those mutual funds bought some stocks thinking they’d go up and instead they went down: Mutual funds that invested billions in big technology startups are now suffering losses in newly public companies and are being forced to mark down their holdings of private companies that are no longer investor darlings. The collapse of the initial public offering of WeWork parent We Co. and the steep decline of Uber Technologies Inc. shares and other recent IPOs have backfired on funds that hoped big stock gains would give them market-beating performances. … When private-market valuations were soaring, funds marked up their holdings, some more than others. We was valued at $102 a share in July 2018 by mutual fund giant Fidelity Investments, and $110 a share in November 2018 by Hartford Financial Services Group Inc., John Hancock Investment Management and Principal Financial Group. That $110 price tag—67% higher than the figure some other fund managers at that time valued the same type of We shares—matched the value put on the office-sharing company by its largest investor, SoftBank Group Corp. The valuation turned out to be overly optimistic. Before We pulled its IPO last month, its bankers were looking to price the offering at well below $55 a share, according to people familiar with the matter. Fidelity marked down its We holdings to $54 a share in March, nearly half its valuation eight months earlier. On one level, the story here is “private markets are the new public markets” and everything is fine. Mutual funds buy stocks hoping that they will go up, and sometimes they go down instead, and that is life when markets are volatile and stock selection is hard. Now some of the stocks that mutual funds buy are private, but nothing fundamental has changed. The mutual funds are diversified, and their investors have not been wiped out because of bad bets on Uber or We. Still it is not completely satisfying. It is plausible that professional public investors like mutual funds are better at public investing than they are at private investing, that they are able to make better choices after reviewing standard public-company disclosure documents and audited financials and IPO roadshow presentations than after doing private-company due diligence. (I think that is kind of the point of public-company disclosure requirements?) Certainly they are taking more risk by buying illiquid pre-IPO shares than they would by buying in, or after, the IPO. The traditional theory would be that mutual funds are compensated for the lack of standard information, and the illiquidity, by a much lower price ; traditionally private companies were small and you could expect a big return from the ones that succeeded and went public. But that’s not a guaranteed essential feature of the world, and it is a mistake to sort of assume “this company must be cheap because I am investing in it before its IPO.” It is of course easy to say in hindsight, but when you’re a mutual fund investing in an illiquid private company with limited disclosure at a $60 billion valuation, you are kind of getting the worst of all worlds.

If you are worried that ordinary people did not have access to the fast-growing innovative private companies, what should you do about it? I think that depends on what you think is the underlying explanation for why companies are staying private longer. One theory is that companies stay private longer because it is harder to go public than it used to be: There are so many disclosure requirements, so much risk of shareholder lawsuits, that being public is no longer all that attractive. The words “Sarbanes-Oxley” are often mentioned in this explanation. If this is your theory then you will want to make it easier to go public, perhaps by relaxing disclosure requirements or limiting liability to shareholders. The other theory is that companies stay private longer because it is easier to stay private than it used to be: There is so much more money sloshing around in private markets, so the historical advantage of public markets—they’re where the money is—has disappeared. The words “SoftBank Vision Fund” are often mentioned in this explanation. If this is your theory then … well, I suppose you could make it harder to stay private , by reducing companies’ ability to raise money privately, but in this deregulatory age that does not seem especially viable. No, really, if you believe this theory then what you want to do is make it easier for ordinary investors to buy shares of private companies , for instance by relaxing “accredited investor” requirements, allowing more small-dollar private offerings to retail investors, and allowing more pooled vehicles to invest in private companies on behalf of ordinary investors. These changes tend to have the odd side effect of making it even easier to stay private longer: If your fix is to allow more investors to invest in private companies, then those companies will have even less need to go public to access capital. I tend to be a believer in the second theory, that companies are staying private longer not because it’s so hard to go public but because it’s so easy to stay private. Anyway here’s a paper: The deregulation of securities laws—in particular the National Securities Markets Improvement Act (NSMIA) of 1996—has increased the supply of private capital to late-stage private startups, which are now able to grow to a size that few private firms used to reach. NSMIA is one of a number of factors that have changed the going-public versus staying-private trade-off, helping bring about a new equilibrium where fewer startups go public, and those that do are older. This new equilibrium does not reflect an IPO market failure. Rather, founders are using their increased bargaining power vis-a-vis investors to stay private longer. That’s “The Deregulation of the Private Equity Markets and the Decline in IPOs” by Michael Ewens and Joan Farre-Mensa. I would be surprised if any one particular law is the cause of the unicorn boom, whether that law is regulatory (Sarbanes-Oxley) or deregulatory (NSMIA), but in general I am sympathetic to the idea that the increased supply of capital to late-stage private startups, rather than the nuisance of being public, is what keeps companies private longer.

Huh: WeWork’s bankers are scrambling to complete a new debt financing package as soon as next week to buy time to restructure after the company’s failed initial public offering left it running short of cash at a faster rate than expected. Two people briefed on the fundraising efforts said the office company’s cash crunch was so acute that it had to raise new financing no later than the end of November. Fitch Ratings downgraded WeWork’s credit rating last week to CCC+, warning that the lossmaking company’s liquidity position was “precarious”. I mean the IPO was supposed to launch last month? And now they’re gonna run out of money next month? You don’t see a lot of companies do multibillion-dollar IPOs with quite so much urgency, Like, there are risk factors in the prospectus about We’s financial condition, but not one saying in bold type “we’re gonna run out of money in two months.” Of course, pro forma for the offering, they wouldn’t have, so that was not actually a risk faced by potential IPO investors. Still this is not the sort of news that is going to make public investors regret missing out on the WeWork IPO. If you passed on the IPO because the business didn’t seem sustainable to you, you will feel vindicated by watching WeWork run out of cash five minutes later. Elsewhere, here is a profile of WeWork founder Adam Neumann’s houses. And sad news for random We projects: WeWork informed parents on Friday that it would no longer operate its private school in Manhattan after the 2019-20 school year, HuffPost has learned. “WeWork will continue to operate WeGrow through the remainder of the 2019-2020 school year, providing a quality education and classroom experience for all students,” a WeWork spokesperson said in a statement. “As part of the company’s efforts to focus on its core business, WeWork has informed the families of WeGrow students that we will not operate WeGrow after this school year.” Given We’s rapid and absolute pivot away from growth I guess it would have been too ironic to keep operating WeGrow.

I have said this before, but the basic jobs of a capital markets banker are to (1) win a client mandate for an initial public offering, in part by promising the client a high valuation, and then (2) deliver the client an actual IPO at a valuation it is satisfied with. One lovely way to do this is, like, you promise a $3 billion valuation, you launch the IPO at a $4 to $4.5 billion valuation range, and you price it at a $5 billion valuation, but it often doesn’t work out that way for obvious auction-dynamic reasons. If the company is really likely to price at a $5 billion valuation, some other bank will be telling it it can get $6 billion, and the company is going to prefer that bank’s aggressive approach over your cowardly $3 billion. So instead your incentives are to, you know, pitch with a $7 billion valuation, win the mandate, and spend the next few months subtly walking the client back to the point that it’s happy with a $5 billion valuation. This requires a lot of skill, but that’s what you’re getting paid for. The Saudi Aramco IPO is a little different because the client more or less announced its valuation—$2 trillion—ahead of time, so its bankers didn’t have to put a lot of effort into overpromising on valuation when they pitched the deal. But the basic process is the same: Now that they are mandated on the deal, they have to verrrrrrrry tactfully start walking down the price. Here’s the Wall Street Journal: Saudi Arabian Oil Co.’s investment bankers could deliver, as soon as Friday, their final recommendations on the valuation of the state-owned energy giant in an initial public offering, with the headline number expected to fall well short of the $2 trillion targeted by Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, according to people familiar with the matter. The crown prince has indicated he wants the IPO to value Saudi Arabian Oil, or Aramco, at $2 trillion. But that target has already met some resistance from company executives working on the planned offering, who have suggested $1.5 trillion is more realistic. That valuation is gaining support among the underwriters who are tasked with drumming up investor interest for the offering, a group that includes JPMorgan Chase & Co., Goldman Sachs Group Inc. and Morgan Stanley among others, according to people familiar with the matter. “Gaining support,” yes. In general I tend not to ascribe that much importance the the bankers’ pre-launch “final recommendations on the valuation” of an IPO, because the real price of an IPO is set after meeting investors during the roadshow and taking their orders. (“Aramco officials and advisers would spend two weeks educating potential investors on the company starting by the end of October, followed by a two-week book-building process,” reports the Journal.) The proposed valuation at launch can influence investors’ views, but ultimately the price that investors are willing to pay is what sets the actual price. Aramco is a little different though because some portion of the IPO will be bought by more or less literally captive investors: The Saudi government is expected to require some members of the country’s elite, who had been arrested for alleged bribery in 2017 and held in Riyadh’s Ritz-Carlton luxury hotel until late last year and in some cases into early 2019, to buy “large stakes” of the offering to help ensure the IPO’s success, according to some of the people. We have talked before about how unusual it is for a company to have the option, while marketing its IPO, of threatening potential investors with kidnapping and torture. Here though I just want to point out that the compelled investors are unlikely to be extremely price sensitive; if you are held against your will until you put in an order in the IPO, you are unlikely to put in an order only at the low end of the price range. Whatever price the bankers pick, some anchor investors are going to pay it!

An under-appreciated innovation of the cryptocurrency world is the concept of the “airdrop.” In an airdrop, you create a digital token and just hand it out to a lot of people, freely, without their asking for it. You copy and paste the Bitcoin blockchain, put the name “Mattcoin” at the top, and announce “hey everyone who owns Bitcoins now also owns the same number of Mattcoins.” Airdropping tokens onto owners of some other, more established token is the norm, but you could imagine other ways to do it. Airdrop one Mattcoin on each U.S. Social Security number, why not. There are a range of reasons why you might do this. At one end of the spectrum, there will be a deep philosophical divide among members of the developer community of some established cryptocurrency, and so it will “fork”: One day, a copy of the blockchain will be created, and everyone who owned a WhateverCoin will now own two things, a WhateverCoin Classic and a WhateverCoin Advanced, and then they will start trading separately and each side will hope that it will achieve dominance and its rival will wither away. But for quite some time, possibly forever, both coins will trade robustly and be worth a lot of money and gravitate to different holders and be used by different communities for different purposes. Less fundamentally, someone could have an idea for some sort of crypto token but worry that it will be hard to get a lot of people to adopt it. Airdropping it on a large group of people—say, every Bitcoin holder—might speed up adoption; if every crypto enthusiast suddenly owns some Mattcoins, then they might start trading the Mattcoins and ascribing some value to them. By giving away a lot of product for free you can spark adoption. At the other end of the spectrum, any dumb hobbyist prankster can just say “hahaha everyone owns Mattcoins now.” I want to stress how absolutely strange this is. Twenty years ago, if I had printed up a bunch of certificates saying “One Mattshare” and mailed one to every person in America, that … I mean, it wouldn’t even have been a good prank. There would be no meaning to it, it would not occur to anyone to start trading Mattshares, also the postage costs would be prohibitive. But the rise of Bitcoin was an extraordinary proof of concept, demonstrating that an electronic asset could become enormously and persistently valuable purely because people freely adopted and valued it. And then the rise of Ethereum and other cryptocurrencies was also an important proof of concept, demonstrating that what worked for Bitcoin could be replicated an arbitrary number of times. Why not just copy a blockchain, hand out some Mattcoins, keep some for yourself, and see if you become a Mattcoin billionaire? What is the downside? You’re not even paying for postage. Cryptocurrency systems have thus, kind of by accident, opened the possibility of pure ex nihilo value creation in which absolutely anyone can (1) announce a purely abstract thing, (2) distribute it broadly to people who didn’t ask for it, (3) ask people to ascribe value to it, and (4) have some non-zero chance of success. That is a new thing in the world, and while it has some advantages—“Dogecoin millionaire” is a possible career path now,[1] as it was not for most of human history—it also creates some novel problems, because our legal and economic institutions are not really set up for this sort of thing. So we have talked a couple of times about how crypto exchanges deal with forks and airdrops. If an exchange holds Bitcoins on behalf of its customers, and I distribute one Mattcoin to every Bitcoin holder, then the exchange suddenly owns some Mattcoins on behalf of its customers. Does it have to distribute them? Does it have to list Mattcoins for trading? If it loaned out Bitcoins to short sellers, does it have to demand Mattcoins back from the shorts? We have talked about a concept of “forkiness,” in which exchanges might want to adjust for serious forks that split the value of a cryptocurrency but not adjust for random prankish airdrops, but it is not always easy to draw lines. Or what about taxes? Cryptocurrency holders know more about what the Internal Revenue Service expects to see on their tax returns, thanks to new guidance from the agency. The IRS released a ruling and a question-and-answer document Wednesday that tell virtual currency investors and their tax advisers how the agency expects them to report income from their holdings. … The guidance says that taxpayers are required to pay taxes on income when a coin splits in a transaction known as a “hard fork” and when coins are distributed through a so-called air drop. “One unfortunate consequence of this guidance is that third parties can now create tax reporting obligations for you by simply forking a network whose coins you own, or foisting on you an unwanted air drop,” Jerry Brito, executive director of advocacy group Coin Center, said in a statement. I have read the airdrop sections of the ruling and FAQ and find them pretty incomprehensible,[2] but they do seem to leave open the possibility that if I airdrop Mattcoins on everyone, and then there are a few Mattcoin trades at some price, then everyone has taxable income. At some philosophical level that’s right: Everyone does have income; everyone has gotten some valuable thing that they didn’t have before, without asking for it or even necessarily knowing about it. It seems pretty weird as a matter of tax policy! But that’s mostly because it’s weird as a matter of economics.
