In other words can we bankrupt warren buffet by issuing a trillion coins to his website's SSL cert, 1 coin via mining, and then establish a market value of at least $1/coin for this asset (not particularly hard to do since there would be only the one coin in circulation until warren started moving his)?”

The way I like to explain initial coin offerings is that “they’re like if the Wright Brothers sold air miles to finance inventing the airplane.” There are two parts to that explanation. One part is the idea of the currency: There is some good or service that will be offered at some point on some platform, and some currency—some cryptocurrency token—that will allow people to pay for that good or service. The other part is the idea of the financing: The people planning to build the platform will raise the money for it by selling the currency before the platform actually works; then they will spend the money to build the platform, and the currency will become useful. Obviously there are ways this can go wrong (the people building the platform can take the money and not actually build it, etc.), though there are ways for any financing mechanism to go wrong. But the strongest case for the ICO is that it represents a genuinely new and interesting way of financing economic activity, in which the development of a platform is funded not by owners but by users . In the fun early days of ICOs, you could believe that they pointed to a glorious future in which new open decentralized internet protocols would be funded not by private companies—which would then own the protocols and make socially destructive decisions in order to maximize their profits—but by their future users, who would then govern the protocols in a responsible way to maximize their social value.[1] But this idea fits awkwardly with U.S. securities laws. Oversimplifying, those laws say that you can’t sell securities of a venture broadly without registering them with the Securities and Exchange Commission and giving investors a lot of disclosure about your venture. If ICO tokens are securities, this raises lots of problems. Doing the registration is costly and requires a lot of administrative overhead. If the tokens are securities, they should probably trade on regulated securities exchanges, which limits their usefulness as currency on your platform. And in a decentralized un-owned platform, it is hard to understand what sorts of financial disclosures are even required: If the venture is not a “company” in a traditional sense, if it has no managers, how can the managers tell investors about its financial performance? What would it mean to file a 10-K for Bitcoin? One solution to the problem is to say that ICO tokens are not securities. The argument here is that ICO tokens are—well, like airline miles, which are not securities. They are a currency that can be used to pay for goods and services on a platform, so they should not be regulated as securities. The popular term is “utility token,” meaning a token that has utility on the platform rather than being a pure investment. This can be a hard argument to make, though, especially if your platform isn’t running yet. (Because you still have to build it, which is why you are raising money.) It seems pretty clear that selling a token to raise money to build a platform, based on promises that buyers of the token will make a profit when the platform is running, is a securities offering. Certainly the SEC thinks that. Another solution is not to sell ICO tokens to U.S. investors, or to sell them only to “accredited” (rich) investors in private offerings that don’t require registration. This is not a great solution, because if you want your platform to be widely usable, you can’t limit it to accredited investors—everyone has to be able to buy or sell whatever it is that runs on your network. There is another solution, blessed by several law firms, that has become sort of the popular best-practices approach. It goes like this: Sell something—call it a “ pre-token ”—to accredited investors (institutions, venture capitalists, etc.) to raise money to build your platform. Concede that the pre-token is a security. When the platform is built, it will run on a token , a cryptocurrency that can be used for transactions on the platform and that is not a security. At some point—at or after the launch of the platform—the pre-token (the security) flips into the token (the non-security), and all the people who bought pre-tokens to finance the platform now have tokens to use on it. (Or to sell to people who will use them.) This seems to honor the intention of securities law—you’re not selling speculative investments to retail investors to fund the development of a new business—while also honoring the intention of the ICO: Your platform is financed (indirectly, eventually) by the people who use it; the people putting up the money do so not in exchange for a share of the profits but for the ability to participate in the platform itself. In this model the pre-token will be called something like a “Token Purchase Agreement” or “Simple Agreement for Future Tokens”: It’s a security wrapper for the eventual utility token. On Friday the SEC brought an enforcement action to halt an initial coin offering by Telegram Group Inc. From the SEC’s press release: “Our emergency action today is intended to prevent Telegram from flooding the U.S. markets with digital tokens that we allege were unlawfully sold,” said Stephanie Avakian, Co-Director of the SEC’s Division of Enforcement. “We allege that the defendants have failed to provide investors with information regarding Grams and Telegram’s business operations, financial condition, risk factors, and management that the securities laws require.” “We have repeatedly stated that issuers cannot avoid the federal securities laws just by labeling their product a cryptocurrency or a digital token,” Steven Peikin, Co-Director of the SEC’s Division of Enforcement. “Telegram seeks to obtain the benefits of a public offering without complying with the long-established disclosure responsibilities designed to protect the investing public.” But that is not really fair to Telegram. Telegram did not try to “avoid the federal securities laws just by labeling their product a cryptocurrency or a digital token.” Instead, Telegram did the best-practices-y thing, selling early accredited investors a security that was meant to eventually flip into a non-security token. From the SEC’s complaint: From January through March 2018, Telegram entered into Gram Purchase Agreements with the Initial Purchasers. Under the agreements, TON Issuer Inc., a wholly-owned subsidiary of Telegram Group Inc., would “issue a new cryptocurrency called ‘Grams’ . . . following the development and launch of a new blockchain platform” called the “TON Network.” The Initial Purchasers, in turn, “subscribe[d]” to Grams by buying them at fixed prices, and Telegram committed to deliver them after the development of the TON Blockchain. … Telegram has taken the position that the Gram Purchase Agreements were investment contracts, i.e., securities, and placed a restrictive legend on the Gram Purchase Agreements. The legend warned United States residents that “the offer and sale of this security has not been registered under the U.S. Securities Act of 1933” and “may not be offered, sold or otherwise transferred . . . except pursuant to an effective registration statements.” Telegram, however, claimed that Grams, the heart of the Gram Purchase Agreements, without which the agreements have no value or purpose, were not securities but rather currency. Telegram thus placed no restrictive legends on any Grams, nor were purchasers advised that they may not sell Grams in the United States absent a registration statement. Purchasers of Grams are not restricted from reselling them to others, other than as provided for by certain contractual lockups placed on some Grams sold to Initial Purchasers. Telegram sold $1.7 billion of Grams—well, Gram Purchase Agreements, my “pre-token”—to accredited investors, including leading venture capital firms like Kleiner Perkins, Benchmark and Sequoia. It used some of the money to develop its blockchain project, and is now getting ready to launch it. It will launch it by distributing some tokens for free to users of its Telegram messaging app, and by distributing other tokens to developers building products on its blockchain system, and of course by flipping those Gram Purchase Agreements, the securities it sold to finance development, into Grams, the non-security utility tokens that will be usable on the system. Again from the SEC complaint: In March 2019, Telegram released a beta version of the TON Blockchain, a network designed to test the functionality of TON and Grams. This was a necessary precursor for Telegram to eventually launch the TON Blockchain and deliver Grams to Initial Purchasers. Telegram is preparing to imminently deliver Grams sold to Initial Purchasers, and will do so at the latest by the Deadline Date of October 31, 2019. Indeed, Telegram recently launched the TON Wallet and, on or around October 2, gave Initial Purchasers until October 16, 2019 to provide it with a blockchain address in which to receive Grams. Defendants also currently intend to set aside 500 million Grams (or approximately 10% of Grams issuable) for use as incentive payments to third-party developers of products for the TON Blockchain. … Defendants also intend to transfer approximately 250 million “free” Grams (of the 1.4 billion remainder) to Messenger users “in the days/weeks immediately following” the launch in order to help create a liquid market for Grams, including the Grams Telegram still hold. But the SEC wants to shut them down. It wants to shut them down because … the blockchain ecosystem isn’t live yet? The TON “ecosystem” did not exist and does not exist today. There are not now and have never been any products or services that can be purchased with Grams. The TON functionalities as pitched by Telegram were (and remain) entirely dependent on the funds provided by investors. Meanwhile, the principal means by which investors would reasonably expect to profit is through their resale of Grams. And because the initial investors bought a lot of tokens? Grams were and continue to be investment contracts from which Initial Purchasers and others reasonably expect to reap enormous profits once the Gram market launches. Grams are not a currency because they have no realistic currency uses at this time. Telegram sold and will deliver Grams in amounts that far exceed any anticipated “use” on the TON Blockchain. For example, all but three of the United States Grams Initial Purchasers bought more than 2.5 million Grams each. Nor did or will Telegram restrict sales only to individuals who would actually “use” Grams. To the contrary, Telegram contemplated that Initial Purchasers would resell their Grams immediately upon delivery, as evidenced by its inclusion of certain lock-up provisions as to some Grams. Moreover, the $1.7 billion raised in the Offering so far exceeds what Defendants project they will need to develop the TON Blockchain. I don’t really get it? The SEC’s basic position seems to be that all ICOs are securities offerings, that there is absolutely no legal way to develop a decentralized un-owned platform by pre-selling the tokens for that platform.[2] If you pre-sell those tokens to retail investors without registration then that is a securities offering and of course you are violating the law. But if you pre-sell them to institutional investors in an exempt transaction, with the hope that one day, when the platform is up and running, you can flip them into utility tokens and the institutions can sell them to real users, that is also a securities offering, when you flip them into utility tokens. It is a securities offering in part because you sold them to the original investors as an investment, with the pitch that they could make money reselling them.[3] (Of course you did!) And it’s a securities offering in part because, at the moment you flip the switch and turn it into a utility token, it doesn’t have that much utility, because not that many people are using it, because you haven’t distributed it widely yet—you’ve only sold it to the big institutions. Look, I am not familiar with the Telegram ecosystem, and I can certainly believe the SEC when it says that it doesn’t do much. Really every time the SEC brings a case like this,[4] it has that rhetorical advantage: There aren’t exactly a ton of economies running on cryptocurrency blockchains, except arguably for Bitcoin and Ethereum, both of which have been more or less grandfathered out of securities law. “You can’t buy much stuff with this token so it must be a speculative investment” is a pretty good argument. But that’s (partly) the SEC’s fault! If you can’t distribute tokens broadly to (potential) users of your network, then they can’t be broadly useful; there is a simple chicken-and-egg problem that Telegram’s two-step approach was supposed to solve. First you raise money by selling pre-tokens to build the network, in a financing transaction that you treat as a securities offering; then you distribute tokens broadly for use on the network, in non-financing transactions that you don’t treat as a securities offering. The SEC collapses those two steps so that every distribution is a securities offering, so you can never distribute your tokens to users, so they can never be useful, so the SEC can always say “well these tokens aren’t useful.” Perhaps there’s a way forward? I don’t know, maybe you have to lock up the pre-tokens longer; maybe you have to (1) sell pre-tokens to institutional investors, (2) launch publicly by distributing free tokens to users, and (3) a year or so later, when the ecosystem is running robustly, let the original investors flip their pre-tokens into tokens and sell them. I suspect that would not satisfy the SEC either. I’m not exactly a crypto enthusiast, but I was once fascinated by the promise of the ICO as a way to finance decentralized un-owned ecosystems that could develop independently of corporate ownership. That just seemed like an interesting and promising new approach, and I was excited to see it develop. If that’s your view then I think it is reasonable to be disappointed in both sides here. On the one hand, the SEC really does seem to be going out of its way to stifle innovation, harshly rejecting the careful good-faith efforts of ICO promoters to try to comply with the securities laws in a way that still captures the spirit of decentralized tokenization. On the other hand, it is not like those promoters have all that much to show for their efforts? A lot of the actually existing ICOs look a lot like fundraising efforts for regular old businesses rather than truly novel decentralized protocols; also they tend not to do much. I am not the least bit persuaded that, if the SEC just got out of the way, Telegram would have revolutionized commerce with its $1.7 billion token project. Still, I would like to see the SEC let someone try.

In surprisingly short order, the general consensus on WeWork has shifted from “high-flying, innovative, fast-growing tech-ish unicorn” to “gigantic bonfire of money.” If you think that WeWork (now the We Co.) is a potentially world-dominating tech startup, then obviously (?) it should be under the total and perpetual control of its brilliant, charismatic, unpredictable founder; that’s just how tech startups work in 2019. If you think it’s a money bonfire then, well, look, there is not a ton of corporate-governance precedent for money bonfires, but just from first principles it stands to reason that whoever is shoveling in the money should be in charge of the temperature. In WeWork’s case, the vast majority of the money that it has incinerated belongs to SoftBank, so sure why not: SoftBank Group Corp. has prepared a financing package that would give it control of WeWork and further sideline its founder Adam Neumann in exchange for relieving the shared-office startup’s looming cash crunch, according to people familiar with the matter. … SoftBank, which already owns one-third of WeWork, is aiming to invest several billion dollars in new equity and debt, some of the people familiar with the matter said. Should there be a deal with SoftBank, much of Mr. Neumann’s voting power—already diminished from its peak but still substantial—would shift to the Japanese conglomerate, which would take a bigger role in turning around We’s operations, people familiar with the matter said. This is apparently one of two options that WeWork’s board is seriously considering; the other option is tapping a group of banks led by JPMorgan Chase & Co. to raise $5 billion of debt. That would involve “raising $3 billion or more of the debt package through the sale of high-yield bonds,” and after equity investors’ reaction to the initial public offering prospectus, imagine how much debt investors will enjoy the bond one. What is the endgame for SoftBank here? I don’t see why a new IPO in February, with a WeWork controlled by SoftBank instead of Neumann, would go over any better than the last one. Arguably WeWork’s kookiness is more SoftBank’s fault than Neumann’s anyway. My theory of WeWork, which I actually did not write as a joke though it is starting to sound like one, is that it is supposed to be a basically sound and profitable business that happens to be losing billions of dollars a year to fund the rapid growth that tech startup investors were supposed to like. Investors turned out not to like it, so, never mind, forget about the whole rapid growth thing. What’s left? I keep quoting a line from the prospectus in which WeWork says that “the flexibility to manage our growth by focusing on our existing pipeline of locations and allowing them to mature presents us with an opportunity to manage our profitability profile.” That sounds like it means—it had better mean!—that if WeWork shuts off the rapid growth, it can become profitable in short order.[5] Not all that short (“Executives at SoftBank figure We needs at least $3 billion to get through the next year”), but once you stop lighting all of the money on fire to attract the attention of public markets, maybe you can just, like, rent some buildings and spruce them up and sublet the space for more than you’re paying? It is not a fantastically innovative business model, it is not particularly “tech,” it will not change the world, but maybe it will bring in more money than it costs? And then SoftBank could just, you know, have that money? Pay itself a dividend? Make a positive return on its umpteen billion dollars of investment? I dunno, I guess it sounds pretty far-fetched. SoftBank is not in the business of making bold multibillion-dollar bets on tech companies run by visionary founders in the hopes of one day owning a majority stake of a company that makes a modest steady profit in the traditional old-economy business of renting out office space. It is in the business of making huge bold tech bets and then flipping them at a multiple of its original investment; the goal is to put in the money, prove the concept, grow really fast, and then sell to other investors who are entranced by the growth. But that pretty definitively didn’t work here, and among the unpleasant options that WeWork/SoftBank could now pivot to, the one that is like “just collect rent checks, make money, and pay some of it to the giant tech fund that accidentally wound up owning this real-estate company” seems … you know … fine? By the way, here’s an amazing sentence from the Wall Street Journal story: Some of SoftBank’s cash could also be used by Mr. Neumann to repay hundreds of millions of dollars of personal bank loans, one of the people said. Ah! Yes, most of the billions of dollars of fresh capital will be shoveled into the money furnace to keep WeWork running for another year, but some of it—hundreds of millions of dollars of it—will be handed to Adam Neumann to pay for all the houses he bought back in better times. This is one of those if-you-owe-the-bank-$10-billion-that’s-the-bank’s-problem situations, with SoftBank in the role of the bank: SoftBank, at this point, needs WeWork to work more than Neumann does—he’s already been pushed out, and he already lives in all the houses—and so presumably he can hold them up for more money. He gives them control, they pay off his debts, they call it even; fine, I get it, but for SoftBank it must hurt to have to pay Neumann even more for the rights to the money furnace that incinerated all their cash.

s.h: People are worried about non-GAAP accounting
s.t: U.S. generally accepted accounting principles tell companies how they have to calculate and disclose their income. Generally speaking, if you have income, you disclose it; “net income” for a year is more or less the money that comes in that year minus the money that goes out. Some money comes in from the daily business of selling your product, and some goes out to the daily expense of making it, but there are also more abnormal, one-off income and expense items. Sometimes lightning hits your factory or whatever and you have the cost of repairing it. It all gets rolled up into net income. That number is useful information for investors, but not that useful. By the time they get the income statement for a year, that year is long over, and they are much less interested in how much money you made last year than they are in how much money you’ll make next year, or five years from now. You can’t really tell them that, since you don’t know, but last year’s net income is a decent starting point for predicting next year’s. Parts of it are more useful than other parts. The regular, repeatable parts—the income from selling your product and the expenses of making it—are predictive; the lightning strikes are less so. If you could tell investors “our ‘real,’ repeatable, apples-to-apples net income this year was $X, and we also had $Y of unusual items that we don’t think are relevant to our future business,” then that would be more informative than just telling them the net-income number. And so companies do that, frequently, in the form of non-GAAP adjusted earnings figures, and they are endlessly criticized for it, and for good and obvious reasons: Companies like to make themselves look good, so they have a bias towards assuming that positive earnings items are real and recurring but that expenses are “extraordinary” and one-off. So there is evidence that, when companies report non-GAAP adjusted earnings numbers, those numbers tend to be inflated. We talked last month about a paper finding that “investors are misled by firms that exclude particular expenses in calculating non-GAAP earnings in order to beat analysts’ earnings forecasts.” The market treats companies’ adjusted earnings numbers as more predictive than GAAP earnings, when in fact they are not. On the other hand here’s a paper called “ Core Earnings: New Data and Evidence,” by Ethan Rouen, Eric So and Charles Wang, finding that adjusting GAAP earnings numbers to exclude “non-operating and less persistent income-statement items” leads to better predictive power: Using a novel dataset that comprehensively classifies the quantitative financial disclosures in firms' 10-Ks, including those hidden in the footnotes and the MD&A, we show that disclosures of non-operating and less persistent income-statement items are both frequent and economically significant, and increasingly so over time. Adjusting GAAP earnings to exclude these items creates a measure of core earnings that is highly persistent and that forecasts future performance. Analysts and market participants are slow to impound the implications of transitory earnings. Trading strategies that exploit cross-sectional differences in firms' transitory earnings produce abnormal returns of 7-to-10% per year. What’s the difference? I mean, fairly obviously, the difference is that if outside researchers try to construct a consistent method of adjusting every company’s GAAP earnings to create a good measure of persistent recurring earnings, they might be able to do that: There are some elements of GAAP that obscure the fundamental economics of the company’s ongoing business, and if you strip out those elements you will get a better picture of the real economics. On the other hand, if every company does its own adjustments, they will all just make themselves look as good as possible in a way that is not necessarily helpful to investors.

Here is a fun story about the stimulative effect of negative interest rates: In the Swiss canton of Zug, officials are going to extremes to avoid getting penalized by the world’s lowest interest rate. To minimize the amount of cash on hand that would get hit with a charge, Zug’s treasury postponed recouping nearly a billion francs in capital gains tax revenue from the federal government. The canton, or state government, also has plans to pay bills and staff Christmas bonuses early. Literally paying Christmas bonuses early! The staff aren’t going to want to hang onto that money either, with bank rates below zero, so they are going to do their Christmas shopping in October, and then retailers are going to pay their bonuses early, etc. etc. etc., the system is working exactly the way it is supposed to.

[1] I once wrote: “The popular analogy is to email. Email is a good system for sending messages to people over the internet. It is also a universally available protocol. People invented and developed it, but no one owns it. Anyone can build software that uses it. Twitter, meanwhile, is also a good system for sending messages to people over the internet. Twitter Inc. owns it, though, and makes money from it, and constantly tweaks it, and can exercise its power over the system in arbitrary ways. A lot of technology and media people, frustrated with this situation -- and with the particular ways in which Twitter exercises its power -- wish that Twitter had been a protocol. But of course if the founders of Twitter had just released it as an open protocol they wouldn't be fabulously wealthy now. And their venture capitalist backers wouldn't have made tons of money. And so those VCs wouldn't have backed them. And so there wouldn't be Twitter. So ICOs are a way for the next Twitter -- or file storage network, or whatever -- to (1) be an open protocol and (2) get funded. You think up a network protocol that you expect to be valuable to a lot of people, you pre-sell some of that value to people who might use the protocol (or who want to speculate on its adoption), you use the proceeds to build the protocol (and reward yourself for your labor), and you get out of the way. You fund yourself from people who expect to get value from using the network, rather than from venture capitalists who expect to get value from owning it.” [2] I have in the past interpreted SEC statements to suggest that the SEC was more open-minded than this, and that there was some narrow path forward for the best-practices pre-token-y approach. I seem to have been wrong! [3] That is, as a matter of securities law, you sold them to the initial investors as “underwriters,” and when those investors turn around and sell them to the public that is effectively a continuation of your securities offering. [4] We’ve talked a few times about the case against Kik Interactive Inc. over its token offering, which did not really follow the pre-token-y best practices but which does not in any case seem to have a ton of utility. [5] Technically I suppose it could mean that a fast-growing WeWork is extremely unprofitable, while a steady-state non-growing WeWork would only be moderately unprofitable. I hope that is not actually the investment thesis, but it has been a weird few months.

Well there you go: Corporate governance is important to our company. We are making a number of changes to our proposed governance structure in response to market feedback. As a result, our board of directors and Adam have agreed to implement the following changes to our governance structure: We will appoint a lead independent director by the end of the year. Our high-vote stock will decrease from 20 votes per share to 10 votes per share. The voting power of our high-vote stock will sunset and automatically decrease to one vote per share in the event that Adam becomes permanently incapacitated or dies. ... We will maintain a board consisting of a majority of independent directors and all of the committees and sub-committees of our board will consist of at least a majority of independent directors. No member of Adam’s family will sit on our board. Any chief executive officer who succeeds Adam will be selected by our board of directors, acting as a group. We will not rely on a succession committee. Our board has the ability to remove our chief executive officer. In addition to appointing Frances Frei to our board of directors, we have committed to adding another director to our board within the next year, with a commitment to increasing the board’s gender and ethnic diversity. Adam has also decided to take the following actions: Adam will give to the company any profits he receives from the real estate transactions he has entered into with the company. As previously disclosed, Adam no longer has the power, discretion or authority to make investment and management decisions affecting the properties he transferred to be managed by ARK and will not enter into future real estate transactions with the company. As previously disclosed, Adam has entered into a lock-up agreement for one year with the underwriters in this offering. Adam will also limit his ability to sell in each of the second and third years following this offering to no more than 10% of his shareholdings. As previously disclosed, we have unwound an issuance of partnership interests to Adam that he received for transferring “we” family trademarks to the company. That is from the amended initial public offering documents that the We Co., formerly WeWork, filed this morning. I am not going to pretend that this is an industry-leading list of corporate-governance best practices, but it is a meaningful change from the WeWork of a month ago. Founder-CEO Adam Neumann will still control the company through dual-class stock for the rest of his life, but only for the rest of his life; the previous version gave him control from beyond the grave. There will be a bit more board independence and supervision. “Our board has the ability to remove our chief executive officer,” super. Before the IPO, Neumann made some money by buying buildings and renting them to WeWork, while cashing out hundreds of millions of dollars of WeWork stock and somehow selling We the name “We”; now he will knock all that off. It’s all standard-issue 2019-era tech-company governance, which is to say it’s better than August-2019-era WeWork governance but still worse than a normal public company. But enough about the list; what is interesting here are those first two sentences. “Corporate governance is important to our company.” Has anyone ever said that before?[1] It gives off the strongest possible doth-protest-too-much vibe; the only time you would ever say “corporate governance is important to our company” is if people had just spent a month relentlessly criticizing your terrible corporate governance. Corporate governance is important to We, in a way that it is not important to other companies, because it is so saliently bad. It’s so important to We that it almost scuttled its IPO. “We are making a number of changes to our proposed governance structure in response to market feedback.” Has anyone ever said that before? Or done it? I am sure the answer is yes, there are a lot of companies, but it is not the norm. I suggested earlier this week that it might be a good idea for We to do something like this, but I am as surprised as anyone that they actually did. It is not the pattern that we have discussed in recent years. That pattern is that tech companies launch IPOs with shareholder-unfriendly governance terms, and investors grumble that those terms are unconscionable and that they must not stand, and then all the investors buy the IPO anyway and the terrible governance terms become market standard. It is not that investors do not push back on bad governance terms; it is just that they do not push back effectively. Until now! Now they have! It’s a big moment. This does not mark the end of tech unicorn founders keeping lifetime control of their companies; Neumann still mostly gets that. But it is a line in the sand that, if you want to take your tech unicorn public, you can’t also charge it $6 million for its name. It’s something. Is it enough? One big area of investor pushback against We’s IPO was the governance stuff; that is now improved, though a cynic would say that as long as Neumann has majority voting control of the company governance changes can never be all that binding. There were other areas of pushback. There have been doubts about We’s business model and unit economics, and about whether We was giving investors enough information to evaluate those economics; obviously the business model has not changed in the amended filing, but the disclosure hasn’t changed much either.[2] Investors who didn’t like the business model before won’t like it now, despite the governance changes. Really the biggest pushback that We got seems to have been on valuation, and it seems safe to say that investors are winning on that one. No one is now expecting We to go public at a $65 billion valuation, as its bankers once proposed, or for that matter at $47 billion, the headline valuation in its last private funding round. I suspect that lopping tens of billions of dollars off the valuation will do more to get this deal done than changing the terms of the super-voting stock, and that changing those terms won’t add tens of billions of dollars back to the valuation. One should not overemphasize the importance of governance here. Still, every little bit helps.

One basic lesson of finance is that bid/ask spreads exist. You pay for liquidity. If there is a thing, and there is some Platonic natural true price for that thing, and you want to buy a lot of it right now, you will have to pay a bit more than the true price. If you want to sell a lot of it right now, you will have to accept a bit of a discount to the true price. How big the premium or discount is will depend on what the thing is and how it trades and how much you want to buy or sell and how soon you need to do it and so forth, and a basic goal of a lot of markets is to make this spread as small as possible, but it never goes away entirely. Being able to buy or sell a bunch of something all at once is valuable, and you pay a bit for that service. This is a basic lesson of finance but it is not really a lesson of classical economics, which sometimes has a reputation for assuming away transaction costs. Nor is it a lesson of everyday life, where you normally get volume discounts for buying a lot of stuff all at once. And so when people encounter this phenomenon in finance they can find it very annoying and counterintuitive. But you find it in a lot of places. Most simply, there is the fact that some high-frequency trading firms make money every day, which normal people tend to interpret as conclusive evidence that they are cheating, but which is just as easy to interpret as evidence that they are buying at the bid and selling at the offer. More subtly, there is the phenomenon of the “IPO pop.” Most of the time, when companies go public, their stock tends to rise above the initial public offering price on the first day of trading. Whenever this happens—really almost every single time—there will be journalists and venture capitalists and corporate executives saying that Wall Street underprices IPOs to reward its greedy investor friends, and that is not exactly untrue, but most finance people will interpret it differently. They’ll be like, well, you wanted to sell a lot of stock all at once in a market where no one had ever bought any of that stock before. There was no liquidity, and you demanded a ton of liquidity. Of course you had to sell at a discount.[3] As with stocks, so with municipal bonds, except way way way less. Here is a Wall Street Journal analysis of municipal bond offerings: About $60 billion, or roughly 5%, of newly issued bonds in negotiated offerings between 2013 and 2017 were sold to customers who turned around and sold them to dealers within a single day of the initial offering, usually for a profit, the Journal found. Prices on those flipped bonds were then marked up further as they were sold to longer-term investors, bringing the total market-adjusted profits to more than $900 million. A graphic explains that, out of $1.24 trillion of new bonds, $59 billion trade on the first day after the offering, with first-day gains of $291 million, or about 0.5%. “By the end of 10 days of trading, the prices of many of those bonds had risen further. Market-adjusted profits from all of the post-offering trading totaled $901 million,” or about 1.5%.[4] So on average, when a municipality sells a brand-new bond for $100, that bond is worth $100.50, maybe as much as $101.50. That is an average, and sometimes it is worth less; sometimes it is even worth less than $100, and buyers will take an initial loss on their bonds.[5] (Just like some IPOs, rather than popping, go down.) But in expectation the buyers get a bit more than they paid for, to compensate them for providing liquidity to the issuer, and for the risk that these new uncertain bonds might go down. You could argue (how?) about what actual numbers are appropriate there—if you are used to 20% IPO pops, a 0.5% muni-bond pop won’t bother you at all[6]—but my main reaction is that the concept is fine. There has to be some positive number there. When an issuer needs a big chunk of money and decides to raise it by selling a brand-new instrument into the market for $100, the instrument should have a theoretical value of more than $100. That is how financial markets work. Others disagree: “That’s money being left on the table that costs taxpayers and rate payers and governments,” said Patrick Clancy, who recently retired after 30 years as a financial adviser to local governments issuing bonds. “That’s not the way it’s supposed to go.” … After the Journal shared its findings about post-offering trading with the West Contra Costa district, then-Associate Superintendent John al-Amin said that those findings “are deeply concerning and would undermine the faith bond issuers have in the municipal market.” I do think that from, like, first principles of human society, it is not totally unreasonable to think that investors should not make a profit by buying newly issued bonds from municipalities that want money. It is just not how I tend to think of things.

Here’s an odd statistic for you: SmileDirectClub Inc. shares sank 28% from their initial public offering price in Thursday’s debut, becoming the first U.S. firm since at least 2008 to raise more than $1 billion and price its IPO above range, yet sink in its opening trades. One way to spin this—it is not what I think, but let’s entertain it anyway—is that this makes SmileDirectClub the only successful IPO since 2008. SmileDirectClub’s underwriters figured the stock was worth $19 to $22 a share, went out and marketed it at that level, were able to talk enough investors up to $23 that they could allocate the whole offering there, priced the deal at a price they knew was too high, sold the stock to investors for more than it was worth, and it immediately cracked, opening at $20.55 and closing at $16.67. The underwriters developed a relatively clear-eyed view of what the stock was worth, and shared it with the company, and were able to convince investors to pay more than the stock was worth, and then the stock opened for trading and the underwriters were right and the investors were wrong. Usually stocks trade up after the IPO and people complain that the company left money on the table; here SmileDirectClub took in an extra $143 million by pricing at $23 rather than the opening market-clearing price of $20.55. (Or an extra $370 million versus the close.) High fives everyone! Except investors. Like I said, I do not really think of it that way; underwriters and also issuers are in a repeated game and want to gain the confidence and goodwill of investors rather than holding them up for every last penny. To me the straightforward interpretation of this IPO is that its banks messed up and misread the demand for the stock. But that’s just my view. If you hate IPO pops, it seems to me you should be jazzed about about this one.

Remember when the Business Roundtable, an association of chief executive officers of big U.S. companies, put out a big statement saying that businesses shouldn’t just be run for the benefit of shareholders but should instead care about workers and communities and the environment and whatever? And people were like “this is a revolution in capitalism,” and I was like “nah this is just CEOs saying that they don’t want to have to listen to shareholders?” This was like a month ago? The easiest prediction in the whole world to make then, or now, is that no CEO of any company that signed that letter will ever make any decision to put the interests of workers or communities or the environment ahead of shareholders because of that letter . Like when some CEO says “we need to stop providing health insurance to the workers we pay to burn down rain forests,” the Head of Stakeholder Relations is never going to pipe up and say “wait we signed a letter , we can’t do this.” Sometimes companies will do nice things for their workers or whatever, but it will always be for the same melange of reasons—tight labor markets, long-term profit motives, real or pretend CEO benevolence, genuine culture of respect for colleagues—that motivated U.S. public companies in 2018, or 1998, or any other point during the long reign of shareholder capitalism. The letter, the explicit commitment to considering stakeholders, changes nothing. Anyway “Whole Foods is cutting medical benefits for hundreds of part-time workers,” reports Business Insider. “Jeff Bezos, the CEO of their parent company, signed the Business Roundtable letter about doing more for employees less than a month ago,” notes Bob Bryan on Twitter. It is definitely an irony! It is definitely an irony that Jeff Bezos does not care about!

You know who is not really a stakeholder capitalism kind of guy? Carl Icahn. The New York Post has an incredible story about Icahn’s letter to employees announcing Icahn Enterprises’ move from New York to Florida next year. The letter starts with a pretty generous relocation offer—including a bonus guarantee and a promise not to fire you before 2023—but then moves on to this: But for those who don’t relocate to the Sunshine State, “the Company will not contest your unemployment claim,” the memo says. “The current maximum weekly Unemployment benefit rate is $450, which you can receive for a total of 26 weeks,” it adds. Sure he could have said something like “you will have to move if you want to keep your job,” but “the Company will not contest your unemployment claim” is a million times harsher. That’s like “as a special favor, you will be allowed to leave with your shoelaces.” The man just sat down and gave some real thought to how he could most cold-bloodedly convey that moving was mandatory, and because he is Carl Icahn he came up with the correct answer. It is honestly impressive. It’s rough for the employees, but then they do work for Carl Icahn , they can’t be entirely surprised.

This month has marked a real changing of the guard at Goldman Sachs Group Inc., which seems to be ushering out a lot of Lloyd-Blankfein-era partners to make the partnership smaller and cooler. We said goodbye to former chief information officer Marty Chavez last week, and now current co-CIO Elisha Wiesel has an exit interview with Bloomberg’s Amanda Gordon that includes this bit of Lloyd Blankfein humor and Gary Cohn … not humor: At J. Aron he worked for Lloyd Blankfein and Gary Cohn, who would wind up leading the firm for the longest stretch of Wiesel’s tenure. He remembers Blankfein chastising him in the lobby of 85 Broad when he arrived on Rollerblades. “He’d say, ‘I’m invested in that head, get a helmet!’” Wiesel recalled. His first encounter with Cohn was when he “screamed at me for being an idiot, because I was being an idiot,” Wiesel said. “He kept asking me about an implied volatility for the option price, and I didn’t know what an option was yet, because I’d literally just arrived.” Also there is a puzzle hunt: When Elisha Wiesel was promoted to chief information officer at Goldman Sachs Group Inc., his colleagues in the securities division, riffing on the all-night scavenger hunt he founded to raise money for charity, locked him in his office with puzzles to solve. When he got out, his reward was a baseball cap emblazoned with the tagline “SecDiv Escapee.” Wiesel is probably best known around Wall Street for founding the Midnight Madness puzzle hunt. Disclosure, I used to work at Goldman; further disclosure, or just a programming note really: I will be doing the Compass puzzle hunt, a successor to Midnight Madness, tomorrow. If you’re there, say hi.

National Basketball Association player Spencer Dinwiddie is planning to securitize his contract with the Brooklyn Nets, selling a share of his future income to investors for a lump-sum payment. It’s a thing! People have done this occasionally for years, and talked about it incessantly forever, it’s fine, whatever. “It’s unclear how much of the contract amount he wants to raise upfront, but it would likely be less than the total amount,” reports the Athletic, and you’d hope so. If you could take a $34.36 million three-year NBA contract and sell 100% of it today at some reasonable discount rate, you could take all that money and just stop playing basketball. I mean, he probably enjoys playing basketball, so there’s that, and I’m sure (sure-ish?) the securitization has some provisions requiring him to perform in good faith and so forth, but really if you sell all of your future income to someone else that reduces your incentives to actually earn the income. If you just sell a fraction of that income then you’ll probably show up to earn the rest. Oh but the real novelty here is it’s a token, a token, a toooooooooookennnnnnnnnnn, on the blockchain, blah blah blah. Obviously if you are an athlete contemplating selling stock in yourself in 2019 you should do it in the form of a token! People love talking about securitizing pro-sports contracts, and they love cryptocurrency stuff, and the people who love securitized pro-sports contracts are the same people who love cryptocurrency stuff, it is the most natural fit in the world. Elsewhere in, let’s say, tokenization, here’s a federal criminal case against a travel agent charged with stealing $1.75 million worth of Delta SkyMiles.

Here’s a story about a “Man Clump” of men who meet outside 160 Pearl Street in New York’s financial district every morning to psych themselves up for a day of cold calling to pitch small business loans: Man Clumping, we discovered, is a useful mechanism for boosting morale within your sales staff — provided, it stands to reason, that your sales staff is male and AMPED. The Man Clump's chief architects, Omar Soliman and Vince Garcia of Synergy Capital (an apparently very persistent telemarketing-based loan company, whose motto is: "We finance all businesses..."), told Gothamist that this is just how they do pitch meetings: Out on the sidewalk, where "elite" deal-makers-in-training can inspire one another to new financial heights through mutual screaming and encouragement. The method involves group chants (the preferred rallying cry, which Gothamist witnessed, ends with the men of the Man Clump woofing in unison) and inspiring aphorisms. "We found these jobs on Craigslist, and we've seen that, if we could start on Craigslist in a random spot and get to the level we did — once we brought all these guys in, we put what we did into them, and now everybody’s becoming elite," Garcia explained. With respect to office culture, Soliman said, "We make it like a sport, almost." I hope this becomes a tourist attraction now? Like why visit the New York Stock Exchange or the Charging Bull or some other boring downtown symbol of American financial capitalism when you can go watch the Man Clump woof?

[1] Googling “Corporate governance is important to our company,” in quotes, suggests that no one has written it on the internet before. [2] To be fair there are some additions to the business discussion in the S-1, including a bit more information on turnover rates, presumably driven by investor questions. But overall it is pretty similar. The redline is not especially colorful. [3] A related explanation of the IPO pop is that IPO investors are taking a risk by buying a stock that has never traded before with an uncertain valuation, so they expect to be rewarded for that risk with a discount to the “true” value. You can also interpret that as a form of bid/ask spread; market makers charge a spread not only for the service of providing liquidity but also, specifically, for the risk of adverse selection, the risk that they might be buying at the wrong price. Obviously the new-issue discount on IPOs and bond offerings is not *literally* the same thing as a bid-ask spread in trading markets, but it is a related concept. [4] That is, $901 million is about 1.53% of that $59 billion notional amount, but that is an upper bound. It is not entirely clear to me if that $901 million was limited to the $59 billion of bonds that trade on the first day, or if it includes other bonds that came loose later. Obviously $901 million of trading profits on the total $1.24 trillion of bond issuance rounds to nothing, just 0.07%. [5] In fact it’s an average based on the price of bonds *that are flipped*, bonds that are resold on the first day of trading. Most bonds (95%) aren’t flipped, and presumably some issues won’t have any first-day flip trades at all. Presumably that will often be because they haven’t gained any value so no initial buyer is looking to make a quick buck. A bond that goes up to 101 is more likely to get flipped than a bond that goes down to 99. So it is plausible that the actual average *value* of new-issued bonds is much closer to $100. [6] It seems to be in line with the average first-day pop for investment-grade corporate bonds.

In general there are two ways to make money investing in public stocks: Figure out which stocks are going to go up and buy them, or Buy some stocks and push the companies to do things to make their stocks go up. I think it is fair to say that, for a long time, the normal approach for most institutional investors was to focus on No. 1 and ignore No. 2. Your expertise was in analyzing stocks and picking the ones that will go up, and you mostly did that. You didn’t tell executives at the companies you owned how to do their jobs, both because you figured they knew that better than you did, and because it might interfere with your main job: If you annoy executives, they will give you less information and you’ll have a harder time picking stocks.[1] Telling companies how to run their businesses was a niche left to specialists called “activist hedge funds,” and while big respectable institutions would occasionally get involved in activist battles, they did so uncomfortably and reluctantly. That seems to have changed in recent years, and now there is more of an expectation that regular old institutional investors will be more involved in monitoring the companies they invest in. Not a ton more involved, but a little more; they have to think about and justify their stewardship a bit more than they used to. This change has occurred for a variety of reasons—changing social and political norms of corporate engagement, academic theories about governance, effective persuasion by activist investors, rules about shareholder voting on “say-on-pay” and other topics, the rise of shareholder proxy proposals, etc.—but one obvious big one is the rise of passive investing. If you run an index fund, you are not in the business of picking the stocks that will go up. That doesn’t necessarily mean that you are in the business of pushing companies to do things to make their stocks go up. You could quite reasonably take the view that the whole point of an index fund is to do neither thing, to be a low-cost provider of generic access to the stock market and not expend any effort on picking stocks or lobbying companies or anything else. But in practice, you know, there you are, going to your office every day; you need to fill your time somehow. You want to be able to justify your existence, to explain to people—customers, or maybe a broader audience—why you are adding value to society. Jack Bogle could convincingly say that he invented a way for ordinary investors to save billions of dollars, but the second wave of index-fund moguls can’t quite say that, so they devote some time to pushing companies to be socially responsible or long-termist or whatever.[2] While I have been talking about approaches to making money in public stock investing, you might have different goals for your investing, and you can apply exactly the same analysis to those goals. For instance, if you run a fund that focuses on environmental, social and governance (“ESG”) factors, and if you advertise yourself to investors as an ESG fund, you could: Figure out which stocks are good for the environment, etc., and buy them, or Buy stocks and push the companies to do things that are good for the environment, etc. In principle you could imagine an ESG fund that, for instance, only bought stock in fracking companies and then single-mindedly lobbied them to stop fracking. In practice that is not a viable approach.[3] On the other hand, you could very easily imagine an ESG fund that screened stocks based on some list of ESG criteria, bought the ones that scored the best, and called it a day. That seems to be the norm, really; “ESG fund” traditionally kind of means “fund that doesn’t invest in tobacco or gun or fracking companies.” But even companies that score relatively high on a list of ESG criteria could be better. And just as the norm in regular investing has shifted a bit, with institutions now expected to be more actively involved in the companies they own, so it is becoming awkward for ESG funds to just pick ESG stocks without actively pushing them to be ESG-ier. Or, anyway, here is a funny story from the Financial Times about ESG funds that don’t vote for ESG-ish shareholder proposals: For environmental and social proposals that received strong support from investors, six BlackRock sustainability funds voted with a company’s management 72 per cent of the time. … At Vanguard, two ESG funds, which combined have almost $7bn of assets, voted with management on environmental and social issues 93 per cent of the time when the proposals won support from at least 40 per cent of investors. ... State Street’s gender diversity ETF, and State Street funds broadly, frequently voted in 2019 for shareholder proposals supporting political spending disclosures, Morningstar said. But the ETF, which is sold under the “SHE” ticker and has $296.8m of assets, abstained from a gender pay gap proposal at Mastercard and voted against a proposal for disclosure about gender, race and ethnicity pay equity at The TJX Companies, according to the 2019 SEC data. That “SHE” fund advertises that it invests in “companies with the highest levels within their sectors of gender diversity on their boards of directors and in their senior leadership.” It picks companies with a lot of female directors and executives, and then it buys their stocks. But now it is apparently also supposed to vote for more gender pay gap disclosure. I am sort of sympathetic to the implicit laziness of the traditional approach: Arguably making a list of stocks that are good on some criteria, and then buying those stocks, is a valuable service, and evaluating and supporting shareholder proposals is a different and lower-value service. (These proposals tend to be non-binding, and to call on companies to produce reports rather than make substantive changes.) Still if people want their ESG as an all-inclusive bundle, it seems silly not to give it to them.

Hedge funds, the saying goes, are “a compensation scheme masquerading as an asset class,” but I have always found the case for the compensation scheme easier to understand than the case for the asset class. The compensation scheme is, like, if you find a really smart person who knows how to pick investments that will go up, you should let her invest your money, and you should be happy to pay her a large fee for that service. She should charge a lot! That is a hard and valuable thing to do. It all makes perfect sense. The asset class is, like … what is she doing ? Maybe she is betting that a company’s bonds will outperform its stock, or trading on changes in statistical relationships between emerging-market currency pairs, or funding lawsuits, or exploiting weird life insurance contracts, or buying large concentrated stakes in U.S. public companies and pushing them to make management changes, or making large concentrated short bets on U.S. public companies and announcing that they are frauds, or, I dunno, there are a lot of things that hedge funds do. If you had a strong detailed thesis on what would happen in the world economy in the next few years, that thesis might inform whether you’d want to buy or sell U.S. stocks or Latin American bonds or Chinese yuan or oil or gold or lots of other asset classes, but I am not sure it would tell you much about whether to buy “hedge funds.” There are a lot of them! Some of them are betting on economic collapse, lots of them are betting on a general rise in the prices of financial assets, some are probably hedged such that they are not much correlated to broader economic conditions, you never know. I suppose if the asset class is “people who generate alpha,” that is, people who reliably generate returns in excess of the market return, then, sure, that’s an asset. That’s a good thing. But I tend to think of that as an individualized, artisanal, direct-sold sort of thing. Like you meet a hedge fund manager and look at her track record and ask about her investing process and experience her charisma and decide that she is or isn’t an alpha generator, and then you do or don’t give her money. You don’t just say “eh, if she’s a hedge fund manager that’s good enough for me, sign me up.” I’m wrong though. Here’s Bloomberg’s Katia Porzecanski: Aberdeen Standard Investments and Hedge Fund Research Inc. are charting new territory by creating a fund that tracks HFR’s broad index of 500 hedge funds. The product will allow wealthy investors and institutions to play in the rarefied world of hedge funds without having to kick their tires or deal with the egos. “For the first time you can have access to the space without having the internal costs of selecting managers or paying a premium for someone to externally handle that manager-selection alpha for you,” said Russell Barlow, global head of alternative strategies at ASI, which oversees about $670 billion. “You can just buy the passive version.” … The new ASI-HFR product will allow clients to passively invest in hundreds of actual flagship hedge funds, as opposed to separately managed or liquid alternative versions of them, said HFR founder Joe Nicholas. The fund is expected to start trading in January, along with 30 strategy and sub-strategy index funds. The hedge funds in the new, underlying index are being selected for their liquidity -- quarterly or better -- and size. They are required to report their performance and assets under management monthly to HFR. Investors will be able to subscribe or redeem from the index fund quarterly. Investors will need to put up a minimum of $5 million to get into the fund. Okay.[4] Passive investing is the great triumph of the efficient markets hypothesis: You assume that it is impossible (for you (to identify people who are able)) to reliably beat the market, so you give up and buy all the stocks. Hedge funds are the great rejection of the efficient markets hypothesis; the whole pitch is “I can reliably beat the market, for you, for a fee.” It just seems kind of strange to mash them together.

Congrats everyone, we did it: Passive investing styles have been gaining ground on actively managed funds for decades. But in August the investment industry reached one of the biggest milestones in its modern history, as assets in U.S. index-based equity mutual funds and ETFs topped those in active stock funds for the first time. … August fund flows helped lift assets in index-tracking U.S. equity funds to $4.271 trillion, compared with $4.246 trillion run by stock-pickers, according to estimates from Morningstar Inc. Investors added $88.9 billion to passive U.S. stock funds while pulling $124.1 billion from active this year through August, the firm estimated. One thing that I think about this development is that it represents not so much the demise of stock-picking as what I have called “the hollowing out of the investing middle class.” People still want charismatic stars to make their investments for them, but if that’s really what you want you are not going to settle for some portfolio manager at a big mutual-fund company who buys the same big public stocks as everyone else. There are swaggering activist investors and far-seeing venture capitalists and exclusive private offerings and Warren Buffett and, I don’t know, somehow Bitcoin. If you just want a normal respectable public stock investment, index funds are fine; if you want something bold and unusual and ambitious, there are so many bolder and more ambitious options than active mutual funds. Active mutual funds are more exciting than index funds and less exciting than hedge funds, which does not strike me as a great place to be.

Well, it is; I don’t make the rules. If a U.S. public company does a bad thing, or if a bad thing happens to it, that is probably securities fraud: The company didn’t tell investors about the bad thing as soon as it did it, or it didn’t adequately warn investors about the risk of the bad thing happening to it, etc., so investors were deceived when they bought the company’s stock. This is not a literal statement of the law, and occasionally companies do or experience bad things and nonetheless convince courts that those things are not securities fraud. But it is a good rule of thumb: If a bad thing happens at a company, and you are trying to analyze the consequences of the bad thing for the company, one of those consequences is pretty much always going to be a group of shareholders suing it for securities fraud. If your chief executive officer gets really sick, that is generally a bad thing, and so, I am sorry to say, it might be securities fraud: Oracle Corp. said Chief Executive Officer Mark Hurd is taking a leave of absence for unspecified health-related reasons, disclosing the move along with quarterly earnings on Wednesday afternoon. The software company made the announcement a day earlier than the results were scheduled to be released, after Bloomberg News contacted Oracle in relation to a story about the executive’s health. The company grappled for more than a year with one of the most harrowing dilemmas a corporation can face: when – and whether – to disclose a serious illness that has befallen a senior executive. … Securities law can be unclear about when a company is obligated to disclose a CEO’s ill health, allowing some to hold out as long as possible, while others have erred on the side of speaking out early. The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission hasn’t settled the question, but in general says shareholders should be told about “material” matters, defined as issues on which “there is a substantial likelihood that a reasonable person would consider it important.” ... “The default position for a company whenever any senior executive is facing health issues should be to disclose, because it is something investors need to know when they assess a company,” said Stephen Davis, associate director of Harvard Law School’s program on corporate governance. “It may not be an issue if there’s a strong board, a strong succession plan, and strong investor confidence in the company. But when it’s a company such as Oracle where you really have a long history of shareholders not having confidence in issues around executive pay, for instance, it’s that much more important for them to know what’s going on.” I don’t really expect investors to sue Oracle for not announcing Hurd’s illness earlier, but I wouldn’t be that surprised if they do. The rules are the rules.
