[1] This norm probably developed before Regulation FD, back when getting material nonpublic information from executives was a reasonable way to pick stocks. Now it is … still … that? [2] Also, if you run an index fund and a company in the index is obviously terrible and lighting shareholder money on fire, you can’t sell your stock, so the only way to preserve your investors’ money is by telling the company to knock it off. When exit is not an option, you have to rely on voice. [3] Or you could imagine an ESG fund that buys stocks in every company and then pushes the bad ones to get better. That seems like a very viable approach, actually! It’s just that you wouldn’t call it an ESG fund. You’d call it an index fund, but you’d also publicly push companies in the index to get better on the social issues you care about and hope to appeal to ESG-conscious investors. Is that how BlackRock’s broad index funds work? I don’t know, kind of, a little? [4] By the way, “The HFRI 500 Fund Weighted Composite Index is a global, equal-weighted index of the largest hedge funds that report to the HFR Database which are open to new investments and offer quarterly liquidity or better.” Presumably many of the better alpha generators are closed to new investments (because if you consistently generate alpha why not keep it for yourself?) or offer limited liquidity (because good hedge fund managers will be good at the main job of a hedge fund manager, keeping investors’ money).

s.h: You win some, you lose some
s.t: Let’s start with the bad news: In yesterday’s newsletter I told you about a hilarious lawsuit between the estate of Lehman Brothers and a broker called Exotix, in which Lehman and Exotix both thought that they were trading $7,000 worth of bonds but Lehman ended up sending Exotix $7 million worth, because bond numbers are confusing and it is surprisingly easy to be off by a factor of 1,000. I was mostly interested in the details of how the trade got messed up, but I … somehow got the verdict wrong? I wrote that Exotix won, but actually Lehman won. I am very sorry for the error but, in my defense, it was weirdly appropriate. I was demonstrating how easy it is to be off by a factor of 1,000 by getting the verdict entirely wrong, or something. Let’s go with that. Now the good news. In Monday’s newsletter, we talked—as we have every day lately—about the initial public offering of the We Co., formerly WeWork, which does not seem to be going particularly well. WeWork last raised money privately at a $47 billion valuation, and was hoping to be valued as high as $65 billion in its IPO, but the recent talk has included phrases like “as low as $15 billion.” I suggested on Monday that, if WeWork is unhappy with its reception by public investors, there is something it could do about it: Some of the pushback to WeWork has focused on its investor-unfriendly governance, the triple-class stock that cements founder Adam Neumann’s control for his lifetime and beyond, and the conflicts of interest between Neumann and WeWork’s shareholders. That all seemed fixable: WeWork wants to go public, it does not want a low valuation, its weirdo sparkly unicorn governance is contributing to a low valuation, so maybe it could give up the weirdo governance? If investors want, say, single-class stock without absolute power concentrated indefinitely in the founder, maybe they’d be willing to pay up for it, and maybe WeWork would give it to them? I did not want to push that idea particularly hard: It is not at all clear to me that investors value governance as much as they say they do, WeWork has plenty of issues beyond the governance, and a lesson of the modern unicorn boom seems to be that startup founders really care about maintaining absolute lifetime control with super-voting stock. Still it seemed worth suggesting: If investors want good governance and are willing to pay for it, and if WeWork wants to go public and is willing to compromise, then maybe there is a deal to be done. And here we maybe are! WeWork is considering major changes to governance to assuage investor concerns ahead of an initial public offering this month that’s even given pause to some of its own bankers, according to people with knowledge of the situation. Both of its lead financial advisers -- JPMorgan Chase & Co. and Goldman Sachs Group Inc. -- have concerns about proceeding with an IPO that could value the company as low as $15 billion, the people said, asking not to be identified because the talks are confidential. That’s set off a push to make the public sale more palatable to potential investors with governance reforms. Any decision ultimately rests with the venture’s co-founder and chief executive officer, Adam Neumann, who maintains voting control through a three-class share structure and has been an adamant proponent of the IPO, the people said. Look, to be clear, if (1) WeWork actually changes its weird governance stuff to be more palatable to investors, and (2) that actually makes it more palatable to investors and the IPO goes well, I will be pretty surprised myself. I will start charging more for this newsletter, I tell you what. Also if that happens my Bloomberg Opinion colleague Shira Ovide has promised to purchase and eat a hat. It will be a weird time! Except that what I want to suggest here is that it won’t be that weird, and that maybe the last few years have been the weird time. In parallel, apparently, with considering governance changes to get the IPO done, WeWork has also been talking to its existing investors (particularly SoftBank Group Corp.) about postponing the IPO and remaining private. If it does that, it will miss out on as much as $10 billion of new funding (in IPO proceeds and bank loans contingent on the IPO), which will slow its rapid growth. But Neumann will keep his absolute control and avoid the invasive scrutiny of public investors, independent directors and periodic disclosure. If he wants to rename the company again and charge it for the name, or if he wants to borrow money against his We stock to buy more buildings to rent to the company, who is going to object? Who, outside of a pliant board and a small group of enthusiastic and captive investors, will even hear about it? This is a textbook, normal choice, exactly what you’d expect if you forgot about the last five years of tech-company funding. The tradeoff is: If you take your company public, you have to conform to public-market norms: You have to give public investors full disclosure, and sell to anyone who wants to buy even if they are mean activists, and suffer the scrutiny of quarterly financial results and evil short-sellers and meddling journalists, and give up ultimate control of your company to shareholders who, if they are unhappy with your leadership, can vote you out. The company that was your baby, that was absolutely identified with you personally, doesn’t belong to you anymore; now you are managing on behalf of the shareholders. But you might want to go public anyway because that’s where the money is. A theme of this newsletter in recent years has been the dissolution of this traditional tradeoff. On the one hand, the public markets aren’t where the money is anymore; you can raise arbitrary billions of dollars from venture capitalists and mutual funds and SoftBank while remaining private, so big private tech companies feel less pressure to go public. On the other hand, that gives them more leverage when they do go public, which means that they have more freedom not to conform to public-market norms. And so dual-class stock has become common, and tech companies regularly go public without giving shareholders any say at all, and their IPO documents say things like “our mission is to elevate the world’s consciousness” to make it clear to shareholders that the mission is not to have consistent growing quarterly profits. But now WeWork seems to be facing the traditional tradeoff: Stay private, keep control, but lose access to billions of dollars of funding, or go public, raise unlimited money, and have to act normal. If it does either of those things, that will mark a sort of end of an era. At the height of the unicorn boom, big tech companies could stay private without giving up the benefits of being public, or they could go public without taking on the burdens of being public. Now they might have to make hard choices again. Elsewhere in WeWork, it is facing new competition from regular office landlords who are launching co-working businesses. Its bondholders are getting nervous. Fidelity Investments’ Contrafund is marking its WeWork stake at about an $18.3 billion valuation. And at Axios, Dan Primack suggests that “if WeWork doesn't go public, SoftBank needn't write down the value of its investment.” That does sound like a calculation that SoftBank would make, but I don’t know, man. If you announce an IPO, it’s widely reported that you can’t get it done at a $20 billion valuation, and then you pull the IPO, that doesn’t exactly support a $47 billion valuation, does it? Like if I were investing in SoftBank’s second Vision Fund, and the marketing documents mentioned that the first Vision Fund had a profitable investment in WeWork marked at $47 billion, I’d have some questions.

At the New York Times, Nellie Bowles writes about an education-technology venture capitalist named Jason Palmer who tweeted a mean thing about a failed startup, and then a bunch of other venture capitalists and founder types tweeted mean things about him, and he was sorry and promised not to tweet mean things about any more startups even if they were obvious nonsense. “By not knowing the rules,” writes Bowles, “he showed exactly what those rules are, and just how the Silicon Valley positivity machine runs.” It runs by cheerleading for startups that you like, and not saying anything at all about startups that you think are worthless. Honestly that is just basic politeness, but on the other hand financial markets do not generally prioritize politeness. One way to read this story is as an extension of the theory that there is a bubble in private technology stocks driven by the structural features of the private market. In public markets, anyone can buy shares and anyone can sell shares. You can buy stock as a committed long-term bet or as a tactical trade that you’ll exit if the company misses earnings by a penny. You can sell your stock at any time if your opinion changes, and you don’t even have to own stock to sell it: If you think a company is bad, you can short the stock to bet on its decline. Private markets are different: You often have to buy the stock directly from the company, which often requires not just coming up with the money but also convincing the founders that you are a true believer in their story and will support them through thick and thin. If you change your mind, you can’t just dump your stock on the exchange; you may not be able to sell it at all, or only with the founders’ permission and after finding another true believer to buy it. And if you think a much-hyped startup is an obvious fraud, you can’t bet against it by shorting its stock. You can’t even tweet mean things about it! A strategy of being long good things and short bad things is impossible: You can’t get short the bad things, and even just saying you’d like to short the bad things makes it harder for you to get access to the good things. (“No founder in edtech should ever pitch their company to you again,” one disgraced startup founder told Palmer.) If there is a diversity of opinions—if some people think some things are good and others think other things are good—then all the things will get positive feedback and none of them will get negative feedback and they will all be happy little unicorns until etc. etc. etc. etc. you can write your own crash narrative, or just read what I wrote above about WeWork I guess. I think this is a reasonable reading of Bowles’s article, but in all fairness I should say that it is not a complete description of the ecosystem. I write rude things about startups all the time, it’s fine, I don’t get invited to invest in other startups but then I wouldn’t anyway. It is not a system that is completely closed to negative feedback, even if it is not exactly optimized to make constructive use of that feedback.

Peloton Interactive Inc. is pressing right on with its IPO: The home-fitness startup plans to offer 40 million Class A shares at $26 to $29 each, it said Tuesday in a filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. A listing at the top of that range would value Peloton at about $8.1 billion based on the shares to be outstanding as listed in its filing. The company is planning to start its IPO roadshow Wednesday, with presentations this week in Frankfurt and London, according to a schedule obtained by Bloomberg. That seems to be a retreat from an earlier valuation target of $8 to $10 billion, but it’s still well above the most recent private round last year. Net income is negative and obviously there is dual-class stock. Maybe everything is fine, I dunno.

s.h: Elsewhere in bank errors in your favor
s.t: If a bank just deposits $120,000 in your account by accident, can you spend it? I do not give legal advice around here but, just as it was for Exotix, the answer is apparently no. You call the bank and tell it to come get its money: Robert and Tiffany Williams of Montoursville, Pa., did not call the bank, police say. When a non-hypothetical $120,000 intended for a business was accidentally transferred into their BB&T bank account because of a teller error, the couple splurged on a camper, a Chevy and a racecar, state trooper Aaron Brown told the Williamsport Sun-Gazette. Authorities say they also distributed $15,000 to friends who needed the money. ... The couple now face three felony charges of theft and receiving stolen property. “All I’m going to say is we took some bad legal advice from some people and it probably wasn’t the best thing in the end,” Robert Williams said Monday in court, according to WNEP. Felony charges! Receiving stolen property! Seems a little harsh. Exotix did the same thing with Lehman’s $7 million, and all they had to do was give the money back. The lesson is that, from the perspective of criminal law, it’s better to have more money than less money.

If you are a public company you have to disclose a lot of information about your business so that investors can make informed decisions about whether to buy your stock. This is good for the investors but arguably bad for the business, since your competitors can read your disclosure to understand your business and get better at competing with you. Arguably this gives private companies a competitive advantage over public ones; also, as we have discussed, it arguably gives big companies a competitive advantage over smaller ones, just because the big companies have less fine-grained disclosure so competitors can’t learn anything useful from their securities filings. (Try competing with YouTube by reading its financial disclosure in Alphabet Inc.’s filings.) Here’s a theory that securities disclosure led to the decline of U.S. manufacturing: U.S. manufacturing employment fell by more than 40 percent over the last two decades, from 18 percent of the total U.S. workforce in 1997 to just 10 percent by 2018. Prior work identifies increased import competition from foreign competitors as a primary cause of this decline. Against this backdrop, the economics literature argues that indirect trade costs, such as information frictions, have a stronger effect on import competition than direct costs, such as tariffs and quotas. We explore the effects of a potential source of information frictions in trade that is unrelated to trade policy. Specifically, we find that the information created by and about public firms helps foreign competitors overcome information frictions and compete with U.S. manufacturers. That’s from “ Did Public Firms’ Financial Reporting Affect U.S. Manufacturing?” by Stephen Glaeser and James Omartian; here is the related paper. There seems to be a not particularly energetic push from the Trump administration to reduce public-company disclosure requirements, either as a way to encourage long-termism in public companies or as a way to encourage more companies to go public. Reducing public-company disclosure requirements as a way to fight a trade war with China was a new one to me, but might have some political appeal.

We have talked before about Patrick McKenzie’s explanation of “ How Discount Brokerages Make Money,” to which the short but somewhat counterintuitive answer is “net interest income”: Customers keep cash balances in their brokerage accounts, and the brokers invest that cash and earn interest on it, and they don’t pass much of it on to the customers, and that is basically the entire business model. Stocks, bonds, mutual funds, branch offices, call centers, blah blah blah, it all exists to justify the only pricing page that matters, and all the verbiage on the pricing page is about how much you pay the customer. This is an exaggeration, but not much of one. 57% of Schwab’s revenues are from net interest. The firm could literally give away every other service; discount the mutual fund fees to zero, do away with commissions, etc etc, and they would still be profitable. Naively you might think that what matters for Charles Schwab Corp.’s business would be, like, whether people wanted to do a lot of stock trades, or whether it was good at executing those stock trades for them, or whether it introduced good financial-advising or mutual-fund or robo-investing products, or whether evil high-frequency trading firms were paying it for order flow, or whatever. But no mainly it’s interest rates. And now: Charles Schwab Corp. is cutting about 600 jobs as it deals with the impact of lower interest rates. Chief Executive Walt Bettinger discussed the coming layoffs, which would amount to roughly 3% of the San Francisco brokerage’s staff, in a recent town hall with some employees, according to an attendee. The cuts are part of an effort to rein in expenses as falling interest rates pinch profit at Schwab’s banking arm, said people familiar with the situation. “We initiated a process to review our expense base to ensure we remain well-positioned to serve clients while navigating an increasingly challenging economic environment,” a Schwab spokeswoman said.

It is a little off our usual subjects but I just want to mention that this New York Times Magazine article about U.S. college admissions by Paul Tough is so, so, so good. One thing that I notice in the world is that there are some domains in which it is uncontroversially accepted that tradeoffs exist, and other domains in which it is considered rude and out of bounds to even suggest the possibility of tradeoffs. I feel like most of what I read about college admissions blithely assumes that colleges can be engines of socioeconomic mobility and maintain high admissions standards and fund themselves; the idea that colleges should admit underqualified rich people in order to keep up their revenue just seems unspeakable in polite society, though also it obviously happens. Tough’s article is brutally clear on what the actual considerations are for working admissions professionals. “Everybody wants to have more selectivity and better academic quality and more socioeconomic diversity, and they want more revenue every single year,” his main character, Trinity College admissions director Angel Pérez, says. “Part of my job since arriving at Trinity College has been educating this community about the fact that you can’t have it all at the same time. You’ve got to pick which goals you’re going to pursue.” It’s also clear on how those tradeoffs actually get made: There is a popular and persistent image of college admissions in which diversity-obsessed universities are using affirmative action to deny spaces to academically talented affluent students while admitting low-income students with lower ability in their place. Boeckenstedt says the opposite is closer to the truth. If you’re an enrollment manager, he explains, the easiest category of students for you to admit are below-average students from high-income families. Because their parents can afford tutoring, they are very likely to have decent test scores, which means they won’t hurt your U.S. News ranking. They probably won’t distinguish themselves academically at your college, but they can pay full tuition.

One thing you could do is, you rent some buildings, and then you make them fancier, and then you convince people to rent offices in the buildings from you for more than you pay for them. If this is a good business and you do it well, more money will come in than goes out, and you can use some of the extra money to rent some more buildings and make them fancier, so the business will grow. If it is not a good business, on the other hand, or if you are not good at it, then more money will go out than comes in, and you should stop doing it, because why are you doing a business that loses money. This lemonade-stand sort of financial analysis is oversimplified, of course. Basically every business is going to have more money going out than coming in at first—you have to spend money to rent the buildings and make them fancier before you ever get a tenant—and so you’ll need access to some capital at the beginning. And if this is a good business, you will probably want it to grow rapidly early on so that you can have a head start on being the dominant player in the industry and making a lot of money from it. So you might want to raise a lot of capital early on, so you can rent lots of buildings all at once rather than waiting to make enough money from the first building to rent a second one. You could imagine a range of possible growth paths. At one (quite common) extreme, you start as small as possible and bootstrap growth using only the money you make from doing the business; you are always profitable but you grow very slowly. At the other (purely imaginary) extreme, you start by imagining the total size of the business in the distant future when it has achieved total market dominance around the globe, and you raise enough money on the first day to get there immediately. If you can do that then you will grow very fast and take maximum advantage of the opportunity for your business, but on the other hand, if you’ve never executed the business profitably why would people give you all that money? I mean: They probably will! Modern tech funding markets can get you arbitrarily close to this extreme. Still the “why” seems like a reasonable question. The We Co., the parent company of WeWork, has raised about $12.8 billion from private investors in its nine years of operations. Naively you might think that that much money could pay for renting and sprucing up a lot of buildings, and that WeWork could then find tenants for those buildings and make a lot of money. If your goal was to rapidly scale your building-renting business, $12.8 billion would probably get you a lot of the way there. But not all the way? In fact, WeWork had a net loss of about $1.9 billion in 2018, and of about $904 million in the first half of 2019. “As we continue to pursue rapid growth,” WeWork explains, “we continue to operate in a state where the majority of our locations are non-mature and have not reached stable operating performance.” It could be profitable, but it would rather grow: If we stopped investing in our growth and instead allowed our existing pipeline of locations to mature, we would no longer incur capital investments to build out new spaces or the initial expenses associated with driving member acquisition at new locations. Rather, we expect that each mature location would generate a recurring stream of revenues and contribution margin. We believe that the flexibility to manage our growth by focusing on our existing pipeline of locations and allowing them to mature presents us with an opportunity to manage our profitability profile. And so it is seeking to raise $9 or $10 billion from an initial public offering—$3 or $4 billion in the IPO itself, and another $6 billion in bank loans contingent on the IPO—to keep throwing into that furnace. That does not seem to be going especially well! But another way to look at it is, no, actually, this is great; it presents WeWork with a golden opportunity to manage its profitability profile. Anyway, anyway, anyway: SoftBank, the biggest outside shareholder in WeWork, is urging the lossmaking property group to shelve its hotly anticipated initial public offering after it received a cool reception from investors, according to people briefed on the discussions. ... The lack of more than $9bn in new capital could force a dramatic change in the We Company’s corporate strategy, including its aggressive expansion that has seen it open 528 locations in more than 110 cities. The company has lost more than $4bn since 2016, burning through capital even as its revenues have doubled each year over that period. WeWork said in its IPO filing that it could slow its expansion dramatically if it needed to become profitable. And here is Bloomberg News on SoftBank’s efforts to postpone the IPO. On the other hand, “the WeWork initial public offering is full speed ahead, sources familiar with the matter tell CNBC’s David Faber.” One possibility here is that SoftBank Group Corp., its affiliated Vision Fund and WeWork’s other private investors own stakes in a high-quality business with fundamentally sound unit economics. Given the attractive market opportunity, they would like it to raise another giant slug of money to continue its rapid growth. But public investors have started to doubt the quality of its business, and are not willing to fund its growth at a price reflecting its strong fundamentals. So WeWork can step back, remain private, slow its growth, flip to profitability and just harvest the rich rewards of renting out office space for more than its costs. Then, after it demonstrates how profitable the underlying business is, maybe public investors will start clamoring to get in to fund more growth. Or maybe they won’t, and SoftBank et al. will just own stakes in a lucrative private business that sends them fat dividends every year from all the money it is making. There are other possibilities! The investors who doubt WeWork’s underlying business model have read that paragraph I quoted above, the one about how WeWork can turn on the profits at any time. They have doubts anyway. One nice thing about postponing the IPO is that you get to find out. Missing out on the $10 billion of public money would slow down WeWork’s growth plans, but if WeWork is right then there is just a dial that it can turn between “Growth” and “Profit,” and dialing down the growth automatically dials up the profits. If you are confident that you possess this dial and that it works this way, then delaying the IPO is a no-brainer: Sure you delay your positive-expected-value growth, but you get to keep ownership of a good lucrative business rather than selling it too cheap. On the other hand, if the dial turns out not to work, then you’ll end up wishing you’d sold it cheap. Elsewhere, Aswath Damodaran makes an effort to value WeWork, and comes up with about $13.75 billion, which is probably not a number that SoftBank wants to hear. And WeWork “plans to rely on junk bonds for funding for the foreseeable future,” and “could also explore whole-business securitizations”; I look forward to reading that prospectus. And: “WeWork Bonds Drop Below Par for First Time Since IPO Filing.” And at Stratechery, Ben Thompson considers the bigger picture: That leads to a much more pressing question: what if the Vision Fund turns out to be a failure? The WeWork investment is not looking great, and the Fund is underwater on Uber. Granted, these are only two prominent examples out of many investments, but they are emblematic of the type of investments the Vision Fund has spent the most money on: high capital burning companies mostly operating at the digital/physical divide, including Didi, Grab, Coupang, OneWeb, etc. If the entire category ends up not being tech companies, at least as far as returns to capital are concerned, not only will the profitability of the Vision Fund be under significant pressure but so will the viability of funds of that size going forward. It is not particularly helpful to have an overwhelming capital advantage if that capital is inevitably set on fire by companies able to put off profitability questions until it’s too late. And here is Fred Wilson on “ Why Positive Cashflow Matters”: “If you have positive cashflow, you can control the timing and terms of your capital raises. … Positive cash flow puts you on control versus the capital markets.”

Ahhh, ahhh, ahhh, AHHHHHHHH: This judgment relates to a dispute as to the terms of a sale (the "Trade") of Peruvian Government Global Depository Notes (each referred to as a "GDN"). The Trade was entered into in early 2014 by the Claimant, Lehman Brothers International (Europe) ("LBIE") as vendor and the Defendant, Exotix Partners LLP ("Exotix") as purchaser. … Ordinarily, it might be thought that, once settled, the subject matter of the Trade should not be in doubt. But in this case it is the subject of dispute. It seems plain that in settling the trade LBIE appears to have materially misunderstood what it was delivering, whilst Exotix had no expectation of receiving assets of such a value as in fact were thus delivered to and received by it. LBIE thought that its holding of GDNs amounted to 'scraps' having a value of some $7,000; Exotix did not expect more and paid some $7,438. In fact, LBIE's holding had a true aggregate value of over $7 million; and it delivered all its holding to Exotix, which, after some internal hesitation, decided to sell on the entirety and pocket a windfall. AHHHHHHHH! What happened here is that the estate of Lehman Brothers was selling off some random scraps of bonds, including 22,955 Peruvian government GDNs. Exotix wanted to buy some different bonds and, to get that trade done, also agreed to take the GDNs off of Lehman’s hands. Each GDN had a face value of 1,000 Peruvian soles (about $354 at the time), but it seems that neither the Lehman trader charged with unloading them, nor the Exotix trader who agreed to buy them, knew that. All they knew was that the bonds traded for 91.5 cents on the dollar, and that on their screens they saw something like “22,955 Peru GDNs.” There is a perennial, extremely low-grade yet haunting problem in finance, which is this: If you look at a screen and see “22,955 Peru GDNs,” does that mean (1) 22,955 soles worth of GDNs or (2) 22,955 GDNs each with a face value of 1,000 soles? (This is not a Peruvian problem, and you might similarly wonder if “22,955 Apple bonds” means $22,955 worth of bonds or 22,955 bonds worth $23 million.) There is no absolutely reliable universal convention, though context generally clears it up. For one thing, Peruvian GDNs seem to come in 1,000-sol units (just as many dollar bonds come in $1,000 units), so you couldn’t actually buy 22,955 soles’ worth of GDNs if you tried. So there would have been no confusion if either trader knew anything about Peruvian GDNs, which they apparently didn’t. For another thing … people usually just don’t have three orders of magnitude of uncertainty about the size of their trades? Like if someone you regularly trade with called you up and offered you “ten thousand bonds,” or “ten million bonds,” you’d be the sort of person who regularly traded $10,000, or $10 million, or $10 billion worth of bonds with them, so you’d just instinctively understand if “bonds” there meant “dollars’ worth of bonds” or “thousand-dollar increments of bonds.” But this trade was a weird scrap that neither side was paying attention to; they had no practice dealing in Peruvian GDNs, and the context was lost. And so somehow both traders just assumed without specifying that 22,955 GDNs meant 22,955 soles’ worth of GDNs rather than 23 million worth. And so Lehman agreed to sell them, and Exotix agreed to buy them, at a price of 91.5 cents on the dollar, or about $7,438 for the lot (if you thought the lot was 22,955 soles’ worth, as they did). And Exotix wired Lehman the $7,438 (plus a little bit of accrued interest), and Lehman sent Exotix $7.4 million worth of bonds. And then Exotix figured it out and, “after some internal hesitation,” decided they’d keep them. I paused at this point to spend some happy minutes in contemplation of that internal hesitation, and almost wrote you a little imagined dialogue to capture Exotix’s reaction to finding an extra $7.4 million of free bonds and its debate about whether to give them back. But then I read further in the court judgment, and that hesitation is actually described in some detail and better than I could have imagined: It appears that Exotix did not appreciate any discrepancy until it received on 24 February 2014 (some 3 weeks after the Settlement Date) a coupon payment on the GDNs in the sum of US$276,321.25, vastly exceeding that purchase price for the GDNs themselves. Mr Damien Marron ("Mr Marron", an associate in Exotix's Dubai office, Middle Office, Trade Support) immediately queried this receipt with Standard Chartered (Exotix's depositary bank) (see email of 25 February 2014 timed at 3:16pm); and he chased the issue by email the following morning, stating: " I think there has been an error on this payment ". … Following several email exchanges (both internally and with Standard Chartered), Exotix eventually realised that the notional value of the GDNs it had received on the Settlement Date was S/22,955,000, and not, as in Exotix's internal records, S/22,955. Mr Hutton [the Exotix trader who bought the bonds in the first place] then emailed Mr David Baskerville (Exotix's Chief Operating Officer at that time), who then undertook some form of internal investigation into the matter. Around this time, in an internal Exotix email regarding the internal investigation, Mr Baskerville warned the recipients (Mr Elliott and Mr Longden) " not to speak to ANYONE about it ". Mr Hutton says that Mr Baskerville did not share with him the results of this internal investigation and was told that " the decision as to what to do about the GDNs was one that was above my pay grade " and that he thereafter had no further involvement in the matter. Ultimately the decision was taken by Exotix at board level that Exotix would keep the GDNs. ... About a year later, on 7 April 2015, Exotix (acting by a Mr Tweedley, in the New York office) on-sold the S/22,955,000 GDNs which LBIE had delivered to it to a third party for US$7,757,921.01 (at a price of 103.581100%), thereby making a windfall of over $8.5m (when added to the coupon payments referred to in the previous paragraph). Lehman eventually figured this out, though only after Exotix had sold the bonds. It sued in an English court, and yesterday Exotix won; I have been quoting from the judgment. It’s … fine? The legal analysis is long and boring but there is a rough finders-keepers logic to it; if you think your bonds are worth 32 cents, and sell them for 32 cents, and they’re actually worth $324, that is kind of on you. Exotix’s lawyer “suggested the analogy of the sale of a picture, which the seller had had for a number of years without focusing on it having been painted by Leonardo da Vinci, and thus, having overlooked its true nature and value, sold it for a fraction of its true worth.”

A basic way to do market manipulation is, you own some stock and you want to sell it, so you do some trades with your friends at high prices, so bystanders thinks the stock trades at a high price, and then you sell the stock to someone else at a high price. This works (sometimes, imperfectly) because practically speaking the main input into most people’s valuation models is the price. If a stock trades at $10, people tend to think it’s worth $10, so you can probably sell it to them for $10. Another basic way to do securities fraud is, you own a company and you want to sell some stock, so you put out fake financial statements that say that your company made a lot of money last quarter and fake announcements that it will make even more money next quarter, and then you sell stock to people who believe you. This works (sometimes, imperfectly) because things like profits and growth are also important inputs into many people’s valuation models. If a company makes money, people tend to think its stock is valuable, that sort of thing. This is all pretty basic stuff and you can only go so far with it. These things—manipulative trading, fake accounting—are pretty closely scrutinized by a lot of regulators. Even beyond that, though, markets just have some (imperfect) self-correcting mechanisms to avoid getting taken in by this sort of thing. I can pump up the price of some thinly traded stock by trading it with my buddies, but I can’t do that very effectively with Apple Inc. stock, because a whole lot of other unrelated people trade it for unrelated reasons and I am just not going to move the price that much. I can put out fake accounts audited by a fly-by-night auditor for some weird penny stock, but if I’m doing accounting fraud at a big company I will have to get my accounts past a real auditor and a bunch of research analysts who closely follow the stock and who will ask hard questions if the Magic Beans Division suddenly starts producing huge profits. The most efficient things to manipulate are the things that everyone pays attention to—the stock price, the financial statements—but they’re also hard to manipulate precisely because everyone pays attention to them. But we now live in a world in which algorithmic traders seek an edge by processing lots of data beyond just historical prices and accounting data. The algos are reading the tweets. They are considering sentiment. They are getting data from satellites and credit-card processors and location-tracking apps. There is a whole world of alternative data out there, and it feeds into algorithms that make trading decisions. What if you manipulated that ? Here’s a fun story from Billy Bambrough at Forbes: It appears Google searches for bitcoin and BTC, the name used by traders for the bitcoin digital token, could be being manipulated–-possibly in order to move the bitcoin price. This week there has been a massive leap in Google searches for "BTC," which usually is lower than searches for "bitcoin"–with search volume for "BTC" around the world now far higher than it was even at the top of bitcoin's epic 2017 bull run. … "Somebody's trying to game the trading algorithms," said Glen Goodman, trading veteran and author of bitcoin investment book, The Crypto Trader, who explained how this could be used to move bitcoin prices on the market. "There are algorithms programmed to look at Google Trends data and try to find correlations between numbers of searches for the word 'BTC' and the movements in the bitcoin price." "If they detect patterns, it may be profitable to trade off that data. This hacker may be buying some BTC, then sending a ton of 'BTC' search queries to Google, the algos see search numbers have risen and are triggered to buy a lot of BTC which pushes the price up, and the hacker then sells their BTC at a profit. Easy money!" This is neither legal nor investing advice, but if you run a hedge fund with a lot of exposure to retailers, you might consider going out and painting a bunch of car-shaped splotches in a bunch of parking lots to trick the satellites into thinking business is better than it is. Manipulating trading prices and accounting numbers is familiar territory and has familiar problems; manipulating alternative data is a whole new world of dubiously legal opportunity. I would really like to see a regulator bring a manipulation case against someone for Googling “BTC” a lot! It doesn’t exactly seem like the sort of thing that is illegal? But who knows. Elsewhere: Analysts at JPMorgan Chase & Co. have created an index to quantify what they say are the growing effects on U.S. bond yields. Citigroup Inc.’s foreign exchange team, meanwhile, report that these micro-blogging missives are also becoming “increasingly relevant” to foreign-exchange moves. JPMorgan’s “Volfefe Index,” named after Trump’s mysterious covfefe tweet from May 2017, suggests that the president’s electronic musings are having a statistically significant impact on Treasury yields. The number of market-moving Trump tweets has ballooned in the past month, with those including words such as “China,” “billion,” “products,” “Democrats” and “great” most likely to affect prices, the analysts found. Buy Fox News ads to manipulate the Volfefe Index! The world is bizarre.

I used to be a capital markets banker, and while I do not think anyone would have said I was particularly talented at it, I at least had a grasp of the basics. For instance, if you had asked me, early in 2019, to pitch WeWork Cos. on an initial public offering, I am not sure that I would have won the mandate, but I am confident that I could have met the minimum standards. Those minimum standards are: I would have rented space in a WeWork office building for myself and my team for a few weeks before the pitch, and then in the pitch meeting I would say things like “we made this deck at a WeWork, it was the best working experience of our lives and we’re never going back to our regular offices,” and make a lot of knowing references to, like, the brand of coffee they have there or whatever; and I would confidently tell them that they could go public at significantly above their last private valuation of $47 billion. That last part is not hard! It’s just, when you get to the part where they say “what do you think our valuation will be,” you have to say a number like “$65 billion.” It is not like saying “$65 billion” is much more taxing on your vocal cords or facial muscles than, I don’t know, “$20 billion.” Now sure sure sure it might tax your financial-modeling skills, or your ability to suspend disbelief, to tell WeWork that it can go public at a $65 billion valuation at the same time its private shareholders are selling into a SoftBank Group Corp. tender offer at $20 billion. But it is a problem with a right answer. If you are an investor trying to decide whether to buy WeWork stock and at what price, you sort of start from a blank slate: You have to come up with your most accurate possible set of assumptions about WeWork’s future growth and margins, and then use those assumptions to model the company and come up with a valuation; your valuation will depend on the assumptions, and the assumptions will always be uncertain. But if you are a capital markets banker trying to get WeWork to go public, you know the right valuation , more or less—it’s “a substantial but not comical premium to the last private round,” or about $65 billion—and all you have to do is adjust the assumptions to get to that valuation. It’s a straightforward algebra problem, not a deep valuation problem. Obviously the next step is hard: If WeWork hires you to do an IPO at a $65 billion valuation, you would like, ideally, to get investors to buy WeWork stock in the IPO at a $65 billion valuation. Or $75 billion even, no one will complain about that. In a pinch, $55 billion will do. Twenty billion will be a problem! Still, in the grand scheme of investment banking, it’s a nice problem to have. First you get the mandate, then you worry about executing it. If you say “$20 billion” in the pitch meeting, you are definitely not getting the mandate. If WeWork then goes public at $20 billion, you have the quiet satisfaction of knowing that you were right, but your competitor who said “$65 billion” has millions of dollars of IPO fees. They get paid even if it goes poorly. Anyway Goldman Sachs pitched WeWork on an IPO early this year, and correctly said “$65 billion,” and got the mandate, and now in a sense probably regrets the $65 billion thing (the backtracking must be awkward!) but in another, more economically relevant sense is probably fine with it. From Bloomberg News on Friday: The New York-based venture, yet to turn a profit in its nine-year existence, is said to be considering a market debut at a valuation of $20 billion to $30 billion, Bloomberg News reported earlier this week. That’s just a fraction of the $65 billion valuation that Goldman Sachs, one of its lead bankers on the deal, told people close to WeWork that it could rise to after the listing, one of the people said. Goldman Sachs made that prediction at a meeting where it was invited to pitch for a role on the future listing, according to another person with knowledge of the matter. SoftBank Vice Chairman Ron Fisher and Mark Schwartz, a WeWork director representing the Japanese conglomerate, arranged the meeting, held sometime in the first quarter, the people said. At the time, $65 billion seemed in the ballpark, at least based on the prevailing market mood. In January, SoftBank had injected more financing into the company at a valuation of $47 billion. Disclosure, I used to work at Goldman, though I am not giving away any state secrets when I tell you that optimism in IPO pitches is rewarded. I don’t know if they made their pitchbooks at a WeWork though. Anyway they’re “one of its lead bankers on the deal,” and I doubt that their optimism is going to cost them that spot now. On the other hand, you don’t get paid for leading an IPO if there’s no IPO. And … uh … maybe? From the Wall Street Journal yesterday: WeWork’s parent is eyeing a valuation for its initial public offering that could fall below $20 billion as some existing investors push the workspace company to shelve the planned offering, people familiar with the matter said. Despite plans to begin a roadshow to market the shares to new investors as early as Monday, We Co. and its underwriters are planning to hold meetings this week among themselves and with investors to figure out what changes may be needed to help garner enough demand for an IPO, the people said. … The startup faces skepticism among potential public investors over its governance, business model and ability to turn a profit while continuing to grow. The latest potential cut comes at a time when IPO demand for companies with a path to profitability is surging and would be particularly painful for investors who have given or committed over $10 billion to the company since it was founded in 2010. ... Should We yank or postpone the IPO, it stands to miss out on nearly $10 billion needed to fund its ambitious but money-losing global-growth plans. The company was planning to raise $3 billion to $4 billion in the IPO and up to $6 billion in debt that is contingent on the IPO raising at least $3 billion. A few weeks ago—after WeWork filed its first, imperious draft prospectus for its IPO, but before it filed its second and more chastened version— I said that it “is going public, sure,” but that founder Adam Neumann “does not need your money.” WeWork, after all, had a spigot of money from SoftBank and from banks eager to win its business by lending. (Neumann had his own spigots of money from loans, stock sales, etc.) I am feeling less good about that claim these days. WeWork’s IPO was going to raise $10 billion, partly in IPO proceeds but mostly in bank loans contingent on a successful IPO. And SoftBank is still, uh, there, but it is not obvious that SoftBank will be happy about putting in billions more dollars specifically because WeWork’s IPO isn’t going great. Also: at what valuation? If WeWork pulls an IPO because it is struggling to get a $20 billion valuation, presumably SoftBank isn’t going to invest more at $47 billion. WeWork’s existing investors don’t seem to love the idea of raising billions of dollars at a down-round valuation, for understandable reasons: They took a risk on a fast-growing company and don’t want to be diluted by selling to skeptical public investors.[1] But WeWork, more than most pre-IPO companies, kind of tied itself to actually doing the IPO; it’s hard for a fast-growing money-burning company to walk away from $10 billon, and it won’t be easy to renegotiate those contingent-on-successful-IPO loans if the IPO doesn’t work out. What will happen? Oh I don’t know, probably something weird. But it is worth quietly noting that there is a middle ground here. Pulling the IPO and giving up $10 billion is bad for the company; doing the IPO at a sub-$20-billion valuation is dilutive for existing investors. But there is, at least in theory, another lever to pull. Part of why WeWork is facing pushback on valuation is for straightforward business-model-y reasons: Investors are worried about profitability and unit economics and competition and other issues that go to the heart of what WeWork does. But part of why WeWork is facing pushback is that it is the absolute limit case of unicorn craziness, a company that is entirely controlled by a quirky and charismatic founder who has cashed out hundreds of millions of dollars pre-IPO while retaining voting control of the company for his lifetime and beyond, employing his family members, borrowing money from the company, owning some of the buildings that it rents, starting a separate fund to own more of the buildings, starting weird side businesses like an elementary school, renaming the company “We” and charging it $5.9 million for the name, structuring it in an unusual multi-level way in which he is a co-owner of the business alongside the public-company parent, and going around saying that WeWork is “ a state of consciousness” rather than a real estate company. WeWork has already walked back some of this stuff: After everyone complained, it canceled the $5.9 million payment to Neumann for the company name. You could imagine—I wouldn’t bet on it, but you could just about imagine—things going further: WeWork wants to go public, it does not want a low valuation, its weirdo sparkly unicorn governance is contributing to a low valuation, so maybe it could give up the weirdo governance? If investors want, say, single-class stock without absolute power concentrated indefinitely in the founder, maybe they’d be willing to pay up for it, and maybe WeWork would give it to them? I have long been a skeptic of this idea, just because investors have long been quite happy to pay up for unicorn IPOs even while complaining bitterly about their governance problems. A boom is no time to push back on terms. And I’m still not sure that governance is worth all that much, economically; I’m not sure that investors would pay a lot more for a one-share-one-vote WeWork than they would for the actual weird WeWork. But I do think that there’s a good case to be made that WeWork’s governance is bad in an economically meaningful way for shareholders. And if the IPO window is closing and investors are getting less receptive to unicorn excesses, and if some unicorns feel the need to go public anyway, maybe the solution is to cut back on some of the excesses.

Well, I just got through saying that there’s not really any reward for being pessimistic and right about valuation when you are pitching an IPO. Your optimistic competitors will get the mandate, and then spend some time walking the company back, and ultimately the IPO will price below their expectations and they’ll be a little embarrassed and you will say “I told you so,” but they will get the fees and league-table credit and you will not. Your job is to do deals, and you’d rather lead a hairy disappointing deal than miss out on principle. On the other hand it is a repeat game and there are occasionally penalties for getting it wrong: J.P. Morgan Chase is close to winning the lead advisory role for the initial public offering of Saudi Aramco, the world’s most profitable corporation, edging out rivals for the plum assignment, according to people with knowledge of the situation. A final decision is expected next week and could still change, the people said. Morgan Stanley, which had been jockeying with J.P. Morgan for top billing on the deal, was hurt by its work leading the Uber IPO, according to these people. Saudi officials, who are large owners of Uber through the country’s sovereign wealth fund, were displeased with Morgan Stanley after its bankers misjudged demand for the ride-sharing giant’s stock in May. The shares tumbled 18% in the first two days of trading and are still well below the IPO price of $45. To be fair Uber Technologies Inc. was the largest U.S. IPO of the year so far and the highest-profile IPO of the whole unicorn boom, and Morgan Stanley got about $40 million in fees plus some amount of stabilization trading profits out of it, so ex ante it made sense for them to pursue the deal even at the risk of it being embarrassing. On the other hand Aramco, if it happens, will certainly be the largest IPO anywhere ever, and it will be rough for Morgan Stanley if winning the biggest IPO prize of the unicorn era loses it the biggest IPO prize of all time. Elsewhere in the Aramco IPO: Saudi Arabia held discussions with some of the kingdom’s wealthiest families about becoming anchor investors in Aramco’s mammoth stake sale, according to five people with knowledge of the talks. Saudi officials made initial contact with some top business families on behalf of the oil giant, the people said, asking not to be identified because the information is private. Aramco may hold more formal meetings as early as next week after banks have been hired for the sale, three of the people said.

I don’t know man; here is an exhausting story about how he’s suing a guy because his fraudulent hedge fund lost money for the guy’s father and the guy pressured him into promising to give it back? Like, to be clear, Shkreli is suing the guy for fraud. Really: In that suit Shkreli claims that George Yaffe “lost” his money because of poor performance of Shkreli’s fund, and that Shkreli “had no legal obligations to pay any money to George Yaffe.” Shkreli’s suit, which alleges fraud, claims that Lee Yaffe falsely advised Shkreli that making the $250,000 promissory note was the “right thing” to do and that Shkreli should “man up.” The suit says the note is “invalid as a matter of New York law because it was given for no consideration and was not given as payment of an antecedent obligation or debt.” “The promissory note also included usurious compound interest that is invalid under New York law,” the suit said. “As a result of Lee Yaffe’s fraud, Mr. Shkreli has a $420,000 judgement against him,” the suit said. Shkreli is asking for monetary damages “to be determined at trial.” This seems like a combination of (1) having too much time on his hands, (2) really enjoying a good confrontation, and (3) having absolutely Yiddish-proverb levels of chutzpah. Like what happened here is: Shkreli set up a hedge fund. The hedge fund lost all of its investors’ money, Shkreli lied about it, and he eventually went to prison—where he is now—for fraud. The son of one of the investors asked Shkreli to give his father his money back because it was the “right thing” to do. Shkreli, in lieu of giving the father his money back, gave him a promissory note for more than twice the amount of the investment, with a high interest rate. That’s … that’s just fraud? Like, that’s just the fraud that Shkreli did? It’s a very standard fraud: You take people’s money, you don’t give it back, but you promise to give them a lot more money later! You can’t sue them , after you go to prison for fraud, saying that they defrauded you by asking you for their money back and that you promised to give it to them! Honestly, what on earth. To be fair, the endlessly weird thing about Shkreli’s story is that he eventually did make a lot of money with his pharmaceutical company Retrophin, and he used some of it to pay off the disgruntled investors in his earlier hedge funds. Including Lee Yaffe! Lee Yaffe testified at Shkreli’s criminal trial that Shkreli proposed to pay him off for his father’s investment in the hedge fund known as Elea by giving Lee Yaffe a $200,000 consulting deal with Retrophin and 15,000 shares in Retrophin stock. Lee Yaffe testified that the agreement, for “research on cluster headaches,” was a sham. He signed a non-prosecution agreement with authorities and also agreed to pay back $355,000, which represents his cash payments under the consulting deal, the Retrophin shares he received and the investment returns on those shares. He gave him the promissory note and the consulting deal? Yeah I mean I guess I can see how he feels a little aggrieved here. Elsewhere in well-known financial criminals serving long sentences in federal prison, Raj Rajaratnam got out recently.

[1] It is not totally clear, but none of WeWork’s early investors seem to have “ratchet” provisions that would protect them from dilution by giving them more shares if WeWork raises money in the IPO at a lower price. The IPO prospectus says that all the existing investors’ preferred shares will convert into common stock at their fixed conversion prices—as high as $110 per share for SoftBank’s Series G-1 preferred—without any adjustment if the IPO price is lower than the conversion price; see page F-48 and, e.g., the listing of SoftBank’s as-converted holdings on page 188, which shows a 1-for-1 conversion of preferred into common stock. On the other hand there are anti-dilution protections for the preferred stock, though they seem to apply only to private fundraisings; see page F-49: “The conversion ratio for the Senior Preferred Stock is adjusted on a broad weighted-average basis in the event of an issuance (or deemed issuance) below the applicable Senior Preferred Stock price, as adjusted.” (Though Will Gornall and Ilya Strebulaev’s well-known study of unicorn financial terms found no ratchets in WeWork’s documents; see the table on page 53.)

I have argued before that the We Co., formerly WeWork Co., is a clever financial engineering company that has managed to tell an appealing fast-growing-tech-company story to equity investors while also telling an appealing stable-real-estate-company story to lenders, but I must say that I am stumped by this: WeWork co-founder Adam Neumann has a message for anyone skittish about the company’s pending IPO: Wells Fargo backs his business. “If Wells Fargo, the largest lender in this country, can get comfortable with this, then everybody should,” Neumann said Wednesday, referring to a $6 billion WeWork credit facility the bank is participating in. “I’m most proud of Wells Fargo coming in. Who’s here from Wells Fargo? Thank you, thank you,” Neuman said at a private education session for analysts in New York, according to a person with direct knowledge of the matter. Uh, no, first of all, that is not the way it works: Equity investors and lenders want different things; Wells Fargo just wants to get its money back, while the people buying the IPO will want a story about explosive growth and expanding margins. But second, Wells Fargo didn’t exactly get comfortable with WeWork: “Under the terms of the financing, banks will have to make good on their commitments only if the initial public offering raises at least $3 billion.” The banks’ comfort is conditional on the equity investors getting comfortable. You can’t tell the equity investors “you should be comfortable with this offering because Wells Fargo is comfortable with it conditional on you being comfortable with it.” Someone has to get unconditionally comfortable! At this point it feels kind of mean to dunk on WeWork? When it first filed papers for its IPO, people made fun of its hubris and conflicts of interest; now that it has filed revised papers and previewed its price range, people are making fun of its quick retreat into humility. The company raised money from SoftBank Group Corp. at a $47 billion valuation earlier this year, but now the price talk involves a $20 billion to $30 billion valuation. Everyone is piling on: “At least two analysts on Thursday said a discounted IPO valuation of $20 billion to $30 billion is still too ambitious.” And: “I’ve heard no bullish views at all,” said Rett Wallace, chief executive of Triton Research, which analyzes pre-IPO companies for investors. “There were Uber bulls, there were Lyft bulls, there were Snap bulls.” He added that “WeWork is exhausting people’s cynicism.” Ouch! To be fair, at the same time WeWork was raising money from SoftBank at a $47 billion valuation, other private investors were selling their WeWork shares to SoftBank at about a $20 billion valuation, which is also about the level where WeWork had raised its previous funding round.[1] The obvious interpretation is that WeWork is a company that has consistently been worth about $20 billion in the private market, with willing buyers and sellers at that price; only SoftBank has considered it worth $47 billion. And now WeWork is (probably!?) going public, and investors seem to think it’s worth about $20 billion or so, which is consistent with every other data point about WeWork’s valuation except one. And so: Adam Neumann, We’s co-founder and chief executive, flew to Tokyo last week to meet one of the company’s biggest investors, SoftBank Group Chief Executive Masayoshi Son, and members of his team, the people said. There, they discussed the possibility of an additional infusion of capital, multiple people briefed on the meeting said. Among the possibilities they discussed was SoftBank serving as an anchor investor in the IPO by buying a significant portion of the roughly $3 billion to $4 billion the company is expected to raise. They also discussed whether SoftBank might invest a chunk of money that would allow We to delay its IPO until 2020, people familiar with the conversations said. Look, if SoftBank thinks WeWork is worth $47 billion, and everyone else on earth thinks it is worth $20 billion tops, then you do not have to be a genius of financial engineering to understand that WeWork should keep going back to SoftBank for more money. SoftBank has put in a ton of money already, and the investment is controversial at SoftBank and its affiliated Vision Fund, and eventually they are going to want an exit, or at least some external validation. And maybe “eventually” is now; the IPO is the traditional time for private investors to get their exit and their price validation. But it doesn’t hurt to go to Tokyo and ask. By the way, the traditional function of an anchor investor in an IPO is to (1) take down a big chunk of the stock so the banks don’t have to sell as much to skeptical outside investors and (2) provide a sort of aura of confidence to reassure those skeptical outside investors: This big famous investor is taking a huge chunk of the stock, so surely you can take a risk on a smaller chunk. Does having SoftBank as an anchor investor … work … here? Like if you learned that SoftBank had a billion-dollar order in the book at a $25 billion valuation, wouldn’t that make you lower your price? We have spent a long time around here talking about the theme of “people are worried about unicorns.” The worry was that private-market valuations had gotten stretched, that private investors—not so much venture capitalists but nontraditional private investors like SoftBank—were paying up so much for big fast-growing tech companies that they had created a private-tech bubble, and that it would all end in tears when those companies rushed to go public and public investors refused to validate their enormous validations. That … uh … that happened , didn’t it? Uber Technologies Inc., the biggest and most famous of the unicorns, had a “down round” IPO (pricing below its last private valuation) in May, and is currently trading below its IPO price. Lyft Inc. rushed to go public before Uber, got a pretty good price, fell immediately, and is now trading below both its IPO price and its last private valuation. Some other high-profile unicorns that have gone public recently—Dropbox, Slack, Snap, Pinterest—have either been down rounds or struggled after their IPOs. And the worry that the IPO window for unicorns might close, that a few rough deals by big unicorns would ruin the market for the rest of them, also might be true, and now WeWork has considered delaying its IPO. And it considered delaying its IPO specifically by going back to SoftBank for more money, specifically because SoftBank will pay more for unicorn shares than the public market will. When people worried about unicorns, what they worried about was that SoftBank was paying so much for stakes in private tech companies that they would not be able to go public at a price it could stomach, and that they’d end up stuck in a weird limbo on the outskirts of the Enchanted Forest of the Unicorns. And now here we are.

s.h: Elsewhere on the outskirts of the Enchanted Forest
s.t: I mean, for instance: Palantir Technologies Inc. is in talks to raise significant funding from private investors, a move that could indefinitely delay one of Silicon Valley’s most hotly anticipated initial public offerings, according to people familiar with the company. The secretive data mining company approached Singapore’s Temasek Holdings Pte, SoftBank Group Corp. and other investors outside the U.S., according to people with knowledge of the situation, all of whom asked not to be identified discussing private information. Talks are ongoing and no deal has been reached. Private markets are where the money is! And where the valuations are high! And why wouldn’t you call SoftBank? Honestly it is a little satisfying when a popular worry works out so neatly. I am generally skeptical of popular worries, on efficient-markets grounds: If everyone is worried that something is overvalued, then that should be reflected in the price, and if people are going on television saying that it’s overvalued while it remains highly valued, that just means that the people with expertise and money on the line disagree with the people on the television. But efficient-market arguments rely on efficient markets, and the unicorn worriers made a decent case that the structure of the unicorn market made it inefficient: Private tech unicorns raised money only when the terms were good, and only from their strongest enthusiasts; it was hard for fed-up investors to dump their shares, and generally impossible for outright skeptics to make short bets against the unicorns. The unicorns lived in an Enchanted Forest where everyone loved them, but the real world would not be so kind. By the way here’s kind of a weird op-ed from Palantir CEO Adam Karp about how tech companies should be like the Marines and not question government orders!

The basic situation with Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, the government-sponsored enterprises that guarantee mortgages in the U.S., is that they were taken over by the government 11 years ago, they have been an arm of the Treasury ever since, everyone expresses deep dissatisfaction with this situation, there are frequent proposals—from interested investors, members of Congress, outside commentators, regulators—to return them to private hands, and nothing ever happens. And I keep blithely saying “actually the status quo is pretty good and nothing is going to happen anytime soon,” and I keep being right. So here we are again. The U.S. Department of the Treasury yesterday released its “ Housing Reform Plan,” a plan for returning Fannie and Freddie to private hands and getting the government out of the business of running them. The plan strikes me as thoughtful, reasonable, middle-of-the-road, realistic. The general vibe is more “Treasury Department” than “Trump administration,” though there are one or two weird political digressions about things like punishing New York and Oregon for having rent control.[2] Also though it probably isn’t going to do much. The basic idea is that Fannie and Freddie would be recapitalized and returned to private hands, and other mortgage-guarantee businesses would be encouraged to compete with them. Those guarantors (Fannie and Freddie and their new competitors) would have capital and risk-management requirements and be regulated by the Federal Housing Finance Agency. Private capital would have to take a substantial first-loss risk on the mortgages they guaranteed, but they’d all be able to pay the government a fairly priced fee for a backstop guarantee. Most proposals for what to do about Fannie and Freddie say similar things; the popular mainstream approach is to mostly re-privatize the mortgage market while keeping a government backstop in case of emergency. But proposals like that have been kicking around for a decade, and Treasury’s does not really add any detail or sense of urgency. So I wrote “the basic idea is that Fannie and Freddie would be recapitalized and returned to private hands,” but the specifics of that are hugely controversial: Would the re-privatized entities be returned to their old owners, who have been suing the government for years, or would the old claims be wiped out and the GSEs raise new capital? How much capital would they have to raise? How much of their earnings will they have to pay to the Treasury during the transition, and how much can they keep themselves to raise capital? Here is the Treasury’s recommendation for recapitalizing the GSEs: Each of these options poses a host of complex financial and legal considerations that will merit careful consideration as Treasury and FHFA continue their effort, already underway, to identify and assess these and other strategic options. Treasury recommends: Treasury and FHFA should develop a recapitalization plan for each GSE after identifying and assessing the full range of strategic options. Yeah they probably should! This is not the plan; this is the recommendation that someone should come up with a plan. It does seem like the Treasury will stop Fannie and Freddie’s “net worth sweep,” allowing them to build up capital rather than returning all their profits to the Treasury. (“Through June 30, 2019, the GSEs have paid a total of $301.0 billion in dividends to Treasury,” says the report, a nice return on the $187.5 billion that Treasury originally invested.) But exactly what the profit split will be and who will end up owning their capital is still unclear. Also many of the proposals in the plan are for Congress to take some action, and there does not seem to be a ton of political will for that right now. The overall tone of the report is very much “don’t expect anything much to happen with the GSEs anytime soon.” Other than that it’s fine though. Treasury is—rightly, I think—fond of the GSEs’ “credit-risk transfer” programs, in which they package and sell some of the credit risk of the mortgages they guarantee to private investors. “As a result of these and other efforts by FHFA, the conservatorships have in some respects reduced the risk to taxpayers, increased the role of private capital, and enhanced the secondary market infrastructure,” says the report.[3] If your goal is to bring back private capital to the business of guaranteeing mortgages, one way to do it is to recapitalize Fannie and Freddie as entities, raise a lot of money from shareholders, and put those shareholders on the hook for mortgage defaults. But another perfectly sensible way to do it is to take the default risk, package it up, and sell it to private investors who will be on the hook for the defaults. The current status of the GSEs means that the first approach is perpetually in the future, but the second approach is totally possible and they’re doing it now. Also, Treasury is very fond of private-label mortgage securitization. For instance, Treasury is offended that Fannie and Freddie’s credit-risk transfer programs are blessed by regulators, while the equivalent activity by banks—selling derivatives that transfer the credit risk of their mortgages to other investors—is treated with skepticism: The capital treatment of securitizations and other similar transfers of mortgage credit risk to third parties is another potentially unwarranted gap between the regulatory capital requirements of banking organizations and the GSEs that merits scrutiny by FHFA and the federal banking regulators. While the GSEs’ CRT provide meaningful capital relief under FHFA’s proposed rule, there is considerable doubt as to whether the banking regulators’ capital rules would permit a banking organization to achieve similar capital relief by structuring a CRT-like transaction as a synthetic securitization. Even for securitizations that do conform to the banking regulators’ capital rules, the credit risk capital charges on a banking organization’s retained securitization exposures generally are considerably greater than the credit risk capital charges on the exposures retained by a GSE in connection with CRT, especially for the more senior interests. What we need is a level playing field for synthetic securitizations of mortgage-backed securities![4] This of course makes sense: The point of the plan is to return private capital to the mortgage market, and the most straightforward way to do that is to get investors to buy and sell mortgages without government guarantees. Still I am old enough to remember when people thought that the enthusiastic securitization of private mortgage-backed securities had caused the financial crisis, and that securitization rules needed to be tightened to keep banks from doing that again. Treasury seems to be going in a different direction.

Unironically really good actually: The billionaire plowed about $500 million into the publicly traded arm of his fund last year, arguing it was significantly undervalued. At the time, Pershing Square Holdings Ltd. was trading at roughly $15 a share. The fund has returned 54.5% on its investments this year through August, fueling a 47% gain for shares of Pershing Square Holdings, which closed in Amsterdam Thursday at $19.02, the highest since January 2016. That translates into a $198 million gain for Ackman in 2019 on his half-billion-dollar bet, data compiled by Bloomberg show. I am an admirer of Ackman’s decision to launch his publicly traded permanent capital vehicle back in 2013, after a long run of good performance. My view is that, while some people think a hedge fund manager’s job is to get good investment returns, they are wrong, and in fact his principal job is to continue to manage a lucrative hedge fund. Continuing to get good returns is the most straightforward way to do that, but straightforward is not the same as easy, and there is no guarantee that any particular hedge fund manager can continue to get good returns. But you can make smart structural choices, like selling shares in a public permanent capital vehicle, that will allow you to continue to run a hedge fund forever even if your performance drops off. And in fact Pershing Square had some bad years—four straight years of losses from 2015 through 2018—and saw investor withdrawals, but kept running plenty of money because its public investors couldn’t take their money out. Smart! But it’s possible that the public vehicle helps with the good investment returns too: In a March letter, Ackman attributed the year’s strong start to a number of factors. The nature of his publicly traded fund meant he no longer had to focus on raising money, and the smaller, more focused investment team was paying dividends. If your model of a hedge fund manager is that (1) he has skill, (2) he has limited time, and (3) his main job is continuing to run a hedge fund, then that implies that he will expend a lot of his skill and time on fundraising, because getting money from investors is what allows you to run a hedge fund. So he will have less time and energy to devote to his second-most-important job, which is picking good investments. And in fact if he has a period of poor performance, he will need to spend even more time reassuring investors to keep them from withdrawing their money, and so he will have even less time to devote to picking good investments, so the performance will get even worse. But if he could just permanently solve the problem of keeping investors, then he doesn’t need to continue working on it and can spend all his time thinking about which investments to pick.

Lol no, says Goldman Sachs: Investors should instead concentrate on firms that generate rapid sales growth during their first three years over short-term profitability, strategists led by David Kostin wrote in a note Thursday. New listings that record sales gains of more than 20% annually are more likely to beat the Russell 3000 Index over three years than a comparable, slower-growth company, the strategists said. Most outperforming IPOs also post positive net income by year three, according to the bank’s analysis. Their research examined 4,500 IPOs completed in the U.S. during the tech boom of 1995-2000, the 2001-2009 cycle preceding the great recession and the latest round starting 2010. During all three cycles “first-year profitability had no discernible impact on the likelihood of outperformance over three years,” the strategists said. In the latest IPO period, profitability in years two and three has indicated outperformance, they said. The obvious cynical take is that Goldman is talking its own book here: It is a leading underwriter of unprofitable tech IPOs, so of course its research analysts are telling clients that it’s a good idea to buy those IPOs. I just like the phrase “first-year profitability had no discernible impact on the likelihood of outperformance,” though. It is such a simple efficient-markets story. It doesn’t mean that this year’s profits are irrelevant to a company’s value, exactly; it just means that whatever the profits mean for the value is already baked into the price. You might think that you can beat the market by buying profitable companies instead of unprofitable ones, but the market has already figured out that trick and priced it in.
