There is a widespread belief that Wall Street traders use complicated derivative products to fool and defraud their unsophisticated clients, but you hear somewhat less about how Wall Street traders use complicated derivatives products to fool and defraud their unsophisticated bosses . Here are Securities and Exchange Commission and Commodity Futures Trading Commission enforcement actions against Swapnil Rege, who was hired by now-closed hedge fund Marinus Capital Advisors in 2015 because it “wanted to expand the Fund’s trading in interest rate products.” “Between 2015 and 2017,” says the SEC, “Rege was the Fund’s primary ‘rates’ trader and mainly traded interest rate swaps and swaptions,” which seems to mean that he knew more about the details of how rates products worked than anyone else there. And he got paid for performance, taking 8% of the profits he made. That is a dangerous combination. If your boss doesn’t know the fine details of valuing interest rate swaptions, you can buy a swaption for $100 and then say “ooh look now it’s worth $150,” book a profit and take your cut. I mean, you shouldn’t , and it’s not quite as easy as that. For one thing, your boss might insist on getting outside quotes to value your swaptions: Even if he doesn’t know the first thing about swaptions, he can find out how much they’re worth just by asking brokers for prices. But you might convince him not to: As of September 2015, at Rege’s suggestion and after discussion, the Fund Adviser stopped using counterparty quotes and began using a model to determine fair value pricing for interest rate swaps and swaptions in the Fund. Well, fine. These are fairly well-understood products and there’s nothing wrong with using a widely accepted model to value them.[1] As long as you have to use the widely accepted inputs to that model, say the ones that come as a default: The model had various inputs, which the Fund Adviser could alter. However, the Fund Adviser instructed Rege and other portfolio managers and traders to use the model’s default inputs and settings. But if you are running the model and want to book a fake profit, maybe you could ignore that instruction: From June 2016 through April 2017 (the “relevant period”), Rege changed the default discount curve setting in the Fund Adviser’s pricing model when valuing certain swaps and swaptions positions. One thing you could do is just change the inputs to make all of your stuff worth more than it is. But you will sometimes have offsetting stuff; you’ll be long one swap and short another. If you change all the inputs to benefit the long swap, you’ll have losses on the short swap that offset the gains. Unless: Generally, Rege used the model’s default discount curve for short positions, and a different discount curve for long positions. Rege used these differing discount curves for positions that otherwise had identical or substantially similar underlying terms, and thus the Fund Adviser’s records should have reflected offsetting or nearly offsetting values for the positions. There was no economic justification for Rege’s use of different discount curves for valuing similar instruments. Rege’s use of different discount curves had the effect of creating artificial gains for what otherwise should have been offsetting or nearly offsetting positions, which led the Fund Adviser to record profits for the Fund that did not actually exist. For example, on December 29, 2016, Rege entered into both long and short positions in swaptions that otherwise had similar underlying terms. Rege used the default discount curve to value the short position and a different discount curve to value the long position. Rege thereby caused the Fund Adviser to record an immediate, single-day profit for these trades of approximately $7 million in the internal accounting records for the Fund, when these offsetting positions should have reflected a net market value at or close to $0. Well look that sounds bad! You pay $100 to go long one swaption, you get paid $100 to go short an identical swaption, you value the short one at $100 and the long one using different assumptions at $150, boom, you’ve got a $50 profit. It seems like the sort of thing that would be easy to catch, doesn’t it? Like, “hey wait you have different valuations for the same exact thing here, that can’t be right.” But notice the SEC doesn’t say it’s the same exact thing. “Similar instruments.” “Swaptions that otherwise had similar underlying terms.” They were different . They were close enough—says the SEC—that the differences shouldn’t matter and that they should be worth almost the same. (Rege settled without admitting or denying the charges.) But not exactly the same, which means that, if you are the firm’s swaptions expert and no one else knows what is going on, you can sort of bluster and hand-wave and patronizingly explain that the small differences support wildly different valuations. “No no no we have to use a different discount curve on this swap, the confirm is printed in a different font, don’t you know anything about swaptions.” So when your boss notices that you changed some inputs but not others— In early January 2017, the Fund Adviser’s CEO discovered that Rege was valuing certain positions using a discount curve other than the model’s default discount curve. The CEO asked Rege about his practice of using the default discount curve in some instances and a different discount curve in other instances. —your best move is probably to bluster and hand-wave: Rege falsely told the Fund Adviser that this was an accepted practice that led to accurate market valuations, and that quotations from counterparty dealers would support the valuations Rege derived by using the differing discount curves. And what can your boss do? If he is not an expert in the details of swaption valuation, but he is a sensible trader type, he will tell you: Okay, if your valuations are right, prove it. Sell some of the stuff at your marks: The CEO asked Rege to exit certain positions so the Fund Adviser could compare actual transaction prices to the internal model valuations. The CEO also asked Rege to obtain broker quotes for positions the Fund continued to hold. And then your move is … I don’t know, fleeing the country seems a bit extreme. But this really is where things should come crashing down: You have engineered yourself a profit with hand-waving and math, but it is not an actual profit, and selling the stuff will reveal that. But maybe not! You could sell at a loss but then bluster and hand-wave about how the market unexpectedly moved against you; “My marks were right but the market suddenly changed.” You lose the profit, but maybe you can avoid being fired and investigated. Or you could do this I guess: Rege engaged in multiple deceptive trades to cover up the fact that he could not exit existing positions at prices that matched his inflated valuations. Specifically, contrary to instructions from the Fund Adviser’s CEO to exit completely out of certain positions, Rege often would enter into new positions at the same time as part of a “package” trade with a single counterparty. Counterparty confirmations for these package trades would show NPVs for the entire package. Trading multiple instruments simultaneously in a package allowed Rege to shift losses from existing positions onto newly-entered positions and to hide the overstated values he had caused the Fund Adviser to record and report in monthly statements to Fund investors. Yeah none of that is wonderful. I feel for the boss here. He had to shut down his hedge fund over this, and he did ask more or less the right questions and get bamboozled anyway. You ask why a thing is marked a certain way, your trader stuns you with math, you say “well never mind that just sell it at this mark,” and he manages to do the sale in a way that stuns you with math anyway.

Well part of this Wall Street Journal story is about how WeWork Cos. founder and chief executive officer Adam Neumann has cashed out about $700 million from his WeWork stake and spent a lot of it on weird stuff like “a 13,000-square-foot house in the Bay Area with a guitar-shaped room.” The implication is not just that Neumann has unusual taste in room shapes but also that founders of startups are not supposed to cash out huge amounts before their companies go public. You are supposed to wear hoodies and eat ramen and live in monkish asceticism while you build your company; you are supposed to have 100% of your net worth wrapped up in that single obsessive vision. Then when your company is big enough to go public and raise hundreds of millions of dollars from big institutional investors, you get to cash out and be a rich person. You know what I am going to say about this theory. Private markets are the new public markets. Neumann has built his company already. It has raised $14.2 billion in private markets over the years, much of it from SoftBank, sure, but some from regular old public investors like Wellington and T. Rowe and Fidelity. It had an equity valuation in its last funding round of $47 billion, sort of, which would put it in the top half of the S&P 500 by market cap if it was public. What are you waiting for? He already did the thing! The guy is the CEO of a $47 billion company that just happens to be private, let him buy all the houses. Or as the Journal puts it: Later-stage investors often are willing to provide more money to startups than traditional venture capitalists, enabling companies to stay private for much longer. That has made it more acceptable for founders to sell small stakes—typically ranging from a few million to tens of millions of dollars—to these bigger investors, especially if a company has remained private for nearly a decade. Sometimes, venture capitalists also sell some of their stakes in these later rounds. “Over the last five years there’s been a growing level of comfort among the VC community to let founders sell,” said Andrea Walne, a partner at Manhattan Venture Partners, a firm that helps arrange such sales. But this is not just an exogenous change in VC culture. The point here is that some “startup founders” are no longer running small scrappy firms that are speeding toward an IPO and still have coin-flip odds of making it; they are running giant multinational conglomerates that can fund massive growth indefinitely in private markets. The financial realities have changed, so the expectations should too. In addition to buying whimsical houses, Neumann has been using the money from his WeWork stock to buy more WeWork stock: Mr. Neumann, 40 years old, has sold shares during most of the investment rounds since 2014, although he didn’t take money out in the round this past January, according to people familiar with the matter. He has also taken out loans of several hundred million dollars backed by his WeWork shares, people familiar with his finances said. He has used some of the proceeds to purchase more WeWork shares by exercising his stock options early, some of the people said. By doing so, Mr. Neumann is betting that the value of WeWork’s shares will rise while also minimizing his taxes, the people added. It’s a tax trade, but it is also a little aggressive to borrow against your illiquid private-company stake to buy more of it. The bank providing the loan—JPMorgan Chase & Co.—is taking a risk not only that the stock will go down, but also that it won’t be able to sell it. But private markets are the new public markets, WeWork is a giant public company that happens to be private, and if you go to a bank and ask for a loan against its stock, it seems silly for the bank to turn you down on a technicality like “we can’t easily sell the collateral if its value declines.” Oh and then Neumann has been using the money from his WeWork stake to buy, um, buildings to rent to WeWork? He has used some of the proceeds from his WeWork loan to invest tens of millions of dollars in commercial real estate, including several properties in downtown San Jose, Calif., where WeWork has been planning an urban campus, and in New York City, people familiar with the deals said. Four of his properties are leased to WeWork—a controversial practice given that WeWork is paying him millions a year in rent. WeWork recently said Mr. Neumann intends to transfer his property holdings to a WeWork-run fund at cost. We have talked before about the conflict of interest involved in WeWork’s CEO renting buildings to his company. The added element of borrowing against WeWork stock to do it is … look why not I guess? Again it seems aggressive. Borrowing money against your concentrated stake in the real-estate company you founded to diversify is one thing; borrowing the money to buy more real estate for that company is kind of the opposite. Despite the luxury housing, this story suggests that Neumann is wrapping up much of his net worth in the WeWork vision, broadly conceived. He has got this WeWork stock, and he leverages it to buy both more WeWork stock and more WeWork buildings. It is an odd form of obsessive focus on his company’s vision, but then it’s an odd vision.

Senator Elizabeth Warren is not a big fan of private equity: Private equity firms raise money from investors, kick in a little of their own, and then borrow tons more to buy other companies. Sometimes the companies do well. But far too often, the private equity firms are like vampires — bleeding the company dry and walking away enriched even as the company succumbs. So she has announced a “Stop Wall Street Looting Act” (summary here, full text here, economic analysis here) that would crack down on private equity firms in a variety of ways. The bill “prohibits target firms from making a capital distribution during the 24 months following a leveraged buyout transaction” and “prohibits interest on excessive debt obligations from being tax deductible by target companies.” It has rules to increase worker protections in bankruptcy, rules about taxing carried interest as ordinary income instead of capital gains, rules about private equity firms’ fiduciary duties and disclosures to their limited partners. But here’s the big one, Section 101(a): Notwithstanding any other provision of law, or the terms of any contract or agreement, a private fund shall be jointly and severally liable for all liabilities of each target firm with respect to the private fund, and any affiliate of such a target firm, including— (1) any debt incurred by the target firm or an affiliate of the target firm, including as part of the acquisition of the target firm by the private fund; (As well as other liabilities like legal penalties and compensation and benefits liabilities.) Warren’s campaign post describes this as “putting private equity firms on the hook for the debts of companies they buy, making them responsible for the downside of their investments so that they only make money if the companies they control flourish.” One thing that I often think about the private equity business—and really about the financial industry generally—is that it is largely a matter of pursuing good basic structural features of capitalism to their logical conclusions. It is just a foundational feature of law and finance, for the past several hundred years, that shareholders are not on the hook for the debts of companies they buy. “The limited liability corporation is the greatest single discovery of modern times,” like the man said; you can’t have big modern business without letting shareholders walk away from a failed company. If you are clever and think about this for a while, it might lead you to a business model specifically built on arbitraging limited liability. You buy all the shares of a company with a lot of borrowed money, the leverage gives you a high expected return with a correspondingly high risk of total loss, and you repeat this a dozen more times until you have a portfolio of risky bets. Some will work out great and you’ll get all the upside; some will fail, but your losses will be limited to your (relatively small) equity investment and your lenders will eat most of the downside. Maybe this model is good (maybe managers of public firms are too afraid of leverage and so do not take optimal risks, and the private-equity model encourages more risk-taking, growth and creative destruction), or maybe it is bad (lotta bankruptcies), or maybe it depends on the circumstances. Warren’s approach is briskly radical: Private equity built a business model on taking advantage of limited liability? Guess what, then, private equity doesn’t get limited liability anymore. I don’t really want to evaluate the merits of this, since, among other things, it is not going to become law any time soon. My bias is, you know, limited liability is good and you want to get rid of it only in specific egregious circumstances, not for huge categories of investors.[2] Private equity firms probably create value, and it seems a bit harsh to just ban them, as this bill effectively does.[3] But I do want to say that I admire the tactical ingenuity here. Elizabeth Warren is proposing to ban private equity, but not in so many words. She’s just proposing one little tweak to the business model: If you want to buy a company with a lot of debt, you have to be responsible for the debt. She understands how revolutionary that would be for the model, and certainly the private equity firms do, but, especially to a non-financial audience, it just sounds so reasonable . And the other side doesn’t .[4] “We want to be able to walk away from companies that we own that go bankrupt” is both a central feature of modern law and finance, and also a little counterintuitive.

Well, you win some, you lose some: A federal appeals court on Thursday upheld the criminal conviction of notorious “pharma bro” Martin Shkreli. The three-judge panel in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circut also upheld the more than $6.4 million in foreiture that a judge imposed on Shkreli last year when she sentenced him for his conviction on two counts of securities fraud and one count of conspiracy to commit securities fraud. Shkreli, 36, is serving a seven-year sentence in a federal prison in Pennsylvania. In its ruling, the appeals panel disagreed with Shkreli’s claim that his trial judge’s instructions to the jury at his trial were incorrect and confusing to jurors. Here is the (brief) ruling. Among other things, Shkreli had objected because the trial judge told the jury that he could be convicted of fraud even if he caused “no ultimate harm” to his victims. In fact Shkreli is an unusual fraudster in that all of the investors in his—really quite fraudy—hedge funds made money: He took their money, lost most of it, lied about it, founded a pharmaceutical company, gave shares of that company to his hedge funds to appease angry investors, and then the company turned out to be worth a lot of money and the investors got all their money back with profits. No harm done! It is not a good defense, legally, but it has a certain intuitive appeal. But the appeals court found that that’s exactly why the judge has to warn the jury against it: We agree with the government that a securities fraud charge without the NUH instruction would actually have constituted a windfall for Shkreli, whose defense was “exactly the kind of improper argument that the NUH instruction was designed to address: that despite his many misrepresentations and omissions to the MSMB Capital and MSMB Healthcare investors, he did not have the requisite intent to defraud those investors because he believed that the investors would ultimately make money from their investments.”

Huh: Slack went cheap on Wall Street. So perhaps Wall Street felt obliged to return the favor. Several major brokers started coverage on the newly public maker of enterprise collaboration software on Tuesday. These weren’t the IPO underwriters per se since Slack didn’t go public via a traditional underwriting. However, the company did engage several of the Street’s biggest names as “advisers” on its direct listing last month and they are evenly split on the stock. Of the eight who set coverage Tuesday, four are neutral on the shares. This contrasts with the typical initiation of research coverage after an initial public offering, when most or all of the underwriters will come out with positive research ratings. People always like to raise their eyebrows at this and hint that it’s a quid pro quo, that the underwriters’ research analysts are only giving the company Buy ratings because the company just wrote their investment bankers a big check. An extension of that cynicism is that the checks for direct listings are smaller, so they buy you fewer Buy ratings. Perhaps I am a hopeless romantic, but I don’t see it that way. To me an underwriting means that, at least in some vague and vestigial way, the underwriting banks are vouching for the company. The banks’ names are on the cover of the prospectus; their sales forces are going out and pitching the stock to their customers; the banks are, technically, momentarily, buying the stock from the company for their own accounts and then re-selling it to investors. The underwriting banks spend intense weeks communicating one consistent message: You Must Buy This Stock. If a month later, when their analysts are allowed to initiate coverage, they said “no we were kidding, never buy that stock,” that would look really bad . They were selling you a stock they didn’t believe in themselves! That’s a scandal! A direct listing isn’t like that. The banks aren’t “underwriting” the offering or vouching for the company; they’re not buying the stock for their own account and re-selling it to investors. The banks are just advising the company on its listing, and advising its shareholders on how to sell their stock directly on the stock exchange. The banks’ names are buried deep in the prospectus; in Slack Inc.’s, they don’t show up at all until page 47. Their sales forces are involved, yes, but in a curiously two-sided way; the banks spend their time before the direct listing helping the company both to find buyers for its shares (among public investors) and to find sellers (among its existing private investors). The message is less clear and consistent—they’re trying to convince some people to buy and some to sell—and in any case it is less clearly attached to the banks’ reputations. If a month later the analysts say they don’t like the stock, well, fine.

We have talked a few times about a conceptual oddity of antitrust law and what law professor Sanjukta Paul calls “the allocation of economic coordination rights.” If you and I each drive a taxi, and we get together and agree to charge the same prices for our taxi services, then that is an illegal antitrust conspiracy and we could go to prison for it. But if get get together and form a corporation , then we can coordinate on prices and that’s perfectly fine. A single business entity can legally fix prices that its employees charge; a group of independent businesses cannot. This seems obviously right—how could a company not be allowed to decide what prices to charge?—but also, if you think too long about it, weird. The law favors one form of economic coordination (the firm, corporations and partnerships and so forth) and effectively bans other possible ways of organizing people’s economic activity. We can’t just be our own bosses and coordinate with each other; but if we get some shareholders and some bosses then we can. There’s a tradeoff there. This is all particularly acute in the case of Uber Technologies Inc. Uber’s drivers are “independent contractors,” it says, which means that they are not subject to certain employment-law protections. It also means that they can’t unionize , or go on strike, or take collective action to raise their earnings: They’re not employees, just independent business operators, so any of those things could be illegal antitrust conspiracies.[1] But all of this points to a solution proposed by law professor Hiba Hafiz: Ride-share drivers do have another option: incorporating themselves. ... If drivers incorporated their own joint venture, they could reduce their antitrust liability exposure risk while protecting their ability to coordinate in their negotiations with ride-share companies and their interactions with customers. Drivers could maintain the same compensation structure and flexibility as they do contracting directly with the platforms — working flexible hours and receiving per-ride salary commissions — while donating a portion, equivalent to the amount they might otherwise pay in union dues, to their newly formed Uber Drivers Inc. … Further, drivers could develop more longstanding relationships with passengers, competing with Uber “off the app” to provide sales and discounts to customers of Uber Drivers Inc. And the joint venture would reduce their advertising costs. The idea is basically to form a union, but call it a corporation. Uber Drivers (the driver company) would be in the business of supplying drivers, and if Uber (the app company) wanted enough drivers it would need to negotiate with Uber Drivers to get them on their terms. (Presumably Uber Drivers could also supply drivers to Lyft Inc., and other apps, and “off the app,” and maybe even make its own app and cut out the middleman.) I don’t know how practical this is, but it is clever. One way to think about it is: Actual U.S. law strongly favors the corporate[2] form of organization over other, less formal methods of economic cooperation, but The corporation is a pretty flexible thing. The most intuitive form of a Big Taxi Corporation is, like, it sets rates and takes in fares and pays its driver-employees a set wage and pays for their cars and gas and if there’s money left over it goes to a group of outside shareholders. But you can modify many of those premises. Make the employees shareholders, pay them “commissions” or “profit participations” or “salaries” equal to their entire fares, etc.; you end up with a union that calls itself a company. One worry that I’d have is: If Uber drivers become employees of Uber Drivers (as opposed to just co-owners of a joint venture), then is Uber Drivers responsible for healthcare and minimum-wage and other employment protections? It would be ironic if a company set up to protect Uber drivers from Uber got in trouble because Uber doesn’t pay them enough.

A model of consumer financial advice that I find sort of perversely appealing goes like this: Retirement and investment products are unusually difficult products for consumers to evaluate. You don’t, like, buy a product and take it home and see if you like it and write a review online. You buy a product, and 40 years later you have an amount of money, and it’s hard for you to figure out if it’s the right amount of money. All of the documentation and math is confusing. You don’t generally know if what you got was good or not; you certainly don’t know right away. There are efficient providers of retirement savings. You know, index funds that charge four (or zero) basis points a year, that sort of thing. One thing that makes them efficient is that they don’t spend all that much money on advertising. They certainly don’t send people out to knock on your door hoping to earn huge commissions by signing you up for an index fund. There are terribly inefficient providers of retirement savings. You know, weird complicated variable annuity products that charge several percentage points a year in the form of non-transparent pricing, and use those huge fees to (1) make a lot of profit and (2) pay big hidden commissions to sharky salespeople who go out and pitch their products to naive people. It is better for you to get efficient retirement savings than inefficient retirement savings. If the sharky salespeople convince you to put $1,000 a month into the bad annuity rather than the good index fund, that’s bad. It is better for you to get inefficient retirement savings than no retirement savings . If the sharky salespeople convince you to put $1,000 a month into the bad annuity rather than spending it on lattes or whatever, that’s good. Well, maybe it’s not good per se, but it’s an improvement. Obviously this model is not correct , and there is a middle tier of providers of retirement advice who are partly in the business of convincing people to save and who charge a reasonable fee for doing that valuable work. But I think it does capture some economic reality. If someone is cold-calling you to pitch a retirement savings product, they are almost certainly not pitching you the best available retirement savings product. But there are probably some people who will not save sufficiently for retirement if no one cold-calls to give them the hard sell on saving for retirement, and who will if someone does. And most of those cold-call products will be, bad, sure, but not Ponzi schemes. The money will be there, in the end, minus the fees. Some people will end up better off with a bad retirement product than they would have without it. If this is your model, what does it imply for regulation? The number one thing it implies is surely that regulators should focus on expanding opportunities for people to buy the good retirement products. This is sort of how the 401(k) structure works: You make it easy for companies to offer good low-cost mutual funds to all of their employees, you make it easy for the employees to sign up for those funds, you set the default options to encourage savings. You also set up the rules so that companies have incentives to choose good low-cost options rather than take kickbacks for choosing worse high-cost options. You create strong incentives for companies to offer something , and you create fiduciary responsibilities to encourage them to offer something good. You set up the market to nudge people into good savings products. Another thing that it might imply, though, sometimes, is that regulators should be careful about shutting down the bad options. Many of the bad options, in expectation, are as good as the good ones except that they charge higher fees. Those higher fees subsidize the costs of getting reluctant savers to save. If you ban them, you might get less saving. Much of the debate over the “fiduciary rule” for retirement advisers was about this tension: If you stop retirement advisers from getting hidden kickbacks for selling bad high-fee products, then they will sell better low-fee products to some people, but they might also stop selling any products to some other people (the ones who are not profitable to advisers without the hidden fees). If those other people end up going to a cheap robo-adviser or the website of a low-cost index-fund provider, that’s a good outcome. If they end up going to Atlantic City it’s not. Anyway here’s a story about how the U.S. Consumer Financial Protection Bureau is becoming, like, an industry promotion group: The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau is seeking to form partnerships with “parties from cross sectors” to get more consumers to stabilize their financial standing, agency director Kathy Kraninger told a gathering of financial industry executives and lobbyists Wednesday. The plan is part of bureau efforts to strengthen consumer education, and encourage people to start saving so they have money to cover emergencies. Consumer advocates criticized Ms. Kraninger’s invitation to financial companies. “Americans don’t need the main federal consumer protection agency partnering with the financial services industry to conduct studies,” said Linda Jun, senior policy counsel at Americans for Financial Reform. “Americans need a strong CFPB that actually polices the industry from doing harm.” Sure that quote sounds right, but is it empirically true? There is constant talk about a retirement savings crisis in which most people have not put aside enough money for retirement. If the CFPB can partner with financial firms to get 10 million people to save money, but in exchange it lets the financial firms steal 1 million people’s savings, is that … is that an improvement? I don’t know. It’s just something to think about. Not to be pleased about, surely; it is all pretty second-best. The studies do sound weird: Ms. Kraninger said the CFPB had already completed a joint study with H&R Block Inc. to see if consumers could be encouraged to save using the company’s prepaid card during the tax-return season. The test was conducted among the company’s moderate-income customers who receive earned income-tax credit. She said it showed positive results, which the bureau plans to unveil in the near future. “This suggests simple timely marketing messages and small incentives help encourage consumers interested in ways to save during the tax time,” she said. She added that there is “a fantastic opportunity for co-branding for engaging in the kind of studies” to gather data and develop steps to get people to save more. Save … using a … prepaid card? Here’s a list of fees for H&R Block’s prepaid Mastercard. “You will be charged $4.95 each month after you have not completed a transaction using your Card for 60 days.” That is … I dunno, it’s not how I would go about incentivizing saving? Back when I used to get tax refunds, I had them direct deposited in my no-fee checking account and then moved them to a high-interest savings account. That’s a better savings product than this! But maybe this is better than nothing.

Well, if you are in the business of making stuff in a remote area, you will need to pay someone to move the stuff to where the people are. If the trucking company that moves your stuff raises its prices, you might stop using it and get bids from other trucking companies. If all the trucking companies raise their prices, maybe you’ll look into sending it on boats or trains. If all of the transportation methods get more expensive, maybe you’ll raise the selling price of your stuff to pay for your increased costs. If all of the transportation methods get more expensive and you can’t raise your price, you’ll make less money. If the cost of transportation gets so high that you can’t sell your stuff profitably, then I guess you will shut down your factory temporarily, or maybe permanently. Sorry. The natural gas business does not exactly work that way: As shale companies turned America into the world’s top oil producer, they unlocked massive quantities of natural gas as a byproduct and Texas has allowed them to freely burn off vast volumes as area pipelines fill up. The process is known as flaring. Now, shale producer Exco Resources Inc. is seeking to flare nearly all of the gas produced by a group of South Texas wells, even though its operations are already connected to a network of pipelines. Williams Cos., the operator of the pipelines, is challenging the request, in what is believed to be the first such dispute on record. Williams attorney John Hays Jr. told commissioners in a hearing last month that granting Exco’s request would open the door to wasting gas any time doing so is more profitable than transporting it. … Exco has said that rejecting the company’s permit application could force a shutdown of the wells. … Granting flaring permits in cases such as Exco’s could make pipeline companies less willing to risk building new conduits. ... Exco and Williams are fighting over how much the producer should pay to access the pipeline network. If the price is too high, Exco says, then it is cheaper to flare gas than pay for transportation. The article has a lot about the economic and environmental impacts of flaring, but I am more interested in the fact that the pipeline operator is the one complaining. I appreciate the point about the risk of building new infrastructure, but still it is weird to (1) be the only carrier who can transport your customer’s product to market and (2) go ask a regulator to order that customer to keep shipping the product even if it’s not profitable.

Like anyone who writes on the internet, I am inundated with public-relations emails from financial technology startups and crypto projects asking me to cover their thing. I mostly just delete these, but every so often— Wet Pants Denim, Dentacoin—they are funny and I pass them along to my readers. I got one today that I loved, not because it is hilarious or weird or over the top, but because it is so normal and controlled: Just wanted to reach out and let you know about a messaging app that will democratize instant messaging for the world of finance. Budfox will be the first free and secure messaging app to encrypt messages and media files, perfect for anyone in the financial community. As an added security bonus, other features the app will provide include: Ability to clear all chat history Way to create a secret chat set to disappear (self-destruction timer) End-to-end encryption with the highest level of security on the market Budfox also provides complete independence without conflict of interest as it is not owned by a bank or commercial organization. Here’s the website. To be clear I have made no inquiries into this and cannot recommend that you do or don’t download the app. There are other secure messaging services, and I have no idea if this one is better or worse than anything else. I pass it along to you only because, if you are reading this newsletter, there’s a good chance that the name will ring a bell for you. You know who Bud Fox is, right? You know what Bud Fox would do with an encrypted auto-deleting chat app, right? You know what this pitch is about, right?

A giant American company has decided to get into cryptocurrency. It has, with great fanfare but not a lot of specificity, announced plans for its own stablecoin, a cryptocurrency that would be useful in making payments and transferring money but that would not fluctuate in value the way Bitcoin does. These plans are at the very early stage, but the company is big and good at its job and has plenty of ability to hire smart engineers, so there’s reason to think they can work out. At first the stablecoin would mostly just be for the company’s own users making payments within its ecosystem, but over time, if all goes well, it might come to be an important independent part of the global financial system. But the company has some issues. It is big, maybe too big: Politicians are always talking about breaking it up, and if it takes control of the money supply (or something like it) that will not assuage concerns about its bigness. It has had some big scandals in recent years, scandals that might be due to its size and hubris. It is not universally beloved. Its brash chief executive officer—who is sometimes rumored to be a potential presidential candidate—is a polarizing figure, and his embrace of crypto might be a reason for some people to oppose it. And really any crypto project like this will attract a lot of regulatory attention: Will it be used to break the rules that normally apply to banking and payments with U.S. dollars? Will the stablecoin really be stable? Can you trust the big company with your money, particularly if it’s this new and strange form of money? Also Congress did not hold a hearing on this company’s cryptocurrency yesterday, and no one is particularly upset about it. Of course I am talking about JPMorgan Chase & Co. We discussed its crypto project—“JPM Coin”—earlier this year, and then I kind of forgot about it because, let’s face it, it’s just one more blockchain project at one more big bank. Libra , on the other hand: Republican and Democratic Senators sharply questioned Facebook Inc.’s plan to create its own digital money, adding to a chorus of skepticism across Washington and underscoring the challenges the company faces in getting its cryptocurrency off the ground. At a hearing Tuesday before the Senate Banking Committee, lawmakers compared the social media giant to a toddler playing with matches who burns the house down, blasted it for repeatedly violating consumers’ privacy and accused the company of cheapening social discourse and polarizing America. Many expressed incredulity that Facebook would be able to safeguard people’s finances. “Do you really think people should trust Facebook with their hard earned money?” Ohio Senator Sherrod Brown, the top Democrat on the banking panel, asked. “I just think that is delusional.” What is the difference? Some huge part of it is just competence in specific domains. When you hear “JPMorgan is doing a crypto,” some obvious things that you’ll think—that I think anyway—are: This crypto will probably comply with U.S. anti-money-laundering rules, because JPMorgan is really focused on that sort of thing. It will probably be hard to buy drugs over the internet with this crypto. This crypto probably will not share your personal data with advertisers. If you have some of this crypto with JPMorgan, JPMorgan will not lose it. If JPMorgan needs a banking license to issue this crypto, that’s fine, because JPMorgan is a bank. If JPMorgan needs some other sorts of licenses to issue this crypto, that’s fine, because JPMorgan has lots of lawyers who will figure out what licenses it needs and then get them, and it probably has them all already anyway. If any financial regulatory agency anywhere in the world has any questions or concerns about this crypto, JPMorgan will send a team of very soothing lawyers to that agency’s offices to talk to them in soft tones until their concerns are assuaged. Etc. Also JPMorgan already dominates the financial system, and people already trust it with their hard earned money, so even if you don’t like JPMorgan much, those aren’t new scary things to worry about. With Facebook … you know! Their expertise is in getting people to use and engage with their products, and they are amazingly good at that—way better than JPMorgan—but that is not exactly the expertise you want here. (That expertise, here, is frankly scary to regulators; instant widespread adoption of a rickety minimum viable product, in the space of money , would be bad.) Mark Zuckerberg once told his critics “Calm down. Breathe. We hear you,” and if you said that to a banking regulator they would throw a chair at you.[1] Still. At some level of size and profitability, you’d think you could just buy domain expertise. Surely Facebook could just identify the 100 best lawyers and regulatory experts and payments-plumbing people at JPMorgan and quintuple their salaries without too much trouble. And then it could do this rollout like, you know, a bank. If you’re a bank and you want to launch a weird new thing, you start working on a prototype and you get the lawyers involved early and you keep in careful touch with your regulators and you don’t announce anything that would make them mad and you iterate slowly until you have a functioning product with all the necessary regulatory buy-ins. That’s not Facebook’s approach. My Bloomberg Opinion colleague Shira Ovide tweeted, “Facebook basically revamped its vanity in-app payments system, dressed up with a vague white paper with hand-waving about virtual currency, and now is in the absolute muck over this. This is the most Facebook thing that ever Facebook-ed.” It’s weird, right? And unnecessarily, maximally confrontational. As Max Read writes about yesterdays’ hearing: What’s worrisome to senators about Libra — and why today’s hearing was such a bipartisan display of mistrust and skepticism — isn’t merely that Facebook itself is untrustworthy. It’s that Libra is an expression of power. … Senatorial dislike of Facebook’s cryptocurrency arises because Libra represents, to a degree of clarity no other Facebook project quite does, a threat to U.S. sovereignty. Facebook’s approach is so baffling that it told Congress that “for the purposes of data and privacy protections, the Swiss Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner (FDPIC) will be the Libra Association’s privacy regulator,” and then the FDPIC announced “Until today we have not been contacted by the promoters of Libra.” What? No! That is not how you do any of this. You call FDPIC first, come on. Why announce something so vague and grandiose that people can project whatever fears they want onto it? Why get everyone so angry without a product? “Facebook has a move fast and break things culture” is not, I think, a good answer: This is a white paper ; they haven’t really done anything. (“Move fast and break things” would mean launching Libra and daring regulators to do something about it, which is kind of a standard move in the crypto world.) “Facebook is a tech company and unused to the scrutiny that comes in financial services” is also not especially satisfying: It might have been true once, but Facebook gets a lot of scrutiny these days! More than banks, even! “Facebook is a tech company and so is incurably utopian and always surprised when people question its motives” is … plausible, really, though it is kind of late in the day to still think like that. I don’t really know the answer, but one thing that is really striking about Facebook’s Libra proposal is the lip service it pays to decentralization and openness. Libra is not, in Facebook’s telling, the Facebook cryptocurrency; it’s an open cryptocurrency that will be governed by a democratic consortium of stakeholders and run, eventually, on a permissionless open blockchain. Perhaps this is purely cynical marketing—get people to trust Facebook’s cryptocurrency by pretending it’s not Facebook’s—but I suspect that they mean it at least at some level. For one thing if you are hiring cryptocurrency enthusiasts to build your cryptocurrency, then the engineers building it, if not necessarily the executives in charge, will tend to be true believers in the decentralized dream of cryptocurrency. But also Facebook is an internet company ; it is very familiar with the power of open decentralized networks, is in some sense built on them, and believes in them in a way that banks don’t. JPMorgan, ha, no, it’s a bank. The idea of a permissionless blockchain, in which anyone can be involved in confirming transactions, is just facially insane to JPMorgan: You need to do diligence and know-your-customer on every counterparty, you can’t just open up your network to any hacker who wants in. You, your shareholders and your regulators expect top-down control of every aspect of the ecosystem. You can have a blockchain, sure; people love blockchains. But the blockchain has to be managed by you, or at least you and a small hand-picked universe of counterparties. These philosophical differences lead to process differences. JPMorgan wants a stablecoin, so it builds it. It calls up regulators and involves lawyers and thinks about the best way to achieve its goals within the rules. Facebook wants a stablecoin, but it can’t just build it, because a Facebook cryptocurrency defeats the purpose of a Facebook cryptocurrency . It has to be a not-Facebook cryptocurrency, blessed by and integrated into Facebook. It has to get buy-in from lots of people, not just—not primarily—regulators but also e-commerce sites and payments processors and venture capitalists and crypto exchanges and people who spend a lot of time on message boards talking about the transformative potential of crypto. It has to crowdsource the design, the structure and features and governance, of Libra, which means that it had to go public with Libra before it knew what Libra was. And then everyone got mad about what Libra might be. Arguably that shows Facebook’s modesty—it is humbly asking for advice rather than just barging ahead on its own—but I don't know. The other way to think of it is that JPMorgan is trying to build a JPM Coin for JPMorgan, while Facebook is trying to build a stablecoin for the world. JPMorgan sees itself as an actor in a system, and is trying to accomplish its goals within the rules of that system. Facebook sees itself as the system ; it has decided that the world needs a new currency, and so it sets up its own new worldwide governance body to solicit input from others about how to build that currency. Of course the other governance bodies—like Congress—will be annoyed.

The basic way that I think about a lot of shareholder activism is that it is about who gets to make investment decisions with the company’s money. A company makes widgets, it is good at making widgets, the widgets are profitable, they bring in a lot of money. The company’s managers want to use the money to build a sprocket factory, because (they say) their widget-making skills will be easily transferrable to the sprockets business, and there will be valuable synergies from cross-selling sprockets to the widget customer base, and when the widget business eventually declines shareholders will be happy that the company diversified into the more modern sprocket industry. An activist comes along and says, no, actually, management has no business getting into sprockets, they are just doing this to build an empire and pay themselves more for running a bigger company, they should use the money to pay dividends and buy back stock so that the shareholders can make their own decisions about where to invest the profits. Then the managers accuse the activist of being a short-termist and undermining the company’s long-term plan for profitability, and the activist accuses the managers of being entrenched and wasteful. I do not think there is any general right answer here, but one question you might ask is: Who is likely to have an advantage in picking new investments , the shareholders or the managers? In some cases the managers will have a long track record of making bold counterintuitive decisions to get into new businesses in ways that turned out to be wildly profitable in the long run; nobody is clamoring for more buybacks at Facebook or Amazon. In other cases the managers will be, you know, good widget-makers: They’ll be perfectly good at operating the business they’ve always operated, but they’ll have no special ability to pick new ones. Meanwhile the shareholders will be mostly professional investors whose whole job is about allocating capital to good ideas. (Or, well, some of them will be index funds, but the rest will be capital allocators.) Surely a professional capital allocator should be better at allocating capital than at least some professional business operators. What if the business is a capital allocating business though? Bill Ackman’s publicly traded Pershing Square Holdings Ltd. has an activist of its own. Asset Value Investors Ltd., or AVI, which owns a 3% stake in the London-listed firm, is pushing back against Pershing Square Holdings’ decision to issue $400 million of 20-year debt without consulting shareholders. The firm already has more debt than most of its peers and selling more bonds will constrain its ability to narrow the gap between its stock price and net asset value, according to a letter AVI sent Tuesday to Pershing Square Holdings Chairman Anne Farlow. It wants the firm to halt the debt plan and pursue a more aggressive share buyback program to close that gap. On the one hand, if you’re investing money in Bill Ackman’s public investing vehicle, it’s not because he makes a fine widget. You’re buying shares because you think he can do a good job of investing your money. He is a famous investing guy and you, probably, aren’t. Investing in his fund and asking him to give the money back to you is sort of self-defeating: If you think you can do a better job of investing than he can, why’d you buy the stock in the first place?[2] On the other hand … like … you can just … look at the results? The sprocket factory is a long-term pivot in the widget company’s business model, and you may not fully see the results for years, and there is endless room for subjective argument. With a publicly-traded vehicle for a hedge fund that owns mostly liquid publicly traded stocks, it is easier and more objective to see how it’s doing. How’s it doing? From AVI’s letter to Pershing Square: It seems remarkably presumptuous for the Board to be issuing debt with a twenty-year tenor when shareholders who invested in PSH at IPO have experienced a share price total return of -26% over a period when the S&P 500 has returned +74%. The uncomfortable fact is that if you just bought stocks at random you would have outperformed what Bill Ackman has done with your money, over some arguably relevant time period, which undermines the argument that you should keep trusting him with the money. Though Pershing Square is up about 48% this year, so maybe you should. Alas the only really relevant time period is the future, which is unknowable. Meanwhile the stock of Pershing Square Holdings trades for less than the value of the underlying assets. Effectively the debate here is: If Pershing Square Holdings just sells all of its investments for cash and gives the money back to shareholders, the shareholders will get an immediate largeish gain: Pershing Square Holdings trades at about a 28% discount to NAV, according to Bloomberg, so if it could sell its assets at their current trading value it could buy back its stock at about a 39% premium.[3] If Pershing Square Holdings instead raises more money by issuing debt and uses that money to double down on Bill Ackman’s investing expertise, then the discount will not dissipate immediately, but maybe all of those investments will work out great—much better than Pershing Square’s much-less-famous shareholders could have done with their money—and the share price will go up, making them far more than 39%. (Also the discount will eventually dissipate because people will stop worrying.) Obviously these are the two extremes—AVI is calling not for liquidation , just for some buybacks—but they clarify the issues. The question is, do you trust the manager’s long-term vision for the company, or do you want the quick price jump of a stock buyback? It’s the standard question of activism, but in an especially pure way.

Meanwhile how are the big-bank blockchain projects going? Companies, including banks, large retailers and technology vendors, are investing billions of dollars to find uses for blockchain, a digital ledger used by cryptocurrencies like bitcoin. ... But a review of 33 projects involving large companies announced over the past four years and interviews with more than a dozen executives involved with them show the technology has yet to deliver on its promise. At least a dozen of these projects, which involve major banks, exchanges and technology firms, have not gone beyond the testing phase, the review shows. Those that have made it past that stage are yet to see extensive usage. I think that if your argument now is that blockchain is a somewhat better database architecture for keeping track of some kinds of financial assets, and so can be implemented selectively in certain products to improve efficiency, sure, yeah, go to town. But I have in my time read white papers about how all of our financial lives would be translated into a single integrated blockchain, and securities would be traded for currency instantly on the same blockchain, and you could get a loan instantly because a lender could see everything about you on the blockchain, etc. etc. etc., a single universal system for everything, through the magic of blockchain. And, yeah, no.

Meanwhile how are the disruptor non-bank crypto-finance businesses going? On Saturday, the company behind Tether mistakenly created more than $5 billion of the digital coins in an instant—more than doubling the amount in circulation. The sudden flood spooked the market and drove down the price of bitcoin, the most actively traded cryptocurrency, by about 12%. … Saturday’s problem came about because cryptocurrency exchange Poloniex needed to move $50 million of Tether from a blockchain network called Omni to another called Tron. The Tether employee who processed the order accidentally created and sent to Poloniex $5 billion in new Tether instead of $50 million. A $3.9 billion market suddenly swelled to $8.9 billion. Tether’s chief technical officer, Paolo Ardoino, tweeted that the mistake was due to “an issue with the token decimals.” On Wall Street, that is called a “fat finger” error. To be fair, as that implies, it happens at regular banks too, though not usually in a “create $5 billion out of nowhere” way.

This is sort of satisfying: Using a novel database, we show that the stock-price impact of analyst trade ideas is at least as large as the impact of stock recommendation, target price, and earnings forecast changes, and that investors following trade ideas can earn significant abnormal returns. Trade ideas triggered by forthcoming firm catalyst events are more informative than ideas exploiting temporary mispricing. Institutional investors trade in the direction of trade ideas and commission-paying institutional clients do so earlier than non-clients. Analysts generating trade ideas are more established and are more likely to produce ideas for stocks with high dollar trading commissions in their coverage universe. That is from a paper titled “ Are Analyst Trade Ideas Valuable?,” by Justin Birru, Sinan Gokkaya, Xi Liu and René Stulz. Analyst “trade ideas” are short-term recommendations (usually about some event in the next one to three months) that sell-side research analysts issue in addition to their formal long-term Buy or Sell or Hold recommendations and price targets. If you think a company has good fundamental long-term business prospects that are not fully priced by the market, you issue a Buy recommendation; if you think it’s going to announce a big stock buyback at the end of the month that will push the stock up temporarily, you put out a trade idea. The most obvious intuitive model of what analysts do might go something like this: They cover a bunch of companies and write a few formal research reports, deep dives on a company and its valuation, each year. They also write occasional brief updates after big events like earnings. This doesn’t take that much time, really. What do they do the rest of the time? They spend some of their time talking to the companies they cover, getting to know the executives and the business, trying to understand how it works and what might be coming in the future. They spend some of their time talking to the investors who, ultimately, pay their bills: Investment banks provide sell-side research as a service to their institutional investor customers; if the customers get good quality research coverage from a bank, then they are more likely to do more trading with that bank and pay it more commissions. (Or, in Europe, they will just pay for the research directly.) Good quality research coverage means good written research reports and Buy/Sell recommendations, but that is just the most basic level of coverage, the stuff that any retail customer can get. The big customers want to be able to call up the analysts and ask questions, talk about the companies, exchange ideas, learn something. They spend some of their time just setting up meetings between the investors and the companies so they can talk to each other directly. (This is called “corporate access” and we talk about it occasionally.) Something happens in all of those meetings and phone calls. When the analysts talk to the companies, they learn something. When the analysts talk to the investors, the investors learn something. When the analysts introduce the investors directly to the companies, the investors learn something. None of these are purely social events; people are talking to each other to learn things, and if they keep doing it it must be because it works. This model would predict (see points 4 and 7) that analysts will sometimes have good ideas about “forthcoming catalyst events”: By getting to know a company and talking to its executives frequently, they may know more than the average investor about what the company is likely to do and when. And in fact: Our results document that trading buys (sells) are associated with significantly positive (negative) risk-adjusted returns. In terms of economic magnitude, the buy portfolio generates a daily DGTW alpha of 4.5 basis points, which corresponds to about 90 basis points on a monthly basis. Magnitudes are about twice as large for sells. There is no reason to think that this means that CEOs sometimes tell analysts “hey we’re gonna do a buyback, pass it on.” That definitely used to happen, and there are arguments that it is a good mechanism for diffusing information, but it is more or less illegal now. Still if you spend a lot of time paying attention to a company and talking to its executives, you may get more clues about what it is going to do, and be better at reading those clues, than an average generalist investor will be. The model might also predict (see points 5 and 7) that big commission-paying institutional customers will get good trade ideas from analysts before everyone else. And in fact: When we focus only on trading activity by institutional clients of the broker generating the trading call, we find that commission-paying institutional clients exhibit statistically significant increases in trading activity as early as three days ahead of the announcement of trading call. What does that mean? There’s a simple possible explanation, which is that, when an analyst has a good trading idea, she first calls up her big institutional clients and gives it to them, and then she calls up her smaller clients and gives it to them, and finally she writes it up and publishes it to all of her clients. This sort of multi-tiered service, with better service for better customers, is common in, um, every industry—have you ever boarded an airplane?—and it wouldn’t be that surprising to see it here. But it is, for reasons that I have always found a bit baffling, sort of illegal-ish in investment research; analysts are not supposed to tell big clients about research recommendations before publishing them. That doesn’t mean it doesn’t happen, though, and in fact banks periodically get in trouble for doing it.[1] But it’s worth saying there are other possibilities. Remember the analyst’s job is, among other things, to talk to the big clients. Those clients are also in the business of thinking about the companies she covers, and they also employ smart people who are good at that. Maybe sometimes they give her ideas, and she likes them and decides to publish them. Maybe her conversations with those big clients stir up or clarify her ideas, and she and the clients both go off afterwards and come to the same conclusions about trade ideas. This is not, just, the naked trading of factual tips ; it is an intellectual process, an exchange of ideas; of course the clients who participate in that exchange will get better ideas out of it. Also here’s a good paragraph on how analysts think about their jobs: We examine the incentives for an analyst to issue trading calls. Compared to other analyst outputs, a trading call is riskier for an analyst as it is much easier to assess whether a trade idea is correct or not than it is to assess whether a stock recommendation is correct or not. A recommendation has a long investment horizon and is generally based on fundamental analyses, so that a recommendation may not pay off for a host of intervening factors that the analyst could not have foreseen. The same argument applies for target prices. With a trade call, the investment horizon is short, and the call is based on a specific trading opportunity. While a successful trading call could make an analyst’s name, an unsuccessful one may damage her reputation with investors. ... In our setting, the evidence likewise suggests that analysts with more established reputations are more likely to issue trading calls. As expected, we find that these calls are more likely to be issued by more experienced analysts (i.e., longer general forecasting experience, industry experience, or stock-specific experience) and all-star analysts. We also find that trading calls pay off for analysts who make them. Analysts who produce such calls are more likely to be subsequently included in the All-American Research Team roster. When you are starting out as a research analyst, you do a lot of fundamental financial analysis and industry research and try to develop a good long-term model of how your companies work. When you’ve been doing it for long enough you can be like “they’re gonna do a buyback next month, buy some stock quick.” Some of that is just the value of experience: When you’ve been doing it long enough, you can spot patterns with enough specificity and confidence to make specific actionable short-term predictions. Some of it might be access: When you’ve been doing it long enough, maybe you have more frequent or informative conversations with management than you did when you started. Some of it is just confidence: When you’ve been doing it long enough, getting a specific short-term call wrong is less damaging to your career, so you can take more risks.

Oh man, Deutsche Bank owns a big and valuable ice cube, and then the temperature rose, and now it is just standing next to a bonfire juggling the ice cube while trying to convince BNP Paribas to pay for it: When Deutsche Bank AG said it was exiting the business of servicing hedge funds as part of its historic retreat, French rival BNP Paribas SA seemed poised to benefit. The reality is more complicated. The two European banking giants are discussing how to transfer 150 billion euros ($168 billion) of balances linked to hedge funds at Deutsche Bank’s so-called prime-brokerage unit along with technology and potentially hundreds of staff, people familiar with the matter said. Yet the German lender’s clients have been pulling about $1 billion of funds per day and going elsewhere as the firms iron out the details, placing pressure on them to complete a deal soon, said the people, who requested anonymity as the talks aren’t public. We talked about this situation a couple of weeks ago, before Deutsche Bank announced that it was getting out of the prime brokerage business and handing its clients over to BNP Paribas. Back then clients were running away on the rumor that Deutsche Bank was not interested in being their long-term provider of prime brokerage services. The lesson, I suggested, was that if you’re thinking about selling a big and valuable but non-core business whose clients can easily leave, you gotta do it quick, because if it just sits around being non-core for too long it stops being valuable. Now that it’s official, yeah, $1 billion per day. “Potentially hundreds of staff!” There are a lot of people working at Deutsche Bank right now whose job is to support and service prime-brokerage clients, and who are hoping to continue doing that job at BNP Paribas, and who are doing their best to keep the clients there long enough for that to happen. I suppose some of the clients are happy with their service at Deutsche Bank and confident that they’ll get a similar level of service when the group moves to BNP Paribas, and other clients just really like their Deutsche Bank coverage teams on a personal level and don’t want to abandon them, and other clients have just somehow not been paying attention. If you’re a Deutsche Bank prime brokerage customer relationship person, are you … marketing? Are you drawing up targeting lists and getting on planes to meet with potential new clients? Are you showing them a deck about your capabilities and then saying at the end “oh also it’ll probably all still work at BNP Paribas”? How are those meetings going?

One put that I am short, in my pontificating career, is that I keep saying that Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac will never be re-privatized and will remain forever in conservatorship for the benefit of the U.S. government. Actually I don’t exactly say that, or even believe it really, in so many words. All I think is that people will keep talking very sincerely about how important it is to return Fannie and Freddie to private ownership, and will keep announcing plans and blueprints to do that, and the optimal time to do it will perpetually be a year or two in the future. One day this delay will probably collapse and something will happen, but I keep confidently predicting that that day is not soon, and I keep being right. It is really inevitable that one day I will be wrong, so I am sorry in advance for that, but today is not that day: The Trump administration is growing wary of taking bold steps toward freeing Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac from federal control before the 2020 election, said people familiar with the matter, in part because of the political risk of potentially upending the U.S. mortgage market. While White House and Treasury Department officials are eager to end the companies’ decade-long conservatorships, they see the task as arduous, slow-moving and extremely complicated, said the people who asked not to be named in discussing internal deliberations. Before this you could occasionally read articles saying that they were planning to take bold steps to free Fannie and Freddie, or that their eagerness to end the government-sponsored enterprises’ decade-long conservatorships might lead to some actual action to do so, but I was not fooled. We’ll just check back in 2020 when there will be no distractions and the mechanics of privatizing Fannie and Freddie will undoubtedly be at the top of the political agenda. Incidentally there is another way to look at this situation. The old, pre-2008 Fannie and Freddie were private companies that took on the default risk of a large chunk of U.S. mortgages, in exchange for a fee, and were backed by a nudge-and-wink informal guarantee from the U.S. Treasury. Then in the financial crisis they were taken over by the U.S. government, at which point they took on the default risk of U.S. mortgages for a fee, and were backed by a much more formal (though still not quite absolute) guarantee from the U.S. Treasury. The (quasi-)private guarantee became public. But since 2008, Fannie and Freddie have gotten a lot more aggressive about selling off the default risk of the mortgages they guarantee: Fannie and Freddie, backed by the Treasury, guarantee the mortgages against default (and package default-risk-free mortgage bonds and sell them to investors, etc.), but then they sell “credit risk transfer” securities to private investors who want to take on the default risk. They are no longer ultimate guarantors of mortgages against default; they are just conduits for packaging that default risk and selling it to investors. (I mean, partly.) “Credit Risk Transfer and De Facto GSE Reform,” is the title of this paper from the New York Fed. The reform—returning the default-guarantee function of Fannie and Freddie to private hands—is already happening, just without returning Fannie and Freddie to private hands. If that’s what is happening, maybe the right way to think about Fannie and Freddie is that they are a sort of administrative agency, in charge of setting the rules and running the mechanics of the mortgage market. They decide the best way to run the mortgage market, how the default risk and interest-rate risk and prepayment risk of mortgages should be split up, and then they parcel out those risks in market transactions to investors. They administer the market, but the actual work of funding and guaranteeing mortgages is (increasingly though not entirely) done by private capital. If that’s the right way to think about it, then maybe government should be in the business of declaring victory , announcing that private capital has returned to the mortgage business, finishing the job (by doing more risk transfers until you’ve transferred all of the risk[2]), and accepting that Fannie and Freddie are government agencies for supervising the market for mortgage default risk, rather than businesses—businesses that will one day be re-privatized—for absorbing that risk. I am not sure that this is right, and I certainly don’t expect it to happen soon . But the longer Fannie and Freddie spend as arms of the government, and the more they pass their economic risk on to private investors, the more it makes sense to think of them this way. If they stay in government hands long enough, they might become government.

If I told you that a loan fund was an “enhanced” loan fund, would you guess that it: Holds higher-quality loans than a regular loan fund, or Holds lower-quality loans than a regular loan fund? “Enhanced” is a good word, so you might naively guess 1, but of course no the answer is 2: Since November of last year, three different money managers have issued $1.6 billion of so-called enhanced collateralized loan obligations that are set up to hold a much larger amount of loans with extremely low credit ratings than typical CLOs. At least two more managers are expected to follow suit in the coming months. The enhancement is not in the loan quality; it’s in the interest rate: “Because they can hold lower-rated loans, the structures pay higher interest rates on the bonds they issue.” Enhancement![3] There is something rather lovely about this, the deep acceptance of the relationship between risk and return, the confidence that flaws can always be compensated with price. In finance, the way to enhance something is to make it worse.

I dunno, this sounds like a challenge: Richard Hayes plans to leave a $45 million coin on the streets of Manhattan all day Tuesday, but he isn’t particularly worried about a thief carting it off. The coin—with Queen Elizabeth’s profile pressed onto one side and a mid-hop kangaroo on the other—is beyond the wiles of the average pickpocket. It measures nearly 32 inches in diameter and is almost 5 inches thick. Oh, and it weighs about 2,200 pounds. Really if you’re in New York today and feeling adventurous, you should mosey up to the coin, get to chatting with Hayes about cricket, and then, when his guard is down and he’s feeling pretty smug about how unstealably heavy his gold coin is, bam, your accomplices swoop in with a big crane—and striped shirts and burglar masks and little mustaches, why not—and carry it away. Not legal advice, but so little of modern finance is this tactile and cartoonish. So many of the things worth stealing these days are, like, data sets, Swift keys, email addresses, entries in cryptographic ledgers, different sequences of zeroes and ones in a computer somewhere. This is a colossal gold coin with a picture of a kangaroo on it! You don’t get to steal that every day.
