[1] Here I am using “public offering” and “private placement” in a sort of legalistic way, what you’d find in an offering document. In the business, most people would call Ligand’s deal a “ Rule 144A offering,” technically private but not as narrowly restricted as a true “private placement.” [2] This is generally described in Ligand’s Form 8-K announcing the deal, and specifically described in the indenture, both of which say that Ligand has the option to settle either entirely in cash or in a mix of cash and stock. For, I assume, accounting reasons, last year Ligand elected to settle only in cash. [3] Ha, I mean, that is the theory. In practice if you just lied in the offering memo you’d have a huge securities fraud lawsuit. [4] Look, it sometimes happens. [5] Last time we talked about it, I offered to buy him a drink, and that offer stands. I understand that he suffered no worse consequences than embarrassment for this, which is as it should be; mistakes happen. [6] If you’re curious, it’s in the definition of the term “Daily Share Amount” on page 6, which says “ Daily Share Amount’ means a number of shares equal to (i) the excess of the Daily Conversion Value for such VWAP Trading Day over the Daily Principal Portion for such VWAP Trading Day, divided by (ii) the Daily Principal Portion for such Trading Day,” and should say “… divided by (ii) the Daily VWAP for such Trading Day.” [7] See section 9.01(b), page 51 of the indenture. [8] Vice Chancellor Laster writes, correctly: “The Conforming Amendment Provision ensures that the terms of the Indenture match the original terms of the deal as marketed in the Offering Memorandum. Although nominally styled as an ‘amendment’ for purposes of Section 9.01(b), invoking the Conforming Amendment Provision does not amend the deal at all. It maintains the original deal by conforming the terms of the Indenture to the original terms.” [9] Also they probably got the original offering memo for this deal anyway, though by 2018 maybe they had lost it. [10] That’s GAAP net income for the years 2009 through 2018, from Bloomberg. Adjusted net income available to common shareholders for those years is a healthier 31.4 billion euros, still not much more than the capital raises so far.

There seem to be two basic approaches to financial fraud. One approach is to pretend to do a real thing as accurately as possible, with the minimum necessary tweaks to make it a fraud. You run a real company and come to work every day doing real stuff, but then you quietly change a few numbers in the financial reports to get yourself a bigger bonus. You set up a hedge fund and tell people that it will do some real strategy in which you can plausibly claim expertise, you give them sensible-looking account statements showing their money growing at an impressive but realistic rate, and then you steal it all. The implicit theory here is that people know what the real thing looks like, and if you can make your fake thing look exactly like the real thing then you will be able to steal a lot of money and not get caught. The other, opposite approach is just to accumulate fantasy. You set up a hedge fund that will use quantum algorithms based on astrology to trade prime bank certificates on the Ruritanian Exchange, and that promises a risk-free return of 100% per month, over the blockchain, and the portfolio manager is Elvis. And then you steal the money and tell your investors that aliens took it. The theory here is harder to pin down. One possibility is the sort of Nigerian-scammer-typo theory: You make the scheme implausible to attract only the most gullible victims, the ones who have no idea what the real thing looks like and who will give you all of their money. Another possibility is that, you know, not all scammers are entirely right in the head themselves, and many have only a sketchy knowledge of what is plausible in legitimate business. My favorite explanation, though, is that people just like fantasy. If you sell them a Ponzi scheme with risk-free 100% returns, all you are offering them is money. If you sell them a Ponzi scheme that achieves its risk-free 100% returns by infiltrating an international cabal of central bankers and taking back power for the people by using the magic of math, or whatever, then that’s a story . That’s something they can get excited about investing in, not only for the promise of money, but also for the feeling of being part of something bigger than themselves, something stranger and more magical than they get in their daily lives. The point is not for the scam to be financially plausible; the point is for it to be psychologically evocative. This is part of why I am skeptical about “financial literacy.” Sure, fine, teach classes in school about budgeting and compound interest and whatever. But your students have read, or at least watched, “Harry Potter”; they have felt the power of believing that there is a secret group of people with special powers who control the world. That is what you are up against, not just people who invest in scams because they can’t do the math, but people who invest in scams because they want to be part of something more exciting than what they learned in their high-school financial literacy class. Anyway here’s a Securities and Exchange Commission case against an alleged pyramid scheme that was also an alleged illegal offering of crypto tokens, sure: Pacheco conducted a fraudulent, unregistered offering of securities through two California-based companies he controls, IPro Solutions LLC and IPro Network LLC (collectively, “IPro”). IPro raised more than $26 million from investors by selling instructional packages that provided lessons on e-commerce. Investors also received “points” that could be converted into a digital asset known as PRO Currency. Investors who contributed additional funds could earn a mixture of cash commissions and additional convertible points by recruiting new investors into the IPro network. As alleged in the complaint, however, IPro was a fraudulent pyramid scheme. It’s just such a lovely sludge of words. It’s multilevel marketing where the product that you’re marketing is instructions on how to do marketing! But also with crypto! Here’s the defendant talking in a marketing video: Now the binary bonus. Now, folks, I love the binary. I’ve been in the binary since day one, and I absolutely love the binary and here’s the reason why … You can earn from you down to infinity with no levels to qualify. You get to override every single person’s volume in your organization, including spillover, including the volume that I get just for being in a good, strong team where people are placing people below me even though I didn’t put them there. And so that is huge because you get to override everything and 10 percent of your weaker team volume is what you’re going to get … Now I’ve been – I made seven figures – multiple companies, multiple times in this industry because of the binary. To be fair, if you are an expert in multi-level marketing this probably sounds like perfectly reasonable technical terminology, but it is hilarious gibberish to me. Of course the SEC alleges that “IPro’s inevitable collapse was hastened by Pacheco’s fraudulent use of investor funds, which included, among other things, the all-cash purchase of a $2.5 million home and a Rolls Royce.”

We talked yesterday about a move by Sirius Computer Solutions to restrict its lenders from also buying credit default swaps that would pay out if Sirius’s debt defaulted. The idea here is to prevent “net short debt activists” from buying Sirius’s loans and pushing for a default in order to get a payout on their CDS; Sirius’s loan documents would prevent net short lenders from voting on events like defaults. The original reports suggested that this provision would apply to any lender who owned CDS, and I wrote: “Notice, though, that there is nothing here about being net short.” This was wrong; Bloomberg News later reported that the provision does apply only to net short lenders.[1] So Sirius’s move isn’t quite so drastic, and won’t prevent its lenders from hedging their loans, as long as they don’t have more protection than they have loans. Sorry for the error. Still I want to stand by my basic point, which is that banning net short creditors is not just about protecting upstanding companies from evil hedge funds trying to destroy them. It’s about protecting companies that have defaulted on their debt from being punished for that default . That is, mostly, a reasonable thing to want: Lots of companies default for reasons beyond their control, and it’s often best for them and their creditors and their employees and everyone else for them to negotiate with sympathetic creditors who want to maximize value, rather than with rapacious creditors who want to minimize it. But there are other companies who default on their debt for opportunistic reasons, because they want to extract value from creditors and give it to shareholders or managers. Banning short sellers does tend to enable that sort of behavior. We have spent a few years talking about various flavors of CDS shenanigans, and one constant refrain is that these shenanigans will need to be outlawed or else they will kill the CDS market. The theories for how they’d be outlawed, and for how they’d kill the CDS market, have mostly focused on CDS market participants themselves: Maybe the International Swaps and Derivatives Association will reform CDS (and in fact it has proposed banning one popular shenanigan), and if it doesn’t, maybe investors will just stop trading it because it doesn’t behave the way it’s supposed to. Occasionally there were theories about how regulators would reform CDS (by treating some of these shenanigans as market manipulation), or even make it go away. But the idea that companies would reform CDS trading, or kill it, was less prominent, and for a fairly straightforward reason: Companies have nothing to do with CDS. The issuer of a bond isn’t party to CDS contracts referencing that bond; it doesn’t get to regulate what happens in the CDS market. But that turns out to be at least a little bit wrong. If the Sirius provision becomes popular, then companies will have a way to regulate the market for CDS on their debt, or at least, to restrict how CDS can be used to hedge their debt. It is not clear that the interests of debt issuers and the interests of debt (and CDS) buyers will be aligned. Debt issuers, after all, have been enthusiastic participants in, and beneficiaries of, lots of the recent CDS shenanigans, most notably by “manufacturing defaults” to extract some money from CDS traders for themselves. Debt issuers want as much flexibility, and as much leverage over their creditors, as they can get; the creditors tend to want tight restrictions on borrowers and to keep some leverage for themselves. If the issuers have control over the CDS market, then that is good for them, but it’s not obvious that the results will be good for the market.

Here is a story about how Palantir Technologies Inc., “one of the most hotly anticipated IPOs of this year,” might actually wait until next year to do its initial public offering. There are various good reasons for that: Its governance and financial functions are not quite mature enough to be public, and it doesn’t actually need the money. But this puzzles me a little: All it needs is for the market not to implode—as some economists fear could happen after 2019, a sentiment that has helped fuel the larger rush out the 2019 “IPO window.” I mean … didn’t that … happen? Already? Not the stock market imploding, exactly, but you’d hate to base a big corporate decision on your prediction of what the stock market will do in a year. But the 2019 IPO window was, I would have thought, largely a story about the big tech unicorns going public before the public’s appetite for unicorns was sated. You could imagine that going like: Lyft Inc. going public first to get out ahead of Uber Technologies Inc., and Lyft’s IPO trading up, and Uber going public into that momentum, and Uber trading up, and everyone realizing that public demand for the current flock of tech unicorns is robust, and WeWork and Airbnb and Palantir and all the rest taking advantage of that demand to price their own IPOs. Success would build on success, the profits that investors made on one hot IPO would encourage them to buy the next one, and a rising tide would lift all boats. But the actual thing that happened is that Lyft flopped and then Uber flopped. The spillover effects, if anything, were negative. If there was a window in 2019 in which public investors were clamoring to buy big private tech companies well above their private valuations, it seems to have shut already. Why go public into that, if you can afford to wait? In 2020, who will even remember the Uber IPO? Being one of the herd of 2019 unicorns seemed like a good idea in February; in May, the better idea might be to distance yourself as far as possible from that herd.

s.h: Is it good for you if your investment adviser is a fiduciary?
s.t: I mean yeah probably, seems reasonable. Here’s a paper on “Fiduciary Duty and the Market for Financial Advice” by Vivek Bhattacharya, Gaston Illanes and Manisha Padi. They study sales of annuity products by a big financial-services firm, and find that, in states where broker-dealers have a fiduciary duty to clients, those brokers behave differently from brokers in states with no fiduciary duty.[2] For one thing, they tend to sell simpler products: We find that extending fiduciary duty to broker-dealers leads to a compositional shift in the set of products purchased by their clients. More specifically, broker-dealers sell fewer variable annuities relative to fixed indexed annuities under fiduciary duty. The effect of fiduciary duty on variable annuity sales is substantial: about three-fourths of all annuities sold by a typical broker-dealer are variable annuities, and imposing fiduciary duty on broker-dealers reduces this proportion by around 9 percentage points. This is not the case for registered investment advisers, whose sale composition does not change. Unfortunately, it is difficult to make welfare statements about this shift, as fixed indexed annuities do not dominate variable annuities (or vice-versa). However, variable annuities have been under significant scrutiny by regulators, given their poor reputation as high fee, low yield products. That’s a story about different types of annuities, but you can easily imagine extending it to other investments. For instance, brokers with fiduciary duties to clients might sell those clients fewer actively managed mutual funds (which have developed a bit of their own “poor reputation as high fee, low yield products,” at least in some circles) and more passive index funds. This might well be good for many clients—most of my money is in index funds—but you still might find it a bit disturbing. A fiduciary broker who genuinely believes that an actively managed mutual fund is the best product for her client might hesitate to recommend it, just because she knows she is liable to be second-guessed by a regulatory preference for simplicity and low fees. A fiduciary standard might push investors into simpler and cheaper options, which is surely mostly good, but perhaps not entirely good; the ones for whom the more complicated products are better might miss out. Still, there is direct evidence that the fiduciaries are just better: By focusing on a single product type and on characteristics that have a straightforward welfare interpretation, such as fees, we are able to make clearer statements about advice quality. Annuity products have complex and multidimensional fee structures, and we find that extending fiduciary duty to broker-dealers causes their clients to purchase products with lower fees on many of these dimensions. Moreover, under fiduciary duty broker-dealers steer customers towards products with a larger and more diverse set of investment options that, under several alternative assumptions on the portfolio allocation, lead to improved mean returns. We then aggregate all these dimensions by formulating and solving a dynamic programming problem to compute the net present value of all variable annuities in the dataset, assuming optimal execution by a risk-neutral individual. We find that broker-dealers with fiduciary duty sell their clients higher-return variable annuities. Again, you can make the analogy to mutual funds. There are cheap passive funds; there are good, moderate-cost active funds; and there are bad, high-cost active funds that happen to pay large fees to brokers for recommending them. A standard that leads brokers to shift all of their clients from active to passive might be a mixed bag, but a standard that leads brokers to shift all of their clients from bad expensive active funds to good cheap ones seems more straightforwardly positive. Elsewhere, the Securities and Exchange Commission’s version of fiduciary-duty-lite will probably go into effect soon: Stockbrokers will soon have to disclose more about conflicts of interest that can bias investment advice under a government plan favored by Wall Street. The Securities and Exchange Commission plans to vote on a final rule on June 5, the agency said on Thursday. … The SEC is expected to for the first time explicitly require brokers to act in the best interest of their customers—not their own paychecks—when they recommend stocks, mutual funds and other products. The proposal didn’t succinctly define “best interest,” which frustrated some brokers and investor advocates. … One requirement, expected to be included in the final rule, is disclosure of all major conflicts of interest, such as how much a broker earns from a sales recommendation. It couldn’t be learned whether the final rule would effectively ban other conflicts beyond certain sales contests.

We have talked a few times about allegations of interest rate manipulation at Australian banks, which are a lot like the allegations of Libor manipulation at U.S. and European and Asian banks, except that the Australians’ trader-chat slang was even funnier than everyone else’s. Here is a story about “ the scandal inside ANZ,” the Autralia & New Zealand Banking Group Ltd., and while it doesn’t add much either to the pile of sweary trader chats or to the financial story of how and why Australian interest rates were manipulated, it is quite a story about banking culture . Here’s a description of an ANZ executive: In London, according to one newspaper report, he'd gotten into a trading room brawl that left him with a black eye. He had also reportedly rented out Richard Branson's Caribbean island at a cost of $40,000 a day for his wedding. His 40th birthday was said to have lasted three weeks. He was successful at his job. He loved money and he was good at making it. The 48-year-old returned to Australia and was hired to lead ANZ's global markets team. Trips to strip clubs were not uncommon under Bellotti's leadership, former traders from ANZ have told the ABC. One club became known as "The Boardroom", because, according to one employee, you were more likely to get one-on-one time with your boss there than in the office. Now, I know, you are yawning. “Ooh, violent hair-trigger traders, expensive parties, team meetings at strip clubs, whatever, I have heard this before, this is every stereotype of the financial industry in a few paragraphs,” you say. Yes! True! The amazing thing is the self-awareness. “It felt a little bit like the Wild West,” says one former trader; “it felt a little bit like a caricature of investment banking with all the excesses, but none of the substance.” What a sentence! If there is one textbook that every young investment banker and trader has read, it is not “Security Analysis” or “Principles of Corporate Finance,” it is “Liar’s Poker.” The thing that unites the industry is not the substance but the stereotypes.

[2] U.S. financial regulation is complicated. Some annuities are sold by broker-dealers, who do not have a fiduciary duty to clients under national law, but who do under state law in some states (but not other neighboring states). Other annuities are sold by registered investment advisers, who are fiduciaries under federal law. The authors study both, and mostly find that RIAs behave similarly in states with and without broker fiduciary rules (because they are fiduciaries either way), while brokers behave differently in response to different rules.

In 2015, a rural wireless company called Windstream Holdings Inc. spun off some of its assets into a separate company. This put those assets beyond the reach of Windstream’s creditors, in pretty clear violation of the covenants in Windstream’s bonds. Much later, in 2017, a hedge fund called Aurelius Capital Management LP acquired some of those Windstream bonds and sued, claiming that Windstream had violated its bond indenture and was in default. Windstream fought back hard, but eventually Aurelius won. This February, a federal judge ruled for Aurelius and awarded it $310.5 million plus interest; a few weeks later, Windstream filed for bankruptcy. In a sense, this is a straightforward vindication of the rights of creditors: Windstream violated its indenture, and Aurelius called it out and punished the violation. But it doesn’t seem to have done much good for Windstream’s actual creditors: Other than Aurelius, most of Windstream’s bondholders supported the company and voted against the default, and Aurelius’s court victory and the subsequent bankruptcy drove down the value of Windstream’s bonds. It was an abstract vindication of creditors’ rights that happens to have cost the creditors tons of money. Why did Aurelius want that? Well, perhaps they just have a moral or aesthetic commitment to holding companies to their covenants. But everyone assumes—Aurelius has never confirmed this, but everyone assumes it—that Aurelius also owned a lot of credit default swaps on Windstream, derivatives that would pay out if Windstream defaulted on its debt. When Windstream went bankrupt, those swaps were triggered,[1] and when the value of Windstream’s bonds collapsed, the value of the CDS soared. Aurelius owned a lot of Windstream bonds—that’s why it got to call a default—but it seems reasonable to assume that in total, between the bonds and the CDS, it was short Windstream’s debt: The worse that debt performed, the more money Aurelius made. People find this very objectionable. “ Net-short debt activism,” is the term for it, the idea that someone who is betting against a company will acquire some of its debt and use that position to call defaults, make trouble, and generally try to drive an otherwise healthy company into bankruptcy over a minor technical default.[2] It seems bad. After Windstream, a sense developed that companies should be careful about the motivations of creditors who buy CDS. Neiman Marcus Group did a technical transaction that made life easier for CDS owners, and an investor called it “a spectacular ‘Devil’s Bargain.’” United Natural Foods Inc. did a technical transaction that made life easier for CDS owners, and then sued its investment bankers for not telling it that that was a bad idea. Here is the obvious conclusion of that trend: Data services provider Sirius Computer Solutions wants to stop derivatives holders from influencing business decisions to benefit their bottom line at the expense of the borrower. Language in the financing package backing Sirius’ buyout by private equity firm Clayton, Dubilier & Rice (CD&R) prohibits lenders that own derivative positions from voting on company matters, according to three sources familiar with the loan credit agreement. As investor activism rises, the borrower wants to prevent these holders from declaring a default that could pay off for their hedged trades. The new provision curbs Credit Default Swaps (CDS) holders’ ability to call a default by removing their right to vote on creditor decisions. In the future, companies may also consider blocking CDS holders from owning a loan altogether, two other sources said. If you don’t want CDS owners to be able to call a default on your loans, just write your loan agreement to say that.[3] If you don't want your lenders to be able to buy CDS at all, you can write that too.[4] Notice, though, that there is nothing here about being net short . This is not “if you lend us $50 million and buy $200 million of CDS, giving you an economic interest in our failure, you can’t vote.” If you lend $200 million and buy $50 million of CDS, giving you an economic interest in Sirius’s success, but a somewhat hedged interest, you still can’t vote. This is just: If you lend Sirius money, you have to choose between (1) hedging your exposure or (2) having the usual right of creditors to vote and call defaults. In the future it might be: If you lend a company money, you can’t hedge your credit risk at all.[5] Presumably this would make loans more expensive: Companies that borrow money and prohibit hedging would, you’d think, have to pay a higher interest rate than companies that allow hedging. (I mean, theory would suggest that, but who really knows.[6]) But that’s not necessarily a reason not to do it: Companies might be happy to pay a higher interest rate in order to cut off any risk that what happened to Windstream would happen to them. But what did happen to Windstream? The story is not exactly “an evil hedge fund bought CDS and bankrupted the company.” It’s more like “the company violated its agreement with bondholders, in a pretty egregious way, and then a hedge fund bought CDS and bankrupted it.” Both parts were necessary. If Windstream hadn’t tried to put one past its bondholders, Aurelius wouldn’t have had any ability to bankrupt it. Now, a well-intentioned company might still worry about net-short debt activists: Many companies end up defaulting on their debts not due to cynical gamesmanship but because their business runs into trouble. A company could quite reasonably want to have supportive creditors in case it runs into trouble, creditors who’d be willing to work with it on a sensible value-maximizing solution, rather than net-short creditors hoping to drive it into bankruptcy. On the other hand, Sirius is not just some random company running its business the best it can and hoping that its creditors will be understanding of any mistakes. It is a private equity buyout. Private equity, as an industry, is famous for being tough on its lenders, extracting value for itself by being tricky and technical with creditors.[7] A private equity fund that wants to do something aggressive with one of its portfolio companies—pay itself a generous dividend, say, in arguable violation of its credit agreements, or, you know, spin off assets to put them out of reach of creditors—might find it useful to ban CDS, just because that would tend to scare off the sort of clever thoughtful hedged investors who might push back. If you’re doing something tricky, you’d rather face off against a long-only buy-and-hold investor than, you know, Aurelius. Your model here could be that there is a trickiness competition between private equity firms, on the one hand, and credit hedge funds, on the other, with each side trying to use its cleverness to extract value from the other. In this model, the Sirius provision is about the private equity firms escalating the stakes by cutting off one of the credit funds’ main sources of trickiness. One other model here might be that the CDS market has come full circle. One important original purpose of CDS was to let banks get rid of the credit risk of making a loan without actually getting rid of the loan. Keeping the loan, staying involved as a lender, is an important part of client service for a bank, but clients were traditionally less concerned about whether the bank hedged the credit risk.[8] Decades later, clients have discovered a dark side to that tradeoff: Staying involved as a lender while not having any credit risk, or while actively betting against the company’s credit, might be worse than selling the loan. CDS was invented because companies wanted their lenders to stick around and support them after making a loan, but it might be killed for the same reason. This section contains “Game of Thrones” spoilers so maybe skip it if that is a problem for you If (spoiler alert!) you have a psychotic break while riding on a dragon and you incinerate tens of thousands of innocent civilians in an entirely fictional medieval fantasy universe, is that securities fraud? Hahaha no, everything is securities fraud, but that is not securities fraud, come on. Nonetheless here’s this! The final season was a disaster. Talk about blowing an opportunity. Never have so many exciting characters met such boring deaths. Never have so many brilliant possibilities been thrown away. Never has so much time, money and talent been wasted mailing something in. … The only question that remains now is whether some enterprising limo-chasing lawyer is going to file a class-action suit against the company on behalf of the stockholders. Don’t rule it out. Stephenson specifically cited the value of “Game Of Thrones” when he announced his company’s massive $85 billion takeover of HBO’s parent company, Time Warner, in 2016. The takeover deal would be a “game-changer” for AT&T because of Time Warner’s “marquee businesses, including HBO,” and “blockbuster shows like ‘Game of Thrones,’ ” he wrote to all of AT&T’s employees at the time. Instead, after completing the takeover last year, he ran the “blockbuster series” for just six more episodes — each more ludicrous than the last. Look, I like to think that I have a decent ear for this sort of thing, and I am going to say: You can rule it out. Nobody is going to sue AT&T Inc. for securities fraud because the final season of “Game of Thrones” was bad.[9] But I have been wrong before, and I have to say, I hope I am wrong now. If you are a securities class-action lawyer with a sense of adventure, please, go ahead, file that lawsuit! I assume the theory would have to be, like, AT&T senior executives were going around telling shareholders that “Game of Thrones” would be good, but in fact they knew it was bad, and when the market finally got the news that it was bad, AT&T’s stock plummeted and shareholders lost money. AT&T’s stock is actually up a tiny bit since the season began, but never mind, never mind! An interesting question, in a lot of everything-is-securities-fraud cases, is how the company could have avoided committing securities fraud. Generally the issue is that a company did a bad thing and didn’t tell anyone about it, and then later the bad thing was discovered and the stock dropped. This is arguably securities fraud because the company concealed the bad thing: It made an untrue statement of a material fact, or at least omitted to state a necessary material fact. But if the company had fully disclosed the bad thing, there’d be no fraud. This never really happens— as I once put it, “Who puts in the risk factors of a 10-K ‘our CEO is a sex pest’? No one, that’s who”—but it’s theoretically possible. If you put out a press release saying “our CEO is planning to commit an egregious act of sexual harassment this afternoon, and it will destroy morale at our company, drive away clients, and lead to a messy and distracting boardroom power struggle,” then, you know, go ahead, I guess. (I mean, don’t, but if you fully and promptly disclose it then the harassment shouldn’t be securities fraud.) But if AT&T had put out a press release in March saying (spoiler alert!) “just FYI Daenerys gets stabbed by her nephew-lover for war crimes and Bran ends up king without ever doing anything useful,” then, yes, shareholders would be on notice of their possible artistic disagreements with the “Game of Thrones” showrunners, but also: You’d spoil the ending! You’d avoid the (entirely hypothetical!) securities-fraud claims, but you’d do much more damage to shareholders. And viewers, sure, but the shareholders are the ones who count.

There is a lot of worrying about automation coming for investment banking jobs. The traditional thing to think—it’s mostly what I think—is that there is a lot of room for robots to take over some of the mechanical and analytical tasks of investment banking, building discounted cash flow models and putting together working group lists and formatting pitchbooks and so forth. This might eliminate some jobs, but it doesn’t really strike to the core of the business. The business of investment banking is not primarily about corporate valuation; it’s about personal relationships and insight into human behavior. The job of a senior investment banker is to go out and talk to corporate executives, to win their trust, to listen to their needs, to dream up a product or transaction that responds to those needs, and to pitch it in a way that resonates with them at a deep emotional level. Also an analyst will run some numbers, whatever, but everyone knows that the best pitches are the ones where you never open the deck. That’s how important the analysis is! The good news is that the robots can do the analysis, but they can never replace the human touch and emotional intelligence of a great investment banker. The bad news is, um, wait, can they? Amazon.com Inc. is developing a voice-activated wearable device that can recognize human emotions. The wrist-worn gadget is described as a health and wellness product in internal documents reviewed by Bloomberg. It’s a collaboration between Lab126, the hardware development group behind Amazon’s Fire phone and Echo smart speaker, and the Alexa voice software team. Designed to work with a smartphone app, the device has microphones paired with software that can discern the wearer’s emotional state from the sound of his or her voice, according to the documents and a person familiar with the program. Eventually the technology could be able to advise the wearer how to interact more effectively with others, the documents show. Never mind then. It’s going to be awkward to lose a deal to a robot because the robot listened more carefully and responded better to the emotional subtext of what the client said. “But we formatted our pitchbook so nicely,” you'll shout, as the client goes off with the robot.

[1] Arguably they were triggered earlier, when Windstream did the thing that the court concluded was a default, but in any case they were certainly triggered by, at the latest, the bankruptcy. [2] I mean, that is the concern. I do not mean to suggest that Windstream’s spinoff of its assets was a minor technical default. Apparently many of its bondholders—the ones who didn’t object—more or less did think that, but I am not sure I’d agree. [3] Incidentally there doesn’t seem to be any CDS outstanding on Sirius. Perhaps that will change after this loan, or perhaps it would have changed if the loan didn’t have the anti-CDS provision. [4] I think that one would be harder to do with *bonds*, which trade fairly freely, as opposed to loans, which often give the borrower some right of approval over new lenders. But the voting stuff should be doable with bonds too. [5] Well, you can’t hedge it with CDS. Presumably bankers will try to find new hedging methods that they can plausibly say are not CDS and don’t fit into the loan agreements’ prohibition, and then the companies would ban that, etc. [6] For one thing, investors do not seem to be perfectly and smoothly responsive to the legal terms of loan documents: They tend to go along and accept a lot of bad terms without demanding a yield premium for them, and then occasionally have a revolt and refuse to accept a bad term at any price. For another thing, if you ban CDS then you ban hedging, but you also ban net-short debt activism, which is plausibly bad *for creditors*: Windstream’s bondholders might, in hindsight, wish that their bonds had had this provision. So maybe companies with this provision should have *lower* financing costs. There is a literature, though not, I think one that accounts for the modern worries about net-short debt activism. Here is a paper providing “evidence of credit default swaps (CDS, hereafter) playing new economic roles as a commitment device for the borrower (i.e. the firm) to repay its debt to the lender (i.e. the creditors),” and showing “that firms a priori most likely to face the limited commitment problem (i.e. firms with high strategic default incentives) experience a relatively larger reduction in their corporate bond spreads following the introduction of CDS.” Intuitively that fits with the discussion in the text: The more likely a company is to want to mess with its creditors, the more it will want to ban CDS (and the more creditors should charge it for that). [7] “PE firms’ lawyers have become specialists at burying ‘carve-outs’ deep in the hundreds of pages (sometimes 1000+) of documentation accompanying a bond sale,” as Robert Smith puts it, and he tells the incredible story of a company that tried to make a subtle two-word change to its bond documents that would allow it to pay dividends to its shareholders even after defaulting on its bonds. More generally there is a long history of private equity firms extracting value for themselves—by dividends, fees, spinoffs, etc.—from portfolio companies that eventually have to restructure their debt, essentially reversing the normal order of seniority and paying the equity while leaving creditors holding the bag. This is the sort of stuff that debt covenants are supposed to prevent, but private equity firms are at the forefront of pushing covenant-light debt that leaves them relatively unrestricted. [8] The classic account is in Gillian Tett’s book “ Fool’s Gold.” Chapter 3 describes an early CDS trade involving JPMorgan and Exxon, in which Exxon asked JPMorgan for a large credit line after the Valdez oil spill. “Like so many of J.P. Morgan’s corporate loans, it would produce little, if any profit, yet would gobble up credit, pushing the limits, and would require a large amount of capital reserve. In theory, the bank could have dealt with that headache by selling the loan to a third party, since a market for selling such loans did exist. But that would have violated its commitment to client loyalty.” The solution was to invent credit default swaps, keep the loan, but sell the credit risk. [9] There are non-securities-fraud reasons for suing companies on behalf of shareholders—“waste,” breach of fiduciary duty, etc.—but I think you can even more confidently rule those out here.

We’ve talked on and off for a few weeks about reports that early investors in Lyft Inc. hedged their investments by selling Lyft’s stock short after its initial public offering in March, and that these short sales helped drive down Lyft’s stock price. This was weird, because those early investors all seemed to be subject to lock-up agreements that forbade them from selling or hedging their stock for six months after the IPO. There were reports that the investors had found a loophole that allowed them to use some sort of hedging product that didn’t count under the lock-ups, but I was skeptical, because the lock-ups really clearly banned hedging. That doesn’t mean that banks didn’t market a hedging product, or that investors didn’t use it; it just means that, if they did, it violated the lock-up. But here is another, more plausible, possible loophole: One theory gaining ground centers on the high number of special purpose vehicles that invested in the twin ride-hailing giants when they were private companies. SPVs are often set up to invest in fast-growing startups, especially those like Uber that stay private for many years. Many employees with equity want an exit and won’t wait for an initial public offering, so those vehicles are formed to buy their stock. … There are at least 100 Uber SPVs, according to Atish Davda, chief executive officer of EquityZen Inc., a firm that handles private market transactions. He doesn’t know how many there are for Lyft. But a regulatory filing by the U.S. company in June listed seven SPVs among about 75 total backers. This creates a new set of investors who may be keen to sell -- or hedge their positions by short selling -- when the IPO finally happens. Short-selling of Lyft shares was particularly heavy after its debut. By May 9, short interest in the No. 2 U.S. ride-hailing company was 27 million shares, or 82% of the total available stock, according to financial analytics firm S3 Partners. For Uber, it was 12% on Wednesday. Less than 1% is considered normal. The simplest possibility is: When Lyft and Uber Technologies Inc. went public, they had most of their big pre-IPO shareholders, including special-purpose vehicles, sign lock-up agreements promising not to sell or hedge their stakes for 180 days after the IPO. But the SPVs’ own investors—hedge funds or other investors who funded the SPVs, who don’t own any Lyft or Uber shares directly and have no direct relationship with the companies—didn’t sign the lock-up and so aren’t bound by it. They can’t sell their shares—because, again, they don’t exactly own any—but they can hedge them (by selling shares short) because they don’t have any contractual obligations to Uber or Lyft. That theory might not be right: To be sure, SPVs often have rules that subject their backers to the same lock-ups as other shareholders. In the case of Lyft and Uber, stockholders can’t sell or short for 180 days. But it might be right- ish : Even if you are not allowed to hedge your SPV stake, who’s going to check? Lyft and Uber might not be able to enforce lock-ups against people who didn’t sign them, and might not even know who the indirect SPV holders are. The SPVs have no particular ability or incentive to check. SPV holders might even have entered into forwards to hedge before the IPO, and their forward counterparties—who never signed a lock-up—might have sold short afterwards. Another possibility: Investors in such vehicles are allowed to short, or bet against, other stocks. So some investors in Uber SPVs may have shorted Lyft to hedge their positions, and vice versa. There are more Uber SPVs than Lyft SPVs, so this could explain why Lyft stock was shorted so much more than Uber’s shares. That’s not a perfect hedge, but the companies have similar businesses and are affected by the same external factors, such as the supply and legal status of drivers. That one doesn’t even rely on SPVs; even a direct Uber investor—even Travis Kalanick—could have gone out and shorted Lyft stock when it went public. This would, in hindsight, have been bad for Uber’s stock; Uber’s own IPO priced disappointingly and traded below the IPO price, and many people blamed Lyft’s weak trading for turning investors off the Uber IPO. But, whatever, if you were an Uber investor who shorted Lyft, you were hedged against that possibility. And Uber didn’t think to require its shareholders to agree not to short Lyft ; maybe it should have. An aside: We talk sometimes about the potential anticompetitive implications of all the big shareholders in one company also being big shareholders in its competitors. But if some of the big shareholders of Uber were also short Lyft, as a hedge, then that would seem to have pretty positive competitive implications! Like those shareholders would push for aggressive competition to gain market share, because anything that Uber gains at the expense of Lyft would benefit its shareholders twice, on the long side and the short side. Private markets, I say a lot around here, are the new public markets—or at least they were back when Uber and Lyft were private. One notable difference between public and private markets has traditionally been that private companies knew who their shareholders were. They had direct relationships: Every shareholder in a private company would normally be either a founder or employee of that company, or a financial backer who negotiated with the founders to invest and then gave the company money in exchange for shares. Secondary transactions—an investor buying shares from an existing shareholder rather than from the company—were uncommon and tightly controlled; if you wanted to buy secondary shares you had to meet and negotiate with the company too. Public companies, meanwhile, trade on stock exchanges, and anyone—high-frequency traders, activist investors, hostile acquirers, disgruntled ex-CEOs—can buy their stock. But there might be some size limit on the traditional control of private companies: If your company has $1 or $10 or $100 million of outside investment, you can know all your shareholders personally; if it has $10 billion of outside investment, a lot of that is going to come in the form of special-purpose vehicles and funds for private-wealth clients and mutual-fund managers you’ve barely met. You won’t know them all well; you might not even know who they are .[1] Traditionally, this wasn’t an issue, because the size limit on being private was smaller than the size limit on knowing your investors; companies went public long before even considering raising $10 billion of outside financing. But if you can raise unlimited cash while staying private, the tradeoff might be that you lose that direct connection with your shareholders, and they just become like public-company shareholders. Elsewhere in the Uber and Lyft IPOs, here is a story about how rival banks are trying to win IPO mandates away from Morgan Stanley, Goldman Sachs Group Inc. and JPMorgan Chase & Co. by pointing out that those guys didn’t exactly do a bang-up job with Uber and Lyft. On the other hand here is a story about how Michael Grimes, the Morgan Stanley banker who led the Uber (and Facebook Inc.) IPOs, “will emerge unscathed” from those troubled deals. I think one possible lesson here is that the pricing and performance of an IPO just isn’t that important ; the IPO banker’s job is much more about befriending the company’s executives, getting them ready and confident for the glare of public markets, telling their story back to them in a way that makes them feel good, etc., than it is about actually getting them the most proceeds or a high trading price.

It was only a few weeks ago that I wrote about the possibility that Deutsche Bank AG might be “just an autonomous inflictor of misery, an emergent entity beyond the control of any human or combination of humans, pursuing its own inscrutable purposes as everyone involved looks on in impotent despair.” I was expressing some cautious optimism that that might not be true, that Deutsche Bank was instead a tool for pursuing the conscious aims of some group of humans, that it might respond to human control. But hahaha what: A software glitch at Deutsche Bank has for almost a decade prevented some potentially suspicious transactions from being flagged to law enforcement authorities, Germany’s biggest bank has discovered. … A Deutsche spokesman said one of the bank’s several anti-financial crime systems had been affected. The software, which was put in place around 2010, was designed to retrospectively to look for suspicious patterns of payments processed by clients of the corporate and investment bank. “Two of 121 parameters [of the IT application] were defined incorrectly,” said the bank on Wednesday, adding that the fault was discovered by employees of its anti-financial crime unit after it started work to improve its internal processes last autumn. “Deutsche Bank is working on correcting the error as quickly as possible and is in close contact with the regulators,” it said. I was kidding, a little bit, anyway. Every big international bank really is an emergent entity that is beyond the conscious control of its directors and senior executives; every day at every bank, thousands of people do thousands of things without getting explicit approval from the chief executive officer. If the CEO decides that the bank should not do any money laundering, he can send out a company-wide memo saying “don’t do any money laundering,” but that is probably not enough. The CEO’s job is not just to tell people what to do, at a general level; it is to set up systems that make them likely to do it. You have to delegate to good people, and set up good incentives, and foster a good culture, and build a good set of controls to check that people are doing the stuff you want. And it still won’t be perfect; even with good managers and incentives and culture and checks, there’s a risk that people will do bad stuff and embarrass the bank. People are unpredictable, and if you employ thousands of them they won’t all do what you want; the job is to build organizational and cultural and technological systems that maximize your chances of getting it right, while preparing for the certainty that someone will find a way to get it wrong anyway. But you really ought to program the software right! I’m not going to say that that’s easy—I couldn’t do it—but it is the easy part . You have to give yourself a chance. If you build a system of compliance checks and clever, unpredictable, complicated humans circumvent it, then that is life in a big organization. But if the system circumvents itself then that’s a problem.

s.h: Who should you trust for investment advice?
s.t: Not me, is the main answer. But if you are debating whether to buy any financial asset, you can, for free, consult the aggregated wisdom of all of the top professional investors whose full-time job is to figure out how much the asset is worth, and who mostly do a very good job of that. It’s an incredible convenience! The only downside is that the considered conclusion of these experts is that the asset is worth its current price. (This is called the “efficient markets hypothesis.”) So this is not a shortcut to vast wealth: If the thing is going to be worth a lot of money tomorrow, it will cost you a lot of money today. So what you want is advice from a specialized top professional who is even smarter than the aggregated wisdom of all the other top professionals, and who can identify things that are actually worth more (or less) than their current price. And who is willing to share her wisdom with you. And who will charge you a fee that is less than what that wisdom is worth. The existence of any such experts is … debated … but let’s say there are some. You might expect them to share certain characteristics. They’d probably be full-time professionals in the field of valuing and choosing financial assets. They’d probably be narrowly specialized in a particular kind of investing where they have developed deep expertise that is better than the more generalist aggregate of the market. Surely they’d be investing their own money in their ideas, and would be wealthy, and ideally their wealth would derive more from their own personal investing returns than from selling their ideas to people like you. Or you could just listen to journalists, what could possibly go wrong! Back in the second quarter of 2017, Bloomberg’s Joe Weisenthal suggested on Twitter that going long assets that journalists flag as bubbles would make for a great exchange-traded fund. Paul McNamara, who helps oversee $135 billion in assets as investment director at GAM Investments in London, took him up on it — in theory, anyway. “I plugged a bunch of securities into the Bloomberg Terminal Portfolio function to test how easy it was to make money shorting stuff that ‘everybody knows’ is overvalued,” McNamara explained to MarketWatch on Tuesday. The portfolio takes long positions in such “overvalued” favorites as Netflix, Tesla, bitcoin and, considering McNamara covers emerging markets, the “no-brainer” Argentine century bond. How did it fare in 2017? As you can see, it surged by almost 80%. Honestly! Compared to the market— the aggregated wisdom of professional investment managers with their money on the line—journalists tend to (1) spend much less time (and have much less training) on valuing financial assets, (2) be generalists, (3) not even be allowed to invest their own money in what they write about, (4) certainly not make most of their money from their personal investment decisions, and (5) um, I am sorry to say, not have as much money. Also there are professional incentives to over-identify bubbles: If you identify a bubble and it crashes, you look smart; if you identify a bubble and it keeps going up, everyone forgets; if you cheerlead for an asset and it crashes, you look super dumb. (Professional investors have mostly opposite, though also distorting, incentives: If they lose money when everyone else is making money they get fired, but if they lose money when everyone else is losing money it’s fine.) What on earth do journalists, no offense, have to recommend them? Why would you think “this newspaper columnist knows more about the value of financial assets than the aggregate of market professionals”? One possible answer is that you wouldn’t; there’s no real evidence that mobs of people actually go out and short stuff just because journalists call it a bubble. Another possible answer is just visibility: You actually read the newspaper column, or watch the TV show, where the journalist calls a thing a bubble; the aggregating work of the market is done quietly and anonymously. But another possible answer has to do with psychological plausibility. The things that journalists identify as bubbles tend to be things that look like obvious bubbles . There tends to be a one-sentence way to dismiss them—“how is a tiny car company that has never made money valued at $50 billion?” “How is a country that defaulted in 2001 and a little bit in 2014 selling 100-year bonds?”—that sounds neat and irrefutable. The market’s response is subtle and various, an aggregation of divergent views that sum up to a price that no one might want to make a direct case for. There’s not much story to it. The people who tell stories for a living sound better.

Tether is a type of cryptocurrency called a stablecoin, which means that each Tether is always supposed to be worth one U.S. dollar. Tether (the entity that managed the stablecoin) told people that the way it managed that peg was by keeping one U.S. dollar in a bank account for every Tether (the stablecoin) that was outstanding. This would be a good way to make sure that a Tether was worth a dollar, but some people claimed that Tether didn’t actually have the money, and Tether wasn’t particularly forthcoming about where the money was, so there was room for doubt. Then last month the New York State Attorney General brought a lawsuit against Tether. The lawsuit pretty convincingly refuted the popular theories that Tether didn’t have the money. No, things were even weirder than that. Tether did have the money, in cash, in bank accounts, but then it went and loaned a lot of it to Bitfinex, its affiliated cryptocurrency exchange, after hundreds of millions of dollars of Bitfinex’s client money was frozen. So Tether was 100% “backed” by “dollars,” but the backing consisted not just of cash in bank accounts but also of loans to an affiliated party. And now there is this: Tether, a stablecoin that has overlapping management and ownership with Bitfinex, admitted the company has historically used some of its reserves to make investments in bitcoin and “other assets,” according to court documents obtained by The Block. It’s the latest insight from recent court proceedings into the operations of Bitfinex and Tether — two entities that have played a major role in crypto markets whilst operating mostly opaquely. In April, the NYAG issued a court order against Bitfinex in which they alleged the firm commingled client funds and borrowed money from its sister company Tether to cover-up the seized funds. Jean Louis van der Velde, CEO of Bitfinex, responded by saying that the lawsuit is “filled with inaccuracies and false assertions.” Throughout these court proceedings, new details about how Bitfinex ran its business have been revealed. For instance, the market has learned that only 74% of outstanding Tether tokens were backed by cash held in its reserve. Bitcoin! I have vaguely defended Tether on the theory that it looks a little bit like fractional-reserve banking. Sure, yes, it did not keep 100% of its money in dollar bank accounts; it used some of the money to make interest-paying loans. But banks do this, and a dollar in a bank account is nonetheless generally treated as being worth exactly a dollar. Now there are reasons that that is true for banks, reasons that do not apply to Tether—banks have deposit insurance, and diversify their loans, and try not to make big loans to affiliated companies—but the basic shape of the thing seemed plausible enough. You have some dollars, you lend them out, you get them back with interest, it’s fine. Your Tethers aren’t 100% backed by cash , but they are 100% backed by senior claims that mature for the right number of U.S. dollars. But … if you … if you … if you take the money backing Tether, and you invest it in Bitcoin, then if Bitcoin goes up you have more dollars than there are Tethers, and if it goes down you have fewer dollars than Tethers. And Bitcoin moves around a lot! And the whole point of Tether is to avoid exposure to that! New York Supreme Court Judge Joel M. Cohen questioned the logic, noting the paradox of a stablecoin being invested in a volatile asset like bitcoin. He said: “Tether sounded to me like sort of the calm in the storm of cryptocurrency trading. And so if Tether is backed by bitcoin, how is that consistent? If some of your assets are in a volatile currency that Tether is supposed to somehow modulate, that seems like it’s playing into what they are saying.” It was “a small amount,” says Tether’s lawyer, but it’s the principle of the thing. Meanwhile Bitfinex has apparently raised enough money to pay off the Tether loans, so it’s … all … fine?

I have written before about my model of stock-exchange fees. The basic idea is that big professional traders—bank trading desks, high-frequency trading firms—mostly get to choose which exchanges they trade at , but they don’t get to choose which exchanges they connect to . If you see 100 shares for sale at the same price at the same time at different exchanges, you can buy them at whichever exchange you like most, probably the one that charges you the lowest trading fee. But for various reasons—to maximize your arbitrage opportunities and minimize risks, to know what the market looks like, to comply with best-execution obligations—you pretty much need fast connections and direct data feeds at every exchange. One implication of this is that traders will be price-sensitive to per-trade variable trading costs, but will have no choice but to pay whatever fixed data and connectivity charges the exchanges demand. Another implication is that a smart exchange will charge basically zero trading fees[1] (in order to maximize its volume and importance[2]) and extremely high fees for fast connections and data (in order to maximize its revenue from captive customers). That is not quite what happens—trading costs are not zero[3]—but it’s a decent intuition; “revenues from ICE’s and Nasdaq’s various data-related businesses rival what the companies make from trading.” Here is a paper from Eric Budish, Robin Lee and John J. Shim about “A Theory of Stock Exchange Competition and Innovation.” Their model is a lot like my model: Our model, shaped by institutional and regulatory details of the U.S. equities market, shows that under the status quo market design: (i) trading behavior across the many distinct exchanges is as if there is just a single “synthesized” exchange, as opposed to traditional platform competition; (ii) as a result, trading fees are perfectly competitive; but (iii) exchanges capture and maintain significant economic rents from the sale of “speed technology” (i.e., proprietary data feeds and co-location)—arms for the arms race. If you think of all the U.S. stock exchanges as “a single ‘synthesized’ exchange,” then obviously trading firms (ii) will prefer to trade on whichever part of the synthesized exchange is cheapest but (iii) have to see all of them. But that’s not Budish, Lee and Shim’s main point. Their main argument is that this situation discourages innovations that could make the stock market better: We then use the model to examine the private and social incentives for market design innovation. We show that the market design adoption game among incumbent exchanges is not a coordination game, but rather a repeated prisoner’s dilemma. If an exchange adopts a new market design that eliminates latency arbitrage, it would win share and earn economic rents. However, imitation by other exchanges would result in an equilibrium that resembles the status quo with competitive trading fees, but now without the rents from the speed race. This means that although the social returns to market design innovation are large, the private returns are much smaller and may be negative, especially for incumbents that derive rents from the status quo. Intuitively, if the market worked perfectly and there was no way to make money by moving information from one exchange to another faster than everyone else, then there’d be no pressure to connect to every exchange, and so exchanges wouldn’t be able to make much money selling data and connectivity. Budish is well known as an advocate of frequent batch auctions in stock markets to eliminate “the high-frequency trading arms race,” so he is perhaps more fond of “new market design that eliminates latency arbitrage” than actual market participants are, but if you are worried that U.S. stock-market design favors fragmentation, complexity, and advantages for high-frequency traders, then this might help explain why.

Here is a delightful story about a firm called Potamus Trading, which “shuttered its proprietary HFT business in January 2018, shifting its strategy and expertise to focus solely on serving asset managers as a broker-dealer”: Potamus uses two-sided trading strategies that play to its stengths as a former market-maker. While most brokers typically use a one-sided algorithm to move the necessary amount of stocks — either buying or selling in various increments — Potamus will play both sides of the market. As an example, if a client wanted 10,000 shares of Apple, Potamus might buy 50,000 shares and sell 40,000 shares in the process of filling the order. Doing so allows Potamus to fly under the radar. "We find that the size of the client orders that we fill are much harder for the other HFTs out in the market to detect, because our system does not systematically send 1,000 shares every second that HFTs are built to seek out," Linnell said. Potamus doesn't charge clients a commission fee, another uncommon practice amongst brokers. Instead, it takes a share of the profits made from the market-making that took place while handling the order. The client also gets a cut. Intuitively, the way many high-frequency trading firms work is that they run essentially market-making-type strategies: They post bids and offers to buy and sell a stock, and try to buy at the bid and sell at the offer, capturing the small spread between them while carefully managing the risk of the stock moving against them. The goal is to make a tiny bit of money on each trade, but never to own a lot of any one stock for any long period of time. You’re not getting paid to pick stocks that will go up. You’re getting paid for providing liquidity, being willing to buy at the exact microsecond when someone else wants to sell. But you could tweak that, right? Instead of buying 100 shares and selling 100 shares within a second or two, you could buy 100 shares and sell, like, 90 shares, capturing some bid-ask spread, carefully managing your risk, and also, slowly, accumulating some stock. Instead of just going to buy stock, you do your market-making with a slight long bias. That way, you can (perhaps) end up both buying the stock and getting paid for providing liquidity—for buying when others want to sell and vice versa—rather than paying someone else to give you liquidity (by selling you the stock you want). A similar basic idea has been kicking around in the bond markets for a while. People complain all the time about bond market liquidity, by which they mean basically that big banks no longer carry large inventories of bonds and so aren’t willing to provide liquidity by buying and selling bonds, at their own risk, when investors want to trade. But big bond investors do carry large inventories of bonds, and might not care all that much about exactly which bonds they own: Of course they have preferences, but they own lots and lots of bonds and no one bond is all that important, so if you really want to buy one of their bonds or sell them a similar bond, then for the right price they might be willing to swap. So there is a lot of talk about the buy-side—big institutional bond investors—becoming liquidity providers, augmenting their basic business (of picking, buying and holding bonds) with a little extra income from buying bonds other people want to sell, selling bonds other people want to buy, and clipping a bid-ask spread. Potamus seems like the same basic idea, but for the weird electronic world of equity trading. Still I feel like there will be objections? People do not like high-frequency traders. One thing that they dislike about HFTs is that they create a lot of unnecessary trading, that the stock market becomes just a game between computers rather than actually reflecting supply and demand; a strategy that lets people buy 10,000 shares by trading 50,000 shares seems a bit wasteful. Another thing that people dislike about HFT is that they think it is synonymous with “spoofing”: HFTs are constantly entering and canceling orders, and there is a popular sense that they are doing this to manipulate prices rather than for normal risk-management purposes. If you want to buy 100 shares of stock, it can make sense to put in an order to sell 10,000 shares to try to drive the price down (as long as that sell order doesn’t execute), but that is illegal spoofing. If you want to buy 10,000 shares, and the way you go about it involves selling 40,000 shares in order not to overpay for the 10,000, well, that isn’t spoofing, but to a casual observer it might seem to have a certain family resemblance.

Libor, the London interbank offered rate, is the world’s main reference interest rate for floating-rate debt and interest-rate derivatives. People do not like Libor, both because there was a giant scandal in which banks were caught manipulating Libor for their own profit and vanity, but also, and more fundamentally, because Libor is basically a made-up number and so it is easy to manipulate. Libor is the interest rate on short-term unsecured loans between banks, and there are not all that many of those loans, and so when banks are asked—as they are, in setting Libor—what rate they would have to pay to borrow money unsecured from another bank, they kind of have to guess. Why wouldn’t their guesses be biased? And so there is a big worldwide movement, strongly encouraged by regulators, to replace Libor with something more real. The favored replacement in the U.S. is SOFR, the secured overnight financing rate, which is based on the market for overnight loans collateralized by Treasury securities. A big advantage of SOFR is that it is based on real transactions, so it’s hard to manipulate.[4] Another advantage of SOFR is that it is useful as a risk-free rate: It’s for very short-term loans backed by very high-quality collateral, so it doesn’t really incorporate credit risk. A major use of a reference interest rate is as a risk-free rate, and in fact Libor was also widely used, back in the day, as a sort of stand-in for a risk-free interest rate. Then everyone remembered that banks can be really risky, Libor went up a lot, and it stopped being useful as a risk-free rate. On the other hand, Libor was kind of useful as a reference rate for bank loans exactly because it reflected some of the banks’ own costs: It was a way for banks to make loans on a sort of cost-plus basis, reducing their risks and thus encouraging the growth of the loan market. So replacing it with SOFR, and putting the interest-rate risk of loans on the banks, has some negatives. The “mismatch” between SOFR and the banks’ own costs arguably “would make banks reluctant to lend during a period of stress.” There are other problems with SOFR. It’s an overnight rate, which is annoying; a floating-rate loan whose rate changes every three months with three-month Libor is more administratively manageable than one whose rate changes every day with one-day SOFR. There are ways—averaging, futures curves—to bootstrap SOFR into a longer-term rate, but they’re not as simple and intuitive as just having a ready-made three-month Libor rate. Anyway here is an article about how SOFR adoption is going slowly. It mentions those problems, but a key problem is something different and dumber: The Fed’s working group is also reaching out to designers of accounting and trading systems about speeding development of products that can function with the new rate. Many investors and companies can’t buy or sell debt linked to SOFR because their accounting and trading systems aren’t properly configured for it, said Venetia Woo, principal director of North American regulatory strategy at Accenture. “The reality is, people want to trade and people want to hedge,” Ms. Woo said. “Physically their infrastructure is not ready for it.” Imagine that everyone agreed that SOFR was a perfect replacement for Libor, superior in every respect. Theory would tell you that they’d all adopt SOFR, and they probably would. But it wouldn’t be instantaneous. There’d be some period—years?—of people going around saying things like “well obviously SOFR is better but we haven’t upgraded our computers yet” or “well sure but it takes time to renegotiate 200 contracts” or “yeah half of my clients haven’t heard of SOFR yet.” In the long run finance tends to proceed through logic and self-interest, but in the short run the computer systems cause a lot of frictions.

Here’s a story about some businesses that conspire together to charge higher prices to consumers: Every night, several times a night, Uber and Lyft drivers at Reagan National Airport simultaneously turn off their ride share apps for a minute or two to trick the app into thinking there are no drivers available---creating a price surge. When the fare goes high enough, the drivers turn their apps back on and lock into the higher fare. … “All the airplanes we know when they land. So five minutes before, we turn all our apps off all of us at the same time. All of us we turn our apps off. They surge, $10, $12, sometimes $19. Then we turn our app on. Everyone will get the surge,” one driver says. This driver explains how they organize it. “Someone is standing by that corner. I stand by this corner and the other one stands at this corner and we say turn the app off and then go online." We have talked before about law professor Sanjukta Paul’s discussion of “the firm exemption” in antitrust law, the fact that a business firm is a legal way to coordinate actions in a way that would be illegal for private individuals. Imagine if instead of a bunch of independent-contractor Uber drivers waiting at the airport, this was just a story about a bunch of drivers employed by Uber, charging prices set by Uber and getting paid a wage by Uber.[5] If that was how Uber Technologies Inc. operated—if its drivers were employees—then Uber could set whatever prices it wanted. If its strategy was like “we will raise fares from the airport when a plane lands, and lower them again when there are no planes,” that would be a perfectly legal and sensible strategy; people would complain—people really don’t like surge pricing—but it would basically be fine. It’s a company, it can charge whatever prices it wants, as long as people are willing to pay. Similarly, if Uber’s drivers felt that they were being underpaid—and they do; that’s why they’re turning the app off—then they could go to Uber and negotiate for higher wages. They could coordinate to do this, starting a union and bargaining collectively and maybe striking to put pressure on Uber. The result might be higher wages, paid for by higher prices to consumers, kind of like what is happening here. But that isn’t quite what is happening here. Instead of Uber setting prices, telling its employees what to charge, and negotiating wages collectively with employees, there are just a bunch of independent businesses, linked only by the fact that they all use the same software app to market their services to riders, conspiring to push up consumer prices. They are openly discussing, with their independent-businessperson competitors, coordinating to raise prices for consumers—and using the app to implement their agreement. If they were all coworkers this would be legal, but they aren’t, so it’s, at least, troubling. It is somewhat strange how much turns on that distinction. People often talk about how important it is for Uber and Lyft that their drivers be classified as independent contractors rather than employees, because the companies don’t want to have the legal obligations (minimum wages, overtime, health care) that businesses have to employees. (“Our business would be adversely affected if Drivers were classified as employees instead of independent contractors,” says a risk factor in Uber’s initial public offering prospectus.) On the other hand if the drivers are just independent businesses, and if the app gives them a way to coordinate with their competitors to raise prices on consumers, isn’t that … also a problem? “The Legal Argument That Could Destroy Uber,” is how Jalopnik described it, citing Paul’s work, and I might not go that far, but Uber’s setup does seem to raise some weird antitrust problems that would be avoided by just employing the drivers.

There are different skill levels of fraud. There is the kind of fraud where you lie to people to get them to invest with you, and then you steal their money and either run away (skillful) or get caught (bad). There is the more impressive kind of fraud where you lie to people, steal their money, and then explain everything to them so persuasively that they are satisfied with their losses and don’t complain to the authorities. Even better is the kind where you then get them to invest more money with you to continue the scam. I particularly enjoy the kind where you lie to people to get them to invest with you, steal their money, and then explain that their money was actually stolen by shadowy nefarious characters and promise to track down the thieves and recover the money, if they just give you some more money first to cover your expenses. I suppose an additional level would be stealing people’s money, getting caught, getting fined by the Securities and Exchange Commission, and then managing to avoid paying the fine: The Securities and Exchange Commission over five fiscal years that ended in September 2018 took in 55% of the $20 billion in enforcement fines set through settlements or court judgments, according to agency statistics. During the prior five years, from 2009 through 2013, the SEC collected on 60% of $14.6 billion. Some of that is for sort of double-counting settlements in which the SEC imposes a fine but lets the defendant pay it to some other regulator, allowing both the SEC and the other regulator to count the fine in their wins column. But some of it is for “those behind Ponzi schemes who spent the funds they took from defrauded investors.” I would think that if you’re good enough at stealing money, you should also have an aptitude for hiding it from the SEC. Still there is a further level of difficulty; really the move is to do a Ponzi, get caught and fined by the SEC, not pay the fine, and get the SEC to pay you . I am not sure exactly how it would work but, you know, there’s a lot of money in whistle-blowing. There’s that guy who did tax fraud, went to prison for it, and got a $104 million whistle-blower award from the Internal Revenue Service; I bet you could figure out a similar trade with the SEC.
