Remember how Lyft Inc. went public, and there was some selling pressure on its stock, and Lyft complained that Morgan Stanley was supposedly “marketing a short-selling product” to early investors in Lyft who were subject to lockup agreements, and Morgan Stanley denied it, and none of it made any sense? In particular, what made no sense is that the lockup agreements—which restrict pre-IPO shareholders from selling stock until at least six months after the initial public offering—really really clearly prohibited hedging of the stock, so the “short-selling product” sort of obviously would not work. I chalked it all up to a misunderstanding. But here is a tantalizing clue: One of those pitfalls was a big hedge related to a trade between investing legends George Soros and Carl Icahn that was seen as weighing on Lyft shares. Uber’s lawyers have scoured Lyft’s lockup agreement—which prohibits early investors from selling the shares until a set time after the IPO—for the kind of loopholes that permitted the hedge, so that Uber might close them ahead of its IPO. Mr. Soros bought a 2.7% stake in Lyft from Mr. Icahn in the days leading up to the San Francisco company’s IPO. Before buying the shares, for about $550 million or $60 apiece, Mr. Soros hedged a big chunk of the stake, people involved in the process said. Hedges, which can take various forms, are typically used to mitigate potential losses on an investment. You could just about imagine something that almost worked here. Like here is my pure speculation about how this sort of trade could go: Icahn is a pre-IPO Lyft shareholder subject to a lockup agreement that prohibits public sales and hedging after the IPO. He calls up Soros before the IPO and says “hey wanna buy my stock? I’ll sell it to you for $60, well below the IPO price of $72.” Soros says “hang on a minute.” Soros calls a bank and asks it to synthetically short some Lyft shares for him after the IPO. It is not clear exactly what the trade would be, but it could be “write me a swap on Lyft stock based on the average price over the first few days of trading,” something like that. They enter into a contract before the IPO, but the price will be set after the IPO, when the bank hedges by selling stock. If they used the average price over the first three days, for instance, the strike price on the swap would be about $72.07. The swap would have some term—at least six months, one assumes, until the end of the lockup—and at the end of the term if the stock price is below the strike price, the bank pays Soros the difference; if it’s above, Soros pays the bank. Also at the end of the term Soros sells his stock. Effectively he locks in a price—the strike price of the swap—for his shares in the first few days of trading. (You could do some other, more complicated trade—collars and so forth—but this is the basic template.) The bank says “sure, you’re not a Lyft insider, we can just sell some stock when it becomes public and give you the economics of that short.” Soros signs that deal with the bank. He picks up the line with Icahn and says “okay now I’ll buy your stock.” Icahn says “my lawyers tell me you have to sign a lockup saying you won’t sell or hedge it for six months.” Soros says “oh sure I’ll sign the lockup now .” It all makes me a little nervous but maybe it could work. The lockup obviously prohibits hedging, and Soros apparently did sign the lockup, but if he did the hedging before he signed the lockup then there’s no problem. I guess. And if Soros bought the stock from Icahn at $60 before the IPO, and hedged it in the $70s or high $60s during the first few days of trading, he did great; the stock fell rapidly from there and is now in the low $60s. And if it did go something like this, you can see why Lyft (and its banks) would hate it. Not only would Soros’s counterparty bank be selling a fair bit of stock during the volatile first few days of trading to hedge the trade, but also the story that Lyft told to prospective investors in the IPO—a story about how its early investors were locked up and couldn’t sell or hedge for six months—was not quite true, because Soros found a loophole. The people who bought stock in the IPO, thinking that insiders were all locked up, and then found out that they weren’t and were dumping stock, have some cause to complain, not only about Soros but also about Lyft. There is more about the Lyft IPO’s troubles in that Wall Street Journal article. For instance: Meanwhile, JPMorgan was tasked with stabilizing the stock. This role is coveted because of the prestige and potential additional fees and trading commissions it can generate. As the stabilization agent, JPMorgan played a major role in deciding whether to exercise the so-called green shoe option to buy additional shares from the company to support the stock. The bank tried to use the green shoe on the second day of trading, according to people familiar with the matter, but it was largely ineffective given the torrent of sell orders. Some investors in the IPO questioned whether JPMorgan could have supported the stock more aggressively to stem the tide of selling. The way the greenshoe works is that, in the IPO, the underwriters sold 15 percent more stock than Lyft did. That is, Lyft sold the underwriters 32.5 million shares of stock in the IPO, but the underwriters placed 37.4 million shares with investors. (The underwriters sold the shares for $72, but bought them from Lyft at $70.02; the $1.98 difference is their fee for the underwriting.) The underwriters were short the extra 4.9 million shares. If the stock went up in the days after the IPO, stabilization would be unnecessary, and JPMorgan would cover that short position by buying the extra shares, from Lyft, at the IPO price. (This is called the “overallotment option,” or “greenshoe.”) If the stock went down , though, or threatened to go down, JPMorgan would cover the short position by buying back the extra shares in the market, which would have the effect of stabilizing the price, because JPMorgan would be a big buyer. There is an interesting economic dynamic there. If the stock went up and stayed up, the underwriters would exercise the greenshoe and buy 4.9 million shares for $70.02, after already selling them for $72. That’s an extra $9.7 million in fees for the underwriters, of which JPMorgan would get 32 percent, or about $3.1 million. If the stock did not trade well, and after going up for a while started going down again and threatened to break through the IPO price of $72, JPMorgan would instead use its short position to stabilize the stock, buying shares in the open market at $72 to try to prevent the stock from breaking through that level. The underwriters would forego the extra $9.7 million by buying back at $72, but they’d help stabilize the stock. But a third possibility is that the stock would threaten to break through $72, and JPMorgan would buy some stock at $72 to defend that price, but it would be “largely ineffective given the torrent of sell orders,” and the stock would trade below $72 anyway. And then JPMorgan would defend the new price, buying back stock at $71.50 or $71 or $70 or whatever on the way down. This would be profitable: If you sell stock short at $72 and buy it back at $71, you make a dollar. It’s more profitable the lower the stock goes: If for some reason JPMorgan didn’t buy in its entire short position on the second day of trading,[1] it could have covered on the third day, when the average price of the stock was about $68.40. That’s not only lower than $72, it’s also lower than $70.02: The underwriters would make more money buying back their short in the market than they would exercising the greenshoe. So what are their incentives? Well, if you are a stabilization agent, and the stock is just above $72 and heading down, you can put in a giant bid at $72, and just stand ready to buy as much as there is to sell at $72. You’ll eat through your entire 4.9 million shares, and the stock won’t go below $72, and then when you run out of firepower it will. It is not at all clear that this is a good idea: If everyone knows that the stock is going to break through $72 as soon as you run through your 4.9 million shares, you will become a target; a lot of people will sell stock trying to push the price down, and when you do run out of the 4.9 million shares the price will collapse rapidly. Also you will make zero dollars on this trade, because you sold at $72 and bought back at $72. Or you can put in a smaller bid at $72, and buy some stock at $72, but if it looks like there is no other support there, you can try to lead an orderly retreat, buying more stock on the way down to cushion the fall. The stock will break through $72 sooner, but it won’t be a disorderly collapse; your trading will be less of a predictable target, which will perhaps reduce teh selling pressure. Also you will make money on this trade, because you sold at $72 and bought back at lower prices. You have made more money, and you have at least a plausible justification for why it was a better tactical choice, but on the other hand someone will question whether you “could have supported the stock more aggressively to stem the tide of selling.”

There are three main lessons in this story about how Goldman Sachs Group Inc. developed a hard-won deep relationship with Uber Technologies Inc., but then ended up losing the lead role on Uber’s initial public offering to Morgan Stanley anyway. The first lesson is that the only way for a bank to develop a relationship with a client is for human bankers to develop a relationship with human client executives and directors . Sure, the bank as a corporate entity can do favors for the client as a corporate entity—it can give the client a loan, or use its franchise to sell the client’s securities, or whatever—but the corporate entity will not really feel gratitude; only humans feel gratitude. In the long run maybe you can build so deep a relationship that it becomes ingrained in the corporate cultures, so that every employee at the client thinks fondly of the bank and is naturally inclined to call its bankers for advice and deals, but at least in the beginning the relationship is going to be about a handful of senior bankers building trust and friendship with a handful of client executives. And if those executives get tossed out, oops, there goes the relationship: It was over meat pies and beers in a Dublin pub that Stanford first met Uber founder Travis Kalanick. At the time, Stanford was leading Goldman Sachs’s internet investment-banking practice and had previously secured investments in other companies, such as Facebook Inc. and LinkedIn Corp., from other corners of the bank. Before long, he had become a trusted counsel to Uber. … [In 2017], Uber’s top management was swept out, following allegations of boorish behavior and toxic workplace culture. Morgan Stanley kept edging into more conversations, private placements and debt deals. If you are going to build trust and loyalty with a client executive, you have to show loyalty to him too; you have to stand by him in tough times. If the times get so tough that he stops being a client executive, well, that’s the risk you take. The second lesson is that, while having the skills and knowledge and diligence to underwrite a securities offering is lucrative, having the skills to pick the right early-stage technology investments is way more lucrative: Goldman Sachs Group Inc. is missing out on leading the hottest IPO in years, Uber Technologies Inc. The consolation: a potential $600 million windfall from a mere $5 million wager that Goldman’s bankers made using the firm’s own money back in 2011, only a year after Uber had started offering rides. Yeah Morgan Stanley isn’t getting $600 million in IPO fees for Uber. Total fees look to be about 1 percent of the $8 or $9 billion that Uber is looking to raise, meaning that Uber’s 29 underwriters will probably share something less than $100 million between them. A third lesson is that bankers maybe overrate prestige a little bit. The story emphasizes how sad it is for Goldman that Morgan Stanley is “lead left” on the deal—the first underwriter listed on the cover page of the prospectus, and the one most responsible for leading the IPO: It’s a spot on the page that investment bankers pursue with zeal -- and then tout for years. “The types of people attracted to the banking world are competitive in nature,” [former Goldman President Gary] Cohn said. “One of the measuring sticks for competition is lead left.” Sure fine whatever, but Goldman is also an underwriter of the Uber deal. (Disclosure, I used to work at Goldman.) It’s listed second on the prospectus. It still gets to put this deal on all its credential pages and count it for league-table credit. It will still get a lot of money in underwriting fees: The breakdown isn’t public yet, but consider that in the Lyft IPO the lead left underwriter got 32 percent of the fees and the second underwriter got 27 percent. And the second does a lot less work! I am sure that Goldman is just devastated to be listed second on Uber’s long list of underwriters, but I am sure that, say, Canaccord Genuity LLC is thrilled to be listed 18th. That’s basically just free money.

There are two problems with insurance that are so well known as to be clichés. One is adverse selection: The person buying insurance usually knows more about her particular risks than the insurance company does. The person buying health insurance knows how healthy she is; the person buying car insurance knows how carefully or recklessly she drives; the person buying fire insurance knows about the stash of fireworks in her basement; the insurance company doesn’t know these things firsthand. So there’s a good chance that the people who buy the most insurance will be the most unprofitable customers, the ones who will make the most claims. This is not always true in practice—I suspect “wanting a lot of car insurance” and “driving carefully” are related personality traits—but it has a lot of truth to it and is in any case a cliché. The other problem is moral hazard: Once the customer buys the insurance, she doesn’t have to worry as much about the risk, so she might get more reckless. If you have fire insurance, go ahead and light those fireworks; if you have car insurance, go ahead and crash your car. Again this is not always true in practice—getting a big car-insurance payout doesn’t help much if you die in the car crash—but again it is both an important insight and a cliché. There are well-known though imperfect approaches to mitigate these problems. Car insurers, for instance, can look at your driving record, at your demographic characteristics and the type of car you drive to try to guess how well you drive and reduce adverse selection, and they can use deductibles and the threat of higher premiums to reduce moral hazard. But these are all pretty imperfect. What would be ideal is if the insurance company could drive your car for you . Then there’d be no adverse selection: The insurance company would know more about how you drive than you do, because it is doing the driving for you. And there’d be no moral hazard: You won’t drive recklessly once you’re insured, because the insurance company will be doing the driving, and it will bear the (financial) cost of any accidents.[2] So! Tesla Inc. is creating its own branded insurance program, a move the electric-car maker believes will enable it to offer a lower-cost product to drivers. Tesla Chief Executive Elon Musk has been working with a unit of Virginia-based Markel Corp. and another company, which hasn’t been named, to offer the branded insurance, according to Markel and regulatory insurance filings in California, where Tesla is based. Revealing the program’s existence in an earnings call last month, Mr. Musk said the goal was to more accurately take into account the safety benefits of the cars’ Autopilot driver-assistance system. Tesla says it has far better data on the performance of its vehicles and their drivers than other insurers do, and believes it can use this information to offer customers lower-cost insurance, according to the California filings. In the call, Mr. Musk said buyers would have “to agree to not drive the car in a crazy way.” If they do, their insurance rates would be higher, he said. I mean, obviously. If Tesla is driving the car for you, it its best positioned to give you insurance. If you try to get insurance from some other company, and you say “no I am a very safe driver because my Tesla does all my driving for me,” then the insurance company will say “but how do I know that your Tesla is a safe driver” and will have only imperfect and disputed statistical information to go on. But if Tesla is giving you the insurance, then it knows all there is to know about how safely Tesla’s Autopilot drives. And it has good incentives to make Autopilot drive more safely, because it has to pay for any accidents. Also if somehow Tesla’s insurance ends up being twice as expensive as anyone else’s, you know not to turn on the Autopilot! The far future outcome here is presumably that (1) all cars are self-driving and (2) self-driving-car manufacturers are strictly liable for all accidents caused by their cars. Tesla is just approaching that outcome in a free-market sort of way.

Well, sure: Bridgewater Associates co-Chief Executive Officer Eileen Murray has held repeated conversations inside and outside of the firm about leaving the world’s largest hedge fund, according to people familiar with the matter. Ms. Murray was recently contacted by representatives of Wells Fargo & Co. about the bank’s open CEO role, people familiar with the matter said. Wells Fargo representatives also called people close to Ms. Murray as part of that process. Ms. Murray subsequently tipped off the job possibility to others at Bridgewater, these people said. Sometimes I make fun of Bridgewater’s culture of radical transparency and endless self-examination, but this sounds kind of nice? Like if you work with a bunch of smart people for a long time, and you get a job offer elsewhere, it would be nice to come into work and tell all your colleagues about it and be like “do you think I should take this new job?” And then they respond with radical honesty, and use their firm-issued iPads to rate the advantages and disadvantages of leaving for the new job. At most workplaces it would be a little awkward to talk to your colleagues about quitting for a new job; at Bridgewater, as far as I can tell, everything is so awkward that this is fine.

s.h: Public markets are the new private markets are the new public markets wait what?
s.t: For a few years now I’ve had a schtick around here that “private markets are the new public markets.” A whole bunch of private venture-backed technology companies started and grew and became enormous without ever bothering to go public. This seemed to reflect deep changes in the capital markets, as the globalization of capital and the rise of technology made it easier for companies to access deeper pools of private capital, changed the balance of power between entrepreneurs and capital providers, and reduced the need for companies to go public to become large and famous. Being public was no longer a necessary condition for being big, and the implications for public markets and corporate governance and growth and inequality seemed important and complex. And then they all went public. I mean, they haven’t all gone public yet, but Lyft and Spotify and Pinterest did, and Uber and Slack and WeWork have filed to go public, and Palantir and Airbnb are rumored to be in the works. I suppose there will always be venture-backed technology companies with multibillion-dollar valuations that haven’t gone public yet, but the big herd of unicorns that we all know and love is dying out. The cool thing, for a certain type of big global technology company a year ago, was to be private, now it is to be public. And the SoftBank Vision Fund has a pretty good sense of what’s cool in technology investing: SoftBank Group Corp. is considering audacious fundraising plans, including a public offering of its $100 billion investment fund and the launch of a second fund of at least that size, as it looks to seize on an exploding startup scene, people familiar with the matter said. … A Vision Fund IPO is the most ambitious of the plans under consideration and would take place after the fund is fully invested, likely by this fall, according to people familiar with the matter. The hope is to create a smaller version of Warren Buffett’s Berkshire Hathaway Inc. —only loaded with young technology companies, many of which have yet to turn a profit, instead of a stable of well-established utilities, insurers and energy companies. An offering like this is largely unprecedented. If successful, it would tap into a new pool of money—mom-and-pop investors—who typically can’t invest in venture-capital funds due to regulations meant to protect unsophisticated investors from risky assets. SoftBank executives are working to overcome those regulations, some of the people said, and it might not happen. I mean it doesn’t sound especially legal, at least under U.S. law. Berkshire Hathaway, for all that we think of it as a Warren Buffett stock-picking vehicle, is actually an insurance company with a bunch of other wholly-owned operating businesses. A fund consisting entirely of minority stakes in other companies—that is, a venture fund—would seem to count as an “ investment company” under U.S. law, and U.S. rules do tend to discourage widely marketed investment companies that buy mainly illiquid private stakes. One thing that is happening here might just be the flip side of Elon Musk’s pretend going-private transaction for Tesla Inc. Musk tweeted that he was going to take Tesla private but allow all of its current public shareholders to keep their stakes, and everyone scratched their heads and said “well how would that work,” and the answer turned out to be that it wouldn’t and there was no plan at all to make it work. It just seemed to Musk that it would be nice if Tesla was not publicly listed, and so he figured there had to be some way around the investor-protection rules that mostly limit retail investors to public companies. Those rules, to a visionary like Musk, seemed trivial. Similarly, here, there’s a visionary involved (SoftBank founder Masayoshi Son), and a vision, and fund literally named the Vision Fund, so it seems a little silly to get bogged down in investor-protection rules designed to prevent venture capital funds from raising billions of dollars from retail investors. Maybe the explanation is that the last few years really have knocked down the boundaries between public and private capital. As companies like Uber raise billions of dollars from retail investors and mutual funds, as SoftBank and its Vision Fund buy public and private stakes and compete with venture capitalists and mutual funds for private deals, those legal categories have just lost some of their practical importance for bankers and companies and investors. In high finance, the public/private distinction just doesn’t matter nearly as much as it used to, and so people take it less seriously. Everyone Masayoshi Son or Elon Musk talks to can invest easily in public or private companies, so they forget that lots of people can’t. Anyway the rest of that SoftBank article is worth reading, because the Vision Fund is pretty wild even beyond the IPO stuff. “Mr. Son recently returned from China, where he negotiated informal deals worth several billion dollars that the Vision Fund doesn’t yet have,” is one pretty magical sentence. Also governance at a public Vision Fund would be a hoot: Another challenge is the existing Vision Fund has struggled with some investments. One plan to boost its returns, on hold for now, was to transfer the fund’s stake in chip maker Arm Holdings back to SoftBank, which bought it in 2017 and then sold a stake to the fund, people familiar with the matter said. Arm Holdings’ weaker-than-expected performance—exacerbated by the high price Mr. Son paid for the company—has pushed returns below what the Vision Fund wanted to show its investors, the people said. What? Like: SoftBank invests in companies. It has a habit of “transferring the stakes to the Vision Fund—often at a higher price,” making a profit for SoftBank at the expense of Vision Fund investors. But if the Vision Fund investors don’t make enough money, that’s embarrassing for SoftBank, so it might buy the stakes back? Perhaps all of this is done in an arm’s-length way that is fair to both SoftBank shareholders and Vision Fund investors, or perhaps Masayoshi Son has such a finely tuned sense of justice and aesthetics (and is such a good investor) that everyone gets a return they’re satisfied with, but it is a pretty curious way to run an investment fund and a public company.

Three things that bankers do in an initial public offering are: Figure out who might want to buy the stock; Talk to those investors to see how much stock they want to buy and at what price; and Try to persuade those investors to buy more stock and at a higher price, by talking up the prospects of the company and by creating a sense of scarcity and FOMO around the deal. The goal is not exactly to get the highest price possible for the company. You want the stock to trade up after it’s priced. There are good standard reasons for this: The investors are taking a risk on a new stock and so expect a positive return; the company itself may need to come back to the capital markets, and its executives and early investors probably still own big stakes, and so they want the stock to trade up so that investors will be happy. But the most important reason that bankers want the stock to trade up is that they are repeat players in the business of doing stock offerings , and the investors who buy those offerings (and who are also repeat players) will be happier to buy the next offering if they made money on the previous one. This can look a little awkward from the outside—it sounds like the bankers are putting the interests of their own franchise over the interests of their issuer clients—but that is, I think, a misunderstanding; the reason the clients hire the bankers in the first place is that they have a valuable franchise, and the bankers preserve that value for the long term so that they can use it to help all their clients. Still, I mean, at some point. Like if you sell stock in an IPO at $25, and it opens for trading the next day at $45 and then closes at $65.75, you have made a mistake. Maybe your list of who might want to buy the stock was incomplete, and you missed out on huge sources of demand, people who wanted to buy the stock but whom you never called. (Perhaps these were retail investors, who tend not to have much input into IPO pricing but who sometimes flock to buy hot stocks on their first day of trading.) Or your list of buyers was fine, but you didn’t do a good job of finding out how much stock they wanted to buy and at what price: You asked them “how much stock do you want to buy and would you pay $19 or $20 or $21,” and they were like “we want to buy everything you’ve got and we’d pay more than that,” and you were like “okay we’ll sell an extra 1 million shares and price it at $25” but you neglected the possibility of, um, $45, or $65. Which is actually an understandable omission. If you launch an IPO with a price range of $19 to $21, and then demand is really good, you can raise the price range, but you can’t really raise it to $45. There are legal reasons for this—increasing the price by more than 20 percent from the initial range requires going back to the Securities and Exchange Commission and can delay the IPO—but the psychological anchoring reasons are probably more important. If you offer people stock at $21 and they’re falling over themselves to buy it, you can sell it to them at $25 and they’ll say “fair enough, yeah, we love this stock.” If you offer it at $21 and they’re falling over themselves and you raise the price to $45, they are going to think you’re a bit of a price gouger. They might want the stock at $45, but they also want a deal, and doubling the price feels like a bad deal. Also, at least in some vague sense the price range for an IPO is a valuation ; it’s not just the bankers saying “here’s what people might pay,” but also the bankers saying “here’s what we think this company is worth based on discounted cash flow models and comparable stocks and our own long experience of bringing companies to market.” If you say the company is worth $19 to $21 and everyone wants to pay $25, fine, there is a difference of opinion, let them pay $25. If you say it’s worth $19 to $21 and everyone wants to pay $45, then something serious and hard-to-admit has gone wrong with your analysis. Anyway: Beyond Meat Inc. went where no company had gone in more than a decade as shares nearly tripled in their first day of trading. The 163 percent surge for the maker of vegan beef and sausage products was the best debut session of any U.S. listing since at least 2008 among IPOs that raised at least $200 million. Beyond Meat saw its market value balloon to $3.83 billion at the close of trading. Oops. It’s not a trivial error—Beyond Meat sold about 18.5 percent of itself in the IPO at $25 per share, to raise about $277 million[1]; at $65 per share it could have raised that much by selling 8 percent of itself—but neither is it the end of the world. Beyond Meat’s venture capital investors and executives didn’t sell any stock in the offering, and can’t for six months. If the stock keeps going up, they’ll keep getting richer, and they won’t worry too much about an underpriced IPO.

I hope if Occidental Petroleum Corp. ends up succeeding in its bid to upset Chevron Corp.’s deal with Anadarko Petroleum Corp. and acquire Anadarko for itself, that’s what they end up calling the combined company. Here is a detailed account of how the Occidental bid for Anadarko came together, and here are some skeptical reactions from Occidental shareholders both to the deal and to the proposal to finance it with $10 billion of expensive preferred stock and warrants from Warren Buffett. And here is an account of how the financing deal with Buffett came together, which involved Occidental’s banker (well, the CEO of one of its banks) Brian Moynihan calling Buffett to make an introduction, and one lesson here is that if you have to choose between hiring a banker who has Warren Buffett’s phone number and one who doesn’t you should probably go with the one who does. Also there is this gem: The deal started to come together over the weekend, the same time that flight-tracking data showed an Occidental plane in Buffett’s hometown in Nebraska, spurring speculation about his potential involvement in the negotiations. The billionaire, whose annual shareholder meeting kicks off Saturday in Omaha, took that as an opportunity to plug his NetJets business. “I should point out to anybody out there who wants to do business with us, that if they take a NetJets plane, nobody will be able to track them,” Buffett joked. I know that Warren Buffett has a lot of qualities that a lot of people admire, but I just can’t get over his focus and dedication here. Way to cross-sell! “I am glad to see that you like my $10 billion, can I interest you in my private-jet-charter business?” And it’s a good pitch; like, he noticed the customer’s pain point and proposed a solution that directly responds to its problems. The man is always working, good for him.

Is starting wildfires securities fraud? Everything is securities fraud: The Securities and Exchange Commission has opened an investigation into Pacific Gas and Electric’s accounting for its losses related to three years of wildfires in Northern California, the utility reported to shareholders Thursday. PG&E told investors that it learned in March that investigators from the S.E.C.’s San Francisco regional office had begun the review of public disclosures and accounting by the utility and its parent corporation for the 2015 Butte Fire as well as wildfires in 2017 and 2018. The fires killed scores of people, and the Camp Fire, which destroyed the town of Paradise last year, was the most destructive wildfire in California history. With utilities this all gets particularly abstract and convoluted: The utility (meaning its shareholders) has to compensate homeowners for fire damage, but the utility is also entitled to raise rates on homeowners to compensate shareholders for that compensation, and meanwhile the utility also might have to compensate shareholders for not warning them sufficiently about the risk the fires posed to their money, but of course if the utility does have to compensate shareholders a lot of that compensation will come out of the shareholders’ own money. “Everything is securities fraud” seems to me to be a useful rule of thumb but there’s no real sense in thinking about it too deeply; it will not make sense.

s.h: The Twelfth Law of Insider Trading
s.t: The other day I promulgated a Twelfth Law of Insider Trading: If you insider trade by buying short-dated out-of-the-money call options on a merger target, and the Securities and Exchange Commission freezes your profits, don’t show up in a U.S. court to ask for them back. The reason the SEC freezes your profits is because they have discovered suspicious trading—usually heavy trading in short-dated call options immediately before a merger, by an account that had never traded options before—but they can’t (1) prove that it was based on inside information or (2) find you. If you show up, they can find you, and they can try to tie you to corporate insiders to prove that you insider traded, and then you are in real trouble. Just let the money go. This was not, of course, legal advice. And of course if you are innocent—if your well-timed first-time options trades were just super lucky—then, um, I guess you should ask for your money back? I don’t know, that’s not legal advice either. (Innocent people get convicted too!) But Dan Walfish pointed out by email that there is a case. Sort of. In 2010, a Spanish citizen named Luis Martin Caro Sanchez bought a bunch of call options on Potash Corp. of Saskatchewan, and a few days later an acquisition bid for Potash was announced and Sanchez made a quick profit of almost $500,000. The SEC got suspicious, froze his assets, and sued him for insider trading. The SEC’s only evidence was the suspiciously well-timed trades. Well, that, and this: Sanchez "threw away" his laptop computer in December 2010, even though he was directed by court order to preserve all documents and information related to the case. He further installed a software cleaning program on his desktop computer in April 2010 that deleted temporary files, files in the recycle bin, and temporary internet files. He still won. The SEC had no evidence of an actual insider tip, just suspiciously well-timed trades and a suspiciously blank computer: eyebrow-raising stuff, but not proof of insider trading, and it turns out that the SEC can’t win an insider trading case without some actual evidence of an insider tip. The lesson here … look, this is probably the very least legal-advice thing I have ever typed, but … the lesson here might be, if you insider trade by buying short-dated out-of-the-money call options on a merger target, and the SEC freezes your profits, go ahead and show up in court to ask for them back as long as you’ve deleted all the evidence first . No, no, sorry, I am sticking with the original Twelfth Law, this is an absolutely terrible idea. Don’t insider trade, don’t ask for the money back if the SEC seizes it, don’t destroy evidence, none of it. Still. It seems like it might work?

We talk occasionally around here about two stereotypes, which are: Public stock markets are short-termist, focused on consistent quarterly profits, and unwilling to invest in ambitious long-term growth; while Private markets are willing to throw limitless amounts of money into unprofitable businesses as long as they offer rapid growth and some distant future prospect of world domination. Neither of these stereotypes is entirely right, and I am particularly skeptical of the first one. The fact that so many fast-growing unprofitable unicorns are going public this year, and investors are cheerfully buying them, suggests that public markets are perfectly able to focus on long-term stories. Still, the stereotypes have some intuitive appeal; there does seem to be some difference in how public and private markets trade off long-term growth and near-term profitability. For instance, I wrote not too long ago that “A big public tech company that came back to the stock market every year to raise billions more dollars to subsidize its losses probably would not be doing that at ever-increasing valuations.” Even as I typed those words I thought, in the back of my mind, “well, except Tesla, obviously.” And here we are: Tesla Inc. plans to raise about $2 billion through debt and stock offerings, after Elon Musk overestimated the ability of the Model 3 sedan to generate enough cash for the company to be self-sustaining. The electric-car maker filed Thursday to sell $1.35 billion in convertible notes and about $650 million in shares. Tesla stock, which had plunged 30 percent this year, rose 2 percent to $238.65 at 10:09 a.m. in New York, and its bonds advanced. It’s not quite “ever-increasing valuations”—Tesla last sold stock in 2017 at $262 per share—but, still, the fact is that Tesla spent a long time saying that it would be profitable and wouldn’t need to raise capital, and now it is going out and doing $2 billion of equity to cover its cash burn, and the stock is up. Tesla’s investors believe in Elon Musk’s long-term vision and are happy to throw in some money to subsidize losses on the way to achieving it. The weird thing is that no one believes those stereotypes more than Elon Musk. The guy complains constantly about the distractions and short-term pressures of the public markets. He launched a pretend going-private transaction for Tesla because he wanted “an outcome where Tesla can operate at its best, free from as much distraction and short-term thinking as possible,” and because he thought the only way to do that was by being private. Whatever, man. By the way, imagine if Musk had taken Tesla private. Imagine if he’d been able to just snap his fingers and Tesla was no longer a public company. It would not be raising $1.35 billion of convertible bonds right now, I tell you what. (Convertibles work a lot better if the underlying stock is publicly traded, so that arbitrageurs can hedge them.) I suppose it might have been able to go to Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (which Musk seems to have thought was willing to put up limitless money to take Tesla private, though that turned out not to be true), or the SoftBank Vision Fund I guess, for a couple of billion dollars of private growth capital; that’s definitely a thing that big private tech companies do these days. Maybe it would even have gotten better terms? (Remember Musk’s pretend buyout was at $420 a share , and if somehow that had happened maybe his private investors would pay a higher valuation now to avoid the embarrassment of a down-round—not really a thing in public markets.) Still, the public markets are pretty good to Musk; it seems silly to complain.

A basic issue with cryptocurrencies is: They are often touted as a way to escape the governmental censorship of fiat currencies, allowing people to keep their money safe from repressive confiscatory governments (or tax collectors) and use that money to buy things that governments don’t approve of; but You mostly need to buy your cryptocurrency with fiat currencies. There is a problem, a tense standoff at the militarized border between crypto and fiat. If you have dollars and want to turn them into Bitcoins, you need some sort of dollar-based intermediary to agree to hand over your dollars to a Bitcoin-based intermediary. The dollar-based intermediaries are going to be cautious about that, because dollar-based intermediaries are heavily regulated, because the dollar-based financial system really is a tool of governmental control. Like, the crypto people are not wrong: The U.S. government does use the financial system as a general-purpose regulatory tool, cracking down on drug trafficking and implementing foreign policy through its control of the banking system. If you want to buy drugs or do business in Iran, the dollar banking system will be an impediment to you, and you might reasonably want to use Bitcoins instead. The problem is that the dollar banking system knows this and might not want to help you buy the Bitcoins. The upshot of this is that if you want to buy some Bitcoins with U.S. dollars, it is not always as simple as having your bank wire some money to a Bitcoin exchange’s bank account so you can buy Bitcoins on the exchange. The Bitcoin exchange might have trouble finding a bank, or it might have a shady bank that your bank doesn’t want to wire money to, or it might have a perfectly respectable bank that would ask too many questions if it was constantly receiving transfers from hundreds of investors. There are two noteworthy solutions here. One is: The crypto exchange ingratiates itself into the U.S. financial system. It complies with U.S. anti-money-laundering and know-your-customer rules, it gets itself a license from a state regulator, it generally makes nice with governmental officials so that it can get treated like an upstanding corporate citizen with access to the banking system. This is not easy, and was maybe impossible in the freewheeling early days of crypto, but it is definitely possible now, and there are big respectable exchanges that take this approach. If your goals in using crypto are super libertarian this might be unattractive, though, because these exchanges will have some of the same governmental-censorship downsides as the dollar financial system. Like if you’re using proceeds of your drug trafficking business to buy Bitcoins on Gemini, the “ Revolution Needs Rules” crypto exchange, Gemini will probably narc on you to the government. Another solution is, I mean, this is a little embarrassing, but the crypto exchange could just pretend not to be a crypto exchange when it opens its bank account. Like instead of opening a bank account as XYZ Crypto Exchange, it opens a bank account as Upstanding Generic Trading Co., and tells the bank that it is in the import/export business or something, so the bank will open its account and let it do transactions without too much inquiry. This approach probably involves a middleman: Instead of the crypto exchange putting on a fake mustache and dark glasses to walk into a bank and open an account, a completely separate generic company can open the account and then serve as more or less a front for the crypto exchange. Then, if you want to use your dollars to buy Bitcoins on the crypto exchange, you tell your bank to wire dollars to the account (at a perfectly respectable bank) of some perfectly generic sounding import/export company, and the front company tells the crypto exchange that you’ve deposited dollars, and the crypto exchange gives you back Bitcoins. There are … problems … with this approach. One is a simple mechanical one, which is that it’s a way for you to wire your money to the front company, but it doesn’t solve the problem of how to get the money from the front company to the crypto exchange . Like, the crypto exchange still has whatever banking problems it would otherwise have. This problem is solvable too—maybe the front company seems respectable enough, and is a big enough customer, that it can convince its bank to wire money to the crypto exchange—but it is not always solved . There is a gap between the front company and the exchange that creates risk. The New York attorney general’s lawsuit against crypto exchange Bitfinex (and affiliated cryptocurrency Tether), which we talked about last week, is in part about this problem: Bitfinex allegedly used a firm called Crypto Capital Corp. as a “payment processor,” meaning that it was a company with bank accounts that took money from investors who wanted to buy cryptocurrency on Bitfinex and gave money back to them when they sold their cryptocurrency. Or it was supposed to. In practice, Crypto Capital seems to have taken several hundred million dollars of customer money from Bitfinex and not given it back to investors, or to Bitfinex. Crypto Capital told Bitfinex (and Bitfinex now asserts) that this is because some of its bank accounts have run into regulatory problems, but the attorney general hinted at the possibility that it might have just trousered the money. When you are, let us say, operating in a legal gray area, that is always a risk. The other problem with the front-company approach is that it is super dicey legally, as you can tell from the words “front company,” which are not nice words. And so on Tuesday federal prosecutors brought a criminal case against two people accused of fronting for crypto exchanges: U.S. Attorney Geoffrey S. Berman said: “Reginald Fowler and Ravid Yosef allegedly ran a shadow bank that processed hundreds of millions of dollars of unregulated transactions on behalf of numerous cryptocurrency exchanges. Their organization allegedly skirted the anti-money laundering safeguards required of licensed institutions that ensure the U.S. financial system is not used for criminal purposes, and did so through lies and deceit. Thanks to the investigative work of the FBI and the IRS-CI, they will be prosecuted for their actions.” And: FOWLER and YOSEF, who worked for several related companies that provided fiat-currency banking services to various cryptocurrency exchanges (the “Crypto Companies”), allegedly participated in a conspiracy in which FOWLER made numerous false and misleading statements to banks to open bank accounts that were used to receive deposits from individuals purchasing cryptocurrency, and in which FOWLER and YOSEF falsified electronic wire payment instructions to conceal the true nature of a voluminous cryptocurrency exchange business. Hundreds of millions of dollars flowed through the Crypto Companies’ accounts from banks located across the globe. … Oops. The indictment is very light on details of the allegations, but what there is is intriguing. Fowler and Yosef allegedly had accounts in the name of Global Trading Solutions LLC, which The Block reports “was used by Crypto Capital to process fiat deposits for Bitfinex.” The indictment mentions that in October and November 2018, U.S. officials seized money in several bank accounts, including a Global Trading Solutions account at HSBC Bank USA with account number 141000147. That account was reportedly used to process payments for Bitfinex in October 2018. The New York attorney general last week alleged that Bitfinex started having trouble getting its money back from Crypto Capital at around that time, and there was some uncertainty as to whether that was because (as Crypto Capital allegedly told Bitfinex) “the unavailable funds have been seized or otherwise restrained by governmental authorities in Poland, Portugal, and the United States,” or because (as Bitfinex allegedly started to worry) “Crypto Capital’s principals may be engaged in a fraud.” Well, now we know that authorities in the United States seized at least some of the money! When we talked last week about the attorney general’s lawsuit, I wrote that “in some (very tendentious) sense it is the fault of regulators … that Bitfinex and Tether find themselves in this pickle.” I mean, yes, right? In some very literal sense, the reason that Bitfinex customers had a hard time getting their money back, and that Bitfinex ended up borrowing some money from the pot of dollars backing Tether, seems to be that U.S. authorities grabbed some money from Bitfinex’s payment processor and wouldn’t give it back.The New York case against Bitfinex and Tether, and the federal case against Fowler and Yosef, seem to be about the same basic thing, but from opposite sides. The New York case is essentially about customer protection: If a crypto exchange takes money from investors, the New York attorney general wants to make sure that it keeps the money safe. The federal case is about systemic concerns: If a crypto exchange takes money from customers, federal prosecutors want to make sure that it’s keeping track of those customers and not helping them launder money. Those are not necessarily inconsistent goals, but they do obviously conflict here.

A question of weirdly frequent relevance in modern banking is: If a bank lends a country a lot of money, and the country’s officials are corrupt, and the bankers working on the deal are also corrupt, and the country’s leaders steal a lot of the money for themselves, but they also use a lot of it to pay big bribes to the bankers to push the deal through the bank’s compliance checks, should the country have to pay the bank back? Like at some level the country ought to be financially responsible for the actions of its officials; you shouldn’t be able to say “I don’t have to pay you back the money you loaned me, because I stole it.” On the other hand, the bank ought to be responsible for the actions of its bankers, and if it loaned money that was then funneled to its own bankers as bribes, then in a sense it already got the money back—it went out as a loan and came back as a bribe—and it shouldn’t demand repayment again. (Or, it should demand repayment from the bankers who took the bribes.) There is a certain symmetry here: The rights and responsibilities of the bank and the country as entities are tied up with the malfeasance of the particular humans who represented the bank and the country in the deal (and who stole the money), and you will sympathize more with the bank or the country depending on how much or how little you identify them with the actions of their individuals. I am not sure there is or should be any sort of bright-line rule. But in general, at least when the corrupt administration of the country has been replaced by a new administration, people tend to sympathize more with the country. “We overthrew that dictator and now we want to get out from the mess he left” is a sympathetic thing to say; “we fired that managing director and don’t want to be responsible for his crimes” is not. Also there is a tendency in these cases for the country to be poor (like, the per capita income of its people is low) and for the bank to be rich (per capita income of its employees is high), which also seems relevant to the balance of sympathies. Anyway: Credit Suisse Group AG’s recent shareholder meeting took an awkward turn when a Mozambican activist questioned Chairman Urs Rohner over the bank’s role in fraudulent deals that saddled her country with $2 billion of debt. The confrontation halfway through Friday’s meeting was the latest example of the rising international pressure on Credit Suisse to forgive loans it made to Mozambican state-owned companies engaged in an alleged complex fraud, and potentially, to pay damages to victims. We talked about those deals a few months ago. They were not good! Lots of people, including officials of a previous Mozambican government, allegedly stole lots of the money from a bond deal run by Credit Suisse, but the lead Credit Suisse banker allegedly got $45 million of kickbacks, which does I think make it a bit awkward for Credit Suisse to demand its money back.

I am sorry but I can never get enough of stories like this: Goldman bankers began fanning out across the U.S. two years ago to pitch companies once deemed too small to warrant regular attention. They’re now setting up a dedicated team. It’s a dramatic cultural shift for a firm whose elite bankers long prided themselves on chasing the most lucrative deals. Now, they just have to overcome all of the skepticism. “I was intrigued to understand why they were reaching out,” Chris Fraser, the former head of a Texas-based chemicals company said of an unsolicited email from a Goldman banker a couple of years ago, as its push began. “I even asked the question, ‘Don’t you have more important or bigger potential clients to spend time with?”’ Fraser eventually struck up a dialogue and hired the bank for a secondary stock offering in 2017 for his company, KMG Chemicals Inc. The clincher, he said, was a banker on the ground. “It wasn’t someone flying in from New York, filling up their calendar for the week and flying out,” he said. I just mean, disclosure, I used to work at Goldman Sachs Group Inc., and now I don’t, and there were days when my job certainly felt like it consisted mostly of sending unsolicited emails to random companies, and it somehow warms my heart to see that that’s now an official focus. And that it works! Honestly if you are running a Nigerian-prince scam you should consider switching to a Goldman-banker scam: Email small companies being like “I can get you $100 million; you just have to pay me $1 million first.” It has the ring of authenticity! Not legal advice. By the way, Goldman made about $1.4 million on that KMG deal, which is not going to get anyone a partnership but which is not nothing either. You send out a thousand unsolicited emails, you convert 1 percent of them into $1.4 million deals, and you’ve got a business that can at least support, like, a vice president. Anyway this is also a great quote: “For Goldman this is a bit more of a novelty than for JPMorgan or Bank of America,” said Ana Arsov, who covers global investment banks at Moody’s Investors Service. Goldman Sachs has long been considered “a premium player,” she said, but “it’s logical to say, ‘Is there a wallet out there that we simply have not penetrated that we could?” Man, that is a logical thing for Goldman to say. “Hi, I’m from Goldman Sachs and I’m here to penetrate your wallet.”

“Uber IPO Is Oversubscribed by Day Two of Roadshow,” it says here, but I would say that Uber Technologies Inc.’s initial public offering was oversubscribed by 2016 at the latest. Like if you’d given me 24 hours, at any time in the last three years, to line up $8 or $9 billion of orders for public Uber stock, I could have done it. You wouldn’t have to give me a prospectus or audited financial statements[1] or talking points for the sales pitch or even the names and phone numbers of big portfolio managers, I would just call the publicly available customer-support lines at Fidelity and Capital and be like “hey Uber’s going public, you guys want a couple of yards?” and they’d be like “oh sure” and I’d be done by lunchtime. This is easy, easy stuff. I mean, at some price, anyway. Imagine if Morgan Stanley was mandated to lead Uber’s IPO, and they went out on the road and pitched investors, and the investors were all like “Uber? Never heard of them, pass.” I think it’d be the most embarrassing event in the history of capital-markets banking. Morgan Stanley raised $475 million for Uber privately, three years ago, from retail-ish investors, without financial statements. Uber sold $9 billion of stock—a bigger deal than the IPO—in one private deal last year. Of course the IPO was oversubscribed immediately. Now, oversubscription is a pretty low bar. The fact that there is billions of dollars’ worth of demand for Uber stock is very very obvious; the question is at what price: Demand for the share sale is currently focused on the lower end of Uber’s targeted share price range, though that could still shift as talks with investors continue, the people said. That would put the amount that would be raised in the IPO closer to $7.9 billion. ... The world’s biggest ride-hailing company is offering 180 million shares at $44 to $50 apiece, according to a regulatory filing last week. At the top of the range, the listing would value Uber at almost $84 billion, based on the number of shares outstanding after the offering as detailed in the filing. If Uber goes public at the low end of the range then that will be about an $80 billion fully diluted valuation, not much above its $72 billion private valuation last year. But this doesn’t tell you much: It’s early in the roadshow, and the bankers’ job from here on out is to try to push the price up. Including, obviously, by leaking on day two that the deal is oversubscribed, and then going back to investors to say “this deal is very popular and you’re not going to get anything unless you are willing to raise your price.”

Online pet-supply retailer Chewy Inc. filed for its initial public offering on Monday, and it is not as high-profile as Uber or the other unicorns stampeding to go public this year, but in some ways it feels, even more than them, like the 2019iest of IPOs. First of all, as is de rigueur in postmodern IPOs, Chewy is a fast-growing but money-losing company. “Chewy is comically unprofitable, even by startupy standards,” tweeted the Wall Street Journal’s Liz Hoffman, noting that it lost $268 million on sales of $3.5 billion last year. “Also sure, Uber is unprofitable but ride-sharing and self-driving cars are new and expensive things. Chewy ... sells dog toys online?” We have talked a lot about the strange startup economy in which venture capitalists subsidize consumers by pouring money into startups that sell their product below cost in the hopes of building global dominance in some newly invented, highly scalable, winner-take-all business. (“ Blitzscaling,” it’s sometimes called.) Does selling dog food and prescriptions fit that category? I don’t know. It doesn’t seem all that new, or winner-take-all. But maybe everything fits that category now; maybe losing money to achieve global monopoly scale is the only business strategy left. Second, Chewy will have dual-class stock: Public shareholders who buy stock in the IPO will get Class A shares with one vote each, but a majority of its votes will be held by a controlling shareholder who has Class B shares with 10 votes each. This is quite common these days; pretty much every buzzy tech startup now goes public with dual-class stock so that its charismatic founder(s) can keep control of the company. But Chewy isn’t controlled by its charismatic founder, or by an adorable and financially savvy dog for that matter. It’s controlled by PetSmart Inc., another pet-supply retailer that acquired it in 2017. PetSmart is in turn controlled by Argos Holdings LP (stellar classical pet reference!), which in turn is controlled by a consortium of private equity firms. Dual-class stock is very much a thing these days—controversial but widespread—because lots of startups run by visionary perfectionist founders are going public, and those founders want to maintain control, and investors grumble about it but at some level think that it is actually value-enhancing to surrender control to the founder whose vision you believe in. That’s sort of a situation-specific story that happens to be repeated over and over again with Facebook and Snap and Lyft and so on. But I guess it’s possible that dual-class stock could be disconnected from that story and just become a standard feature of IPOs. If you’re a private equity firm or a corporate parent or whatever, you can just sell a majority stake in an IPO but keep control with super-voting stock. If investors will buy it, why not do it? Finally, I don’t want to be rude here, but we did have a previous giant internet boom, and it was followed by a giant internet bust, and the very most famous symbol of that boom and that bust, the one that everyone still refers to all the time to capture the insanity of that era, the one that “has become synonymous with the dot.com bust,” was an online pet-supply retailer. “I can’t believe people bought the IPO of a money-losing online pet food company” is a thing that people really went around saying for like a decade within living memory. Anyway.

This is not a complete description of the difference or anything, but one important difference between a mutual fund and an exchange-traded fund is that an ETF is a mutual fund that doesn’t pay taxes. When a mutual fund has some appreciated stock, and sells it, that creates a taxable gain, and shareholders in the mutual fund have to pay taxes on it that year. When an ETF has some appreciated stock, and sells it, that doesn’t create a taxable gain, and the shareholders in the ETF don’t have to pay taxes until they sell their ETF shares, because the ETF never sells the stock . Why would it sell stock? An ETF normally tracks an index, which doesn’t change much, so it rarely sells stock for stock-picking reasons. When investors redeem, they don’t get cash from the ETF (which would require selling stock); instead they sell their ETF shares to market makers who then hand them in to the ETF and get back shares of the underlying stock. Due to a quirk of the tax law—a quirk at the center of the modern ETF industry—this in-kind redemption is not a taxable transaction. And if the ETF needs to get rid of a big chunk of stock for reasons unrelated to redemptions—for instance because a big stock is coming out of the index—well, a bank will just create a bunch of ETF shares (by delivering the underlying index basket to the ETF), wait a few days, and then redeem those shares for a “custom basket” consisting of the shares the ETF wants to get rid of. No sale, no taxes. Bloomberg Businessweek had a story about these transactions—sometimes called “heartbeats,” because the ETF’s assets have a big spike up followed almost immediately by an offsetting spike down—in March, and we talked about it at the time, and I recommend those links to you if you want a more complete explanation of how this all works. Today I want to talk about a follow-up story on the heartbeat trade, by Bloomberg’s Zachary Mider, Annie Massa and Christopher Cannon, called “ Vanguard Patented a Way to Avoid Taxes on Mutual Funds.” The trick is actually pretty straightforward, once you understand (1) the heartbeat thing and (2) that ETFs are mutual funds that don’t pay taxes. Vanguard Group Inc. has long had a bunch of large index-tracking mutual funds. When it got into the exchange-traded fund business, instead of setting up new ETFs, it added them to the existing funds: Rather than establish new, freestanding ETFs, Vanguard proposed to add an ETF share class to existing mutual funds. ETF and mutual fund investors would jointly own the same underlying pool of stocks. The concept made sense for Vanguard. Investors who preferred ETFs could easily convert without selling. And the Vanguard ETFs would have a head start in the marketplace. They’d be able to point to decades of performance history and benefit from the existing mutual funds’ scale, ensuring low fees. So now Vanguard had hybrid entities that were partly mutual funds (which pay taxes) and partly ETFs (which don’t). How would that go? Some observers thought taxes were a drawback to Vanguard’s plan. Investors expect ETFs to be more tax-efficient than mutual funds. Why buy a Vanguard ETF if it might get burdened with the tax bills of its sister mutual fund? “The fund will exhibit little of the ETF’s characteristic tax efficiency,” one skeptical ETF consultant told Investment Management Weekly in 2004. Hahaha nope, that’s not how it works. If you combine a tax arbitrage with a normal tax-paying thing, you get a bigger tax arbitrage, not a bigger tax bill; otherwise you are doing it wrong. Now Vanguard can use heartbeat trades in the ETF side of its funds to avoid taxes in the whole fund, a trick that tax analyst Robert Gordon calls a “dialysis machine” for taxes: Vanguard’s trading in Monsanto Co. in June showed the dialysis machine in action. The agrochemical giant had agreed to be sold to a German rival for $56 billion in cash, and the Vanguard Total Stock Market Index Fund was one of Monsanto’s biggest shareholders. It had owned shares since the early 1990s and, over the decades, the stock had risen more than 25-fold. That meant Vanguard probably faced a big taxable gain. On June 4, an unidentified investor pumped $1 billion into the fund’s ETF. Two days later, when Monsanto was scheduled to exit the index, the same investor took $1 billion out. It looked like a classic heartbeat trade, except it was five times too big. The ETF portion of the fund had only $184 million of Monsanto to get rid of, and no other large stock was leaving the index that day. The size of the deal makes sense, though, considering that the entire fund had $1.3 billion of Monsanto to unload. The ETF didn’t just dispose of its own small stake in the company—it got rid of most of the mutual fund’s much larger stake as well. An investor created $1 billion of ETF shares and redeemed them two days later, presumably receiving back Monsanto shares—both the ETF’s and the mutual fund’s—for its in-kind redemption. The fund didn’t have to sell its appreciated Monsanto stock, and so didn’t create capital gains taxes for its investors. Those investors, I should disclose, include me: A lot of my money is in Vanguard index funds, including this one, and (basically out of laziness) none of it is in ETFs. So like a chump I expose myself to having to pay capital-gains taxes every year despite not selling any of my funds, but my friends at Vanguard are working hard to save me from that fate. So I am biased, but I think this is fine? My reaction to the story about the heartbeats was, well, if you think ETFs should pay taxes, this is bad, and if you think “ETFs are mutual funds that don’t pay taxes,” it’s good, and if you are totally agnostic about whether ETFs should pay taxes then it does look a little tricky, sure. But in fact in our actual world the proposition that ETFs are, and should be, mutual funds that don’t pay taxes is really popular and widely accepted: A lot of middle-class people love investing in ETFs and not paying taxes until they sell their shares, and politicians and regulators seem pretty happy to let them do it. It is also quite reasonable: People who buy ETFs pay taxes on their gains when they sell the ETFs and actually realize the gains, which feels like the right time to pay taxes, whereas people who buy mutual funds have to pay capital gains taxes at random times that have nothing to do with their own investment decisions or cash flows. From that perspective, the heartbeat trades are not an evil tax dodge but just a sensible mechanical use of the rules to achieve the logical result that everyone wants. If you believe that, then Vanguard is just taking the logical next step: If “mutual funds that don’t pay taxes” are a widely accepted superior product, then why not just use the same mechanical procedure to make sure that your other mutual funds don’t pay taxes? Once you accept that it’s good for some kinds of mutual funds to defer capital gains taxes, then it’s only fair to let other kinds of mutual funds do the same thing. Really Vanguard is just rationalizing the tax system. My only complaint is that Vanguard has patented this method, so nobody else can immunize a mutual fund from taxes by bolting on an ETF; as a Vanguard customer I’m fine with that personally but it does undercut the fairness argument. Fortunately Vanguard’s patent is “valid until 2023,” so soon enough no mutual funds will pay taxes and the world will make sense.

The good news is that the absolutely heroic UBS Group AG investment banker who sat next to a competing banker on a train, noticed that the other guy was getting messages on his phone about a deal, and emailed his colleagues back at the office to put together a pitch to try to win a role on the deal, will not get in trouble: UBS Group AG and two bankers were cleared by French enforcers after facing accusations of inappropriately obtaining a tip about a secret $15 billion Iliad SA takeover plan and then approaching the French carrier to offer financing. At the heart of the case is a Eurostar trip between London and Paris five years ago where a former UBS investment banker Alexandre Zaluski caught glimpses of messages that popped up on his neighbor’s mobile phones. A Lazard Ltd. dealmaker on the train was working on an attempt by Iliad to take over T-Mobile US Inc., and was unknowingly also providing Zaluski a window into the deal. It was part of Zaluski’s job as an investment banker to share the tip with his UBS colleague and telecom sector specialist Christian Lesueur, the Autorite des Marches Financiers’ enforcement committee ruled. Similarly, Lesueur can’t be criticized for putting together a team of a dozen UBS bankers, briefing them, and making a financing pitch with Iliad. Yep! We talked about this case last month, and I was fully on Zaluski’s and Lesueur’s side. “It is the prime directive of investment banking,” I wrote: “If there is a deal in your sector, you had better either be involved in the deal, or have a really good answer when your boss asks you ‘why aren’t we in this deal?’” They saw a deal happening, right there on the train, and the panic kicked in and they got to work. They didn’t actually get the mandate, but you can’t fault their commitment. The bad news, of course, is that now other investment bankers have no excuse not to do this. If you collapse into your train seat after a 16-hour day only to find the guy next to you carelessly emailing about a deal, or if you go out on your first date in months and the people at the next table are talking about a merger, sorry, back to work! Zaluski and Lesueur have set the standard for everyone else, and if you aren’t at least occasionally pitching for deals based on overheard conversations then you’re not working hard enough. Important people like to sit next to important people on trains, are you one, etc. If the Autorité des Marchés Financiers had declared this illegal, then expectations would be lower. If they’d announced a bright-line rule that it’s illegal to do investment banking on trains, then everyone would get a bit more free time.

Huh: UBS Group AG is telling executives in its large wealth management business to be more selective when hiring bankers as it seeks to cut costs following a challenging first quarter, according to people familiar with the matter. The bank has introduced an informal rule to allow hiring of one back-office employee only if five are leaving, the people said, asking not to be identified because the matter is private. For client-facing staff, the rule is less strict: Managers can hire one banker for two departing ones, the people said. I must say, if you’re the fourth person to quit your back-office wealth management group at UBS, that’s a little insulting. “Yeah you and your three friends weren’t doing anything important so we’re not going to replace you,” ouch. I assume that if Zaluski or Lesueur quits they’ll immediately have to be replaced by two new bankers, but not everyone is that diligent.

Every year Institutional Investor publishes a perfectly sensible ranking of how much money “the world’s richest hedge fund managers made” the previous year, and every year people write articles describing the list as a ranking of how much hedge fund managers got paid, and every year I point out that (1) it is not a ranking of how much they got paid , since it mostly measures return on their own capital invested in the fund, and (2) it is not a ranking of how much hedge fund managers made, since the top spots usually include a lot of people who are retired from managing hedge funds but who still have their money in those funds. Anyway this year congrats Ray Dalio, who really does manage Bridgewater Associates, and who came first in the ranking. Second place was Jim Simons, who has not run his hedge fund for almost a decade; David Shaw, who “has not run D.E. Shaw on a day-to-day basis since 2001,” came in eighth.
