[3] One thing perhaps worth noting here is that a lot of Tether owners probably acquired their Tethers through Bitfinex, so in a sense the money backing Tether came from Bitfinex. A sympathetic view of all of this would be: Look, all of the money held by Tether and Bitfinex at Crypto Capital or Deltec or anywhere else was all there to back customer claims, either customer accounts at Bitfinex or USDT/dollar parity at Tether, and it’s all basically the same set of customers, so shifting money from Tether to Bitfinex to pay the more urgent customer claims is fine, especially if you think you’ll eventually be able to recover or make up for the lost money at Crypto Capital. The attorney general’s view—which I think is clearly correct—is, no, if you go around saying that Tether is fully backed by dollars it needs to be fully backed by dollars, and you can’t— in her words—“treat Tether’s cash reserves as Bitfinex’s corporate slush fund” or use them “to hide Bitfinex’s massive, undisclosed losses and inability to handle customer withdrawals.” [4] You can tell because Uber is offering 180 million shares, and in its “ Use of Proceeds” section it says that “Each $1.00 increase (decrease) in the assumed initial public offering price of $47.00 per share would increase (decrease) the net proceeds to us from this offering by approximately $178.2 million, assuming the number of shares of common stock offered by us, as set forth on the cover page of this prospectus, remains the same and after deducting the underwriting discounts and commissions and estimated offering expenses payable by us.” If you net $178.2 million from increasing the price of 180 million shares by a dollar, that means you’re paying $1.8 million in fees for every $180 million you raise, or 1 percent.

I write a fair amount around here about how Tesla Inc. Chief Executive Officer Elon Musk has a habit of saying things about Tesla on Twitter that turn out not to be true. I have my reasons for writing about this: It’s funny, for one thing, and material corporate disclosures via a CEO’s tweets are still sort of a novelty, and, most notably, the Securities and Exchange Commission has spent a lot of time in court arguing that Musk should not be allowed to say untrue things about Tesla on Twitter. But it is important to keep some perspective here and remember that Musk also has a habit of saying things about Tesla on earnings calls that turn out not to be true. This is not a novelty—he’s far from the first CEO to do that—and it does not particularly raise interesting legal questions or objections from the SEC. Also: It’s fine. Everyone just sort of understands that you can say things on earnings calls that turn out not to be true. Earnings calls traditionally begin with a magic incantation of the words “forward-looking statements,” and a warning that “actual events or results could differ materially” from what is discussed on the call, and people understand and accept that risk and are more or less not allowed to sue if in fact things turn out differently. So if Elon Musk says on an earnings call that Tesla expects to be profitable in every future quarter, or that it will not need to raise capital, and if in a subsequent earnings call he says that it won’t make a profit next quarter and might need to raise capital, that’s fine. Or if he says in an investor day that Tesla will have a fleet of robot taxis on the road by next year, and if in 2020 Tesla does not in fact have a fleet of robot taxis on the road, no one will complain. I mean, good lord, people will complain, but their complaints will be about Tesla’s execution and Musk’s overconfidence. Obviously it is better to make lavish promises on earnings call and follow through than to make those promises and fall short. But people won’t complain that they were deceived . They weren’t. They understand that a purpose of an earnings call is for the market to get a sense of what the CEO is thinking about and what he wants to achieve, and that an earnings call is, to some extent, within some limits, a place for optimism and predictions and plans and hopes and dreams, not just for hard facts. And the ambition and whimsy of those hopes and dreams will depend on the personality of the CEO. Tesla earnings calls are a place for Elon Musk to be Elon Musk. Twitter is a place for Elon Musk to be way, way, way more Elon Musk, so from a certain perspective it’s weird that anyone would try to limit him there. Obviously the tweets do not all start with a disclaimer about forward-looking statements, and are a bit less qualified in their phrasing. Still. It is just the case that Tesla is an outgrowth of Elon Musk’s imagination, in some obvious bad ways but also in a lot of extremely compelling good ways. You know, when you dial into an earnings call, that you’ll be getting a certain amount of Musk’s imagination. Surely you know that on Twitter too. Anyway Tesla announced earnings yesterday and they were bad and also this: Elon Musk’s declarations that Tesla Inc. was done losing money and needing to raise more cash turned out to be premature. The chief executive officer is reopening the door to seeking capital for the maker of the electric Model 3 sedan after posting a bigger-than-expected loss for the first quarter. A record drop in deliveries, combined with the company’s largest-ever debt payment, depleted cash to the lowest level in three years. Musk, 47, assured investors that higher deliveries and cost cuts will help Tesla post a narrower loss in the second quarter and return to profitability the following three months. But he also went a step further than his hint earlier this week that Tesla may seek more funds as he embarks on a hugely ambitious pursuit to unleash fully autonomous robotaxis in a shared service next year. Also here is a funny exchange on the earnings call between Musk and Morgan Stanley analyst Adam Jonas: Jonas: And just as a follow-up, Elon, and you kind of alluded a little bit, there is just so much drama around Tesla's share price and quarterly results. From the outside, at least, it just looks like a huge distraction. And at the same time, there is so much alternative capital and large amounts of strategic capital that is incrementally deployed in domains where Tesla has real leadership. So, how important is it for Tesla to be a publicly traded company, Elon? Musk: Well, mate, I don't want to surprise you, but I would prefer we were private, but unfortunately, I think that ship has sailed, so... Jonas: But is it important? I mean, do you think the Company's value is maximized being public? Is there just only so much you can do and you just got to play the hand you're dealt? Musk: Well, I mean, being public, does feels like the sort of price of the stock is being set in kind of a manic-depressive way. And I think Warren Buffett's analogy is just like perhaps being a publicly traded company is like having someone stand at the edge of your home and just randomly yell different prices for your house every day. It's still the same house. This is funny because, you know, ha ha ha Musk sort of tried to take Tesla private and look how that worked out. But it is also a bit weird and interesting for a public-market analyst to basically say to a public-company CEO: Aren’t you sick of us? Aren’t our expectations and questions a waste of your time? It is also interesting because, traditionally, public markets are where the money is , and so of course a capital-intensive business should be public so that it can raise as much money as possible. Now that story has changed: Jonas talks about “alternative capital,” which I assume is a reference to the oceans of money available in private markets, and there is a sense that private investors are happier to fund big ambitious growth projects than public ones are. If Tesla was private, it would probably be looking to raise a lot of money right now to build its robot taxi fleet, but no one would be making fun of it for that. Private investors love to invest billions of dollars in robot taxi fleets. Instead Tesla is public, and capital-raising is sort of automatically disfavored.

This is so pleasing: The employer, UnitedHealth Group Inc., allows workers to buy shares twice a year at a 15 percent discount. There’s no minimum holding period, meaning participants can sell the shares immediately and pocket the difference. “It’s arbitrage in its purest form,” Shapiro said. “The money was just sitting there and could have been hers, if she’d just been able to afford payroll deductions.” … Shapiro’s eureka moment prompted him to found Carver Edison, a fintech startup that provides interest-free loans to workers unable set aside money from their paychecks to buy stock on the cheap. That’s from this Bloomberg story about Aaron Shapiro, the 26-year-old founder of Carver Edison. The essential insight is such a fundamental one in finance, which is: There is an arbitrage. The arbitrage cannot be exploited because no one will fund it. We should fund it. Then the people who do the arbitrage will make a lot of free money and give us some of it. In this case, the arbitrage is simply that many employers have employee stock purchase plans that let their employees buy unrestricted stock at a discount. The employees often do not have the money to buy the stock, so they don’t benefit from the program, or the discount. This seems like a very solvable problem. If a stock trades at $100 and you can buy it at $85, someone should be willing to lend you the $85 for, like, 10 seconds, so you can buy the stock for $85 and immediately sell it at $100. (Or $99 or $101: There is some risk of the price moving, but not, in 10 seconds, that much.) Then you pay the lender back the $85, plus something for its troubles—10 seconds’ worth of interest, plus maybe some compensation for the teeny risk of the stock going down so far, so fast, that the lender loses money—and you keep the rest. Now actually it is a little bit more complicated than that, but only in a good way. In fact you don’t put up the money, get the stock immediately, and sell it 10 seconds later. Instead, you put up the money, wait three or six months, then get the stock and sell it immediately. Borrowing money for months is more expensive than borrowing money for 10 seconds, but in this case there is a lovely compensation, which is that you don’t have stock-price risk over those months. “The shares are bought at a discount of as much as 15 percent to the market price at the start or end of each period, whichever is lower.” That is, it’s not like you put up $85 today for a stock worth $100 today, wait a few months, and then get the stock when it might be worth $125 or $100 or $85 or $50. Instead, you put up the money today, and then in a few months you get back stock at the lower of (1) the stock price at the beginning (when you put up the money) or (2) the stock price at the end (when you get the stock). In either case, minus 15 percent. So if you put up $1,000 today when the stock is at $100, and the stock ends up at $125, you buy stock at $85 ($100 minus 15 percent, or about 11.8 shares for $1,000). If the stock ends up at $80, though, you buy stock at $68 ($80 minus 15 percent, or about 14.7 shares for $1,000). You get all the upside if the stock goes up over the period, but none of the downside: If the stock goes down over the period, you buy it at the end price and don’t participate in the losses. One obvious benefit of this is that it remains an arbitrage, there’s no market risk, and so a lender should be confident in funding it: The lender can always get its money back, because you’ll always get stock at at least a 15 percent discount to the market price at delivery, and so there’ll always be enough to cover the loan. But there is a subtler benefit, which is that the company is not just giving its employees free stock in the form of the 15 percent discount; it is also giving them free optionality in the form of the buy-at-the-lowest-of-the-start-or-end-price deal. Loosely speaking, and ignoring the 15 percent discount, the company has written the employees a call option on the stock at the starting price. (The employee gets all the upside above the starting price, but none of the downside, which is the profile of a call option.) That option has some value; if you offered it to a bank, the bank would pay you some money for it. Of course it is not explicitly a call option, it’s not transferable, and you can’t just sell it to a bank. But you kind of can! In cases when the stock price increase over the six-month period exceeds a certain threshold -- say 25 percent ... -- Carver will collect and sell a few extra shares. Some of those may be sold in the open market, while others will be sold to banks via options, allowing Carver to generate revenue by collecting a small fee on each contract. Carver Edison doesn’t charge the employees interest on its loan; instead, it takes a portion of their optionality and sells it to banks to make money. (“Carver Edison generates revenue by selling options to financial institutions that allows the financial institutions to realize the benefit of the stock price exceeding the 25% cap … on the Loan Repayment Shares,” says Aon Plc, a partner of Carver Edison, in this explanation of the deal.) The employees give up some of their upside—if the shares go up more than 25 percent over the period, they only get the 25 percent appreciation—in exchange for the interest-free loan. The company has given them a weird option, and Carver Edison has figured out how to turn it into a normal option and sell it to a bank. One reasonable question here is, why would companies do this? I suppose the answer is that whatever the reason is for doing an employee stock purchase plan in the first place, that’s a good reason to let someone fund employees’ participation. “Companies benefit by increased engagement, cash flow and tax savings,” says Aon, and “shareholders benefit from the increased ‘owner mentality’ and greater employee alignment.” I mean, less so if the employees sell all the shares immediately to capture the discount, but that creates a kind of engagement too.

I really can’t stress enough how weird it would be for a big bank intentionally to do something that its employees don’t want, its shareholders don’t want, its customers don’t want and its regulators don’t want. I mean it is common enough for a bank to do something that one or several of those groups don’t want, but all of them? Your model of big banks can be that they are shareholder-value-maximizing corporations, or socialist collectives run for the benefit of workers, or public-private partnerships run as essentially regulated utilities, or businesses whose mission is to delight their customers, or some combination of those things, but you have to have some model. They have to be trying to make someone happy. The alternative view—that a big bank is just an autonomous inflictor of misery, an emergent entity beyond the control of any human or combination of humans, pursuing its own inscrutable purposes as everyone involved looks on in impotent despair—is too horrible to think about. Anyway here you go: Deutsche Bank AG and Commerzbank AG ended talks on a historic tie-up, throwing the future of the lenders into question after a series of failed turnaround plans. More than five weeks of negotiations and the Finance Ministry’s push to forge one strong institution out of two struggling firms failed to overcome the economic and political obstacles to combining the country’s biggest listed banks. Here’s the Deutsche Bank press release, which says “that a combination with Commerzbank would not have created sufficient benefits to offset the additional execution risks, restructuring costs and capital requirements associated with such a large-scale integration.” I mean no one is entirely happy about this result either. Maybe the autonomous-inflictor-of-misery model, for Deutsche Bank and Commerzbank at least, is correct. “Without a deal, both banks face myriad challenges.” German Finance Minister Olaf Scholz is particularly sad, since he and his deputy “had been the key political agitators behind the merger plan” and the only people who seemed at all happy about it: “Besides Scholz and Kukies, nobody wanted this merger,” says one German politician. And now everybody won’t get the merger they didn’t want. It still feels pretty gloomy.

AI I used to be a capital markets banker, which means that I went around to companies trying to persuade them to issue securities. (Convertible bonds, in my case; other capital markets bankers try to persuade companies to issue equity or investment-grade bonds or high-yield bonds.) There are two main skills for a capital markets banker[1]: Remembering all the convertible bonds (or whatever) that have been issued in recent years, and who did them, and what their terms were, and how well or poorly they went over in the market, and how they traded afterwards, and what terms the market pushed back on, and what terms ended out working out poorly or well for the issuer or for the investors, etc.; and being able to spot patterns in this data and apply them to a potential issuer’s situation, and to interpolate pricing for a particular issuer’s new securities based on pricing for comparable securities, so you can advise that issuer’s managers on whether they can issue a convertible bond (or whatever) and on what terms and who will buy it, etc.; and Being pleasant company when you meet with a potential issuer’s managers, and taking them out to dinner, and remembering their kids’ names, and making appropriate jokes, and explaining the mechanics of convertible bonds (or whatever) in a hearty and nonthreatening but confidence-inspiring way. The second part is just a matter of generic sales and interpersonal skills that are not at all specific to the financial industry. Once, when I was a banker, I left my office briefly to buy shoelaces or something, and the guy who sold them to me talked me into getting a sit-down shoeshine, an experience that I find uncomfortable and would never actually seek out and also did not have time for. But he was very persuasive, and I did it, and hated it, and walked back to my office with the unsettling certainty that the shoeshine guy would be better at my job than I was. The convertible-bond stuff can be taught; the sales skills are hard. The first part is the finance-specific part; it’s the knowledge and insight and market feel that allows you to advise companies confidently and helpfully on what they should do. It is a form of expertise that is developed over time through a sort of apprenticeship model, but it is also … like, you could have a database. Most banks do. Each time a convertible bond (or whatever) is issued, someone writes down the details in a spreadsheet, and then you have a big list of all the relevant information that your clients might need to plan and price a new convertible bond (or whatever). You can’t just hand them the list; interpreting the list, pattern-matching, interpolating pricing for a new issuer, are all specialized skills that you have developed over time by looking at the list over and over again and seeing how new bonds make their way onto it. But they’re not magic . They’re basically a sort of regression: You write down some characteristics of the last 20 or 200 companies that issued convertible bonds (or whatever), and how their bonds priced, and then you write down the characteristics of the current issuer, and you infer pricing from that. Anyway: Now technology could be about to change the traditional ways of doing things, just as it has in other old-school business lines such as the trading of stocks and bonds. The next frontier is the “primary” side of the banks’ capital markets businesses, which helps companies issue debt and equity. Bank of America Merrill Lynch, for example, has spent time collecting and cleaning up internal information on initial public offerings it has managed, and fed the 50-gigabyte data set into a machine-learning tool it calls “Predictive Intelligence Analytics Machine”, or Priam. Since September the bank has used Priam to help predict which investors will be interested in European listings, and it now plans to apply the tool to US and Asian deals too. “Once we’d cleaned all the data, it was unbelievable what we could do,” says Elif Bilgi Zapparoli, the bank’s co-head of global capital markets. “[Priam] is learning and improving with every deal.” Honestly ( as we’ve discussed before) it seems like low-hanging fruit: Instead of having an analyst type all the deals into a spreadsheet and then having a vice president eyeball what it means, you have the analyst type all the deals into a program with a spiffy name, and then have the program eyeball what it means. Instead of an informal eyeball regression, you just do a regression. On the other hand I object a little to this: “We are transforming ourselves,” says Ms Zapparoli. “It used to be purely about relationships, now it’s about marrying that with data analytics . . . The possibilities are huge, and that’s what’s exciting.” Come on, it wasn’t purely about relationships. Your capital markets bankers didn’t just win business by buying the fanciest dinners and making the wittiest conversations at them. They also did some “data analytics.” It was just a very informal sort of “data analytics,” the sort of thing that goes by the name “market knowledge” rather than “machine learning.” And in fact if you outsource all the data analytics to a robot, then that means that the human doing the job will be focused more on relationships; if all the market knowledge is in the computer, the human’s only value-add is the dinner conversation. Similarly: Some senior bankers are dismissive, sneering at efforts to graft artificial intelligence on to what is an essentially relationship-driven business. And even enthusiasts argue that AI will not be a game-changer, given it works best on vast sets of data with billions of observations, rather than the thousands of IPOs and bond deals that banks tend to have in their databases. I often read claims like this about how machine-learning algorithms can never be great investors or bankers because they have not had enough experience of markets and deals, and I always think: Compared to what? How many observations have the human bankers had? The job is a pattern-matching job, and it is hard to the extent that the patterns are uncertain and shifting, but that makes it hard for the robots and the humans alike.

Cryptocurrency blockchains work on the principle of public-key cryptography. Each blockchain account has a private key, which is an enormous number—64 hexadecimal digits in the case of the Ethereum blockchain—known only to the account holder, and which is required to send any cryptocurrency from the account. The private key is run through a public encryption algorithm to generate a public key, which is publicly available and can be used by other people to send cryptocurrency to the account holder. There is no practical way, yet, to use the public key to figure out the private key, so the account is secure. On the other hand, it is easy and mechanical to generate the public key from the private key. One thing that this means is that if you guess someone’s private key, you can pretty easily check to see if you’re right: You run the encryption function on the private key that you guessed, and if it returns the person’s public key then you’re probably right. You can further check by using the combination of the public and private keys to send yourself all the money in the account. If that works then you were right. Also now you have their money. This is not a problem that people worry about very much, just because there are so many more possible private keys (2^256) than there are actual ones (“ nearly 50 million public Ethereum addresses,” on the order of 2^25, meaning that for every Ethereum address in use there are more unused ones than there are atoms in our galaxy), so your odds of guessing someone’s private key are infinitesimal. Unless of course their private key is their birthday, or their phone number, or literally the number 1: What if an Ethereum owner stored their digital money with a private key—the unguessable, 78-digit string of numbers that protects the currency stashed at a certain address—that had a value of 1? To Bednarek's surprise, he found that dead-simple key had in fact once held currency, according to the blockchain that records all Ethereum transactions. But the cash had already been taken out of the Ethereum wallet that used it—almost certainly by a thief who had thought to guess a private key of 1 long before Bednarek had. After all, as with Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies, if anyone knows an Ethereum private key, they can use it to derive the associated public address that the key unlocks. The private key then allows them to transfer the money at that address as though they were its rightful owner. Hey look 1 is a 64-digit hexadecimal number, if you put 63 zeroes in front of it. That is from a Wired article titled “A ‘Blockchain Bandit’ Is Guessing Private Keys and Scoring Millions.” Bednarek is security consultant Adrian Bednarek, and this is the paper that he wrote (and the accompanying video) about what he found, and it is hilarious. Once you know about wallet 1, you might as well move on to wallet 2, and wallet 3, and the Spaceballs Wallet, and a whole bunch of other wallets whose private keys are mostly zeroes.[2] Bednarek did that, and he found hundreds of actual wallets, but in each case someone had been there first: The researchers not only found that cryptocurrency users have in the last few years stored their crypto treasure with hundreds of easily guessable private keys, but also uncovered what they call a "blockchain bandit." A single Ethereum account seems to have siphoned off a fortune of 45,000 ether—worth at one point more than $50 million—using those same key-guessing tricks. If you open a bank account online, and the bank asks you for a password, and you propose “1,” the bank is probably going to reject it and tell you that your password needs to be at least 12 characters and include an uppercase letter, a lowercase letter, a number, a special character, an emoji, a hand gesture and an unexpressed thought, because the bank knows that if it lets you choose an easy password and someone guesses that password and steals your money, the bank is going to get in trouble. Ethereum can’t get in trouble: Ethereum isn’t a thing; it’s a decentralized network that functions on cryptography and market incentives. You have really good incentives not to choose 1 as your private key—if you do, your Ether will get stolen—but no one is actually going to prevent you. There is no ex ante check on individual stupidity; there are only incentives. A lot of people in the cryptocurrency world think that this is a good thing, that the weak and stupid ought to be punished while the fittest survive, that password paternalism is unnecessary among free adults. Probably the blockchain bandit thinks it’s a good thing. We talked last week about about bots who trade crypto assets on decentralized exchanges on the Ethereum blockchain, and who make a profit by arbitraging other users’ typos. “It’s sort of an embarrassing way to make money,” I wrote, “but it apparently works.” This is a million times dumber! This one is so dumb that it stops being embarrassing; if you can steal someone’s Ether because their private key is 1 then that is so ridiculous that you ought to be proud of it. You are the incentives; you are what makes the system work: People will choose random impossible-to-guess private keys because if they don’t you’ll steal their money. Really you are doing them a favor.

Oh man, sorry, this newsletter is in your spam folder now. Anyway I have nothing really to say about this Commodity Futures Trading Commission enforcement action except: Can you believe this stuff keeps happening? Like, setup: In the course of their fraudulent scheme and during the Relevant Period, Defendants made material misrepresentations to pool participants, including that: (1) all pool funds would be used to trade forex; (2) pool participants would receive a minimum 12% guaranteed annual return from this forex trading; (3) the Oasis Pools were profitable and returned 22% in 2017 and 21% in 2018; (4) the Oasis Pools had never had a losing month; (5) money being returned to pool participants was from profitable trading; (6) there was no risk of loss with the Oasis Pools; and (7) pool participants earned extra returns by referring other pool participants to the Oasis Pools. Punch line: Of the approximate $75 million Defendants received from pool participants during the Relevant Period, Defendants deposited only $21 million into forex trading accounts in the names of the Oasis Pools, all of which has been lost trading forex . Defendants misappropriated over $28 million of pool funds to make Ponzi-like payments to other pool participants. Defendants misappropriated over $18 million of pool funds—at least $7 million of which was transferred to Relief Defendants—for unauthorized personal or business expenses such as real estate purchases in Florida, exotic vacations, sports tickets, pet supplies , loans to family members, and college and study abroad tuition. (Emphasis added.) Pet supplies! Probably the worst allegation here is that they actually invested a meaningful chunk of their alleged victims’ money in the thing they said they’d invest it in, and then lost it all .[3] Like there is some basic criminal respectability in telling people you will invest their money in can’t-lose foreign-exchange trading, using some of it to make Ponzi payments to maintain the pretense, and stealing the rest of it to spend on Florida real estate and study abroad.[4] That is how Ponzis work; the craft is in lying to investors about your investing acumen and plans. But if you actually do the forex trading, and are terrible at it, then that suggests that you weren’t just lying to investors to steal their money; you were also deceiving yourself about your can’t-lose forex trading skills.[5] It is all a bit sadder, although I will say that it seems to be common in Ponzi schemes, which are often as much about self-deception as they are about theft. Plus if you just Ponzi some of the money and spend the rest on stuff, the authorities can seize the stuff and recover some money for your victims.[6] If you lose money trading, then it’s gone for good. Anyway the moral of the story is if someone guarantees you 12 percent returns with no risk of loss from trading foreign exchange, they are definitely going to steal your money, but if you are reading this you already knew that and there is no real value in my pointing it out. Same for the CFTC, same for everyone. The supply of suckers for foreign-exchange trading scams is constant and mysterious and impervious to education.

Well, if you are in the business of plowing limitless amounts of money into buzzy tech things at higher-than-ever-before valuations, sometimes this is going to happen: Masayoshi Son, the billionaire founder of SoftBank Group Corp., made a huge personal bet on bitcoin just as prices for the digital currency peaked, losing more than $130 million when he sold out, according to people familiar with the matter. … The exact size of the bet couldn’t be determined, but it came at the peak of the bitcoin frenzy after the digital currency had already risen more than 10-fold in 2017, the people said. Bitcoin peaked at nearly $20,000 in mid-December 2017, and Mr. Son sold in early 2018 after bitcoin had plummeted. … With a net worth estimated by Bloomberg LP at $19 billion, Mr. Son will hardly notice, though it dents his reputation as a patient and prophetic investor. Look I’m going to allow it. Masayoshi Son is not a deep-value investor who scours the Earth for unloved overlooked assets to buy them at bargain prices and waits for the market to come around. He’s the biggest and most entertaining momentum investor around, a guy who scours the Earth for its buzziest and most popular assets so he can pay tremendous prices for them and then wait for them to go up even more. It’s his whole thing, and it has not exactly worked out poorly: He’s super rich, and people who control vast pools of money are lining up to invest with him. It’s a perfectly reasonable strategy, as long as you have some edge at picking which super-hyped buzzy expensive thing really will work out. But that edge is never going to be 100 percent reliable, and every time it isn’t, you’ll buy a faddish thing at the top and it will be embarrassing.

Six months ago, if Lyft Inc. had secretly sent Uber Technologies Inc. a 274-page memo saying how much an average Lyft ride costs, and how much of that Lyft takes and how much it gives to its drivers, and how much it spends on operations and marketing and research, and what its plans are to make more money, and if Uber had replied with a similar 368-page memo, and if the memos had leaked: That would have raised some eyebrows. Why does Uber need to know all that pricing stuff about Lyft, and vice versa? What are they getting up to with all that competitive information? One possibility is that each side could figure out the price that the other could afford to charge for rides, and then set its own prices there: If Uber knows that Lyft can’t make money at less than $12 per ride, or whatever, then Uber can safely charge $12 and not worry too much about Lyft undercutting it. Of course Lyft could undercut it, and in fact both Uber and Lyft lose tons of money so in an obvious though debatable sense they’re both selling rides for below cost. The main explanation for that behavior seems to be that they are spending a lot of money on growing their networks and trying to become the future of transportation, rather than worrying about being profitable now. But it is possible that part of the explanation could be that they don’t exactly know each other’s cost structure, and so they compete on price somewhat blindly, lowering their own prices because they overestimate each other’s ability and desire to undercut them. If they did have frequent granular detail on how much the other guy was losing per ride, that pressure might relax and they might each decide to lose less per ride. Anyway, if they had sent each other those memos six months ago, probably the antitrust authorities would have had questions. But now , Lyft is public and Uber is on its way to being public, and they are legally required to hand out that sort of financial information to anyone who wants it, and you can go read Lyft’s discussion of its financial results and competitive strategies here, and Uber’s here. And here’s this: Uber and Lyft have battled each other for years in a price war that wildly undercut taxicab fares, thanks to billions of dollars in venture capital that subsidized the lower prices and supported the companies’ massive losses. Those days of cutthroat U.S. prices may be numbered. With loss-wary public-market investors likely to add pressure, numerous investors in both companies, former ride-hailing executives and academics who study the market believe Uber and Lyft will ultimately need to raise fares amid the growing red ink. “You have shareholders who want you to generate profits,” said Mitchell Green, founder of Lead Edge Capital, an investor in Uber. “There are lots of different levers, and one of them is pricing....These companies have more pricing power than people think.” We have also talked about this dynamic in terms of “loss-wary public-market investors” versus profligate venture-capital investors: Private investors, the stereotype goes, are happy to subsidize consumers as long as it generates growth; public investors, the stereotype goes, are myopically focused on the short term and want consistent quarterly profits. Obviously those stereotypes aren’t the whole story, and public investors are pouring billions of dollars into money-losing unicorns these days so they have some tolerance for money-losing growth. But another possibility is just that the disclosure dynamics of public and private companies are different. Public companies all tell each other (and everyone else) how much money they make and how they think about their business and strategy. Private companies mostly don’t share that sort of stuff with each other, and if they did share it privately with each other they’d probably get in trouble. It’s possible that sharing that sort of stuff leads to a more profitable equilibrium, in which each competitor can see and understand the others’ strategy and so they can get to a pricing structure that works for all of them. You see hints of this sort of thing sometimes: suggestions that competitors are communicating with each other on pricing via public disclosures and conference calls, worries that disclosures that are good for investors might be bad for consumers, discussions of when unilateral disclosure of information might “ facilitate anticompetitive harm.” And a big problem for cartels is monitoring your competitors to see if they’re cheating; if they publish detailed financial information then that’s easier to do. We talk a lot around here about whether index funds are an antitrust problem, and it probably goes a bit too far to suggest that public markets themselves are an antitrust problem. Still it is possible that disclosure itself has a sort of normalizing effect on pricing and competition, that companies that know how much their competitors make and that have to disclose their own financials will tend to converge on pricing that makes money rather than losing it, and that the demand for profitability in public markets is a feature of their structure rather than a result of investor psychology. Elsewhere, “April 23 will mark the end of a 25-day quiet period for banks that underwrote Lyft’s initial public offering,” allowing them to start publishing research notes; it’ll be awkward if they are sell recommendations. And “Uber Technologies Inc. secured a $1 billion investment from three Japanese companies” in its self-driving-cars unit, valuing it at $7.25 billion. (We talked about this deal, in option-valuation terms, last month.)

If you want to buy corn, you can go to a supermarket and pick out your corn and take it to the cash register and buy it. If you want to buy a lot of corn, you can go to a big corn farm and negotiate a price for some bushels, or enter into a long-term contract to assure your supply of corn, or whatever. It’s a thing, you can buy and sell it in all the ways that people buy and sell things. Also the Chicago Board of Trade lists corn futures. If you want to do your corn trading in sort of an abstract financialized world, you can trade corn futures. They are a good liquid way to bet on corn prices; if you are a big corn user or producer, they are a way to hedge your corn-price risk. They are not really a substitute for the supermarket, or the farm. For most natural corn uses, you don’t want the regulated standardized financialized futures contract. You want corn. There are more convenient ways to get the corn than through a futures contract. This is not exactly new news, but I was tickled to learn that the physically settled Bitcoin futures that Intercontinental Exchange Inc.’s “Bakkt” project is planning will be one-day futures: Atlanta-based ICE is trying to attract institutional investors by providing Bitcoin futures that differ in a crucial way from derivatives already offered by CME Group Inc. and Cboe Global Markets Inc.: When Bakkt’s one-day contracts expire they would pay out in Bitcoin tokens instead of U.S. dollars. Customarily, a “future” is an exchange-traded derivative contract that allows you to bet on the price of the underlying thing in the future . You don’t need a contract to bet on tomorrow’s Bitcoin price. You can just buy a Bitcoin today, and tomorrow it will be worth tomorrow’s Bitcoin price. No, the whole point of a one-day Bitcoin future is that you don’t want to buy a Bitcoin today, because buying a Bitcoin is a terrible experience. I don’t mean that (just) from a subjective “oh you have to remember your password” sort of perspective; the bigger problem, for an institutional investor, is that the places where you can buy Bitcoin have a tendency to be … not especially institutional. Many Bitcoin exchanges, which will sell you Bitcoins and keep custody of them for you, are not subject to U.S. regulation and have a tendency to get their Bitcoins stolen. Buying Bitcoins and keeping custody of them for yourself might give you more security (unless you lose your private key), but if you are a regulated audited fiduciary investment manager it raises its own problems. How do you convince your auditors, and your clients, that you actually have the Bitcoins and that you have taken the proper steps to safeguard them? With cash or securities there are standard steps—custodian banks, etc.—that everyone recognizes as legally effective; with cryptocurrency, the norms are still developing. It’s definitely a booming industry— old-school financial firms and new crypto-y firms are constantly announcing plans for custody solutions—but it is not yet a mature one. None of these problems exactly go away with one-day futures, but they are … deferred? By a day? When you enter into the futures contract, you are doing something that is entirely conventional for an institutional investor to do: You’re entering into a regulated futures contract on a regulated futures exchange. You don't have to worry about tricky questions of custody. The next day, of course, the trade settles, and you have a Bitcoin.[1] You still have to figure out all the custody stuff. But the trade itself is normal and tractable: Trading Bitcoins on a Bitcoin exchange is still weird, but trading futures on a futures exchange is a perfectly normal thing to do. The fact that the futures immediately transform into Bitcoins is a nice convenience, a way to use a normal trade to get a still-abnormal asset. And whereas the regulatory apparatus of trading on a futures exchange subject to U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission oversight is maybe a bit of overkill if you just want to buy corn, it is soothing if you want to buy Bitcoins. Much of the time, financial products are structured to minimize regulation; with Bitcoin futures, you might turn a spot transaction into a “future” just to opt in to more regulation. In financial transactions among sophisticated institutions, there is often a sense that the optimal amount of regulation, for the parties, is a bit less than the default amount. In Bitcoin transactions, the optimal amount is often a lot more. Anyway Bakkt still has to figure out all the custody stuff: The launch date for the project -- known as Bakkt -- has been delayed for months because of skepticism from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the U.S. regulator that polices Bitcoin futures. The issue that that has made the CFTC the most concerned is how clients’ tokens will be stored, and thus safeguarded from possible theft and manipulation, according to people familiar with the matter. To placate the agency, ICE is considering seeking a license from New York financial regulators that would permit Bakkt itself to hold custody of customers’ tokens, said three of the people, who asked not to be named because the discussions aren’t public. Should ICE secure a state license it would still need sign-off from the CFTC on the broader Bakkt project. I suppose that once you perfect and normalize custody, the endgame is really for Bitcoin to be a normal asset that can trade in a normal spot market, making one-day futures somewhat superfluous. But we’re still pretty far away from that point.

What even: Elon Musk’s war with Tesla Inc. short sellers just got weirder. The electric-car maker claims a California man who it says is part of an online group of short sellers has been stalking its Fremont factory and harassing its employees -- including dangerously swerving his car toward a Tesla Model 3 that was on a freeway test drive and injuring a Tesla security guard in a hit-and-run on company property. … Tesla claims it was able to identify the harasser as Randeep Hothi from the license plate of the vehicle he drove -- and that it also traced Hothi to the Twitter account he allegedly shares with his brother that frequently tweets with the hashtag “$TSLAQ" in solidarity with others who want to see the company fail. … On April 16, the company alleges, Hothi was behind the wheel of an Acura that variously drove ahead of, beside and behind a Tesla-owned Model 3 on the freeway for a period of 35 minutes -- while Hothi was taking pictures of the Model 3. The Acura swerved so close to the Model 3 that the vehicle’s side-collision safety feature engaged in an emergency maneuver to avoid a collision, according to the court filing. Look, this just isn’t a thing . People short Ford Motor Co. stock but don’t try to run its cars off the road. They short Herbalife Nutrition Ltd. but don’t put poison in its powders. In general , illegal sabotage of public companies by short sellers is the sort of thing that a certain kind of public-company CEO loves to imagine and complain about, but that doesn’t happen much. Not never! But not much. And so in the past I have been fairly dismissive of Elon Musk’s frequent complaints about short-selling saboteurs, which—like so much of Musk’s online activity—can feel a little kooky and half-baked. On the other hand this … is pretty concrete? Like maybe they imagined the whole thing, but that would be pretty weird even for Tesla. A real lawyer signed a real court document making allegations of physical harm. Maybe Musk is on to something with all the sabotage talk. Wouldn’t it be amazing if Elon Musk is somehow the one CEO who really is hounded by evil short sellers who are constantly sabotaging his cars? One well known and mostly positive fact about Musk’s ... muchness … is that he attracts passionate fans, that his over-the-top public persona resonates with some people who become devoted buyers of Tesla’s cars and stock. That’s good for sales, and good for the stock price. But maybe the (well, a) downside of that is that he also attracts passionate short sellers , that his over-the-top public persona resonates in a bad way with some people, who become devoted short sellers of Tesla’s stock and also, like, harassers of its employees and rammers of its cars? Somehow something that he does drives them crazy, and then they start driving crazily near Teslas. Meanwhile, “the company is hosting an investor day on Monday, expected to focus on the progress of its technology for self-driven vehicles.” And Musk is now “in a rare public dispute with a critical supplier: Panasonic Corp., the company that makes all of the lithium-ion battery cells that power Tesla Inc.’s electric vehicles.” And “Tesla Inc. said it’s looking into a fire in Shanghai involving one of its vehicles after a video of a car bursting into flames was circulated on social media in China.” But there’s some chance it was sabotage, right?

I assume that there are consultants out there whose business is thinking about pricing strategy for hedge funds, but I have never met them, so my completely naive view is that this seems smart: D.E. Shaw & Co. is making it more expensive for investors in its biggest hedge fund, raising fees while many of its rivals have been forced to slash them. The New York-based investment firm is reverting to a fee model that it held for the better part of the 2000s, according to a person with knowledge of the matter. The new structure will charge 3 percent of assets and 30 percent of profits and will take effect at the start of next year. The move cements D.E. Shaw’s standing as one of the pricier funds in the industry. Hedge funds, subject to backlash from investors frustrated by mediocre returns, have been trimming fees and offering more concessions to investors over the past decade. Fees now average 1.45 percent for management and 17 percent for performance, according to a Credit Suisse Group AG survey released in August, down from the traditional 2-and-20 model. Let’s say you charge 2 and 20 and clients are grumbling. Oh sure you can go to 1.45 and 17, but … really? Clients who think that 2 and 20 is expensive will not think that 1.45 and 17 is cheap; there are index funds that charge 0 and 0. Zero is cheap! A hedge fund is never going to look competitive with truly inexpensive products. Charging high-but-not-quite-as-high fees just looks, like, cheap in the bad way. Weak. Unsure of your ability to offer value to your clients, and trying to make up for it with discounts. On the other hand: 3 and 30! Charging 3 and 30 is a way to advertise that you generate alpha, or that your clients think you generate alpha, or that you think you generate alpha, or that you think you can get people to think you generate alpha, or something else on a continuum of “you are good at being a hedge fund.” Obviously it is helpful to have performance numbers here but honestly even without them I’d be tempted to just charge a lot of money. In general it feels like there has been, and will continue to be, a sort of hollowing-out-of-the-middle-class of investment options, in which there is room for very low-cost mechanical approaches and high-cost high-alpha specialized approaches; self-consciously taking yourself out of the middle just feels like sensible marketing.

Well we talked about this a couple of weeks ago, before Zoom Video Communications Inc. went public, but here you go: Zoom Technologies Inc., a Beijing-based maker of mobile phone components whose shares traded for less than 1 cent each just two months ago, has soared more than 70,000 percent since March 12. The catalyst? Who knows, but confusion spurred by the trading debut of a much bigger company, Zoom Video Communications Inc., is one very plausible explanation. Zoom Technologies has that sweet sweet “ZOOM” ticker and, now, an $8 million equity market capitalization. I feel like $8 million would be a reasonable price for Zoom Video (ticker ZM, market cap $15.9 billion) to pay for that ticker. I am going to say that this is a case of market efficiency that should naturally conclude with ZM Zoom acquiring ZOOM Zoom, shutting down its (apparently rather limited) business and stripping it for its ticker. I mean or it’s just a case of confused people and confused algorithms and other, cleverer people and algorithms taking advantage of the confused ones. That is also possible. Probable really. But what if it just worked out this time? Zoom, buy ZOOM, come on; you will be getting a better ticker for yourself, and you will be giving the rest of us a gift, a world that makes just the tiniest bit more sense.

If you are a private equity fund, you borrow a lot of money to buy a company, and then you try to operate the company in a way that makes enough money to pay back the debt and make you rich. Sometimes this works and everyone is happy. Sometimes it doesn’t work and at least some people are sad. If you are a smart cutthroat private equity fund you try not to be the one who is sad. Traditionally you will be the holder of the equity in the company (thus: “private equity ”), and if there is not enough money to go around you will try to arrange matters so that the equity gets the money and the debt does not. This is hard, because the point of debt is that it is senior to equity, but you are smart and you might find a way. There are dividend recaps and ways to shuffle assets around and loose covenants that allow equity payouts even in default. And in fact the financial press is absolutely full of stories of creditors complaining about private equity firms putting one past them, finding clever ways to get paid themselves while stiffing the creditors. But that’s just the typical conflict. There are other possibilities. For instance here is the story of a time that Apollo Global Management LLC acquired a company and got its executives to pay Apollo to work there . The dust-up involves CEVA Logistics AG, a Swiss company that Apollo acquired more than a decade ago. Former executives today say Apollo double-crossed them. In a $34 million class-action lawsuit against Apollo and CEVA, they say the buyout firm looked out for its own interest and used a deft stroke of financial engineering that ended up wiping out their equity. Apollo denies wrongdoing. … Interviews with 35 current and former CEVA managers, as well as presentations made to prospective executives, reveal how Apollo and CEVA persuaded, pressured or required managers to put their money in. Over the years, Apollo and CEVA told executives they could make as much as 15 times their investment when Apollo eventually took CEVA public. “It didn’t even enter my mind that I could lose this money,’’ said Smit, who signed a document promising she wouldn’t sue over the investment. “It feels like they robbed hundreds of people by legal means.’’ Apollo bought most of the equity of CEVA in a buyout, and let (or required) executives buy some equity too “since it would give them ‘skin in the game.’” When CEVA ran into trouble you might have expected Apollo to maximize the value of the equity even at the expense of its creditors. But instead Apollo bought a bunch of CEVA debt cheap, became a creditor, and then wiped out the equity: Apollo started buying CEVA debt at a discount in 2007, according to the lawsuit and an Apollo document. That made it possible for Apollo and other big creditors in 2013 to swap debt for equity in a new company that would own CEVA. The lawsuit says the move erased the shareholders’ stake and let Apollo maintain control with minority ownership of a going concern with less debt. This wiped out Apollo’s equity (but then Apollo got new equity in the recapitalization), and it also wiped out the executives’ equity (and they got nothing). In response to the lawsuit, Apollo and CEVA said they had no fiduciary duty to CEVA executives, and that even if they did, it wasn’t breached. Apollo said it lost its equity stake, too, and that a recapitalization was needed because CEVA was close to defaulting on some interest payments. Huh. Look, this is fine. Executives ought to be compensated in part through equity ownership of their company, and when a company can’t pay its debts, that’s supposed to wipe out the equity, including the equity owned by the executives. Their equity is supposed to be at risk, to pay off if the company works and not if it doesn’t. “It didn’t even enter my mind that I could lose this money” is a terrible thing to say about paying cash to buy illiquid unlisted stock in your own highly levered employer , come on. There is one general lesson here, which is that when a portfolio company runs into trouble, a smart aggressive private equity firm will tend to do a good job of maximizing the value of its own stake in that company rather than the total return to all stakeholders. (Also it will do that openly and proudly, saying things like “what, we had no fiduciary duty to anyone else”: Every unsympathetic story like this makes Apollo look great to its actual investors, who are pleased to see it working hard and smart on their behalf.) There is also a more specific lesson, which is don’t pay Apollo to work at one of their companies . Honestly, when you write a check to Apollo to work at their portfolio company, and then you sign a document saying you won’t sue about it, what do you think is going to happen?

Here is a pretty interesting investor presentation from the Blackstone Group LP, pitching a project that it expects to have a negative net present value. Specifically Blackstone has decided to pay more taxes. Not too many more taxes; it’s a “relatively modest additional tax cost,” as the presentation puts it, so that’s nice. Still it will cost more than $50 million a a year, possibly much more.[1] There is no offsetting financial benefit to Blackstone the entity; those extra taxes won’t buy it more business opportunities or lower costs or anything like that. Still they think it’s a good idea, and they’re pretty smart so they’re probably right. What the extra taxes will buy for Blackstone is the corporate form: Blackstone is currently a publicly traded partnership (so it doesn’t pay corporate tax), but now it will become a corporation (and will pay corporate tax). Again this won’t change its business in any material way, other than the extra taxes. All it will do is make it easier for some people to become Blackstone shareholders. Most public companies are corporations, and many public investors are limited to owning shares of corporations. Many stock indexes, too, include only corporations, so indexed investors can’t buy partnerships. And retail investors might find it a pain to own shares in a partnership; you get some weird tax forms when you own a partnership. “Conversion unlocks opportunity for equity value appreciation by removing ownership restrictions and meaningfully expanding global investor universe,” says the presentation. “60%+ of U.S. long-only and index fund / ETF market restricted from owning partnerships,” it says, “resulting in under-ownership of BX relative to peers and leading companies.” Presumably all the formerly restricted people will go buy Blackstone stock and the stock price will go up, which will be good for Blackstone’s existing shareholders and executives. As of 11:15 this morning the stock was up about 7 percent on the news. Isn’t it a little weird? There are two basic ways to think about stock prices, the corporate finance approach, in which a stock price is the discounted present value of the company’s future cash flows, and the simpler supply-and-demand approach, in which a stock goes up when more people want to buy it. The efficient markets hypothesis suggests that these approaches are the same, that people’s desires to buy stocks are correlated with the expected cash flows, and that if for some reason a lot of people shun a stock with high expected cash flows then arbitrageurs will step in and nonetheless push the price up to the fair level. But in the real world executives sometimes decide to do things to reduce future cash flows in order to, as Blackstone’s Stephen Schwarzman said on Bloomberg Television this morning, “reach a dramatically larger audience.” Blackstone’s stock was up this morning on news that its future cash flows will be lower, but that more people will be able to buy it.

Ooh here is “Bloodsport on Wall Street: Hedge Funds Make Mayhem for Profit,” a nice recap of many of the fun credit default swap trades that we have talked about over the years. ( Codere! Hovnanian! McClatchy! Sears!) As is always the case in discussions of these trades, some people are amused and appreciative: “The participants in this CDS market are all incredibly sophisticated, with wonderful lawyers,” says Henry Hu, a law professor at the University of Texas at Austin who studies swaps. “They’re endlessly creative.” While others grumble: Some in the industry worry that aggressive traders will undermine confidence in the market for swaps. “I don’t know how long the CDS market can survive if it is untethered by the underlying credit risk,” says Robert Pickel, who until 2014 was chief executive officer at the International Swaps and Derivatives Association, the trade group that in March proposed new default guidelines. I am not sure that’s true. For one thing, people have said it about every weird CDS trade, and this genre of weird CDS trade dates back at least five years, and the CDS market has survived. But also I think that it underestimates the aesthetic component of high finance. People like this stuff! Some people, anyway. If you work at a distressed-debt hedge fund you have to do something all day. One thing you could do is analyze companies’ cash flows to decide if they are good credits independent of any action that you could take, but that is only one tool in your kit; instead of just trying to understand the world, you might also want to affect it. Doing stuff with CDS expands your palette, gives you more opportunities to make things happen, and lets you test your intelligence and creativity against other smart hedge funds in an intellectual contest, which is honestly why you got into the distressed-debt investing business in the first place. A derivative that gives you exactly the underlying credit risk that you expect is a fine and good mass-market instrument, sure, yes, but a derivative that gives you some adventure has its own kind of appeal.

The way it works is: A company reveals some bad news. Its stock drops. People sue it for securities fraud because it didn’t disclose the bad news earlier. Sometimes step 3 is pretty tenuous: The bad news was disclosed instantly, leading immediately to the stock drop, but shareholders sue the company for not previously disclosing the conditions that led to the bad news, or for not warning shareholders that the bad news was a possibility, or for saying in its securities filings “we try to avoid bad things happening” when in fact bad things were going to happen, or whatever. The theory is pretty flexible, is the point, which is why I say that “everything is securities fraud.” Still this strikes me as a novel extension of the theory: Lyft Inc. was sued by investors who claim the ride-sharing company overstated its market position when it went public last month, leading to a dramatic plunge in its stock price. Two separate class-action complaints against Lyft, as well as its officers and directors and underwriters, were filed Wednesday in state court in the company’s hometown, San Francisco. The novelty here, it seems to me, is that these lawsuits omit step 1: Lyft hasn’t disclosed any bad news . It went public (three weeks ago) at $72 per share, and then the stock dropped, not because some new bad news about Lyft came out—Lyft hasn’t even made a securities filing since its IPO, nothing is going on—but just because it sold stock at a price that, in hindsight, the market didn’t quite want to pay. Traditionally you would wait for Lyft to announce something bad—at least a first public quarter of disappointing earnings—and then say “aha, they didn’t warn us about this bad thing in the IPO, fraud!” But here the shareholders got impatient. I think the theory has to be something like: There was some bad news about Lyft that the market didn’t know when Lyft went public. Therefore the market bought Lyft’s shares at $72, a price that did not reflect the bad news. The market subsequently learned the bad news. You can tell because the market price fell to the $50s, a price that does reflect the bad news. You don’t need to know what the bad news was ; the whole story is contained in the stock price. It is a lovely informational-efficiency theory: The market knows something bad now that it didn’t know three weeks ago, because the price is lower. Maybe every time a stock price drops, that is securities fraud. It is a real triumph of the efficient-markets hypothesis. (Fine, the “plaintiffs also dinged the company for failing to tell investors that it was about to recall more than a 1,000 of the bikes in its ride-share program,” I guess that is subsequent bad news, but it seems pretty thin.)

s.h: Insider trading is not about theft, it’s about fairness
s.t: Well, that’s what I always say. I also admit that prosecutors often say otherwise, that they go around saying things like “the stock market is supposed to be a level playing field” when they are bringing charges against accused insider traders. I just think this is wrong, that a moment’s thought will make it obvious that the stock market is not a level playing field and is not supposed to be, that the whole point of the stock market is to provide incentives to professionals to find out information that nobody else knows. Still they say it. And juries tend to find it persuasive. So I appreciate that Sebastian Pinto-Thomaz’s lawyers came up with the novel legal strategy of asking them not to say it, and that it worked: Federal prosecutors walked away Tuesday from a time-honored tactic of telling jurors that the stock market should be a “level playing field,” after Manhattan U.S. District Judge Jed S. Rakoff agreed with counsel for a former analyst on trial for insider trading that such language isn't grounded in reality. In a morning bench ruling, Judge Rakoff sided with lawyers representing former S&P debt analyst Sebastian Pinto-Thomaz, who argued in a pretrial motion that such language, a fixture in previous insider trading trials, doesn't properly characterize how the stock market works. They argued that U.S. Supreme Court precedent, including Dirks v. U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, provides that the stock market is not supposed to be fundamentally fair, or a level playing field, as traders routinely seek out ways to gain an advantage over their competitors to increase profits. Rakoff agreed, saying, “Anyone who thinks that the stock market is a level playing field obviously has no contact with reality.” Obviously they can still say that he insider traded and that that was bad and so forth, they just have to stick closer to the actual law, rather than pretending that the stock market is supposed to be fair to everyone.

Look, I don’t know what’s going on here, but it’s the sort of thing that we sometimes discuss around here so here you go: Hong Kong Airlines was in turmoil on Wednesday after an apparent boardroom coup in which a former director claimed he had taken control due to financial irregularities on the part of shareholder HNA Group. Zhong Guosong proclaimed himself chairman of Hong Kong’s third largest carrier just a day before supposed chief Hou Wei assured staff in a memo that he was still at the helm of the financially fragile company. … It was not clear who was officially in charge but neither side appeared to be backing down, as the carrier fights for its future amid financial instability. “The current issues have no impact on our operations and we will continue to run our business as normal,” said Hong Kong Airlines (or at least one possible instance of Hong Kong Airlines) in a press release. Good to know! We talk a lot about how to decide who controls a corporation when there is a dispute, with shareholders and directors and executives and courts and national governments and the guy with the keys to the front door all having some claim to make that decision. But often that decision is sort of abstract and second-order; the dispute over who “controls” the company is really about who gets to appropriate the profits or fire his enemies or make strategic plans, while the actual day-to-day operations of the company just keep on going despite the dispute at the top. You don’t necessarily need to know who the chief executive officer is for the planes to go where they’re supposed to go; the pilots and mechanics and flight attendants can do their jobs with any CEO, or none. In some sense no one is in charge; the company is in charge of itself.
