When a company buys another company for cash, and hedge funds think that the deal price is too low, they can seek “appraisal,” meaning that they can go to a judge and ask him to decide what a fair price for the target company would be and make the acquirer pay them that price. His name is Travis Laster. The judge, I mean. That’s his name. If you think that a merger price was too low, you go to Travis Laster and you ask him to decide the right price, and he will then award you that price, which might be higher or lower than (or the same as) the agreed-upon deal price. He has sort of a curious power to rewrite merger agreements and decide, in a legally binding way, the value of giant companies. Also he is having a weird time at work these days, and I am going to tell you about it because it combines corporate finance with a particularly specific sort of legal realism. Well, fine, I am exaggerating a little, it is not just Travis Laster. But most big U.S. corporations are incorporated in Delaware, which means that if you want appraisal you will end up in the Delaware Court of Chancery. That court has seven judges, and you could get any one of them, but Laster has been involved in a number of the most important recent appraisal cases, and writes long and thoughtful and controversial opinions in them. And he seems to be in a bit of a fight with his bosses on the Delaware Supreme Court, a fight that is affecting how much various public companies are worth. The story starts with the buyout of Dell Inc. by its founder, Michael Dell, in 2013. Some investors thought he was getting a sweetheart deal in buying his own company, and they sought appraisal, and Vice Chancellor Laster heard the case and decided that Michael Dell really had bought Dell too cheaply. He wrote an opinion finding that the fair price for Dell was higher than any price that anyone had been willing to pay: The deal price had been $13.75, and he awarded the appraisal plaintiffs $17.62 per share. I thought at the time (2016) that this decision was a little weird, since a lot of people with a lot of money on the line had all concluded that Dell was worth less than $14. But it was weird in the way that appraisal just kind of is weird; the whole point of it is that it allows a judge to substitute his determination of value for that of the parties to a merger. In 2017, the Delaware Supreme Court reversed the Dell decision, finding that the market for Dell’s stock, and also the auction process for the buyout of Dell, were both more or less efficient and so provided better evidence of its value than the tastes of one judge. So it threw out Vice Chancellor Laster’s decision awarding Dell’s objecting shareholders a higher price. When that decision was handed down, Vice Chancellor Laster was in the middle of hearing another appraisal case, about Hewlett-Packard Co.’s acquisition of a company called Aruba Networks Inc. And so he sent a letter to the parties to that case. “In the letter, the Vice Chancellor requested supplemental briefing on ‘the market attributes of Aruba’s stock’ in part because he ‘learned how many errors [he] made in the Dell matter.’”[1] And then he decided that case, last February, by finding that the fair price for Aruba’s stock was its unaffected trading price . The deal price had been $24.67 per share, but HP had paid a premium for Aruba, and Vice Chancellor Laster decided that that premium was not part of the fair value of Aruba that should be paid to its shareholders. (Mostly it reflected synergies of the combined company, which are not part of the appraisal value.) Instead, the trading price of the stock before the deal was announced—$17.13 per share—was the best evidence of the fair price, so that’s what he gave the plaintiffs. This decision was also weird! It was the extreme opposite of the Dell decision: Whereas in Dell the judge discarded all of the evidence of the market to come to his own conclusion about Dell’s value, in Aruba he discarded basically every argument about value and just used the market price. Not only was his judgment of value irrelevant, but so was the judgment of HP , and Aruba’s board, and other potential buyers, and every other identifiable human with a view on value. The impersonal invisible hand of the stock market was all that counted. Whereas Vice Chancellor Laster’s original Dell opinion staked a pretty robust claim for the power of appraisal, his Aruba opinion suggested that appraisal was dead. If the unaffected stock price is generally the correct deal value, then no one should ever seek appraisal again, and Delaware appraisal rights are worthless. This was so extreme a decision that, among appraisal-arbitrage types that I talk to, a popular theory was that the Aruba decision was sarcastic , that Vice Chancellor Laster’s message to the supreme court was: “Oh yeah? You don’t like me substituting my own judgment for that of the market? Well, fine, here’s the market price, do you like that?” They don’t like it, it turns out. Yesterday the Delaware Supreme Court reversed Vice Chancellor Laster’s Aruba decision. Here is the opinion, whose tone is sort of … hurt? Basically the supreme court reads Vice Chancellor Laster’s Aruba opinion as an attack on its Dell decision, and it doesn’t understand why the vice chancellor is so mad: Like any human perspective, the trial judge’s broader reading of Dell and DFC is arguable, but the trial judge’s sense that those decisions somehow compelled him to make the decision he did was not supported by any reasonable reading of those decisions or grounded in any direct citation to them. Among other things, the trial judge seemed to find it novel that DFC and Dell recognized that when a public company with a deep trading market is sold at a substantial premium to the preannouncement price, after a process in which interested buyers all had a fair and viable opportunity to bid, the deal price is a strong indicator of fair value, as a matter of economic reality and theory. The apparent novelty the trial judge perceived is surprising, given the long history of giving important weight to market-tested deal prices in the Court of Chancery and this Court, a history that long predated the trial judge’s contrary determination in Dell. Aruba is not exactly a giant unqualified win for appraisal plaintiffs: The Delaware Supreme Court awarded them $19.10 per share, based on the deal price minus an estimate of expected synergies that were allocated to Aruba (again, synergies are not part of the fair value in an appraisal case), and you would never bring an appraisal case if you knew that your award would be 20 percent below the deal price. Still it is sort of a normal appraisal decision. It leaves open appraisal as a possibility , it assumes that sometimes there is information about the value of a public company that can be known but that is not incorporated into the stock price. From the opinion: HP had more incentive to study Aruba closely than ordinary traders in small blocks of Aruba shares, and also had material, nonpublic information that, by definition, could not have been baked into the public trading price. For example, HP knew about Aruba’s strong quarterly earnings before the market did, and likely took that information into account when pricing the deal. Based on the record evidence, the Court of Chancery could easily have found that HP and Aruba’s back and forth over price, HP’s access to nonpublic information to supplement its consideration of the public information available to stock market buyers, and the currency of the information that they had at the time of striking a bargain had improved the parties’ ability to estimate Aruba’s going-concern value over that of the market as a whole. In particular, HP had better insight into Aruba’s future prospects than the market because it was aware that Aruba expected its quarterly results to exceed analysts’ expectations. Appraisal is an uncomfortable topic because it assumes inefficient markets; the only reason you’d seek an appraisal is because you think that the market got the wrong price for a company, but that a judge will get the right (higher) price. That sometimes seems like a weird thing to think, and sometimes Delaware judges themselves conclude that it’s a weird thing to think and just defer to the market. Other times they don’t. If you are seeking appraisal, you want to catch them on the days when they don’t.

That is: If you think that it’s bad to invest in like tobacco companies or gun companies or whatever, is betting against those companies by selling their stock short (1) also bad or (2) actually good? This is such a good late-night-dorm-room question of financial capitalism question that I was a little shocked to realize that I’d never thought about it. But I am apparently not alone; here is a Pensions & Investments article about how “hedge funds by their very nature are somewhat ill-equipped to handle the rising emphasis on ESG [environmental, social and governance factors] in investing,” and there seems to be genuine, though vague, disagreement on the question: It's a simpler equation for long-only investors. Don't like a company for its poor ESG practices? Don't buy its shares. But are you allowed to sell short the same company — and potentially profit — from those same lax principles if the stock falls? ... "It's fair to say a lot remains to be done," [one allocator] said. "There's not yet a common understanding on how to interpret hedge funds' short positions in terms of ESG." The Church of England is against both long and short bets on industries on its exclusion list because it believes that either way, it's wrong to profit from those activities, Mr. Mason said. But Mr. Lindenbaum pointed out that by shorting a stock, you can help increase a company's cost of capital. On the one hand, there is a certain force to “either way, it’s wrong to profit from those activities”; if you think that some activities are just socially icky, then making your money from them, either long or short, is icky. “Church of England profits from short bet on pornography company” doesn’t sound good, exactly, does it? Arguably a short seller is competing with the company it is shorting—for the capital of investors who want to buy shares of that company, and who can either buy shares issued by the company or shares borrowed and shorted by the short seller—and you might not want to become a competitor in a sinful business. On the other hand, particularly in the case of hedge funds , shorting a stock can be part of a strategy of harming the company. Increasing its cost of capital, sure, but also lots of short-selling hedge funds tend to be activist shorts: They don’t just short the stock and hope it goes down; they also use (preferably legal) methods to make that come true. They go to regulators and complain that the company is doing something illegal, they lobby legislators to pass laws against the company’s activities, they file to invalidate its patents, they publish research reports exposing that it is a fraud, whatever. If you don’t like guns, you should really like a hedge fund that shorts gun manufacturers and then lobbies banks not to finance gun production. That’s not just lip service to ESG; that’s actually doing something about it! One more abstract consideration is Cliff Asness’s point that the goal of ESG investing really ought to be to drive up expected returns in sin industries: By refusing to invest in companies that do bad things, you raise their cost of capital, causing them to finance fewer (bad) projects. “That means quite simply that fewer sinful projects will show positive NPVs and fewer will be undertaken,” writes Asness. But “one man’s discount rate is another man's expected return,” and so if ESG investing is successful in driving up the cost of capital for bad companies, that means that the returns to people who do invest in those companies will be higher . So why would you short them?

A pretty standard stereotype of how hedge funds work is: A hungry ambitious young investor convinces a few true believers to give her money, and works really hard to invest it well in niche conviction ideas. The ideas are great and her returns are high. On the strength of those returns she raises billions of dollars in locked-up capital. Her good ideas do not have capacity for billions of dollars, so she invests it in whatever, while spending most of her time fundraising and going on television and shopping for yachts. The returns are bad, but they are bad returns on very large amounts of money, so the fees remain high. I do not mean to suggest that this is always true in every detail, but it sometimes has a certain amount of explanatory power. So it’s sort of heartening to see that Bill Gross’s career was the opposite: Results for Bill Gross, the famous bond investor who spent the bulk of his career running the Total Return Fund at PIMCO, provide a noteworthy comparison. The average monthly spread between the fund’s risk-adjusted gross return and the benchmark return, gross alpha, was 0.10 percent over Gross’s first five years running the fund. His skill allowed him to extract about $1.9 million per month in 2018 U.S. dollars from the market. In his last five years ended in September 2014, the average monthly spread was 0.18 percent, and the average fund AUM was $271 billion. Gross’s monthly value extraction was roughly $500 million. The magnitude of his alpha in the later years was roughly double what it was in the early years, leading to value extraction that was roughly 270 times larger because of the substantial increase in AUM. That’s from a note called “ Looking for Easy Games in Bonds” by Michael Mauboussin of BlueMountain Capital Management, which is mostly about the possibilities for active management in bonds. (Better than in stocks!) One way that Mauboussin evaluates active managers is on “value extraction,” which is basically gross alpha (above-benchmark returns) times assets under management. Getting a high percentage return on a small pool of assets is, in this view, less impressive than getting a somewhat lower return on a much larger pool of assets. The goal is to make more total money for investors. But when Gross’s fund got huge, he had higher (percentage) alpha than when it was small. (And when he left Pimco to run a small fund, his returns were disappointing.) Nor is that even unusual, exactly, in bonds; Mauboussin graphs bond mutual fund performance (gross alpha and value extraction) in 10 buckets of fund size, and finds “a decline in annual gross alpha as you go from the first to the eighth decile,” but: Gross alpha then rises again for the largest funds. In general, the opportunity set shrinks as funds get larger because of ownership and liquidity constraints. But the reversal in the trend for large funds suggests some sources of edge. These include superior allocations to new issues, better access to information, and more flexible mandates. This is what was often said of Gross, that because his fund was so big it “was the market”: He could know where all the bonds were, push around Wall Street to get favorable pricing, get any new-issue allocations he wanted, and generally have advantages of bigness that outweighed the constraints of not being particularly nimble. But it is a more general pattern: As they get bigger, bond funds get less nimble and worse, until at a certain point they get so big that the advantages of bigness outweigh the disadvantages. There are economies of scale. This is a nice story. The stereotypical hedge-fund story is a gloomy one; it suggests that skill is sort of worthless, since anyone who has it will end up squandering it on a fund that is too big to actually take advantage of it.[2] The bond-fund story suggests that skill is useful and can persist,[3] that if you do a good enough job of investing to amass a lot of assets, you can invest those assets even better than you did the earlier ones. It’s a virtuous cycle; the system works; the rewards go to people who can use them.

This is adorable: The worlds of art and finance aren’t that far apart. That’s what students from the Yale School of Management and the Yale School of Art learned last semester during an independent study course that brought them together. The students took part in a cryptocurrency workshop organized by the two schools, exploring the relationship between art and money by creating new “currencies,” based on the cryptocurrency structure that has produced decentralized digital currencies like Bitcoin. Renowned German conceptual artist and filmmaker Hito Steyerl worked with the students. “There’s an interesting relationship between art and money,” says William Goetzmann, the Edwin J. Beinecke Professor of Finance and Management Studies and director of the International Center for Finance, who helped shape the course along with Ayham Ghraowi, assistant dean for research and public projects at the Yale School of Art. I mean, one particularly interesting relationship between art and money is that if you make certain kinds of art you can sell it for lots of money. I am not sure whether the point of art school is just to give you the technical skills to make art, or also to teach you which kinds of art you can sell for lots of money, but surely the point of a joint art-school/business-school class is to teach you the latter. And, yes, as this class correctly concluded, one type of art that can make you lots of money is a cryptocurrency project. “Essentially everything in cryptocurrency is simultaneously serious and a joke,” I once wrote, which is a decent working definition of art. Anyway I am glad they all had fun; here’s an MBA student: “Art is about more than making ‘art’ pieces,” he says. “It really is about taking in the world and questioning what it means. It was an interesting parallel to business school, where we do more than figure out how to make profits. We explore how business affects society, individuals, and citizens.”

Sometimes an asset will trade at one price on one trading venue, and another price on another venue. If you notice this discrepancy, you can buy the asset at the lower price in one place, sell it at the higher price in the other place, and make an instant guaranteed profit. But if you notice this discrepancy there’s a pretty good chance that someone else will too. I mean, it’s free money, why wouldn’t other people notice? And so then a pretty important question in market structure is: How do you decide who gets the free money? There is a straightforward canonical answer that is used in most financial exchanges, which is that whoever gets to the exchange first gets the free money. These days, people complain endlessly about this method of allocating the free money, because it seems unfair (people with fast computers who pay to rent space next to the exchange have an advantage over the little guy, etc.) or because it encourages a socially wasteful arms race (people keep building microwave towers to get their signals to exchanges faster, etc.). Sometimes they suggest other methods for allocating the free money, for instance randomly or pro rata among people who notice the free money within a certain amount of time, etc. Meanwhile there are trading exchanges in the blockchain world. There are things called “decentralized exchanges” that run on the Ethereum blockchain and match buyers and sellers of assets, where by “assets” I mean mainly crypto tokens issued in initial coin offerings to fund various blockchainy projects. There are enough of these exchanges, and the prices are volatile enough, and the overall operational standard is sloppy enough, that sometimes there are large price discrepancies between the exchanges, and free money is available. How does the blockchain allocate the free money? The answer is: Whoever pays the most for the free money gets it. This is a general method of operation on the Ethereum blockchain: Transactions are executed on the blockchain when they are included in blocks of transactions that have been “mined” by Ethereum miners, and miners are incentivized to include transactions in their blocks by the transaction fees (called “gas”) attached to the transactions. If you bid a high gas price, everyone will want to do your transaction first, and so you will get the free money. I mean, you’ll get some of it, most of it probably; the miner who mines your block will get a cut too. Here is a paper called “ Flash Boys 2.0: Frontrunning, Transaction Reordering, and Consensus Instability in Decentralized Exchanges” about this mechanism. “‘Flash Boys’-like trading manipulation is rampant on certain cryptocurrency exchanges,” is how Bloomberg News summarizes it: Special arbitrage bots are anticipating and profiting from ordinary users’ trades on decentralized exchanges, which let them trade more directly, the authors said in a report released last week. The firms that deploy the autonomous trading programs manage to get priority ordering by paying higher fees, and use that advantage for practices such as front running, in which traders can see orders from others and manage to place their own first. The deeper point of the paper is to suggest possible risks to the stability of the Ethereum blockchain as a whole, but I prefer to read it as a funny examination of what a bad idea it is to put a financial-asset exchange on a public blockchain, and as a nice encapsulation of the essence of blockchain, and how it differs from traditional finance. First: At its heart, the blockchain is a slow database. For all the “Flash Boys 2.0” stuff, and the comparison to high-frequency traders racing for a microsecond advantage in the stock market, the fact is that the arbitrages here work because the Ethereum blockchain does not execute transactions instantly in the order that they come in, but instead spends a lot of time broadcasting proposed transactions to all of the different nodes on the network so they can come to a consensus about which transactions executed and in what order. It creates more time for anomalies to persist and for people to compete to take advantage of them. Second: The fundamental libertarianism of “decentralized” blockchain applications tends to mean in practice that everything is ruled by a market mechanism. This is true at a very general level: A lot of crypto projects are basically about taking some activity that traditionally would be done by a firm , and doing it by a decentralized market instead. The basic trick is to find some way of aligning incentives so that unaffiliated unscreened strangers will just have the right incentives to make the thing work. It is in many cases sort of a pleasing vision, a perfection of the free market as a mechanism for coordinating cooperation. But in this context—the context of executing transactions on an exchange—the market mechanism is just: The people who decide what transactions execute in what order, make those decisions based on who pays them the most. The authors argue that this creates the possibility of skewed incentives that might lead to “time-bandit attacks” undermining the Ethereum blockchain as a whole, but you don’t even have to consider that argument to realize that this situation feels weird. The New York Stock Exchange doesn’t go around saying “whoever pays us the biggest fee will get to jump the line and execute trades first.” In fact people do complain that stock exchanges give unfair advantages to their biggest customers, and that they charge excessive fees for fast access and necessary data, but those things are very different from just holding explicit auctions for priority. In the regular financial system, firms make decisions in lots of different ways to maximize lots of different things. In the blockchain financial system, there are no firms, and all decisions tend to be made based on price. Third: Everything that happens in the crypto space always ends up looking like deep sophisticated cutting-edge theory backed up by incredibly dumb practice. When I wrote above that “the overall operational standard is sloppy enough” to create arbitrage opportunities, this is what I meant: Figure 1 shows one example of a pure revenue transaction, executed on November 15, 2018. In this transaction, two trades are executed on a decentralized exchange, TokenStore, which features a design conceptually similar to that of Etherdelta. The first executed trade buys Free Coin, an obscure token. By inspection, this difference in rates is a clear result of someone using the exchange API and committing an off-by-one error, offering to buy tokens at 10x the market rate. This created a cross in the order book (sell order at more than a buy order would pay), which when both executed by the same arbitrage counterparty, generates the flow of funds in Figure 1. While this opportunity probably arose from a typo, a variety of revenue sources exist. For example, inconsistent price feeds, or variance across exchange designs that respond to market movements at different speeds can also create pure revenue. That last sentence is a bit of face-saving—“no no no, this is about arbitrage , which is a fancy thing, not about typos , which are a dumb thing”—but in fact typos seem to be a rich source of decentralized token exchange profits: The top sender in Figure 6, for example, appears to often profit off typographical errors users make in their decentralized exchange trades. One user, “Getcoin Hub Inc.”, pleads with this arbitrage bot, saying “This was obviously a mistake transaction - any chance you can find it in your heart to send it back?”. Another, Benjamin Huffman, pleads with the bot that “I am a single parent trying to make ends meet at a job I hate. Please have some mercy.” Yet another, Alfie, leaves a comment requesting the return of their ETH, stating “Please I ask you to send me the ETH back as I really need it to continue my education. I might need to sell my car to pay what is already due for this semester.” The bot, of course, was merciless. Imagine going to your hedge-fund bosses and saying “I have identified a highly reliable profit opportunity, people keep making typos in their orders to buy and sell crypto tokens, and if we pay high enough fees the exchanges will allow us to exploit those typos.” It’s sort of an embarrassing way to make money, but it apparently works!

People, you may have heard, are worried about bond market liquidity. The main form that this worry takes is that big-bank bond dealers, who used to buy and sell big blocks of bonds for their own account in order to intermediate trades between customers, are now too hesitant to do that. They are constrained by capital requirements and risk limits and regulation, and don’t want to take the risk of buying bonds for themselves, so they focus on lining up trades between buyers and sellers at no risk to themselves. Without their willingness to take risk, trades tend to be small and slow, and in bad times they might dry up altogether. There are two fundamental approaches to fixing this problem. One is to say, well, okay, we can’t rely on dealers as middlemen anymore; bond investors are going to have to trade with each other, so let’s build the most efficient possible system for matching them with each other. The old system made it essentially impossible for an investor who wanted to buy a bond to find an investor who wanted to sell that bond: There was nowhere for them to meet and discuss what bonds they wanted to buy and sell; all of that information was monopolized by the dealers. When the dealers were providing a valuable service of taking one side of each trade, that was fine, but now that the dealers are so reluctant to put their capital at risk, there is no good reason for them to have a monopoly on the information. Instead you could just, like, have a bond exchange, and let everyone put their orders to buy and sell bonds on the exchange, and if someone put in an order to buy that crossed with someone else’s order to sell, then they would trade their bonds. The goal would be to concentrate as much information as possible (about investor desires to buy and sell bonds) in one place, so that people who wanted to buy or sell can find each other as conveniently as possible. This has an obvious intuitive appeal, but that doesn’t necessarily mean that it’s right. You can see the objections to it when you look at the stock market. The stock market does this—it has big centralized electronic venues to expose everyone’s orders to buy and sell stocks—but in fact (1) those venues still involve a lot of middlemen (market makers) who intermediate between “real” buyers and sellers and (2) lots of people dislike those venues, think they’re getting front-run, prefer to keep their orders secret, and use tools (dark pools, splitting up orders, etc.) to do that. Oversimplifying, the way to encourage me to trade is to give me as much information as possible about other people’s trading intentions, but let me keep my intentions secret. An open transparent all-to-all system may not strike that balance perfectly. The other approach is to say, well, the poor dealers, their job is too hard, we should make it easier for them to make money because then they will take more risk in intermediating trades. One way to do this would be to give them more of a monopoly on information. For instance, for most bonds these days, people know what price they have recently traded at. If people didn’t know that, then the dealer who last traded the bonds would have a big informational advantage: If she knew that the last trade was a big seller unloading a ton of bonds to her at a big discount, but nobody else knew that, then she could go around selling those bonds at a higher price than she paid. Supply and demand dynamics would suggest that the price should go down—a lot of supply has just come onto the market—but if nobody knows that, and she can keep it secret, then she can make a profit. The industry seems to be pursuing Option B: The Financial Industry Regulatory Authority will likely test the market impact of delaying the disclosure of large corporate bond trades after some of the biggest investors argued that such a move would improve liquidity. Finra last week proposed running a pilot program that would give traders 48 hours before having to reveal their so-called block trades to other investors. The effort would allow the industry-funded brokerage regulator, which is overseen by the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, to evaluate how delayed transparency might affect corporate bond trading. Here is the proposal. Bond trades below a size threshold—basically $5 million for high-yield and $10 million for investment-grade—would be reported within 15 minutes on the Trace (Trade Reporting and Compliance Engine) feed, so that everyone would know what bonds were trading and at what prices. But trades above the threshold would not be reported for 48 hours, meaning that a dealer who buys $20 million of bonds will have two days to work out of her position before the market finds out that she bought any. This will encourage her to buy the bonds, since she won’t be—ugh—“front-run” by other traders seeing her big position and lowering their prices. Here are some comments to the Securities and Exchange Commission on a previous version of the proposal. It’s all kind of what you’d expect. Dealers like it. Here is JPMorgan Chase & Co.: Providers of liquidity accept heightened risk when transacting in block trades, and these trades are immediately disclosed to the market with masked trade sizes. We believe as a result of this immediate disclosure, broker dealers now prefer smaller trade sizes on average, particularly for less liquid and lower rated bonds. This changes the risk/reward for the broker dealers and is reflected in their pricing. Similarly, we observe that asset managers at times can experience challenges in transacting large trade sizes. We believe that it is important to study whether increases in the delay of public disclosure for block trades, as well as in the dissemination caps, would support larger trade sizes and tighter pricing, which would make the market more effective and be beneficial to market participants. At least some big bond investors feel the same way; here is Wellington Management Co.: We have observed that bids to purchase fixed income securities tend to decrease in response to the dissemination (via TRACE) of a broker-dealer's purchase of a large block of securities … unless there is an immediate dissemination of a corresponding sale. We believe that this decrease occurs because the TRACE prints are serving as a signal to other market participants that there is an eager seller, and therefore they lower their published bids. Indeed, we have often seen situations where some market participants, anticipating this price decline, will short a security in response to multiple TRACE dissemination indicating broker-dealer purchases. The practical result is that immediate publication of large blocks on TRACE leads to artificially depressed bids and therefore serves as a disincentive to brokers to purchase securities in large blocks. “High-frequency traders,” or whatever, do not like the proposal; here are comments from Flow Traders LLC and Jane Street Capital LLC, which make markets in bond exchange-traded funds and would prefer for bond prices to be transparent. Jane Street: A 48-hour dissemination blackout for large trades would introduce a material amount of information asymmetry and adverse selection to the corporate bond market. Block liquidity providers would have the freedom to hedge large block trades for up to two days prior to informing the market that the large block trade has occurred. Counterparties who end up on the other side of those trades would be unaware that the market is likely poised to move against them given that the block liquidity provider would likely conduct additional hedging trades in the same direction. There is not really much to choose from in these positions. Dealers and big bond investors say: We would prefer to be able to sell a lot of bonds without the price dropping. Electronic traders say: We would prefer to be able to lower our prices if someone is going to be selling a lot of bonds. On first principles I am more sympathetic to the electronic traders—if someone is selling a lot of bonds then the price should drop!—but as is so often the case in market structure debates it is hard to see much of a moral component to it. Somebody will be better off and somebody will be worse off and Finra will just get to pick who it is. It is weird though that this comes so soon after all of the prosecutions of bond traders for lying to customers about the prices they paid for bonds. Those bond traders tended to trade things—certain kinds of mortgage securities, etc.—that, at least at the time, did not print on Trace. So they could make up the price that they paid and their customers wouldn’t immediately know they were lying. This was generally perceived to be a bad thing, though I will say that there was a strong countercurrent of “no it’s fine lying about bonds is great,” and in fact many of those bond traders ended up beating the charges. It does seem to me though that if you think that dealers lying to customers about bond prices is a serious problem, making the dealers publicly print the prices they paid for bonds is a reasonable solution—more reasonable than after-the-fact prosecution, anyway—and actively changing the rules to make it easier for dealers to conceal the prices they paid is a weird way to go.

There are at least two reasons why hedge funds might have invested in IEX Group Inc., the startup stock exchange that was built to disrupt the big exchanges by building a “speed bump” to make it harder for high-frequency traders to trade ahead of fundamental investors. One was: They wanted what IEX was offering (a dark pool, then a stock exchange, that was relatively less favorable to high-frequency traders than existing exchanges), so they gave it money to make that happen. The other was: They thought that everyone would want what IEX was offering, and so it would rapidly displace the incumbent exchanges, dominate the market, and make them billions of dollars on their investment. Now IEX is an operating, profitable, mature-ish U.S. stock exchange, so if you want what it’s offering you can have it. But it is also a pretty small exchange that does not seem to have disrupted the New York Stock Exchange or Nasdaq all that much, so if you were betting on it to take over the world then, um, that bet has concluded. And so: Some of the earliest investors in IEX Group Inc. recently sold their stakes in the upstart stock exchange, including activist hedge funds Third Point LLC and Pershing Square Capital Management LP, people familiar with the matter said. The funds exited their stakes in a transaction that valued privately owned IEX at more than $700 million, up from its previous valuation of about $500 million, according to people briefed on the deal. The deal was all secondary—“IEX didn’t raise new capital in the transaction”—presumably because it didn’t need any money. It’s profitable, but it does not have the sort of rapid growth opportunities that would require it to raise a ton of money. The bet was fine! I mention it really only for this paragraph: IEX has also explored a potential foray into the videogame industry, discussing whether its technology could be used in online multiplayer games to help level the playing field between people with slower and faster network connections, according to people familiar with the matter. I think that my perception of IEX was way too narrow. I thought of IEX’s essential proposition as “a stock exchange, but nice and anti-HFT.” That suggested to me that an obvious place to branch out was in listings: Corporate executives probably have at least as much vague paranoia about high-frequency traders as activist hedge fund managers do, so going to those executives and saying “hey list with us, we are nice and don’t like HFTs either,” seemed like an obvious winner. But in fact IEX has only managed to get one listing so far, though more may be on the way. But the dream is much bigger, and IEX’s essential proposition is apparently “ we will correct the unfairness of time itself .” Is it unfair that a high-frequency trader buys a stock before you can buy it? IEX will let you buy it first. Is it unfair that someone killed you in Fortnite because your connection was too slow? IEX will let you kill him first. Is it unfair that your knees hurt? IEX will make you 20 again. Maybe not that one. The point is that equalizing the effects of time is a much bigger and weirder and more interesting market niche than thwarting high-frequency traders on the stock exchange, and if that is in fact IEX’s niche then those bets could turn out to be more interesting.

I think that, as humans-vs.-robots-in-financial-markets stories go, this one is kind of good news for the humans: For as long as companies have hosted quarterly conference calls, analysts and journalists have tried to parse not just what a company’s executives say, but how they say it. Software from Amenity Analytics promises to automate this process by spotting when chief executive officers try to duck tough questions. The software, its makers say, can even pick up on the signs of potential deception that CIA and FBI interrogators look for—including stalling and the use of qualifiers—and can gauge the sentiment of what is said on calls and reported in public filings, issuing a positive or negative numeric score. The goal is to make it easier for investors to wade through information and quickly make trading decisions. … Barclays Capital, in an October 2018 research report, concluded that using Amenity Analytics’ software to examine earnings calls—and using the sentiment score to decide whether to buy or sell short the shares of those companies—produced an annual return 12.97 percent greater than a benchmark index. Sure this is a case of robots muscling into a domain—literary analysis?—that was previously reserved for humans. But at least the robots are paying attention to the humans . If you are going to have robots sitting around analyzing the tone and nuance of an earnings call, then there will be opportunities for the humans, since you’ll need them to stall and qualify on earnings calls. Also in the near term you will probably need humans to ask the questions. In the medium term, the next generation of NuanceBots will dial in to earnings calls and ask algorithmically generated questions designed to elicit the maximally informative amounts of stalling. I guess in the long term, a specialized NuanceBot will also be tasked with answering the questions and the earnings calls will become perfectly uninformative again. But for now, the humans are providing the alpha; it is just being filtered through a robot analysis. Honestly it is a little wild that an analysis of sentiment on earnings calls can produce a 13 percent excess return. Actual insider trading by corporate executives themselves doesn’t do nearly that well, though I suppose they usually need to wait a few days after the earnings call to trade. This suggests that the executives themselves do not fully understand whatever subtle hints about performance they are coding into their earnings calls: When they’re ducking questions, they’re not just hiding information from analysts, but also from themselves. Meanwhile my guess is that if you took a smart sensitive human with no financial training and asked her to listen to some earnings calls and make trading decisions based only on how confident and trustworthy the CEO sounds, she would not reliably beat the market. (If she would, this would probably … be a thing?) She has a big advantage over the robot in that she is also a human and can instantly understand and contextualize a lot of behaviors that the robot needs to learn about from scratch, but somehow when it comes to actual trading decisions the robot is better off. Being an alien objective observer of human behavior gives the robot a clearer view. The humans subconsciously make excuses for each other, cover for each other, give each other the benefit of the doubt, put themselves in each other’s shoes. The robots are just like “he ducked the question, sell.” There is something poignant about this result, a suggestion that the robots can know the humans better than we know ourselves. It is the highest purpose of quantitative finance, revealing truths about our humanity that we couldn’t see before because, as humans, we were too close to them. Elsewhere in robots: Maths-savvy, computer-toting investors have already disrupted traditional tactics in asset management. Next in their sights is the red-hot private equity world. … Some so-called quants are now exploring whether their systematic, data-intensive investment process can also work in more opaque, private corners of the system, potentially significantly lowering industry fees. The knock on using quant techniques in private investing is that it “consists primarily of bespoke, negotiated, multiyear investments in private companies, where information is often murky and exiting a trade can be tricky.” You have fewer observations and a less robust link between those observations and performance, so it’s hard to develop data-driven techniques. But to the extent “quant techniques” starts to mean “understanding humans better than they understand themselves,” you know, why not? The NuanceBot will do your bespoke negotiating for you. Here is something else in that private-equity story: Man Group’s Numeric unit last year launched a fund that attempts to replicate the returns of a typical private equity fund but at a fraction of the cost, by investing in small, listed companies that can mimic the profile of a typical private equity portfolio. It is interesting sometimes to think about what it is that quantitative investors are doing. One possible answer is that they are doing the basic functions of investing—allocating capital to productive uses, providing liquidity, that sort of thing—just like regular fundamental investors, but faster. Another possibility is that they are providing a statistical simulation of that work. If you can break, say, Warren Buffett’s investing approach into a list of statistical factors, then you can put together a mechanical strategy that partially replicates Buffett’s return profile without necessarily owning the stocks that he owns. You can give investors exposure to hedge-fund-like returns without hedge-fund-like fees. You can use a toolkit of statistical similarities to build stuff that looks like other stuff. There is often a lot of overlap between these descriptions. A quant fund that loads on the value factor can be described as simulating a value investor, or it can be described as actually allocating capital to stocks that are underpriced relative to their fundamentals. There is no meaningful difference between those descriptions; in simulating human value investors, you are doing some form of the same thing that they are actually doing. But sometimes they are different. If there is a high statistical correlation between some list of public stocks and some index of private-equity returns, then you can use those public stocks to create a product that simulates private-equity returns. But in simulating the returns of private-equity investors you are not simulating what they are doing, because you are not actually allocating capital to private businesses. You can simulate what they are doing, but you cannot replace it.

One of my worse recent takes was probably when David Solomon became chief executive officer at Goldman Sachs Group Inc., and there were a lot of articles about how Solomon (who grew up in investment banking) marked a dramatic change from former CEO Lloyd Blankfein (who grew up in sales and trading), and I was like, nah, it’s not that big a deal, money is money, the relative size and power of the different divisions of Goldman Sachs is probably more a function of the economic environment than it is of the personal loyalties of the CEO. But investment banking keeps being good under Solomon, while trading keeps being bad: This is the second straight quarter that revenue from investment banking, the business that Chief Executive Officer David Solomon previously led, cushioned a steep drop from the firm’s trading business. Goldman’s new management team is getting closer to finishing a firmwide review that’s already led to changes in the trading operation, including scaling back some commodities businesses. Here are Goldman’s results and presentation, which have a pleasing symmetry: Investment banking revenue posted a surprise jump from a year earlier to $1.8 billion, while the fixed-income trading business fell 11 percent to $1.8 billion. Equities trading had an even bigger drop to $1.8 billion. Revenue from the bank’s investing and lending business was also down -- to $1.8 billion. I like it, very fair-minded of the new guy to make sure that every division is the same. (Investment management came in at $1.56 billion, oops.) Disclosure, I used to work at Goldman, technically in investment banking though many of my deals were allocated half to banking and half to trading, so I suppose I am biased to enjoy this sort of even-handedness.

On my old derivatives structuring desk, we had a sort of Zen method of hazing analysts and imparting wisdom in which we tried to answer questions at a level of abstraction that was so high as to be meaningless. It would be like: Analyst: Can you explain to me how to model a prepaid variable-share forward? Vice president: See, it’s a thing, and you can do it. Analyst: Thank you for this. It was probably my favorite part of investment banking, and good preparation for financial journalism honestly, but I don’t think I ever achieved the heights of style that Todd Boehly manages here: “Most things are boxes that own things. And it’s not the box itself that’s good or bad—it’s what’s in the box,” Boehly tells Barron’s. “Everything is structured.” Most things … are boxes … that own things! Are the things that they own also boxes that own things? Logic and empiricism suggest yes! An infinite series of nested things that are boxes, all of them structured. It is a beautiful quote. As is traditional in this genre of financial wisdom literature it is also completely incomprehensible. More explanation: Generally, Eldridge provides the capital to build the box, which is a company, and then money from Security Benefit buys the things to put in the box that Eldridge built. Those things generate cash flow, which provides income to purchasers of Security Benefit annuities. Often, they have been bundled and punched out in a neat securitization package. Other times, Eldridge puts up money to build or seed a company, and then Security Benefit buys whatever securities that company ends up issuing. Eldridge Industries is Boehly’s investment firm. Security Benefit is a life insurer that Boehly acquired for Guggenheim Partners when he was a managing partner there, and that he purchased for Eldridge when he left Guggenheim. At the most generic level—well, the second-most generic, I guess—the strategy is one that we have talked about recently, which is: Own a life insurer. Own an investing firm. Have the life insurer use its policyholders’ money to fund your investing firm’s investments. If your investing ideas are good then you make money on the investments, and your policyholders make money by funding them, and also you make money by growing the life insurer. It is a controversial strategy because of the obvious potential for conflicts of interest: You’re using policyholder money to fund your own investment ideas that can make a separate profit for you. A Security Benefit policyholder sued Guggenheim last year for using policyholder money to buy a stake in the Los Angeles Dodgers (“Boehly personally owns 20%” of the team), and there is something awkward about using policyholder money for personally glamorous investments like sports-team ownership. On the other hand it is also an appealing strategy for people with a pure love of investing, which is why so many hedge fund managers and also Warren Buffett end up funding some of their investing through insurance companies. You just get to use every part of the investment, you know? To explain, Boehly draws rectangles on a whiteboard, filling them with hypothetical, income-producing loans, or leases for warehouses, or Pizza Hut franchises. “These are institutional asset strategies where we have two vectors working for us: We make the rate of return here”—on the whiteboard he taps the things inside a scribbled rectangle—“within the warehouse, and we make the rate of return here”—the business equity, the rectangle itself—“as we build the business.” For a certain kind of investment geek, earning a high rate of return is almost secondary to earning several different rates of return. Look at all those vectors!

If you build software that allows a trader to “spoof”—submitting orders that he doesn’t intend to execute, in order to create the illusion of demand and so move the price of a financial instrument in his favor—can you yourself be guilty of spoofing? It seems like there is a sense in which the answer has to be yes: In many financial instruments, most traders are software , and so if the person who builds the software isn’t responsible for what it does then perhaps no one is. You can’t put the algorithm in jail. On the other hand if an actual human trader comes to you and asks you to build software that will let you submit an order and send it to the end of the queue for execution, and you do, and he uses it to spoof, are you guilty of spoofing? Man, I have no idea; people barely know what spoofing is or why it’s illegal, so it seems silly to analyze a question that’s this subtle. That is basically the conclusion of the court system too: The case of Jitesh Thakkar, the first non-trader charged under anti-spoofing laws, ended [last] week in a mistrial. Jurors in Chicago were split over whether he broke the law by developing software that someone else used for fake market orders, even after hearing detailed testimony from his client, convicted Flash Crash trader Navinder Singh Sarao. To be fair, “when an FBI agent showed up at his home at 7 a.m. in late 2017” to ask Thakkar what he thought Sarao was doing with his program, Thakkar replied “I mean in a sense – spoofing,” which is not a great look. Meanwhile Sarao—the poor guy who was charged with causing the 2010 “flash crash” through his spoofing— testified during Thakkar’s trial that spoofing is “something that’s incredibly common in the trading environment,” and “something most traders do,” which strikes me as not especially true, and probably not what prosecutors wanted to hear, but also the sort of thing that a spoofer would tell himself when he went out to commission a spoofing program. Everyone else is doing it, so why not me? I suppose the question would be: Is there some legitimate non-spoofing reason to submit orders to a stock exchange while simultaneously trying to make them be last in line to execute? This feels like a tricky question for a jury to answer, for reasons having to do with the difficulty of defining criminal spoofing generally. The legitimate reason to try to be last in line to execute is something like “there are some circumstances in which you’d want your order to execute, but fewer than if you were trying to be first in line.” Professional traders sometimes do feel that way; they enter all of their orders with contingent or probabilistic expectations and desires about when they will execute. But to prosecutors and jurors it can be more tempting to think, well, if you enter an order you should want it to execute, and if you don’t want it to execute it must be spoofing.

Well, if you get rid of your founder and chief executive officer in a boardroom coup two years before your initial public offering, your IPO prospectus can’t really feature an inspirational letter from that founder explaining the deeper meaning of the company. I mean, you could ask, but the letter you get might be peevish and weird. And so Uber Technologies Inc., which publicly filed its long-awaited IPO prospectus yesterday, does not have a letter from founder and ex-CEO Travis Kalanick in that prospectus. Instead it has this: Letter from Dr. Ronald Sugar Chairperson of the Board of Directors Dear Stockholders, Over the last two years, Uber has undergone an incredible transformation, buoyed by new leadership, the tireless work of our innovative employees, and a commitment by our board to the highest standards of corporate governance. As we go public, our board is focused on providing careful oversight to ensure this progress continues. World-class governance will be our north star, as we strive to responsibly manage risk, ensure transparency, and stand accountable to our stockholders. It goes on for three more paragraphs but they’re just as boring. And, yes, fine, there’s also a letter from Uber’s current CEO, but it is also boring. Dr. Ronald Sugar! He’s 70 years old, was the CEO of Northrop Grumman Corporation from 2003 until 2010, and is also on the boards of Apple Inc., Chevron Corp., Amgen Inc. and Air Lease Corp. He joined Uber’s board last July. And he wrote you a letter. The purpose of his letter is to say: Hi, I’m here. There’s a board chairman. This is a mature serious company, with an independent board. There are grown-ups. When Lyft Inc. filed its IPO prospectus last month, we talked about its standard tech-startup missionary tone, and I expressed some hope that Uber’s prospectus would be different, clear-eyed and disillusioned and brutal. Well, not quite. Here too there is a certain amount of missionary rhetoric; Uber repeatedly says “our mission is to ignite opportunity by setting the world in motion,” which is even less edifying than Lyft’s “improve people’s lives with the world’s best transportation.” But what is striking about Uber’s prospectus is that its tone is so often … apologetic? The IPO is not so much Uber’s opportunity to introduce itself to the world—everyone knows about Uber already!—as it is an opportunity for Uber to say, uh, sorry about all the old Uber stuff, let’s start over. “Of course, in getting from point A to point B we didn’t get everything right,” says the CEO’s letter. The corporate governance section says: We are on a new path forward with the hiring of our Chief Executive Officer Dara Khosrowshahi in September of 2017, following many challenges relating to our culture, workplace practices, and reputation. Our workplace culture and forward-leaning approach got us to where we are today, but it was clear to our new management team that Uber needed to make a commitment to resolve our historical cultural and compliance problems. Our leadership team has sought to fundamentally reform our workplace culture by improving our governance structure, strengthening our compliance program, creating and embracing new cultural norms, committing to diversity and inclusion, and rebuilding our relationships with employees, Drivers, consumers, cities, and regulators. Several risk factors hit this apologetic note. “Our workplace culture and forward-leaning approach created significant operational and cultural challenges,” Uber says, and I would love to have been in the drafting sessions that came up with the euphemism “forward-leaning.” “Our focus on aggressive growth and intense competition, and our prior failure to prioritize compliance, has led to increased regulatory scrutiny globally.” And: In 2017, the #DeleteUber campaign prompted hundreds of thousands of consumers to stop using our platform within days. Subsequently, our reputation was further harmed when an employee published a blog post alleging, among other things, that we had a toxic culture and that certain sexual harassment and discriminatory practices occurred in our workplace. Shortly thereafter, we had a number of highly publicized events and allegations, including investigations related to a software tool allegedly designed to evade and deceive authorities, a high-profile lawsuit filed against us by Waymo, and our disclosure of a data security breach. And while last month I wrote that Uber is perhaps most closely associated with surge pricing during emergencies, surge pricing—the Randian heart of the Travis Kalanick-era Uber—barely comes up in the prospectus. It’s mentioned a few times in the risk factors, but in the description of the business there is only a paragraph on the merits of “dynamic pricing.” What else? There are other good risk factors. The very first risk factor is, reasonably enough, competition: “The personal mobility, meal delivery, and logistics industries are highly competitive, with well-established and low-cost alternatives that have been available for decades, low barriers to entry, low switching costs, and well-capitalized competitors in nearly every major geographic region.” What is interesting is what Uber sees as its competition: Our Personal Mobility offering competes with personal vehicle ownership and usage, which accounts for the majority of passenger miles in the markets that we serve, and traditional transportation services, including taxicab companies and taxi-hailing services, livery services, and public transportation, which typically provides the lowest-cost transportation option in many cities. In Ridesharing, we compete with companies, including certain of our minority-owned affiliates, for Drivers and riders, including Lyft, OLA, Careem, Didi, Taxify, and our Yandex.Taxi joint venture. First of all it is funny that Uber’s competition, in some markets, is itself: As part of various competitive truces it has struck over the years, it is a part-owner of Didi, Grab and Yandex.Taxi, and while it has agreed not to compete in their home markets, they have not agreed not to compete with Uber elsewhere, and in fact they do. I suppose this is a mixed bag; if you buy stock in Uber you do get sort of an index fund of ridesharing companies. More broadly, it is funny and sort of ominous to think that Uber’s fiercest competitors are (1) cars that people own and (2) public transportation. Uber is a tough competitor, and you hate to think what they’ve got planned for your car and your subway system. There’s a map in the prospectus showing Uber's market share in different regions, and it is somewhat comically the same—under 1 percent market share—everywhere, on the theory that any time someone travels anywhere they could be traveling in an Uber. This is perhaps overly modest—there’s also a more useful breakdown of “ridesharing category position,” showing that Uber actually has a majority share in the ridesharing market in many of its regions—but it’s a strategic modesty. “We include all passenger vehicle miles and all public transportation miles in all countries globally in our” total addressable market, says Uber, for an estimated $5.7 trillion annual opportunity. If Uber is really only 1 percent of the way to its goal of dominating the transportation market, its $100 billion valuation doesn’t look so high.

I dunno, here are some more Uber things. First, until yesterday it was universally reported that Uber lost $1.8 billion in 2018. In fact Uber’s net income for 2018 was $997 million. This was not a mistake on the part of journalists; Uber has for several years been pretty transparent about its finances, for a private company, and that $1.8 billion loss came directly from the company. It was just an “adjusted” loss. Under generally accepted accounting principles, it had a profit. (In fact the loss is what Uber reports in the prospectus as “Adjusted EBITDA,” of negative $1,847 million; among other things it adjusts out Uber’s $3.2 billion gain on divestitures—of its Russia and Southeast Asia businesses—and $2 billion unrealized gain on the value of its Didi investment in 2018, both of which are line items that it hadn’t reported in prior years and that don’t necessarily feel like “real” income.) People love to complain about companies using non-GAAP accounting to make their numbers look better, but in Uber’s case, when it was not public and was releasing unaudited non-GAAP numbers, those numbers made it look worse ; now that it is going public and forced to emphasize GAAP numbers, it has to reluctantly report a profit. Second, here’s a story titled “ Uber and Pinterest pore over their IPO lock-up agreements,” apparently in reaction to the weirdness around Lyft’s lockup agreements that we discussed earlier this week, in which Morgan Stanley allegedly marketed a hedging solution to locked-up Lyft shareholders that would allow them to hedge their stock despite being locked up. (Morgan Stanley denied this, and it didn’t really make any sense, though that doesn’t mean that it can’t have happened.) “Everybody is taking a fresh look at these agreements and making sure they have the desired effect,” said one Wall Street banker. “[Lock-up language] is now just part of the discussion, at the top of the list.” And in fact if you look at the lockup section in the Uber IPO prospectus, it is a little different from the precedents! A very little. Specifically, where Lyft said that its locked-up shareholders couldn’t sell stock or “enter into any swap or other arrangement that transfers all or a portion of the economic consequences associated with the ownership” of the stock, Uber says that they can’t sell stock or “enter into any swap, hedging transaction, or other arrangement that transfers to another, in whole or in part, any of the economic consequences of ownership of our common stock.” The change is the words “hedging transaction.” I suppose the theory in Lyft was that if you call something a “hedging transaction,” instead of a swap or option or collar or forward or any other standard word, maybe it wasn’t covered by the lockup. Uber has closed that loophole, I guess, though I suspect it was always tiny to nonexistent. Third, speaking of Lyft, oops: Lyft Inc. shares took yet another nosedive on Wednesday amid reports that larger rival Uber Technologies Inc. could be filing for an initial public offering as soon as Thursday. The shares ended the day at a record low, falling 11 percent in New York. … “Given the substantial market opportunity and investor interest in the secular ride-sharing opportunity, Lyft will likely benefit from being the only direct publicly traded play on the ride-sharing market,” Susquehanna analyst Shyam Patil said ahead of Lyft’s trading debut. “However, once Uber goes public (expected in the mid-April timeframe), we could see outflows as investors seek to invest in Uber.” Lyft’s stock fell below $60 this morning, the lowest in its brief time as a public company. And it does make sense that, if you want some fixed dollar amount of exposure to ridesharing, you’d put all of those dollars into Lyft when it came public and then, when Uber goes public, shift 80 or 90 percent or whatever of them to Uber. Still it has been like two weeks? It is a little weird that this wasn’t priced.

A lot of financial technology companies want to disrupt some area of banking, but end up needing a bank. They may have a better idea for how a bank-like thing—payments, savings, lending, etc.—should work, but find that for regulatory reasons some bits of the process still need to run through a traditional bank. Sometimes this will be a high-profile co-branding situation—the Apple x Goldman Sachs credit card, etc.—but sometimes the bank is just an anonymous service provider. LendingClub Corp. does peer-to-peer lending, but that requires an “issuing bank,” and it uses WebBank, NBT Bank and Comenity Capital Bank to issue its different types of loans. It seems fairly clear who is in charge here. LendingClub had the idea, has the technology, runs the marketplace, makes the loans happen; those banks are just sort of renting out their regulatory status for a modest fee. On the other hand a lot of banks want to bring some technology to their banking offerings, and end up needing a tech company, and … there too it is fairly clear who is in charge? Fiserv and two competitors— Fidelity National Information Services Inc., known as FIS, and Jack Henry & Associates Inc.—are little known outside the banking world, but their infrastructure now makes up much of the modern banking system’s financial plumbing, especially for smaller banks. They provide the technology behind everything from keeping track of customer deposits to powering mobile apps. As the number of community banks has shrunk, the three companies have grown, partly through acquisition of other tech providers, in both revenue and profit. These companies, known as “core providers,” say they can affordably bring to small institutions big-bank technologies, including the newest tools such as open-data platforms and on-demand services. But discontent is starting to simmer at the small banks that most depend on them. Smaller lenders and some industry groups say the service providers’ onerous contracts and sometimes mediocre digital offerings have made it harder to keep up with big competitors. Executives at some small banks say they feel like they are becoming franchises of the core providers because they are so reliant on their technology. There is an old-timey model in which the key elements of banking are, like, having a local branch, looking customers in the eye and giving them a hearty handshake, knowing their parents, etc. But in modern banking the importance of having a website and a payments app and, uh, “keeping track of customer deposits” is relatively higher, and the handshaking is relatively less important. For big banks, this means that they are increasingly and self-consciously becoming tech companies, building apps and hiring developers and blathering about blockchain. For small banks, it means that they are increasingly and unhappily becoming franchises of tech companies.

This is sort of mind-bendingly beautiful: A federal bankruptcy judge has authorized McKinsey & Co. to devise industry conflict-of-interest guidelines, even as the firm recently has paid $32.5 million to settle allegations that its undisclosed conflicts tainted its own bankruptcy work. The surprising move by Judge David Jones of Houston will allow the big consulting firm to craft a conflicts protocol that will be used in a current chapter 11 case, Colorado coal miner Westmoreland Coal Co., and could serve as a model for all bankruptcy practitioners, including law firms and financial advisers. In court papers, Judge Jones approved McKinsey’s request to develop new disclosure guidelines, saying: “The court hopes that the protocol to be developed by McKinsey will lead to a comprehensive national standard for all professionals.” I … look, you are not going to like this, but I think the intuition here is something like “if a big fancy institution like McKinsey can’t follow the current rules, then that is not a problem with McKinsey, it is a problem with the rules, and who better to fix the rules than McKinsey?” That is not really an uncommon intuition in complex regulatory areas, nor is it necessarily even wrong. ( Here is an argument that McKinsey’s failure to disclose conflicts came from an ethical commitment to client confidentiality.) Still usually it is the sort of thing that is achieved in back-channel lobbying, not literally commissioning the rule-breakers to write the new rules.

s.h: People are worried about bond market liquidity and also duration
s.t: Here you go: Behind the rally in global debt markets lurks a disaster just waiting to happen. At least, that’s what some long-time market watchers are warning. While dovish comments by the Federal Reserve and other central banks have prompted investors to pile back into bonds, two troubling developments could make buyers uniquely vulnerable to deep and painful losses, they say. One is the sheer amount of ultra-low yielding debt, which means investors have almost no buffer in the event prices drop. That’s compounded by the worry liquidity will suddenly evaporate in a selloff and leave holders stuck with losses on positions they can’t get out of quickly. … Currently, the duration of $52 trillion of investment-grade bonds tracked by Bloomberg globally stands at about 7, close to a record high. (Bonds with low yields and long maturity dates tend to have the highest duration.) That means if yields rose a full-percentage point, the bonds would lose 7 percent of their market value. For a half-percentage point jump, that works out to 3.5 percent, or a $1.8 trillion loss. One way to interpret the existence of $52 trillion of investment-grade bonds with an average yield of 1.8 percent and an average duration of 7 years is that the markets have made a very large collective bet that the probability of long-term interest rates rapidly rising to 2.8 percent is very low. But of course any time the markets make a large collective bet that the probability of a bad thing is low, that creates an opportunity for long-time market watchers to point out that it is not zero.

Here is a rather obsessive examination of where to sit at a venture capital pitch meeting, with diagrams and a call to disrupt pitch-meeting seating arrangements: Both investor and entrepreneur have honed their performances – the conversation itself – over many years. Each side knows exactly how to execute their part in the pitch meeting dance. But the stage itself – the meeting room – lags woefully behind in terms of optimization. This is an opportunity!
