It’s sort of fun to go back through old news articles about Uber Technologies Inc.’s financing rounds. Here’s one from June 2014: Only a few months ago, Silicon Valley start-ups were celebrated for drawing investors into paying for multibillion-dollar valuations. But on Friday Uber, the car ride service, climbed to an entirely new level. The company announced on Friday that it had raised $1.2 billion from investors at an eye-popping $17 billion valuation. Seventeen billion! Ooooooh! Different times, man. Less than a year earlier Uber had raised money at a $3.5 billion valuation. Less than a year later, in May 2015, it raised money at a $50 billion valuation. And then … well, then it kept raising a lot of money, but the valuations stopped rising so rapidly. They crept up a bit: $68 billion, $72 billion. And now Uber is apparently planning to file publicly for an initial public offering tomorrow, to price sometime in May, and “ is seeking a valuation of between $90 billion and $100 billion, influenced by the poor performance of smaller rival Lyft Inc’s shares following its IPO late last month.” In the four years leading up to the IPO, its value has about doubled. Alphabet Inc. is up 123 percent in that same time period; Facebook Inc. is up 126 percent. These are good results! But if you got into Uber in May 2015, you didn’t get—and you can’t have expected—an early-stage-venture-capital-style reward for the risk you were taking by backing a (then and now) money-losing company with dreams of world domination. Instead you invested in a large mature public tech company that happened to be private and losing money. There is something a bit anticlimactic about an Uber IPO: It is already huge, it has already raised oceans of money, its financials are already more or less public, how big a deal is an IPO really? “Still a pretty big deal” is the realistic answer. It’s a big IPO! It’s the standard-bearer of the unicorns, the biggest and most noteworthy of the current crop of pre-IPO venture-backed tech companies, “the largest U.S. IPO this year and among the 10 largest of all time.” If it goes public at well above its last private valuation, it will be a nice vindication of the current model of private financing. People, for a long time, were worried about unicorns, worrying that private-market valuations had gotten too far ahead of public-market ones and that venture investors were doomed to lose money. But the unicorns waited out those worries and, meh, it’s fine. Anyway I am sure we will be examining every detail of the IPO in the coming weeks. For now: “Morgan Stanley Wins Stabilization Role for Uber IPO.”

An advantage of doing an initial public offering is that it produces an IPO price: The company sells its stock to the public at one price, and then when the stock starts trading there is at least some tendency to be anchored to that price. This is not an unmixed advantage, since if the stock falls below the IPO price a lot of people will tut-tut that the IPO was a failure and something is wrong with the company. But it is mostly a nice thing: During the IPO, the company gets a week or two to tell its own story its own way, with intensive face-to-face marketing, no negative sell-side research notes or short-selling pressure, and a general atmosphere of enthusiasm and goodwill. The day-to-day trading of a public stock is an uncontrolled random walk; the IPO is a carefully managed marketing pitch. You’d expect it to produce a relatively high price. And in fact, while the evidence is mixed, most companies do tend to underperform in the years after their IPOs, suggesting that in fact their anchoring was a bit high. If you do a direct listing, though, you don’t get an IPO price: You just list your stock for trading on an exchange, and one day it doesn’t trade, and the next day it does. You don’t … well, actually, I don’t know what you do and don’t get to do; there has only been one big direct listing in the U.S. in living memory, and so it’s hard to say what the traditional marketing elements of a direct listing are. You do do some marketing, probably; perhaps not a road show but a presentation and some talking points for bank salespeople. But it’s not the full-on marketing push of an IPO, and you don’t take a bunch of orders and set a price to satisfy all the demand you’ve whipped up. You just start trading. Conceivably—again there is not much precedent to go on—there’s no anchoring price at all. You might expect—I did expect, before Spotify Technology SA’s direct listing, though in hindsight I was mostly wrong—a lot of volatility in the early trading, as there is no recent big trade to anchor anyone’s expectations. And this is fine, sure, who cares, except that the main point of being public—especially for a direct-listing company that isn’t going public to raise money—is to let your employees and investors sell stock, and they’d rather sell the stock at a high and certain price than a low and volatile price. (And the way a direct listing works is that they can sell stock immediately , on the first day or the second day or whenever, whereas in an IPO early shareholders either sell directly in the coordinated IPO process or sign lockup agreements and aren’t allowed to sell for six months.) Anyway this seems smart: In the next few months, anyone will be able to buy stock in Slack Technologies Inc. In the meantime, wealthy investors are paying big premiums to snap up shares of the workplace software maker on private markets. Investors are buying stock in some cases for more than double the price of Slack’s last fundraising round in August, which valued the company at $7.1 billion, said people familiar with the transactions. Shareholders have sold stock to private buyers in the last two months at prices as high as $25 or $26 a share, which implies a company valuation of about $16 billion, said two of the people, who asked not to be identified because the details are private. A third person said deals were discussed at a price range of $24 to $27 a share. ... The recent string of private stock transactions in Slack is part of a company strategy to test what public investors might be willing to pay, a person familiar with the matter said. Music streaming provider Spotify Technology SA, which went public in a similar fashion to Slack last year, also allowed private share sales ahead of its direct listing. Spotify is up 7 percent from its first trade a year ago. … Bloomberg Beta, the venture capital arm of Bloomberg LP, is an investor in Slack. It’s not a coordinated marketed road show, but it does give the public markets some prices to think about—prices paid by particularly enthusiastic investors in the run-up to the direct listing—in figuring out what the right public trading price will be.

Traditionally, there are two main ways for big companies to borrow money. They can issue bonds, which are securities sold to institutional investors (pension funds, insurance companies, hedge funds, etc.) and underwritten by an investment bank, which will technically buy the bonds from the company and re-sell them immediately to the investors. Or they can take out bank loans, in which they borrow money directly from commercial banks. There are some structural differences—term, security, fixed vs. floating rates, covenants, etc.—between traditional bonds and traditional loans, but the main historical difference was about who was lending the money. Bonds were sold through investment banks to institutional investors and were freely tradable; loans were borrowed from commercial banks, who kept the risk on their balance sheets. That is not really true anymore though. Loans are now normally syndicated: The bank arranging the loan for a company will find other investors to buy most of it, rather than keeping the loan on its own books. Institutional investors—not just banks—regularly participate in those syndications and buy big chunks of loans. There is an active trading market for loans. Investment banks and commercial banks are the same banks now, and the league tables of bond underwriters list the same universal banks as the league tables of big loan arrangers. Loans and bonds are just sort of interchangeable ways for companies to borrow money from institutional investors, with banks acting as coordinators and middlemen rather than actually putting up the money, and the choice between loans and bonds tends to come down to the structural features rather than the different investor bases. This is not necessarily obvious to everyone, and the historical difference between bonds and loans—bonds were sold by investment banks to investors, loans were made by commercial banks on their own balance sheets—still motivates some of the discussion and regulation of lending. So U.S. regulators have spent years scolding banks for doing leveraged loans at too-high levels of leverage. But just loans. Not bonds. It is somewhat unclear to me what exactly the regulators are worried about. The most obvious thing they could be worried about is that if a bank lends a risky company $1 billion, then it has large concentrated risky position, but given the actual workings of the syndicated loan market this just isn’t true: The bank arranging that loan will sell most of it before funding, rather than keeping that risk. There are other things they could be worried about—just that high corporate leverage is systemically risky, for instance, or that banks that underwrite risky loans have a higher risk of getting stuck with them if syndications fail—but if you were worried about those things I think you would be equally worried about loans and bonds. “Companies shouldn’t borrow more than six times their earnings” is a perfectly coherent statement, but “companies shouldn’t borrow more than six times their earnings in loans but just go nuts with bonds, no problem,” is an odd one. Meanwhile the fact that bonds and loans are the same is so obvious and matter-of-fact to people who work in the leveraged finance business that sometimes misunderstandings arise. Here’s a weird story: UBS Group AG fired a senior investment banker because he allegedly failed to apprise his managers of details of a leveraged-buyout loan, highlighting the pressure Wall Street firms are under to keep a lid on risk in the lucrative business. The Swiss bank in December dismissed James Boland, who ran its leveraged-finance group in the Americas, and a lieutenant. Their alleged offense: not informing superiors and the bank’s compliance officials that they had reclassified a bond the firm was underwriting as a loan, according to people familiar with the matter. … UBS had planned to finance the deal with a bond, the people said. But after officials at the Swiss bank realized they couldn’t provide enough disclosure for such a deal to pass legal muster, they switched it to a loan, which carries less-stringent disclosure requirements. Unlike bonds, however, loans are subject to the guidelines regulators put in place as part of broader efforts to limit excessive risk taking in the wake of the financial crisis. There is no sign that the loan ran afoul of government guidelines. Even though the loan was successfully syndicated to investors, UBS temporarily held on to a piece of it, and that is what caused the guidelines to come into play, one of the people said. (He denies wrongdoing and “is appealing his dismissal,” and “the matter is headed for arbitration.”) If this were a substantive difference—if UBS had been planning to market $250 million of bonds to investors, and then at the last minute decided instead to lend $250 million of its own money to the company—then you would not expect the change to be made casually and without high-level approvals. Someone would have to go find the $250 million! But it’s not a substantive difference, not really; UBS just changed its plans from marketing one piece of paper to investors to marketing another piece of paper to investors. One of those pieces of paper is regulated and the other isn’t, but that doesn’t make much sense, and you can see how it might slip someone’s mind.

We talked yesterday about a new kind of non-transparent exchange-traded fund, developed by Precidian Funds, that has received preliminary approval from the Securities and Exchange Commission. Unlike regular ETFs, this sort of ETF would not publish its holdings in real time, which would allow it to be actively managed without giving away the secrets of what stocks it buys. But in order to keep prices fair, the ETF would publish its net asset value every second. My view was, you know, fine, whatever, but it’s a bit rough on the ETF arbitrageurs who don’t know what’s in the portfolio and therefore can’t arbitrage it. I received about one million emails and tweets from stock-arbitrageur types all laughing at me for my naivety: Just by publishing the value of the portfolio every second, the ETF will make it easy for arbitrageurs to figure out what’s in the portfolio. As Vivek Rao put it in email, “there are 6.5 * 3600 = 23400 seconds in a trading day, and an ETF’s returns are a function of the returns of constituents, so someone with second-by-second returns of all U.S. stocks could solve a set of linear equations to find the weights of a non-transparent ETF that invests in U.S. stocks. ... So non-transparent will really mean transparent to high-frequency traders.” As someone else said on Twitter, “if NAVs are published every second you have 24,000 observations each day, which is enough to reconstruct the underlying with high accuracy using sparse regression techniques, so only retail investors are blind to the portfolio.” Now, to be fair, this is an argument that Precidian and the SEC considered, and they think they have a solution. The main trick is that the ETF’s published asset values will be rounded to the nearest penny (and will be based on about a $20 share price), meaning that they will sand away the precision you’d need to perfectly reconstruct the portfolio. (A secondary trick is of course that the point of the non-transparent ETF would be to allow active trading, and so the composition of the portfolio could be obscured to the extent it changes often.) The ETF’s sponsors “have represented that they will operate the ActiveShares ETFs in a manner designed to minimize the risk of reverse engineering and the Commission anticipates that the ActiveShares ETFs will have the ability to minimize such risk,” says the SEC, but that is not quite definitive. Here is a memorandum from the SEC’s Division of Economic and Risk Analysis describing several analyses of whether the portfolio can be reverse-engineered. The rough answer is: It’s pretty easy with an unrounded net asset value; with rounded values and a large universe of possible stocks it’s harder, but you can still recover some useful information. I don’t … know what to tell you? Clearly the goal of the non-transparent ETF is to allow active managers to keep their holdings secret, but I am not entirely sure that that is a good or important goal. It’s possible that active stock managers believe that their secret sauce is more valuable than it is. It’s possible that if algorithmic trading firms figured out what stocks non-transparent ETFs were buying, they could trade in ways that harmed those ETFs; it’s also possible that if they figured out what stocks they were buying they could trade in ways that would mostly help investors in those ETFs by providing tighter arbitrage-based pricing. It’s possible that an open-secret ETF—one whose holdings are known to anyone who can do the math, but not disclosed to its retail investors—would be just fine, that it would provide the benefits of arbitrage-based pricing with the advantages of, um, not explicitly disclosing its portfolio so that its manager feels better about the whole thing. It’s possible that a good product for retail investors would be one that doesn’t tell them what stocks it buys, even while all the professionals involved know perfectly well. It does feel weird though.

The dominant theory of how corporations work is, to exaggerate only slightly, that chief executive officers spend their time trying to enrich, aggrandize and enjoy themselves at the expense of the corporation, while shareholders use a variety of crude mechanisms—incentive pay, proxy proposals, shareholder activism, the threat of hostile takeovers, etc.—to try to make the CEOs act in the interests of shareholders. It is sort of a strange theory. It is not how most of us do our jobs. But there is a real appeal to it. “Incentives matter,” people say. “Lots of CEOs are psychopaths,” people say. “Humans are rational maximizers of their own self-interest,” economists say. It makes sense that if you want to analyze how a corporation functions, you should focus on the incentives and constraints facing the CEO. An alternative theory is something like: Most CEOs try to do a good job running their companies, and if you want to analyze how a corporation functions, you should focus on the CEO’s actual beliefs about what a good job would be. This is fuzzier and more subjective than looking at incentives, but I think it also has a real and underrated appeal. For instance here is a delightful finding (and a related 2018 paper) from Jiwook Jung and Taekjin Shin about what CEOs learn in business school. Jung and Shin focus on diversification of businesses: “Up until the 1960s, business school professors viewed diversification as a valuable strategy,” but “thoughts on diversification turned into skepticism in the 1970s and outright criticism in the 1980s,” as “agency theory views diversification as a prime example of managerial opportunism at the expense of shareholders’ wealth.” In the 1960s conglomerates were viewed as good diversification; in the 1970s and 1980s, that same diversification was viewed as bad for shareholders (who could more efficiently diversify by buying other stocks), but still good for managers (who got to build large empires and diversify their career risk). The dominant theory would be that CEOs would still pursue diversification—because it’s good for them—but that shareholders would try to stop them with activism, more finely-tuned incentive pay, hostile takeovers, etc. But Jung and Shin have another theory: While theories and evidence against diversification emerged in the 1970s, many U.S. firms remained diversified well into the 1980s. Why did the decline of corporate diversification unfold so slowly? We believe it was because corporate strategy reflects the views of top decision makers, and change in strategy follows only from a new crop of decision makers. It took 20 to 30 years for those MBA students who absorbed a skeptical view on diversification in the 1970s and the ‘80s to climb up corporate hierarchies, replace CEOs at major firms, and put the brakes on diversification. To test our argument, we collected data on 2,031 CEOs who ran 640 large U.S. corporations from 1985 to 2015. We also gathered information on their educational background, such as the school they attended for an MBA and their year of graduation. We split our sample into three cohorts—CEOs who earned an MBA before, during, and after the 1970s—and examined whether these groups made different strategic choice about diversification. Here’s what we found: Compared with CEOs without an MBA, CEOs in the first cohort, who earned an MBA before the 1970s, were 17% more likely to pursue diversification at some point during their career. The later cohorts of CEOs, those who earned an MBA in the 1970s and later, were less likely to pursue diversification than their non-MBA counterparts, by 24% and 30%, respectively. We also conducted some additional tests. A quarter of CEOs with an MBA in our data graduated from HBS, where Michael Jensen taught agency theory beginning in 1985. Given his elevated role in popularizing agency theory, we expected that being exposed to his teaching had an enduring effect on students’ views of diversification. We found that CEOs who attended HBS after Jensen joined the school were 83% less likely to engage in diversification than those who went to HBS before that. Obviously it is hard to untangle the effects over time in data like this, but I do find it sort of nice to think that CEOs who learned from Michael Jensen would take a different approach to their businesses from CEOs who never heard of him. It says something nice about the value of teachers and scholars, for one thing. But it also says something nice about CEOs. It suggests that they want to do the right thing, and they have a socially developed framework for deciding what the right thing is, and that framework changes over time for intellectual reasons rather than just because of constraints and incentives. There is really nothing weird or surprising about that, but it just tends not to be how corporate-finance theory works. We talk a lot around here about the theory that common ownership of different companies in the same industry by a handful of big shareholders might reduce competition in that industry. One big controversy in that theory is: How would common ownership reduce competition? It is hard to believe that the big index-fund managers are calling up the companies they own and saying “hey don’t cut prices because we own your competitors too.” Some subtler mechanism—in incentive pay structures or voting patterns or oversight or lack thereof—must be involved. Scott Hemphill and Marcel Kahan have a recent paper (and a related blog post) on “The Strategies of Anticompetitive Common Ownership,” laying out and evaluating some possibilities. But the mechanism that seems obvious to me, but that no one takes that seriously, is just: CEOs want to do a good job, and their understanding of what a good job is changes with intellectual currents. They learned in business school that their job is to maximize shareholder value; they learned in another class in business school that shareholders ought to be, and generally are, broadly diversified. Their understanding of their job is that they are supposed to make shareholders happy; their understanding of shareholders is that they own the market portfolio. Why wouldn’t they have internalized those lessons, and make choices that maximize the wealth of diversified shareholders?

Ah: “I envision a whole new equity market for higher education in the next five years where today there’s only debt,” says Chuck Trafton, who runs hedge fund FlowPoint Capital Partners LP, which has invested in ISAs [income-sharing agreements], including Purdue’s. ISA experts say they have fielded calls from some of the world's largest investment managers that are considering investing in the contracts. And Tony James, executive vice chairman of money manager Blackstone Group LP, formed the Education Finance Institute to help schools study and develop ISAs. That is from a story about how income sharing agreements, an equity-like way to finance higher education, are slowly catching on: Students borrow money from investors and, instead of agreeing to pay it back with interest, agree to pay the investors a fixed percentage of their income for a fixed time period, letting the investors share the upside and downside of their careers. I always love stories like this, and I have since the early 2000s, when I first wrote about them as a law student. There is a constant fascination with the possibility of funding education with equity rather than debt, and people are always starting companies to do it, but as far as I can tell it is perpetually five years in the future. Why doesn’t this ever take off?[1] I don’t know. Part of it is that people find it icky for vague indentured-servitude reasons. Part of it is just that nobody understands student loans, so people want to do the simplest most normal thing rather than some weird financial-engineering experiment. Part of it is that young ambitious people at the beginning of their careers may have a bias against giving up upside: If everyone thinks that they’ll get rich, then no one will want to sign away a percentage of their future earnings. In America, James Baldwin wrote, “spiritually speaking, there are no workers, only candidates for the hand of the boss’s daughter.” And so: “Purdue, for example, caps total payments at 2.5 times what a student borrowed, so the most successful don’t feel gouged,” which is less than a 10 percent annual return over 10 years, hardly a great cap on equity returns. I’m tempted to guess that these reasons work together: If you are a cold-hearted calculating money-motivated student, then your financial upside is high and there’s no reason to sell shares in it for cheap. If you’re a fuzzier and more emotional type who doesn’t care that much about making a lot of money, then this might be a good deal for you, but you’re also the sort of person who would find it icky or confusing and wouldn’t take it. The target audience is people who are focused on financial optimization but don’t plan to make a lot of money, and I am not sure how big a group that is.

What is the point of an exchange-traded fund? I feel like there are two answers, an inside answer and an outside answer. The outside answer—the one relevant to normal investors—is that it’s a mutual fund that (1) allows you to buy or sell shares, at about the net asset value, on the stock exchange, at any point throughout the trading day and (2) doesn’t pay taxes. The inside answer—the one relevant to ETF-industry professionals—is that it is a sort of quasi-derivative version of a basket of stocks that trades at the correct price (one close to its net asset value) because of a clever arbitrage mechanism: Market makers and arbitrageurs know what is in the ETF basket, so if the ETF trades at a higher (lower) price than the underlying stocks, they can sell (buy) the ETF and buy (sell) the underlying stocks to capture a risk-free profit.[2] These two answers work together: The arbitrage mechanism keeps the price of the ETF in line with its net asset value, meaning that if you buy and sell shares of the ETF during the day you will get a price that is very close to the net asset value.[3] Once you understand the inside answer it is tempting to believe it is the “real” one, but I guess that’s not necessarily true. Yesterday the Securities and Exchange Commission said that it plans to approve a new sort of “non-transparent” ETF that will basically break the arbitrage mechanism.[4] The ETF’s holdings will be secret, which will be good for active managers who don’t want to report their trades in real time. (“We can couple the benefits of the ETF wrapper with active management expertise, while protecting investors and our portfolio managers’ intellectual property,” one person involved says.) Market makers and arbitrageurs will not be able to trade the ETF against the underlying basket to keep prices in line with net asset values. Instead the ETF will publish its net asset value every second, so people will know what it’s worth and, presumably, only buy or sell it at prices pretty close to what it’s worth. If prices get too far out of line, there is a sort of arbitrage-ish mechanism to get them back in line: A single “Authorized Participant Representative” will know what the underlying stocks are; if the ETF’s price is below the net asset value, you can give the AP representative cash (to buy the underlying securities, which the AP representative knows but you don’t) and get ETF shares back; if the ETF’s price is above the net asset value, you can give the AP representative ETF shares and get cash back (based on the NAV). As a way to keep the price of the ETF close to its net asset value, that sounds … plausible? It is effectively the same as letting people buy and sell shares from the ETF at net asset value.[5] But from the classic ETF arbitrage perspective it is a bit of a mess: Market makers can’t trade in the underlying securities to hedge their ETF positions, and arbitrageurs can’t keep the prices in line in real time, because nobody (except the AP representative, who can’t tell anyone) knows what the underlying securities are. Aesthetically I find that kind of weird because I am used to the inside answer, the arbitrage mechanism, the delicate market structure that lets ETFs work. But practically I guess it is fine? Like the basic idea here is: This is an actively managed mutual fund, That you can buy and sell throughout the trading day at pretty close to the net asset value, and That doesn’t pay taxes. Point 2 is maybe not as crisp and perfect as it is in a traditional ETF, but that is not the relevant comparison; the relevant comparison is that you can’t do intraday trading in a regular actively managed mutual fund at all . (Also: This is more tax efficient.) The SEC is concerned with investor protection, and so it requires the new ETFs to have a big warning saying “This ETF is different from traditional ETFs,” and “The price you pay to buy ETF shares on an exchange may not match the value of the ETF’s portfolio.” It is not so concerned with letting ETF arbitrageurs have a fair shake at arbitraging every new ETF, but perhaps it doesn’t have to be.

Zoom Video Communications Inc. filed a draft prospectus for its initial public offering back on March 22. Yesterday it updated the prospectus with a marketing price range that could value the company, which provides a video conferencing platform, at more than $8 billion. Zoom will list on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker symbol ZM. ZM, you might notice, is not the optimal ticker. ZOOM would be a better ticker for a company named Zoom. ZOOM is taken. It is taken by a company called Zoom Technologies Inc. Zoom Technologies is not listed on the Nasdaq. It de-registered its stock in 2015; it still trades over the counter here and there, but not all that much, and not for all that much money. In February of this year, for instance, fewer than 5,000 shares of Zoom Technologies traded, according to Bloomberg data, at a high price of $0.004 per share, a low of $0.00 (what?), and an average of $0.0026. That is, about $12.32 worth of Zoom Technologies stock traded, total, in February, and its market capitalization peaked at $12,000. Yesterday Zoom Technologies closed at $1.00 per share, for a market cap of $3 million, up … infinity percent? … from its February lows. (Up 24,900 percent from its February highs, too.) Volume yesterday was 127,116 shares, or more than 1,000 times as many shares as traded in all of February. The price and volume started rising on March 22, the day that Zoom Video filed its prospectus, but things really got going in the following weeks. If you saw Zoom Video’s prospectus filing, thought (incoherently!) “huh, Zoom is going public, I should buy some before that happens,” and ran out and bought 1,000 shares of Zoom Technologies for $60, you are … well, “rich” is an exaggeration (you have $1,000), but your rate of return is excellent. Obviously—it goes without saying—there is no recent news out of Zoom Technologies. I don’t want to make too much fun of this. The numbers involved are small, and for many participants the trades are surely rational. (The stock has gone up pretty consistently over the past couple of weeks, so if you thought not “I am going to buy this $8 billion unicorn cheap” but rather “I am going to buy this nano-cap company to profit from other people’s confusion” you have probably done well.) We talk about this stuff from time to time, and it always seems to me like an amusing backwater of inefficiency rather than a deep flaw in the capital markets. Still, if you run a defunct-ish nano-cap public company, there is no time like the present to rename it Universal Best Executive Research and gun for that UBER ticker. You won’t get it, of course, but even an unsuccessful gesture at confusion might pay off.

We talked a bit last week about Patagonia’s decision to stop making co-branded fleece vests for finance and tech companies, but here is a full Wall Street Journal A-hed about the controversy: On weekdays, foot soldiers in New York City’s business-and-finance army parade through Manhattan wearing Patagonia vests embroidered with such names as JPMorgan Chase , Nomura and BMO Capital. Like a pair of $1,500 John Lobb oxfords, these co-branded power vests can intimidate and draw envy. To the dismay of those yearning to be swaddled in one, Patagonia said last week it was keeping new orders of the torso-hugging showpieces reserved for “mission-driven companies that prioritize the planet.” I assume Bridgewater will find a way to get them. Anyway my point here is, we have to make this happen: That same day, workwear and outdoor apparel retailer Carhartt reached out to Patagonia vest-wearers on Twitter. “130 years of workwear speaks for itself,” the company wrote. “We’d be glad to help.” I just went to Carhartt’s website and there is a whole category called “flame-resistant.” I really cannot stress enough how good it would be if the hedge-fund uniform stops being branded Patagonia fleece vests and starts being branded Carhartt flame-resistant deluxe coveralls. Really, if you make a bad call, won’t you feel more confident facing your boss’s white-hot rath in the safety of flame-resistant coveralls? At the very least, if I order some Money Stuff branded coveralls, who will buy some?

[1] Some part of the reason may be that the U.S. government now offers income-based repayment of student loans, which provides some of the advantages of true equity student financing without giving up upside. It’s not a perfect substitute, but I do think there is some amount of “why would I do an income-sharing agreement with some weird investor when I can get a better version of the same deal from the government?” [2] To make the profit really risk-free, there is a creation/redemption mechanism that allows arbitrageurs to exchange shares of the ETF for the underlying basket, or vice versa, directly with the ETF. (Well, technically it allows “authorized participants,” a handful of big banks and market makers, to do this, not just anyone, but the no-arbitrage result is basically the same.) [3] And because you are buying and selling on the exchange rather than cashing in and out of the ETF directly—and because even when you do trade directly with the ETF it is via in-kind creations and redemptions rather than with cash—the ETF doesn’t pay taxes. [4] We talked about this way back in 2014, when the SEC rejected a previous version of the idea. [5] So why not just do that? Why bother with the complexity of the AP representative? You know the answer: So that the ETF doesn’t pay taxes! If you could trade with the ETF for cash, it would create potential tax recognition events. If you only trade with the AP representative for cash, and the AP representative does in-kind creations and redemptions, then the ETF doesn’t have to pay taxes. I keep stressing the tax stuff in the footnotes because it is so central to the structuring of ETFs, even though it has no apparent connection to the market-structure arbitrage-y stuff in the text.

In my former career, I was in the business of structuring derivatives, which in my case often meant that I was in the business of saying no to derivatives. “Derivatives” is sort of a vague term, and there is a persistent folk belief that they have magic powers, that any legal or financial problem can somehow be solved by doing a derivative. In this folk belief, the derivative structurers are wizards with arcane powers, respected and feared as long as they can make the rains come, but also treated with great suspicion when the harvest fails. I had a lot of conversations like this: Coverage banker: Our client has some shares of XYZ, and he would like to eliminate his downside risk in the stock. He doesn’t want to pay much for that protection, but he is willing to give up his upside exposure. Can you structure some sort of derivative to help him hedge? Me: He owns the stock, he doesn’t want to lose money if it goes down, and he doesn’t care about making money if it goes up? Banker: Exactly, yes, can you help him? Me: He should just sell the stock. Banker: Oh no he can’t do that, he signed an agreement with the company that doesn’t let him sell the stock. Me: Did he also agree not to hedge it? Banker: I don’t think so, I’m sure hedging is fine. Me: Really? Banker: Let me send you the agreement. [ Sends contract ] Me: It says right here “you shall not sell, hedge, reduce your exposure, trade in options or swaps or other derivatives, or otherwise do anything at all that anyone might even think looks a little bit like hedging.” Banker: Well but we were thinking there might be some sort of … derivative? Me: Come on! Banker: This is not very helpful. Are you even a real derivatives structurer? At this point I would say I had to jump to another call, but it is important to point out that I wasn’t very good at this. If you were really good, you would construct a magical derivative that would somehow thread the needle, hedge the client’s risk and not violate the agreement. If you were slightly less good, you would construct a derivative that wouldn’t hedge the client’s risk, but you’d be a good enough salesperson to pitch it to the banker and maybe even to the client. (Short a basket of correlated stocks, sure!) If you were … let’s say, average … you would construct a derivative that would hedge the client’s risk and definitely violate the agreement, sell it to the client, and let him worry about getting sued. Anyway here’s a goofy story from The Information about the initial public offering of Lyft Inc. Lyft threatened Morgan Stanley with legal action earlier this week, demanding in a letter the investment bank stop marketing a short-selling product that the ride-hailing firm believed was disrupting trading in its stock, according to four people familiar with the situation. The letter, sent on April 2, cited an article in the New York Post published on Monday night that said the bank was marketing a product that appeared to offer Lyft’s pre-IPO shareholders a way to get around lockup agreements that prevent them from selling for at least six months after the IPO. If true, the letter said, Morgan Stanley “is engaged in tortious interference” and the company demanded the firm stop sales of the product or face legal action. ... For weeks during the roadshow, Morgan Stanley salespeople had been calling early Lyft investors and pitching them on a short-selling transaction that would enable them to lock in gains, regardless of the lockup, the executive said. … One of the transactions was called a “total return swap,” a way for the investor to get the returns from short-selling the stock, while not technically selling the stock. We talked about these rumors last week, and I pointed out that the lockup absolutely clearly prohibits Lyft’s pre-IPO shareholders from using total return swaps to hedge their exposure. “A person familiar with the situation said the lockups were bullet proof and the Morgan Stanley product was clearly in contravention of the agreements,” and: “Some of the VC firms who were contacted checked with Lyft’s bankers and their own lawyers to see if the suggested trades would breach the lockup agreements,” and were told that they did. So, yeah. A total return swap is not a way around the lockup, except in the narrow sense that Lyft can keep track of its shares but can’t necessarily keep track of who’s doing total return swaps. It’s a way around the lockup if Lyft doesn’t notice . Meanwhile CNBC reports that Morgan Stanley denies Lyft’s claims, saying that its “activity has been in the normal course of market-making,” and that it “did not market or execute, directly or indirectly, a sale, short sale, hedge, swap or transfer of risk or value associated with Lyft stock for any Lyft shareholder identified by the company or otherwise known to us to be the subject of a Lyft lock-up agreement.” And it does seem somewhat unlikely to me that a big investment bank would go around marketing a lockup-violation product. I wouldn’t be at all surprised if someone asked for one, though.

Okay here’s a math problem I guess? You run an index fund. It has a billion dollars in it. It costs you $500,000 to run it, paying rent and salaries and index licensing fees and whatever. It also generates $800,000 of securities lending revenue: The fund owns a bunch of stocks and lends them out to short sellers to make a bit of extra money. As the manager of the index fund, you are in charge of doing that lending, and so you could in theory keep the securities lending revenue for yourself. Or you could say, no, this revenue belongs to my investors, I will just put it back in the fund (increasing the returns that the fund makes for investors). Or you could split it somehow, giving some of the revenue to yourself and some to the fund. Here’s the math problem; it has two parts: How much of the securities lending revenue should you keep for yourself and how much should you give to the fund? What fees should the fund charge to investors? Fine, it is not really a math problem, it is more of an aesthetic problem. There are different possible answers. Here are three decent ones: You keep $500,000 of securities lending revenue for yourself, give $300,000 to the fund, and charge fees of zero. You keep all $800,000 of securities lending revenue for yourself and charge fees of negative 3 basis points. “We’ll pay you to invest with us,” you can tell investors. You give all $800,000 of securities lending revenue to investors and charge fees of 5 basis points. “We are fully transparent,” you tell investors: “We charge you an honest price for our work, and pass all of the securities-lending revenue on to you.” All of these answers have the same economic result: You make zero dollars running the fund, and your investors get the return on the underlying index plus 3 basis points. There are of course other possible answers that are simply worse for investors—ones where you make more than zero dollars—but let’s assume that, in a highly competitive environment for index funds, those get competed away. There are other possible answers that are worse for you—ones where you make less than zero dollars—but let’s assume that, in a rational market for index funds, you don’t go there.[1] And there is an infinite spectrum of answers that are economically the same (you keep $400,000 and charge 1 basis point, etc.), but those three—minimum fees, maximum revenue sharing, and solving for zero fees—seem like the most salient. Which do you like? I am sort of partial to answer 1. Free is a good price for a product. When you tell people that something is free, they tend to be happy, and want it. When you tell people that something costs a little less than zero —that you’ll pay them a small amount of money to do it—they tend to get suspicious. “Wait if you’re paying me to do this then it must be bad,” they think, “and also you should pay me more.” On the other hand, when you tell people that something costs money but is superior to the free thing—“we charge you fees, but we give you this extra source of revenue that makes up for the fees”—then they also get suspicious and just want the free thing. I guess if I were starting an index fund today, and the numbers shook out roughly like my hypothetical example,[2] I’d try to make the fees zero by subsidizing them with securities lending revenue. It’s nice and round, easy to explain and advertise. But people tend not to start index funds from scratch these days; index funds tend to live at big fund companies that already have histories. Oversimplifying, those histories include: charging much higher fees for their funds, back before the rise of indexing and the fee wars pushed fees near zero; and feeling pressured to share securities lending revenue with their funds rather than keeping them for themselves, leading to more or less investor-friendly splits of that revenue in which the funds get most of the money and the firms get relatively little.[3] And so the norm is to charge positive fees but give most of the stock-lending revenue back to investors. Just on first principles it is weird! These things are offsetting; it doesn’t really matter economically whether you make your marginal dollar from fees or from securities lending.[4] If you think, as I do, that investors tend to notice and like “zero fees” but are less likely to pay attention to the relative split of securities lending revenue, you’d want to make the fees more investor-friendly and the securities lending less so. But that’s not really the way the industry works. Anyway here’s an article from Jeff Sommer about how index-fund “fees are on the verge of falling below zero,” with securities lending revenue being part of the explanation. (Though with vicious competition being the main explanation.) It feels to me like there is a correct number, and it is zero, and we might just sail right by it on our way from one incorrect number to another. You see this sort of strange math problem from time to time. Another example is Robinhood Markets Inc. and payment for order flow. Retail brokerages generally charge investors a commission for executing trades and sell those investors’ orders to wholesale brokers. The wholesalers pay for that order flow in the form of (1) “payment for order flow,” direct cash payments to the retail brokers and (2) “price improvement,” tighter bid/ask spreads for the trades that give the brokers’ customers better execution. In a competitive market, you would expect that the total benefit would be passed on to the customers: The tighter bid/ask spreads directly save the customers money, while the payment for order flow gives money to the retail brokers that allows them to reduce their commissions. The split between those two things is kind of arbitrary[5]: One broker could demand a higher payment for order flow, pass it on to customers in the form of lower commissions, and accept less price improvement; another broker could demand more price improvement, accept lower payments for order flow, and charge higher commissions. It seems to me that the sensible and salient commission rate would be zero, and that retail brokers would want to solve for the amount of payment for order flow (and the corresponding amount of price improvement) that would get them to zero commissions. But in fact retail brokers traditionally charge commissions, while also taking less payment for order flow than they could, and giving customers relatively more price improvement. And then Robinhood came along and quite sensibly offered zero commissions, subsidized, apparently—there is some dispute—by a lot of payment for order flow. This strikes me as obviously good and correct, and the sort of thing that a tech-y upstart can do when it examines the business from first principles and is not beholden to legacy structures. And then of course people got mad at it.

Imagine you’re a banking regulator and a bank comes to you and says: “Hey, funny story, we were looking at our books and realized that a bunch of loans that we’ve been telling everyone are good are actually bad. Anyhoo, now we have a lot less money than anyone thinks we do. We were thinking of selling a bunch of stock to raise the money, but that will be hard to do if we tell people about the bad loans, so we were just going to keep it quiet. Are you cool with that?” Are you? I am sure that the textbooks for banking regulators stress how important accurate accounting is for overall confidence in the system, and that it is healthy to subject banks to the discipline of the market and to let bad ones fail. On the other hand, we have lived through a pretty nervous decade or so for bank regulators, and one central conclusion of that decade seems to be that the main cure for nervousness about banking is more capital. If you have a bank that is bad, “raise a bunch more capital” always sounds like a good solution, and “come clean to the market about how bad it is at the risk of sparking a panic” tends to sound like a bad one. So: The ECB gave Banco Popular the green light to proceed with its ill-fated capital raise in 2016 despite being in possession of evidence that indicated serious financial irregularities in the Spanish lender’s accounts, according to a confidential ECB report seen by IFR. Investors eventually lost every cent of the €2.5bn raised by Popular in the rights issue as part of the resolution of the bank a year later. The capital call, which launched in May 2016 and closed the following month, is now the subject of a legal battle in Madrid, with disgruntled former shareholders claiming that they were misled into backing the deal by false numbers. One thing to say here is that a securities regulator might have a different perspective from a banking regulator. A regulator whose primary focus was the protection of investors and the integrity of the capital markets would push hard for full disclosure, while a regulator whose primary focus was the safety of the banking system and the protection of depositors and taxpayers might be willing to throw shareholders under the bus here and there.

On Thursday Elon Musk walked into a federal court for a contempt of court hearing, and a couple of hours later he walked out again, which is a not-to-be-underestimated victory. You have to figure that any time Elon Musk walks into a contempt of court hearing there’s like a 20 percent chance that he’s spending the weekend in jail. But not this time: A federal judge gave Elon Musk and the Securities and Exchange Commission two weeks to resolve a dispute about whether Mr. Musk had violated a settlement he reached with the commission in October and should be held in contempt of court. Judge Alison J. Nathan of Federal District Court in Manhattan told both sides to “take a deep breath” and put on “their reasonableness pants” after a roughly 90-minute hearing attended by Mr. Musk, the chief executive of the electric car company Tesla. Please do not send me a drawing of Elon Musk’s reasonableness pants. I assume they’re form-fitting, see-through and somehow rocket-boosted. What do you think will happen here? The current court order requires Musk to get a lawyer’s approval before tweeting anything that might be material to Tesla Inc.; the SEC thinks he violated that order by tweeting about Tesla without pre-approval, while he thinks he’s fine because he reasonably thought his tweet wasn’t material. One obvious solution, which the SEC would probably like, would be to change the settlement to require him to get approval before any tweet about Tesla, but Musk seems pretty adamant about not agreeing to that. Another solution, which Musk would probably like, would be to let him tweet anything he wants about Tesla, material or not, true or not, and have Tesla just put a disclaimer on its website saying like “Elon’s tweets may not be true, use them at your own risk.” The SEC would probably not be okay with that. Maybe a good compromise would be that he can tweet as much as he wants about Tesla, but he only gets, say, three material tweets: Once he tweets three material things about Tesla without pre-approval, then he’s cut off, and he needs to get pre-approval for any more Tesla tweets, material or not. (I am not sure who would determine materiality, maybe the SEC?) Obviously the SEC would prefer not to let him make three materially false announcements without consequence, but, to be fair, they’ve let him do that in the past and it was fine. We just are not in the normal world of securities law! Everyone—Musk, the SEC, the judge, Tesla shareholders—has kind of accepted that sometimes Musk will tweet things about Tesla that aren’t true; the question is just how much of a sense of humor people should have about it.

I am not sure it rises to the level of a Law of Insider Trading, but this is rude: During the afternoon of June 9, 2017, Family Member A had a telephone conversation with Wife. Family Member A and Wife had a close personal relationship. They routinely shared confidences with each other and kept the other’s confidences. While discussing another family member’s upcoming medical procedures, Family Member A shared material nonpublic information with Wife. In explaining why Family Member A would not be able to travel to attend the medical procedure, Family Member A disclosed to Wife that Family Member A was engaged in work related to the [not-yet-disclosed deal in which Amazon.com Inc. bought Whole Foods Market Inc.]. By virtue of their history, pattern, and practice of sharing confidences, Wife owed a duty of trust or confidence to Family Member A, and Family Member A expected that Wife would maintain the confidentiality of the material nonpublic information. Immediately following Wife’s discussion with Family Member A, Wife relayed the material nonpublic information about Family Member A’s involvement in the proposed transaction to Yang in the context of discussing why Family Member A would not be able to travel for the medical procedures. By virtue of their spousal relationship, Yang owed Wife a duty of trust or confidence and Yang knew or was reckless in not knowing that the information Wife disclosed was confidential and that he should not trade on the information. Less than an hour later, Yang purchased 40 Whole Foods call option contracts with a strike price of $25 and an expiration date of January 18, 2019 … “Is Cousin Jane coming out for Grandma’s surgery?” “No, she’s stuck working on a big deal for Whole Foods.” “Cool, I’ll just buy some call options.” Come on. Tai-Cheng Yang agreed to pay the Securities and Exchange Commission about $57,000 for this, and I hope the medical procedure went well, because otherwise he probably feels really guilty. Did Donald Trump’s likely Fed nominee Herman Cain use an email mailing list to promote worthless penny stocks? There is only one conceivable answer.

If you are an entrepreneur thinking of doing an initial coin offering, what should you make of the “ Framework for ‘Investment Contract’ Analysis of Digital Assets” that the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission issued yesterday? I think the correct answer is probably “that is a trick question, the ICO market is dead, nobody is thinking of doing ICOs anymore.” It is not uncommon for financial innovation to get a bit ahead of the rules that are supposed to regulate it, but the ICO market got so far ahead of the rules that it started, boomed, peaked and died before the rules came along. No, I’m kidding, at least a little. First of all, the decline in ICOs probably is due not only to crypto prices being well off their highs, but also to indications—and enforcement actions—from the SEC suggesting that most ICOs are more or less illegal. That has probably put a damper on ICOs. Second, there are still no real rules about ICOs; the SEC’s framework begins with a footnote saying that “it is not a rule, regulation, or statement of the Commission,” just some hints from the SEC’s staff about how they interpret the existing securities laws. Specifically, it describes the staff’s thoughts about when a digital token counts as a “security” under U.S. law. If a token is a “security,” then an ICO issuer needs to either register the token with the SEC like any other initial public offering, or make sure that it is sold only to “accredited investors”; the security designation also limits how the token can trade. Even if a token is a security, you can do an ICO; there have been ICOs of security tokens that are sold only to accredited investors, and other ICOs that have actually been registered as securities offerings. But being a security does make things harder, particularly for the classic use case of a crypto-token that is intended to finance the development of some decentralized platform and then be used as a currency connecting buyers and sellers on that platform. If you don’t register your security token, and limit it to accredited investors, then that makes it less useful as a token: People selling stuff on the platform will get back tokens that won’t necessarily be freely tradable, and everyone will have to worry about transferring tokens to non-accredited investors. If you do register your security token, and make it freely tradable, then you have to file quarterly disclosure documents and financial statements, and … like … whose financial statements are you filing? Who are “you”? Who is auditing them? How? The securities laws are written for companies that issue stocks and bonds ; it is not clear how you would write securities disclosure for a decentralized ecosystem of buyers and sellers who convene on a blockchain, or how you’d gather the data to write that disclosure, or how you could get lawyers and accountants to sign off on it. So if you are a big believer in ICOs as the way to finance the enterprises of the future, to fund decentralized platforms that will not be owned by corporations but will be maintained by their users, what should you think of the SEC’s guidance? I think it is … mostly positive? There has been a certain amount of noise out of the SEC suggesting that all ICO tokens are securities, and that there is no way to issue an interesting utility token that complies with the rules. But the framework doesn’t say that. It does seem to chart a narrow course by which a token could not be a security. A legal non-security token is possible! Not a non-security ICO , maybe, but a non-security token . (We’ll get to the difference.) The framework is based on the “Howey test,” the U.S. Supreme Court’s test for deciding if something is a security. The key questions, for tokens, are: (1) Do you expect to make money from buying tokens, and (2) do you expect to make that money through “the efforts of others”?[1] Do you expect to make money? Here the question is basically, are people buying tokens mostly as investments, or are they buying them to use them on some platform? Bad facts, for the SEC, include “the digital asset gives the holder rights to share in the enterprise's income or profits or to realize gain from capital appreciation of the digital asset,” “there is little apparent correlation between the purchase/offering price of the digital asset and the market price of the particular goods or services that can be acquired in exchange for the digital asset,” that sort of thing. (Also, not dispositive but a bad fact: “The digital asset is transferable or traded on or through a secondary market or platform, or is expected to be in the future.”) Good facts include “the value of the digital asset has shown a direct and stable correlation to the value of the good or service for which it may be exchanged or redeemed,” “the trading volume for the digital asset corresponds to the level of demand for the good or service for which it may be exchanged or redeemed,” etc. Does it come from the efforts of others? Here the essential question is: Is the person or company or group that launched the ICO—which the SEC calls an “Active Participant” or “AP”—essential to the continuing operation of the network? Bad facts here include “an AP plays a lead or central role in deciding governance issues, code updates, or how third parties participate in the validation of transactions that occur with respect to the digital asset,” “an AP creates or supports a market for, or the price of, the digital asset,” etc. But the most interesting bit to me was this negative factor: There are essential tasks or responsibilities performed and expected to be performed by an AP, rather than an unaffiliated, dispersed community of network users (commonly known as a "decentralized" network). What that suggests is that if the thing really is a decentralized network, it’s okay .[2] That is not an easy test to satisfy—it certainly describes Bitcoin, and probably a few other cryptocurrencies, but most ICOs are designed to fund a centralized developer’s work in building and maintaining the platform—but it does seem like the right test. If you are building a token to run a decentralized platform, and if you plan to disappear once the platform is up and running, then the SEC will let your token work as a token, not a security. Well, with the small caveat that your token won’t work while you’re building the platform. The SEC has not really blessed the classic non-security ICO, in which you issue tokens to raise money to build a decentralized platform and then get out of the way. Those tokens would obviously be speculative—the platform hasn’t been built yet—and your role in building the platform is still central. “Where the network or the digital asset is still in development and the network or digital asset is not fully functional at the time of the offer or sale, purchasers would reasonably expect an AP to further develop the functionality of the network or digital asset (directly or indirectly),” says the SEC, basically foreclosing the possibility that any ICO like that could avoid being a security. This is not fatal! Lawyers have thought much the same thing for a while now, and have developed technology like the “ simple agreement for future tokens.” The SAFT is a security, and you issue it (to accredited investors or in a registered offering) to fund the development of the platform, and then once the platform can stand on its own the SAFT poofs into non-security tokens which can work on the platform. The SEC’s framework suggests that this idea might work. (Or even: You could issue security tokens to fund the platform, and then at some point when the platform works and the developer disappears, the tokens just become non-securities. This seems a bit hazier than the SAFT, but unlike the SAFT it is explicitly mentioned in the SEC’s framework, which describes “evaluating whether a digital asset previously sold as a security should be reevaluated at the time of later offers or sales.”) So the SEC’s framework strikes me as a reasonable compromise: You can issue speculative tokens to fund the development of a decentralized platform, but they will have to be treated as securities and sold in a registered or exempt offering. But then once the platform is (1) working and (2) decentralized, they can stop being securities and start being just pure tokens. Alongside the framework, the SEC staff also issued a no-action letter approving one particular token.[3] This no-action letter is not that helpful! The token involved is for a company called TurnKey Jet, Inc., and it is just a way to do prepaid private-airplane time on a blockchain. It satisfies the SEC’s framework not by being a decentralized network—it looks like TurnKey Jet would mostly operate the platform—but by not offering an expectation of profit. The tokens are usable only for private jet usage, and can’t really appreciate in value. The SEC’s approval conditions—particularly “TKJ will sell Tokens at a price of one USD per Token throughout the life of the Program, and each Token will represent a TKJ obligation to supply air charter services at a value of one USD per Token”—are super boring. This is a useful precedent if you are planning to, like, put your retail gift cards on the blockchain, but not if you are planning a genuinely novel way of financing the development of decentralized economic activity. Still, if that is what you’re planning, the framework probably offers some encouragement.

Look, if you are an investment bank, and you are going to sell structured notes whose payoff is based on a basket of large venture-backed private technology companies, I think you are obligated to acronym it up and call the thing a UNICORN. It ends with an “N,” for “note,” so you’ve got a head start. Unregistered Non-IPO Corporate Option Reverse Notes, something like that.[4] Ooh, or Using New $1-billion+ Companies to Originate Retail Notes, UN1CORNs, I like that, mix it up a bit. Forge and BNP Paribas, shoot me an email and I’ll tell you where to send my royalty checks: Forge Global Inc., a five-year-old company that matches private companies and their employees with investors, plans to raise as much as $1 billion in the next year through the sale of a series of structured notes linked to the shares of startups. French bank BNP Paribas SA will offer the derivatives to both institutions and wealthy individuals in Europe and Asia, the companies said. … BNP Paribas’s clients outside the U.S. have long sought to invest more heavily in emerging Silicon Valley companies but may not have the resources to research individual companies or access the venture-capital funds that own them. “For them it was really about accessing private tech as an asset class as opposed to picking individual names,” said Benjamin Kieffer, BNP Paribas’s head of equity-derivatives structuring. Private tech stocks will invariably go through downturns, but they will endure as a viable investment option in part because these companies are no longer racing to go public as once were, Mr. Kieffer said. Today’s privately held companies are bigger and the pool of available cash to fund them is much greater, he added. When we last talked about structured notes around here, I described how banks ordinarily manufacture them by trading in the underlying stocks. I assume that, here too, BNP Paribas is not just going to make naked bets on unicorn stocks against its customers: It’s going to buy baskets of unicorn stocks (from Forge, “the leading marketplace for pre-IPO securities,” according to the press release), and issue notes that mirror those baskets. On the other hand, traditionally structured notes have complicated option features that banks dynamically hedge by actively trading in and out of the underlying stocks throughout the life of the notes; that’s a lot harder to do with unicorn shares, just because they tend not to trade all that often. So I assume the structured notes will be fairly simple, not so much a complicated barrier option product as “here’s a basket of unicorn stocks wrapped up in a note.” That is, they will be somewhat dressed-up unicorn index funds, or commoditized late-stage-venture-capital funds, that sort of thing, but their legal form will be a note issued by a bank so that BNP Paribas clients can easily buy them. Honestly this seems like a good and obvious idea, which is why people keep announcing variants on it. I don’t know if Forge’s and BNP Paribas’s version will stick, but I suspect that eventually one will. Private markets, I keep saying around here, are the new public markets, and if that keeps being true then they will just sort of accrete all of the trappings of public markets, index funds and structured notes and retail sales forces and all the rest.

Here’s kind of a weird story about Lyft from the Wall Street Journal: Carl Icahn sold his roughly 2.7% stake in Lyft Inc. to fellow billionaire George Soros ahead of the ride-hailing company’s initial public offering last week, according to people familiar with the matter. ... The activist investor, who rarely invests in private companies, had been unhappy with Lyft’s plan to use supervoting shares to give its two founders near-majority voting rights, some of the people said. It isn’t clear what price Mr. Soros paid, but the investment was sure to be a successful one for the 83 year-old Mr. Icahn. He had invested roughly $100 million in Lyft in 2015 at a valuation of $2.5 billion, and later added $50 million at the same valuation. The IPO valued Lyft at $24 billion, or $72 a share, though he likely sold it for a bit less than that. … Lyft’s pre-IPO investors are prohibited from selling shares until a lockup expires 180 days after the offering, and Mr. Soros remains subject to that. Unlike many other tech IPO’s, Lyft’s was all primary, meaning that all of the $2.3 billion of stock sold in the IPO went to financing Lyft rather than cashing out early investors. That makes sense both as a marketing matter (“we’re using your money to grow” is a better story than “the smart money thinks this is the top and wants out”) and as a financial one (Lyft needs the money!), but it does mean that if early investors wanted to get out they had to do so in somewhat odd ways and, presumably, at a discount. Soros, meanwhile, got a big slug of shares—more than he likely would have gotten in the oversubscribed IPO—and, again presumably, at a discount, but now he’s stuck with them for 6 months, and the stock has spent much of this week trading below the IPO price. (It got back above it this morning.) It sort of feels like the point of an IPO is to bring together all the supply of shares, and all the demand for shares, in one big transaction and let the price sort everything out, but here it didn’t quite work that way. Meanwhile here’s kind of a weird story from the New York Post: Lyft investors who bought the ride-hailing company’s shares well before its high-profile initial public offering Friday are protecting themselves against a decline in the high-profile stock despite “lock-up” agreements intended to block them from doing just that, numerous sources told The Post. Morgan Stanley, a lead underwriter for Lyft rival Uber, is one of the brokerages selling a “short” product to pre-IPO investors, three sources close to the situation said. ... Driving the unusual bets is language in Lyft’s lock-up agreements that has hedge funds and other early Lyft investors giving themselves a green light to make limited “short” bets, which make money on a stock’s decline. It’s weird, for one thing, because there is nothing unusual in the lockup language in Lyft Inc.’s IPO prospectus, which says quite clearly (as these things go) that the pre-IPO investors cannot hedge their stakes for six months.[5] Perhaps they misread the agreements? “People who own the stock are allowed to hedge their positions. You are not allowed to reduce your economic interest,” says one investor, incoherently. (Hedging is reducing your economic interest.) It’s weird, for another thing, because hedging Lyft seems really expensive: A surge in demand for short positions in Lyft Inc., the ride-sharing company that went public last week, has made it the most expensive bearish bet in the U.S. equity market. Tuesday was the first day investors were able to borrow shares to settle short sales, and the cost of funding a new short stake rose 100 percent, according to IHS Markit. That makes Lyft the “most expensive to borrow” U.S. equity with over $5 million in balances, the firm said in an emailed statement. The straightforward way to hedge stock is to sell it short, but doing that with Lyft is prohibitively expensive: If stock-borrow rates stay this high (they won’t), locking in a $70 share price for six months (until the lockup expires and early investors can sell) would cost about $35 in borrow costs. Hardly seems worth it. There are other ways to hedge—basically doing an option or a swap or a forward with an investment bank—but those tend to require your bank to short the stock; if stock borrow is expensive then those methods will be expensive too.

A genre of financial news story that I enjoy these days is “stories about the integration of back-office systems that don’t use the word ‘blockchain.’” Like here, for instance, is a story about how Bank of New York Mellon and BlackRock Inc. both have computer programs that they offer to customers, and those computer programs don’t work well together, and now they will, not because they’re being put on a blockchain but just because they will work together: BNY Mellon, which keeps investment firms’ books, plans to deliver real-time information on trades, asset prices and cash positions to the 40-50 clients it shares with BlackRock’s Aladdin, a system money managers use to analyze their investment portfolios and manage their risks. The companies said those overlapping clients will be able to access information faster and cut down on phone calls and emails. Custody banks normally deal with investment firms’ compliance and risk staff, who in turn relay information to the fund managers. Seems sensible! The basic idea of, like, investors have a lot of computer systems that keep track of different bits of their business, and if all those computers worked together then the job would be easier, seems hard to argue with. Sometimes “blockchain” is used as a metaphor for that basic idea, but it’s the basic idea that’s really compelling. Elsewhere here’s a story about how Goldman Sachs Group Inc. “plans to release on GitHub, the popular developer-collaboration site, some of the code that its own traders and engineers use to price securities and analyze and manage risk,” and “is offering $100,000 in annual funding for engineers to build new applications using the bank’s code.”
