Remember when people were worried about unicorns? It was a specific worry; the worry was not just that a lot of technology companies seemed to have valuations that were not justified by fundamentals, but particularly that a lot of private technology companies seemed to have valuations that were bound to lead to disappointment when they went public. There was a theory that the public and private markets for tech-company shares had become disconnected, that venture capitalists and (particularly) non-traditional venture investors like mutual funds and (most particularly) SoftBank were now willing to pay higher prices than the public markets were, and that when those private investors eventually tried to sell to the public markets they’d run into trouble. I won’t exactly say that I shared that worry—my basic rule around here is never to worry about market prices—but not because I thought its premises were wrong. Instead I thought that the relationship between private and public markets had changed, not by becoming disconnected , but by becoming the same . “Private markets are the new public markets,” is a thing I say a lot around here. Because hot tech companies can stay private longer and raise much more money privately, and because the investors in those private companies are increasingly the same investors as those in the public markets, and because there are more opportunities for secondary liquidity in the private markets, the distinction between public and private companies has blurred. And if big private tech companies are essentially public companies, then, just like real public companies, their stock price can sometimes go down. The old pattern was that small companies raised small amounts of speculative capital from venture capitalists at speculative valuations, and then the ones that worked out went public at much higher valuations. The new pattern is that large companies raise large amounts of not-particularly-speculative growth capital from mutual funds at mature-company valuations, and then eventually they sort of quietly slip into being public. Going public is not an important rite of passage in their corporate lives; it doesn’t validate their arrival as a big company, and it doesn’t really change their valuation much. If a big tech company is worth $20 billion the day before it goes public, it should be worth $20 billion plus some random stock-price movement the day after. And so if you are a mutual fund investing in huge mature private companies at high valuations, you should not expect venture-type returns (a lot of zeroes, some 10x returns); you should expect mutual-fund-type returns: some stocks going up 10 percent, some stocks going down 10 percent, that sort of thing. But, nah, never mind. Things are pretty good in the Enchanted Forest right now, or rather, right now the path out of the Enchanted Forest is paved with gold: Pinterest Inc. has sped up the timing of its initial public offering as the image-search company looks to tap into a red-hot market for new issues, according to people familiar with the matter. … The backdrop for public offerings could hardly be better right now, with major stock indexes trading near record highs after a late-2018 market swoon. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite is up about 18% so far this year. Many highly valued startups had been reluctant to tap the public markets, but that has changed as investors bid up the shares of one newly public company after another. Lyft Inc., the leader of this unicorn stampede, raised money privately at a $15.1 billion valuation last year; it is going public with a $23 billion target valuation and is oversubscribed at that price. Uber Technologies Inc. last raised money privately at a $72 billion valuation and could supposedly go public at about $120 billion. At least for now, we seem to be back in a world where public markets pay a lot more—for more mature companies with better governance, disclosure, liquidity and access to capital—than private markets do. It’s all pretty normal. And people still worry about unicorns, but for the normal reasons: Executives of companies in the IPO pipeline and their underwriters are mindful that the good times will end sooner or later and are eager to have their shares start trading before that happens. By moving forward with an IPO in mid-April, Pinterest will likely beat Uber, which is expected to stage one of the largest IPOs on record as soon as late April. See, if you are worried about the IPO window shutting, it’s because an IPO is a big rite of passage in the life of a private company (even Uber), and it’s important to make sure that it goes right.

After Bill Ackman’s Pershing Square Capital Management had a run of pretty bad investing returns and investor redemptions, Ackman decided that he would “curtail all of his own marketing and public relations meetings” and instead spend his time “in the office, concentrating on financial analysis.” I was, I am sorry to say, a bit skeptical about that move at the time: I have in the past expressed admiration for Ackman's ability to retain assets while losing money. "The measure of success as a hedge fund manager," I said, "is, roughly speaking: Can you keep managing a lucrative hedge fund?" Being good at that is a skill, a skill related to making profitable investments, but certainly not identical to it. There is an argument that if you have a series of horrendous losing years, but still have a huge public profile and a lot of money under management, then what you have discovered is that you are (1) really good at marketing and being the public face of a hedge fund but (2) indifferent at actually making the investment decisions. How’s it going? From today’s Wall Street Journal: About a year after the shareholder activist stopped raising money for his private hedge fund in the wake of a pair of disastrous bets, Mr. Ackman has told his investors he is avoiding hard-to-understand companies, staying out of the media spotlight and returning to the basics of investment analysis that first catapulted him to success. … Mr. Ackman says he is embracing a more Zen-like approach that allows for more days spent in his Manhattan office and less time traveling the world to hunt for new funds and hold investors’ hands. … So far, the approach seems to be working, with the public fund up 31.9% this year. Fine fine fine, he was right and I was wrong. Apparently he is good at making investment decisions, as long as he’s not too distracted by being a famous hedge fund manager. There is a notorious style-drift phenomenon among hedge fund managers, where someone makes a lot of money in one weird investing niche, concludes from this success that he is a universal genius, scales up his fund and invests in entirely different areas, starts making macroeconomic calls and political pronouncements, and never repeats his earlier success because, it turns out, he was actually good at the one thing and not a universal genius at all. But this seems like a slightly different phenomenon. If you want to be a billionaire hedge fund manager, early in your career the best thing you can do to maximize your chances is probably to make a lot of correct investing decisions. At some point, though, that might change, and the marginal expected value to you of making one more good investment decision is lower than the expected value to you of, like, being on television a lot, or hanging out with deep-pocketed investors, or setting up a permanent-capital vehicle to ensure that you’ll still have a fund even if investors turn on you. I suppose the dynamics can shift back again though: Once you have the permanent capital vehicle, and are famous, the investing decisions become relatively more valuable again. Speaking of that permanent capital vehicle—Pershing Square Holdings Ltd., the publicly traded $3.6 billion entity that provides much of Ackman’s outside capital these days—here’s something odd: In an indication of lingering investor jitters, the shares are trading at a sizable discount to their net asset value, which most recently stood at $22.81. The shares closed Wednesday at $16.54. And: [Ackman] joked that he prescribed changes for his own firm as he does at companies he invests in: “I went activist on Pershing Square.” Well, sort of. That’s new-style activism, the kind where you show up at a company and give it pushy, detailed, somewhat condescending operational advice on how to run its business. “The CEO is spending too much time on planes and television and not enough time at the office doing the hard work,” Ackman told a company (his own) about its boss (himself). But there is an older school of activism that focuses on financial engineering. “This company is trading below the value of its parts, and you need to do a trade to unlock that value,” would be the more traditional thing for an activist to tell a company like this. It’s not so clear what that trade is, though. A below-NAV stock buyback? (In fact Ackman has done some buybacks of the public vehicle.) A leveraged recap? A spin-off? A merger? It does seem like there might be an opportunity here for a really focused activist investor.

I dunno, here’s a trade: I buy a lot of short-dated put options that will pay off if a company’s stock goes down. I publish an article on a financial website saying that the company is a fraud and is going to go bankrupt. The stock plunges as people read my article and worry that it might be right, and the drop is “compounded by high-frequency trading algorithms activated by price swings and negative keywords.” I sell my put options for a quick profit. The stock never recovers from the dark cloud that I put it under, and it still trades at depressed levels months later. Oh by the way my article was completely made up and I published it under a silly Latin pseudonym. What do you think? This clearly happens , which I find frustrating, because it looks so dumb when I type it out like that. As a fan of efficient markets, I am just annoyed to think that people and algorithms are like “well, this pseudonymous person on Seeking Alpha said this company is a fraud, so it must be true.” I want the market to be a bit more self-correcting than that, to give weight to claims based on their factual basis and the credibility of their proponents, not just to say “HEADLINE BAD SELL STOCK.” But I suppose the market is not that robust, and if you decide to take advantage of that there is money to be made. Here is an article about “a new, ugly phase in a war between companies and activist short sellers, with businesses fighting back against social-media fueled attacks and investors accusing executives of trying to muzzle critics.” “The game was rigged,” says the chief executive officer of a $200 million public company about a negative blog post published under the pseudonym “Rota Fortunae” (“wheel of fortune”) that sent the stock down by 40 percent. (The company has “issued a public rebuttal,” which prompted R.F. to make “limited factual corrections.”) Look, obviously you should not lie about companies for profit, and if you do the Securities and Exchange Commission should go after you, and occasionally they do. But I am not convinced that this is a particularly big problem or that the SEC is devoting insufficient resources to it. I hypothesize that: In the history of capital markets, there are many more CEOs who have said positive things about their companies that turned out to be false than there are short sellers who have said negative things about companies that turned out to be false. Those CEOs have cost investors orders of magnitude more money than those short sellers.[1] I don’t particularly have any statistical evidence for this, though it seems likely to me; it takes a lot of penny-stock short-and-distorts to add up to one Enron. Even if it’s true it doesn’t tell you how to evaluate any individual case. And there is a statistical problem, which is that there are just a lot more noisy CEOs than there are noisy short sellers, which means that my hypothesis could be true even if most CEOs are scrupulously honest and every short seller is always lying. Still it leaves me a bit skeptical of CEOs who complain that the market is rigged in favor of the short sellers. The CEOs can put out press releases too, and the market can evaluate the two sides, and you’d hope that it would take a company’s official statements at least as seriously as an anonymous blog post.

s.h: Don’t forget to tip your loan shark
s.t: A good general rule about debt is that normal individuals tend to think of their debts as moral obligations, while big companies and institutions don’t.[2] This is partly a matter of legal and market dynamics—companies just have more ability to call up their lenders and renegotiate their debts, and can come out of bankruptcy stronger than they go in; individuals often have no human being they can call at their lender to even try to renegotiate, and really don’t want to go bankrupt—and also partly a matter of, like, a human is a moral agent and a company isn’t quite. Part of it is also that the companies are right and the individuals are wrong, and that a debt is a specific set of legal entitlements rather than an overriding obligation to repay the money in any possible state of the world. But the point here is that this is a mostly true descriptive fact about the world; whatever you think about the morality of debt, most people most of the time try to repay their debts even if they have legal arguments to avoid them. We talk a lot around here about sophisticated hedge funds who comb through bond indentures and credit-default-swap documents to find counterintuitive loopholes, and to be fair there are a few individuals like that, but for the most part if you lend a lot of regular middle-class people money they will mostly try to pay you back. There is a trade here. Here’s a New York Post story about “Earnin, an app that fronts workers part of their paychecks early”: Once Earnin users have entered their personal details, bank account number and login, they can take out cash advances in increments as large as $100. When users request money, they can tip any amount up to $14, which the company uses to pay for the service. While skipping the tip altogether is an option, the app suggested tipping $9 or more for a one-week, $100 loan, in order to “pay it forward to someone else,” according to screenshots of the app provided to The Post by Smith. You don’t have to pay interest, but you should . (Also it is not “interest” but a “tip,” which is genius: a $9 interest payment on a $100 one-week loan “would amount to a 469 percent APR,” an obviously usurious annual percentage rate, but a $9 tip on a $100 transaction is only 9 percent, which feels positively stingy.) There are apparently some enforcement mechanisms—the article suggests that if you don’t “tip” you’ll have a low borrowing limit and reduced convenience—but surely the main way that Earnin gets people to pay is by asking them to. If you’re supposed to pay for a service, mostly, you do. You don’t even have to pay back the loan: “Even the concept of a pay cycle is only a few centuries old,” [Earnin CEO Ram] Palaniappan told The Post. “There’s a reference in the Bible that employees would be paid before sunset.” He went on to say that Earnin’s cash advances aren’t loans at all, but rather “nonrecourse transactions” that don’t charge interest or give Earnin the right to collect. Again there is an enforcement mechanism—“Earnin requires that users give the company the right to automatically debit their account,” and “reserves the right to sue users for violating its terms of service”—but I suppose you could evade it (just don’t keep any money in that account). The idea appears to be not that the enforcement mechanism is ironclad, but that it is mostly unnecessary; people will just pay back the loans even if you tell them that they’re not loans and don’t need to be paid back. There are, of course, objections: “Critics say Earnin’s marketing and business models resemble those of Payday 2.0, and that its tactics may be intended to skirt regulations on payday lending.” But I have to say that this is a real disruptive financial innovation. Bloomberg News recently ran a series of articles about short-term high-interest lenders who had pioneered a new way to enhance their legal rights to collect on loans, but here is a short-term high-interest lender who just doesn’t care about its legal rights to collect on the loan, which is way stranger. If you worked at a bank, and you came up with an idea to give people high-interest cash advances, and your legal team came back to you and said “how can we make sure that these loans are enforceable and that we can collect our principal and interest,” and you said “we won’t, we’re just going to skip all of that, there’ll be no binding contract and people who don’t want to pay won’t have to,” you would definitely not get approval to do that . But Earnin recently “raised $125 million from Silicon Valley venture capitalists,” and for all I know the model might even work. Traditional finance operates by being very very sure of what your legal rights are, which is why we are always talking around here about hedge funds battling over CDS documents. But the tech industry has made a lot of billionaires by understanding people’s actual behavior , and if you notice that people pay back their loans even if they don’t have to then maybe there is money to be made there.

Uh: JPMorgan Chase has also started experimenting with a new behavioral science-based assessment technology called pymetrics in its application process. pymetrics is a series of engaging online games, based on decades of scientific research, that have shown to be very accurate in measuring a wide range of relevant social, cognitive and behavioral features – things like attention, memory and altruism. “The concept behind pymetrics,” says CEO and co-founder Frida Polli, “is that there is no right or wrong answer, no ‘smart’ vs ‘not smart’. We aim to provide a platform that helps every person find their place in the world of work.” Once an individual candidate completes the assessment, pymetrics software then compares the student’s results to the profile of successful employees at our firm. Do they … want … altruism? That paragraph is from a blog post by Matt Mitro, JPMorgan Chase & Co.’s head of campus recruiting, about how the bank is changing its application process for college students. I suppose if you take the test and get a zero in altruism they make you a derivatives trader, while if you get a somewhat higher score then you are a good team player who puts clients’ interests first and they make you an investment banker. But is there some level of altruism that is too high? At some point, does the software gently take you aside and say “look, we want you to find your place in the world of work, and that place is not at an investment bank”? I mean! To be fair! I used to be an investment banker, and I sometimes interviewed college students for investment banking jobs, and I am not going to sit here and tell you that I never rejected anyone for being too altruistic. I wouldn’t have said that, exactly, on the evaluation forms; I think the normal expressions would be more like “not commercial” or “no real commitment to investment banking.” But if you ask a candidate “if you had a million dollars to invest right now, what sector would you choose and why,” and she replies “oh I would give it all to the homeless”: That’s a pass! Nice sentiment, high score in altruism, not what we were looking for. Here is more from Business Insider about the changes to JPMorgan’s on-campus recruiting process, which will now be less on-campus: JPMorgan Chase's investment bank, one of the largest in the world, is scrapping the annual college-recruiting visits that have launched generations of investment bankers and traders. Instead, the bank will ask its next generation of workers to apply by submitting video interviews and taking online behavioral-science tests. The company began notifying college career counselors today about the change in policy, which applies to prospective interns and has been almost a year in the making, according to a memo seen by Business Insider. The change is intended to widen the funnel for intern candidates in a way that doesn't disadvantage minorities or students from schools the bank wouldn't have visited in the past. "This is really all about leveling the playing field," Katie Pankhurst, the head of campus recruiting North America for the bank, said. The traditional interviewing method is that a bank takes a bunch of current bankers who went to Penn, it sends them back to Penn to interview current students for internships, and the bankers choose which current students to hire based on criteria like “she seemed comfortable walking through a discounted cash flow model in the interview” or “he’s in my old fraternity” or “we talked about lacrosse for 30 minutes.” It can be a little unscientific, and there is a lot of crude pattern-matching: The banks tend to focus their recruiting at a small number of traditional feeder schools, and to choose applicants in part based on criteria—referred to by terms like “cultural fit” and “the airport test”—that come down to “is this person like me?” The promise of video interviews, online behavioral games, etc., is that they will replace the crude pattern-matching with somewhat less crude pattern-matching: not “does this applicant resemble the person interviewing her in immediately apparent ways,” but instead “does this applicant resemble other successful JPMorgan bankers in somewhat subtler and more consistently applied ways?” One obvious concern is that, if your existing practices of hiring people and deciding who’s successful are biased, then a more objective approach can actually perpetuate those biases: When Amazon.com Inc. built a machine-learning tool to automate its hiring process, it turned out to favor men over women, probably not because robots naturally favor men but because Amazon was already favoring men. This is not really an argument against the technology—it could well be better , and less biased, than the humans it’s replacing—but it is sort of awkward. If humans are doing the evaluations of cultural fit, they can always come up with a nice-sounding explanation for their choices, and it’s hard to prove bad intentions. If an algorithm does it, it’s a little more cut and dried. I rejected candidates for not being commercial enough; the algorithm might reject them for scoring too high on the altruism factor. Same idea, but one sounds bad! The other problem is that if you send humans to campus to recruit, they will tend to favor the people who interact with them most comfortably, but if you send robots to campus to recruit they might favor the people who interact with them most comfortably. From Mitro’s blog post: In recent years, we began integrating pre-recorded video interviews into our application process so students had an opportunity to put their best foot forward, telling the story beyond their resume. And to be sure students really benefit, we offer them practice questions in advance to get comfortable with the technology and the chance to re-take if something goes awry. Our questions are read on video by real recruiters and do not typically have one correct way to answer. I dunno, still sounds weird. I do not think I’d want to be stuck in an airport with a pre-recorded video, and I’d worry that that would be obvious in my interview.

Occasionally, for fun, I do puzzle hunts, scavenger hunts in which teams of players run around the city solving difficult puzzles to figure out where to go next. (It is a little hard to capture what this looks like, but here is an article about one hunt, and a podcast about another.) These hunts, at least in New York and London, tend to be full of financial-industry types: There are usually a lot of Goldman Sachs teams, high-frequency traders, some hedge funds. There is an obvious connection to the day job: Large sections of the financial industry are about synthesizing information, seeing unexpected patterns in data, drawing connections, and solving puzzles faster than everyone else late at night in an intensely competitive environment. It is no surprise that people who enjoy building electronic trading algorithms, or designing derivatives, or combing through bond indentures and credit-default-swap documents to find surprising ways to make money, might also enjoy wandering around doing cryptography on their Saturday nights. Obviously the financial industry has social value—financing new ideas, moving resources to where they’re needed, etc.—and even the tricky puzzle-solving bits of the financial industry tend to have the intangible but important benefit of making markets more efficient. Still it is sometimes tempting to imagine replacing them with high-stakes puzzle hunts. Sometimes we talk around here about situations where one hedge fund has read a document more cleverly than another hedge fund in a way that allows the first hedge fund to extract a bunch of money from the second hedge fund, and, you know, fine, but I think they might all have more fun if they did puzzle hunts instead. In addition to publishing the credit derivatives definitions, the International Swaps and Derivatives Association could publish puzzles, and each hedge fund could put up $100 million to enter the ISDA puzzle hunt, and whichever fund won would keep the money. Hedge funds would still compete against each other in a test of cleverness and ingenuity and hard work and quickness, but the test would take place in an entirely closed universe; no one else would notice, except for a few pedestrians who would wonder what all these people in fleece vests were doing wandering around examining code sheets. I’m kidding, of course; there is plenty of social value in reading documents super carefully in order to make sure that their terms are rigorously enforced, I’m sure, probably. But … sometimes, maybe, a little? Here is an article about how Aurelius Capital Management, the hedge fund that Mark Brodsky started after leaving Paul Singer’s Elliott Management Corp., is facing off against Elliott in the Windstream Holdings Inc. bankruptcy. Aurelius put Windstream into bankruptcy, by scouring its bond documents to find an arguable default and then suing to make that default come true. That’s a move that you might remember from the time Aurelius and Elliott teamed up to do something similar to the nation of Argentina. But now: Aurelius is believed by market participants to have bought derivatives insuring against a Windstream default, with Elliott taking the other side of that trade. That would hand Aurelius a payout on the contracts, known as credit-default swaps, while Elliott could be faced with losses. Moreover, as Windstream begins to navigate bankruptcy proceedings, Aurelius and Elliott have what would appear to be very different agendas. Aurelius, which started the year with $2.4 billion in assets, likely remains focused until the auction on preserving its CDS return. Elliott, which manages about $34 billion, holds a position in Windstream’s secured debt that gives it leverage in bankruptcy negotiations. “Given the sophistication of the players -- Aurelius and Elliott -- I think the interesting stuff starts now,” said Erik Gordon, a professor at the University of Michigan’s Ross Business School. “Nobody will do a more sophisticated analysis than these two and nobody will be more willing to fight than these two.” If you think about this as a pure cleverness competition between two sophisticated hedge funds that have gotten rich off of creative puzzle-solving, or as an Oedipal struggle between Brodsky and Singer, then, yes, there is lots of interesting stuff here. But in the actual world, the cleverness competition—which at its core involves a zero-sum bet between Elliott, which sold CDS, and Aurelius, which bought it—happens to have bankrupted a real company. Isn’t it a little tempting to ask them to take their bets offline? Like what if we created an entirely fictitious company, and Elliott and Aurelius negotiated its governing documents and bond indentures and tried to build little booby traps into the documents while spotting the other side’s booby traps, and then when the documents were done they could sue each other in Pretend Puzzle Court and some mutually agreeable judge would decide whose booby traps worked? And they could just make a big real zero-sum bet on the outcome, and whichever hedge fund was cleverer at this game would win real money, and no actual companies would need to worry about it? Again, I do not want to make too strong a claim here; the document-enforcement stuff that distressed-debt hedge funds do is generally very hard to separate from real-world, often efficiency-enhancing, effects. (And often the competition works out well for real companies.) But just, like, try it out once, maybe? If they need someone to be the dungeon master for a real-money distressed-debt role-playing game, I would be up for it.

If you think that a company is bad and you want to bet that its stock will go down, the normal way to do that is to sell the stock short: You borrow the stock, sell your borrowed shares, wait until (you hope) it goes down, and then buy it back at a lower price. To do this, you need to borrow the stock from someone who owns it. Intuitively, you might think that this would be an awkward conversation: “Hey, you know that stock you really like, the one that you own a lot of and that you’re counting on to fund your retirement? I think it is bad and would like to bet it will go to zero. Would you lend me some stock so I can do that?” In practice, it is all pretty anonymous and mediated by institutions: You borrow the stock from a broker, and your broker gets it from an impersonal stock-borrow market, and much of the supply of stock loan comes from big institutional money managers, often passive index funds and exchange-traded funds. And you pay some money—usually a little bit of money, but a lot of money in the case of stocks that everyone wants to short and no one wants to lend—to get the lenders to give you their stock. Still, there are occasional reminders of that intuitive awkwardness. People entrust their savings to an index fund, and then they find out that the index fund is lending out the stocks it owns to help people betting against those stocks, and they get a bit scandalized. Chief executive officers of the companies being shorted get particularly scandalized. Elon Musk, of course, has a thing about it. (“There is no rational basis for a long holder to lend their stock to shorts, as it dilutes the shareholder base & gives the short a strong incentive to attack the company by whatever means possible, including regulators,” etc.) People who are very enthusiastic about a stock are sometimes offended to think that other people who own the stock might be conspiring with short sellers to drive down the stock price. I think that this view is mostly misguided, and that if you are bullish on a stock you should be happy to lend it to short sellers: You are right (right?), they are wrong, and they are paying you to help them lose money. In the long run the stock price will reflect the fundamentals, not the sentiments or desires of short sellers, and if you believe in the fundamentals and people want to give you money to bet the other way, you should take their money. But some long investors—and many CEOs—seem not to think this way; they think that short sellers are both a moral affront and a real danger to the long-term value of the company, and so they can get touchy about the stock-lending business. If you are a real Bitcoin enthusiast, what do you think about this? BlockFi, a fintech startup backed by billionaire Mike Novogratz’s Galaxy Capital, began providing interest-bearing accounts this month that offer up to 6.2 percent in annualized returns paid in Bitcoin or Ether. Since a March 5 launch, they’ve attracted at least 10,000 customers, 90 percent of whom are retail investors. The company has taken in over $35 million in deposits, with large accounts pulling the average balance up to about $40,000. BlockFi’s interest rate is set on a month-to-month basis and is based on a combination of rates BlockFi sees in the institutional cryptocurrency borrowing market, as well as a budget it set for customer acquisitions, Zac Prince, chief executive of New York-based BlockFi, said in an interview. “We expect the interest rate in the account to be higher in times when prices are falling, and lower when prices are rising because demand to borrow Bitcoin is partially driven by market sentiment,” said Prince. “We are bullish on the cryptocurrency market and on Bitcoin long term,” he said, which would ultimately result in lower interest rates. “The company lends the funds to crypto investors for arbitrage, short-selling or market-making trades at rates ranging as high as 12 percent,” takes a cut, and passes the rest to its customers (investors? depositors?). Just as with stocks, there are reasons other than a fundamental short thesis (cross-exchange arbitrage, etc.) that might make you want to borrow a Bitcoin, but overall it is probably the case that providing a big pool of Bitcoins to borrow has the effect of making it easier for people to bet against Bitcoin. If you think that Bitcoin is the future of money and that its fair value is enormous, then you presumably think those people are chumps and you should be happy to take their money. If your model of Bitcoin is that it is a pure reflection of current trader sentiment, and you are long, then you might think short sellers are your mortal enemy and that getting paid 6.2 percent to help them out isn’t worth it.

Lyft Inc. is a ride-sharing company that loses a lot of money every year and is in second place in an apparently winner-take-all industry. It is going public as part of a huge wave of expected initial public offerings by big-name tech companies, including, presumably, its much bigger competitor Uber Technologies Inc. Its founders “will own just under 5 percent of the company’s stock but control 49 percent of the company’s votes” after the IPO, a dual-class structure that big institutional investors vocally oppose and that will cause Lyft to be excluded from some indexes. How do you think its IPO is going? “Amazing, couldn’t be better,” is the obvious answer, not only because I wouldn’t have bothered with that whole setup if the answer was “bad,” but also because Lyft wouldn’t have bothered with that whole setup if the answer was going to be “bad.” Lyft is going public with huge losses and dual-class shares because now is an amazing time to bring a tech company public with huge losses and dual-class shares; it’s doing it as part of a unicorn stampede because everyone else recognizes that too. (It’s doing it before most of those other unicorns, and especially Uber, because it is smart and eventually the window will close.) Everything in that previous paragraph is not just a random independent fact about Lyft; it’s a sign of the market’s high level of receptivity to big tech IPOs. So of course the market is going to be receptive to this one. Anyway yeah the answer is “amazing, couldn’t be better”: The San Francisco-based company has only been on the road marketing its initial public offering for two days, but investors have already been informed that the listing is oversubscribed at the current price range, said people familiar with the matter, who asked not to be identified because the details are private. Based on early commitments, Lyft executives and bankers see demand far exceeding the number of available shares, making it likely that the company will surpass the $23 billion valuation it’s seeking, said the people. Lyft is expected to price its shares on March 28 and begin trading on the Nasdaq the next day. If excessive demand continues, the company could decide to sell more shares or price them above the original range of $62 to $68 a share. Once Lyft is public, there will be a stock price, and there will be news about Lyft, and the news will be good or bad, and if it is good the stock will go up and if it is bad the stock will go down. Expectations will be built into the stock price, and the price will move as reality meets or misses or exceeds those expectations. But before it is public there is not quite a stock price, and expectations aren’t quite built into it. So when the stock price goes up—which is a reasonable way to read “the IPO is oversubscribed at the current price range”—that is a sign not so much that Lyft is exceeding the market’s expectations as that it is still figuring out what they are.

In my experience, when I read a news story about algorithmic traders—particularly of the “electronic market maker”/“high-frequency trader” variety—it will usually say that they use complex algorithms, but when I talk to algorithmic traders, they will usually say that their algorithms are comically simple. This might be a matter of false modesty, or caution about revealing proprietary secrets, or just that people who do it all day have a different standard of complexity from the people who write about it. But there’s also a basic nub of truth to it. There are ways to think about (or program a computer to think about) buying and selling securities that are as complicated as the world, that take into account macroeconomic variables and geopolitical tensions and bottom-up fundamental analysis and social-media sentiment data and sunspots. But there are also ways to think about buying and selling securities that are as simple as the simplest computer game, algorithms that are like “bid a bit lower than the market price, offer at a bit higher, and if someone buys from you raise your price a bit to reflect demand.” If your basic business is market-making , buying and selling to customers and trying to make money by charging a spread rather than by predicting long-term market movements, then much of the time you can ignore the fundamental analysis and macroeconomics and sunspots. Your goal is not to predict the long-term value of the securities that you are buying and selling, but just to buy and sell roughly equal quantities of them so that your book is flat, your risk is low, and you get paid a spread. Anyway: Headlands Tech Global Markets LLC, a firm founded by former senior executives at Citadel LLC, is using complex mathematical formulas and powerful computers to buy and sell state and local government securities, seizing on the sometimes divergent prices in a market where the vast majority of bonds only rarely change hands. Headlands’ five-man band of algorithm-driven traders have become a major, if little known, force in the industry, bidding each day on about 13,000 municipal securities that are put up for sale on electronic trading platforms. That’s placed it among a group of companies that are bringing technology that has swept through other corners of Wall Street to state and local-government debt trading, challenging a long-held view that a market that finances everything from factories to state governments requires detailed research to gauge prices. “This idea that every bond is a unique snowflake and a story -- they say ‘balderdash’," Paul Daley, a managing director at BondWave LLC, a financial technology company, said of Headlands’ approach. “All these bonds are mathematical equations, and if we can model it, we can price it." There is obviously an approach to municipal bond trading that involves, like, reading the prospectus for a local water-authority bond, and poring over the financial statements, and reviewing the minutes of the water authority’s public meetings, and traveling to the town to taste the water, but it is not the only approach. Another approach would be like “meh, all munis are basically the same, if you know the price of one bond you can infer the rough prices of other bonds with simple adjustments for credit ratings and geography, and then if the bid-ask spread is wide enough and you get to buy at the bid and sell at the ask you will be fine.” This approach is not perfect, and every so often you will own some water-authority bonds that idiosyncratically default, and you’ll look a bit dumb because you didn’t read the prospectus or taste the water, but if you are doing your job right they will be a tiny part of your portfolio and you won’t hang on to them for long so the risk is manageable. Particularly if you are trading with retail investors: “We felt like given our experience providing liquidity to retail-sized orders in other asset classes, even though munis were very different, that we could potentially add value as a liquidity provider," Mannion said in a phone interview. He declined to disclose Headlands profitability. People who work at electronic market-making firms tend to spend almost no time thinking about fundamental financial analysis, and a lot of time thinking about adverse selection: If you are a high-frequency trader buying stock for an instant, your big risk is not that the stock will turn out to be the next Enron. Your big risk is that the stock you buy is part of a large sell order from Fidelity, and there is more coming, and the price will continue to decline for the next few seconds and you will lose money on your trade. If you leave that business for retail muni market-making, there are some downsides—the bonds trade less often, there are more of them, their prices and order books are less informative, etc.—but it does seem like there aren’t many businesses with less risk of adverse selection than selling municipal bonds to retail accounts. If you’re going to trade thousands of bonds without knowing anything about them, it’s best if the bonds are so fragmented that they mostly trade in retail size, and if no one else who trades them knows anything either. Elsewhere, my Bloomberg Opinion colleague Brian Chappatta writes about Headlands, and about the growing influence of quants in the bond markets.

s.h: Should index funds be illegal but over the blockchain?
s.t: If you put a week’s worth of Money Stuff columns in a blender, you might get something like this: The US financial regulator is set to examine whether investors’ choice of asset management companies will be damaged by competitive pressures that threaten to destroy smaller players. … “I am concerned about what it will mean for investors, particularly main street investors, if the variety and choice offered by small and midsized asset managers becomes lost in a wave of consolidation and fee compression,” said Dalia Blass, director of the division of investment management at the SEC. … Many distributors have culled funds from their platforms as investors shifted to low-cost index trackers. … Ms Blass said the SEC would look at whether technologies such as blockchain could improve access to fund distribution for small and midsized managers. First of all, I love that the Securities and Exchange Commission’s goal here is to protect expensive mutual funds from competition. I am not being purely sarcastic here; that does seem, somehow, like part of the SEC’s historic mission. You could imagine an investment regulator whose main goal was to steer retail investors to reasonably safe, low-cost, broadly diversified investment portfolios, to tell uninformed investors the right answer rather than to overwhelm them with “variety and choice.” (I am not at all sure that would be a good thing—there is a lot to dislike about a government regulator deciding what investors should invest in—but you could certainly imagine it, and a lot of people do.) That would be a very different regulator from the SEC. Second, I love that the way to protect the small mutual funds would somehow be blockchain: Small mutual fund manager: Please buy my fund, it underperforms the S&P 500 but on the other hand it pays me 1 percent a year. Investor: Hmm I’d rather buy an S&P 500 index fund that charges 0.015 percent a year. SMFM: … Investor: … SMFM: Blockchain? Investor: Oh, why didn’t you say so, here’s some money. Blockchains: Is there anything they can’t do? Maybe if I put this newsletter on the blockchain it will write itself.

I’m a little embarrassed that I wrote so much, not so long ago, about Bitcoin futures. (Not embarrassed enough to stop me from doing it again!) In my defense, the only cost of me writing about Bitcoin futures was my time, and yours I guess, sorry. Cboe Global Markets Inc., meanwhile, actually listed the Bitcoin futures, and presumably had a lot of highly paid people working hard on it, and now, never mind: Cboe Global Markets Inc., the first mainstream exchange to let people buy and sell Bitcoin futures, said in a web posting that it’s reviewing its approach to cryptocurrency derivatives and doesn’t currently plan to list more contracts. The Wall Street Journal calls this “the latest sign that mainstream financial firms are losing their enthusiasm for cryptocurrencies,” though to be fair CME Group Inc. still lists Bitcoin futures and has more volume than the Cboe. The problem is that there are basically two kinds of reason to want to buy Bitcoin: You have some fundamental use for, or belief in, Bitcoin: You think it has some properties that make it a better store of value than other currencies, or a better transaction mechanism; you want to store or transfer value outside the control of national authorities, or buy drugs, or whatever. You see a future of money that is in some deep way different from the current financial system, and owning Bitcoin is a way to take a position on that future. The price of Bitcoin is a number that was once low and is now high, and your job as an investor is to find numbers that go up, so you better buy some Bitcoins. There was never all that much reason to believe that many large institutional investors fell into category 1; they are the current financial system. But if you do have some fundamental use for, or belief in, Bitcoin, buying Bitcoin futures is not a great to express it: If you think that Bitcoin is a disruptive innovation that will fundamentally upend the financial system, or if you just want to buy drugs with Bitcoins, buying Bitcoin futures on the Cboe seems misguided. The mainstream exchanges, again, are part of the financial system that is going to be upended, and you can’t use the futures to buy drugs. Category 2 was a perfectly good reason for institutions to buy Bitcoin futures in 2017: They could get in on the buzz of Bitcoin, and bet on its continued rise, without actually doing any of the complicated legal and technological work to buy and hold and store and account for actual Bitcoins. They could just get raw exposure to the number , the price of Bitcoin, without having to touch any of the weird squishy bits of an actual Bitcoin. The problem is that, pretty much the second Bitcoin futures were introduced, this stopped being true : The price of Bitcoin peaked at over $18,000 in December 2017, shortly after Cboe’s futures were introduced; it’s down almost 80 percent since then. So never mind! If the point of Bitcoin futures was to allow traditional investors to get economic exposure to the price of Bitcoin without having to deal with actual Bitcoins, it worked great, but that price exposure was terrible and the people who got it now regret it.

s.h: Don’t forget to re-sign your rock band
s.t: We talked last week about the time that a private equity firm called Vintage Capital Management LLC agreed to buy Rent-A-Center Inc., and then Rent-A-Center got cold feet, and then Vintage forgot to send a one-sentence letter extending the deadline to close the deal and Rent-A-Center was able to get out of it. It was pretty weird! Vintage was working so diligently on all of the complicated issues involved in getting the deal closed that it just forgot that random little ministerial task, and it was working so closely with Rent-A-Center to resolve the other issues that it figured Rent-A-Center wouldn’t be a big stickler over that one-sentence letter. But, nope, ha, Rent-A-Center took the opportunity to get out of the deal, and its stock is way up since then. Reader Brad Goldman emailed to point out a weirdly similar anecdote in “Runnin’ With the Devil,” Noel Monk’s memoir of managing Van Halen. As a Forbes article describes it: As the new manager, Monk's first task was the impossible — find a way to get the band out of the"hellaciously bad" and ironclad contract they had signed as unknowns. "They were the best stage band I'd ever seen," says Monk, speaking by phone from his Colorado home, "and they were getting absolutely screwed. Warner Bros. had the option to renew the same terms every 2 years for life. I told them we have to get out of this." Monk's solution? "I flooded the record company with so many paper requests, for royalties and accounting, that they were sick of me and my people. They were snowed with all the things I would throw at them and somehow they did what I was hoping – they missed the option date to renew the contract." In the book, Monk tells of meeting with WB Chairman Mo Ostin and dropping the news that the company's hottest young act was now a free agent. Renegotiating the contract "made the band members instant multimillionaires." In the Rent-A-Center deal, there was actually a lot of work to do, and it distracted Vintage from the extension deadline. In the Van Halen deal, there wasn’t particularly, so Monk cleverly created a lot of work to distract them, and it (apparently) worked. One lesson here is, keep a checklist of your deadlines. Another lesson might be, just because you have a deal with someone and you are working hard together to achieve some goal, don’t just blindly assume that you are partners and your interests are aligned: Think about what the other person’s interests actually are, and keep in mind what your contract actually requires. A third lesson might be, it is common in finance and economics to assume optimal exercise of options: If someone has the right to do something, and it is in her clear economic interest to do it, that is assumed to be equivalent to “she will do it.” That is a good enough assumption for most cases, but in the real world, sometimes people just forget.

There is a kind of financial capitalism that is pure and heartless and single-mindedly focused on maximizing shareholder value, but you won’t find it at big banks. Partly this is because of the old half-joke that I frequently make around here, which is that big banks are socialist collectives that are run for the benefit of their employees: Compared to normal companies, big banks have a lot of employees who get high and variable pay (and so are basically residual claimants on the earnings of the bank), their senior executives tend to identify more closely with those employees than with the shareholders, and the business of the bank is so hard to understand that shareholders don’t have a lot of control over those senior executives. But it’s not just the employees. Compared to normal companies, banks have more leverage, so they have to think more carefully about the interests of their creditors than normal companies do. They are more (and more subjectively) regulated, so they have to think more carefully about the demands of their regulators. The proper model for thinking about big universal banks might be that they are both public-private partnerships (with fiduciary-like duties to the central bank and the government) and worker-owned collectives (with fiduciary-like duties, or affinities anyway, to their employees), which can make it much more complicated to figure out, in any particular scenario, whose interests they are looking out for. It is sort of amazing to read down the list of people who don’t want Deutsche Bank AG and Commerzbank AG to merge. Employees, obviously: The trade union for bank employees opposes a merger “in view of the risk to tens of thousands of jobs,” Jan Duscheck, who sits on Deutsche Bank’s supervisory board as labor representative, said in an emailed statement. As many as 30,000 positions could be at risk in a merger, according to people familiar with the matter. Senior executives also transparently hate the idea. My Bloomberg Opinion colleague Elisa Martinuzzi writes: Deutsche Bank Chief Executive Officer Christian Sewing had pleaded for more time when speculation about a deal first emerged. He was hoping to complete more of his own revamp, including integrating the two consumer brands the firm already owns, before adding yet more risk and complexity. Regulators don’t love solving the problems of too-big-to-fail banks by making them bigger and more systemic; as my Bloomberg Opinion colleague John Authers points out, Deutsche Bank is already “not so much TBTF as it is FTBTF (Far Too Big To Fail) or even TBTR (Too Big To Rescue),” and “nobody would have dared suggested in public 10 years ago that Deutsche Bank and Commerzbank should be allowed to merge.” The ECB shares his concern: The eurozone’s top financial supervisor has criticised the idea of creating national or European champions to compete with global rivals, potentially putting the European Central Bank on a collision course with Berlin’s efforts to protect its banking industry via a merger of Germany’s two biggest lenders. Shareholders are pretty unenthusiastic—“Several influential Deutsche Bank investors have said they’re wary of a merger as it will dilute their stakes at a low valuation”—though both stocks were up on the formal announcement that the two banks have started merger talks. Here’s a representative supportive shareholder reaction: One of Deutsche Bank’s largest shareholders who for months lobbied hard against a merger with Commerzbank has acknowledged that despite widespread scepticism, the momentum towards a deal “looks all but impossible to stop”. … “We are still not convinced a merger makes sense but we won’t go in fundamental opposition,” a person close to the top-five investor told the Financial Times. There’s a random assortment of supporters from various constituencies—“The potential deal is supported by Germany’s Social Democrat finance minister, Olaf Scholz; Deutsche’s chairman, Paul Achleitner; Commerzbank chief executive, Martin Zielke; and US private equity group Cerberus, which is a big investor in both lenders”—but it is strange to see a deal plodding forward that executives, employees, investors and regulators are all so sad about. At least if you are trying to maximize shareholder value, you have a goal. At least you’re trying to make someone happy. If you’re trying to optimize for so many constituencies, you may end up with something that none of them want. It seems like a symptom of the banks’ too-big-to-fail/manage/whatever-ness that this deal keeps lurching gloomily forward: These banks are so big and systemic that no one can control them, and even their potential merger seems to be proceeding on its own power over everyone’s objections. In other Deutsche Bank news, here is a story about the bank’s relationship with Donald Trump: Over nearly two decades, Deutsche Bank’s leaders repeatedly saw red flags surrounding Mr. Trump. There was a disastrous bond sale, a promised loan that relied on a banker’s forged signature, wild exaggerations of Mr. Trump’s wealth, even a claim of an act of God. But Deutsche Bank had a ravenous appetite for risk and limited concern about its clients’ reputations. Time after time, with the support of two different chief executives, the bank handed money — a total of well over $2 billion — to a man whom nearly all other banks had deemed untouchable.

“SEC Stunned That Musk Failed to Get Pre-Approval of Tweets,” it says here, but I say to you: No! They! Are! Not! Elon Musk literally said on television that he was not going to have a lawyer pre-approve his tweets! He further clarified that the reason he was not going to do this, even though it was arguably required by the terms of his settlement with the Securities and Exchange Commission, was that “I do not respect the SEC. I do not respect them.” The fact that he then tweeted without getting his tweets pre-approved is the least surprising event in the history of the capital markets, and I guarantee you that the SEC is not surprised. They don’t even really say that they’re stunned. They say that it’s “stunning.” Very different. It’s stunning, sure, but no one, at this point, is stunned. Anyway here is the SEC’s latest filing in its effort to get Musk held in contempt of court for tweeting stuff about Tesla without pre-approval. We talked about that effort here, and about Musk’s response here. Musk’s view is that he only has to run tweets by a lawyer if he thinks they might be material, and so now he tries to only tweet non-material things about Tesla. The SEC disagrees: The Court-ordered pre-approval requirement for Musk’s written communications lies at the heart of the settlement. Musk’s unchecked and misleading tweets about Tesla are what precipitated the SEC’s charges, and the pre-approval requirement was designed to protect against reckless conduct by Musk going forward. It is therefore stunning to learn that, at the time of filing of the instant motion, Musk had not sought pre-approval for a single one of the numerous tweets about Tesla he published in the months since the Court-ordered pre-approval policy went into effect. Many of these tweets were about the topics specifically identified by Tesla in its own policies as potentially material to shareholders. Musk reads this Court’s order as not requiring pre-approval unless Musk himself unilaterally decides his planned tweets are material. His interpretation is inconsistent with the plain terms of this Court’s order and renders its pre-approval requirement meaningless. Ehh. Look, I see Musk’s lawyers’ point: The settlement doesn’t literally require him to pre-clear all of his tweets, but only to pre-clear the tweets that might be material, which gives him some wiggle room. I see the SEC’s point: Musk has uniquely terrible judgment about what he should tweet about his company, which is why we are here in the first place. One path forward would be to change the settlement slightly to make this determination simpler, for instance by requiring Musk to pre-clear all tweets about Tesla, whether or not he thinks they are material. Obviously Musk would object to that. When we last talked about this, I suggested an opposite approach of just letting him tweet whatever he wants and declaring it automatically immaterial. Obviously the SEC would object to that. It feels a little like Musk and the SEC don’t have a settlement at all: They reached an uneasy (and short-lived) truce by signing a piece of paper, but they don’t agree on what the piece of paper means.

Honestly even I am tired of this: Credit-default swaps on German autoparts company Schaeffler AG whipsawed amid investor speculation that its bond financing plans could either trigger payouts or render the contracts worthless. The cost of insuring Schaeffler’s debt surged after Chief Financial Officer Dietmar Heinrich said he may dissolve Schaeffler Finance BV, a unit used to issue outstanding debt, according to two people who attended a company event on March 15 and asked not to be identified. The contracts had plunged earlier last week when the company said it would issue as much as 5 billion euros ($5.7 billion) of bonds out of a different entity, known as Schaeffler AG. Schaeffler has previously issued its bonds out of Schaeffler Finance BV. Credit-default swaps on Schaeffler therefore reference SFBV’s bonds. Schaeffler plans in the future to issue bonds out of Schaeffler AG. That likely means that, over time, the supply of SFBV bonds will dry up, which will leave Schaeffler CDS—that is, SFBV CDS—more or less worthless. If all of SFBV’s bonds go away, the CDS will be “orphaned”: SFBV will have no debt, and so will not be able to default, and the CDS can never be triggered. If only most of the bonds go away, the CDS won’t technically be orphaned, but if there ever is a default (presumably at both SAG and SFBV) there will not be many bonds to deliver into the CDS auction, and so in practice the CDS probably won’t pay out much on a default. But if all of the bonds go away and also SFBV itself goes away , then the situation might improve. If you have CDS on a company, and the company pays off all its bonds, then you have CDS on a company that will never default and you are sad. But if you have CDS on a company, and the company vanishes , then, um, maybe someone will do something to fix your CDS. I am not sure what that something is; it might be deciding that SAG has become a successor to SFBV and moving the CDS over there, or it might be deciding that SFBV’s disappearance has somehow triggered the CDS: Uncertainty about what could happen after that has split the market. Citigroup Inc. analysts recommended buying Schaeffler swaps in a note on March 13, saying that a dissolution of the existing unit could constitute a bankruptcy credit event and prompt compensation to swaps holders. Barclays Plc analysts argued against that outcome in a note on Monday. If SFBV’s bonds go away a little bit, that is bad for CDS holders; if they go away entirely, that is worse; if they super-duper go away, that is better. The logic is not particularly intuitive. It all works the way it works, but that rarely feels like the way it is supposed to work. Elsewhere, here is a nice client memo from Davis Polk & Wardwell LLP about the recent crop of CDS nonsense. What I found particularly useful is the very clear explanation, on pages 2 and 3, of how CDS settlement auctions work, which is helpful when thinking about semi-orphaning situations.

One bit of CDS nonsense that we talked about last year was the proposed refinancing at McClatchy Co. McClatchy agreed to a deal with one of its investors, a New Jersey hedge fund named Chatham Asset Management, to refinance its debt in a way that would orphan McClatchy’s CDS; Chatham had sold CDS on McClatchy and would have a windfall from the orphaning, which it would presumably share with McClatchy in the form of attractive financing. That deal fell through because other hedge funds—including those who had bought CDS—made a better offer, which is exactly how I think this stuff should go, so good work everyone. But there was a further oddity to Chatham’s proposed deal last April. Basically McClatchy was planning to raise new first-lien term loans at interest rates in the neighborhood of 7 percent and maturities in 2030 and 2031: not cheap debt, exactly, but not bad for what is after all a newspaper company with a low-junk credit rating. But at the same time, McClatchy had some senior unsecured bonds (so junior to the proposed first-lien term loans) with an interest rate of 6.875 percent (equal to the cheaper of the two term loans) and a maturity of March 2029 (close to that of the term loans), and those unsecured bonds were trading at something like 128 cents on the dollar , for a yield of about 3.7 percent. (Bloomberg shows them currently priced at about 124.5 cents on the dollar, for a yield of about 3.9 percent.) If McClatchy had 11-year unsecured debt outstanding that traded at 3.7 percent, it was odd for it to go out and raise 12-year secured debt at 7 percent. Why not just reopen those 11-year bonds and sell more super-cheap unsecured debt, rather than bothering with new more-expensive secured debt? For that matter, it is also weird that these senior unsecured bonds of a troubled newspaper company, which had deep junk ratings of Caa2/CCC-, were trading at a 3.7 percent yield. For comparison, Apple Inc. has a senior unsecured bond due in 2027 that was trading at about a 3.7 percent yield last April; Apple is giant, rated AA+, and not a newspaper company. How were McClatchy bonds trading at the same level? Well, you might wonder if those prices were quite firm. The oddly high-priced bond trades fairly infrequently and in small sizes,[1] and it’s entirely possible that if McClatchy were to try to sell more it would not get much interest at 120+ cents on the dollar. Also most of that bond is owned by Chatham, so there is not necessarily a robust market with many buyers and sellers all transacting at those very high prices. Anyway here is a Bloomberg News article about Chatham, which has a lot going on. It is a major owner of other newspaper companies, including Postmedia Network Canada Corp. and American Media Inc. (which owns the National Enquirer): In all three cases, Chatham bought most of the subordinated bonds, plus stock. Those investments amounted to a bet that the companies would acquire competitors and cut costs. Chatham has been restructuring their debt to give them more time. Their bonds, though, haven’t suffered. And given the strains in the print-media business, the strong price of the debt is difficult to explain, traders say. Postmedia, where Pecker sat on the board until last August, has posted annual losses for most of the past decade. Its bonds rarely change hands. Yet its junior bonds offer yields comparable to more senior securities. The notes don’t pay regular interest in cash, a sign of their inherent riskiness. At least five other traders who’ve looked at the bonds say their prices seem too good to be true. A similar story has unfolded at newspaper publisher McClatchy, which has posted annual losses since 2015. Its bonds staged an improbable rally last year, charting a steady climb over 50 percent from 80 to 125 cents on the dollar. That made it one of the best performing bonds in the world at the time. It even offered lower yields than some blue-chip companies. “That’s just not how bond math works,” said Michael Terwilliger, a portfolio manager at Resource Credit Income Fund. “I wouldn’t even begin to consider owning it at that level. Something other than fundamentals are playing a huge factor in those bonds.” I don’t know! We talk constantly around here about weird ways in which the mechanics of CDS can diverge from the economic realities of the underlying companies. But bonds can too, sometimes.

I guess I would characterize this story as: Banks are the entities in our society that keep lists of who has how much money. When banks need to update those lists—to reflect that I have sent you money, for instance, so now I have less money and you have more—it is very hard for them, and it takes them a long time to do it. When two banks are involved—when my money is at one bank and yours is at another—it is virtually impossible, don’t even ask, it could be days, weeks even. And if we are in two different countries , forget about it. International Business Machines Corp., a big computer/consulting/business-machines company, has gone to the banks to propose a way of keeping the lists of money on computers , so that if I want to send money to you, our banks could just make the relevant entries electronically, almost instantaneously, rather than spending days trying to figure it out. The banks are like “oh man yes, that sounds amazing, sign us up.” Like: Fine, yes, that would be a reasonable story, if it was set in the 1950s . Sure! The banks had armies of clerks who kept handwritten ledgers by the smoky light of whale-oil lamps, and a clean-cut young International Business Machines Corp. salesman showed up to say “how about a business machine,” and the banks were like “it’s so crazy that it just might work, let's do it,” and they were brought out of the darkness into the electronic age. Why not, I might be a bit off on some of the details of the historic atmosphere but basically it feels believable. But this story is set in 2019! It’s set now! Now, today , when you can order any physical object on earth from Amazon.com and get same-day delivery, IBM salespeople are showing up at banks and being like “what if we told you there was a way to transfer money without putting gold coins in a sack, loading them on a horse and crossing a mountain range to reach their destination?” And the banks are like “what is this witchcraft?” International Business Machines Corp., a provider of technology for creating digital currency, said at least two “major U.S. banks” are considering whether to follow JPMorgan Chase & Co.’s lead in issuing a coin. Jesse Lund, IBM’s vice president of blockchain, said that the company has held initial discussions with the two lenders on issuing a so-called stablecoin -- a digital token that is pegged 1:1 to an established currency like the U.S. dollar. JPMorgan, the largest U.S. bank by assets, announced in February that it would issue a digital currency tied to the dollar, called JPM Coin. … Digital coins can enable instantaneous transfers of funds between institutional accounts, reducing settlement times and making it easier to move money internationally. JPMorgan, which moves more than $5 trillion in wholesale payments each day, said its coin will use its own private blockchain to speed payments among corporate customers. “Stablecoin,” in this context, I don’t think means much more than “a way to keep a list of dollars on a computer, but faster.” I worry that the proper conclusion here might be that tech companies know how to be banks and that banks, never mind not knowing how to be tech companies, don’t know how to be banks. At this point Amazon probably could ship me a sack of gold and horse faster than my bank could do an electronic wire transfer. And! And! And and and! The digital currencies can be used to settle transactions between customers of different banks. By loaning the coins, banks can earn interest income and charge transaction fees, Lund said. “There’s a new revenue opportunity for banks,” he said. “Banks are now starting to catch the buzz.” If you put the dollars on computers, you can lend them out and charge interest! It’s a new revenue opportunity! How are these banks banks?
