[2] In fact, when I write about the theory that common ownership of multiple companies in the same industry by large passive institutional investors might reduce competition, people sometimes email me to suggest voting swaps as the solution: Just make the index funds sell their votes to someone else who cares. [3] I am being careful to say it this way. It is not equivalent to say “My Cab Co. could acquire Your Cab LLC”: Employees of a single firm can coordinate on prices in ways that would be illegal for employees of different firms, but *acquisitions* that have anticompetitive effects are their own area of antitrust law. Organic growth, hiring, etc., by one firm might reduce competition, but mostly gets a pass from antitrust law; acquisitions, however, are treated differently. [4] Just as with the agreement on prices, of course, the corporation doesn’t insulate us from *other* competitors; again this only gets you economic profits if there are some barriers to entry or economies of scale. This matters to the question of whether we earn monopoly profits, but it does not generally matter to the question of whether there is a violation of U.S. antitrust law: Horizontal price-fixing agreements between competitors are “per se illegal” even if they don’t work, while a company setting its own prices is obviously fine whether or not it has competitors. [5] We talked a little bit about an earlier version of this argument last year. [6] This is the result of the Supreme Court’s decision in Copperweld Corp. v. Independence Tube Corp., which “held that a parent company is incapable of conspiring with its wholly owned subsidiary for purposes of Section 1 of the Sherman Act because they cannot be considered separate economic entities.” Paul writes: “At the broadest level, what Copperweld did is to extend the antitrust privilege of firm status beyond formal firm boundaries. In this way, it made colorable various firms’ legal claims to control activities beyond the borders set by corporate law itself.” [7] I mean, fine, take the stock and then sell it the next day after the IPO pop, that could be a good trade. (Not investing advice, no guarantee of IPO pop, etc.)

Imagine, as I do every day, being the Tesla Inc. “Designated Securities Counsel” whose job is to review Elon Musk’s draft tweets before he sends them out. (Bloomberg News calls this unnamed but undoubtedly accomplished lawyer “ Musk’s Mystery Twitter Sitter.”) The first problem is of course that Musk doesn’t actually let the Designated Securities Counsel review the tweets before they go out, so right there the job is basically impossible. But even if he did share his drafts, it would not be easy. So for instance: Elon Musk is out tweeting again, teasing about some Tesla news, barely a day after his social media behavior brought him more regulatory trouble. A "Thursday 2 pm" tweet came first, followed by "California" and then "Some Tesla news." Musk tweeted “Some Tesla news” at 3:21 a.m. Eastern Time last night, so the second problem is that if you are the Twitter sitter you are working a lot of late nights. But the third problem is, even if Musk does show you his drafts in advance, during business hours, what do you make of them? Like: Musk: If I tweet “Thursday 2 pm,” is that the sort of thing that “contain[s], or reasonably could contain, information material to Tesla or its stockholders”? No, right? Mystery Twitter Sitter: Why do you torture me. Musk: And surely tweeting “California” is fine? Nothing material or misleading about “California.” MTS: I was an editor of my law review you know. Musk: And then “Some Tesla news”? MTS: What have I ever done to—wait, yes, obviously “some Tesla news” could be material to Tesla and its stockholders. Musk: But there’s nothing misleading in the tweet, so you can pre-approve it, right? MTS: Well I don’t know, depends on what the Tesla news is. What is it? Musk: You’ll find out Thursday, lol. MTS: What if, instead of doing this, you just went to bed. Musk: Show me what in these three tweets is illegal or misleading. MTS: Look, as your lawyer, I am telling you that this seems like a bad idea, and you should at least wait until after your contempt-of-court hearing to do anything that might look like a violation of your settlement with the Securities and Exchange commission. Musk: Nope! I am a smart guy and I like to get into the details of every aspect of my business. I second-guess expert engineers all the time, and often it works out for me; I’m not going to do whatever you tell me just because you are a lawyer. I think these tweets are fine. If you don’t, you have to explain to me, specifically, how they violate the settlement. MTS: The world is not as black and white as many tech founders wish it was, and the legal system is not just a list of unambiguous written rules applied in a mechanical fashion. Whether you like it or not, regulators and courts operate in large areas of discretion; they have lots of ways to make life more difficult for you and for the company that you manage as a fiduciary for others, and they are used to being treated with a certain amount of deference by the people they regulate. Here they have you dead to rights on a technicality—you didn’t get your “500,000 cars” tweet pre-approved, as you promised you would, and it had to be corrected—and how they respond to that will depend on your overall attitude and behavior. My job as a lawyer is not just to look up rules and show them to you; it is to make predictions, grounded in research but also in experience and a certain professional connoisseurship, about how officials will react to particular fact patterns, and to advise you on the wisest course of action in shaping their reaction. (This is sometimes called “ legal realism.”) My expert advice to you is that the benefit to you, and to your company and its workers and shareholders, of sending out these inscrutable late-night tweets is very low, while the risk of further antagonizing the SEC and the courts seems pretty high. I am not giving you a formal legal opinion that it is illegal for you to tweet “California.” I am just telling you that it’s dumb. Musk: Well are they going to put me in jail for sending these tweets? MTS: I mean, probably not, no. Musk: I have a big drill you know. MTS: I know. Musk: That’s a kind of legal realism too. Apparently the compromise was that Musk tweeted the tweets, but first he changed his Twitter name to “Elon Tusk,” with an elephant emoji, to make them … less official? Less contemptuous? More annoying? Also, here are stories about what might happen next in Musk’s long dumb dispute with the SEC from Bloomberg News (“Judges don’t like to be ignored, and they have a lot of power”) and the Financial Times (“The SEC here is trying to avoid having to take extreme action, but [Mr Musk] keeps pushing them”—but also “The agency has actually revealed here how completely toothless it is”). Oh and Tesla has a $920 million convertible bond coming due on Friday.

s.h: People are worried about stock buybacks
s.t: The New York Times has a story about how corporations are “the single largest source of demand for American stocks,” making these two apparently contrary points: People—retail investors, pension funds, mutual funds—have been selling U.S. stocks because they don’t expect a lot of growth from big U.S. public corporations: “Facing the prospect of a period of relatively low returns — or even a bear market for stocks — many investors are eager to protect their gains or to find more appealing investments, like emerging markets and corporate bonds, outside the American stock market.” Big U.S. public corporations, meanwhile, are buying a ton of their own stock, because they have a lot of cash and nothing better to do with it: “The persistent flow of corporate money into the stock market has been a pivotal element in its recent rise.” Here’s one way to describe that story: Corporations and retail/institutional investors have opposite views. Corporations think that their stocks will go up, and are big enthusiastic buyers. Individuals and institutions think that stocks will go down or be flat, or that there are better opportunities elsewhere, and so are net sellers. Here’s another way to describe that story: Corporations and retail/institutional investors have identical views. Individuals and institutions think that large public U.S. corporations will not provide a lot of great growth opportunities in the near future, so they prefer to invest their money elsewhere. Those large public corporations, meanwhile, look around at their own businesses and also conclude that they will not provide a lot of great growth opportunities in the near future. But they’ve provided a lot of cash in the recent past, and the companies have to do something with the cash. Spending it on bad opportunities—investing it in projects that will not provide much return—would be bad. Giving it back to shareholders,[1] so the shareholders can invest it somewhere more promising—abroad, or in private companies, or sure I guess in bonds—is the sensible use of that cash. Imagine that there were no corporations. People who had money just invested it in machines for producing widgets or whatever. Occasionally you’d read a trend story that was like “people do not expect a lot of growth in the U.S. widget market these days, so American investors are dumping their widget machines and investing their money in Chinese sprocket factories.” And you’d be like, yes, sure, that makes sense, economics. Interposing the corporate form between the people with money and the widget machines shouldn’t change those basic economics. If people do not expect a lot of growth in the U.S. widget market, and want to cut back their widget-machine investments and put their money in China instead, then they need a way to get their money out of the widget machines and into China. And the simplest way would be for the widget corporation that has their money to give it back to them.[2] Look, there are a lot of more complicated issues involved in stock buybacks. There are differential taxation issues and market-manipulation worries and concerns about the effects of buybacks on executive compensation. And sometimes companies are wrong about the opportunities available to them, and are too quick to return money to shareholders instead of investing it in positive-expected-value opportunities. (Though traditionally the more common complaint was that corporate managers were too optimistic about their opportunities and too willing to spend shareholders’ money on dumb ideas instead of giving it back to them.) But the barest simplest issue is: When investors don’t think that U.S. public companies have a lot of especially compelling investment opportunities, and the managers of those companies agree, shouldn’t the managers give the investors their money back so they can put it somewhere more attractive?

Hmm: A U.K. reinsurer has sold the first terror catastrophe bond, giving investors the chance to lock in high yields in return for taking on terrorism risks. ... Modeled on Catastrophe bonds, the new notes will suffer losses if insurers have to pay out on terror attacks including chemical, biological or cyber. Catastrophe bonds, which pay out after natural disasters such as hurricanes or earthquakes, have found a market by offering investors a high-yield asset uncorrelated to economic or financial-market risks. “What’s the manufactured default on this gonna look like,” Sujeet Indap joked on Twitter, but really if you think through the incentives here they seem fine. The buyers of the bonds might be unscrupulous hedge funds or whatever, but they make money if there are no terror attacks, and lose money if there are. If they are going to do anything to manipulate the payout, it will be, I don’t know, finding terrorists and paying them not to commit attacks. (Possible lucrative terrorist business model?) The seller of the bonds is a reinsurer, which presumably has not laid off all of its risk, so its incentives are also fine. Credit-default swaps on the bonds will be credit - default swaps; they’ll pay off if the reinsurer can’t pay the bonds when due, not if the bonds lose principal due to terror attacks. In theory, someone could build a terror-default swap that paid off if these bonds lose value due to terrorist attack, but (1) I doubt there is much demand for that—people are buying these bonds specifically to get that uncorrelated exposure, so why hedge it?—and (2) no, come on, financial markets tend toward completeness but there are some limits, and I think an explicit naked “profit from terrorism” bet would be too much. I guess you could sell the bonds short and then arrange for a terrorist attack. That could be the plot of your financial thriller if you want. But realistically if your plan was “sell some securities short and commit a terrorist attack to drive down their value,” you don’t need terror cat bonds for that. Terrorism is bad for lots of securities. There is an actual case of a guy who sold Borussia Dortmund stock short and then bombed the team bus. If you want to do a bet-on-terrorism trade where you manipulate the outcome—and please don’t!—you shouldn’t do it by shorting cat bonds. That’s the first place they’ll look! Obviously this is not legal advice. By the way, there was a story last week about how the World Bank sold “pandemic bonds” (catastrophe bonds but for pandemics), but then the bonds didn’t pay out because the World Bank did not correctly anticipate the course of an Ebola epidemic when writing the bonds: Just a year later, a severe attack of Ebola hit the Democratic Republic of Congo. So far it has claimed almost 500 lives and become the second-largest outbreak ever recorded, according to Médecins Sans Frontières. Yet the bonds have yet to pay out a penny. A linked emergency cash facility at the World Bank has paid the DRC more than $11m and is preparing to disburse more. But the lack of support so far from the pandemic bonds, which mature in July 2020, has prompted questions about the limits of financial innovation. The bonds’ criteria include the requirement that a disease must spread across an international border before the affected nation can receive the cash — which has so far not been the case with the DRC and Ebola. Do you think that anyone at the World Bank was a little tempted to smuggle one Ebola patient over an international border to trigger the Ebola cat bonds?

Boy oh boy: U.S. refiner Citgo Petroleum Corp is formally cutting ties with its parent, state-run oil firm Petroleos de Venezuela SA, to meet U.S. sanctions imposed on the OPEC country, two people close to the decision told Reuters on Tuesday. … Citgo has halted payments to its parent, subscriptions to corporate services, email communications and minimized mentions to PDVSA on marketing materials and its website. Corporations are people, my friend, and every so often people become estranged from their parents and stop speaking to them, so at first glance this may not seem that weird. But it’s super weird! PdVSA is Citgo’s “parent” in the sense that it is Citgo’s sole shareholder; it would not be at all unusual to say that this means that PdVSA “owns” Citgo. If you owned a car, and your car one day decided to formally cut ties with you, you’d be perplexed. Of course Citgo is not just a machine, or a collection of machines; it’s also a collection of humans, and those humans are always free to cut ties with their corporate bosses. Normally people do this by “quitting their jobs.” But that’s not what they’re doing here. They’re keeping their jobs, and the corporate structure, and the corporate name and the business relationships, and still going to work each day with the machines. The entity has survived intact and mostly unchanged; its ownership has not. So who … does … own Citgo? The U.S. government has rendered it impossible for PdVSA to own Citgo’s shares, but it hasn’t confiscated those shares; the U.S. Treasury does not own Citgo. The workers and managers of Citgo are still going to work after cutting ties with their corporate parent, but they have not expropriated the company for themselves; it is not a worker-owned cooperative. It is not a non-profit. It’s just a sort of floating ownerless anomaly? The real answer seems to be that Citgo is still owned by PdVSA, but not by the actually existing PdVSA in Venezuela; Citgo is owned by a hypothetical future PdVSA that will be controlled by a Venezuelan regime that is recognized by the U.S. (Or perhaps by a semi-hypothetical present PdVSA that has no operations, but that does have a skeletal management appointed by the U.S.-recognized opposition Venezuelan regime? Or perhaps Citgo’s shares are held in trust for the future PdVSA?) Like Venezuela’s interim opposition government, Citgo’s emancipation is a provisional interim step, and eventually things will get back to normal. But what if they don’t? What if the government of Nicolás Maduro remains in power, and the sanctions remain in effect, and the hypothetical PdVSA never merges with the real one? What if the opposition loses its credibility and its claim to govern Venezuela, and Venezuela just continues indefinitely under U.S. sanctions? Will Citgo just continue indefinitely as an ownerless corporation? Who will appoint its board and its managers? What will it do with its profits? Who will it work for? How will it decide? Sometimes corporations are a mystery. Elsewhere: “The U.S. is considering sanctions against Wall Street billionaire David Martinez as part of its effort to topple Nicolas Maduro’s regime by cutting off its access to financing.” And: “ Evolving Venezuela Sanctions Pose Problems for Banks.”

[1] By the way, whenever I write that buybacks give money back to shareholders, someone emails or tweets to say “no, buybacks do not give money back to shareholders, the shareholders don’t get the money, only people who sell their shares do.” This is a terrible objection! If I borrow $100 from you, and then later I give you back the $100, and I say “I spent $100 paying back a creditor,” would you really reply “oh no, you don’t owe me money any more, so you can’t have paid back a creditor”? Come on. “Contempt of court” is a term of art, and it’s possible to be held in contempt of court without actually having any particular contempt for the court. If the court orders you to do something, and you don’t do it—because you forgot, or because you had other priorities, or because you are a big company and it’s hard to get everyone to comply with a court-ordered policy—you might be dragged back into court and held in contempt, even if your personal feelings about the court are neutral or abstractly respectful. On the other hand, if you go around giving television interviews about how much contempt you have for a court order, and also you violate it , then you are asking for trouble. After Elon Musk (1) tweeted some material false statements about taking Tesla Inc. private, (2) settled the resulting securities-fraud charges with the Securities and Exchange Commission by paying a $20 million fine and agreeing to have his tweets pre-approved by a lawyer, (3) went on television to say that he is not getting his tweets pre-approved and that “I want to be clear. I do not respect the SEC. I do not respect them,” and (4) again tweeted material false statements about Tesla’s production projections , I think it is fair to say that he is in contempt of court? The SEC sure does anyway: The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday asked a judge to hold Musk in contempt for violating a settlement that required him to get Tesla approval for social media posts and other writings that could be material to investors. He breached that deal with a Feb. 19 tweet that said Tesla would make about half a million cars in 2019, the agency claims. The CEO posted a few hours later that deliveries would only reach about 400,000. Here is the SEC’s motion asking a New York federal judge to hold Musk in contempt. (Here are Musk’s subsequent tweets criticizing the SEC some more, though at least he added “I have great respect for judges.”) The problem is that last week, after market hours, Musk tweeted that Tesla would produce 500,000 cars in 2019; four hours later, he corrected that to say that actually it would be about 400,000. It seemed unlikely at the time that that first tweet had been pre-approved, given that (1) it was wrong and (2) Musk had said on television that no one would ever pre-approve his tweets . But the SEC went and asked, and Tesla’s lawyers confirmed that, nope, no pre-approval. (“Although the 7:15 PM EST tweet was not individually pre-approved,” they wrote to the SEC, “Mr. Musk believed that the substance had already been appropriately vetted, pre-approved, and publicly disseminated”—which was not the deal.) Tesla does have a “ Senior Executives Communications Policy,” which says that Musk and other senior executives must get their potentially material tweets pre-approved. Musk just doesn’t follow it. On the other hand, someone is reading Musk’s tweets after they go out: “The Designated Securities Counsel continually monitors Mr. Musk’s tweets,” wrote Tesla’s lawyers, and imagine the years of hard work and high achievement that put that person on a path to end up in that job. That person was definitely a valedictorian somewhere, and now: “Upon seeing the 7:15 PM EST tweet, the Designated Securities Counsel immediately arranged to meet with Mr. Musk at the Fremont factory. Mr. Musk and the Designated Securities Counsel together drafted a clarifying tweet,” which went out at 11:41 p.m. Eastern time. Just another day at the tweet factory! Tesla’s general counsel—who does not appear to be the same person as the Designated Securities Counsel—quit the next day. What should the SEC, and the judge, do about this? I had some thoughts last week, but really I don’t know. I doubt the SEC does either; their motion and proposed order just ask Musk to “show cause, if any, why he should not be found in contempt.” (But only Musk: Apparently the SEC thinks that Tesla, which has told Musk to get his tweets pre-approved but hasn’t gotten him to listen, is doing the best it can, and has not asked the judge to hold Tesla in contempt even though it is not really complying with the terms of its settlement.) What will the judge do to him? What can she do? Yell at him? Tell him, no this time he really needs to do what she already told him to do? Put him in jail? You can’t put Elon Musk in jail; he has a whole company for drilling tunnels! Let’s be fair to Musk: On the one hand, absolutely, he has been going around saying that he does not respect the law and is going to ignore the SEC and a court order, but on the other hand he has also been going around saying that he’s got a big drill. Also rocket ships, submarines, flamethrowers, possibly flying cars, basically the whole arsenal of supervillain technology. The message is not just “I do not care about the law”; it is also “and you can’t stop me bwahahaha.” Obviously I want the endgame here to be that Musk gets clapped in jail in New York for contempt, his cellmate is El Chapo, they become friends and exchange tunneling tips and war stories, a Boring Company intern drills a big hole in the side of the jail and busts them both out, they make an elaborate escape via tunnel and submarine, and ultimately they fly off to live a picaresque life of space crime on Mars. But probably what will happen is that Musk will go to court and the judge will yell at him and he will say he’s sorry and then six minutes later he’ll tweet “my fingers were crossed and I am NOT sorry” and he’ll go on TV that night and be like “you know what I have contempt for? Court,” and everyone will just be like “ehhhhhhhhhh good enough.” The whole thing is exhausting and dumb and demeans everyone involved. In general it seems like the American justice system can grind down anyone caught in its grip, but in this particular case I think Elon Musk might grind down the justice system first.

Look, nothing about the Windstream situation is a “manufactured default.” A “manufactured default” is when a company gets together with a hedge fund that has bought credit-default swaps on the company (which pay off if the company defaults on its debt) and agrees to do some sort of minor optional default on its debt in order to trigger the CDS. In return, the hedge fund gives the company some money, at the expense of other hedge funds who had sold CDS and lose out from the default. I think that this trade is rather neat—it takes a zero-sum synthetic bet between hedge funds and turns it into a source of financing for a real company—but lots of people think that it is market manipulation and I suppose I can see where they’re coming from. Windstream is not that at all. In Windstream, a hedge fund (Aurelius Capital Management LP) discovered that a company (Windstream Holdings Inc.) had already violated the terms of its bonds, so it bought those bonds and sued for a declaration that they were in default. Nobody agreed on the default, or manufactured it, or cut any backroom deals. Last week Aurelius won in court, and yesterday Windstream filed for bankruptcy. But this does not, on its face, look all that great for Aurelius. Aurelius bought about $310 million of Windstream bonds at some time before Sept. 21, 2017, when those bonds were generally trading between call it 70-ish and 90-ish cents on the dollar. After Aurelius won its court ruling, the bonds fell below 40 cents on the dollar. After yesterday’s bankruptcy filing, they are trading below 20 cents on the dollar. The court ruled that the bonds were in default and that Aurelius could demand immediate payment of its $310 million, but it can’t guarantee that Windstream can actually come up with the money, and the odds are pretty good that it can’t. Everyone assumes that there is something else going on here, and the thing that they assume is going on is that Aurelius bought a lot of CDS protection on Windstream and is now due for a big payoff—bigger than its losses on the bonds—from driving Windstream into default. (This is sometimes called “ net-short debt activism,” meaning that Aurelius acts like an activist investor in Windstream’s debt even though its net position is a bet against that debt.) Windstream Chief Executive Officer Tony Thomas talked about it in the press release announcing the company’s bankruptcy: “The Company believes that Aurelius engaged in predatory market manipulation to advance its own financial position through credit default swaps at the expense of many thousands of shareholders, lenders, employees, customers, vendors and business partners. Windstream stands by its decision to defend itself and try to block Aurelius’ tactics in court. The time is well-past for regulators to carefully examine the ramifications of an unregulated credit default swap marketplace.” “Windstream’s accusation of market manipulation is nonsense,” says Aurelius, and that is completely correct as far as it goes. As far as Windstream is concerned, all that Aurelius did was read its bond documents, assert its rights under those documents, go to court to argue its position, and win in court. None of those things could be market manipulation. If Aurelius also bet in the CDS market that it would be correct, well, (1) that doesn’t sound like manipulation to me and (2) Windstream wasn’t selling CDS so the integrity of the CDS market isn’t its problem. But of course the overall result is very much Windstream’s problem: Windstream is bankrupt now because Aurelius came after it, and it’s hard to imagine Aurelius coming after it if Aurelius hadn’t bought a lot of CDS on Windstream first. (Windstream’s other bondholders were very willing to forgive Windstream’s covenant violation, tried to help it fend off Aurelius, and are now facing huge losses due to Aurelius’s activism.) It is not hard to sympathize with Windstream’s view that something is wrong with the CDS market, if this is the result. A basic drive in modern finance is to make markets complete. If there’s a possible future state of the world that will have some financial payoff—if airlines might lose money if fuel prices go up, or if farmers might make money if grain prices go up, etc.—then there ought to be some way to quantify and bet on the current value of that possible future payoff. If there’s a security or an asset or a contract or a state of the world that comes with a bundle of different rights, then there ought to be a way to buy or sell each individual right in the bundle. If there’s a way to invest in something, then there ought to be a way to sell it short. And if there isn’t, some financial engineer at some bank somewhere is working on a way to do it. This is not just a strange compulsive hobby of financial engineers; it is a basic point of finance. The social value of the financial industry is in ever more finely allocating risk, shifting risks from people who naturally bear them but don’t want to (farmers, airlines) to people who are willing to bear them for a price (investors, speculators, insurers, people with natural exposure the other way). The better a society is at managing and allocating risks, the more prosperous and happier it will be. Obviously other things go into prosperity and happiness besides risk-shifting, but risk-shifting is the thing that the financial industry does, so it takes it seriously. Out in the rest of the world, market completeness is not generally viewed as the top goal. There are all sorts of laws against betting on sports or presidential elections, against selling kidneys or votes, against taking out insurance on your neighbor’s house. (Many people think many of these laws are bad and should be changed, but that mostly seems to be a minority opinion.) There is a belief that some things are more important than money, or that involving money in those things creates incentives for people to behave badly. But finance is about money, and is ruled by monetary incentives, and so in general it is unusual to have these sorts of objections to purely financial transactions. But, maybe, sometimes? One way to think about the Windstream situation is that the market for corporate credit exposure has become a bit too complete. It used to be that corporate credit was a bundle: The people with credit exposure to the company (its lenders and bondholders) were the people with the legal right to foreclose on it, and they had incentives to use that right sparingly and only when it enhanced the overall value of the credit. But modern finance can separate bonds into their component atoms: You can buy a bond and sell off the interest-rate risk, or the credit risk, or the exchange-rate risk if you want. If you buy a bond and sell off all the credit risk, then you end up with the right to foreclose and no incentives to use it responsibly. You can even sell off more credit risk than you bought, leaving you with bad incentives, which seems to be what happened here. I don’t really know what to do about this. One thing you could imagine would be to ban this sort of thing, but that does require some pretty fine slicing of what “this sort of thing” is. Would you ban bondholders from hedging their exposure? How confident would you be that regulators would measure their exposure correctly? Would you force bondholders to choose between hedging their risks and enforcing their legal rights? There is an almost natural tendency of financial markets toward completeness, and it’s hard to stand in the way. I suppose another possibility is to just want more market completeness? An important stylized fact about Windstream is that this situation seems to have destroyed value. Windstream was worth a certain amount of money before Aurelius came along, and now it is worth less, and Aurelius has not captured all of that difference. Aurelius has (presumably) gotten a CDS payoff, but some other hedge fund is on the other side of that; there’s no net gain there. And meanwhile a lot of value will be destroyed in fees and delay and uncertainty in bankruptcy, which will mostly profit no one. (The fees will be profitable for the lawyers and bankers.) In a perfect market, someone would have stopped that. Windstream’s other bondholders could have gotten together with the CDS sellers to pay off Aurelius, for instance. Or maybe those bondholders could have hedged their Aurelius risk by buying net-short activism default swaps, I don’t know. It is all just money, just financial transactions; surely someone could have found a way to move money around to allocate these risks and prevent this value destruction. Hopefully some financial engineer somewhere is working on it.

Doesn’t it feel like it’s time to revive the heritage brands of investment banking? We live in an age of constant cyclical nostalgia, banks are looking to the past for a sense of credibility and stability, and the scandals that brought down many of the old banks are half-forgotten by now. Plus everyone who has gone to work at an investment bank in the last 20 years did it because they read “Liar’s Poker,” and that book is about Salomon Brothers, which hasn’t been a live brand in ages. Bring it back! If you asked Citigroup Inc.’s traders whether they’d rather answer their phones “Citi” or “Salomon,” I am confident what they’d answer. I don’t know who owns the rights to the Drexel Burnham & Lambert, but, I mean, the Michael Milken brand is pretty good these days, so I have to think the Drexel one would be valuable. UBS AG seems to own Dillon Read, PaineWebber and Kidder Peabody, without doing much with them. When I worked in banking, not all that long ago, “First Boston” was still a common, though obviously pretentious and hipster-ish, way to refer to Credit Suisse AG. Bear Stearns, maybe you want to give it a few years, but if Lehman Brothers feels a little too-soon for you there is always Shearson Lehman Hutton. Though actually “a group of E.F. Hutton alumni bought the E.F. Hutton brand” back from Citigroup during the crisis (great idea!) and it’s still around, so maybe just Shearson Lehman. Kuhn Loeb! Loeb Rhoades! Hayden Stone! Hornblower & Weeks! The Lehman family tree is great. Anyway sad news: Bank of America Corp. will drop Merrill Lynch from its investment-bank brand, while keeping the name Merrill for wealth management. The investment bank is to be called BofA Securities and the U.S. Trust name will be dropped from the private bank, Charlotte, North Carolina-based BofA said Monday in a statement. Here is the official announcement of the “Brand Updates.” Look, fine, I can see that “Bank of America” has some appeal as a brand: It is a bank, it’s in America, it’s easy to spell and remember, etc. (“BofA”seems a bit more suspect, I have to say.) And while Merrill Lynch has a proud tradition as an investment bank, it has an even prouder tradition as a wealth manager—Thundering Herd, etc.—so it makes sense to rationalize the brand I guess. It’s probably clearer for clients. It’s sad for the bankers, though, especially the ones who worked at Merrill Lynch back when it was independent. If you work at a firm whose name is just two people’s last names—or five, and until recently the investment bank would make at least occasional use of the full “Merrill Lynch Pierce Fenner & Smith”—then it feels like an investment bank, you know? Part of a long tradition of Wall Street partnerships, etc. If you work at a firm whose name is “Bank of [a geography]” then it’s just a bank, and if the geography is “America” then it feels like a really big anonymous bank.

If you are a hedge fund manager, and the stocks that you buy go up, it’s not too hard to write your annual investor letter. “We bought some stocks, they went up, our process works great, now I have a yacht”; it’s all pretty straightforward, and in any case your readers will give you the benefit of the doubt. You have made them money, which is what they really wanted, so if you send them a boring letter it’ll be fine. On the other hand, if the stocks that you buy go down, that’s when you need to break out the classical quotations, sharp analysis and measured self-deprecation that make your readers think “sure we hired this guy to pick stocks that go up and he picked stocks that went down, but he sounds pretty smart in this letter, let’s give him another chance.” It’s a much harder exercise; you need to state forthrightly that the buck stops with you and that you won’t make any excuses for your poor performance, and then make some pretty good excuses. And then there is Warren Buffett! Come on with this stuff: [Berkshire Hathaway Inc.] posted a staggering net loss of $25 billion in the fourth quarter, the biggest loss in its history. That was largely due to a new accounting rule that Buffett disagrees with, which requires companies to report changes in the value of investments as part of earnings. For most corporations, that’s a relatively minor figure, but Berkshire’s $170 billion stock portfolio means big gains and losses each quarter. The firm’s operating earnings, meanwhile, soared 71 percent from a year earlier. That’s Buffett’s preferred metric because it excludes stock swings and measures how Berkshire’s underlying businesses are performing. Those units benefited from better insurance results, gains at the company’s railroad and a lower corporate tax rate. And: In his annual letter to Berkshire’s shareholders that accompanied its results, Mr. Buffett urged investors to focus on the performance of Berkshire Hathaway’s broad array of companies, which includes insurers, energy firms, railways and manufacturers. These firms did well last year, posting a 36 percent increase in earnings. Before 2018, Berkshire did not include the performance of its stock holdings in its income statement, unless it sold the shares. But a new accounting rule requires that the company include the paper gains and losses. That is something Mr. Buffett has criticized, saying the rule would cause “wild and capricious” swings in Berkshire’s bottom line. In this year’s letter, he wrote, “Indeed, in the fourth quarter, a period of high volatility in stock prices, we experienced several days with a ‘profit’ or ‘loss’ of more than $4 billion.” Look, fine, if you admire Warren Buffett as the foremost insurance underwriter and railroad operator of his generation, you should definitely focus on the strong cash flows from his operating businesses. But just for me personally, when I think about Warren Buffett, the first thing that comes to mind is that he is, in all of human history, the single person who has become most famous for his ability to pick stocks that go up. That’s kind of his thing! So it is a little silly to see Buffett complaining that, just because he put $36 billion into a volatile tech stock, his results look volatile. That’s what you get! If you buy stocks, and they go down, then you have losses. Or “losses,” with the quotation marks, if you must. “Paper losses,” sure. But it is hard for me not to feel like, well, yes, if your business is stock-picking, then your business results ought to reflect what happens to the stocks you pick. The accounting has just caught up to the reality. Or maybe not. In fact there’s another big shift in Berkshire’s accounting, one that goes the other way. On the one hand, generally accepted accounting principles now require Berkshire to reflect the quarter-to-quarter results of its stock-picking in earnings. On the other hand, Berkshire’s own description of its results will stop focusing on book value, because book value is most appropriate for describing an investing company, and Berkshire is not an investing company anymore. From Buffett’s letter: Long-time readers of our annual reports will have spotted the different way in which I opened this letter. For nearly three decades, the initial paragraph featured the percentage change in Berkshire’s per-share book value. It’s now time to abandon that practice. The fact is that the annual change in Berkshire’s book value – which makes its farewell appearance on page 2 – is a metric that has lost the relevance it once had. Three circumstances have made that so. First, Berkshire has gradually morphed from a company whose assets are concentrated in marketable stocks into one whose major value resides in operating businesses. Charlie and I expect that reshaping to continue in an irregular manner. Second, while our equity holdings are valued at market prices, accounting rules require our collection of operating companies to be included in book value at an amount far below their current value, a mismark that has grown in recent years. Third, it is likely that – over time – Berkshire will be a significant repurchaser of its shares, transactions that will take place at prices above book value but below our estimate of intrinsic value. This is all totally reasonable, but it does over time mean that Berkshire’s financial results have become a less clear picture of Warren Buffett’s success as an investor. While the GAAP changes mean that Berkshire’s financial results will be a less clear picture of Berkshire’s success as an operator. It will all be mixed together, and the mix will tell you less about each part. Obviously the letter is really good, by the way, though you don’t need me to tell you that. Like, if you gave Warren Buffett your money hoping he would pick good stocks with it, then over the long term you have very little reason to be dissatisfied with him (even in 2018 he beat the S&P 500), but even if you are dissatisfied with recent performance you will probably be assuaged by the letter. Buffett, more than any other investor, has really mastered the art of sounding smart when his stocks go down, a talent that I attribute to (1) being smart and (2) a long history of the stocks going up. This year’s quotes are from Abraham Lincoln and Christopher Wren.

Last year Sinovac Biotech Ltd., a U.S.-listed Chinese biopharmaceutical company incorporated in Antigua and Barbuda (why not), held an annual general meeting of shareholders to re-elect its board of directors. Some shareholders showed up at the meeting (in Beijing) and took the board by surprise by demanding to vote for different directors. This is generally viewed as somewhere between “extremely impolite” and “totally illegal,” because: Who goes to shareholder meetings? In most of the world, most of the time, the answer is almost nobody; all of the business of the meetings is conducted by proxies. If you want to nominate directors, you send in a notice months in advance, and navigate a bunch of tricky procedural formalities, and if all goes well you get to send a proxy card to all the shareholders asking them to vote for your directors, and if more shareholders send back proxies for your slate than for the management slate then your directors get elected. You don’t just show up at the meeting, nominate your directors and ask for a show of hands. The company’s managers will quite properly tell you that you are out of order, and you will respond “the whole system is out of order,” and there will be a lot of shouting and confusion. But that’s what some shareholders at Sinovac did, and there was a lot of shouting and confusion—you can read a partial translated transcript in the court decision that eventually came out of it—and the insurgent slate of directors did get more votes than management’s incumbent slate. But management refused to accept the results, leaving Sinovac with two boards of directors, one approved by the shareholders and the other approved by the managers. (Obviously the one approved by the managers was, in every practical sense, the real board of directors—“the Incumbent Directors remained in control of the Company following the disputed election,” says the court decision—which might trouble you if you think that the shareholders are the owners of a corporation.) Everyone went to court in Antigua and Barbuda, and the court handed down its decision in December, and of course the incumbent directors won: Again, there is a procedure, and you really can’t just show up at a shareholder meeting with your own ballots and a moving speech and try to get everyone to vote for your directors. If anything at all dramatic happens at a shareholder meeting, you are doing it wrong. But that is not where the story ends. Sinovac is apparently so mad at the shareholders who tried to elect their own directors that it triggered its poison pill . Here are Sinovac’s press release and Form 6-K announcing the pill trigger, and they are wild stuff, though perhaps you can’t tell from the boring legalese of the 6-K: On February 18, 2019, the Board of Directors (the “Board”) of Sinovac Biotech Ltd. (the “Company”) determined that 1Globe Capital, LLC, Chiangjia Li, OrbiMed Advisors LLC, and those additional shareholders who voted together with the foregoing at the annual meeting held in February 2018 (collectively, the “Collaborating Shareholders”) became “Acquiring Persons,” as defined in the Company’s Rights Agreement, dated March 28, 2016 (as amended, the “Rights Agreement”), at or prior to the Company’s last Annual General Meeting held on February 6, 2018. As a result, a “Trigger Event” occurred under the Rights Agreement, and the approximately 28.7 million preferred share purchase rights (the “Original Rights”) under the Rights Agreement held by the Collaborating Shareholders or their Affiliates or Associates (as defined in the Rights Agreement) automatically became void under the terms of the Rights Agreement. Pursuant to the Rights Agreement, the Board approved an exchange (the “Exchange”) of all valid Original Rights as of the close of trading in the United States on February 22, 2019 (the “Exchange Date”) for 0.655 of the Company’s common shares (the “Common Shares”) and 0.345 of the Company’s newly created Series B Convertible Preferred Shares (the “Series B Preferred Shares” and, together, each an “Exchange Share”). So, first of all, any poison pill trigger is wild. The basic idea of a poison pill is that if one Bad Shareholder acquires too much of the company’s stock, then every other shareholder gets some free extra shares, diluting down the Bad Shareholder. Traditionally the Bad Shareholder was a hostile bidder trying to acquire the company at (supposedly) less than its intrinsic value, and the justification for the poison pill was that it protected shareholders from coercive takeover tactics. But standards have shifted over time, and now anyone who owns enough shares, and is rude to management, can count as a Bad Shareholder and be diluted by the board. But the point of the pill, generally, is to be a deterrent: Because everyone knows that the pill exists, and is a disaster, no one ever triggers it. Someone triggered a pill in 2009, and it was a mess; trading in the company’s stock was suspended for a month, and as far as I can tell there hasn’t been a trigger since. Last year we talked about an activist shareholder at a penny-stock company who went around saying things like “I have intentionally triggered your poison pill” and “I/we dare you to proceed with the poison pill,” but he just seemed to be confused, and it looks like he eventually backed down. But Sinovac is going and doing it! Nasdaq has halted trading in the stock, and Sinovac says that the halt will last “until at least March 8, 2019 in order to facilitate the orderly distribution of the Exchange Shares.” Eventually all of Sinovac’s shareholders, except for the Bad Shareholders, will get an extra share for each share they currently hold[1]; the Bad Shareholders will not, and so will have their stakes cut roughly in half. So that right there is pretty extreme, but it gets weirder. The traditional poison pill singled out one Bad Shareholder—typically a hostile bidder—and diluted away its shares. Modern pills focus on deterring coordinated action by groups of Bad Shareholders, so they count anyone “ acting in concert” against management as one Bad Shareholder Group, and aggregate all of their shares for purposes of triggering the pill. This means that you can’t, for instance, get together with other shareholders and conspire to oust the directors and vote in a new slate, without risking triggering the pill. But in the U.S., it is considered bad form to completely ban shareholder democracy, and so even the “acting in concert” pills don’t count shareholder voting as acting in concert. If Carl Icahn runs a proxy fight, and he calls you up and gets you to agree to support him, you might be counted with him as part of a group triggering a poison pill, but if he just quietly sends every shareholder a proxy card, and you vote for his slate, you’re safe. That’s how it works in the U.S., but not necessarily in Antigua and Barbuda, and it is not Sinovac’s approach. As the 6-K says, the pill will catch not only 1Globe Capital (the 15-plus-percent holder that led the insurgent group) and a few other funds that coordinated with it, but also “those additional shareholders who voted together with the foregoing at the annual meeting held in February 2018.” Anyone who voted against management at the annual meeting now gets their shares diluted away. That’s pretty strict! It comes to about 40 percent of the shares outstanding: 28.7 million shares voted the wrong way at the meeting, and will get diluted; 42.4 million shares voted the right way and will get the extra shares.[2] We have talked a lot recently about the question of who controls a corporation, and I have consistently pushed back on the naive view that shareholders “own” the corporation and get to choose its managers and directors and control how it operates. Here some shareholders wanted to vote out the old directors and vote in some new ones, and their new directors got more votes than the old ones did, and not only did this not have the effect of replacing the old directors with the new ones, but the old directors have decided to punish the shareholders who voted against them by taking away some of their shares. Whatever is happening here, it is hard to see it as the shareholders owning the corporation.

Here is a story about how BlackRock Inc. decided to start a big private-equity business, but is running a bit behind schedule. (It “set a goal of raising at least $12 billion to buy and hold long-term stakes in companies” last year, but “is still waiting for its first check.”) I loved this bit: The company decided not to staff the fund with a full team at first and test the appetite of investors with a seven-page slide presentation, refining the concept as it went along. Several potential investors were concerned that a team wasn’t yet in place, and that BlackRock had no record to show, according to people familiar with the matter. The firm didn’t want BlackRock’s own balance-sheet capital at risk for its first deals, said three people familiar with the matter. Just sort of imagine how that went: BlackRock: Do you want to invest in our private equity fund? Investor: Probably! Can I hear more about the background of the people who will be running it? BlackRock: Oh we haven’t hired them yet. Investor: And there is no track record we can look at? BlackRock: Nope. Investor: Well, that’s okay, you guys are pretty smart, and I assume you’ll be investing alongside us? BlackRock: Oh no, that would be too risky for us. Investor: Okay well how would the strategy work? BlackRock: We’re still refining that. Investor: Ah. BlackRock : So are you in or what? Here’s the thing. The answer, sure, seems to have been a consistent “no.” But this isn’t that crazy. Like I have written it to sound crazy, and I guess it does sound crazy. But if I just generically asked if you wanted to invest in a big BlackRock private equity fund, without telling you any more about it, wouldn’t you be tempted? There just seem to be a lot of favorable institutional factors. BlackRock is so big! It is going to see a lot of deal flow: Given BlackRock’s importance in other businesses, every bank is going to want to win its favor by showing it good private-equity deals. When it does bid for a target, the target might be favorably disposed to it given its strong brand and Larry Fink’s penchant for running around talking about long-termism and the social purpose of business. (In fact, BlackRock’s private equity venture is apparently called “Long Term Private Capital.”) For similar reasons you might also expect it to have an easy time fundraising, and so be able to deploy your capital quickly and efficiently, though apparently that would be wrong. It is going to be able to hire well: It is a prestigious firm with a lot of money, so you can assume that the people it eventually hires for private equity will be smart and hard-working even if you don’t know who they are yet. All of the back-office-y stuff will be efficient and competent, because BlackRock is a big competent institution; unlike with other private-equity startups, you probably will not have to do a lot of due diligence to make sure it’s not a Ponzi. And given its economies of scale and general approach, you might expect the fees to be low, and they will be: “Long Term Private Capital is offering to charge clients a management fee below 1%, and 10% of profits, and its management fees would fall as the fund gets bigger,” versus the standard 2 and 20. There is a lot to like, even in a purely imaginary BlackRock private equity fund. People talk from time to time about the “value of the person” versus the “value of the seat”: If you bring in $100 million of revenue trading bonds for Goldman Sachs, how much of that is due to your own hustle and skill, and how much of it is due to Goldman’s reputation and client network and the fact that a monkey could make money trading bonds for Goldman Sachs? What if BlackRock’s pitch had worked, and they had raised $12 billion for a private equity fund with no managers or strategy or track record? And then they had to go out and hire people to invest that money? How much should those people get paid, if they were an afterthought at the fund they run?

We talked last week about Aurelius Capital Management LP’s victory against Windstream Holdings Inc., when Aurelius got a federal judge to rule that a 2015 sale-leaseback transaction violated the terms of Windstream’s bond indentures and therefore put Windstream into default. I found the decision troubling, but also correct; ”the covenants included a specific promise not to do this exact thing,” I wrote, and Windstream “ignored the spirit of the covenant, and mostly also the letter.” But Stephen Lubben at Credit Slips is less impressed: The court readily concedes that the plain language of the indenture does not cover the transaction on its face. Rather the court repeatedly argues that the “economic realities” of the transaction bring it within the terms of the indenture. In essence, the court has granted Aurelius covenant protection that it (and its predecessors) were not savvy enough to negotiate in the first place. That’s the kind of interpretive stretch that law professors expect to see with sympathetic plaintiffs – the classic “widowers and orphans.” But Aurelius? As the author of a law school corporate finance text, I’ve read my share of these sorts of opinions. I often tell my students that the one constant theme running through the bulk of corporate finance jurisprudence is that “if you want protection, you’d better contract for it.” The Windstream opinion represents a clear departure from that trend. Instead, the theme seems to be, “I know what you really meant.” Obviously Aurelius didn’t negotiate for this protection: They didn’t own the bonds when they were issued, or even apparently at the time of the sale-leaseback; instead, they bought the bonds later because they read them and concluded that they did protect bondholders against the sale-leaseback that Windstream actually did. A judge agreed with them, and so did I, but Lubben knows more about bond indentures than I do (and probably more than the judge does) so perhaps they were wrong. And it’s certainly true that the only reason to give Aurelius a win here is if the documents support Aurelius: Possibly bankrupting a real company to make money for a (possibly net-short) hedge fund is not a particularly desirable outcome; you might have to do it if it’s what the documents say, but not if it’s just what they should have said.

Crudely, there are two ways for things to trade: Someone can set up an all-to-all platform that lets anyone who wants to sell a thing sell it to anyone who wants to buy it, or Someone can act as a dealer, buy the thing from people who want to sell it, and sell it to people who want to buy it. Aesthetically, there is a lot to like about the first approach. It feels honest, transparent, natural; the people who want to buy for fundamental reasons are buying from the people who want to sell for fundamental reasons, without a grubby middleman imposing himself to take a cut. The gains from trade are shared by the principals, instead of being siphoned off by intermediaries. Everyone can compete on a level playing field, instead of some middleman controlling information for his own advantage. And yet it is striking that, wherever there is an all-to-all trading platform, dealers seem to spring up. We talk about this all the time in the context of U.S. stock exchanges, which are in some theoretical sense not dealer-driven markets—anyone, through their broker, can post an order to buy or sell on the exchange—but which in practice are so dominated by market makers that whole books are written about how high-frequency traders take a cut of every trade. But there is also Amazon/EBay arbitrage, which means listing something for sale on EBay and, when someone orders it, just buying the thing (cheaper) on Amazon and having it sent to your customer, clipping the spread between the two prices. The only thing you are doing for your money is cutting and pasting an Amazon seller’s ad onto EBay, and hoping that people will notice your EBay ad before they notice the original seller’s ad. And that happens enough to make this a viable business. Even though people tend to feel like it’s a scam! Arguably it is a scam, but arguably it is providing a valuable service at a market price. Awkwardly, the service is “selling stuff to people who don’t have time to look at the second link in the search results,” but time is finite and human attention is precious and that service might actually be worth what people pay for it. The general lessons might be: People really, really value what in the market-structure jargon is referred to as “immediacy”; Trading platforms that rely on matching natural buyers and sellers have a hard time guaranteeing immediacy; Intermediaries who use their own capital to provide immediacy—who buy from sellers as soon as the sellers want to sell , sell to buyers as soon as the buyers want to buy , and take on the risk and hassle of waiting—are valuable. Anyway here’s some news about Zillow: Zillow Group Inc., the housing search website that’s taken a hit to its stock price as it pursues an ambitious plan to buy homes and originate mortgages, is bringing back its first chief executive officer to lead the transformation. … Zillow’s plan would transform the way Americans buy and sell their homes as it has changed the way they shop for them, with mouse clicks on satellite maps. In April, the company announced plans to launch a Big Data-driven spin on flipping homes, using its price-estimating software to buy properties, then making some minor repairs before reselling a few months later. And here is a recent deeper dive from Bloomberg Businessweek into that transformation, in which Zillow is trying to change from a company that helped inform buyers and sellers and agents—“a partner to real estate agents, not a disrupter”—into a dealer that offers immediacy and tries to earn a spread. One possibility is that this is just a dumb idea. (“Zillow, the skeptics said, was moving from a high-margin business—online advertising—into a capital-intensive, low-margin one,” and will face adverse selection because “sellers will pull the trigger only if they know they’re getting a good deal.”) But maybe it is a good and necessary idea, because people don’t particularly want a platform that helps buyers and sellers find each other; they just want to buy or sell a house. “People expect to press a button and have magic happen,” said Zillow’s former CEO. And magic —instant results—might require a capital commitment. One theme in modern finance is that big banks want to be tech companies. Partly this means that they, you know, hire a lot of programmers to make their computers work better, but there is also a structural meaning: It means that banks, chastened by the financial crisis and limited by regulation, want to reduce their reliance on capital-intensive risk businesses and get more into the business of providing technology-driven platforms for their customers. Don’t buy and sell bonds from customers; build a trading platform that lets your customers trade bonds with each other (and gives you a cut). So it is a useful data point to see actual tech companies moving the other way . Zillow built a computer platform that helped buyers and sellers find each other, and that gave it (in the form of advertising) a cut of the action with no risk. And it decided that it would rather take risk, commit capital, and be a bank.

s.h: People are worried about bond market liquidity
s.t: The standard story of bond market liquidity is: Big banks used to trade bonds by buying a large slug of bonds from a customer and holding on to them for as long as it took to find another buyer, smoothing out the market but also taking a lot of price risk for themselves. Since the financial crisis, new regulations (higher capital requirements, rules against proprietary trading, etc.) have made it more difficult for banks to trade bonds on their own books as dealers. Instead, banks have just matched up buyers and sellers without intermediating risk themselves, which is less convenient for the buyers and sellers. Also if anything goes wrong, the banks will not be there to take on their historic dealer role of smoothing out price moves, and there could be an ugly crash. People who do not want there to be an ugly crash tend to think this is bad. Other people think it is fine, though: If bond prices go down and someone has to lose some money, much better for it to be long-term fundamental bond investors with stable funding than for it to be banks . Banks are systemically risky, as we know, because losses at banks caused a massive systemic crisis in 2008. I’m not saying that this story is true , and you could object to many of the particulars, but it gives you a rough sense of the controversy. In simplest form, the controversy is that post-crisis regulation has made the financial system safer at the cost of making the market worse . That might or might not be a good tradeoff, depending on the magnitude of the two effects—both quite hard to measure!—but it intuitively seems like it could be a real tradeoff. Here is a Federal Reserve staff working paper by Nathan Foley-Fisher, Stefan Gissler and Stéphane Verani about “ Over-the-Counter Market Liquidity and Securities Lending.” It offers a different explanation for (part of) the post-crisis decline in bond market liquidity and the banks’ ability to act as dealers. This story also starts with banks buying and selling bonds for their own account as dealers. When a customer wants to sell, the bank will buy. When a customer wants to buy, the bank will sell, if it has the bonds . But there are lots of bonds, and no guarantee that the bank has the particular bonds that the customer wants to buy. If it doesn’t, it can refuse to do the trade, or tell the customer to wait and try to go out and find someone who’s selling; either result would seem to count as bad for bond market liquidity. But there’s a third option: It can borrow the bonds from someone else, and sell them short to you. A dealer that receives a buy order from a client will try to find another client with a matching sell order. While searching, the dealer can fill the buy order using its own inventory, by locating the security in the interdealer market, or by borrowing the security from a securities lender. In exchange for paying a fee and posting collateral, dealers borrow securities from other financial institutions with large portfolios of securities, such as insurance companies. To be sure, the lending market itself may not be frictionless and impediments to the ability to borrow securities could impinge on market liquidity. Such frictions may arise from high lending fees for borrowing certain securities … or from search and bargaining in the securities lending market .... Nevertheless, when the costs of interdealer trading and inventory are relatively high, securities lending can improve market liquidity by reducing the costs of dealing securities. If dealers can borrow bonds from bond investors, then they can sell bonds to customers without being constrained by what they actually have in inventory, and so they can function as classic two-sided dealers. If they can’t borrow bonds from investors, then all they can do is try to match up buyers and sellers: They can’t take the risk on their own balance sheet as intermediaries, because they can’t sell bonds that they don’t have. A stylized story you could tell here would be: Before 2008, dealer banks could borrow lots of bonds in the securities lending market, so they could regularly intermediate bond trades on their own balance sheets, but “the corporate bond securities lending market collapsed by about half towards the end of 2008,” and so it got harder for dealers to source bonds and thus to act as dealers. This looks a lot like the story we started with, except that instead of being a consequence of regulatory changes, the decline in liquidity is due to a decline in securities lending. Still, what caused the decline in securities lending? The short answer is that American International Group Inc. was a huge player in the securities-lending market, and its securities-lending activities were systemically risky (basically because AIG invested the cash it got for short-term securities lending in long-term risky mortgage-backed investments), and eventually those activities blew up in a catastrophic way and took AIG down in a way that had huge systemic repercussions for the financial system, but also , after that happened, AIG pretty much stopped doing securities lending. “AIG experienced a complete shutdown of the securities lending program operated by its life subsidiaries, falling from over $80 billion to almost nothing in less than one year.” And so: Applying a difference-in-differences empirical strategy, we show that the shutdown of AIG’s securities lending program in 2008 caused a statistically and economically significant reduction in the market liquidity of corporate bonds predominantly held by AIG. We also show that an important mechanism behind the decrease in corporate bond liquidity was a shift towards relatively small trades among a greater number of dealers in the interdealer market. Oversimplifying wildly, before AIG collapsed, if you wanted to buy a bond, you’d go to a dealer, and she would borrow the bond from AIG’s universal portfolio of bonds and sell it to you. After AIG collapsed, if you want to buy a bond, you go to a dealer, and she will put you on hold and call around to all the other dealers to see if she can find enough bonds to sell you. It’s slower and less certain, and the market is worse.The tradeoff is that the market used to be better because AIG was accumulating huge systemic risks that no one really understood. “Our findings highlight the importance of the shadow banking system as a potentially fragile determinant of market efficiency,” the authors write, but that fragility can affect more than just bond market liquidity. It might be worth having less market efficiency if the tradeoff is less fragility.

One of these days we are going to need a new Linnaeus to clean up startup cryptozoology. Start with “unicorn,” the now-completely-standard term for a private technology company with a valuation of $1 billion or more. This became jargon in 2013, but it was just an extension of the common usage of “unicorn” to refer to any sort of rare, desirable thing. In 2013, billion-dollar startups were rare and desirable; now they are common and a lot of them seem kind of terrible. A good term these days for a startup with a $1 billion valuation might be “startup.” At some point, a big and dingy flock of unicorns just starts to look like a bunch of horses. Meanwhile a billion dollars isn’t cool, you know what is cool, some round number that is larger than a billion dollars. But this leads to etymological and anatomical difficulties, because the word “unicorn” comes from the Latin words for “one” and “horn,” but people who use it to describe startups seem to think that it comes from the Latin words for “one” and “billion dollars.” And so a startup with a $10 billion valuation is, with some frequency, referred to as a “decacorn.” If a unicorn is a rare, elegant and desirable horse with one horn, is a decacorn a rarer, more elegant and more desirable horse with 10 horns? Would that be elegant and desirable? Where do the horns … go? How does it work? Please do not send me a drawing of a decacorn. I am pretty sure that I coined the term “quinquagintacorn” for Uber (50 horns!), but now it seems to be a thing. On the other hand, a $100 million startup is, not a decicorn (one-tenth of a horn, in SI units), but a … centaur? I mean, I don’t know if that is a particularly common usage, but here it is in Fortune so at least someone has said it once. The idea here might be that a centaur (a mythological half-man-half-horse) is midway between a merely human early-stage startup and the equine elegance of a unicorn. But I worry that “centaur” might instead be formed from the Latinate prefix “cent-,” meaning “hundred,” and “aur,” which means “million dollars” in the same hypothetical language in which “corn” means “billion dollars.” But there are further extensions of the menagerie that abandon numerical notions entirely and are just like “hey, here’s a mythological thing, let’s call some startups it.” For instance, it is relatively easy to achieve a $1 billion valuation—if I give you a dollar for a 1/1,000,000,000 stake in your company, congratulations, now it’s a unicorn—but (somewhat!) harder to actually raise $1 billion in cash. So here’s Felix Salmon at Axios: Meet the minotaurs — our term for the companies that would be worth more than $1 billion even if the only thing they did was to take the cash that they have raised and put it in a checking account. ... Axios has found 55 minotaurs as of early 2019. That's more than the 39 unicorns found by venture capitalist Aileen Lee when she invented the concept just over 5 years ago. (There are well over 300 unicorns today.) ... The rise of the minotaur reflects a new form of investing, epitomized by Japan's SoftBank, and a new form of company-building, dubbed "blitzscaling" by entrepreneurs Reid Hoffman and Chris Yeh. … It's a deliberate attempt to build a monopoly that can't be competed against unless you have pockets that are billions of dollars deep. It's the promise of monopoly rents in the future that makes billion-dollar investments attractive in the present. On the one hand, there is nothing in the term “minotaur” that suggests raising a lot of cash, or anything having to do with a billion dollars, or a genetic resemblance to unicorns. On the other hand, if you are worried about the rise of instant monopolies, then I suppose “minotaur” does capture the notion of something that is rare and mythical like a unicorn, but scarier. “I know that I am accused of arrogance and perhaps of misanthropy, and perhaps even of madness,” says Borges’s minotaur, which might as well be a critique of blitzscaling. Incidentally I feel like I have seen this concept—a company that has raised a billion dollars—described before under a different mythological name. Here is a claim that a company that has raised a billion dollars in a single round is called a “dragon.” Here, on the other hand, is a claim that “A dragon is a company that returns an entire fund — a ‘fund maker.’” Meanwhile a “pegasus” is either (1) a decacorn, (2) “ a unicorn that has grown its wings and actualized its value” (that is, sold or went public at a billion-dollar valuation), or (3) um a lifestyle startup I think? The point is that there is absolutely no science to any of this taxonomy, no hierarchical classification, and really almost no set of terms with agreed-upon meanings that allow conversations to happen efficiently at a deeper and more technical level. It’s just a series of funny words that you can say onstage at conferences so that everyone feels vaguely good about the chirpy cute ecosystem that they’re investing in. Look at all the adorable horsies! How could anyone object to all the horsies.

Oops! “I feel like I’m wasting my life,” he told me. “When I die, is anyone going to care that I earned an extra percentage point of return? My work feels totally meaningless.” He recognized the incredible privilege of his pay and status, but his anguish seemed genuine. “If you spend 12 hours a day doing work you hate, at some point it doesn’t matter what your paycheck says,” he told me. There’s no magic salary at which a bad job becomes good. He had received an offer at a start-up, and he would have loved to take it, but it paid half as much, and he felt locked into a lifestyle that made this pay cut impossible. “My wife laughed when I told her about it,” he said. That’s from a Harvard Business School graduate making $1.2 million a year in asset management business, and, um, what lifestyle is that? If you think “lifestyle” is synonymous with “mortgage and private-school tuition,” then the actual style of your life might end up being pretty bad.
