What is going on in this Wall Street Journal story about how “Deutsche Bank AG racked up a loss of $1.6 billion over nearly a decade on a complex municipal-bond investment”? The basic plot seems to be: In 2007, Deutsche Bank bought a “$7.8 billion portfolio of 500 municipal bonds,” insured by monoline insurers. In 2008, getting nervous about the municipal and monoline credits, Deutsche Bank bought credit-default swaps from Berkshire Hathaway Inc. “in a complex deal,” paying $140 million up front. The market got worse, and Deutsche Bank did not mark down the overall position as much and as quickly as some people think it should have. In 2016, Deutsche Bank got out of the position, with total losses, over the course of the trade, of about $1.6 billion. As part of the unwind, Berkshire Hathaway paid Deutsche Bank $195 million to terminate the CDS. First of all, that is a big loss, no? Looking at the total return of the Bloomberg Barclays Municipal Bond Index, it was up more than 50 percent over the life of this trade, with only two down years in 2008 (down 2.5 percent) and 2013 (down 2.6 percent). You could have steadily racked up losses of more than 20 percent on a diversified municipal-bond trade over that eight-year period—and some of Deutsche’s bonds seem to have been from Puerto Rico, so sure—but it would have taken either careful security selection or a certain amount of structuring. There was a certain amount of structuring: When the trade unwound in 2016, Deutsche Bank’s then-chief executive officer said that it had “unwound a particularly long-dated and complicated structured trade.” But what was the structuring? The story suggests that Deutsche bought bonds, and then it bought CDS from Berkshire Hathaway for $140 million, which ought to have hedged its risk of losses on the bonds. And then it sold the CDS back eight years later for $195 million, suggesting that Berkshire had a small loss. If Deutsche suffered billion-dollar-plus losses on the portfolio, and bought insurance on that portfolio from Berkshire, it’s odd that Berkshire only lost $55 million on that insurance. What was Deutsche paying it for? I assume the CDS was some sort of out-of-the-money super-senior-type deal, but I basically have no idea what happened here. In any case the implication is that Deutsche Bank should perhaps have recognized losses on the trade earlier than it did: Rather than bleeding in losses over the years, should it have taken a big hit early on? Maybe! To the extent Deutsche Bank’s position was a portfolio of municipal bonds , it is hard to imagine this being a big problem; those don’t necessarily trade as liquidly as stocks, but over the course of eight years they are going to print a few trades and you’ll be able to mark the portfolio to market. Presumably the main problem involved Deutsche’s valuation of some sort of illiquid bespoke derivative trade, and there was some debate about whether Deutsche did a good job of that. In 2011 it sent its auditors a white paper that “argued that the bank was doing a good job surveying the market and estimating municipal-bond recovery and default probabilities”; in 2017, it “opened an internal investigation into whether it had misled investors or needed to address problems with how it valued certain complex positions.” So there’s a bid/ask there, but without knowing anything about the trade or how Deutsche Bank valued it, it is hard to have a view. Still it is a good reminder of the mysteriousness of bank accounting. “A bank is a collection of reasonable guesses about valuation,” I once wrote; “There is no objective reality.” Don’t get me wrong, there are accounting rules; you can’t just make any guess you want. And over some timeframe, observable reality will catch up to you: If you buy $7.8 billion of stuff, wait eight years, and sell it for $5.2 billion, it is hard to escape the conclusion that you lost $1.6 billion. But the question here is, when did you lose the $1.6 billion? Naively, there is an argument that you lost it all at the end of the eight years, when you actually crystallized the loss by selling it; before that everything was uncertain. And I suppose there is an abstract argument that you lost it all at the beginning of the eight years, when you bought stuff that was inevitably-in-perfect-hindsight going to lose value. (You should have known, etc.) Neither of these arguments will be too persuasive to accountants, who try to impose more objective market- and evidence-based tests to determine when to recognize losses, but with complicated illiquid instruments those tests won’t necessarily produce clear-cut results. Just because you lost money later doesn’t exactly mean your earlier marks were wrong, but it doesn’t exactly not mean that either. A good rough intuitive test, though, would be that if you buy $7.8 billion of stuff, sell it eight years later for $5.2 billion, and spend the intervening eight years complaining and fretting about how bad the stuff is, you probably should have recognized bigger losses earlier. That, again, is not the sort of test that will be recognizable to accountants, but it does seem like a decent heuristic for how newspapers and regulators and the public are going to think about things. If you know your bonds are going to go bad, then in some loose accounting sense they already have.

By the way, it’s a cliché by now to point out that Warren Buffett criticizes derivatives as “weapons of mass destruction” while also constantly and gleefully trading weird derivatives, including the ones that apparently caused some mass destruction to Deutsche Bank’s balance sheet. But this is not unique to Buffett; in general, my “prudent risk management” is your “opaque financial engineering.” Here’s a funny story about how Vivendi SA is fighting with activist hedge fund Elliott Management over equity collars: Elliott acquired a stake in Telecom Italia SpA last year and “wrested control of the board from 24 per cent shareholder Vivendi,” and Vivendi has been harshly critical of Elliott because it acquired and hedged that stake with a collar: Elliott last month stepped up its stake in Telecom Italia to 9.4 per cent after renegotiating a hedging facility called an equity collar with JPMorgan, which it used to help build its initial stake and protect just over half of its shares from any falls in price. Vivendi has repeatedly hit out at Elliott’s use of collars as it has shielded the New York-based firm from some of the losses on its investment. A spokesperson for Vivendi told the Financial Times on Wednesday that Elliott’s use of “financial engineering tactics” had handed the firm a “€300m profit so far”, following a steep fall in Telecom Italia’s shares since May last year. Yes but: But despite Vivendi’s anger at the ploy, the company itself used an equity collar to help build its own stake in Telecom Italia. It has also used similar facilities to hedge its holdings in other companies. Ha, well. Vivendi argues that it used the collar “to quickly build a position in Telecom Italia and unwound its collar after only three months,” while Elliott “uses a collar on a much longer period with the aim of benefiting from the shares’ downside, hence not being aligned with the interests of the company’s other shareholders.” I will say that if you are going to be an activist in a stock, and you have hedged your downside in the stock, that definitely seems like a fair subject for criticism. You are not, in an important sense, along for the ride that you are taking the other shareholders on. The collar as a stake-acquisition tool is a fun piece of financial engineering, incidentally. The basic idea of a collar is that a bank takes away most of the upside and downside risk of the customer’s stake. If the stock is at $100, the bank might sell the customer a $90-strike put and buy back a $110-strike call, with the result that the customer is only exposed to a narrow range of price moves: If the stock goes down a bit, the customer loses money; if it goes up a bit, the customer makes money; if it goes up or down a lot, though, most of the move is the bank’s problem (or gain). At a very general level, you can just think of this as the customer selling a lot of its stock to the bank: The customer owns some stock, but the bank gets most of the gains and losses on the stock, so economically it’s as though the bank owns most of the stock and the customer owns less.[1] (Legally, though, the customer still owns all the stock.) The bank does not want to economically own a lot of stock—it is not in the business of taking stock-price risk on huge stakes—and so it will have to sell the stock in order to hedge its position. But since it doesn’t actually own the stock—it is economically exposed to it, but the customer still technically owns it—it will have to borrow the stock and sell it short to do the hedge. This creates the possibility of the collar as stake-acquisition tool: If the bank is borrowing the stock to sell it short to hedge the collar, why not borrow it and sell it short to the customer? The mechanics are: A customer wants to buy a lot of stock, and then economically sell most of it to the bank to hedge its stock-price risk. If the customer does that, the bank will want to economically sell most of the stock to hedge its stock-price risk. So the bank can just borrow the stock and sell it directly to the customer, so that the customer can sell it back to the bank, making everything quick and tidy.[2] It definitely feels like a sleight of hand: Before the trade, neither the bank nor the customer owns any stock, but then they each sell each other some stock, and the result is that the customer ends up with a big chunk of stock (but limited economic exposure). If you were the CEO of a public company, and one day you discovered that an activist hedge fund has acquired a big voting interest in your company because a bank sold some stock short to the hedge fund in exchange for the hedge fund economically selling it back to the bank, you would probably be annoyed too.

Here is a story about the last days of Theranos Inc., the Blood Unicorn ( Elasmotherium haimatos ) that imploded in fraud charges last year. It is full of amazing details. For instance, after John Carreyrou of the Wall Street Journal started reporting that Theranos’s technology was fake, Chief Executive Officer Elizabeth Holmes developed “an unconventional plan for redemption” that involved buying a Siberian husky puppy, naming him Balto, and bringing him to the medical lab without bothering to house-train him, sure. It also clears up one question I had, which is why Holmes seems to have run a huge fraud without ever selling stock or taking much money out for herself. One possible answer is that Holmes had a lavish lifestyle, and that everything—private jets, security, “all those Birkin bags,” publicists, “meals, clothing and other social activities”—was expensed to the company. You don’t need to steal cash if you can bill your entire life to the company. But the image that I could not get over was this: After the Journal broke the news that the company was being investigated, the board suggested that Holmes take the Theranos blood test and compare it with results from two other competing labs and one university lab, this person said. If all the results were the same, Theranos could prove to regulators and the media, so went the logic, that their blood-testing products worked perfectly. If the tests showed that Theranos’s results were off, the board suggested that Holmes could direct the company’s considerable raised capital toward fixing the problem. Holmes agreed to the trial but then withheld the results, the former board member told me. When the board asked about the findings, Holmes seemed to offer a series of obfuscations. Sometimes she would say she was waiting on results; at other times, she said there had been problems with the tests. Eventually, this got heated. Just … just sort of imagine being a director of a revolutionary blood-testing company, and spending years congratulating yourself for how cutting-edge the technology is and how much money the company is worth, and then one day reading in the paper that your company is being investigated for fraud, and coming in to the next board meeting and being like “hey uh so this might be a dumb question but have we ever considered checking to see if our blood tests work?” If you are asking that question at that point, everything is irretrievably ruined. When the company is in early stages and asks you to join its board, sure, go ahead, ask it to validate its blood-testing technology against outside labs. When you’re on the board and the CEO tells you that the product is ready to go to market, sure, absolutely, ask that she validate the technology first. But when the company has already spent years telling everyone that its technology works perfectly, and using that technology on thousands of actual live patients, and you read in the paper that the technology is fake, it is waaaaaaaaaaaay too late to check. I mean, fine, you might as well ask, better late than never, but at that point you have to know that you’re not going to like the answer. And if somehow you don’t know that, you definitely figure it out at the next board meeting when you are like “okay so first order of business, we were going to check to see if our blood tests work, how’d that go,” and Holmes stares straight ahead without blinking for a long time and then says “great, great, everything is great, unfortunately the puppy ate the results but trust me they were perfect.”

We talked last month about how much IEX, the Investors Exchange, enjoys trolling the other stock exchanges about their high connectivity and data fees. Oversimplifying: IEX makes its money by charging traders to trade, while the other exchanges make more money from fixed fees for data feeds and high-speed connections; this tends to make IEX cheaper for relatively infrequent traders (who pay by the trade), and the other exchanges cheaper for the most frequent traders (who can amortize their connection fees over a lot of trades). I tend to think that either model is a perfectly plausible way to make money, but it is also the case that trading firms don’t have much choice but to pay the other exchanges’ high fixed prices to connect, and that those prices, which have nothing to do with the exchanges’ cost of providing connectivity, can feel arbitrary and annoying and monopolistic. And so last year the Securities and Exchange Commission rejected some price increases for data feeds that had been proposed by the New York Stock Exchange and Nasdaq, because the exchanges hadn’t provided a good enough justification for the price increase. Since then IEX has embarked on a merciless trolling campaign to try to make investors and regulators suspicious of the data and connectivity fees, including last month’s white paper comparing those fees to the cost of providing them. The latest is a fake infomercial on YouTube in which a guy in a fleece vest pitches “the WonderCable,” which allows you to connect to “those fusty old exchanges and the data they distribute.” It’s kind of funny, if you like this sort of thing. “Other places might try to sell you this cable for 100 bucks—let’s be honest, it’s just a cable—but if you call in the next 10 minutes it can be yours, not for $100, not for $75, we’re talking recurring monthly payments of $19,999.95.” It makes the same point as the white paper, but more vividly. Really more non-consumer-facing businesses should make high-production-value videos attacking their competitors. If you run a hedge fund and you hire actors, make a professionally produced 90-second YouTube video insulting another hedge fund, and send it to me, I cannot promise that I will write about it here, but I will definitely give it some consideration.

[1] Obviously this is very loose. Derivatives people would compute the Black-Scholes delta of the put that the bank sold and the call that the bank bought, and add them up to get a number, usually expressed as a percentage, that you could loosely describe as “the amount of the customer’s position that the bank economically owns.” Collar deltas are quite commonly well above 50 percent, meaning, as I say in the text, that “economically it’s as though the bank owns most of the stock and the customer owns less,” though you would not ordinarily describe it that way. Remember when Tesla Inc. Chief Executive Officer Elon Musk committed securities fraud by falsely claiming on Twitter that he had secured financing to take Tesla private? Remember how Musk and Tesla settled with the Securities and Exchange Commission by agreeing to pay fines and have Tesla lawyers review Musk’s tweets before he sent them out? Remember how Tesla hired a high-powered Washington litigator as its general counsel and Musk’s Twitter babysitter? Remember how Musk then said in a 60 Minutes interview that he and Tesla were absolutely not ever going to comply by the terms of the settlement that they had signed, that he does not respect the SEC, and that no lawyer would ever pre-clear his tweets? How’s that working out? Elon Musk corrected a prediction for how many cars Tesla Inc. would make in 2019, just hours after tweeting that production would reach about 500,000 vehicles this year. The electric-car pioneer, who has a track record of snafus on Twitter, said he intended to tweet that Tesla expects to be making cars at an annual rate of about 500,000 by the end of 2019. Musk said Tesla still forecasts deliveries of about 400,000 vehicles this year. “Meant to say annualized production rate at end of 2019 probably around 500k, ie 10k cars/week,” Musk tweeted, four hours after saying it would make 500,000 cars in 2019. “Deliveries for year still estimated to be about 400k.” It was all after trading hours, so whatever, but it’s the principle of the thing. The principle apparently being that Musk should have an absolutely unfettered right, as the CEO of a large public company, to make false statements of material fact about the financial and operational results of his company, whenever he wants. “Hello, First Amendment,” Musk actually said, once, on television, about this subject. Honestly, imagine being Tesla’s lawyer and waking up to this nonsense. I would quit! I am not alone; Tesla’s lawyer actually did quit this morning: Tesla Inc.’s general counsel is leaving just two months after being hired in the wake of Elon Musk’s run-in with U.S. securities regulators. Shares of the electric-car maker declined on the news. Dane Butswinkas, the Washington trial lawyer who represented Musk in his legal battle with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission last fall, will return full-time to his legal practice in Washington, Tesla said in an emailed statement. Jonathan Chang, a vice president in Tesla’s legal department, takes over effective immediately. Man, that is the way to do it. That guy has plenty of money, and who needs this aggravation? Good for him. At least he can quit. What on earth would you do here if you were the SEC, though? The SEC has a settlement with Tesla, approved by a federal judge, requiring the company to “implement mandatory procedures and controls to oversee all of Elon Musk’s communications regarding the Company made in any format … and to pre-approve any such written communications that contain, or reasonably could contain, information material to the Company or its shareholders.” Tesla has made it absolutely clear that it never intends to comply with that settlement, that it will continue to allow Musk to make material public statements without any sort of controls whatsoever, and that no lawyer can ever tame him. Don’t get me wrong, this is funny , and I enjoy it, but it is also a genuine problem for the SEC. It is hard to enforce securities laws against everyone else if you’re openly letting a high-profile CEO ignore them. At the same time, though, the SEC’s relatively lenient settlement with Musk and Tesla was probably correct . Musk is important to the success of Tesla, which is a $50 billion company with an admirable social mission and cool cars, and, despite the volume of false statements he keeps making about his company, most of them are fairly harmless and have no malicious intent. Keeping him off Twitter, as the SEC has been trying to do, would be good, but keeping him from running Tesla —as the SEC’s original lawsuit halfheartedly gestured at doing—would be bad. That is just as true now, after Musk’s months of flouting the settlement, as it was when they signed the settlement in the first place. If the SEC’s mission is protecting investors, it can’t move too harshly against Musk: Banning him from running a public company would seriously harm Tesla’s investors, even if it might be good in some generic sense for the integrity of markets. Still they could go back to court and try to fine him a whopping great amount for breaching the settlement: If a $20 million fine didn’t stop him from tweeting, maybe a $200 million fine will? Also, if I were the SEC I might consider trying to go after Tesla’s board of directors. Shouldn’t they be, you know, acting like directors? Shouldn’t they be supervising the CEO, and making sure their company complies with the terms of the settlement that it agreed to? Musk is a liability for Tesla—the tweets, the drama—but he is also an asset; the board, on the other hand, doesn’t seem to be adding much value, or taking its role at all seriously. Maybe the SEC should put them on the hook, threatening to fine them or ban them from serving as public-company directors if they can’t make their company follow the terms of its settlement. Of course that is a little unfair; it’s not like they can control Musk either. But somebody has to try! “We can’t stop him,” the SEC might reasonably say, “so let’s make it your problem.”

We talked yesterday about Aurelius Capital Management LP’s lawsuit against Windstream Holdings Inc., which resulted on Friday in a $310 million judgment for Aurelius and a declaration that Windstream is in default on its bonds. Aurelius also had something to say about the case yesterday, in a truly amazing victory-lap press release that I am going to quote at length: We take no pleasure in Windstream's resulting financial predicament. Windstream could easily have averted it – first by not playing fast and loose with its noteholders in 2015, hoping nobody would hold the company to account, and second by settling. Instead, Windstream wasted an exorbitant amount – more than would have been needed to settle with us at the time – on an ineffective exchange offer and then on litigation. In our view, a management and a board with an extreme and unwarranted assessment of Windstream's legal case chose to bet the company. The company lost. According to its statement last Friday, Windstream now intends to appeal. This is welcome news for our fund, as it will require Windstream to post a surety bond exceeding $300 million. That surety bond will pay in full the notes our fund owns when Windstream loses the appeal. We are happy to take the surety company's credit over Windstream's. To noteholders who chose to play the company's game even after it had broken its promise, we wish you luck with your exchange notes. Between their dubious status and their OID risk in bankruptcy, we suspect you will need it. “We take no pleasure in Windstream's resulting financial predicament,” says Aurelius in what might be the most pleasure-taking financial press release I’ve ever read. In general financial press releases do not bother to say “we take no pleasure in” whatever, because it goes without saying; on the rare occasions when they do, you can pretty much believe them. “I take no pleasure in reporting a fifth consecutive year of losses,” a hedge fund manager will say, and, right, probably. Here, though, the whole thing just oozes pleasure, although of a somewhat perverse kind. Aurelius’s last paragraph—wishing the exchange noteholders good luck—hits on what might turn out to be the nuttiest thing in this case. Windstream violated a covenant in its bonds, and Aurelius called it out, and Windstream scrambled to defend itself by retroactively getting bondholders to consent to the violation. Most bondholders were happy to go along, but the problem is that Aurelius had bought a majority position in one series of bonds, the 6.375 percent notes due 2023, and so could force a default on those bonds even if the holders of other bonds consented. Windstream had the clever idea of asking its other, more pliable bondholders to exchange into additional 6.375 percent notes, diluting Aurelius’s majority of that series and giving their consent. This almost worked—Windstream issued $560 million of new 6.375 percent bonds to exchanging bondholders who then outvoted Aurelius—but Aurelius argued, and the court agreed, that the exchange offer violated the terms of the indenture and so was invalid. It’s clear enough what that means for Aurelius’s case: It means that the 6.375 percent bonds didn’t consent to the covenant breach, and so Aurelius gets to declare a default and accelerate its bonds. But it’s not so clear what it means for the investors who exchanged their old bonds for $560 million of new 6.375 percent bonds that a judge just declared invalid. I asked yesterday: “Do they not have the 6.375 percent bonds? Do they still have their old bonds? The opinion is not clear. It seems bad!” Aurelius has gotten Windstream’s other bondholders into quite a mess, and it wants to make sure that they know it. Elsewhere, here is Julia Hoggett, Director of Market Oversight at the U.K. Financial Conduct Authority, speaking about manufactured defaults in credit-default-swap trades: We have observed behaviour in the CDS market in other jurisdictions that appears to involve intentional, or ‘manufactured,’ events. As Andrew Bailey said in a Bloomberg interview last year, we feel this behaviour is on ‘the wrong side of the line’. It goes against the intended purpose of these instruments. Manufactured credit events may also constitute market abuse by the involved parties. We have been speaking to firms, ISDA and other regulators and support the work being undertaken. We look forward to swift and effective action being taken by the industry. Where necessary, we will take appropriate action to uphold our statutory objectives. To be clear, whatever you think of Aurelius’s attack on Windstream, it is not a “manufactured default”: Aurelius didn’t connive with Windstream to do a fake-o default to trigger a CDS payout; instead, it discovered a real default on Windstream’s bonds and then put Windstream to the sword to enforce the terms of the bonds. (And, everyone assumes, to get a CDS payout.) For the company , this is obviously much worse—instead of getting some cheap financing, as usually occurs in “manufactured default” cases, Windstream gets a possible bankruptcy—but I suppose it does look better to a market regulator. It’s not collusive, not market manipulation; unnecessary though the default might be, at least it is real .

All else equal, short-term debt should usually have less credit risk than long-term debt. Partly this is a matter of predictability: If you lend to a creditworthy borrower now, it will probably still be creditworthy in a year, but more can go wrong in two years, or 20. Partly it is a sort of practical seniority: If a borrower has a limited amount of money, it will tend to pay its debts in the order in which they come due, which means that it might pay its one-year debt in full in a year and not have enough money left over to pay its two-year, or 20-year, debt. Here is an unusual counterexample: Top Deutsche Bank AG executives were so concerned after the 2016 U.S. election that the Trump Organization might default on about $340 million of loans while Donald Trump was in office that they discussed extending repayment dates until after the end of a potential second term in 2025, according to people with knowledge of the discussions. Members of the bank’s management board, including then Chief Executive Officer John Cryan, were leery of the public relations disaster they would face if they went after the assets of a sitting president, said the people, who asked for anonymity because the discussions were private. The bank ultimately decided against restructuring the loans to the Trump Organization, which come due in 2023 and 2024, and chose instead not to do any new business with Trump while he is president, one of the people said. If the president of the United States owes you money, and you send him a quarterly statement saying “you are a valued customer and we love doing business with you, no payment is currently due, just wanted to say hi,” then that’s fine. If on the other hand you send him a bill for $340 million, he might not pay it, and then what do you do? You sue him for defaulting on his debt, and he says things like “no” or “fake news!” or “Deutsche Bank is the enemy of the people,” and then you are in a horrible mess forever. Sure your legal arguments might be impeccable, but law is not exclusively a matter of contracts and statutes and precedents and arguments; if the president of the United States decides that he does not owe you money, then he has a certain amount of power to make that come true. But if you wait until he is not the president anymore, then (you hope!) normal legal arguments resume their normal importance. Best to wait until then to send him the bill. By the way, imagine being a borrower and having your bank call you up and just volunteer “hey, we don’t need you to pay us back in seven years, why don’t you take nine?” It just feels like a pretty good sign that they’re terrified of you. You gotta take advantage of that. It’s weird because they are already negotiating against themselves, but that doesn’t mean you can’t negotiate against them too. “Sure, fine, I guess I am willing to take some extra time to pay you back, but only if you cut the principal in half and reduce the interest rate to zero.” You’re never going to have more leverage than when your bank calls you up and begs you not to pay them back.

“That is absolutely silly,” says Glenn Hubbard, in this joint interview of him and Joseph Stiglitz in a Columbia Business School investment newsletter. “I haven’t seen that as a major problem, but I haven’t really been following it,” adds Stiglitz. Without getting into the details of their responses, I want to make two more general points: Some people who have thought about the rise of common ownership of multiple firms in the same sector by large institutional investors have concluded that it reduces product-market competition, and others have concluded that it does not, but everyone who hasn’t thought about it instinctively assumes that it is absurd. I do not know if that is useful information—most facially counterintuitive things are false, but some are true—but it does strike me as interesting. As I have written before, the premises of this theory are very straightforward and intuitive, and really “if all the companies are owned by the same people then they won’t compete with each other” seems more like the simple obvious naive view than the arcane galaxy-brain take. It might be wrong , but it is just a bit strange that everyone’s immediate reaction is to laugh at it. People are now asking Nobel-Prize-winning economists, perhaps even with a straight face, “should index funds be illegal,” and it is clearly my fault. (The interviewer quotes me.) I do not think that the theory itself is silly, but obviously that question is silly— that’s why I always phrase it that way, as a sort of maximalist reductio-ad-absurdum joke—and I am pleased to have done my small part to make high-level economics a bit sillier.

Ugh, nobody looks particularly good in this Windstream case, do they? Windstream Holdings Inc. is a rural telecommunications company that, in 2015, spun off its copper wires and fiber-optic cables into a real-estate investment trust (now called Uniti Group Inc.), and then leased the wires back from the REIT, because that’s how business works now. The problem is that Windstream had issued some bonds, and those bonds had covenants, and the covenants included a specific promise not to do this exact thing.[1] Now this is not necessarily a dealbreaker: The covenant doesn’t mean that you can’t do it, though it does say that; it just means that you need to ask the bondholders’ permission to do it. If the sale-leaseback transaction is good for the company, and not too harmful for the bondholders, you can go out and seek a consent from the majority of your bondholders. You offer them a bit of extra money, they give you the consent, you do the thing. Windstream did not do that. Instead it just sort of ignored the covenant. I mean, not quite; Windstream did some structuring that allowed it to argue that it had complied with the covenant, but that argument was pretty weak, weak enough that I’m only going to discuss it in a footnote.[2] Certainly it ignored the spirit of the covenant, and mostly also the letter. So Windstream was rather unpleasant to its creditors in all of this structuring, but on the other hand, the creditors don’t seem to have minded all that much. They never did anything about it, anyway. They never sued, or declared a default. And Windstream kept making its interest payments. It was fine, whatever.[3] Or it was fine until 2017, when New York hedge fund Aurelius Capital Management LP bought a bunch of Windstream’s bonds and sued Windstream, claiming that it had defaulted on those bonds two years earlier and demanding immediate payment of the bonds. Windstream defended itself vigorously, including by using an exchange offer to try to get bondholders to consent retroactively to the sale-leaseback. The bondholders—other than Aurelius—mostly did consent, but the exchange offer didn’t work for technical reasons that I will also relegate to a footnote.[4] And on Friday, Aurelius won its lawsuit in federal district court. Here is the opinion, by Judge Jesse Furman, declaring Windstream in default and awarding Aurelius $310.5 million plus interest. But Aurelius comes out looking pretty unpleasant too. For one thing, there is that two-year delay: If Windstream defaulted on its bonds in 2015, that didn’t hurt Aurelius, because as far as I can tell it didn’t even own the bonds at the time. Windstream and its bondholders were just bopping along, perfectly satisfied with each other, and then Aurelius showed up and bought bonds, by all indications, purely to call for a default. Rude! Mary Childs writes at Barron’s: “This whole thing arose, credit market participants say, in part because there was not much better to do in distressed debt at the time, so bored former lawyers sitting at hedge funds trolled old bond documents looking for something to do.” Or as Windstream put it, “the proverbial egg has not only been scrambled, but eaten and digested by marketplace investors long ago.” And then Aurelius came along and, um, I guess you can extend that digestive metaphor if you want. For another thing, there are credit-default swaps. I mean, everyone supposes there are, though Aurelius has not confirmed it, and it’s oddly not mentioned in the opinion. Aurelius probably bought its Windstream bonds at a discount, and now has a judgment requiring them to be paid off at par, but that can’t really be the whole game here: Windstream “has warned that a defeat could force it to seek bankruptcy protection or liquidation,” and in fact Aurelius’s bonds were trading below 40 cents on the dollar this morning, well below what it paid for them. Accelerating bonds doesn’t necessarily get you paid back at par, if you accelerate the company right into bankruptcy. Instead, the universal assumption is that Aurelius has also bought a lot of credit-default swaps that will pay out if Windstream defaults on its debt: By pushing Windstream into default, Aurelius will make a profit on its CDS, even if it loses money on the bonds. And, look, in general, I am all for CDS creativity, but here even I find it distasteful. “We, along with others in the market, found Windstream’s arguments that Aurelius pursued this litigation in bad faith and in order to ensure a payout on its CDS to be compelling,” wrote analysts at CreditSights. And my old law firm, Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, wrote a memo last summer about “The Rise of the Net-Short Debt Activist,” that is, activist investors who own more CDS than debt and use their debt positions to agitate for default: The Windstream situation, regardless of how it is resolved, exemplifies the risks that net-short debt activism can pose to companies. Aurelius has publicly questioned Windstream’s financial position and threatened Windstream with an outcome—defaults on its bond debt—that could cause significant damage to Windstream’s other stakeholders, including other creditors, shareholders and employees. While short sellers in the equity markets might “talk down” a stock, they have no similar legal mechanism to inflict such wide-ranging harm on a target. Usually around here when we talk about CDS buyers causing a “manufactured default,” it is in cooperation with the company, and while lots of people find it bad and manipulative, it does help the company get financing. Like, if a hedge fund pays a company to do a quick technical default to trigger CDS, at least now the company has money . It’s a way for real companies to get financing at the expense of CDS sellers, to whom the company after all has no obligations; I tend to think it’s rather neat. But “the Windstream situation represents an escalation of the tactic,” notes Sujeet Indap at the Financial Times, “since Aurelius was offering no benefit to the company.” There’s a zero-sum bet between Aurelius and its CDS counterparties, and in order to get that bet to pay out, Aurelius has pretty much burned down a public company. It seems a bit much. Is there any argument—other than “the bonds say what they say so they have to be enforced”—that this is a good result? “The cop of the credit markets, Aurelius, rides again,” writes Childs, “and we can all rest easy knowing the black-and-white agreements of bond indentures, once written, are immutable.” There is something to that: You can choose to view Aurelius not as an interloper messing up a perfectly amicable situation between a company and its bondholders, but rather a vindicator of the rights of bondholders against an overbearing issuer. The story might be that, in 2015, Windstream flagrantly violated the terms of its bonds and dared its bondholders to do something about it, and those bondholders were too meek or confused to defend themselves. They were simple long-only credit investors, they don’t have the time or inclination to sue, their positions weren’t concentrated enough to make it worthwhile, they weren’t expert document-readers, or whatever: They were mugged by Windstream and had no practical way to stand up for themselves. But eventually they (well, some of them) sold their bonds to Aurelius, and Aurelius stood up for bondholders’ rights. And now other bond issuers will think twice before trying to steamroll their bondholders in the future, knowing that Aurelius may be lurking to call them on it.[5] It’s the principle of the thing, the principle being “don’t do sale-leaseback transactions if you’ve promised your bondholders that you won’t.” Maybe? The problem here is that Windstream’s bond prices have collapsed since Aurelius got involved. Perhaps Windstream’s bondholders had no complaints about the 2015 spin-off, or perhaps they had complaints that they kept to themselves, but now they are looking at huge losses and a possible bankruptcy. When Aurelius came along, Windstream’s other bondholders did not applaud or join its lawsuit: Instead, Windstream asked them to retroactively consent to the sale-leaseback, and they rushed to do so. Windstream might have mistreated its bondholders, but Aurelius’s plans to vindicate bondholders’ rights seems suspiciously terrible for the actual bondholders.

The basic issue in high-frequency trading is: A thing is for sale at the same price on different exchanges. The price changes on one exchange—for instance, because someone bought the thing, pushing the price up. Should you still be able buy the thing at the old price on another exchange, a fraction of a second later? There are three possible answers to that question. One answer is: Yes, you should be able to buy the thing at the old price on other exchanges; there should be a grace period between when a price changes in one place and when it changes somewhere else. This is the actual plot of the book “Flash Boys,” and the basic premise behind IEX, the Investors Exchange, although strictly speaking it is not how IEX currently operates. The problem in “Flash Boys” was that investors would buy stock on one exchange, and then they would want to buy the same stock at the same price on other exchanges, but high-speed traders would update their prices on the other exchanges faster than the investors could send orders to those exchanges, which felt unfair to them. So IEX built a “speed bump” designed to allow people to buy stock on IEX and then buy stock on other exchanges before they could update their prices, though, again, when IEX became a public stock exchange it eliminated that particular aspect of its speed bump.[6] Another answer is: No, you should not be able to buy the thing at the old price on other exchanges, and in fact the people who list the thing for sale on the other exchanges should get their own grace period to update their prices to make sure you can’t buy at the old price. The problem here is that market makers—firms that post bids and offers on a thing for a living—will list a thing for sale on an exchange, and then the price of the thing will change elsewhere, but before the market makers can update their prices, high-speed traders from the other exchange will swoop down on their orders and buy from them at the old price. This feels unfair to the market makers. Exchanges tend to cater to the interests of market makers, and so, since IEX was able to get one version of its speed bump approved by regulators, other exchanges have been experimenting with market-maker-friendly, “last-look”-style speed bumps. We talked in 2016 about a proposed speed bump favoring market makers at the Chicago Stock Exchange (which was put on hold in 2017), and now there is this, in the precious-metals futures market: Exchange giant Intercontinental Exchange Inc., known as ICE, quietly unveiled a plan earlier this month to impose a three-millisecond “speed bump”—or brief delay—on some trades in gold and silver futures. … Under the plan, the three-millisecond delay would apply to incoming orders seeking to hit unexecuted buy or sell orders already posted on ICE. Traders posting new orders to be displayed on the exchange wouldn’t be affected. Such a design would benefit market makers, the firms that facilitate trading by continuously quoting prices for stocks or futures. Market makers would be able to cancel or adjust their quotes without having to wait three milliseconds. The losers from ICE’s plan would be high-speed trading firms that “pick off” slightly out-of-date quotes posted by slower-moving market makers—in other words, buying just as the price is about to tick up or selling just before the price drops. These two answers can look superficially similar: They both involve “speed bumps,” and they both claim to be solving the problem of “high-frequency traders” racing from one exchange to another to take advantage of slower and more honest traders. But they are opposites: One sort of speed bump imagines the market makers as evil high-frequency traders, nefariously updating their prices before honest traders can buy from them at the old price; the other imagines the liquidity takers as evil high-frequency traders, nefariously buying at the old price before honest market makers can update their prices. It is tempting to say “one of them must be wrong,” but it is also perfectly possible that they’re both wrong. The third answer to the question, then, is: Who cares, none of this has any moral valence whatsoever, nobody should get any special grace period. If you get your order to the other exchange before market makers can update their prices, then you get to buy the thing at the old price; if market makers on the other exchange are able to update their prices before you send in your order, then you have to buy the thing at the new price. This answer is not perfect! It rewards people for the probably-not-all-that-socially-useful work of racing from one exchange to another, somewhat disadvantages slow fundamental traders, and encourages arguably wasteful investments in technology to move signals from one exchange to another at high speeds. But the advantage to this answer is that it is intuitively fairer than giving either side its own special grace period. It is also less administratively complicated: You don’t have to debate which orders are morally good and which are evil and high-frequency; you just process them in the order in which they come in.

Here is a New York Times story about the “McKinsey Investment Office, or MIO Partners,” the in-house hedge fund of consulting firm McKinsey & Co., which invests employee money, including in companies that McKinsey advises. “That web of relationships underscores the unusual nature of McKinsey’s hedge fund, and the potential for undisclosed conflicts of interest between the fund’s investments and the advice the firm sells to clients,” says the Times, and I suppose there are some shady elements: When McKinsey advises on a bankruptcy, for instance, and its hedge fund owns one or another slice of the capital structure, then there’s a clear potential for conflicts of interest. Mostly, though, it’s hard to get too worked up about this. For one thing, most of the fund’s money seems to be run by outside advisers, and even the stuff run by McKinsey employees seems to be mostly walled off from the consulting business. For another thing, the incentives are mostly good: McKinsey’s consultants are trying to make the company better, and its hedge fund is invested in the company and wants the company to get better, so there is no problem here. “The firm’s partners stood to profit from their own advice,” says the Times about McKinsey’s indirect investments in Valeant Pharmaceuticals, but why would that be bad? If they do stuff to make the stock go up, then they make money, but that is also what the company wants. (In the event, Valeant’s stock went down, which was bad for both Valeant and McKinsey.) Really companies ought to demand that their consultants buy some of their stock, so they have some skin in the game with their advice. Of course, what would really be scandalous is if McKinsey’s hedge fund shorted companies that the firm advised, and then the consultants tried to give those companies ruinous advice. You couldn’t advertise that strategy, but much of the Times story is about how secretive MIO is, and if you can be secretive enough then maybe you could pull off this trade.

I think if you asked most people what the goal of SoftBank Group Corp.’s $100-billion-ish Vision Fund is, they would say something like: The Vision Fund is designed to buy large stakes in late-stage technology companies at wildly inflated valuations. SoftBank, and the Vision Fund’s investors, probably wouldn’t say that; “wildly inflated valuations” is not the way one describes one’s own investment process. But it seems to be the consensus of tech companies (who love selling stakes to the Vision Fund), venture capitalists (who also love selling stakes to the Vision Fund, but meanwhile complain that its buying spree is pushing up valuations and making it more difficult for them to find their own deals), and outside observers (who love making fun of the prices that the Vision Fund pays). There is something vaguely public-spirited about that mission: Flinging vast amounts of cash at tech companies probably enhances the tech ecosystem, encourages other people to start tech companies, and gives the Vision Fund an important role in shaping the future of technology. But, uh, maybe a little less so if the Vision Fund is mostly buying tech stakes at high valuations from SoftBank? Here is a story about how the Vision Fund’s main investors, Saudia Arabia’s Public Investment Fund and Abu Dhabi’s Mubadala Investment Co., “ are complaining about the high prices the fund’s manager, SoftBank Group Corp., has paid for tech companies and the control wielded by SoftBank Chief Executive Masayoshi Son over investment decisions,” that includes this detail: Investors have also complained about SoftBank’s strategy of investing in companies first, then transferring the stakes to the Vision Fund later. One person familiar with the Middle East investors’ thinking expressed concerns about whether SoftBank was taking advantage of high tech valuations to crystallize gains at the expense of PIF and Mubadala. SoftBank has transferred, sold or is planning to sell to the Vision Fund at least $26.3 billion worth of stakes in companies that it originally purchased for around $24.9 billion during the past few years, according to company filings. … The issue isn’t necessarily the premium over SoftBank’s cost for the investments; it is that the company is buying and transferring stakes while the market is high, potentially setting the fund up for losses. Fair! Though it does feel a little like, well, you signed up for the Tech Stakes At Inflated Valuations Fund, what exactly did you expect?

[1] The key bonds here are Windstream’s 6.375 percent bonds due 2023 (CUSIP 97381WAZ7), which were issued in January 2013. The indenture for those bonds says that “t he Company shall not, and shall not permit any of its Restricted Subsidiaries to, enter into any Sale and Leaseback Transaction,” with some exceptions if, basically, Windstream is not too indebted after the sale-leaseback. (It was.) “‘Sale and Leaseback Transaction’ means,” says the indenture, “with respect to any Person, any transaction involving any of the assets or properties of such Person whether now owned or hereafter acquired, whereby such Person sells or otherwise transfers such assets or properties and then or thereafter leases such assets or properties or any part thereof or any other assets or properties which such Person intends to use for substantially the same purpose or purposes as the assets or properties sold or transferred.” [2] The argument is that the bonds were issued by a company called Windstream Services LLC, which is now a subsidiary of Windstream Holdings Inc., the public-company parent, and the indenture forbade any sale-leaseback by Services, but not by Holdings. Of course all of the copper wires resided at Services and its restricted subsidiaries. (And were part of the assets that supported the bond issuance in the first place.) Services transferred the wires to Uniti (the sale), but Holdings leased them back. Windstream’s argument is that since Holdings, not Services, did the leasing, it’s not a sale-leaseback covered by the indenture. The problem is that Services is the company that (1) sold the assets, (2) uses them now, and (3) comes up with the money that Holdings uses to make the lease payments. In fact, according to Friday’s court opinion in the case, “in internal documents and public filings, Holdings itself reflects the payments from the Transferor Subsidiaries as a form of revenue — ‘[l]easing income from subsidiaries’ — and the Transferor Subsidiaries reflect their corresponding liabilities as ‘[l]ong-term lease obligations’ and associated ‘[p]ayments under long-term lease obligations.’” That is: Services sold the assets to Uniti, and then Holdings leased them back from Uniti, and then Services leased them back from Holdings. There is no lease agreement between Services and Holdings, in order to give Services some argument that it is not a lessor, but practically speaking it is. I suppose there is some argument that this is not quite as credit-negative for Services as a simple sale-leaseback would be. In particular, if Services stopped making payments, it would not be in default on any agreements, as it would be in the case of a sale-leaseback in which it was officially the lessor. Still that is not much comfort: If Services stopped making payments, then Holdings would be in default on its lease (since Holdings has no independent operations and gets all of its money from Services), and so Services would presumably lose access to the wires—which is the problem that sale-leaseback covenants are mostly designed to prevent. [3] Windstream’s 6.375 percent bonds were trading in the neighborhood of 100 cents on the dollar in late 2014 when the spin-off transaction was getting rolling; by April 2015, when it closed, the bonds were south of 90 cents on the dollar. I suppose that is some evidence that the transaction was credit-negative and so it would have been hard to get consent, though on the other hand the fact that the bondholders didn’t call a default at the time is evidence the other way. [4] When Aurelius first sent a notice of default, Windstream went out to try to retroactively get consent for the spin-off and sale-leaseback. This was complicated by the fact that Aurelius had bought a majority of one series of Windstream bonds (the 6.375 percent notes due in 2023) and was not going to give consent, meaning that Windstream would be in default on those bonds even if the other bonds consented. But Windstream had a rather clever court-packing plan: It asked the holders of its other bonds to exchange into 6.375 percent notes, with “entry consents” approving the sale-leaseback. This actually almost worked—Windstream ended up getting a majority of the enlarged 6.375 percent notes to agree to the consent—but it foundered on a weird technicality: The indenture for the 6.375 percent notes allowed the issuance of new notes in exchange for other bonds only if they did not increase the amount of Windstream’s debt. (Or if it met a leverage test, which it did not; the relevant provisions are summarized on page 4 of Judge Furman’s opinion.) But Windstream’s exchange offer did increase the total debt: It issued $560 million of exchange notes, “increasing the principal amount of its overall indebtedness by approximately $40 million.” So the judge found that the new 6.375 percent notes were not validly issued under the indenture, so their votes don’t count. (By the way … I don’t know what that means for those bondholders? Like, do they not have the 6.375 percent bonds? Do they still have their old bonds? The opinion is not clear. It seems bad!) “Services’ financial maneuvers,” wrote the judge, “are too cute by half,” but I actually think that they’re basically fine and not even particularly unfair (most bondholders really did consent!). The problem is that they just messed up the math. The indenture says you can’t issue more debt, so don’t! Just keep the principal amount the same. Sure you need to pay the bondholders a premium to exchange into the new bonds, but pay them in stock or something, or sell new stock and pay them in cash. Windstream blew up its entire capital structure over $40 million of new debt. Seems dumb! [5] Law professor Jared Ellias praised the decision on Twitter, writing of Windstream’s sale-leaseback: “I call this ‘bankruptcy hardball’ because it was an act by a distressed firm to get additional runway in violation of promises it had made to prior creditors. Instead of sitting down and reaching an agreement with those creditors, Windstream came up a highly technical legal argument that may have been correct as a matter of form but, as SDNY points out, was clearly wrong as a matter of substance. It's good to see courts starting to push back on these types of deals. Hopefully it's a start of a trend; most courts have been willing to defer to form over substance when the issuer has an argument that they did not violate a debt covenant.” [6] It kept another speed bump, though, one that allowed midpoint pegged orders to update to reflect the new price. This is closer to my second answer in the text, though not identical (it is not aimed at market makers).

A public-company chief executive officer has two main ways to make money from her job each year: She gets a paycheck, or rather a pay package (salary, bonus, stock options, etc.), in which her company pays her a negotiated amount for her services; and She owns stock in her company, and if she does a good job the stock goes up and she is richer. A company could go with all one or the other, and some companies do: A family-owned company might hire an outside manager, give her no equity, and pay her purely in cash; a startup founder-CEO might take no salary and be motivated solely by her part-ownership of the company. But for most normal public companies, it’s a mix of the two. It is a convention, in discussing public-company executive compensation, to talk exclusively about #1 and ignore #2. The compensation package—the amount of stuff the company affirmatively grants her each year for doing her job—counts as “pay”; the amount that her wealth goes up from owning stock in her company usually does not. This is mostly just a convention, a generally accepted way of using words, and it is not universally followed, but there are some pretty good reasons for talking this way. It roughly tracks how tax law thinks about income (getting a check is income; having your stock go up is not). If the CEO quit her job, she would still own her stock and would thus still profit from the stock going up (though of course it might not go up as much), so isolating #1 focuses on her income that is purely job-related. And if you are interested not in her income but in the company’s expenses—not “how rich is the CEO” but “how much does she cost shareholders”—#1 is a reasonable approximation of that, while #2 is not really an expense at all. But you can’t get carried away and assume that this convention represents the entire truth of the matter, because then you might start thinking things like “wait, Warren Buffett only makes $100,000 a year for running Berkshire Hathaway Inc.? He’s so good at stock-picking; I should offer him $125,000 and have him come work for me.” (Or: “Mark Zuckerberg only makes $1 a year for running Facebook Inc.? I should offer him $3 to stop.”) No, come on, these people have vast amounts of wealth tied to the performance of their companies; Warren Buffett gets, in effect, a base salary of $100,000 and a bonus of 17 percent of the value he creates for Berkshire Hathaway shareholders. In good years, that comes to billions of dollars: Berkshire was up 23 percent in 2016, handily beating the S&P 500, and Buffett personally got about $14 billion richer. In mediocre years, it … also comes to billions of dollars: Berkshire was up 2.8 percent in 2018 (also handily beating the market, to be fair), and Buffett’s take came to more than $2.3 billion. That is not formally part of his pay package, but it is surely part—virtually all—of the economic reward that he receives for doing his job each day. I feel like we don’t quite have a convention for how to talk about hedge-fund-manager pay, but to the extent we do, it’s the opposite of the public-company convention: Every dollar of increased wealth that a hedge fund manager gets from her hedge fund, whether it’s a fee paid by investors or returns on her own investment in the hedge fund, tends to be discussed as “pay.” There is nothing particularly wrong with this convention either! Again, it is just a question of how you use words, and there are good arguments for talking this way too. For instance, if you want to answer questions like “how many world-historically expensive homes can Ken Griffin buy,” focusing solely on his fee income, rather than his investment income, would be a mistake. It’s all money. More broadly, if the question that you want to answer is “who is really good at running a hedge fund,” a quite plausible scoring mechanism would be to rank managers based on how much money they have made—both as a manager and as an investor—from their hedge funds. High investment returns mean that you are good at investing; high fee income means that you are good at gathering assets and extracting fees from them; those are the main skills, so why not add them together to get your score? But, again, you can’t get carried away. If you are counting the manager’s own investment returns as part of her income, which is perfectly reasonable and relevant, you can’t also pretend that the number you get is all fees. And so every year Institutional Investor’s Alpha publishes a list of the world’s “best-paid” hedge fund managers, and every year Alpha quite prominently explains that it is counting both fee income and investment returns, and every year people publish commentary on the list saying essentially “I can’t believe all of these hedge-fund managers got paid so many millions of dollars of fees despite not beating the market, what a grift,” and every year I publish a post saying, well, wait, actually, the income seems to be mostly investment returns on the managers’ own portion of the fund , meaning that it’s not fee income at all, and then we all agree to meet up next year and have the same conversation again. Today Bloomberg published its first ranking of hedge-fund-manager earnings. It too ranks managers based on total earnings, combining fees and investment returns; again, I think this is perfectly sensible, depending on what you want to measure. Jim Simons of Renaissance Technologies tops the list for 2018, making $1.6 billion in “total hedge fund income.”[1] Ray Dalio of Bridgewater Associates, Ken Griffin of Citadel, and John Overdeck and David Siegel of Two Sigma round out the top 5. But Bloomberg also disaggregates the numbers: To compile the ranking, Bloomberg broke out “total income” figures to show estimates of dividend income and return on personal assets. Dividend income is our calculation of the share of performance fees that the manager takes home as owner of the hedge fund. Return on personal assets is our estimate of how much managers earned on their own cash invested in their funds. (It does not count management fees, assuming I suppose that those are mostly spent on staff and expenses.) And there’s a little bar chart breaking down the splits. Most of the top 10 made the majority of their 2018 earnings from investment returns, though fees were usually a substantial contributor. Not always: “Michael Platt of Bluecrest Capital Management returned 25 percent, although hedge fund investors didn’t benefit after he kicked out clients,” and his $680 million of earnings is all investment returns.[2] But from Bloomberg’s chart, the top five total earners were also the top five fee earners, and in almost the same order,[3] which is sensible but also a bit boring. Really 2018 was an anomalously straightforward year for hedge funds: The stock market was down, most hedge funds did poorly, but the hedge funds that did well were disproportionately the big, old, historically successful ones. If you have run a gigantic hedge fund successfully for a long time, and it did well in 2018, then (1) you collected a lot of performance fees on your gigantic pot of assets, and (2) you had a lot of your own money in the fund, and it went up. That’s not how it works every year, but it is kind of how it’s supposed to work.

My usual role around here is to tell you about interesting financial things that have happened, or to argue that boring financial things that have happened are actually interesting, or at least to make fun of dumb financial things that have happened. Occasionally though, we indulge in a bit of speculative fiction and talk about how nice it would be if some really interesting financial thing had happened, even though it didn’t. Here is a Vanity Fair story about Jeff Bezos, an extramarital affair, nude selfies, politics, the National Enquirer, etc., but I just want to focus on this amazing passage about what might have been: One option even included Bezos buying A.M.I.—not such an outlandish consideration given the seriousness of the breach and the fact that, for Bezos, the price of the tabloid company is essentially a rounding error—to find out the source of the leak. “We discussed the possibility to buy A.M.I.—not to kill the story, but to find out the source. They said that’s not a bad idea. We discussed numbers and the name of the LLC that we’d use. It would be called BOBO LCC”—short for Lauren’s helicopter filming company, Black Ops, and Bezos’s space company, Blue Origin—“that’s the level of detail we went into.” Quick explainer: The National Enquirer, a tabloid owned by American Media Inc., acquired some embarrassing photos of Amazon.com Inc. founder and squazillionaire Jeff Bezos, and of Lauren Sanchez, with whom he was having an extramarital affair. Sanchez’s brother Michael has been accused of leaking the photos to the Enquirer, though he denied that in the Vanity Fair article. (“I’m not saying I didn’t do something ,” he says, though.) The quote in that paragraph is from Michael Sanchez, and he is describing a discussion that he had with Bezos and Lauren Sanchez last month after the National Enquirer started asking about their affair. One possibility they apparently considered was for Bezos to buy AMI, not kill the story (???), and I suppose, once in possession of AMI’s records, find out who leaked the information to the Enquirer. Now: This didn’t happen; The person saying that it almost happened is not necessarily an unbiased source; and AMI is not a public company (though it is owned by a hedge fund), so a hostile takeover might not have been possible anyway. But I think I am justified in saying: Never mind all of that, let’s just imagine if it had happened! Imagine if a tabloid owned by a public company threatened to publish nudes of Jeff Bezos, and Jeff Bezos just lobbed in a hostile bid—funded by his personal fortune, not by Amazon—to buy the publisher at a premium. He would have to put out a tender-offer disclosure document, and in the “Purpose of the Offer” section he would just write “revenge,” and in the “Plans for the Target” section he could write “I am going to find out who leaked my nudes and exact ruinous vengeance on them, and that’s it, I haven’t thought about any other plans.” And then management and Bezos would make their respective cases to shareholders: Management and its investment bankers would put together a detailed slide deck explaining their long-term business plans and financial projections, while Bezos would put out two slides, one saying “Vengeance Will Be Mine” over that picture of him looking buff in a vest, and the other printing the price of his all-cash offer in a really big font. And then management’s investment bankers would issue an opinion saying that Bezos’s offer was inadequate and he’d be like “fine double it then, I don’t care, how much could a newspaper publisher possibly cost, do you know how rich I am.” And politicians would rail against short-termism in corporate America, and point to the fact that valuable productive companies could be bought by corporate raiders just to strip them down to a single piece of information, and Bezos would be like “yes that’s true but have you considered how much money I have.” And then he’d win, of course, and he’d gain control of the company and install his board, and they’d appoint a new Bezos loyalist CEO, and Bezos would show up at the office and be like “okay who’s my leaker,” and he and the new CEO would call every employee in one by one to grill them until someone told him what he wanted to know. And then he’d go, you know, write a withering blog post about the leaker or whatever his plan was. But then there’d still be a whole company there! Like he bought this company just to ask one question and exact his amazing personal revenge, but meanwhile there are all the reporters and editors and printers and people who work in accounting, and they all show up to work to be grilled about the leaker, but then after that, like, they just … go on producing a tabloid … for an owner whose … only interest in it has passed? Like I guess he could sell it then, for some fraction of what he paid for it, but what’s the fun in that? Or he could shut it down out of spite, fine, but that seems wasteful. Maybe he could keep running the tabloid, but dedicate it exclusively to publishing mean stories about the person who leaked his nudes. Anyway corporate finance is amazing, but the point here is that it could so easily be so much more amazing. Oh also Amazon won’t be building a big new office in New York.

The way appraisal lawsuits work is that a company agrees to buy another company, and pays for it, and some shareholders of the target vote against the deal and sue the buyer for more money. They go to a Delaware Chancery Court judge and argue that the target was worth more than the buyer paid for it; the buyer argues that it was worth what it paid, or even less. And then the judge decides how much it was worth and orders the buyer to pay that amount. It’s kind of weird! A lot of corporate finance is, you know, willing buyers and willing sellers, negotiated transactions, etc., but then at the end of a merger, you go to a judge and he gets to decide if the market was right or wrong. The way he decides is mostly that each side has a valuation expert to say how much the company was worth, and then the judge makes a decision about which one was more persuasive. These valuation experts tend to be finance professors, hired by the parties through economic consulting firms, who do discounted cash flow analyses of the company to come up with their values; the judge will generally take the more compelling DCF as a starting point for his own valuation. You might expect there to be a sorting process in which the plaintiffs hire an expert who believes that the company was undervalued and the defendants hire an expert who doesn’t. Or yes fine fine fine you might instead expect there to be an entirely cynical process in which each side hires an expert who doesn’t believe anything, but who says whatever they want for a fee. But it could be worse! When Verizon Communications Inc. bought AOL Inc. in 2015, some shareholders sued for appraisal. Last year they lost that lawsuit, when Delaware Vice Chancellor Sam Glasscock III ruled that the fair value of AOL was $48.70 per share, a bit below the deal price of $50. The vice chancellor wrote at the time: The Petitioners hired a well-qualified academic, Dr. Bradford Cornell, a visiting professor at the California Institute of Technology, as their expert witness. Cornell performed a financial analysis, and concluded that the fair value of AOL stock was $68.98 per share. For reasons not necessary to detail, however, the Respondent questioned Dr. Cornell’s impartiality in this matter, and the Petitioners seem content to use the DCF model presented by the Respondent’s expert as a starting point for my analysis. Oh but no, those reasons are necessary to detail, and a few weeks ago the shareholders detailed them, in a new hilarious lawsuit against their own expert: What [Cornell] failed to disclose was that Cornell had only taken on the engagement for Plaintiffs [i.e. the shareholders] to satisfy an admitted “grudge” he held against Plaintiffs’ litigation opponent [i.e. Verizon], which had spurned hiring Cornell in favor of a competing testifying expert. While trying to solicit Plaintiffs’ litigation opponent, Cornell expressed negative views about the strength of Plaintiffs’ case. Plaintiffs and their counsel knew none of this when they retained him. When Cornell’s undisclosed communications surfaced in the midst of the Appraisal Action—after Plaintiffs had disclosed Cornell as their expert and expert reports were issued—the consequences for Plaintiffs were devastating. The disclosure of these communications effectively destroyed Cornell’s testimony, which forced Plaintiffs to essentially abandon him as their expert … It seems that Cornell (who is a visiting professor of finance at Caltech) pitched Verizon on retaining him as an expert, and allegedly sympathized with Verizon over email about “what a nuisance these [appraisal] cases can be.” But they went with his colleague/competitor/frenemy, Professor Daniel Fischel, who was associated with the same economic consulting firm as Cornell. So Cornell switched consulting firms and pitched his services to the appraisal plaintiffs, but not before sending Fischel this email[4]: Dan, Like you I tend to bear grudges. And though I see you as perhaps the best general expert witness in the country, when it comes to appraisal, particularly for tech companies, I think I am uniquely well qualified. So when Verizon/Wachtell chose you without even talking to me further that leads to a grudge against them. Consequently, I have had some conversations with plaintiffs. … Later he allegedly told Fischel that his “main concern is that plaintiffs have a [ expletive ] case (that is not based on conversation just what I have read online) so I will have to be careful to avoid letting my grudge lead to a situation where I threaten my reputation.” Well: oops! Anyway there are absolutely no broader lessons to be learned here[5] and I am telling you all of this out of pure gleeful cynicism. I had a professor in law school whose theory was that any bitter lawsuit over seemingly trivial stakes was really about a love triangle, but it is pleasing to find that a high-stakes litigation over a multi-billion-dollar merger could turn on a valuation expert who was miffed that the other side didn’t hire him.

We talked the other day about how Banco Santander SA did not call its Additional Tier 1 Capital securities when investors expected it to, leaving those investors outraged and stuck holding securities worth, um, 98 cents on the dollar. I was fine with all of this: Santander had an absolute right not to call the securities, and taking the holders’ concerns seriously would undermine the usefulness of AT1 securities as bank capital. “I struggle to find any reason to sympathize with the investors here,” I wrote. But I neglected to mention one actually decent reason to sympathize with them, which is that Santander had just gone out and raised another AT1 security days before the expected call date on this one. If you were an investor in Santander’s old bond, you might reasonably have thought that Santander was raising the new AT1 to pay to retire the old AT1, and you might have participated in the new AT1 deal expecting that you’d quickly get some money back from your old AT1. Santander didn’t exactly say that that was the plan, but it was a reasonable guess, and if you thought that then you got played. So, fine, a little sympathy. One aspect of the new AT1 that particularly made investors expect a call of the old one is that the new AT1 had a short settlement cycle, meaning that Santander would get the cash from the new offering a bit quicker than it normally would. Investors sensibly thought that this was so that Santander would have the cash in time to pay off the old AT1. But in fact that guess was wrong, for this very strange reason: The bond also had an unusually short settlement date of two days, meaning that Santander would have the money in its hands last Friday — which investors believed was the bank’s deadline for calling the coco. This is because a notice had to be filed 30 days before March 12, which fell on a Sunday. But the bank then told investors that they actually had until Tuesday February 12 to make a decision. This is because the bank had legal advice that 30 days should be interpreted as a month, disregarding that there are 28 days in February. None of this actually mattered, in the end, since Santander never exercised the call. Still: what? When bonds don’t work out for investors, in ways that are explicitly allowed by the documents, it is tempting to say—and I often succumb to the temptation—“hahaha, that’s on you, you should have read the documents.” Here, for instance, Santander’s AT1 explicitly said that Santander never has to pay it back, though it could at its option decide to pay it back this month; investors who interpreted that to mean “Santander will definitely pay it back this month” were, I insist, only deluding themselves. Read the documents! On the other hand, if you did read the documents, you would have seen that Santander had to call the AT1 30 days in advance. But Santander’s lawyers said—and for all I know they’re right—that, nah, 30 days actually means 28 days. Reading the very clear words (and numbers) in the document would have gotten you nowhere, would have actively misled you, because the words apparently mean something other than what they say.
