Sure, right, depending on the details, I can see how this might be bad: One hedge fund manager didn't invest much in oil, but a data company's unusual pitch caught his eye. The firm claimed to pinpoint which oil rigs in Texas were operating in real time, information that could be used, for a price, to make better bets on the commodity. How did the company acquire this type of potentially extremely lucrative data? It paid a guy $50 to drive around and stick sensors on oil rigs. The hedge fund manager, who declined to be named, said he immediately passed. I don’t know exactly what this unnamed data firm was telling this unnamed hedge fund, but it does sound like it might be … industrial espionage? Trespassing? Why would the oil companies want to let some outsider to stick sensors on their rigs in order to sell data to hedge funds? Something feels a bit icky about it. But the specific thing that feels potentially icky about it is the possibility of sticking sensors on things whose owners don’t want sensors stuck on them. Imagine a different story, in which, instead of using sensors, the company paid a guy to drive around and look at oil rigs. Like, drive on a public road, pass by an oil rig, look to see if the pumpjack is moving up and down, and if it is, update the spreadsheet to say “yep, this rig is working today.” This would cost more—the guy would have to drive around every day, instead of just leaving the sensor there, and you might need more guys—and would give you daily rather than real-time data. But you could imagine, with somewhat better technology (drones, satellites, remote sensors, I don’t know), getting pretty close to the quality and cost of the sensor approach, without violating anyone’s property rights. Would that be bad? If you just knew “which oil rigs in Texas were operating in real time,” by looking at them, but by looking at them in a capital-and-labor-intensive way that no one else had replicated, that would be “potentially extremely lucrative data.” You would have it, and no one else would, and you could sell it to hedge funds and they could use it to make informed bets on oil prices (and oil companies’ stocks), etc. etc. etc. And someone somewhere would say “this is insider trading and we should ban it.” I think they would be wrong: I think that getting information about the world and incorporating it into prices is the point of capital markets, and that criminalizing difficult differentiated research would obviously be a mistake, but I can also promise you that lots of people would say this. The reason is that there is a tension between this basic goal of capital markets—to give people incentives to find stuff out—and the intuitive popular desire for fairness . If someone goes and hires a bunch of people to look at oil rigs in a difficult way and then sells that information to hedge funds for a million dollars, then I , as someone who lives in New York and has a day job and can’t just drive around looking at oil rigs all day, can’t compete with those hedge funds in oil trading. I cannot possibly think of a reason why I should expect to be able to compete with hedge funds in oil trading but, again, I promise you that this is a thing that people think. Anyway here’s more from that Business Insider story about alternative data: At a recent hedge fund conference in Miami, the possibility of a crackdown in the alternative data space was a huge topic of conversation among data companies, lawyers and money managers. "It's inevitable," said Mike Marrale, CEO of alternative data provider M Science, on a panel at the Context Summits conference in Miami. This fear was shared by several hedge fund managers, who expect the Securities and Exchange Commission to bring a case against one or more investors who used data improperly. But you have to be precise about what “improperly” means. Insider trading, I always say, is not about fairness ; it is about theft . Having information that no one else has is fine , it is good , it is what hedge funds are supposed to do. It gives them an unfair advantage over the people who don’t have the information, but if you are paying a hedge fund 2-and-20 fees, you’d better hope that they have some unfair advantage. No, what is bad is having information that you got from someone without their permission , or, really, that you got from someone without their permission to trade on it . (So: If a company hires an investment banker to work on a merger, and the banker goes and trades some stock for herself with the information, that’s classic insider trading. Or if a CEO tells his therapist or golf buddy about a merger in confidence, and the therapist or golf buddy trades, same thing.) Looking at oil wells: fine. Sneaking in to plant sensors on oil wells: bad. The real risk with a lot of “alternative data” is that it aggregates a lot of information from a lot of people who probably didn’t really give any thought to whether they wanted to let hedge funds trade with it. So you download an app on your phone, and it tracks your location, and it sells that information to a data company, and that data company sells it to hedge funds, and the hedge funds use it to figure out what stores get a lot of foot traffic and then to buy their stocks. Did you give the app company permission to sell your data like that? Did the app company give the data company permission to sell it to hedge funds? Do the terms of your phone’s app store allow or restrict this? Etc. If there isn’t permission at every stage, then arguably the hedge fund is misappropriating your information to trade. (Of course its trading doesn’t actually harm you , but insider trading law doesn’t really care about that; the victim of the misappropriation doesn’t need to be harmed by the trading.) So you want to make sure that all the permissions are correct: If a data provider makes it through that phase, Point72 has its investment team trial the data, which can take anywhere from a couple weeks to "many, many months" based on the complexity of the data. If a trial fills the investment team's needs, a small team of lawyers dedicated to data review combs through it. "We essentially demand to see every contract in the chain," Granade said. Though, of course, there are other approaches: "There are some organizations we work with who are extremely pedantic about ensuring that everything is kosher. They ask a lot of questions, they ask for a lot of transparency, and they're always trying to figure out the ultimate source of a data set," he said. "There are other funds that are pretty chilled out, for better or for worse." I suppose there is an argument that “we bought this data from a provider, we didn’t know it was taken without permission” might be a defense against insider-trading charges, but I’m not sure that being “chilled out” about this is a great idea.

Do you think anyone who manages money professionally has ever made an investing decision based on the ratio between how a company’s chief executive officer’s pay and that of its median employee? U.S. public companies have had to disclose that information since last year, under Securities and Exchange Commission rules that are at least nominally intended to give investors more information about the companies they invest in. “Several commenters” on the regulations, many of them public and union pension funds, “stated affirmatively that they would find the new data points, including pay ratio disclosure, relevant and useful when making voting decisions.” So, sure. I suspect that most investors are more interested in the absolute amount of a CEO’s pay, or how it compares to her competitors’ pay, or to the size of the company or how much money she has made for shareholders, but it’s certainly possible that some investors—particularly environmental-social-and-governance-focused ones, but maybe returns-focused ones as well—need this particular data point to inform their say-on-pay voting decisions or I suppose even, conceivably, their buying and selling decisions. “This CEO makes too big a multiple of her median worker’s pay for this company to be well-managed, so we should avoid the stock,” is not, like, an impossible thing for an investment analyst to think. Still it just doesn’t feel like a regulation that is aimed primarily at investors. Every disclosure requirement for public companies, of course, serves two functions: The disclosure helps shareholders and potential shareholders of those companies evaluate the business and decide whether to buy or sell shares, and it also helps the rest of society understand the workings of the big corporations that are important to our economy and our lives. Both of those seem like they might be good things, but only one of them is the explicit goal of securities regulation. In general the SEC thinks about what information investors should have to make informed investing decisions and avoid being defrauded, and then tells (public) companies to disclose it, and then everyone else gets that information too and there are some good spillover effects. But these are just spillovers, just an accident; securities regulations are not mainly concerned with providing citizens of a democracy with the information that they might want about the power and function of businesses.[1] Anyway here are Steven Bank and George Georgiev on “ Securities Disclosure As Soundbite: The Case of CEO Pay Ratios”: We suggest that the pay ratio disclosure rule represents a unique approach to disclosure, which we term disclosure-as-soundbite. This approach is characterized by (1) high public salience—the pay ratio is superficially intuitive and resonates with the public to an extent much greater than other disclosure, and (2) low informational integrity—the pay ratio is a relative outlier in terms of certain baseline characteristics of disclosure, meaning that the information is lacking in accuracy, difficult to interpret, and incomplete. We find that in its current formulation the rule is ineffectual and potentially counterproductive when viewed as a means of generating useful and reliable information for investors, or influencing firm behavior on matters of worker and executive compensation. The pay ratio is more successful in fomenting or contributing to public discourse on broader societal matters relating to pay inequity and economic inequality, though the quality of the underlying information likely limits the quality of the discourse. Given the low probability of legislative action in this area in the near term, we propose that the SEC should seek to improve the rule’s informational integrity by mandating a narrative disclosure approach that provides information about median worker pay and the resulting pay ratio with more context, nuance, and explanation. We talk a lot around here about how “ everything is securities fraud,” by which I mean, every time a company does a bad thing, it has also violated securities laws by not immediately disclosing that bad thing to investors. I always find this a bit troubling, both because it seems to involve the law in a bit of dishonesty—people get mad at companies for doing bad things to consumers or the environment or the killer whales, but then have to pretend that they’re mad at those companies for doing bad things to shareholders —and also because it seems to privilege the interests of shareholders over the interests of citizens, suggesting that harms to shareholders are more important than harms to society. Trying to address income inequality by passing rules to give the owners of capital more information seems like an obvious non sequitur, and I am not sure that tweaking those rules to make them more useful to those owners of capital will make anyone happy, but that is the odd regulatory system we live in.

“Bezos Exposes Pecker,” reads the Platonic form of a New York Post cover, about the news that David Pecker’s American Media Inc. threatened to publish some nudes from Jeff Bezos, and Bezos preempted them by going public with all of their emails on the matter. Here is Bezos’s Medium post, which I very much enjoyed reading, but it’s sort of a convoluted story that has nothing much to do with the subject matter of this newsletter (money, stuff), so here I will confine myself to two comments. First, this is only very slightly and pretextually related to Bezos’s work as the chief executive officer of a publicly traded corporation, but at the same time, everything in a CEO’s personal life is at least arguably related to his job. A CEO needs to show good judgment, avoid distractions and be a good public face for the brand. Bezos is the founder and CEO of Amazon.com Inc., but as we have discussed before he is not the controlling shareholder and has no extra-voting stock; his grip on his CEO job is maintained not by any special legal rights but just by being good at it. It is hard, though, to think of another CEO anywhere who can be more confident that his performance has earned him perpetual job security. (Maybe Warren Buffett?) As Bezos put it: AMI’s claim of newsworthiness is that the photos are necessary to show Amazon shareholders that my business judgment is terrible. I founded Amazon in my garage 24 years ago, and drove all the packages to the post office myself. Today, Amazon employs more than 600,000 people, just finished its most profitable year ever, even while investing heavily in new initiatives, and it’s usually somewhere between the #1 and #5 most valuable company in the world. I will let those results speak for themselves. Yeah I mean the shareholders are gonna be okay with some nudes. Second, this is an … inspiring? … story about the intangible things that money can buy, if you have really quite a lot of it. AMI threatened to publish some embarrassing revelations about Bezos, and Bezos just went and published them himself because he is too rich to be embarrassed . Most of us go through life trying to avoid embarrassment, because we care what people think and we know there’s some risk that they might think less of us. But Jeff Bezos just has too much money for that to be a practical concern. That’s a good level of rich! Also a good level of rich: hiring a private investigator to smite your enemies and telling him “to prioritize protecting my time since I have other things I prefer to work on and to proceed with whatever budget he needed to pursue the facts in this matter.” I am not sure I would advise you to live your life in such a way that your budget for private investigators is “unlimited,” but it has a certain appeal.

One of my favorite recent financial-markets mysteries was why Herbalife Nutrition Ltd. suddenly got rid of its CEO, Richard Goudis, last month. Herbalife announced at the time that Goudis’s departure “pertains to comments which recently came to light, made by Mr. Goudis prior to his role as CEO, that are contrary to the Company’s expense-related policies and business practices,” which doesn’t explain much. One possibility was that Herbalife is just an absolute stickler for expense-account propriety, and a decade-old instance of taking some paper clips home for personal use ended Goudis’s career, but that … never … seemed … all that likely. There are a lot of juicy things that you can spend corporate money on that might, when they come to a board’s attention, sound bad! The Wall Street Journal has now solved the mystery: When Mr. Goudis was Herbalife’s chief financial officer about a decade ago, he told a colleague working in Hong Kong or mainland China to ignore the company’s expense account limit on entertainment spending, the people said. The phone call was recorded by another employee, they said, and last year a copy reached the Justice Department, which has been investigating whether the Los Angeles-based nutritional supplement seller violated foreign bribery laws in its business dealings in China. … The Justice Department and the Securities and Exchange Commission have been investigating Herbalife’s anticorruption practices in China for roughly two years. Herbalife, which disclosed the probe in January 2017, said in an Oct. 30, 2018, regulatory filing that the probe has mainly focused on entertainment and gift expenditures by the company’s local China external affairs department. Well, right. We have talked a couple of times recently about euphemisms for “bribes.” I have suggested that it never seems like a good idea to call bribes “chickens,” but that “success fees” might sometimes be a decent way of putting it. Let me add that “ignore the company’s expense account limit on entertainment spending” is also pretty good. It sounds so modest and reasonable, like you understand that your internal policies are too penny-pinching so you will waive them to let your managers make better business decisions. But those spending limits aren’t just internal policies, and they’re not primarily about saving money: They’re about not violating bribery laws, and ignoring them can get you in real trouble.

Ahahahahahahahahaha: The fireside chat is a mainstay of the corporate conference. Businesspeople fly in from around the country, check into their hotel and fortify themselves at a coffee buffet as they listen to colleagues drone on in a beige event hall. But on the agenda something beckons – an intimate tete-a-tete between the event’s bold-faced speakers. Billed as a “fireside chat,” it promises the sort of woodsmoke-infused insight that can only come from stacking several important men next to flaming timber. But one thing is almost always missing — fire. At event after event, the fireside chat has no fireplace and no crackling flame. At best, the panelists might get a high-backed leather chair and a glass of water. “Well, yeah, there’s no fire. There’s never been a fire,’’ said a woman helping organize presentations at a bank-hosted investor conference in San Francisco last month. “That’s just what they call it. They call it a ‘fireside chat,’ but there’s obviously no fire.” She turned and hurried away before giving her name. Hahahahahahahahahahahahahahaha. I often find myself defending corporate and financial jargon, since I think it often serves the aims of precision and specificity even at the cost of being off-putting or incomprehensible to outsiders. This is not that; this is just silly.

As part of its efforts to cripple the regime of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, the U.S. government has made it illegal for U.S. investors to buy bonds of Venezuela’s government or of its state-owned oil company, Petróleos de Venezuela SA. U.S. investors can hold on to Venezuelan bonds that they already own, but they can’t buy any more; they can sell their bonds, but only to non-U.S. investors. JPMorgan Chase & Co., meanwhile, runs emerging-market bond indexes that a lot of investors and exchange-traded funds use as benchmarks. The Venezuelan bonds are in the indexes. Should they come out? The trading ban is “a development that typically would prompt JPMorgan to yank the notes from its indexes,” but: Bondholders as well as some Venezuelan politicians aligned with Juan Guaido, the U.S.-backed lawmaker trying to oust Maduro, are now actively lobbying to get JPMorgan to keep the debt in the index. For creditors, the rationale is straight-forward: Removing Venezuela from the index would pressure them to dump the securities at rock-bottom prices. For those in Guaido’s camp, it’s a bit more complicated. Their concern is that by forcing mutual funds, ETFs and other traditional investors to unload the debt, it will wind up in the hands of hedge funds that are more aggressive and potentially even litigious in bond restructurings. That in turn will hurt their efforts to impose a sizable haircut on creditors -- a key part of their plan to stabilize the crisis-torn country if they manage to take power. In some ways that second point feels a little strange: If Venezuela’s bonds are mostly held by long-term indexy investors who bought them at 100 cents on the dollar, those investors will be sad about getting back only, say, 40 cents; if the bonds are mostly held by vulture-y hedge funds who bought them in a fire sale at 33 cents on the dollar, shouldn’t those funds be happy to take the 40? But, ha, no, that is the opposite of how it seems to work in the real world. If you buy a bond at par based on your credit analysis, expecting it to pay normally, and then it doesn’t, you might say “well that’s on me” and take your losses. If you buy a bond at pennies on the dollar after it is already in default, you’re buying it specifically because you plan to be absolutely ruthless in the restructuring. If Guaidó’s Venezuela is going to have to renegotiate Maduro’s debt, they’d rather do it with indexy investors than with whoever buys it next. The first point is also a little strange, though. On the one hand, sure, dropping Venezuela from the index is harsh on people who track the index and already own the debt: They really will have to sell in a fire sale, not only because Venezuela is pretty unsettled right now but also because the market is limited to non-U.S. buyers. On the other hand, leaving Venezuela in the index is harsh on people who track the index, or are planning to, and have to buy the debt. If you run an index-tracking emerging-markets debt fund, and a client puts some more money in, you have to go buy the bonds in your index. But (if you’re in the U.S.) it’s illegal to buy the Venezuelan ones. So you can’t track the index. That’s why the index tends to have rules about dropping hard-to-trade bonds. There is an obvious path dependency to these things. If it is very hard to trade a country’s securities, and that country is not in an index, then investors will argue against adding it to the index, because adding it will force them to go out and buy a bunch of securities and that will be hard. (This was for a long time the argument against adding mainland Chinese stocks to emerging market indexes.) But if the country is already in the index, and its securities become very hard to trade, then investors will argue against dropping it from the index, because dropping it will force them to go out and sell a bunch of securities and that will be hard. None of this is a matter of objectively correct criteria for index inclusion. It’s just, like, the index providers have customers, and the customers are investors, and the index providers should try to do the best they can to make most of their customers reasonably happy.

Elsewhere in Venezuelan financial news, how’s it going at Citgo Petroleum Corp., PdVSA’s U.S. subsidiary? Because of the U.S. sanctions, Citgo’s U.S. management is ignoring directives from oil executives tied to Mr. Maduro’s regime, a person familiar with the matter said. Valued by PdVSA at over $9 billion, Citgo directly employs over 3,000 people in the U.S. but is a major source of critical dollar revenue for Venezuela. Guaidó plans to name a new board of directors for Citgo, and Citgo already plans to go along with it: A Citgo spokesman said in a statement: “We are aware that there may be new members elected to the Citgo Petroleum Corp. board of directors. In corporate governance, as with all matters, we will follow the laws of the United States.” This outcome is not exactly surprising— we talked about it last week—but it is still some pretty extraordinary corporate governance. If I just announced one day that I was appointing a new board of directors for Facebook Inc., Facebook’s existing board of directors and chief executive officer and controlling shareholder would probably all come out and say “wait, what, no, you can’t appoint a new board of directors, you’re just some guy, you don’t even own any of our stock.” But if Facebook’s employees then said “nah we’re good with Levine’s board, wave ‘em in,” and a Facebook spokesman came out and announced “we’re aware of the new board members and, welcome, they are now our board,” that would be super, super, super weird. (Should I try this?) I don’t think it would work , exactly, though it is an interesting exercise to figure out how it wouldn’t work. (“Oh Mark Zuckerberg would go to court and get a ruling saying his board is still the board,” sure, yes, that is easy, but you need the employees to actually do the work; do you have to send the cops in to make the employees swear allegiance to the old board?) That is not all that is going on at Citgo—in particular, it seems like the U.S. legal system will generally accept the legal fiction that PdVSA, Citgo’s sole shareholder, is controlled by Guaidó rather than by the people in Venezuela who actually control it—but it is part of it. Citgo can just throw off its bosses and board and shareholder, and replace them with a new board, in part because the employees who go to the refineries every day and actually do the work have decided that they’re going to ignore their old bosses and throw their lot in with the new board.

I feel like, if you handed me $100 billion and told me to spend it like an insane person, there would be a few weeks in which I’d take some tentative steps while feeling daunted by the sheer scale of the challenge, and then I’d kind of get into the groove and figure out how to blow billions of dollars at a time, and then surprisingly quickly you would find me saying things like “you know $100 billion isn’t all that much when you think about it” and “ugh I am going to have to make some really difficult decisions about where to allocate my scarce resources” and “I would like some more money now thank you.” Anyway: SoftBank Group Corp. has spent at least half of its nearly $100 billion Vision Fund in less than two years, increasing the pressure on the world’s biggest technology investor to raise more money if it wants to maintain that pace. The Vision Fund, which is backed by the sovereign-wealth funds of Saudi Arabia and Abu Dhabi, has taken stakes in some of the world’s most valuable startups, including ride-hailing pioneer Uber Technologies Inc. and shared-office-space company WeWork Cos. LLC. SoftBank said Wednesday the fund has spent about $50 billion of its approximately $99 billion in capital. At the roughly $7 billion-per-quarter spending rate it has logged so far, the Vision Fund’s remaining money will last only another year and a half—likely less, when taking into account amounts already set aside for paying fund employees as well as existing investments that may get transferred to the fund from SoftBank’s own books. Man, good for them, that’s terrific.

We talk a lot around here about coordination problems that investors have in dealing with issuers. A company is selling some securities, and investors don’t like some feature of the securities and would like to change it, but the investors can only get it changed if they all agree not to buy the securities with the feature, and the investors individually all have powerful incentives to hold their noses and buy. Sometimes the issuer wins, and there are articles about how covenants in bonds and loans keep getting weaker. The articles are full of quotes from investors complaining about the covenants, but the investors buy the bonds anyway because everyone else does and they can’t afford to be left behind. Other times the investors are able to find a coordination mechanism, and they win. So Covenant Review, which is what it sounds like, sometimes writes about a bad covenant, and all the investors read it and complain to the underwriters, and because they have all read the same thing—and they all know that they’ve all read the same thing—they stand firm and force the issuer to change the covenant. Or the issuer wins in the short term—Snap Inc. goes public with non-voting stock even as investors all complain—but the investors find a mechanism (changing index rules to keep out dual-class stocks) to stop it from happening again. It can be interesting to think about the various coordination mechanisms available to investors: lobbying regulators or stock exchanges or index providers or proxy advisers, threatening or cajoling underwriters who serve as gatekeepers for deals, writing scoldy public letters to issuers individually or through an investor organization, subscribing to trade publications that stick up for their beliefs, etc. But the simplest thing that investors usually want is to pay less for securities, and the simplest coordination mechanism is for them to just email each other saying “I’m not going to pay more than 260 for this and you shouldn’t either,” and, oops: The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) has fined Paul Stephany, a former fund manager at Newton Investment Management Limited, £32,200 for his conduct in relation to an Initial Public Offering (IPO) and a placing. On two separate occasions, Mr Stephany submitted orders as part of a book build for shares that were to be quoted on public exchanges. Prior to the order books for the new shares closing, Mr Stephany contacted other fund managers at competitor firms and attempted to influence them to cap their orders at the same price limit as his own orders. The FCA found that Mr Stephany risked undermining the integrity of the market and the book build by trying to use their collective power. As a consequence, Mr Stephany failed to observe proper standards of market conduct. It’s not a particularly big fine, and Stephany said in a statement that the U.K. FCA’s action “acknowledges that my honesty and integrity as a fund manager are not in doubt.” And when you read the email that got him in trouble, it seems clear that it never occurred to him that he was doing anything wrong. This is not like the Libor or FX scandal chats, full of dark jokes about how everyone was going to jail. It’s just a calm professional argument about valuation that he “blind copied to 14 External Fund managers at 11 competitor firms”[1]: Sorry for the out the blue email but I wanted to urge those considering or in for the OTB IPO to think about moving to a 260m pre money valuation limit. I have done that first thing this morning with my GBP17m order. I don’t usually do last minute brinkmanship on IPOs but think there are particularly good reasons on this one given- -significant market uncertainty since Fed decision -huge private equity profits bagged by Inflexion given they bought it for c73m two years plus have taken mgmt fees and dividends - the c.15x PER which looks attractive is predicated on significant top and bottom line growth -this is a relatively large placing in a small cap so sensitive to future mkt weakness I haven’t received any indication that the books are well covered or even covered so suspect this one is still very much open to price movement. Please have a think and mention to any colleagues or have put orders in. His model of how an initial public offering works seems to have been that there’s an issuer on one side, and investors on the other, and the investors negotiate with the issuer, and if the investors coordinate their negotiation strategy they will be better off. Whereas the FCA’s model is that an IPO is an auction, and the investors put in their bids to buy stock, and if the investors coordinate their bids then they are colluding to manipulate the results of the auction. The FCA’s model is surely correct,[2] but you can see how Stephany’s model might have made sense to him. Investors can go on television to say that they think the price of a stock is too high, they can lobby underwriters not to bring deals with features they dislike, they can sign joint open letters to companies saying that dual-class stock is bad and they don’t want to buy any more of it. Why can’t they just email each other what they think about the price?

Here is a paper by Guido Baltussen, Laurens Swinkels and Pim van Vliet finding that a handful of classic investing factors (trends, momentum, seasonality, value, carry and betting against beta) have performed well not only in modern times, but also going back more than 200 years. My Bloomberg Opinion colleague John Authers has an excellent summary and analysis that you should read. “On this evidence,” he writes, “it looks as though persistent market anomalies stem from persistent anomalies in human nature and human reasoning (which are not necessarily irrational), and not from rational and predictable responses to changes in risk.” And: “Correlations between factors and between asset classes are remarkably constant over time, even in periods that far predate cross-asset trading, algorithms or even the telephone.” I guess my question is: If you know that some broad market anomaly (not a quirky one like “executives who play a lot of golf have below-average stock returns,” but a general one like “stocks that have been going up tend to keep going up”) has worked for a few decades recently, would you expect that anomaly to have been stronger or weaker in the early 1800s? My intuition is, mostly, stronger. A simple ( though debatable) way to think about these anomalies is that they are instances of market inefficiency, of asset prices somehow not incorporating all available information: Value works because market prices don’t always reflect fundamental performance, momentum works because prices take some time to fully incorporate new information, seasonality works because people go to the beach in the summer instead of buying stocks, etc. It would be weird if markets had not gotten more efficient over the last 200 years. Now, when there’s big earnings news, the company publishes a press release online, and it has financial information in easily comparable numerical formats, and it’s picked up by Bloomberg and sent out widely, and investors know to expect it and read it instantly and react, and they have electronic spreadsheets that they can update quickly, or they have their algorithms read the news even more instantly and react even faster, etc. etc. etc. Two hundred years ago information traveled by, uh, horse. Of course information should be incorporated into prices more quickly now. Computer and communications technology, legal regimes, and investor knowledge about the workings of markets all support much greater market efficiency than they did 200 years ago. Why would any of that introduce new “anomalies in human nature and human reasoning”? Maybe it will get rid of some—maybe when the algorithms get good enough to incorporate all information instantly, trend-following will stop working—but in any case, whatever human foibles survive modern technology were probably there from the beginning. Elsewhere in anomalies: Researchers found that following the 9/11 terrorist attacks, market reactions weakened for forecasts from analysts with Middle Eastern surnames. They also found that following the French and German governments' opposition to the US-led Iraq War, the US market reactions weakened for analysts with French or German surnames. This effect was stronger in firms with lower institutional ownership and for analysts with non-American first names. The researchers measured surname favourability using the US historical immigration records to identify countries of origin associated with a particular surname and the Gallup survey data on Americans' favourability toward foreign countries. I will guess that if you had data on stock prices and analyst recommendations for 1850, that effect would have been even stronger.

The main thing about big banks’ commodity trading businesses is not that they’re particularly risky, or use a lot of capital, or create unusual conflicts of interest between the bank and its clients. What makes the commodity business special is that, if you really dedicate yourself to commodity trading, you end up owning a fleet of oil tankers. Or a network of mysterious aluminum warehouses. A big bank that wants to be a serious player in commodities will find itself drawn to trading “physical commodities,” rather than just contenting itself with derivatives, and physical commodities trading requires a certain physical commitment. You can trade stocks or bonds or loans or currencies or interest-rate swaps or exotic equity options or Bitcoins on a computer in your office, but if you are trading metals at some point you are going to want a forklift. Maybe there is nothing strange about a bank owning a forklift, or a fleet of oil tankers, though there are some historical and legal debates about whether these are non-banking activities that banks should not do. But if you’re a person who is generally suspicious of the pervasive and secretive power of the big investment banks—as a lot of people have been in recent years—then this just feels like a good thing to be suspicious about, a dark emanation of banks’ nefarious power out into the real world. If for instance you think of one particular bank as “a great vampire squid wrapped around the face of humanity, relentlessly jamming its blood funnel into anything that smells like money,” then the fact that that bank runs a “sprawling logistics network that handles the transport and storage of physical commodities” will make you nervous. Lotta places to stick the blood funnel. Anyway Goldman Sachs Group Inc. now has a friendly online bank that will lend you money or let you open a savings account, and also this: Goldman Sachs Group Inc. is planning to cut back its commodities-trading arm, once a huge moneymaker and training ground for a generation of executives including former chief Lloyd Blankfein. The retreat follows a monthslong review under new Chief Executive David Solomon that showed the commodities business’s dwindling profits don’t justify its costs, according to people familiar with the matter. Executives are discussing pulling back from trading iron ore, platinum and other metals, and are ordering cost cuts to the sprawling logistics network that handles the transport and storage of physical commodities. “The pullback in commodities is as symbolic as it is strategic,” in that Goldman’s commodities business, which grew out of its takeover of J. Aron & Co. in 1981, “produced a bloodline of executives who would later run the firm, including Mr. Blankfein and Gary Cohn.” And now Lloyd Blankfein has been succeeded by Solomon, who grew up in investment banking and is “less emotionally wedded to the trading business,” particularly the metals trading business. And, look, investment banking is plenty exciting and risky ( 1MDB!), and I am sure that in the not too distant future I will be writing about some wild conflicts of interest that Goldman faced in some wild derivative trade that it did for some wildly inappropriate customer, and we will all chuckle ruefully and say “ah yes that’s the Goldman we know,” but, man, right now, doesn’t it seem like Goldman has decided to become boring just like all its competitors? Disclosure: I used to work at Goldman building derivatives, and now I have an online savings account with them, so I suppose we have all grown old and boring together. Oh speaking of conflicts of interest and inappropriate customers, here is a story about Goldman’s relationship with “controversial German financier” Lars Windhorst. I do not fully understand what that relationship was, or what was controversial about it—Goldman refused to accept Windhorst as a customer but somehow did some trades in which he was involved in some capacity, and something went wrong, and the sales trader involved was fired, and now that trader is suing the firm saying he was a scapegoat, and the whole thing is sort of confusing—but it is an interesting slice of life. Here’s a tale of social etiquette involving Windhorst and Michael Daffey, who co-runs Goldman’s equities business: At a birthday celebration in October 2015, Windhorst and his girlfriend gave jewelry to Daffey’s wife, according to people familiar with the matter. Accepting such a gift from a potential client can violate internal policies. “Mr. Daffey did not become aware of the source of the gift until much later,” the Goldman spokesman said. “When it was brought to his attention, it was addressed internally and determined that the gift did not act as an inducement.” Daffey told some people at the bank that he gave the jewelry to a maid, a person with knowledge of the matter said. Windhorst confirmed a gift. What? Or here is a story about Windhorst, Daffey and some other Goldman guys meeting to high-five about a trade and talk about future business: The men at the gathering congratulated themselves for having done proper due diligence and getting compliance approval, according to a person with knowledge of the gathering. Honestly a sentence that you don’t want to hear is “congratulations on getting compliance approval.” Like, absolutely, you should get compliance approval, but you don’t want it to be such a close thing that you’re getting congratulated on it. “Can’t believe you got compliance approval on that one, amazing work”: No, that’s bad, that’s not how you want it to be.

Car-dealership company Group 1 Automotive announced earnings yesterday morning, including non-GAAP “adjusted diluted earnings per common share” of $2.31. Analyst estimates had averaged $2.35, according to Bloomberg. “Group 1 Automotive Fourth Quarter Adjusted EPS Misses Estimates” and “Group 1 Drops as Profit Misses, Hurt By New Regulation in U.K.,” were some Bloomberg headlines. Here is how Chief Financial Officer John Rickel started his portion of the earnings call yesterday: Thank you, Earl, and good morning, everyone. Before I cover my prepared remarks, I want to take just a moment and address some confusion around our earnings consensus that’s arisen this morning. As of 10:30 P.M. Central Standard Time last night, the consensus in Bloomberg and in FactSet was basically $2.29 per share. Sometime over the overnight hours, a new estimate was entered into the system from our Morgan Stanley analyst, who increased his quarterly estimate from $2.25 to $2.58, an almost 15% increase in expected earnings. I would note there was no covering note that went with this increase, so I could not able to address what changed his expectations. If you look now in FactSet it still reflects $2.29, which we believe is the more appropriate estimate. Bloomberg, however, has picked up this inflated estimate that came out late and it's now reflecting a higher number. We would respectfully suggest to our covering analysts and to our investors that the appropriate thing to do is to ignore that higher estimate that came in late and continue to reflect what is in FactSet at $2.29 as our agreed consensus for the quarter. It is such a magical thing to argue about. After you report that your earnings were $2.31, why would you say that $2.29 “is the more appropriate estimate” of those earnings than $2.35? I guess it’s true—$2.29 is closer to $2.31 than $2.35 is—but you don’t have to estimate at all anymore: The earnings were $2.31, so the most appropriate estimate is not $2.29 or $2.35 or any other number, but $2.31. Obviously the CFO is not saying “you should estimate our earnings at $2.29,” because he just told you that the earnings were $2.31. No, what he is saying is more like: “You should have estimated our earnings at $2.29, just before we announced them, because then you would have been pleasantly surprised by $2.31.” As opposed to having estimated the earnings at $2.35 and being disappointed by $2.31. This is an argument not about Group 1’s earnings, but about how the analysts should feel about them. Except it’s not quite even that; it’s an argument about how analysts did feel about them. It’s not exactly “you should have estimated earnings at $2.29 and been pleased,” it’s “really, ignoring weird outliers, you did estimate earnings at $2.29, so you are pleased.” Were they pleased? I dunno; the stock opened below Monday’s close, and at one point was down as much as 5 percent, but it started rallying in mid-afternoon and ultimately closed up 0.7 percent for the day. It is … just … possible … ? … that investors read the earnings release, said “$2.31? we expected $2.35,” dumped the stock, listened to the call at 10 a.m., heard Rickel’s argument that they had expected $2.29, thought about it for a while, concluded that they really had expected $2.29, and started buying the stock. None of this makes much sense. Surely the people who expected earnings to be $2.29, or $2.25 or whatever, were pleasantly surprised by the $2.31 result (and maybe bought more), while the people who expected earnings to be $2.35, or $2.58 or whatever, were disappointed (and maybe sold); those were—surely!?—actual subjective expectations held by actual people, and could not be changed retroactively by the CFO saying “actually you expected something else.” Meanwhile surely the (many more) people who had no expectations whatsoever about Group 1’s earnings also had no reason to retroactively develop those expectations after the CFO announced what they should have been. And yet! My implicit crude model is “people expect what they expect, and then are pleased or disappointed by the contrast between reality and their expectations.” The CFO’s implicit crude model seems to be “people are aware of the reported consensus of analyst estimates, and then buy or sell stock based on the contrast between reported earnings and that reported consensus.” Mine feels … sort of sensible? … but his is probably right. You should buy stocks because the market undervalues them, not because you are personally fond of their business; you need to care as much about the market’s view of the company as you do about your own view of its fundamentals; stock markets are Keynesian beauty contests, not regular ones. (Also, you know: algorithms!) It’s just that normally you’d get the expectations from the market (or from analysts, or from data providers), and the earnings from the company; here, the company had to provide both the expectations and the earnings itself. Elsewhere in expectations, Snap Inc.’s stock was up 1.9 percent yesterday on terrible, but less terrible than expected , headlines like “Snap Stems the Flood of Users Leaving Its App” and “Snap’s User Base Stops Shrinking as Revenue Beats Estimates” and “Snap Stock Soaring On News That Not Everyone Has Stopped Using Snap.”

One general piece of not-legal-advice that I like to give about insider trading is that it’s never illegal to trade on your own intentions. If Warren Buffett or Carl Icahn announce that they like a stock, that stock will go up; there is nothing whatsoever wrong with them buying the stock first and then announcing that they like it. There is an important caveat to this rule, though, which is that you have to check to make sure that you are actually the owner of your own intentions. Most people in the investing industry make a living by selling their investment views to someone else, and if you are one of them, then you are no longer necessarily free to use those decisions for your own profit. So if you are one of Warren Buffett’s subordinate stock-pickers, and you first buy stock for your personal account, then buy a lot of the same stock for Berkshire Hathaway Inc., then announce Berkshire’s stake, and then sell your own stock for a profit—that tends to look bad. Or if you are an independent trader and blogger, you can probably first buy a stock and then write a blog post about how good it is, but if you are an investment columnist at the Wall Street Journal, the Journal owns your (for-publication) opinions, and the same exact procedure will get you in trouble. And then there is this, don’t do this, come on: A former equity analyst who made more than 34,000 euros ($39,000) in an hour by investing in Vallourec SA just before he raised his own rating on the French company had his fine doubled by an appeals court. Ex-Kepler Cheuvreux SA analyst Geoffroy Stern will have to pay an extra 100,000 euros after France’s highest administrative court ruled that a lower jurisdiction erred in its ruling. The court found that he benefited from insider information when making trades based on draft recommendations written by him and others that the brokerage was set to publish hours later. I feel like the idea of “what if I buy a stock just before I recommend it” has probably occurred to a lot of equity analysts over time, but mostly these days someone explains the problem to them and they don’t actually do it.

We have talked a couple of times about Quadriga CX, the Canadian cryptocurrency exchange that put millions of dollars’ worth of cryptocurrencies into offline cold storage wallets and then lost the keys to those wallets when its founder and sole employee (!) died suddenly in India. Or did it? Here is the Wall Street Journal: Two independent researchers say publicly available transaction records associated with QuadrigaCX suggest the money may be gone, not trapped. They say it appears Quadriga transferred customer funds to other cryptocurrency exchanges, although it isn’t clear what might have happened to the money from there. “It is extremely likely that there aren’t any cold wallets,” one analyst told the Journal. I suppose if you’re a customer you are rooting for this outcome: If the money was stolen, there’s a chance that investigators can find some of it and get it back; if it was really locked in a cold wallet on a laptop and then the only person with the password died, then it could be gone forever. You’re better off dealing with a dishonest larcenous exchange than an honest one that takes security too seriously. (And dies, I mean.) I’m sorry, I know that this is just the most boring and obvious cliché about cryptocurrency, but still I have like a physical need to say it: If you are a believer in the power of cryptocurrency, if you like its promise of trustless decentralized money, why did you entrust millions of dollars of your money to one guy with a laptop? One guy with a laptop! Ooooooh it was “ the largest crypto exchange in Canada,” sure, but it was also one guy with a laptop, and he died and bricked the laptop and now your money is gone. (Or he didn’t and it’s stolen, or some other dumb combination of those things.) “I don’t trust the banks, but this chap from the internet seems nice, and he has a laptop, I’m sure he can hold my money for me, and what are the odds that he’ll die suddenly?” Gahhhhh come on. This is not how it works! Either you have some sort of stable trustworthy regulatory and investor-protection framework so that you can go to any reputable intermediary and assume that it will do what it says it will do, or you have to do your own careful due diligence on any intermediary before choosing to trust it. But no one seems to have done the diligence of, like, showing up at Quadriga CX’s headquarters/house and asking “wait where are the rest of you,” in the same way that I’ve never gone to Valley Forge, Pa., to make sure that the Vanguard Group is actually there. The problem is that people think they don’t trust the traditional financial system, but in fact its most basic functionality—not forgetting where it put your money—is so reliable that people just keep assuming without evidence that the crypto system must work the same way. Surely a big crypto exchange must have, like, systems, and lawyers, and more than one employee , so you can trust it, right? Wrong! If I ever buy Bitcoins I will keep them at Gemini, the Winklevoss twins’ exchange, just because I am absolutely sure there are two of them. Elsewhere, the guy with the laptop, Quadriga CX founder Gerald Cotten, “filed a will 12 days before his death listing substantial assets,” including a yacht and an airplane. And at a Canadian court hearing yesterday, the court was shown a picture of Quadriga’s bank drafts, which were kept on a stove, next to a lit candle , which feels a little heavy-handed as a metaphor. A Quadriga lawyer said that they’re now “off the stove,” though that doesn’t help any with unlocking the laptop. Uh I don’t really know how to put this, so I am just going to say it. Yesterday Tesla Inc. director Linda Johnson Rice exercised options on 1,700 shares of Tesla stock at a strike price of $319.57, and then sold the stock at $320 per share, for net proceeds of 43 cents per share, or $731 total. The options would have expired in July 2024; Bloomberg’s option calculator estimates that they were worth about $160 per share, or $272,000 total. When Tesla granted her the options in 2017, it valued them at $115 per share. She just gave them away for 43 cents. I do not know why you would do this. Rice did the same thing last month—the exercises and sales are part of an automatic Rule 10b5-1 trading plan that she set up in November—and I was puzzled then too. She has another 10,628 options left, worth well over $1 million, and I can only assume that she plans to throw them away for pennies too. I hope that there is some absolutely mind-blowing tax trade going on here.

s.h: People are worried about stock buybacks
s.t: Here are Senators Chuck Schumer and Bernie Sanders in the New York Times with, mostly, the usual arguments about why stock buybacks are bad: First, stock buybacks don’t benefit the vast majority of Americans. That’s because large stockholders tend to be wealthier. Nearly 85 percent of all stocks owned by Americans belong to the wealthiest 10 percent of households. Of course, many corporate executives are compensated through stock-based pay. So when a company buys back its stock, boosting its value, the benefits go overwhelmingly to shareholders and executives, not workers. Second, when corporations direct resources to buy back shares on this scale, they restrain their capacity to reinvest profits more meaningfully in the company in terms of R&D, equipment, higher wages, paid medical leave, retirement benefits and worker retraining. There are two strands of argument here. One is that the capitalists are wrong about their own interests, that companies that spend money on stock buybacks instead of on research and development will be less profitable in the long term. I think you should be very skeptical of this argument, if for nothing else then on efficient-markets grounds: When the actual shareholders of a company, with their own money on the line, want the company to do one thing, and Bernie Sanders and Chuck Schumer want it to do something else, it is hard for me to believe that Sanders and Schumer are the ones who are maximizing long-term shareholder value. But the second argument is that even if the capitalists are right about their own interests, those interests are adverse to those of workers: Even if buying back stock enhances long-term shareholder value, it might come at the expense of higher wages for workers. At some general level I do not find this especially hard to believe. Workers and owners are not in a zero-sum bargaining game— most good corporate ideas work out well for both workers and shareholders—but, sure, there is an obvious conflict; shareholders would probably mostly like to pay less for labor and workers would probably mostly like to be paid more. Most people who don’t like buybacks want to discourage them generally, while most people who don’t like, uh, the enrichment of capitalists at the expense of workers propose, uh, other things. But Schumer and Sanders have a sort of compromise idea: They want to limit buybacks to companies that pay workers well. That is why we are planning to introduce bold legislation to address this crisis. Our bill will prohibit a corporation from buying back its own stock unless it invests in workers and communities first, including things like paying all workers at least $15 an hour, providing seven days of paid sick leave, and offering decent pensions and more reliable health benefits. In other words, our legislation would set minimum requirements for corporate investment in workers and the long-term strength of the company as a precondition for a corporation entering into a share buyback plan. The goal is to curtail the overreliance on buybacks while also incentivizing the productive investment of corporate capital. “The productive investment of corporate capital” isn’t really what they mean here. If some doomed old-economy firm is slowly lurching towards its inevitable end, the way to productively invest that firm’s money is probably to give it back to investors so they can put it into a better business. Giving the money to workers instead, so they can have health insurance for a few more years as the firm declines, is not primarily a productivity-maximization plan. But that doesn’t mean that it’s wrong! Here’s a weird thing though. Schumer and Sanders write: “Some may argue that if Congress limits stock buybacks, corporations could shift to issuing larger dividends,” and they propose that “we should also seriously consider policies to limit the payout of dividends, perhaps through the tax code.” This is a little odd on first principles. Buybacks and dividends are, roughly speaking, the same thing, and if you think it’s a good idea to limit buybacks to companies that pay their workers well, you should want to limit dividends in exactly the same way. You could just write “our bill will prohibit a corporation from doing buybacks or dividends unless” etc. etc. But there is probably a good reason why they wrote it this way. The reason is that they are U.S. senators, and stock buybacks are mostly a matter of federal securities law .[1] Until about 1982, it was widely believed to be “market manipulation” for a company to buy its own stock in the open market, but then the Securities and Exchange Commission enacted the “safe harbor” of Rule 10b-18, and now buybacks that follow the requirements of that rule are not considered manipulative. Congress could easily change that rule to ban buybacks (by declaring them manipulative), or to add new requirements (like paying workers, etc.). Dividends, meanwhile, are mostly a matter of state corporate law .[2] Corporate law regulates how companies can pay dividends, and corporate law is left to the states, and the courts are generally skeptical of efforts to federalize it. Securities law regulates the buying and selling of securities, and dividends do not involve buying and selling securities, so the SEC and Congress basically leave them alone. So when Schumer and Sanders propose to limit buybacks, it would be pretty easy for them to do it. (I mean they’d need to get the votes and pass the law and so forth, and I don’t think it’s especially likely, but my point is that they, like, work in the right building to do it.) If they proposed to limit dividends, they’d have a tougher time. The people who could most easily limit dividends are the legislators in Delaware (where most big U.S. companies are incorporated), and they have no particular incentive to side with labor over capital. I dwell on this because it is strange that stock buybacks have become a genuine political issue, while dividends have not. From a corporate finance perspective they come to much the same thing: Either way, a company decides that it doesn’t need all of the money that it generates, and so it returns some to investors so that they can invest it in something else. But buybacks are hated, while dividends are mostly ignored. Why? Part of it is probably that buybacks are relatively new—rising to prominence since the 1980s—while dividends are very old and traditional: Buybacks are associated with financial engineering and the shareholder-value revolution and other modern financial developments; dividends are associated with old-fashioned stability for widows and orphans. Part of it is probably that the “market manipulation” intuition is real: People think that, if a company buys its own stock to push the price up, that is somehow dishonest, in a way that freely distributing the cash is not. But part of it might just be these sort of institutional dynamics. Stock buybacks are a legitimate subject for Congress and the SEC to think about; they are essentially a matter of federal law, and so candidates for national office can have positions on stock buybacks. Dividends are mostly a subject for Delaware law, and so national politicians have less to say about them. It’s not that buybacks are a distinctively bad problem; it’s that, if you think they’re a problem, they’re a distinctively solvable problem. Because buybacks can be addressed by national policy, they can become a national issue.

How much do you think Slack Technologies Inc.’s investment bankers will charge it for advising on its direct listing, in which Slack will go public just by listing its stock on the exchange without selling any shares in an initial public offering? When Spotify Technologies SA went public in a direct listing last year, supposedly cutting Wall Street banks out of the lucrative IPO business, it actually paid its Wall Street banks more than $30 million of fees, which is maybe a little on the low side but not a terrible payday for an offering that, after all, didn’t raise any money for the company. But those fees were so high because Spotify and its banks were figuring it out as they went along: There had never been a comparable direct listing by a large high-profile company on modern U.S. stock markets, and so the banks needed to answer basic questions like whether it was even allowed, and what legal documents you needed, and how to tell the company’s story to investors without a traditional roadshow, and how to line up investors for the first day of trading without a traditional bookbuilding. It was all novel and complicated and required a lot of work and a fair amount of skill and market judgment. But then it all worked out great! It will be a lot easier the second time. And the stakes will quickly get a lot lower for the issuer. The work of leading an initial public offering is pretty routinized at this point, but companies still pay banks a lot of money for it, because they are trying to raise money and a good execution can mean the difference between raising a lot of money at a high price and raising less money at a low price. When you do the first direct listing, good execution means basically avoiding some unforeseen disaster that somehow prevents you from listing your stock or gets you in bad trouble with the SEC or investors. But when you do, like, the fifth direct listing, the difference between good execution and mediocre execution becomes unimportant. You’re not selling stock; you’re just letting it trade at whatever price the market dictates, and there is nothing time-sensitive about that price: If it’s lower than you’d like, you can keep meeting with investors and announcing good results until it goes up. So you don’t care very much if the banks do a good or bad or indifferent job of lining up investors and arguing for a high valuation on your first day. Anyway Slack has filed confidentially to go public, and it plans to do so with a direct listing. As we discussed last month, this makes sense, both because Slack doesn’t need to raise money and also because Slack seems to revel in creative corporate finance. Honestly it would probably still be fun and lucrative to be a banker working on the second direct listing. There is still stuff to figure out, still potholes to watch out for, still a good case to be made that the company needs your wise guidance. (The fact that Slack is using the same three banks as Spotify—Goldman Sachs Group Inc., Morgan Stanley and Allen & Co.—suggests that it cares about their expertise.) But you’d also have the nagging feeling that you are eating your own seed corn, and that it won’t take too many more successful direct listings before this stops being a lucrative business—maybe stops being a business at all—for banks. (Would you be a little tempted to take one for the team and mess it up badly, to discourage future direct listings? How?) Elsewhere in IPOs, here is a story about how “Saudi technocrats remain determined to stop [the Saudi Aramco IPO] from ever happening”: At a meeting of Aramco executives in Saudi Arabia’s Eastern Province, the room fell silent when one of them questioned the entire idea of a public listing, that executive recalled in an interview. Aramco, the executive said, spends $5 to extract a barrel of oil and then sells it for 10 to 20 times that much. Where else, he asked, could Saudi Arabia possibly invest to generate such returns? No one had an answer, the executive said.

In general I feel like I read many more stories about Financial Engineering Run Amok than I do stories about Financial Engineering Allocating Risks in a Tidy Way to Solve a Real Problem, so when I do come across the latter category it is always very pleasing. Here is a story about how some people want there to be lynxes in England, while other people do not want lynxes in England to eat their sheep, and how the gap was bridged by the people who want the lynxes buying insurance that will pay the people who do not want the lynxes if the lynxes eat their sheep: A syndicate of underwriters, working through Lloyd’s of London, is offering financial protection to the farmers so they’ll be compensated for lost sheep. “It shows that we were not just paying lip service to stakeholders, we were actually thinking of solutions to engage with them,” says O’Donoghue, who is chief scientific adviser to the Lynx UK Trust. Coasean bargaining! The credibility-enhancing value of bets! Obviously it would be better if the lynxes were buying the insurance for the sheep, rather than the lynx trust buying the insurance for the sheep farmers, but that’s really the point here: Humanity is the only species that uses financial engineering to achieve mutually beneficial outcomes, go us.

Here is a story about a Bridgewater Associates manager fired for an office romance: Bridgewater claimed Bob Elliott, who was head of foreign-exchange research, didn’t properly disclose the relationship, the people said. Elliott told superiors about the relationship with a female colleague and believes he was dismissed without cause, one of the people said. The woman, who was at the firm for three years and didn’t report to Elliott, also was fired. I don’t know what happened here but I would like to believe that both sides are telling the truth and that it is a very Bridgewater misunderstanding: Sure he told his superiors about the relationship, but maybe he didn’t confess it at a firmwide meeting and give everyone the chance to ask him questions about his dating history and his attitude toward commitment. “Office romances are relatively common at the firm,” and how could they not be? Bridgewater combines the general financial-industry problem of bringing together a bunch of young people to work long hours together, with being fairly isolated in Connecticut, with being an intense oversharing therapy cult in which workers spend much of their time analyzing each other. (“It’s kind of a family atmosphere,” says the co-CEO, which I suppose some would consider a deterrent to dating.) Of course some of them will date each other, and of course some of them will not be as transparent about it as Bridgewater wants, because Bridgewater, generally, seems to demand an uncomfortable level of transparency.

s.h: People are worried about bond market liquidity
s.t: Here is Chris White of ViableMkts and BondCliQ: There has never been any statistical evidence that buy-side to buy-side trading can create meaningful liquidity in any financial market…ever…in the entire history of financial markets. However, this idea is consistently raised as the ingredient for a better corporate bond market and continues to spawn new ideas for trading solutions that remove intermediaries (dealers) from the trading process. … For a buy-side to buy-side trade to happen, Asset Manager ABC must have a standing order to sell a specific CUSIP within the same time period that Asset Manager XYZ has a standing order to buy that same CUSIP. The critical catalyst to any potential buy-side to buy-side trade is that one asset manager must have a redemption or need/want to change their portfolio composition while the other has an inflow (cash) or the opposite need/want to change their portfolio composition at the same time. This restriction is what makes Buy-Side Liquidity impractical and unreliable for consistent trading. The illustration I always turn to here is the stock market. U.S. stock exchanges run as all-to-all electronic exchanges; anyone can trade stock with anyone else, without being forced to go to a middleman. And in practice virtually everyone trades with middlemen, in the form of high-frequency traders; platforms that try to exclude the middlemen (by banning evil HFTs, etc.) tend to either have low volume or to get in trouble for secretly sneaking HFTs back in. It’s just unusual for one big mutual fund to want to sell a particular stock at the exact millisecond that another big mutual fund wants to buy it. They could wait around to find each other—and there are venues that will let them do that—but for the most part the preference seems to be to get immediacy from a middleman rather than waiting for a natural trade. With bonds—which already trade less frequently and are more fragmented—it seems like an even bigger issue.
