[1] Of course state corporate law also regulates buybacks, but practically it does not often seem to be the binding constraint. [2] Of course dividends are also a matter of tax law, in the sense that everything is a matter of tax law, and as Schumer and Sanders suggest, Congress could discourage dividends by changing their tax treatment. The problem with this is that their tax treatment, for the companies that pay them, is already not particularly great: Unlike interest on debt, dividends are not tax deductible, so there is no real tax advantage to paying them. Congress could increase the taxes that investors pay on dividends that they receive, or just add some sort of corporate surtax on dividends paid, but there’s not an obvious elegant tax way to discourage dividends.

Should mainland Chinese stocks be included in major indexes of emerging markets? I don’t really know how you’d go about answering that question from first principles. Like you could say “Chinese companies tend to have [better][worse] corporate governance than companies in other emerging markets,” or “Chinese markets tend to have [better][worse] liquidity,” or “the Chinese government tends to be [better][worse] at upholding the rule of law,” or of course “Chinese stocks tend to go [up][down] more than other emerging-market stocks,” or whatever, but I am not sure what any of those things have to do with anything. Or you could say “China exists, and Chinese stocks exist, and so a list of all the stocks that exist should include Chinese stocks”; I am more sympathetic to that argument, but it doesn’t really tell you much about whether to include those stocks in the category of “emerging markets.” A stock market index is mostly a summary of a set of social facts; the “emerging market index” is a list of the sorts of stocks that funds that call themselves “emerging markets funds” want to invest in. If every “emerging markets fund” invests in Chinese stocks, then the index should have some Chinese stocks; if none do, then it shouldn’t; if half do, then … I dunno? Naively I might say “if half do, then half of them should benchmark themselves to a China-inclusive index and the other half should benchmark themselves to a China-exclusive index,” but I suppose that sounds disappointingly relativistic; surely every fund manager shouldn’t get to choose her own index. ( Or should she?) The nice thing is that, if this vague and lazy notion of indexing is correct, index providers have pretty good incentives to get it right. Index funds pay them licensing fees to use their indexes. The more their indexes track the actual desires of investment managers (and, presumably, of those managers’ customers), the more money they will make. If, on the other hand, you think that this notion is incorrect, and that an index has to be based on some sort of objective principle—about governance or liquidity or whatever—then you might sometimes find yourself thinking that an index provider’s decision is “wrong.” And you might think that the index provider was unduly swayed by commercial considerations to abandon its principles and make a decision that pleased its customers and increased its revenue even though that decision was wrong. I tend to take the social/relativistic view—an index is a list of stocks that investors want to be included in the index—and so I tend to think it is incoherent to say that an index-inclusion decision might be wrong. But I suppose some people disagree. Anyway here is a story about “ How China Pressured MSCI to Add Its Market to Major Benchmark”: Last summer, the world’s largest index provider added stocks in China to one of its most prominent global benchmarks, leading billions of dollars to flow into Chinese shares and advancing China’s plans to draw more foreign investors to its markets. The move by MSCI Inc. came after it came under heavy pressure from the Chinese government, which tried to curtail the company’s business in the country, according to people familiar with the matter. MSCI’s decision to include domestic Chinese stocks in its widely followed Emerging Markets Index was received unfavorably by some investors who were concerned about robustness and transparency of markets in the world’s second-largest economy. Since the addition, Chinese stocks have stumbled, as has the global index. Yet business has boomed in China for MSCI and large global asset managers who supported its move. If you think that the goal of the emerging-markets index is to include stocks that will go up, then this is a failure. If you think that it is to include stocks that large global asset managers want to invest in, then it’s fine. “The episode raises questions about the independence of MSCI at a time when the firm wields increasing market power,” and I suppose it does: To the extent MSCI was driven by business and regulatory pressures from the Chinese government, as opposed to pressures from its paying customers, then that would be bad. But if you take the social/relativistic view, all of the words here just sound sort of strange: MSCI said all of its index decisions are made after consultations and feedback from a wide range of global market participants, including asset owners and managers, brokers, local authorities, regulators, stock exchanges and others. The consultation process is “transparent and objective to ensure MSCI indexes remain relevant and accurate investment decision support tools for its clients,” the firm said in a statement to the Journal. The company cited safeguards including the fact that its index-inclusion process is handled by its editorial division, which is separate from its commercial operations, and based on criteria that it has made public. “MSCI acts as a conduit between local policy decision makers and international institutional investors to constructively communicate market feedback; it takes this responsibility very seriously,” it said. Really who cares if the criteria are transparent and objective, or if the decisions are kept separate from commercial operations, or if a wide range of perspectives are considered? It just feels like a better answer would be “our clients wanted to invest in Chinese stocks so we told them it was okay to invest in Chinese stocks.” Making it more objective and less commercial than that feels like a mistake; these decisions can’t be made objectively, and pretending that they can be might get you in trouble.

On Friday I proposed sort of an extreme legal-realist theory of corporate law, suggesting that Citgo Petroleum Corp. will effectively be owned by whoever Donald Trump thinks should own it. I want to be clear that Citgo—which is owned by the government of Venezuela, while the control of the government of Venezuela is disputed—is a very special case, and that my general theory of corporate law is not “it’s whatever Donald Trump wants.” At the same time, though, as a matter of prudent risk management, it does seem sensible not to put yourself in a position of having something that Donald Trump wants and might try to take from you. The president of the United States has a lot of power, is the general, not especially rigorous, but nonetheless worth noting, legal point here. Anyway Deutsche Bank AG knows what I am talking about; here is a story about how the bank, a longtime lender to Trump, denied him a loan during the 2016 presidential election campaign: Senior officials at the bank, including its future chief executive, believed that Mr. Trump’s divisive candidacy made such a loan too risky, the people said. Among their concerns was that if Mr. Trump won the election and then defaulted, Deutsche Bank would have to choose between not collecting on the debt or seizing the assets of the president of the United States. Well, right, imagine it. Some mid-level Deutsche Bank official goes to court and obtains a foreclosure order, and then they call the sheriff to evict Trump from his building, and the sheriff gets there and finds the building guarded by, like, the Marines. Again I am not saying that this is the likely outcome, or that this is the way that the law of secured transactions works in any formal legal sense, but you can see why Deutsche Bank might not have been especially keen to find out. Also this is a very pleasing risk management heuristic from Deutsche Bank: Officials in the private-banking unit protested that Deutsche Bank already had numerous outstanding loans to Mr. Trump and that there was no reason not to make another, two of the people said. The decision was appealed to Deutsche Bank’s top executives in Frankfurt. There are at least three subtly different ways to read that. One is as a theory of efficient time management in underwriting: If you’ve already made a loan to someone, that means you have already concluded that he’s a good credit risk, so you are just wasting time re-analyzing the credit from scratch. Another is a practical analysis of personal risk and reward: If the existing loans go bad, everyone involved will be in trouble, but they won’t really be in any more trouble if some more loans go bad (you can only be fired once), so you might as well collect the fees from the new loans and hope they all work out. But you can also imagine an almost superstitious view, like, “we will be in trouble if the existing loans go bad, so the best thing to do is to tiptoe around very quietly and never say anything negative about those loans so as not to bring cruel fate down upon us, so let’s not raise any questions about making additional loans now.” Elsewhere in Deutsche Bank news, “Congressional investigators expect the House Financial Services Committee to examine Deutsche Bank AG’s efforts after the 2016 election to shed a loan it made to VTB Group, a large Russian state-owned bank.”

An oddity of the current moment in the financial world is that there are a number of famous billionaires who have jobs that consist mostly, but not entirely, of managing their own money. John Paulson manages a multi-billion-dollar hedge fund, and has clients, and collects fees, but “almost 75 to 80 percent of the money” in the fund is his. Steve Cohen, after an enforced hiatus, manages a multi-billion-dollar hedge fund, and has clients, and collects fees, but something like $11 billion of the money that he runs is his, versus about $5 billion of outside money. Bill Gross started his tenure running the Janus Henderson Global Unconstrained Bond Fund by investing $700 million of his own money into it; by the end of last year the fund was down to $950 million. These seem like strange dynamics, particularly for Gross, who works for a big company and has a boss. Why go to the office every day and answer emails from a boss if you are basically just investing your personal fortune? (From the boss’s perspective, why pay someone a salary if he is basically just investing his personal fortune?) You can just, like, get an E*Trade account; if it’s just your money then it doesn’t need to be a job. Certainly a lot of hedge fund managers have reached this conclusion, and have converted their funds into family offices, though of course Cohen went the other way. Anyway, after a run of disappointing performance at Janus—“The issue that plagued Gross was that he was too unconstrained for his own good at Janus,” writes my Bloomberg Opinion colleague Brian Chappatta—Bill Gross is converting into a family office. Or rather he’s doing the mutual-fund-manager version of that, which is called “retiring”: In his next phase, Gross, 74, will focus on managing his personal assets and remain active in charitable endeavors, according to a statement from Janus. He has made philanthropic donations of $800 million in the past 20 years. “I learned early on that without a client, there can be no franchise,” said Gross in his farewell statement, and, um, right.

s.h: You can’t take it with you
s.t: We talked on Friday about the problems of QuadrigaCX, the Canadian cryptocurrency exchange that lost most of its customers’ cryptocurrencies because they were in “cold storage” and it “forgot the password.” But the practical details of how Quadriga forgot the password are even more embarrassing than that: Quadriga’s “ sole director and officer,” Gerry Cotten, was also the only person with the password, and Cotten “ died of complications due to Crohn’s disease in India on Dec. 9, while opening an orphanage.” So you can’t blame him for forgetting the password! You can blame him for everything else, though. (He “left behind no business records,” oops.) And you can certainly blame everyone else at QuadrigaCX for their utter lack of interest in protecting customer deposits. “One of Gerry’s many accomplishments was his ability to build a highly capable and successful management team, which will continue his legacy,” said QuadrigaCX, somehow, in a statement, and I am going to have to partially disagree. Yes, certainly, its management team will continue his legacy, in that he lost a bunch of cryptocurrency and they have continued not to find it. But “highly capable and successful”? Successful? Their first act in charge of a cryptocurrency exchange was to announce that it had lost all of its cryptocurrency. Their failure is absolute and categorical. And I do not think it would be unreasonable to expect that a financial-services executive of average, or even considerably below-average, capability might have asked at some point “hey what is our plan for keeping the money safe other than relying on one guy to remember the passwords?” Also, this is awkward, so I am going to outsource it to Gizmodo: Some other reporting has suggested it is possible some of the funds in question moved after the case was publicized, and though the evidence was not definitive, it and the strange circumstances of Cotten’s death spurred accusations that his demise was either faked or the pretext for an exit scam by other parties with access to the holdings, according to CCN. Well that’s a pretty good plot for my cryptocurrency novel! (Is there a series of world-weary crypto detective novels? Like Inspector Montalbano but on the blockchain? There should be.) The lesson is perhaps that the amount of money you should put into a crypto exchange should be capped at the amount where, if it turned out that all of your money was stolen in a farcical plot, you’d be like “well it was worth it to lose that amount of money to participate in this farce.” People pay money for Knicks tickets; you should think of your crypto investments like that.

Here is an interesting story about how, compared to the rest of Wall Street, the hot business of managing collateralized loan obligations is relatively female-dominated. (Relatively: “Female executives hold only one out of every 10 senior management jobs in the investment industry, according to data provider Preqin Ltd, but in the burgeoning field of CLOs, one out of every four bosses is a woman.”) It is among other things a model of applying value investing principles to your career: “The strong female cadre in CLOs traces back to gender discrimination at banks in the late 1980s,” when banks started hiring women “but rarely placed them in high-profile—and high-paying—roles like trading bonds or chasing merger deals.” Instead they became commercial loan analysts, and years later those skills became valuable for CLO managers. In general it is better to go into a field that is going to be lucrative and glamorous than one that has been lucrative and glamorous, and one could imagine a sort of countercyclical egalitarian current on Wall Street: Everyone wants to go to the currently glamorous businesses, which means that people who face discrimination are more likely to wind up in the currently out-of-favor businesses, which means that they have a better shot of being leaders in the next glamorous business. One should not, obviously, overstate this; again, one out of four CLO managers is a woman.

Honestly capitalism is amazing. If you have a lot of money, you can buy a big yacht. If you have even more money, you can buy priceless artworks and put them in your yacht. And if you have the very most money, you can hang priceless artworks in your yacht, let your children throw breakfast cereal at them, and then hire an art expert to act like this is a genuine problem and solve it for you. Imagine, like, making small talk with the barista at your coffee shop: You: Hey how’s it going? Barista: Pretty good, how are you? You: Not great honestly. My kids threw cornflakes at the $110 million Basquiat that I keep on my superyacht and now it is smudged. Barista: [ sings Marseillaise, constructs guillotine ] But if you have enough money you can just pay the right person—specifically an “Oxford-educated art historian and conservationist” who does this sort of thing, whatever that is—to get the interaction that you want rather than the one that you would ordinarily get: You: Hey how’s it going? Oxford-educated art historian and conservationist: Pretty good, how are you? You: Not great honestly. My kids threw cornflakes at the $110 million Basquiat that I keep on my superyacht and now it is smudged. O-EAH&C: Oh you poor dear, let me give you a hug, now let’s fix that Basquiat right up. Anyway here is what appears to be a real news article.

We have talked about this question a few times in the past, and I have advocated for a sort of legal-realist approach, one that focuses less on philosophical debates about shareholder rights and board accountability and more on practical questions like, who has the keys to the front door and the password to the website? I feel like that approach is soon going to be very useful in understanding Citgo Petroleum Corp. If you look at an org chart, you will notice that Citgo is owned by Petróleos de Venezuela SA, and that PdVSA is in turn owned by the nation of Venezuela, giving the president of Venezuela the ultimate power to appoint (the people who appoint) the people who run Citgo. But if you look at a map, you will notice that Citgo is mostly in the U.S., while Venezuela is mostly in Venezuela, which has important implications for the exercise of that power, given that the U.S. is trying to oust Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and is supporting opposition leader Juan Guaidó’s claim to the presidency. So for instance the president of Venezuela, Maduro, can appoint the president of Citgo and send him to the U.S. to run Citgo, but the U.S. can just not let him come in. That happened: The U.S. State Department last year revoked the passport of Citgo’s current president, Asdrúbal Chávez, who has been presiding over the company from afar. “Presiding over the company from afar” suggests that he at least gets to appoint and order around the subordinates who run Citgo day-to-day in the U.S., but that too is somewhat precarious, as the U.S. government could always lock those people out of the company on national-security grounds. That might also happen: Loyalists to Mr. Maduro inside Citgo may be referred to the Treasury Department for further scrutiny over concerns around their personal access to company assets, a person with knowledge with the matter said. “Loyalists to Mr. Maduro inside Citgo” is a bit of an odd idea in the context of corporate control. Whatever their political loyalties, or nationalities for that matter, presumably everyone who works at Citgo has a boss, and mostly they do what their bosses tell them to do. The bosses have bosses, etc., until ultimately they all answer to Chávez, the president of Citgo, who answers to PdVSA, which answers to Maduro. This is not a matter of political loyalism but of corporate hierarchy. On the other hand, you could if you wanted—that is, the U.S. federal government could if it wanted—chop off the hierarchy at some point near the top, and graft a new top onto it. That also seems like the plan: Mr. Guaidó is planning to install new boards at PdVSA and Citgo, raising complex legal questions about who controls those businesses and potentially creating a governance crisis. Oh I think the governance crisis is pretty inevitable, but let’s focus on how you “install” a board. This is a matter of corporate formalities, shareholder voting, etc., but mostly it is a matter of, when the people you name as directors show up at the boardroom, do they get to come in or not. Deep down at the bottom of all analysis of legal rights, the question is “will men with guns show up and make this thing happen?” To oversimplify, Guaidó right now does not seem to have much ability to send men with guns to PdVSA’s headquarters to install a new board, though he is working on it. On the other hand Maduro definitely does not have any ability to send men with guns to Citgo’s headquarters to keep his board there, and Donald Trump more or less does have the ability to send men with guns to install Guaidó’s,[1] which means that if Trump’s administration backs Guaidó then it should not be too hard for his appointees to take control of Citgo. (Though not, yet, of PdVSA.) Here, when I say “control,” I am not referring to abstract concepts like beneficial ownership of the requisite number of voting shares. I mean, like, do they get to push the button that turns on the refinery or whatever. Anyway all of those quotes are from this Wall Street Journal article about how Citgo is considering filing for bankruptcy as a way to … well, as a way to sort out all the claims of Citgo’s and PdVSA’s and Venezuela’s creditors in an orderly fashion, for one thing, but also as a way to get a U.S. federal court involved in figuring out all of these questions about who controls Citgo: A bankruptcy filing isn’t imminent or certain, people familiar with the matter said. But it is one of several options the company and U.S. government officials are considering to keep Citgo’s Gulf Coast crude operations running and to preserve the assets from being looted by loyalists to President Nicolás Maduro or dismantled by creditors, they said. Obviously the actual legal analysis, in or out of bankruptcy, is more complicated than “this guy is the guy who the U.S. government wants to be president of Citgo, so now he is president of Citgo,” and if your analysis of corporate control generally is as simple as “the government can do whatever it wants” then you will mostly be wrong. I’m not sure you’d be that wrong here though!

Yo, lo: A tiny Vancouver-based cannabis company whose former ticker was YOLO, short for “you only live once,” was declared the winner of the POT stock symbol lottery in Canada. Weekend Unlimited Inc. said Friday that it won the first-ever random lottery for a Canadian ticker symbol. The company debuted on the Canadian Securities Exchange on Oct. 15, two days before the country legalized recreational marijuana. The stock has fallen 57 percent since the Oct. 15 market close, bringing its market value to C$28.6 million before trading opened Friday. Really “Weekend Unlimited” is pretty good too; in its three and a half months as a public company it has managed to have a great name and two great tickers, somewhat undercutting its contention that you only live once. Bloomberg tells me that it “engages in the manufacturing and sale of cannabis glassware and cannabis-related paraphernalia,” so now you know how a Bloomberg DES page says “it makes bongs.” Also, how was its ticker not BONG? We talked about the POT lottery the other day, and I conjectured that it would be worth a lot of money and suggested that an academic should write a paper about it. Well here is your event study. As of 11 a.m. today, on what I am going to assume is not much other news, YOLO/POT was up about 57 percent on heavy volume, suggesting that the POT ticker in Canada is worth about $15 million Canadian dollars, a relatively modest amount but still about half as much as the company’s actual business.[2] If you take a business-school class on securities analysis or corporate valuation, and it doesn’t cover POT, I think your education is incomplete. Anyway I look forward to the Canadian stock exchanges also lotterying off the YOLO ticker, and maybe the BONG one while they’re at it.

Here is a story about how Renaissance Technologies found a way to let its employees invest in its hedge funds through their Roth IRAs, so that they can get all of the investment returns of the fund tax-free. Those returns are, um, good: “The fund has historically averaged annualized returns approaching 80 percent before fees.” Renaissance is rather famous for clever and aggressive tax structuring, but this just seems like the regular amount of tax structuring. Roth IRAs are a thing, and the point of them is that your investments grow tax-free; if the government is going to offer up something like that, Renaissance is obviously going to take it. The moral here is probably as simple as: if you can invest in a really good hedge fund tax-free, you should.

Basically the way cryptocurrency works is that you keep all your Bitcoins in an account on the blockchain, and to get them out you need the password (it’s called a “private key”) to that account, and if you forget the password there is no one who can help you recover it (this is called “decentralization”) and so your Bitcoins are just gone forever. This makes it very important to put your password somewhere very safe and not lose it. This is especially important if you are running a cryptocurrency exchange and holding Bitcoins on behalf of your customers, oops: For the past weeks, we have worked extensively to address our liquidity issues, which include attempting to locate and secure our very significant cryptocurrency reserves held in cold wallets, and that are required to satisfy customer cryptocurrency balances on deposit, as well as sourcing a financial institution to accept the bank drafts that are to be transferred to us. Unfortunately, these efforts have not been successful. That’s from a terse announcement by Canadian crypto exchange QuadrigaCX that it is filing for creditor protection because it seems to have lost its Bitcoins. (They were in “ cold storage,” which basically means that the exchange had written its private key down somewhere offline instead of keeping it online, and now it can’t find where it wrote down the private key.) I really just cannot stress enough that you almost never see big traditional banks announce “hey guys, little problem, we put all of our depositors’ money in a big box, but then we forgot where the box was, sorry about that, anyway we’re bankrupt now.” I mean there are frauds and thefts and trading errors and lots of other ways for banks to lose money and even go bankrupt, but the traditional financial system really does seem to have mostly solved the problem of forgetting where the money is . Crypto, not so much. Do you ever … do you ever get the sense that crypto enthusiasts think this is good? Like there is a sort of Darwinian/Randian notion that the financial system ought to punish inattention, weed out the weak, and reward those who not only laser-etch their private keys on metal plates and bury them in the backyard, but also remember where to find them? It has an appeal not only because it is exciting —so many cool ways for things to go horribly wrong!—but also because in some weird sense it rewards virtue and punishes vice: Those who remember their private keys grow strong and wealthy; those who forget them are justly doomed to suffer. Of course every monetary system rewards virtue and punishes vice. J.W. Mason wrote recently: In the classroom, one of the ways I suggest students think about money is as a kind of social scorecard. You did something good — made something somebody wanted, let somebody else use something you own, went to work and did everything the boss told you? Good for you, you get a cookie. Or more precisely, you get a credit, in both senses, in the personal record kept for you at a bank. Now you want something for yourself? OK, but that is going to be subtracted from the running total of how much you’ve done for the rest for us. People get very excited about China’s social credit system, a sort of generalization of the “permanent record” we use to intimidate schoolchildren. And ok, it does sound kind of dystopian. If your rating is too low, you aren’t allowed to fly on a plane. Think about that — a number assigned to every person, adjusted based on somebody’s judgement of your pro-social or anti-social behavior. If your number is too low, you can’t on a plane. If it’s really low, you can’t even get on a bus. Could you imagine a system like that in the US? Except, of course, that we have exactly this system already. The number is called a bank account. The difference is simply that we have so naturalized the system that “how much money you have” seems like simply a fact about you, rather than a judgement imposed by society. But not only is it a judgment imposed by society, it is a judgment mediated by the design of the financial system. The actual financial system of, say, the U.S. in 2019 mediates that judgment in a lot of opaque and confusing ways. If you work hard and live frugally, the system will let you buy a house, except that it might also let you buy a house if you don’t work hard and live frugally but just sign some weird documents, but if you sign the weird documents you might lose your house even if you do work hard and live frugally, etc. etc. etc., personal responsibility can become somewhat dissociated from the actual workings of the system. The Bitcoin system, by contrast, is refreshingly crude and brutal and libertarian: The main way to impoverish yourself is by losing your etched metal plates with your private key, or by putting your trust in someone else who loses their etched metal plates. You can understand it—a time traveller from the medieval world could understand it—and laugh at the people who get it wrong and take pride in your own ability to keep track of your etched metal plates. It creates its own trivial sort of virtue,[3] and punishes deviations. As a feature of a practical monetary system that mostly seems unhelpful—though, I guess, compared to what?—but I can see how some people might like it.

I guess it’s a little weird that you don’t see more clients suing their investment bankers over the financial advice that they got. I mean it happens occasionally on derivative trades gone wrong, and of course there are shareholder lawsuits against banks for conflicts of interest in mergers-and-acquisitions advisory work, and Carl Icahn has some specialized fun, but for the most part you don’t really see a company’s chief executive officer hire bankers to advise her on a merger, get that advice, do the merger, realize that the merger was bad and the advice was worthless, and turn around and ask the bankers for her money back. I say it’s a little weird just because the value of the advice is so subjective and uncertain, while the price is so high: Surely someone has paid a bank $20 million for advice, gotten the advice, and thought to herself “really, $20 million, for this?” People get insanely litigious about dry cleaning; you’d think some CEO somewhere would decide to fight her bankers to the death over their fees. On the other hand, this is the whole job of investment banking. The job is to win the trust of senior executives at the company at a deep, personal level, so that they rely on your advice and think of you as a friend and are genuinely happy to pay you millions of dollars. And the job is also to make the senior executives feel good about the deal that they are doing, so that if they have buyer’s remorse it is years later and no longer associated with you. Also, to be fair, the CEO is the one actually doing the deal; if she decides a month later that it was a disaster, it’s going to be pretty embarrassing for her to sue her bankers.[1] But United Natural Foods Inc. is suing its investment bankers, led by Goldman Sachs Group Inc., over their work on the term loan that UNFI took out to pay for its acquisition of Supervalu Inc. Here is UNFI’s complaint, which is an illuminating tale of how a client might wind up feeling disgruntled about its bank. (Disclosure: I used to work at Goldman; also, as a young M&A lawyer, many years ago, I represented Supervalu in a previous merger.) Goldman was UNFI’s adviser on the Supervalu M&A deal, and Goldman, Bank of America Corp. and U.S. Bank N.A. had committed to provide a $2.15 billion term loan to finance the deal. The basic way that term loans work is: The lead banks commit to provide the entire $2.15 billion loan on terms that they agree with the client. Then they go out and syndicate the loan to other investors, keeping only a relatively small chunk for themselves. The client agrees to help with the syndication by providing financial statements, showing up at investor meetings and answering questions about the company, and generally partnering with the banks to get the loan placed. A bit more painfully, the client also agrees to help, if it comes to that, by letting the banks “flex” the loan: If they can’t syndicate the loan on the initial terms that they agreed, they are allowed to increase the interest rate or the original issue discount to make it more attractive to investors. The flex provisions are in the commitment letter and they are limited; in UNFI’s case, for instance, Goldman could flex the interest rate by up to 1.5 percentage points, and could add up to 0.5 percent of original issue discount. It is a sharing of risk: The client takes the first bit of downside, paying a bit more interest if things don’t go quite as well as expected, but if markets fall off a cliff the bank takes the rest of the risk and still has to fund the loan.[2] In a loose, general sense, interests are aligned here. The client wants the syndication to go well, because it is a repeat user of capital markets and wants to be on good terms with its lenders. The bankers want the client to be happy, because they hope for repeat business from that client and want a good reputation with clients generally. But in a specific, financial sense, the interests are kind of adverse. Every additional quarter point of interest makes it easier for the bank to sell the loan and reduce its risk, but every additional quarter point also costs the client a quarter point of interest. In general , the bank would prefer a lower interest rate, because that will make the client happy and be a good accomplishment for the bank. But specifically , if it comes down to deciding between two interest rates, the bank is probably going to be pushing for the higher one, and the company will probably prefer the lower one. UNFI’s loan did not go particularly well, is the basic issue in this complaint, and so tempers got frayed. Goldman flexed it as far as it could go,[3] and then came to UNFI and asked to increase the interest rate by another 0.5 percent. UNFI said no—which it was totally allowed to do, but which does indicate a certain breakdown in fellowship between bank and client. According to the complaint, Goldman’s lead banker, Stephan Feldgoise, was not happy: Because UNFI was refusing to agree to concessions demanded by Goldman Sachs, which UNFI was not contractually required to provide and would substantially increase costs to UNFI and its shareholders (such as the unwarranted demand for an additional interest rate increase above that contemplated by the Flex Provisions), Feldgoise told UNFI that it had “forced” Goldman Sachs into “full risk mitigation mode.” UNFI, however, had entered into a Commitment Letter with Goldman Sachs to avoid being impacted by changing market dynamics, or facing any other unexpected changes to the financing. According to UNFI, Goldman did three things to enrich itself as part of “full risk mitigation mode.” First, it made a rather technical argument that UNFI hadn’t given it enough time to market the loan, and so owed it an extra $40.5 million in fees; Goldman then took the $40.5 million out of the closing proceeds of the loan. Having read only UNFI’s side of this story, I have to say that I find it pretty sympathetic: Goldman had the full agreed 15-business-day period to market the loan, which it did with detailed documents and investor meetings, but because Supervalu updated its financial statements toward the end of that period, Goldman claimed that that restarted the clock and left it with too little time to syndicate the loan before closing. Perhaps Goldman has a legal case there, but it does seem unsporting. Second, Goldman withheld its $11.4 million merger advisory fee from the closing proceeds of the loan. UNFI argues that it should not have done this and should have invoiced it separately, but more importantly it argues that the fee should have been discounted by $2 million: On July 25, 2018, however, Goldman Advisory, acting through Goldman Sachs’ Feldgoise, offered to reduce those fees by $2 million. Feldgoise did so in order to encourage UNFI to raise its offer for SUPERVALU from $27 per share to $32.50 per share, which was necessary to beat out the competing bid for SUPERVALU. In part on the basis of Goldman Sachs’ promised $2 million contribution, UNFI ultimately agreed to increase its bid to $32.50 a share. I imagine the dynamic here as: If your customer is a little disgruntled, you offer to reduce your fees as a good-faith gesture to win back his trust (and future business). But when your customer gets really, really, burn-it-down-and-salt-the-earth disgruntled, there is no point to reducing your fees, since you’ll never get any business from him again. So you might as well grab as much as you are contractually entitled to on your way out. The third thing that Goldman did—well, we have talked about it before. There were some credit default swaps outstanding on Supervalu. When Supervalu’s debt went away after the merger, the CDS would, normally, also have gone away. People who wrote CDS on Supervalu would have a windfall—they had bet that Supervalu would not default, and now it never will—while people who bought that CDS would have a loss. But Goldman found an arrangement with some CDS holders: If Supervalu were a co-borrower on UNFI’s term loan, then Supervalu would still have debt outstanding, and would thus still theoretically be able to default, and so Supervalu CDS would be worth something. And some investors who owned Supervalu CDS wanted this enough that they were willing to buy pieces of the term loan to make it happen. So Goldman went to UNFI and asked it to make Supervalu a co-borrower. And UNFI said yes. And now it regrets it. From the complaint: In order to hold up its end of the bargain and avoid orphaning the buyers’ CDS, Goldman Sachs would have to persuade UNFI to add SUPERVALU as a co-borrower. Recognizing that UNFI would never agree to do so if it knew Goldman Sachs’ true intentions, Goldman Sachs falsely claimed to UNFI that the change would have a “[m]uted impact on [UNFI] but [was] meaningful to select accounts.” When UNFI resisted the change, Goldman Sachs threatened it, claiming that if UNFI did not acquiesce it would “scare off the lending group,” which would in turn raise concerns among UNFI’s shareholders. At no time did Goldman Sachs inform UNFI that the “select accounts” were in fact Goldman Sachs’ own clients that had bought CDS on SUPERVALU debt. Believing that Goldman Sachs was acting in good faith, UNFI agreed to the change. By making SUPERVALU a co-borrower on the Term Loan, Goldman Sachs ensured that SUPERVALU would continue to have outstanding debt, thus causing the price of CDS protection on SUPERVALU to immediately triple. As a result, the value of $470 million in outstanding CDS protection on SUPERVALU increased by more than $70 million overnight, and has continued to rise in the intervening months. In exchange for this massive value shift in the CDS market, on information and belief, the holders of CDS in SUPERVALU—who Goldman Sachs could identify through its market-making desk—agreed to fund portions of the Term Loan that Goldman Sachs and the other lenders had committed to UNFI. Stated differently, Goldman Sachs asked for payment (in the form of participation in the Term Loan) in order to change the Term Loan structure with the specific intent of impacting the pricing of SUPERVALU CDS for the benefit of certain of its clients. This scheme allowed Goldman Sachs and the other Term Loan lenders to benefit: they got to move the amount of the Term Loan sold to the relevant SUPERVALU CDS investors off their balance sheets and onto the balance sheets of those investors; while the CDS investors avoided, and in some cases reversed, significant mark-to-market losses on their positions in SUPERVALU CDS, and created the possibility of a significant payout in the event of a future default on the Term Loan. The only loser in this scheme was Goldman Sachs’ client: UNFI. UNFI bargained for a bank loan from what it believed, at the time, to be reputable Wall Street banks, including Goldman Sachs, which UNFI believed would syndicate the loan with good-faith investors. It ended up with a loan funded by hedge funds that are betting that SUPERVALU, and now UNFI (having acquired SUPERVALU), will default on its debt. As loan partners, the CDS purchasers may engage in predatory practices intended to cause a credit event under the CDS contracts, such as declaring technical defaults on the Term Loan or otherwise pressuring UNFI to fail. In the context of a highly leveraged transaction, the lack of good-faith loan partners substantially reduces the value of the Term Loan to UNFI. With SUPERVALU as a co-borrower, UNFI will have much less flexibility in borrowing arrangements for SUPERVALU going forward, in addition to an inability to restructure SUPERVALU’s debt or to sell SUPERVALU outright. While this reduced flexibility might have been a small issue with cooperative lenders whose interests were aligned with UNFI, it has become a much larger issue now that UNFI is partnered with lenders that have bet on UNFI to fail. This strikes me as mostly wrong. You actually have no idea whether those hedge funds “have bet on UNFI to fail.” The one thing you know is that there is $470 million notional amount of CDS outstanding on Supervalu, while the term loan is for $2.15 billion, meaning that in aggregate the lenders are way more long (via term loan) than short (via Supervalu CDS). In fact it is perfectly common for lenders in a term loan to buy CDS on the issuer, in order to hedge their exposure. If they buy CDS in the full amount of their lending commitment then, yes, their interests are less aligned with the issuer; if they buy more CDS than their commitment, then they have an interest in seeing the issuer fail. But that can happen in any loan, before or after the loan is syndicated. I just do not think that corporate borrowers, in 2019, have a right to expect that all of their lenders will be unhedged, or to sue their loan arrangers for syndicating to hedged investors. The fact that UNFI’s lenders are hedged via Supervalu CDS is an interesting novelty—and certainly helped get the deal done, for Goldman—but I don’t think it materially changes anything. Besides, if there is one thing that we have learned from years of weird CDS structuring, it is that CDS is a two-sided transaction, and if an issuer is unhappy with one side it can always go bargain with the other.[4] Oh sure, some people who own Supervalu CDS and UNFI’s term loan have an incentive to see UNFI default—but there are other people who wrote the same amount of Supervalu CDS, and now have an incentive to keep it out of default! By adding a co-borrower, UNFI has created a whole new set of (synthetic) investors who (are mad about all of this but) want it to succeed. If it gets any trouble from the CDS holders, it can always go to the CDS sellers for a better deal.

s.h: I love Bridgewater so much, they are my muse
s.t: Eileen Murray, the co-chief executive officer of Bridgewater Associates, spoke at a hedge fund conference this week, and someone in the audience had the nerve or naivety or lack of imagination to ask her about investments . This guy—presumably a hedge fund manager or allocator—had the chance to put a question to the co-head of the largest hedge fund in the world, and he wasted it on asking “what percentage of Bridgewater's equity investments are in internet/technology companies.” As though anyone at Bridgewater would ever deign to talk about something so pedestrian as sector allocation of equity investments! Obviously she declined to answer. What do they talk about at Bridgewater, all day every day, on videotape? Oh boy do you know the answer! Themselves! Endlessly, lovingly, obsessively, they talk about themselves: She then shared the “secret sauce” to the sustained outperformance at world’s biggest hedge fund, something anyone present could adopt themselves, should they dare: Bridgewater Associates has been so successful, year after year, Murray said, because of its unique and intense culture. Bridgewater’s ethos of “radical transparency” involves videotaping or tape-recording every conversation for review later, constant evaluations of peers across what elsewhere would be called a hierarchy in its “dot system” which aggregates into “baseball cards,” portraits of each employee which indicate that person’s strengths or weaknesses. That makes it hard to fly below the radar with mediocre performance and low accountability. And, given the volume of dots, the odds that your portrait is accurate are pretty high, Murray said. “It’s kind of a family atmosphere,” she said. “I don’t know about you, but for me, my family tells me things I don’t want to hear. But they do it out of a sense of love and kindness...Some people think [the culture] sounds harsh and stressful. I think it’s very kind.” I said on Twitter that Bridgewater does not sound at all like my family, and people with slightly older children replied that it sounds exactly like theirs, so I suppose I have that to look forward to. Bridgewater once had a long-running controversy—including multiple “intense” interrogations conducted by James Comey—about “whether Ms. Murray had been dishonest about her dealings with a lower-level employee regarding his employment at the firm.” I sincerely hope that her family didn’t bring in a senior Justice Department official to interrogate her about her inconsistent claims about Santa Claus. I don’t … even … what? There was a period of pretty meh investment returns at Bridgewater, during which I could make fun of them as being a psychotherapy cult that happens to manage an large hedge fund, but they had a really good year last year so I suppose all the self-analysis is paying off. But it is so fascinating to me that the infinite stories about Bridgewater’s radical candor and believability and videotaping and so forth, all of the stuff about how conscious they are about learning and making decisions as a group, never end with, like, “and so that’s how we decided to increase our allocation to tech stocks.” It’s never “we got in a room, turned on the video cameras, fired up our believability charts, and talked about macroeconomic and technology trends until the most believable people convinced everyone with perfect candor that we should buy more Apple.” It’s always like “we got in a room to talk about how believable Jane is, and Fred discussed her flaws with perfect candor for an hour, after which we gave him some dots, here, would you like to watch?” I guess that I believe that someone is making some sort of investing decisions at Bridgewater. (Obviously a lot of the investment decisions are automated, but someone must touch the model.) And the firm does publish well-regarded research notes about economic and financial topics. Clearly some hedge-fund-like outputs are being produced, somehow, by someone. But from the outside, from what you read in the press and hear from its public statements, Bridgewater’s radical transparency seems to be a perfectly closed system, always and only about itself, never about investing. Don’t get me wrong: That’s really cool! I mean it would be a lot less cool if they didn’t make any money, but they do, and the fact that they seem to make a lot of money mostly by sitting around and gossiping about each other is weirdly inspiring. It is an odd financial form of the paradox of hedonism, or rather an inversion of it: You might naively think something like “if we get together a team of smart people who all have a single-minded focus on making good investment decisions, then the interpersonal dynamics and managerial techniques will take care of themselves.” Many hedge funds—and tech startups for that matter—more or less consciously take exactly that approach, with mixed results. But in fact, at Bridgewater, it is precisely the opposite: If you get together a team of smart people who are willing to spend 100 percent of their time doing weird interpersonal exercises and subjecting themselves to managerial experiments, somehow they will make good investment decisions as a byproduct.

Airlines have become the poster children for the newish antitrust theory that common ownership by the same big shareholders of multiple companies in the same industry will lead those companies to compete against each other less vigorously, preferring to keep prices and margins high rather than fighting for market share, because a zero-sum fight for market share does not help common shareholders but high margins do. We have been talking about this theory around here since 2015, and even back then there was one obvious nagging objection, which was: wait, really, airlines ? Anyway here’s a story about how United Continental Holdings Inc. last year “startled the airline world with an aggressive growth agenda aimed at bolstering hub profits and reclaiming traffic—a strategy to win back passengers rivals had siphoned away in the nine years since the carrier’s chaotic merger,” and how it has “declared the project a success” and is now moving more aggressively against its rivals, and how American and Delta might be displeased, and how “the good news for consumers is that, if the two rivals choose to retaliate, it could trigger a fare war.” Or, I suppose, not. Berkshire Hathaway Inc. is a 9+ percent holder of United, American and Delta, for what it’s worth.

The way “payment-in-kind” securities work is that, instead of giving you cash for your interest payments, the issuer gives you more of its securities, generally more of the same securities. (In “PIK toggle” securities, the issuer sometimes gives you cash and sometimes securities, generally at its choice.) The reason for this is not necessarily that you especially want more of the securities, though you might. The reason is that the issuer can create an unlimited amount of its own securities. It can—assuming the correct corporate formalities etc.—never run out. It will never miss an interest payment, because it can always create the currency for the interest payments out of thin air. PIK and PIG-toggle bonds are thus popular among companies that want to borrow money but that can see themselves having a hard time coming up with the traditional currency—cash—for making interest payments. In theory, there is no reason to limit interest payments to cash and like-kind securities; the only limit is your (and your investors’) imagination, and you could imagine building a bond that pays interest in lottery tickets or crude oil or sandwiches or Netflix subscriptions or Uber rides or whatever. And novelty interest-payment methods are not completely unheard-of in the real world. A lot of those things, though, are somewhere in between cash and securities on the essential question of “can the company run out?” If an oil company pays interest in oil, that does give it a cushion that cash interest does not: A bad scenario for an oil company is if oil prices fall and it has a hard time generating cash; if it can pay interest in oil, it mitigates that problem. But it is not a perfect solution the way that payment in securities is. An oil company could, after all, run out of oil, or run out of money to pay to drill for oil. Securities can be generated infinitely and at no cost; actual physical stuff, even the actual physical stuff of your business, cannot. Anyway: The beleaguered Chinese company that made news last year paying its bond investors in ham instead of cash has a new problem: it’s running low on pigs. The cash crunch that left Chuying Agro-Pastoral Group Co. unable to service some of its debt has now intensified to the point that it’s unable to buy enough feed, according to an announcement on the Shenzhen Stock Exchange. “ PIG toggle” and “ payment in rind” were the jokes here, when we last talked about this. But, yes, if your pork company can’t raise enough cash to pay interest in cash, there is an increased chance that it won’t be able to raise enough pigs to pay interest in pigs. It should try feeding the bonds to the pigs.

I wrote yesterday that you don’t see a lot of biotechnology companies securitizing the cash flows from a single drug to sell to investors, and about a million people emailed me to say, well, you actually do see that a fair amount in the takeover context: Pharmaceutical companies will sometimes take contingent value rights in takeovers, giving target shareholders the right to additional payments based on milestones relating to individual drugs. It’s not quite the same as a standalone issuance but, yes, fair. Conversely, a reader reminded me of Andrew Lo’s idea of a large diversified “megafund” to fund biotech research, on the theory that no one wants to fund individual long-shot projects but that if you put enough of them together you will get a portfolio that people want to invest in. Obviously that is the opposite of what we talked about yesterday, which is letting people invest directly in each individual drug, but on the blockchain.

GE Soars as Subprime Settlement Bolsters New CEO’s Rescue Plan. Meet Tesla’s McKinsey-Groomed, Newly Minted Millennial CFO. Howard Schultz Should Stay in Business, Which He Is Good At. It’s Almost Too Cold in Chicago to Get a Pizza Delivered. Don’t use an electric scooter as a getaway vehicle. Insurance agent pretended to be Voldemort to spook clients. If you'd like to get Money Stuff in handy email form, right in your inbox, please subscribe at this link. Thanks! [1] Also, to be really fair, part of the banker's job is to check all the legal boxes so that even if the client wants to sue they can’t. [2] Don’t think too hard about that. If things really fall off a cliff you could have material adverse events, etc., or of course the bank could just implode. Realistically the client takes the first bit of risk, the bank takes the next bit, and then at some level the bank detaches and true horror is the client’s problem. [3] The complaint argues that even that was illegitimate: UNFI says that “the Flex Provisions that Goldman Sachs exercised unnecessarily, including a 1.5% interest rate increase on the loan (amounting to more than $180 million over the life of the loan) … amounted to significant and unexpected additional costs to UNFI and its shareholders. Defendants should be required to compensate UNFI for the additional and unnecessary costs it now faces in repaying the Term Loan.” I don’t think that there is any actual argument here—it seems pretty clear that Goldman had the right to flex the loan—it is just sort of a disgruntled customer complaining. [4] Reader Brent Wilson made this point to me about UNFI, via email.

Here is a story about how the highly desirable Canadian stock ticker symbol POT, which was previously wasted on the Potash Corp. of Saskatchewan, will now be allocated to a new company (presumably, a cannabis company) via a lottery run by the Toronto Stock Exchange. It does seem like a bit of a failure of imagination for a stock exchange . You run a market! Sell the thing! If you’ve gotten “significant interest” in the POT ticker, as the TSX says it has, you should auction it off to the highest bidder, not raffle it off to the luckiest. Really you should run continuous two-sided markets in all ticker symbols. Why not let the potash company cash in on its ticker when it realized that pot would be buzzier than potash? How much would you pay for POT? Of course there is a literature, though I am not sure that anyone has answered precisely this question. (It’s a paper that someone should write.) But it seems reasonably clear that ticker symbols can be valuable. Here is a paper finding that having a “likeable” or pronounceable ticker leads to a higher valuation. Here is one finding that having a ticker similar to your corporate name can lead to higher valuation. We talked last week about a 2001 paper finding that having a ticker similar to another company’s corporate name can lead to increased correlation with that company, which is desirable if it is a popular hyped company and you are not. The logical extension is that having a ticker symbol that resembles a thing should lead to increased correlation with that thing, particularly if that thing is a popular hyped investing theme. “What should I invest in,” you ask your market-savvy friend, and he replies “pot, pot legalization is a huge opportunity that will mint many billionaires, you should invest in pot,” and off you go to buy POT. When POT is potash, we chalk that up to “hahaha markets are dumb,” but I am not sure the conclusion is much different if POT is a pot company. Some people will do their research, seek out the best and most underpriced pot company, and decide that it’s POT. Others will buy POT because it says POT. Anyway, congratulations in advance to the lucky winner of the POT lottery, and to the academic who does the event study analyzing how much value POT got from being declared POT. I hope it’s a big number. “Canopy Growth Corp., the world’s biggest cannabis company by market value, trades under the symbol WEED in Canada,” and how sure can you be that the ticker isn’t a cause of the valuation?

A basic thing to understand about crypto and tokens and blockchain is that financial engineering existed for a long time, and reached a high degree of sophistication, before anyone came along and invented blockchains. For instance, many crypto enthusiasts might be too young to remember this, but in the early and middle years of the last decade quite a few people made quite a lot of money doing something called “securitization,” which means turning all sorts of previously non-tradeable economic claims—mortgages, say, or credit card debt—into tradeable securities that people could buy or sell with relative ease. Parts of that worked out poorly, but the basic concept seems sound and there is still quite a lot of securitization today. But a popular pattern in the crypto/token/blockchain world is that someone will come along and be like “finally, through tokenization, we have invented a way to slice _________ into bits and let people trade the bits.” I always find this a bit confusing. Whatever _________ is, it is safe to say that before the invention of tokenization there was already a way to slice it into bits and let people trade the bits. Slicing things into tradeable bits has been a very hot area of finance for a very long time, and people got pretty good at it. Real estate is a popular target for tokenization, for instance, and I am confused because real estate securitization—not so much mortgage-backed securities but real estate investment trusts—is a thing that has existed for a long time. This doesn’t mean that actual tokenized real estate proposals wouldn’t be different from existing real estate securitization, or that they wouldn’t work or wouldn’t be good. (For instance some of those proposals involve trading shares of individual buildings, which is a bit different from the typical REIT.) It does mean that if you are evaluating those proposals, you have to try to understand why, given that the technology definitely already existed , nobody went and actually did the slicing and trading that the tokenizers think they will do now. It is possible that the answer has to do with the blockchain: It is possible that having a permissionless open-source method for trading tokens will allow a market to grow up in a way that traditional securitization would not have. But it is also quite possible that the answer is, like, “no one ever traded $100 slices of individual buildings because that is not a particularly appealing investment for anyone.” If that was the problem, then blockchain will not solve it. Anyway do biotechnology companies regularly securitize the cash flows from one individual drug in the development stage? I am not an expert in biotech finance but it seems like the answer is no. I assume the explanation for that is not dissimilar to why consumer companies do not regularly securitize the cash flows from individual cookie brands or whatever: The management of the company is better able to construct a diversified portfolio of individual products, and to focus resources on developing and marketing the most promising products, than outside investors would be. But here you go, blockchain blockchain blockchain: In a novel approach for the biotechnology industry, small-cap company Agenus Inc. is aiming to raise $50 million to $100 million by issuing digital securities backed by future sales of an experimental cancer drug. The digital securities will allow investors to bet on future sales of single products and will have a limited impact on shareholders’ equity, the company said. Agenus plans to offer at least 25 million of what it calls biotech electronic security tokens, or BESTs, to certain high-net-worth individuals and institutional investors starting Feb. 15. “With these types of novel instruments, you have a much more concentrated exposure to a specific product,” Chief Executive Officer Garo Armen said in a phone interview. It’s “inevitable” that other biotech companies will follow suit, he said. Is … it? Why? I am sorry to be quite so dogmatically efficient-markets-y but, you know, if it’s inevitable, why hasn’t it happened already? You don’t need blockchains and digital securities to securitize cash flows from individual drugs; the technology for doing that has existed for decades. If it’s never been used, that might be a problem with the thesis, not the technology.

My simple model of how stock exchanges make money goes something like this: You do not want to charge people a lot of money for trading on the stock exchange, because they are price sensitive to trading costs, and the cheaper the trades are the more trades they will do. (You might just not charge very much, or you might do something more complicated like charge a lot for some order types and give large rebates for other order types, but the point is that you want your overall pricing scheme to encourage trading, not discourage it.) You do want to charge people a lot of money for connecting to the stock exchange—for being able to trade, and for getting useful data feeds—because they are not price sensitive to those more-or-less fixed costs. As long as there is a lot of trading on your exchange—and there is, because of Point 1—then every professional trader will need to pay you for connectivity and data, because they can’t run their trading business without real-time in-depth knowledge of what is going on at your exchange. Between Points 1 and 2, you need to charge a large enough total amount of money to pay for your salaries and computers and electricity and buildings and executive bonuses and so forth. I mean it’s more complicated than that, I suppose, but one thing that probably doesn’t enter very much into the model is your unit costs . You don’t really have unit costs. You’re not sitting around calculating how much it costs you to execute a trade, or to connect someone’s cable to your servers, or to send them a copy of your order book. All of that stuff is done electronically; it costs you, in round numbers, nothing. You charge people money because you have a bunch of overall costs of running an exchange, and you charge them as much money as possible for the services that they have to pay for and as little money as possible for the services where they have a choice, and you optimize the total number. But IEX, the Investors Exchange, did go and calculate its own unit costs of providing data and connectivity, not so much for business reasons but because that is a fun way to troll the bigger exchanges: On Tuesday, Investors Exchange, a small exchange that competes with the NYSE, Nasdaq Inc. and Cboe Global Markets Inc. for stock trades, filed an analysis with the Securities and Exchange Commission comparing its costs of providing comparable market data and connectivity to clients with fees levied by the big exchanges. IEX, which itself pays the big exchanges’ fees for data and connectivity, estimated the big three’s charges are between 10 times and 19 times its own costs for market data and as much as 41 times its costs for physical connectivity. Here is the report. (The headline on IEX’s website is “Overcharged and underserved.”) The backdrop is that the SEC recently rejected some proposed fee increases from the exchanges, demanding that they justify the fees, and IEX’s argument is that the fees are unjustifiable. NYSE and Nasdaq reply, well, come on, that’s not the business model: Representatives of NYSE, owned by Intercontinental Exchange Inc., and Nasdaq said the IEX analysis didn’t reflect a full accounting of the costs of trading on IEX. “They have tens of millions of dollars of costs to run their exchange,” said Phil Mackintosh, Nasdaq’s chief economist. “They are showing you a sliver of their costs.” Josh King, a NYSE spokesman said: “While IEX is free to cherry pick and conflate their numbers, the fact remains that the all-in cost to trade on NYSE is lower than IEX.” I don’t know what any of this tells you. Certainly I sympathize with NYSE’s view that you cannot evaluate its connectivity fees based on the costs of, like, plugging in a wire. On the other hand it is hard not to sympathize with the professional traders who have no choice but to pay whatever NYSE charges for connectivity and data feeds. No wonder they’re trying to start their own exchange, to capture some of those fees for themselves.

We talked a few weeks ago about a series of allegedly corrupt government bond deals in Mozambique, in which a company was awarded lucrative contracts to build a tuna fishing fleet and to monitor the shoreline for pirates, and in exchange allegedly paid massive bribes to the government officials awarding the contracts. There are emails, and in the emails the government officials referred to the bribes by the extremely unhelpful euphemism “chickens.” I wrote: It does seem to me that, if you are looking for a code word for “bribes,” “success fees” is almost infinitely superior to “chickens.” Like if someone finds these emails and asks you “isn’t ‘success fee’ just a euphemism for ‘bribe,’” you can just tough it out and be like “oh no those are success fees, very standard, in every contract, you gotta pay a fee for success. Consulting! Local expertise!” But if someone finds these emails and asks you “isn’t ‘50 million chickens’ just a euphemism for ‘$50 million of bribes,’” what, are you going to be like “no no no we had a legitimate need for 50 million chickens for this coastal monitoring project, the chickens will be stationed on the seashore to look out for pirates”? Come on. On the other hand if they’d been like “I need 50 million pounds of tuna” then, sure, I guess, maybe that would have been harder to spot? Anyway there is an investigation in South Africa right now into another alleged bribery scheme that also used “chickens” as a code for bribes: On Mondays the team would ask: “What is the order of chicken?”, Agrizzi told the commission. This was a code to figure out how much bribe money would be needed that week, he explained. And: One message submitted as evidence at the commission dated March 13 2017 was a request for one tonne of chicken which was apparently a code – one tonne of chicken equalled R1 million, Van Tonder said. Here, however, the company “ran kitchens in mines, youth centres, Lindela Repatriation Centre, and for prisons across the country,” so it did actually have a plausible use for chicken! Like if someone found these messages and asked “isn’t ‘one tonne of chicken’ just a euphemism for bribes,” they could have said “no, we needed a ton of chicken, we cook a lot of chicken in all those prison kitchens,” and the investigators would have been stymied. (Of course as it happens they all seem to have answered “yep that was bribes,” but that is a separate error.) I do not think that any of this is exactly bribery best practices , but I suppose I will have to allow it. Still I am a little confused about how this works. If you are in a non-chicken-related business, and you go around emailing about chickens, on the one hand future investigators will not have too much trouble figuring out that you mean bribes, but on the other hand the people you’re emailing won’t get confused and send you chickens. (They’ll send you bribes.) If you are in the chicken business and you email people asking for a ton of chicken, it does seem like you run the risk that they’ll send you a ton of chicken, when what you really wanted was a bribe. Conversely, what if you do want chicken? Do you have to email, like, “please send me a ton of chicken, but not bribes this time, real chicken, for the kitchens”? That would give the game away. It all seems like it might get a bit hard to manage.

Ah: The Trump administration plans to work with Congress to overhaul mortgage-finance giants Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, a White House spokeswoman said Tuesday—playing down the idea the administration will seek to unilaterally release the firms from government control. Yes right all that it will take to re-privatize Fannie and Freddie will be finding a bipartisan compromise in a divided government when it takes a break from debates over immigration and government shutdowns and election interference. And Fannie and Freddie investors seem confident that this will happen any day now. It would be nice to have some of their optimism.
