Fund-of-funds LCH Invesments NV does an annual ranking of the top 20 hedge funds measured by the total profits that they have made for investors since inception; this years’ version came out recently and you can read about it here or here or here or here. The perennial champ is Bridgewater Associates, which has made $57.8 billion for investors since it started in 1975, adding $8.1 billion last year. Second place is Soros Fund Management, at $43.9 billion from its founding in 1973 until, um, 2017, “ even though in 2011 Soros announced he was returning all outside money to investors.” It’s not an exact science. Renaissance Technologies is way down in 17th place at $16.7 billion, but that “does not include the gains generated by Renaissance’s oldest fund, the Medallion Fund, which has been closed to outsiders for more than a decade and now manages money only for partners and employees.” Still the orders of magnitude are useful. You can measure hedge fund managers’ performance in different ways. The fund with the highest compounded rate of return (or Sharpe ratio or alpha or whatever) over a long time is, arguably, the best at investing . The fund with the most money is arguably the best at marketing (a key skill), and the hedge fund manager with the largest personal fortune [1] is probably best at the subtle combination of skills—investing, marketing, structuring and negotiating fees and lockups, etc.—that, I would argue, is the ultimate measure of a hedge fund manager. This ranking, meanwhile, mingles measures of investing skill with measures of bigness and also just of longevity; 17 of the 20 funds on the list were started last century. But it is arguably the best measure of social value : This is a pretty straightforward measure of how much money these managers made for their investors on their way to amassing their personal fortunes. Those personal fortunes are, at least in theory, a reward for providing value for the investors, and this is the measure of that value.[2] It is interesting—not apples to apples, but evocative—to compare these numbers to other people who made similar amounts of money for investors in other ways. Twitter Inc., for instance, is a company with a market capitalization of about $25 billion, meaning roughly that it has made about $25 billion for its investors, which would put it right in the middle of this list. Meanwhile Amazon.com Inc. has created about $66.5 billion of value for its shareholders this month , more than any hedge fund has created in its history, and that ignores the quite plausibly much greater value that Amazon provides for its customers . Of course Jeff Bezos is quite a bit richer than any hedge fund manager so I suppose the world is as it should be. Still just sort of impressionistically it does seem like hedge fund managers, as a group, seem to be pretty good at capturing a lot of the value that they create. The managers of these top 20 hedge funds seem to be uniformly billionaires in a way that managers of, say, $15 billion industrial companies generally aren’t. And it’s a skewed sample because these are the ones who returned the most value; there are billionaire managers who did not make this list, probably billionaire managers who have captured more in fees than they have returned to investors.[3] Something about this just feels right: If you build a business around manufacturing widgets or creating online connections, it is because you love widgets or online connections, and you are likely to create a lot of value that you do not capture for yourself because you are so busy cherishing your widgets or whatever. If you build a business around finding mispriced financial assets, it is because you love finding every last bit of value, and it is pretty natural that you’ll end up finding a lot of that value for yourself.

Today PG&E Corp., the California utility that might be held responsible for billions of dollars of wildfire damage, filed for bankruptcy, over the objections of some shareholders including BlueMountain Capital Management LLC, and I have a lot of sympathy for both sides here. BlueMountain’s basic point is that “there is no imminent financial crisis” at PG&E: It has enough money to operate normally now, and it will be a long time before it has to actually pay out all those billions of dollars in fire damages, and that amount might turn out to be overstated. Bankruptcy is a way to restructure PG&E’s liabilities and figure out who should get how much, but it’s a very expensive way to do that, and there are other ways. You could just negotiate settlements with fire victims, and do normal liability-management transactions to pay your debts, and ask regulators for rate increases to cover the fire costs, and generally keep operating and try to maximize your revenues and minimize your expenses like, you know, a regular company. But PG&E went the other way: “Instead of rolling up their sleeves and getting to work,”says BlueMountain, PG&E’s board of directors “are poised to concede defeat and pass the buck to a bankruptcy judge.” But in PG&E’s defense: Yes, actually, it seems like it would be exhausting to adjudicate all those claims! And it is what bankruptcy judges are for. PG&E is at this point arguably a big battleground for how society should allocate the costs of wildfires: Should the homeowners themselves be on the hook, or PG&E’s stockholders, or its bondholders, or its utility customers, or the state of California, or someone else? PG&E’s board can try to work out fair and acceptable solutions to these questions, but it has no particular moral or legal standing to do that, and does have some fiduciary obligations to look out primarily for its shareholders’ interests. A bankruptcy judge is more of a neutral arbiter, and a bankruptcy case is a centralized place to fight these things out; that might be a more appropriate judicial-political way for society to carve up the costs than multiple negotiations with a company would be. And PG&E is already punting its obligations to the court: Ahead of an expected filing for Chapter 11 protection this week, the company is skipping payments it agreed to make to people whose property was destroyed in a 2015 blaze in the Sierra Nevada foothills caused by a tree falling on a power line that officials have blamed on the utility. When PG&E’s expected liabilities were smaller, everyone just agreed that its shareholders or ratepayers would have to bear all the costs of wildfires, and homeowners would be fully compensated. I guess it’s not yet certain that that will be the result of this bankruptcy, though, and so PG&E is reopening the question even in the earlier cases. Still it is an expensive way to figure this stuff out: A bankruptcy will probably result in higher bills for customers because it will be more expensive for PG&E to borrow the money it needs to make infrastructure investments it needs to keep the lights on. The company supplies natural gas and electricity to about 16 million people in Northern and Central California. … “With utilities, bankruptcies take multiple years,” Kit Konolige, an analyst for Bloomberg Intelligence, said in an interview before the filing. “There is no such thing as a quick utility bankruptcy. And it creates a lot of uncertainty for everybody involved.” And “bankruptcy professionals may be the only people guaranteed to benefit from a yearslong chapter 11 proceeding, thanks to ballooning fees and the disputes dogging PG&E into bankruptcy.” On the other hand there are purely tactical reasons—having nothing to do with wildfires, climate change, or even solvency—why bankruptcy might be the right choice: The restructuring process could provide an opening for PG&E to amend or cancel some $34.5 billion in longstanding contracts to purchase wind and solar power, many of which were negotiated when market prices were much higher. The fate of those contracts has raised concerns among wholesale power providers like Consolidated Edison Inc. and NextEra Energy Inc. that renegotiation could create uncertainty for future development. The story might end up being “we can find a way to compensate wildfire victims by taking the money from wholesale power providers who have locked in above-market rates for power.” I don’t know if that’s good or bad or what; I don’t know if those companies are better or worse able to bear that risk than homeowners are, or if upsetting their contractual expectations is better or worse than putting the costs on ratepayers. But it’s a pot of money, and PG&E’s board put it into play by filing for bankruptcy, and now a judge will have to figure out whether to make use of it. In other news, PG&E’s bonds are still in the investment-grade bond index until the end of January, which is a little awkward.

I am sort of weirdly offended by this: The Saudi Public Investment Fund hedged most of its 4.9 per cent stake in Tesla with the help of bankers at JPMorgan Chase after the market closed on January 17, according to four people with direct knowledge of the trade. The arrangement means that, although it still holds the shares, the Saudi sovereign wealth fund is left with little exposure should the price fall. Its potential gains are also capped if the stock rises, freezing its $2.9bn bet on the company. Remember when Elon Musk was going around telling everyone how confident he was that the Saudis were willing to give him unlimited financial backing to take Tesla private at $420 a share? Well it turns out they held their stock for like six months and then collared it somewhere in the mid-$300s. But sure, sure, they told Musk that they’d be long-term buyers of the whole company for a much higher price! Honestly the Securities and Exchange Commission should sue him again just for how embarrassing this is. In other news, $920 million of Tesla convertible bonds come due in a couple of months. If the stock averages above $359.87 for the next 20 trading days, Tesla will pay off the bonds half in cash and half in stock; if it doesn’t, then it will pay them entirely in cash. The stock closed at $296.19 yesterday, but earnings are tomorrow and who knows. If the stock does jump, you can imagine weird technical dynamics here. For one thing, convertible arbitrageurs who own the bonds and hedge them by being short stock might be buying back some stock as the bonds tick toward maturity below the strike price, which will push the stock up toward the strike, but if it actually gets there they will probably need to short more stock (to hedge the stock that they’d then be delivered). Also paying the converts partly in stock is probably good for Tesla—“they have the cash, but would rather have people convert,” says an analyst—so if it looks like it might happen then maybe that should push the stock up.

Why do brokers send customer orders to their own dark pools? Brokers will say that it’s because their dark pools offer good execution without the risk of exposing orders to public markets. Critics will say that it’s because the brokers have a financial interest in using their own dark pools (for instance, they don’t have to pay stock exchange fees, and they like touting dark-pool volume to potential customers). Here is the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority’s answer, which is the bad one, as you can tell from the title: “ High Broker-Affiliated ATS Order Routing Associated with Lower Fill Rates, Higher Costs.” “The evidence from this study does not support the idea that when a broker sends a high proportion of orders to an affiliated ATS, these venues necessarily offer a lower-cost option that avoids other market participants from learning of an institutional order,” said Jonathan Sokobin, FINRA’s Chief Economist and Senior Vice President. “The difference across brokers in routing decisions, fill rates and trading costs are persistent over time, indicating that past routing behavior is predictive of future behavior.”

After the financial crisis, former American International Group Inc. Chief Executive Officer Hank Greenberg disputed AIG’s need for a government bailout, and went to court to demand that the government give him his company back. He gave it a good shot but ultimately, and not particularly surprisingly, lost. But the lesson there was that Greenberg has a pretty high capacity for contrarianism, and I guess he likes to keep busy, so now he is debating other, less consequential, AIG questions: AIG says it is 100 years old because it can trace its roots to a company founded in Shanghai in 1919. Mr. Greenberg says AIG dates to just 1967—when he pulled together various operations that had grown from that original Shanghai company—to take public. “You think I’m going to sit quietly by and let them take credit for being 100 years old? They’re not, and I know the answer to that because I formed AIG,” he says. Mr. Greenberg says he has talked by phone twice to AIG’s current chief executive to complain, then cornered him at an industry dinner event—to no avail. His lawyer has compiled a list of what they consider inaccuracies in AIG’s story. I don’t think he gets the company back or anything if he wins this one. This one is just for sport.

I mean the obvious answer is “hahahaha yes of course they are come on,” but it is worth taking the question seriously for a minute. In theory this is how an initial coin offering ought to work: Someone has an idea for a decentralized piece of infrastructure that everyone should be able to use but that no one should own: Think, like, email, or the World Wide Web, or Bitcoin, things that work on a peer-to-peer basis with no central owner who controls them and charges other people to use them. So for instance you could have peer-to-peer cloud-based file storage: Instead of Amazon storing all your data, you could let a decentralized network store your data and rely on cryptography and incentives to make sure that it’s all there. To make this infrastructure work without any owner, there would be a token, a cryptocurrency, that is used to operate it. People who want the thing would buy tokens and then exchange them for the thing; other people would be incentivized to provide the thing by the prospect of getting tokens. The network would run on its own without any owner or supervisor: Providers would have incentives to do a good job of providing the thing and maintaining the network, because they get paid in tokens and want the tokens to be valuable, and the tokens will be more valuable if the network is useful and the thing is good. But you have to build it first: You have to write the code and develop the network and get people to start using it. So the person who comes up with the idea pre-sells some tokens in an ICO. This is good because it gets tokens out into people’s hands so that, when the network is ready, it will have users, and also because it gets cash into her hands so she can pay the expenses of building the network and perhaps, sure, get a little rich. Is that token a security? Maybe! The classic “Howey test” in U.S. law is that a security is “an investment of money in a common enterprise with a reasonable expectation of profits to be derived from the entrepreneurial or managerial efforts of others.” If you buy the tokens in the ICO, before the network is ready, you probably expect them to go up in value, if for no other reason than that you’re taking a risk (the network may never work!) and want to be compensated for it. And if they go up in value it certainly won’t be through your doing; it will be through the hard work of the visionary/entrepreneur who is trying to build the network, and who took your money in exchange for the tokens. There’s an argument the other way—that you are buying the tokens solely as a pre-sold product, as a way to buy file storage or whatever, and not as an investment—but it is a little chancy, since (1) you can’t actually use the tokens to buy file storage today and (2) if the Securities and Exchange Commission interviews you, you are probably going to say “of course I bought the tokens because I expected the value to go up!” Still there is I think a reasonable argument that this shouldn’t be regulated as a security in the same way that stocks are. This is not a philosophical argument about ownership or expectations of profits or whatever, or a legal argument about the Howey test, but a practical argument about how securities regulation actually works. If this token is a security, then the entrepreneur has to furnish you financial statements and risk factors about her enterprise, and in some deep sense there is no enterprise. She doesn’t want to control the network; she wants to build the network and release it into the wild. If all goes well, she will never have an entity that makes any revenue or profits, and your tokens will get their value not from any financial variables but just from how useful they are in buying things on the network. If she sends you financial statements every quarter, and if all goes well, then the financial statements will show some expenses and no revenues for a few quarters, and then nothing forever; the entity will fade away but the network itself will maintain its value. Those financial statements don’t seem like they’d be that useful to you in evaluating your investment. Similarly, maybe she’ll be able to give you quarterly disclosures that describe, say, how many transactions occur on the network, or who the biggest customers and providers are, or other facts about the network that are relevant to your investment. But maybe not; maybe the point of the decentralized network is to preserve anonymity so that no one, not even the founder—and certainly not every token holder—can know who is doing what on it. Maybe all you care about is whether you can use your tokens to buy file storage or whatever, and you’re willing to sacrifice knowledge about who else is doing what on the network, because that sacrifice itself makes the network more valuable. Obviously I am kidding a little about all of this, because in practice many ICOs—and particularly the ones that the SEC has gone after for securities-law violations—look nothing like what I described above. They’re just, like, someone has a vague business idea, and there was a brief period when it was so stupidly easy to raise money by selling tokens, so they’d sell tokens with a half-baked half-plagiarized white paper that focused principally on how much money you could make. That stuff was obviously a securities-law violation, and there is no harm whatsoever in the SEC shutting it down, and the SEC has been busy doing that. But that doesn’t tell you much about the hard and interesting cases, the ICOs that do look like what I described above.[1] The SEC’s statements have been a little ambiguous. But we might have a test case soon! Social-media startup Kik Interactive Inc. of Waterloo, Ontario, plans to fight an expected enforcement action from the Securities and Exchange Commission over a 2017 initial coin online offering, Chief Executive Ted Livingston told The Wall Street Journal, setting the stage for a legal battle that could have broad ramifications for the digital-currency market. The SEC’s enforcement division believes Kik issued an unregistered security when it sold $100 million in “kin,” a digital token that Kik says works like a currency on the its platform, according to Mr. Livingston and documents reviewed by the Journal. … Kik says from the start it marketed kin not as a security but as a “utility token” for developers and the foundation of a new ecosystem of apps and service, of which Kik would be one part. I am generally inclined to be skeptical of claims like this, but if you review the kin white paper and the coverage of the ICO at the time, you can see Kik’s point. They weren’t marketing the thing as a speculative investment, and they made clear that their intent was to create a two-sided unowned marketplace that they would not control. I am not sure that that’s enough to save them, and I’m not even sure that it should be, but they do have a case. One thing to consider is: What if they’re right? What if these sorts of ICO tokens are not securities and shouldn’t be regulated like securities, because the sorts of disclosures and investor protections that are useful in securities law don’t make sense here? Surely that doesn’t mean that no disclosures or investor protections would be useful here; after all, the proportion of shady ICOs to good ones seems to be at least as high as the proportion of shady stock offerings to good ones. Arguments against securities regulation of tokens might be easier to make if they came with practical proposals for non-securities regulation of tokens.

s.h: Who is the president of Venezuela?
s.t: You can try to answer that question with legalistic precision—the constitution, let us assume, specifies methods of electing the president and other methods of overturning those methods, etc., and you can run those procedures and determine the results, etc.—but really the answer is a social fact. “If you could convince everyone in the entire world that you were King of France,” writes David Graeber, “then you would actually be the King of France.” The person who everyone thinks is the president of Venezuela is the president of Venezuela. Most of the time in most countries this is pretty unanimous: A lot of people might prefer a different president, but they generally accept that the current president is the president. But in Venezuela right now there seems to be some genuine controversy about who is in charge, as president Nicolas Maduro and National Assembly leader Juan Guaido each claim power. In general it is conventional to think that, in the absence of unanimity, there is some core group of people that you need to convince you are the president in order to be the president, and the traditional view is that it’s the people who have the guns. (“In fact, it would probably work just to convince a substantial portion of the French civil service and military,” continues Graeber.) Government is about the exercise of power and the monopoly on violence, andif you control the people with the guns then you control the government, that sort of thing. And in fact Maduro and Guaido are jockeying for the loyalty of Venezuela’s military. But there are other constituencies! For instance, if you keep your gold in a vault, the guy with the key to the vault gets to make his own decision about who is the president of Venezuela: Nicolas Maduro’s embattled Venezuelan regime, desperate to hold onto the dwindling cash pile it has abroad, was stymied in its bid to pull $1.2 billion worth of gold out of the Bank of England, according to people familiar with the matter. The Bank of England’s decision to deny Maduro officials’ withdrawal request comes after top U.S. officials, including Secretary of State Michael Pompeo and National Security Adviser John Bolton, lobbied their U.K. counterparts to help cut off the regime from its overseas assets, according to one of the people, who asked not to be identified. … The U.S. officials are trying to steer Venezuela’s overseas assets to Guaido to help bolster his chances of effectively taking control of the government. The $1.2 billion of gold is a big chunk of the $8 billion in foreign reserves held by the Venezuelan central bank. Oops! It does seem a little sloppy, if you are a fiery nationalist president who is openly hostile to many of the major western powers, to keep all your gold at the central bank of one of those powers. But I am not sure that there is a general solution to this. “Keep the gold in Venezuela and have the army guard it”: Fine, sure, but then you gotta trust the army. You probably need to trust the army anyway, if you are going to run a country, but you can certainly imagine a controversial strongman president finding it more prudent to keep gold in a bank abroad than in an army base at home. I joked on Twitter that “this is why I keep my gold on the blockchain,” but it is possible that the real lesson here is that there is no technological way to keep your assets safe, no way to avoid trust entirely. Property, like political power, is a social institution; you own gold because a sufficient group of other people believe that you own the gold. If no one else thinks that you own the gold, then your gold is gone. In other Venezuela news, Felix Salmon argues that if the U.S. really wants to help Guaido, it should issue an executive order preventing creditors from seizing Venezuela’s assets in the U.S., so that a post-Maduro regime will have some time and breathing room to work out a debt settlement. (We talked about this idea a few months ago when Lee Buchheit and Mitu Gulati first proposed it, and I said “don’t hold your breath for the Trump administration to actually do it for Venezuela,” but now that the administration seems to be fully behind Guaido it does seem like a plausible way to help him.) And in other sovereign-debt controversies, Gulati and Mark Weidemaier ask: “ Mozambique’s Guarantees on the Tuna Bonds: Can They be Repudiated?”

I don’t make a lot of investment predictions around here, mostly because I am bad at it, but I have spent the last few years pretty confidently asserting, every time someone announced a new plan to take Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac out of government conservatorship and return them to private shareholders, that it wasn’t gonna happen. So far my record on those predictions has been perfect. And why not? The status quo is great for a lot of people, particularly politicians: Fannie and Freddie generate a lot of profits for the Treasury in conservatorship, and their direct government control makes it simpler to use them as an instrument of housing policy. Re-privatizing them would require the government to make hard choices about how the housing market should be structured, how much risk the government should bear and how much it should be paid for bearing that risk, and whether Fannie and Freddie’s current private shareholders should be rewarded. Beyond all that, it just seems hard to go wrong betting on government inaction, in 2019 or really in general. Congress and the Trump administration have a lot on their plate, and can’t do most of it; making huge risky substantive decisions about a controversial program that no one is paying much attention to seems like too much to ask. But my general rule of thumb is that the market always knows better than I do so here you go: For more than a decade, lawmakers have tried and failed to overhaul Fannie and Freddie, which were placed in conservatorship during the 2008 financial crisis. But recent statements by administration officials indicating the government plans to move soon on taking the firms out of conservatorship have sent shares surging. The common shares of Fannie and Freddie are up more than 170% this year, while the most commonly traded class of the preferred shares, a form of senior equity that used to pay a dividend, are up more than 37%. … “It’s night and day,” said David Barrosse of Washington, D.C., policy analysis firm Capstone LLC, of the change in political will to privatize Fannie and Freddie. “We think that the signs are there for anyone to see, in public statements: This is happening now.” Sure, why not! I found this paragraph promising: A growing cadre of investors who aren’t suing the government, including Paulson and GSO, are behind a proposal by investment bank Moelis & Co. that calls for allowing Fannie and Freddie to recapitalize by ending the profit sweep and issuing new common and preferred stock. Moelis, which is advising some holders of Fannie and Freddie’s preferred shares, estimates the government could make up to $125 billion through the sale of its warrants for the companies’ common stock. The basic situation is that Fannie and Freddie send money to the government every year, and re-privatizing them by ending the profit sweep would (1) stop that and (2) give billions of dollars to hedge funds. Those seem like unattractive features of re-privatization, from the government’s perspective, though obviously attractive to the hedge funds. But the nice thing about capital markets is that they will pay you (the discounted value of) many years’ worth of profits, all at once, up front, and the … possibly less nice … thing about governments is that they’d sometimes rather get a large lump sum payment now than a steady stream of money later. So if the government could raise $125 billion up front by selling Fannie and Freddie warrants, then it might be tempted to take the money and forego the future profits. By the way the largest initial public offering ever was Alibaba’s, which raised $25 billion, and there has been a great deal of excitement over the so far hypothetical $100 billion IPO of Saudi Aramco. A $125 billion offering of warrants— warrants!—would be quite a thing.

My Bloomberg Opinion colleague Tyler Cowen notes that he and Amihai Glazer wrote a paper on our favorite topic—whether common ownership of companies in the same industry by institutional investors undermines competition—possibly as early as the late 1980s, though no journal would publish it because “they all told us it was crazy”: I should also note Ami and I never quite agreed on what the paper meant. I always viewed it as more of a theoretical curiosity. I’m still not sure I understand Ami’s take, but in general he saw it as closer to a real world possibility or maybe stronger than that. I also thought that even if joint ownership came about, forces akin to those discussed in the socialist calculation debate still would require something akin to firm-by-firm competition, rather than managed collusion (what about just picking managers with sluggish temperaments, thus leading to an intermediate solution?) I should say that I write about this all the time, find it plausible at a level of basic theory, and am skeptical of all proposed solutions, which I suppose puts me in the “theoretical curiosity” camp.

Here is Erin Griffith on hustle culture: Perhaps we’ve all gotten a little hungry for meaning. Participation in organized religion is falling, especially among American millennials. In San Francisco, where I live, I’ve noticed that the concept of productivity has taken on an almost spiritual dimension. Techies here have internalized the idea — rooted in the Protestant work ethic — that work is not something you do to get what you want; the work itself is all. Therefore any life hack or company perk that optimizes their day, allowing them to fit in even more work, is not just desirable but inherently good. I think there is a plausible case that finding meaning and value in your work is better than not finding meaning and value in your work. But there are tradeoffs: If you don’t find meaning in your work, it’s easy to leave it behind at 5 p.m.; if you do find meaning in your work, there’s a risk that it will expand to become the main source of meaning in your life. And it’s sort of obviously in your boss’s interests to convince you that it should.

On the other hand here are Devon Zuegel, Andrew Kortina and Namrata Patel on “a decrease in the marginal signalling utility of (conspicuous) consumption goods for all but the highest earners,” its effect on labor force participation and thus economic growth, and their proposed solution: “The somewhat radical idea of a tax on human attention or time spent consuming entertainment media as a way to stimulate productivity.” Okay! I confidently assert that reading Money Stuff increases your productivity, though, so I expect that it will be exempt from the leisure tax.

For some reason young people sometimes ask me for advice about whether they should pursue a career in financial services, and if so what sorts of jobs they should seek and how they should go about it. You should not do this: I do not know anything about anything, and I am busy. But one piece of advice that I try to convey is that “finance” is a very broad field, and that there are lots of different jobs in the financial industry that require different skills and interests, and you should learn something about those jobs and, more importantly, learn something about yourself, before deciding on a career path. Some people are natural salespeople and others are natural flow traders and still others are natural hedge-fund analysts and a select few are natural derivatives structurers, but many of those people would be miserable in any of the other roles. Still there is one financial-industry career path that I would have thought would be equally appealing to almost anyone, and that I would unhesitatingly advise anyone to pursue, which is that if someone is willing to pay you $50 million not to work in the financial services industry, you should hit that bid! That’s my dream job! If any investment bank out there is looking to pay someone $50 million not to work in finance, let’s talk; I will be happy to sign up for that. I’d do it for $30 million honestly. Weirdly though Andrea Orcel has actually been offered that gig and is still thinking it over: Andrea Orcel is facing the trade of his career: collect tens of millions of dollars in deferred compensation from UBS Group AG or keep a career in banking. The former head of the Swiss lender’s investment bank can still contractually qualify for the backlog of compensation if he decides to work in another field or retires, according to people with knowledge of the company’s position. UBS doesn’t believe it would be obliged to make the payments if he joins any sort of financial-services competitor, the people said, asking not to be identified discussing internal decisions. “We can’t comment on individual cases,” UBS said in a statement. “But if someone fulfills the requirements for career retirement at UBS, meaning mainly as long as they don‘t work for another financial services organization following a certain amount of years with UBS, they receive their deferred compensation. It’s granted on the existing deferral schedule.” We talked about this “trade” last week, when I wasn’t sure if Orcel—who left UBS to run Banco Santander SA, and then lost his offer at Santander when neither UBS nor Santander was willing to pay out his $40 million to $60 million of deferred comp—was still in line to get that deferred comp if he didn’t go to Santander. If not, I figured, he should have gone to Santander for less; if so, though, taking the money and going to the beach seemed like a no-brainer. And it looks like, yep, he stands to collect tens of millions of dollars just for not being an investment banker anymore, something that hundreds of investment bankers do for free every year. Look, obviously, at every step along the way as you move from being a young analyst to the global head of investment banking, you are going to be selected and indoctrinated for the sorts of personality traits that would lead you to think things like “why would I take $50 million not to work in investment banking when I could work 80 hours a week for the rest of my life and have a good chance of making even more money?” So offers like this are wasted on people who are inclined to reject them. Still, if you are about to embark on a career in financial services, you might want to think for a minute about whether you’d give it all up for $50 million. It’s not a live offer, now, but maybe write down your answer. And then in 30 years if someone does make you that offer, go and look at what you wrote and see what you think about it.

We talked a little bit earlier this week about the possibility that, as the government shutdown drags on and the Securities and Exchange Commission does not review or sign off on initial public offerings, eventually a company will go the fallback route of doing an IPO without SEC signoff. This is allowed by the rules, but never happens, not only because it seems reckless not to have the SEC sign off on your financials but also because those rules require you to wait 20 days between pricing the IPO and actually selling the stock. I sort of vaguely imagined that would be fine for the new breed of IPO companies that don’t really need the money—they can just price the IPO at an aspirational level, sell stock if people want to buy there, and not if not—but I guess it is not surprising that the first company to actually announce a fixed-price IPO will be one that really needs the money: Gossamer Bio Inc. said in a filing Wednesday afternoon that it would go public by letting its registration become automatically effective “as a result of the shutdown of the federal government.” If all goes to plan, the company will be able to sell shares to investors in 20 calendar days. … Kevin Kennedy, a partner at Simpson Thacher & Bartlett LLP who works on IPOs, said the move is “highly, highly unusual,” although the option has long been available to companies. Many avoid it because it means having to price shares before a firm markets its deal to investors, whose feedback is needed to set the price. Nasdaq and bankers have also worried such deals could be vulnerable to regulatory or legal challenges later, people familiar with the matter said. But some biotechnology firms may take the option during the government’s closure because they need to raise money, Mr. Kennedy said. In addition, many biotechs don’t have revenue yet, so their financial statements are simpler and require less scrutiny from the SEC. “It’s hard to envision this working for too many outside of the life sciences,” he added. “For a lot of them, going public is not optional. They have to find this financing or shut down.” I am enthusiastic about new IPO structures generally, so I’m excited for this, but I cannot deny that it is just a terrible way to do an IPO. You price the stock and then wait 20 days, and a lot can happen in 20 days. If the stuff that happens is bad, then the price that people are willing to pay will go down; if it goes down enough then no one will buy your stock at the price you set. If the stuff that happens is good, then the price that people are willing to pay will go up, and you will be, as people constantly say about IPOs, “leaving money on the table.” If you don’t need the money, you can just make the price high and take your chances. But if you do need the money, you really have to significantly underprice the IPO in order to minimize the risk of it failing, which means that in all likelihood you’ll be leaving a lot of money on the table for investors. It is an ugly trade.

There is a theme in all of our recent discussions of credit default swaps around here, which is roughly: A weird and counterintuitive thing seems to be about to happen in the CDS market. We talk about how weird and fun and counterintuitive it is. Other people talk about how it is a disaster, probably illegal market manipulation, and will undermine market confidence so badly that CDS as a product will disappear. Everyone gets together and says, never mind, the thing won’t happen. There was going to be a manufactured default in Hovnanian Enterprises Inc. bonds, and then there wasn’t. There was going to be a weird CDS orphaning at McClatchy Co., and then there wasn’t. There was going to be a weird corner on Sears Roebuck Acceptance Corp. bonds in the CDS auction, and then there actually kind of was, but the people who were mad about it had settled by the time it happened so it wasn’t a huge deal. And we talked a little while ago about CDS on Dutch telecom company VodafoneZiggo. The issue there was that VodafoneZiggo had issued bonds out of a subsidiary (Ziggo Bond Finance B.V.), and there were lots of CDS contracts referencing that subsidiary. Then one day VodafoneZiggo got rid of Ziggo Bond Finance and transferred all of the bonds over to a different subsidiary (Ziggo Bond Company B.V.), but no one really noticed. This bit of corporate structuring seems to have been a matter of indifference to the bondholders—one Ziggo bond subsidiary was as good as another—and to the company itself, but it caused a problem for the CDS market: ZBF can’t default on its bonds anymore (since it has no bonds, and no longer exists), so if you own CDS on ZBF it appears to be worthless. And if you own bonds issued by ZBC and hedge them with ZBF CDS, you are in trouble: If ZBC defaults, your ZBF CDS will not pay off. This is not an unheard-of thing, and the CDS market has mechanisms for dealing with it, but they require immediate action and no one noticed this one for a while. And then they did, and prices of ZBF CDS dropped—because it might be worthless—and people went to the determinations committee of the International Swaps and Derivatives Association asking it to rule, in essence, ah come on. And this week it did! ZBC is close enough to being ZBF, ruled the determinations committee, that CDS on ZBF is now CDS on ZBC, and everything works the way everyone blithely expected it to work. This is a debatable conclusion on delightfully legalistic grounds. Here is Robert Smith’s analysis at the Financial Times, which turns among other things on the fact that all of ZBF’s Obligations, but not all of its obligations, were transferred to ZBC, and derivatives lawyers cherish the difference between lowercase and uppercase letters.[1] But it is in any case a pretty sensible decision not to enforce the dumbest possible outcome just because it is supported by a literal reading of the contract. Of course there are complaints: “They’ve never fudged the documents before,” says one hedge fund manager. “It’s the uncanniest thing I’ve ever seen.” The point, I suppose, is that any outcome on a disputed issue can undermine confidence in the CDS market: The point of any dispute is that some people think that the documents say, or mean, one thing, and others think that they say, or mean, another thing, and any decision will shake the settled expectations of somebody. Still this one seem fine. It is perhaps helpful here that, unlike in most of our weird CDS situations, this one doesn’t seem to have been engineered . The random orphaning of ZBF CDS would be a windfall for people who had sold that CDS, of course, but it’s not like they worked to achieve that orphaning, or even noticed it. This was not a trade that they put on and then fought to defend; this was just an accident that would have worked out nicely for them but, then, didn’t.

I am not an expert in wildfire causation, but just from vaguely following financial news I was pretty sure that California utility PG&E Corp. was responsible for a bunch of catastrophic wildfires and was going to have to pay billions of dollars in damages. This was not a moral judgment or anything, but California law makes utilities responsible for fires caused by their equipment even if they were not negligent, and California officials were investigating the causes of the fires, and PG&E had announced that it was preparing to file for bankruptcy in anticipation of the results, so it did rather seem like the news was going to be bad. So this was a surprise to me: PG&E Corp. was cleared of blame for a deadly 2017 blaze just days before the California utility giant was set to file for bankruptcy to deal with crippling wildfire liabilities. And yet the company has given no indication that it’s changing course. The finding by the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection on Thursday may reduce PG&E’s projected $30 billion in liabilities from 2017 and 2018 wildfires by $17 billion, state Governor Gavin Newsom told reporters in Sacramento, stressing that the report “isn’t insignificant.” But analysts were giving smaller estimates -- to the tune of $8 billion -- and PG&E said in a statement that it still faces “significant potential” costs. It is unclear what will happen—some analysts think bankruptcy is still likely, while big PG&E investor BlueMountain Capital Management said this “is yet another example of why the company shouldn’t be rushing to file for bankruptcy” and is trying to replace the board of directors—but it is at least imaginable that PG&E will file for bankruptcy, get into court, add up all of its assets and liabilities, and realize that actually everything is fine and it has plenty of money and the whole thing was an overreaction. (Some of PG&E’s remaining projected liabilities are for fires whose cause has not yet been determined by Cal Fire, so maybe it will be cleared for those too.) A normal reason to file for bankruptcy is that your assets are worth less than your liabilities, you have liabilities coming due, and it would be unfair to pay off some creditors in full when you don’t have enough money to pay everyone. So you file for bankruptcy so that you don’t have to pay off anyone—all of their claims are “stayed”—and you go to court and argue about how much you can afford to pay back, and eventually you figure it out and pay everyone off pro rata. But if there is, like, a 50 percent chance that your assets are worth much less than your liabilities—if that will be determined by a coin flip in a week, say—and you have liabilities coming due now ( as PG&E does), then it would also be unfair to pay off some creditors in full when there’s a 50/50 chance you won’t have enough to pay everyone. So you might file for bankruptcy, stay all the claims, wait until after the coin flip, and then either (1) do a full painful restructuring when it turns out there isn’t enough money or (2) say “never mind, back to normal” if it turns out there is. (PG&E “could exit bankruptcy on an expedited basis without impairing creditors,” as BlueMountain puts it.) It’s not something you see every day! Bankruptcy is, you know, bad, and companies do try not to file for bankruptcy only to say “never mind” a week later. But there is a certain logic to it in unusual cases like this. Elsewhere in PG&E, here is “ How Securitization Could Help Save PG&E.” And elsewhere in bankruptcy, here is “Creditors Say Edward Lampert Reaped Billions but Left Sears Insolvent.” I have to say that that headline is just … straightforwardly true? Like, Sears Holdings Corp. is definitely bankrupt, and Lampert—Sears’s chairman, biggest shareholder, etc.— seems to have made a profit out of doing transactions with it. Those are not legally dispositive facts: Sears’s committee of unsecured creditors accuse Lampert of enriching himself by deliberate asset stripping and want to recharacterize his loans to Sears as equity contributions, while Lampert argues that his actions were in the best interests of all Sears stakeholders and that the “processes we followed are unimpeachable.” Ultimately a court will have to decide whether Lampert achieved the results he achieved legitimately or illegitimately. But the crude results are just that Sears once had money, and now it doesn’t, and Lampert does. So you can kind of see the creditors’ point.

Disclosure: I used to work at Goldman Sachs Group Inc., and I didn’t always know what I was doing and had to work pretty fast under a lot of pressure and without enough sleep, and I sometimes made mistakes, and when I did people were nice enough to let me fix them, and that was a good and kind thing to do and I appreciated it, and Goldman employees are people too and there is no reason not to be kind to them. Still, in my current role as a commentator on the financial industry, I feel it is incumbent on me to be cruel and say, if Goldman messes up and sells you some stock too cheap, and then calls you up and says “that stock was too cheap and we’d like you to pay us more for it,” you should probably hang up on them, come on: Goldman Sachs Group Inc. and Morgan Stanley asked some counterparties to cancel or amend trades in Jardine Matheson Holdings Ltd., after a $41 billion flash crash on Thursday saw shares change hands far below the market level, according to people familiar with the matter. Some of the amendment requests were to settle the trades at a higher price, according to the people, who asked not to be named discussing a sensitive topic. We talked about this trade yesterday, when I pointed out that the “$41 billion flash crash” actually cost people—people like Goldman and Morgan apparently—about $9 million in mispriced sales. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley can afford to lose $9 million on ill-timed market orders every now and then, and letting them eat the loss will teach them a valuable lesson about market orders. Just, when you see the actual traders who lost the money, buy them a drink; they will need it.

I slave away all day writing sentences on the internet. David Einhorn, meanwhile, works full time (except for a midday nap and some poker vacations) at his job of managing a multibillion-dollar hedge fund, which may lack some of the spiritual rewards of writing sentences on the internet but which definitely pays better. So it is particularly painful for me to realize that I’ll never write a sentence as good as this throwaway line that David Einhorn put in an investor letter: "We no longer believe there is risk of our assets growing too quickly (other than through improved performance)," Einhorn wrote in a quarterly letter to investors, explaining why he would re-open to new capital. "To be clear, we do not plan to initiate a marketing effort, as we plan to continue to focus on the portfolio," he added. Greenlight Capital, Einhorn’s hedge fund, lost 34 percent in 2018, “coming off six straight years in which Greenlight lagged behind the total return of the S&P 500.” Client redemptions brought assets under management to about $2.5 billion, “down from more than $6 billion a year ago” and $12 billion at its peak. And after seven straight years of poor performance, and the ensuing billions of dollars of redemptions by irate clients, Einhorn took stock of the situation and decided: Hey, good news, we have solved the problem of growing too fast! That risk has been taken right off the table! And that news was so good that he had to share it with clients. And it’s good news for the clients too, because, if they haven’t taken their money out of Greenlight in disappointment after seven straight bad years, now they can put more money in. They can put more money in! What? I have said this before, but I do not actually believe that running a large hedge fund is a coin-flipping contest and that most famous managers’ returns are due mostly to luck. It’s just that it almost always seems both funnier and more analytically productive to think of things that way. Imagine that, just by pure chance, every hedge fund manager gets, say, seven years of beating the market and seven years of underperformance, but the order is determined randomly. Some managers will get the perfect order. They will have a one or two bad years starting out, and their clients will begin to lose faith in them but be persuaded to stick around a little bit longer. Then they will have all their good years in a row. They will look like visionaries who were slightly ahead of their time; clients who trusted in them will be amply rewarded; new clients will gain confidence not only from the string of successes but also from the early failures that presumably taught them valuable lessons about discipline and caution. In the good years, money will pour in and be subject to long-term lockups. They’ll raise permanent capital vehicles. They’ll make billions in performance and management fees. Then they’ll have the rest of their bad years, but at that point, between the lockups and the permanent capital and keeping their own billions in the fund, it won’t matter that much; their wealth is assured. Not only that, though, the clients will actually go out of their way to justify the trajectory. “I feel bad for her; it’s tough to see someone who demonstrated as much skill as she did in those first seven years suffer as much bad luck as she has in these last six,” the clients will say, somehow. Other managers will just have, like, four bad years up front and that will be the end of them. Their seven good years will be wasted trading their own retirement accounts. Why would you invest with someone with such a bad track record, unless she previously had a good track record? I don’t know. This can’t be the whole story, but I will say that I would like to read more stories about hedge fund managers who started with seven straight bad years and then turned it around. I’m sure they exist. And that path is interesting! If you have a bunch of years of good performance in a row, and then a bunch of years of bad performance, then maybe you have demonstrated skill, but it is hard to reject the null hypothesis that you just had some good luck and then some bad luck. But if you have only a bunch of years of bad performance in a row, and keep managing money , and then turn it around and make a lot of money, then I think you have certainly demonstrated some kind of skill. At the very least you are good at marketing. But in year seven of losses, if you go to clients and saying “my investing process is good and here is why,” and they believe you, then whatever you are saying must be pretty compelling! There must be some logical basis to your explanation that can be conveyed to an outside observer with money on the line. And then, if you actually do turn it around, well, there is an out-of-sample test of your process. Whereas if you have the gains first and you go to clients and say “my investing process is good and here is why,” you’ll never know for sure if they were persuaded by your explanation or by the results, and you might never know for sure if the explanation actually explained the results. Elsewhere: “The New Hedge Fund Manager Flies Economy and Stays in Hostels.” Promising!

There is an idea in the stylized imaginary history of economics called the “ double coincidence of wants.” The basic insight is that if I have a sheep and you have a cow, we might both be better off if I gave you some wool and you gave me some milk, but what are the odds that I’ll be thirsty for some milk just when you could really use a sweater? Fortunately money exists,[1] so I can sell my wool for money and you can sell your milk for money, and then we both have money, and we can store it, and we can use the money to buy the stuff we want when we want to. Everyone always wants money, is the point of money. Of course that is not super literally true. If I want some milk in the middle of the night, and I do not have milk, and I go over to your house and wake you up and say “hey go milk your cow here’s a dollar,” you will not be happy about the whole transaction. You don’t always want money. Money and prices are big steps toward solving the coordination problems of the economy, but there are other steps. You need markets: There need to be specific places where people can go at specific times to exchange their money for specific sorts of stuff. And so, to really go overboard on the stylized imaginary history of economics here, people invented medieval market fairs, and then shops, and then shopping malls, and then Amazon.com. Much of the story of modern capitalism is about expanding these markets and making them more efficient and seamless and automated and on your phone, so that you can exchange money for pretty much anything, anytime, anywhere. There does however seem to be a tradeoff between that pervasive efficiency and a kind of goofy irrationality. If a medieval merchant showed up five minutes early to a market fair, and it wasn’t open yet, he wouldn’t just, like, dump his bolts of cloth into the ocean and go home empty-handed. He’d wait the five minutes! But once you put markets on computers, dumb stuff happens: Jardine Matheson Holdings Ltd., Singapore’s largest company by market value, plunged 83 percent on Thursday before quickly rebounding. The exchange said an influx of pre-market sell orders caused the dramatic drop. Shares sank just before the regular session began, with about 167,500 changing hands at just $10.99, compared with Wednesday’s close of $66.47. Jardine, the flagship investment firm of a 186-year-old conglomerate, soon recovered from the $41 billion wipeout and ended up closing 0.5 percent higher. In fact the very next trade, a few minutes after that opening cross, was in the mid-$50s, and it was back above $60 seconds later. The $41 billion wipeout consisted of people selling 167,500 shares at call it a $55 discount, meaning that they lost about $9 million or so—real money, but not tens of billions, or even tens of millions, of dollars. (The stock trades in U.S. dollars. And “it is likely to be one seller selling a bulk amount at the wrong price,” says an analyst.) As is so often the case with flash crashes, the headline numbers are large and exciting but the actual harm seems quite small. Still, what were they thinking? Sell orders overwhelmed bids during the pre-opening phase, Singapore Exchange Ltd. said in an emailed statement, adding that the orders weren’t due to a fat finger error or a malfunctioning brokerage system, and the exchange won’t be canceling the trades. Traders had earlier speculated that a human mistake was to blame. “Trading was orderly and there was no sign of manipulation," SGX said in its statement. The sell orders were mostly market orders, which institutions usually use to set the size of an order but not the price, according to the bourse. “Participants had ample time to react before the market opened," and sellers could have withdrawn their orders if they didn’t want to offload shares at the low price, SGX said. They could have waited a few minutes and sold in the $60s, and they “had ample time” to notice that, but they didn’t.[2] The point of a stock exchange, and the particular point of an opening auction, is to aggregate liquidity. You know that everyone who wants to buy or sell Jardine stock will be hanging out on the Singapore stock exchange, so if you want to sell some, you go to the stock exchange because that’s where the buyers are. And if you want to sell a lot all at once, you tend to focus on the open and the close, because those are salient points that tend to attract a lot of buyers and sellers—and that have specific formal processes for aggregating all of the buyers and sellers into one auction—so there’s a lot of liquidity and really good and efficient price discovery. And then sometimes there isn’t! But you have gone so far down the road of relying on that liquidity that you somehow can’t stop yourself. The formal processes—the exchanges and order types and auction mechanisms and algorithms—have entirely replaced thinking about things like “I want to sell some stock, I wonder if anyone wants to buy it.” That’s mostly good and efficient! Human desires are complicated and reducing them to simple automated procedures saves everybody time and money. But the automated procedures can also erase our intuitions about how to act like humans. If you show up at the market and there’s no one else there, you understand that you have to wait to sell your stuff until other people show up. But if your algorithm shows up at the opening cross and there’s no one else there, it’s easier to forget.

Man, if I was an investor in Bridgewater Associates, the world’s largest hedge fund that is also a weird therapy cult in which workers are constantly engaging in rituals of self-criticism while the computer quietly does the investing, I would want to witness some of that sweet sweet self-criticism for myself. Like if Bridgewater had a mediocre year, I would call them up and demand that they explain themselves in excruciating and humiliating detail. That’s their whole thing, right? Amazingly the San Joaquin County pension fund seems to have done just that: After reviewing the investment for more than a year, the county decided this month to pull its entire $81 million from Bridgewater’s Pure Alpha II fund. The move came even after it gained 14.6 percent last year. The decision underscores the mostly mediocre performance of Bridgewater’s fund since 2012, and the increased frustration fund clients face as their managers fail to make money for them, even as they enrich themselves. … San Joaquin got a 3.1 percent annualized return after fees (6.9 percent before fees) in the five years ending Sept. 30, 2017, a return and fees combination that it was apparently not satisfied with. Fine! But the best part is this: The county’s Pure Alpha investment is minuscule for Bridgewater. It amounted to less than one-tenth of one percent of what Bridgewater manages in its hedge fund strategy. Yet Dalio’s team fought to save the account. Bridgewater crafted a three-page letter -- not including the appendix -- to defend itself and the fund’s track record and fees. “Defend”? How defensive! I assume that that is a shorthand characterization and that Bridgewater actually listened to San Joaquin’s criticism with an open mind and conducted a rigorous analysis of its performance and fees before deciding to tell the county that it had it all wrong. Probably San Joaquin’s believability score was too low. Anyway I hope San Joaquin made its Bridgewater representative come and present its letter in person, and then videotaped that session to share with other public pension funds. One of my favorite things to ponder about Bridgewater is: Do they apply their rigorous self-analysis to the question of whether all that rigorous self-analysis is good for returns? Those returns have been good over the long run (Bridgewater “noted that the investment had returned an annualized 10.4 percent after fees since the pension fund’s initial investment in 2006”), and good last year, but otherwise mediocre for the past few years. What you’d really want is to take half of Bridgewater’s employees, give them half the money, and tell them to keep doing what they’re doing with the self-analysis and constant feedback and so forth, and then take the other half of the employees, give them the other half of the money, and tell them to manage it while bottling up their feelings and being dishonestly polite like workers everywhere else. See who does better! Sure it sounds reasonable to say that rigorous self-understanding and constant honest feedback will lead to better investment returns, but how do you know ?

It’s not hard to see why investment banks, and many other employers, require their employees to agree that if they have any complaints they have to take them up in arbitration rather than the court system. Arbitration tends to be cheaper, faster, more employer-friendly, and more secret, all of which are good things for employers whose employees have problems with them. It is not so great for employees—not only because it is employer-friendly and secret, but also because it tends not to allow class actions and so can be more expensive for the employees—which is why it is controversial. That controversy might be bad enough for morale or public relations that some employers would stick with the courts, but it’s certainly not surprising that many employers prefer arbitration. But if I were running an investment bank I would go a bit beyond insisting on mandatory arbitration. I would also have a separate provision for employees whose specific problem is that they were fired just before receiving their bonus. Those employees, it seems to me—as a person and former investment banker, I mean, not as the hypothetical head of an investment bank—have a 100 percent legitimate grievance. Firing people just before bonuses, so that they don’t get their bonuses, is very mean. On the other hand they have a 0 percent legitimate legal case . It’s a bonus! You’re not entitled to it until you get it. The bank tells employees, really really really clearly and repeatedly, that they will get their bonus if they’re employed when it’s paid, and not if they’re gone. Much of the point of the bonus is to give the bank more flexibility about pay. So, sure, employees who have claims about discrimination or mistreatment I would send to arbitration. But employees who have claims about not getting their bonus I would send to therapy. Their employment contract would say “you agree that all disputes about unpaid bonuses will be adjudicated by binding therapy,” and then if they brought a claim they would have to go talk to a specially trained counselor who would “take their testimony,” reassure them that their feelings are normal and that they are good people whom any bank would be lucky to give a bonus, and then point out that they have not a sliver of a legal entitlement to a bonus so maybe they should just let it go and try to move on with their lives. And that would be the binding non-appealable verdict. Anyway Bloomberg’s Max Abelson reviewed thousands of pages of arbitration transcripts from a guy who went after UBS AG because he was fired before his bonus, and his story will modestly undermine whatever modest confidence you had in the arbitration system. “Like getting stuck at an endless dinner with guests who despise each other,” is how Abelson describes it. One arbitrator—84 years old, legally blind and hard of hearing—allegedly fell asleep during testimony, though he sort of half-denied it: Stewart has no recollection of any naps. “Now, some of these cases, the testimony goes on and on and on, and sometimes the witness is very repetitive,” he says. “It’s a challenge for any arbitrator to have to keep paying close attention.” Another arbitrator was in the bathroom during the closing statements. “I’m sure you can fill me in,” he said when he came back. The guy did not get his bonus, of course, though the arbitrators did award him some of the deferred compensation that he arguably abandoned by refusing to sign a release, which frankly seems generous to me.
