Here’s some career advice from billionaire hedge fund manager John Paulson: He said he opted for a career betting on mergers rather than advising on them because the hours were shorter and he could make more money. “Even though M&A fees are a lot greater than lawyer fees, they’re still capped by the time you have, what you can sell your time for, whereas when you manage money there’s no cap. There’s unlimited upside to what you can do with the capital you manage,” he said. “The other thing I love about this business, when I say why I went into this business, is the fee structure,” he added, detailing how much he could make in charging a 1 per cent management fee and 20 per cent performance fee on different levels of assets. “The more money you manage, the greater the fees,” he said. “Now ultimately we managed over $30bn, and there were years our returns were well in excess of 20 per cent, so to get to those levels, the fees just pour out of the sky.” This is of course the most obvious imaginable reason to go into the hedge fund business, and it would not be worth quoting except that you don’t see successful hedge fund managers spell it out all that often. “I just love the intellectual challenge of understanding trades and testing my belief against the markets, and the money is an accidental by-product,” is what you ordinarily say, when what you mean is “the thing I love most is how the fees just pour out of the sky.” Also if you start losing money you don’t have to give the fees back: “The 63-year-old money manager said that almost 75 to 80 per cent of the money managed by Paulson & Co was now his own capital, reflecting years of disappointing returns that have driven outside investors away”—though also reflecting earlier years of huge returns and huge fees that allowed him to have billions of dollars of his own money in his fund—and “he would consider turning his firm Paulson & Co into a family office ‘in the next year or two.’”

This also seems very reasonable! The day after Christmas, a hedge fund manager who made the remarkable promise that he would never lose investors’ money was accused of stealing from his clients by U.S. regulators. But then the partial government shutdown hit and the Securities and Exchange Commission’s case went into purgatory, with all court proceedings put on hold. In the ensuing weeks, one of the few SEC cops still on the beat put what seemed to be a reasonable request to the fund manager, Statim Holding’s Joseph Meyer. As long as the case was stayed, would Meyer agree not to pull assets from a Statim hedge fund. Meyer refused, the regulator said in a Jan. 17 court filing. I mean! If you are doing scams (Meyer’s lawyer says “we dispute the allegations” and “look forward to vindication”), and the cops come and bust you, the classy move is to say “you got me copper” and go quietly. But if the cops then say “hang on, we lost our funding, we’ll be back in a month or so, just don’t move, wait right here and we’ll come back and take all your ill-gotten gains”—no, I am going to say no, you do not have any obligation to make life easier for them. Obviously this is not legal advice—you probably do have a legal obligation not to run off with your ill-gotten gains, really—but you probably aren’t looking for legal advice. And just as a matter of sportsmanship, if the cops ask to hit pause on their case against you, I don’t see why you should have to agree. If you asked them to leave you alone for a few months they wouldn’t do it!

s.h: Should you day-trade stocks on your phone?
s.t: Look, you do what you want, but I’m with her: “I know it’s not the most responsible way to get into investing,” Ms. Putman said. “It’s easy gambling—on your phone, in your pocket…and you could lose it all in the checkout line.” So is this professor: “Much like easy, self-directed electronic trading allowed people to use broker-dealers to gamble in the stock market, free apps and this bull market are bringing the ability to make foolish decisions to an ever-broader swath of people,” said Ben Edwards, business and securities law professor at University of Nevada Las Vegas. Honestly a good mission statement for, like, half of the modern tech industry would be “bringing the ability to make foolish decisions to an ever-broader swath of people.” With buying stocks on your phone, though, there is a superficially plausible case that it is bringing you the ability to make wise decisions, making it more convenient to save and invest responsibly. Ha no just kidding; here’s the co-founder of Robinhood Markets Inc., the leading trade-stocks-on-your-phone app: Robinhood co-founder Baiju Bhatt said in a September interview that Robinhood’s users engage with the app the way they engage with Instagram or WhatsApp, as opposed to rival e-brokers. Those with positions check the app an average of 10 times a day, he said, adding that those who actively trade tend to do so in low-price stocks. “We generate a ludicrous amount of trades in $1 to $5 stocks,” Mr. Bhatt said. “Because we’re free, we’re the only place where you can day trade stuff like that.” Rival e-brokers charge flat fees for each trade, which isn’t economically feasible for small numbers of low-price stocks. I do not give investing advice around here, but if your broker is bragging in public that your trading activity is “ludicrous,” you might want to listen to him! A lot of what I read about Robinhood seems to take a weird position: It is good to let people trade stocks for free on their phones, but Robinhood is somehow doing it in a sneakily bad way. Principally, there is a controversy about Robinhood’s use of payment for order flow. I find this controversy baffling and annoying because it is absolutely crystal clear that this is good for you : Robinhood charges high-frequency traders for the privilege of selling you stock at better than the market price , and then uses the fees it collects from them to let you trade for free. If you went to a regular broker and demanded that your order be routed to the stock exchange with no payment for order flow, (1) you would pay a commission and (2) you would get a worse price for the stock. Robinhood’s approach is demonstrably better for you in every way. As I once wrote: “‘We make big high-frequency trading firms bid to do your stock trades, and pass the benefit on to you’ ought to be a good talking point.” On the other hand, if you are constantly day-trading penny stocks on your phone, why are you doing that? The main costs of doing that are not the commissions or bid/ask spreads; they are the investment risks that you are taking and the likelihood that your own trading will underperform the market. My view of Robinhood is sort of the opposite of the one I laid out above; it’s: Despite the occasional slip, as far as I can tell Robinhood seems to do a good, efficient, honest job of letting people trade stocks for free on their phones, but That is bad and most people should not trade stocks for free on their phones. Elsewhere, people keep sending me this Reddit story about a guy who claims he lost a ton of money trading a short box spread on Robinhood without understanding—possibly also without Robinhood understanding—the risks of the position. You know what you probably shouldn’t do? You probably shouldn’t trade risky short multi-leg option strategies on levered volatility index exchange-traded funds on your phone!

Uh: The U2 frontman and his business partners at the U.S. private-equity firm [TPG] announced a new company called Y Analytics, which will use a method they developed to measure social and environmental change created by investments. Obvious questions include: Do you agree with Bono and TPG about what “social and environmental change” is desirable? Do you agree with their methods of measuring it, and their results? It seems to me that a lot of responsible investing comes down to personal priorities and preferences, and efforts to create objective quantitative indexes of social goodness are mostly a category mistake. (“We can measure financial returns, why can’t we measure social responsibility?” Well: “Statistics can tell us which baseball player has the highest batting average, why can’t they tell us which one has the highest moral worth?”) But perhaps a lot of people have the same subjective preferences as Bono. Or perhaps a lot of people aspire to have the same subjective preferences as Bono. Honestly I don’t care, I just want an excuse to put in these quotes from Bono: “Math is music here,” Bono said in an interview. “If capitalism is to be a force for good we have to be able to measure when it’s doing good and when it’s doing harm,” he said. “Fuzzy thinking just won’t cut it. We need cold hard facts.” And: “I understand the cynicism,” Bono said. “There is banana skin all over the floor, I think. I am very conscious of it. We have had green-washing or purpose-washing with all manner of halos being offered up as fig leaves for companies who do bad things but then give money away and make up for it. I get that,” he said. Greenwashing by offering halos as fig leaves while avoiding banana skin! My stars.

We talked again yesterday about the theory that common ownership of multiple firms in one industry by diversified shareholders reduces competition, and every time we talk about this, I get emails to the effect of “what if we just banned index funds from voting?” (Or “what if index funds just voluntarily agreed not to vote their stock?” Or “what if index funds asked their shareholders how to vote and just passed those votes through?”) It’s an idea that people seem to like, but I don’t understand it. There are at least three problems: One of the hypothesized mechanisms for how common ownership undermines competition is not that diversified investors call up managers and tell them not to compete, but that they don’t call up managers and tell them to compete: Managers (perhaps) have a natural inclination to avoid risk and follow the status quo, and without investor pressure to grab market share they will reach a less competitive equilibrium. Reducing investor oversight will not improve this. Nothing we talked about yesterday is about shareholder voting, and frankly almost nothing in the practical life of a corporation is about shareholder voting. Shareholders almost never vote on controversial binding proposals; contested takeovers and proxy fights are rare. They operate to check managers in extreme cases, but in most cases managers don’t need to be checked and work diligently on behalf of shareholders all on their own. Managers optimize shareholder value mostly because they have internalized a morality of optimizing shareholder value: They learned it in business school, they were trained in it early in their careers, they are shareholders themselves. If they feel a fiduciary duty to diversified shareholders, then they might do whatever bad anticompetitive things we are worried about, whether or not those shareholders vote on advisory proxy proposals. Nothing we talked about yesterday is really about index funds. It’s about diversified investors, whether they are index funds or large diversified active investors or individual investors who diversify by buying individual stocks. Warren Buffett owns four airlines. Stopping index funds from voting will not have much effect; stopping anyone from voting if they also own shares in a competitor will be intensely fact-specific and might end up with no one (or no one but management) voting. Again, I come back to what I said yesterday. If there is an issue here, it is that (1) shareholders are increasingly diversified and (2) managers are responsive to the interests of their paradigmatic shareholder. It’s not about BlackRock, or index funds; it’s not about the particular tools that investors use to diversify. It’s about two deep intellectual developments in modern capital markets, diversification and shareholder responsiveness. Those developments are obviously good in a lot of ways, but the (quite controversial!) theory is that they are also bad in one specific way (by undermining competition). But if that’s true, then the simple solutions that focus on BlackRock, or index funds, or whatever, probably won’t do any good.

s.h: People are worried about BBB bonds
s.t: Ooh I have high hopes for this one. There are a lot of big companies with lots of bonds with BBB ratings, which are held by investment-grade bond funds; if those bonds are downgraded to BB, then the investment-grade bond funds will have to sell them (and high-yield bond funds will have to buy them), which would presumably be bad for their price. You might think “well yes having a lower credit quality should be bad for the price,” but the point here is that there is—arguably—a step discontinuity; a downgrade from A- to BBB+ demonstrates lower credit quality but doesn’t change your investor base, while a downgrade from BBB- to BB+ is a fundamental shift in your investor base. Obviously this worry intersects with worries about bond market liquidity: What if there is no one to intermediate the shift of a big BBB bond from investment-grade to high-yield investors when it is downgraded to BB? Also I feel like there is some corporate-finance lore that basically every company should aim for a BBB rating: Being investment-grade gives you some opportunities and flexibility that high-yield companies don’t have, but being high investment grade is a waste of leverage capacity. If everyone is targeting BBB, some people are going to miss. Anyway: The fate of BBBs is poised to set the tone for both investment-grade and junk markets in the years to come. With more BBB debt outstanding than all junk bonds and leveraged loans combined, investment-grade problems could get downloaded to high yield in a hurry if there are a slew of downgrades. “You only need a couple of those large names to move into HY to really cause more of a liquidity trap within high yield,’’ George Rusnak, the Wells Fargo Investment Institute co-head of global fixed-income strategy, said in an interview on Bloomberg TV. And: Barclays focused in on the potential high-yield archangels: 13 major issuers that would face acute demand challenges if downgraded to junk because their outstanding debt would “overwhelm” the investor base. The most common high-yield benchmark constrains any one issuer to 2 percent of the index by par value. “A downgrade to high yield for some of the large capital structures could have more drastically negative implication,’’ he writes. “Not only would funding costs increase significantly, but funding a large capital structure -- each of the top 10 BBB would be more than 2 percent of the High Yield Index if downgraded -- in the high-yield market might be downright impossible.’’

If a contract says that you can fix something within “fifteen (30) days,” how many days do you get? The generally accepted view among lawyers is that you get 15 days—that “words prevail over numbers”—and here is a report of a Delaware Chancery Court decision agreeing with that. Perhaps a more correct rule is that if a contract says that you can fix something within “fifteen (30) days,” you should at least make fun of your lawyers a bit. I had real trouble typing “fifteen (30)” just now; I can’t look at it without getting nervous. You want a lawyer like that.

I would watch this movie: Another company, New Fortress Energy LLC, recently launched its IPO roadshow and is pitching shares to investors. The company hopes the shutdown ends by the time it is ready to price its shares, a person familiar with the offering said. If not, it could wind up on an extended or indefinite roadshow. Ordinarily, when a company does an initial public offering in the U.S., it files a prospectus for the offering with the Securities and Exchange Commission, and the SEC reviews the filing and declares it effective, and then the IPO prices. But with the government shutdown, the SEC is not reviewing prospectuses. One approach is to just get out there and start marketing shares and hope the SEC comes back. But what if it doesn’t? You just keep going? In 2021, a New Fortress Energy LLC executive will be on his 100th swing through Baltimore, dead-eyed and rumpled from years spent living in a small plane. “Any more questions for us since we were last here?” “Yes, one, why do you keep coming back?” There is another approach that is possibly even weirder. Nothing in the law requires the SEC to sign off on prospectuses. You can do an IPO without the SEC’s approval; in fact, on its way out the door for the shutdown, the SEC issued an FAQ reminding companies of that. One reason that companies ordinarily do ask for SEC approval is that it feels sort of legally prudent to run everything by the SEC before going public, so that you don’t get sued too much: Proceeding without SEC signoff carries substantive risk, some bankers and lawyers said. If the IPO disclosures given to investors are later shown to have shortcomings, plaintiffs’ lawyers could pounce and point to the unusual way the deals were done. “Historically, companies have taken some comfort from the SEC review of an IPO,” said Karen Garnett, a former senior SEC official who is now a partner at Proskauer Rose LLP. I can see the argument for giving up on this: You can review your own disclosure and determine if it’s accurate and complete, and in any case you’re basically going to get sued if the stock goes down and not if it goes up, whatever the SEC says or doesn’t say. But the more important reason that companies like the SEC review is that, if you go the SEC-review route, the rules allow you to price the deal and sell stock immediately. The deal is marketed with a preliminary prospectus with no price, the SEC declares the prospectus effective, the deal is priced, and then the company sends out a quick notice of the price and the stock can start trading the next day. If you go the other route, you can just file your prospectus, wait 20 days, and sell the stock—but the prospectus has to be complete before the 20 days start, which means that it has to have a price. This means that you need to decide on the price for an IPO 20 days before accepting binding orders for the stock, and then sit around and wait for 20 whole days for something to go wrong. Maybe the market will crash and no one will want to buy the stock at the price you set. Maybe the market will rally and you’ll have sold the stock way too cheap. It is too big and weird a risk for most normal companies to take. But wouldn’t it be fun? I have enjoyed, in recent years, watching private companies slowly move away from the traditional trappings of the IPO. You can go public without voting stock, without a lockup, without an IPO at all. The fact is that a lot of corporate founders are pretty suspicious of the method that Wall Street uses to price IPOs. And if you don’t like the Wall Street bookbuilding process for pricing your IPO, other approaches are now possible. One approach is the direct listing, where you just list your stock for trading and the price sort of comes to whatever it is. Then, if you like the price, you can do a stock offering at the actual market price a few weeks later, why not? But why not just decide what the price is, put it out there, and see if people will buy it? Offer your stock at the valuation you want; if people pay for it, great; if not, meh, you didn’t need the money anyway. As the IPO becomes less important, as it stops being a rite of passage in corporate life and becomes just one more fundraising round, maybe it’s okay to have an IPO fail because the price is too high. What if companies actually start doing that, not as a newfangled corporate finance strategy but just because the SEC is closed and that is, accidentally, the rule now?

You know, we keep talking about this, and everyone keeps assuming that I’m kidding, but meanwhile it is slowly coming true: European lawmakers have taken aim at the influence of the largest index fund managers — and the debate could have implications for the likes of BlackRock, Vanguard and State Street Global Advisors. ... Last week the European Parliament cited OECD research and warned that higher levels of common ownership result in “hidden social cost and reduced product competition”. Sven Giegold, a Green MEP, said the “dramatic change in the asset management industry” posed dangers to the market economy. “The effects of [large passive funds] have to be taken into account and regulated,” he told the Financial Times. He called for action from the European Commission. Margrethe Vestager, EU competition commissioner, last year began looking into whether common ownership impinged on competition. That inquiry has yet to result in policy action. I have to say, as a guy who writes on the internet, I am pleased to see my dorky niche hobbies gaining mainstream acceptance. But as an investor , I’m going to be sad if regulators ban index funds—or all mutual funds!?—and might also feel somewhat responsible. Never mind everyone! I was kidding! Forget about it! Honestly. On the one hand I am kind of sympathetic—more sympathetic than most of my readers anyway—to the basic idea that, if most of a company’s shareholders also own stock in its competitors, the company will have reduced incentives to compete. As Martin Schmalz, the theory’s leading proponent, puts it: “Is there any plausible story why these secular changes in the ownership structure of firms would not lead to a lessening of competition?” I once wrote that the premises of the theory—that managers are responsive to shareholders, that shareholders are increasingly diversified, and that the joint interests of companies in an industry can conflict with the interests of consumers—“all seem, not just reasonable, but like basic textbook stuff.” On the other hand, every proposal to do something about it strikes me as obviously silly. The problem, if you believe it’s a problem, is that firms are responsive to shareholders and that shareholders are diversified. How can you “fix” those things? Most of the debate about what to do about this is confused, focusing on the role of a few big asset managers—BlackRock et al.—and proposing solutions that would constrain them, for instance by “limiting institutional investors to holding either 1 per cent of an industry, or shares in only one company in each industry.” There are obvious ways to structure for that: For instance, just break up each big index-fund manager into, like, 10 still pretty big index-fund managers. This is extremely inconvenient for those managers , and also for investors—who have to pick one of the 10, lose out on economies of scale, etc.—but doesn’t seem to do anything for the problem. Before, a large percentage of each company’s stock was owned by three or so big asset managers, who owned all of the stocks in the industry and had some reason to favor reduced competition. After, the same large percentage of each company’s stock will be owned by 30 or so big asset managers, who will own all of the stocks in the industry and have some reason to favor reduced competition. The names on the shareholder list aren’t what matters; what matters is that the company’s managers can look at the shareholder list, say “all of these guys are diversified investors who also own our competitors,” and draw conclusions about shareholder utility maximization from that. Sure hey look BlackRock is big and owns a lot of stock. But you can actually go look at what BlackRock explicitly, self-consciously does with its power. It writes bland letters to CEOs telling them to be more long-termist and to solve the problems of society. You might think this is bad! (For instance, you might not want those problems solved, or you might want someone else to solve them, or you might object to the letters on stylistic grounds.) But BlackRock doesn’t write letters to CEOs telling them to raise prices and stop trying to take market share from each other. This might be because it is telling them to do that in secret without leaving a paper trail (doubtful), or because it does not in fact care if they raise prices and make more money (quite likely, but rejected by the theory). Or it might be because it doesn’t need to do that , because its interests as a common shareholder of every company are sufficiently obvious to corporate executives. But those interests are fully described by saying “a lot of this company’s shares are owned by people who also own a lot of shares of its competitors.” It doesn’t matter who those people are or how many they are or in what form they own the shares. If 70 percent of your shares are owned by one or three or 10 or 10,000 broadly diversified investors, then you should (arguably) maximize the wealth of a diversified investor. You can understand the confusion. We are talking about antitrust concerns here; if you do not pay much attention to the controversy, you might just say “well sure BlackRock is big and owns a lot of every company, and bigness is an antitrust problem, and common ownership is an antitrust problem, so the solution is to make BlackRock smaller.” But the concern is far deeper and more interesting than that, and it has nothing to do with BlackRock. It’s that people used to buy stock exclusively to bet on individual stocks, and now they mostly buy stock as part of a broadly diversified portfolio. If you were a corporate executive a few decades ago, the image of a shareholder that you could hold in your mind would be someone who bought stock in your company because she understood its fundamentals and wanted it to succeed; if you are a corporate executive now, your image of a shareholder is surely someone who owns a little bit of every company and couldn’t pick yours out of a lineup. That doesn’t mean that you have to concern yourself with the interests of diversified shareholders: There are very good arguments that you should focus on what you should control (your business) and not what you can’t (your competitors), plus, you are relatively undiversified, because you probably get paid largely in your own company’s stock. The point is only that as this paradigmatic shareholder changes, it would not be surprising that corporate behavior would also change. And you can’t fix that by breaking the big index funds into smaller ones.

We talk sometimes around here about how dumb financial literacy is. Someone goes around giving people a quiz about how compound interest works, and most people fail, and people wring their hands about how America’s kids are not learning the skills they need and propose adding mandatory high-school classes about financial literacy, but the questions and answers are always wrong. They’re about math, mostly compound interest. Being able to do math is good! But it should not be confused with financial literacy. If I were writing financial literacy quizzes, here’s the sort of question I’d ask: I have a coin. I will flip it. If it comes up heads, I will pay you $10. If it comes up tails, you will pay me $10. We will do this 100 times. But wait! To sweeten the deal, I will give you insurance: If it comes up tails, the insurance will compensate you for 50 percent of your losses, so you only really have to pay me $5. The question is: Do you want to play this game? You could do math! With 50 percent probability I will pay you $10; with 50 percent probability you will pay me $5; the expected value of a coin toss is +$2.50; the tosses are independent; the expected value of the game is positive. You should probably play, but you could even calculate the variance of returns and decide if it fits with your risk tolerance. But: no. No! No! Do not play this game! Something is going on with this game! I have not told you what is going on, but why would I? I am trying to take your money! Maybe something is going on with the coin: It is loaded, or both sides are tails, or I am flipping it behind a screen and just reporting to you what I got. Or maybe something is going on with the insurance: The contract has a lot of exclusions, or the insurance only pays off when you die, or it is payable only in buy-two-get-one free coupons for cat food, or in some weird crypto token. Or all of the above; the mechanics are not the point here. The point is—the point is, if I offered you, in the safety of a financial-literacy quiz, a fair bet (heads I pay $10, tails you pay $10) then go ahead and take that, or not, whatever. Maybe I just like gambling, and you do too, and we can both enjoy gambling with each other. But if I offer you an unfair bet that is manifestly biased in your favor , run! Run! Why would I do that?[1] Anyway here is a fun website for a thing called Collectiv’Traders that offers “The First Compensation System for Retail Traders.” The idea is that you can sign up through Collectiv’Traders to trade “contracts for difference” with a retail broker, and if you lose money on the CFDs Collectiv’ will refund some of it to you. (Up to 80 percent depending on your leverage levels and how many friends you refer.) A CFD is just a bet on the price of a stock, currency, etc.: If the thing goes up, the broker pays you the amount it goes up; if it goes down, you pay the broker. (Or vice versa; you can be long or short.) If you were going to trade retail CFDs anyway, this is a great deal: If you win, you keep your money; if you lose, you only lose 20 percent of it. But it is worth noting the background fact that “74-89% of retail accounts typically lose money on” CFDs, according to the European regulators who are cracking down on them. You were probably going to lose money anyway; now you will lose less, which is better for you, but still worse than just not doing it in the first place. It is worth asking, well, even so, why would CFD brokers offer to refund you up to 80 percent of your losses? (CFDs are bilateral bets, so every dollar you lose on a CFD trade is a dollar that the broker gets.) Collectiv’ actually answers that question very clearly: Brokers spend billions of dollars every year to acquire more clients. Why? Just because 80% of retail traders are losing money and abandon FX Trading after three months. Acquiring new clients to replace losing clients is an endless vicious circle. We believe that all this money could be used to compensate the losses of retail traders to give them a second chance in the financial markets. The problem here is that CFD brokers are too good at taking your money . You show up, you open an account, you take a nice refreshing sip of coffee, and bam, your money is gone. “I will never trade CFDs with this broker again,” you harumph to yourself. And the poor broker has to go and plow most of the money it made from you into marketing to find someone else who wants to lose all of his money. What if there were a better way? What if you only lost some of your money, and felt so good about it that you decided to stick around to lose more of your money steadily over time? This is of course how casinos work—they take your money, but not all of it, and leave you feeling good enough about the experience that you come back to lose more—and I guess it is not surprising to see it applied to the retail trading industry. Obviously it has nothing to do with investing, but why would it? Also they pay you for your losses in the form of some weird token, but the details are not what is important here.

s.h: Sometimes people buy the wrong stock
s.t: Last week we talked a bit about how people sometimes buy one stock thinking that it’s another stock: Like, they buy Tweeter because Twitter is going public, or they buy Nestor because Google is buying Nest, or whatever. This is from 2001 but it’s still pretty good: This paper examines the comovement of stocks with similar ticker symbols. For one such pair of firms, there is a significant correlation between returns, volume, and volatility at short frequencies. Deviations from “fundamental value” tend to be reversed with in several days, although there is some evidence that the return comovement persists for longer horizons. Arbitrageurs appear to be limited in their ability to eliminate these deviations from fundamentals. I imagine one limit on arbitrage here is just, like, how often is there news about Nest that causes price moves in Nestor? It seems unlikely that you could make a living running a similar-name-arbitrage hedge fund, and if you’re running a different sort of hedge fund you might not have the bandwidth to notice similar-name-arbitrage trades. Still it would be funny to set up a similar-name-arbitrage fund. Bringwater Associates. Renaissance Technicalities. Apparently Quite Respectable Capital Management. Point73 Capital. Eliot Management. Fourth Point. Greenlite. Pershing Rectangle.

s.h: Here is an xkcd comic about technical analysis
s.t: It’s funny (“lumbar support”), but I have nothing really to say about it, and it would be in “Things happen” except that I know how the Venn diagram looks: A lot of people are going to send me this comic, so I might as well tell you now that I have seen it. Also I should say that I have become more sympathetic to technical analysis as I get older. The terminology can be silly, but go read that paper I linked above—about how people are constantly buying the wrong stock because they can’t keep the tickers straight—and tell me that a stock chart is a random walk. A stock chart is a stylized picture of human behavior, and sometimes people are silly in predictable ways.

A scam that you could try, if you are a powerful government official, is: Hire an investment bank to help you raise $6.5 billion for a government investment fund. Steal the money. Say to the investment bank “I can’t believe you helped me raise all that money, you had to know I would steal it, there were red flags everywhere.” Sue the investment bank, on behalf of your government, for another $6.5 billion. I don’t know what step 5 is. Maybe “win the lawsuit and then steal the money again”? This is of course a completely fanciful scam. It does not, for instance, describe what allegedly went on at Malaysia’s 1MDB development fund. It’s close, though! The difference is that Malaysia’s former prime minister Najib Razak and his associates are accused (by U.S. and Malaysian authorities) of doing steps 1 and 2, and Malaysia’s current government is currently doing steps 3 and 4: An apology from Goldman Sachs Group Inc. doesn’t cut it for Malaysia, which said it may consider a discussion to absolve the bank of blame for its role in the 1MDB scandal for $7.5 billion. The country filed criminal charges against the lender in December, the first for Goldman, and may discuss dropping those allegations if the bank pays the sum, Finance Minister Lim Guan Eng told reporters on Friday. Units of the bank were accused of making false statements in documents submitted to a local regulator in arranging $6.5 billion bond offers for troubled state fund 1MDB. This is a very, very, very important difference if you are a government official contemplating trying to do this scam: Razak is facing life in prison, while the current government hasn’t stolen any money at all. If you want to do this scam, you want to both steal the money and remain in power to sue the bank for it; that combination might be impossible. But it is arguably a less salient difference to the investment bank . You can see how Goldman might argue, look, we helped the Malaysian government raise money, and the Malaysian government stole that money, and now the Malaysian government is suing us for helping the Malaysian government steal from itself? How is this our fault? I am not sure that argument will win much sympathy, though. It is no defense at all in the U.S.—where two former Goldman employees have been charged criminally for their involvement, and where Goldman itself seems to be negotiating its punishment with authorities—because facilitating foreign government corruption is illegal in the U.S. even if the foreign government is perfectly happy to be corrupted. And I am not sure it will turn out to be much of a defense in Malaysia, where Goldman is fighting the criminal charges, because the current government is not really likely to consider itself bound by the actions of its allegedly corrupt predecessor. I should disclose two biases here. One is that I used to work at Goldman and generally tend to think fondly of the place. The other is that I am a little afraid of them? They are going pretty scorched-earth in defending against this 1MDB stuff. Here is the New York Times describing Goldman’s efforts to isolate the scandal to its former partner Tim Leissner, who ran the business in Malaysia and has pleaded guilty to criminal charges in the U.S.: In November, for example, the bank met with federal prosecutors in Washington and delivered a lengthy PowerPoint presentation that sought to paint Mr. Leissner as a man practiced in the art of deception, according to two people familiar with the presentation. One slide in the presentation said that Mr. Leissner may have been briefly married to two women at the same time. Another slide included a photo of Mr. Leissner praying with other men, as well as images of a government-issued ID card that showed Mr. Leissner describing himself as Muslim. The people familiar with the presentation said Goldman officials used the slide to claim that Mr. Leissner twice converted to Islam in order to impress wealthy Muslim women he was dating. The inch-thick presentation also accused Mr. Leissner of having had a sexual relationship with at least one Goldman client and of having received a mail-order Ph.D. from a now-defunct university, the people said. I wonder what their dossier on me looks like! I must say that this is all a very mixed bag for Goldman: “We appointed a con man to our partnership, and then he conned us in a way that made us $600 million of fees, really we are the victim here,” is not … entirely compelling? Like Goldman cashed those checks, you know? And if one of your partners is so “practiced in the art of deception” that he can evade even the best compliance procedures then, fine, your compliance procedures are great, but on the other hand your partnership selection procedures need some work. If all of this stuff is proof now that Leissner was an unstoppable criminal mastermind, then it is awkward that Goldman knew about it ages ago. (“Joe Ravitch, a former Goldman partner who helped hire Mr. Leissner from Lehman Brothers in Hong Kong in 1999, said it was common knowledge that Mr. Leissner was misbehaving.”) I don’t know! It does not seem to me that there is any particularly satisfying way to decide when to blame a corporation for the actions of its employees. It always seems so vague and rote: “It’s just a few bad apples who do not reflect our values,” the corporation will say, and its critics will reply “no your corporate culture caused this and your lax compliance procedures let him get away with it.” In theory, you want to give the corporation—its shareholders and directors and senior executives—incentives to set things up in the right way, have good compliance procedures, check up on employees, etc.; if they don’t do that, then you blame and punish the corporation, but if they do everything right and something slips through the cracks anyway, you just shrug and say “happens to the best of us.” (Because it does!) In practice it seems pretty hard to tell ex post what procedures were reasonable ex ante, and the fact that the bad thing happened is at least some evidence that your procedures were inadequate to stop the bad thing from happening.

Lehman Brothers Holdings Inc. filed for bankruptcy on Sept. 15, 2008, making this week the 10 year and, uh, 4 month anniversary of what might be the central event of the global financial crisis. The New York Fed’s Liberty Street Economics blog has a series of posts this week commemorating the occasion, which seems like weird timing until you notice that the posts are not keyed to the anniversary of the bankruptcy filing but to the end of the bankruptcy process. Or, not the end even; the beginning of the end. “This week, we will publish a series of four posts that provide an assessment of the value lost to Lehman, its creditors, and other stakeholders now that the bankruptcy proceedings are winding down,” says the first post. Winding down! “The Chapter 11 proceedings are set to continue for some time,” concedes a later post. Remember Lehman filed for bankruptcy 10 years and 4 months ago. You can actually go read the posts for some calculations of the value lost to Lehman and its stakeholders in bankruptcy, but that timeline alone is enough to give you a rough sense: If you are in bankruptcy for 10 years and 4 months and you’re still not done, stuff is bad. The New York Fed’s authors are interested mostly in a somewhat theoretical question, which is, what was the value lost in bankruptcy? The idea here is that, before Lehman filed for bankruptcy, it had a lot of stuff that was worth some money, and if it could have instantly and seamlessly distributed that stuff to its creditors then they would have been at least partially repaid. But it couldn’t instantly and seamlessly distribute the stuff; instead, it had to go through the bankruptcy process, which took 10 years and counting and involves a certain amount of friction. One friction is fees: Bankruptcy requires bankers and lawyers and accountants and experts to figure out how much stuff there is and who should get it. Another friction is just, you know, the 10 years; getting back 50 cents on the dollar the day the company goes south is worth more than getting back 50 cents on the dollar 10 years later. So there are some calculations, of which the most striking might be the direct costs of the bankruptcy in professional fees and compensation to employees and advisers of Lehman’s bankruptcy estate. Those costs—plus “other operating expenses” of the bankruptcy juggernaut— come to about $7.26 billion. That’s a lot of money! Don’t get me wrong; I am quite sure that Lehman’s advisers worked hard—so, so hard—for that money. It does seem sort of socially wasteful, though, when you just see it written down like that. An investment bank died, and people spent a decade and $7 billion carving up its corpse. Okay. These sorts of calculations are interesting, because big fees are always interesting and also because value destruction in bankruptcy matters in thinking about the costs of the bankruptcy regime, whether Lehman should have been rescued, what should happen with future failed financial institutions, etc. But if you are an actual Lehman creditor, the numbers that might be of more interest are not about the value destruction in bankruptcy but rather just how much you got paid . The biggest problem at Lehman was not the value destroyed by the costs and frictions of bankruptcy, but the value destroyed by the management of Lehman before bankruptcy. “We estimate value destruction” of bankruptcy “to be on the order of $46 billion to $63 billion, or between 15 percent and 21 percent of Lehman’s pre-bankruptcy consolidated assets,” write the authors, which is a gigantic amount of money. But the more important numbers are these: Starting in April 2012, the Lehman estate made sixteen cash distributions to creditors. The total amount distributed was more than $126 billion, out of which almost $94 billion went to third-party creditors. We estimate the total allowed claims to third-parties as $304-312 billion, implying a recovery rate for third-party creditors of about 31 percent. Creditors got back 31 cents on the dollar in nominal terms (about 21 to 26 cents accounting for the time value of taking 10 years to get paid). At the high end, the costs of bankruptcy came to 21 cents on the dollar, meaning that if bankruptcy could have somehow magically been free and instantaneous, creditors would have gotten back about 52 cents on the dollar. The rest of the loss was due to Lehman, not bankruptcy. Besides Lehman, we recently celebrated another big financial-crisis anniversary: Bernie Madoff was arrested 10 years ago last month for running a giant Ponzi scheme. That anniversary is kind of a happy one, as these things go: Madoff’s victims have gotten back about 70 cents on the dollar, and could see a lot more. The numbers are not exactly apples to apples, but it sure does seem like Madoff’s investors did a lot better than Lehman’s. The nice thing about Madoff, as I pointed out last month, is that if you run a big enough Ponzi scheme there is only so much you can do with the money. “You just can’t spend $13 billion on cocaine,” I wrote, and if you spend it on yachts then eventually your bankruptcy receiver can sell the yachts. But if you are engaged in actual transactions in the financial markets, there is no limit to how much money you can lose and never get back.

A very simple scam that you can do, if you are a trader who works for someone else, is: Buy a thing for $100. Tell your boss that it’s now worth $200. Get a big bonus because you made a 100 percent profit. Tell your boss, oops, now it is only worth $100, or $0. Get fired because you made a big loss.[1] Keep that bonus. Really it is the framework scam for a lot of modern finance. Certainly a popular description of the 2008 financial crisis is that it was a bunch of traders buying mortgage-backed securities at delusional prices because they could clip their bonuses before the prices crashed. The tricky part is step 2: Your boss will want to check that the thing is really worth $200. There are ways to address this. A well-known one is that, if you run a hedge fund, you can buy some bonds that don’t trade very often, and then ask your buddy at a bank to give you a high but fake bid to buy the bonds: You can tell your investors that they’re worth a lot, and point to an arm’s-length third-party bid from a big bank to support your valuation, and as long as your buddy knows you’re not going to hit the bid it’s no problem for him.[2] But Thomas Lindstrom found an amazingly simpler, yet so much worse, way to do this, which is that he bought extremely far-out-of-the-money options on Treasury note futures, which were worth approximately nothing. Because they were worth approximately nothing, he would pay very little for them. The Chicago Board of Trade’s rules at the time provided that options like this had to settle each day at a minimum price of $15.625 (one tick) per contract, though they were allowed to trade for a lower price. So Lindstrom could buy an option for like $2 and immediately mark it up to $15.625, showing a big immediate profit. And he could support that valuation by pointing to the official settlement price on the CBOT. Not terrible! The problem is that eventually the options would expire, and they would inevitably expire at $0 (they were really really far out of the money), and so Lindstrom would have lost like $2 of real money (and $15.625 of his nominal position). So when the options expired he’d have to go buy even more to (pretend to) make up for the losses. Like so many scams, it had a built-in snowballing effect. Anyway he ended up getting $285,000 of undeserved bonuses, lost $13.9 million for his employer (and put it out of business), and got sentenced to five years in prison this week. Bad trade! We actually talked about Lindstrom’s trade a few years ago, when the Commodity Futures Trading Commission and prosecutors first brought the case. I bring it up again first of all because it is such a neat pure example of book mis-marking. If you are going to mis-mark your book, that sort of neatness at first seems good—you have these unambiguous CBOT statements supporting your valuation—but then ends up being very bad: There is no subtlety, no room for interpretation, no argument that really the marks were in good faith, and you end up in prison for five years.[3] But it is also sort of a pleasing story about how arbitrary numbers get arbitraged. At first glance, there is something solid and conservative about the CBOT’s approach of settling contracts at a minimum price of one tick.[4] A tick, $15.625, is a nice round number in the curious arithmetic of Treasury traders, and forcing the contract to settle there requires sellers of far-out-of-the-money options to, effectively, post some extra collateral against them. Selling far-out-of-the-money options is a risky business, and you want to keep an eye on people who do it, and this is a simple crude way to get them to be careful. In many areas of life, simple crude safeguards are the best kind: They are harder to game, harder to walk right up to the line. But in finance there are two sides to every trade, and if you create a simple crude safeguard on one side there is the risk that it will lead to a simple crude scam on the other.

We talked a while back about “the Weinstein clause” in merger agreements: Acquirers are now asking target companies to represent that none of their senior employees have been accused of sexual harassment. I pointed out the old deal lawyer cliché that “the point of a representation is to force disclosure”: The fact that the Weinstein representation now sometimes appears in merger agreements is evidence that sexual harassment is now a routine part of mergers-and-acquisitions due diligence; junior M&A bankers and lawyers will now send around checklists asking merger targets to disclose their sexual-harassment investigations as just a normal part of the job. Here is a fascinating interview—on the HR Risk Podcast—with investment banker Greg Bedrosian about “Weinstein clause” issues in M&A. Among other things, he notes that in private-company deals where acquirers might once have held back 10 percent of the proceeds in escrow for a year or two to insure against any representations being false, now sometimes escrows are 15 or 20 percent “in situations where that topic is relevant,” as he delicately puts it. But he also talks about rep and warranty insurance, in which an insurance company will effectively, for a premium, take on the risk of the Weinstein clause and guarantee that the seller will get the escrowed amount: What we haven’t yet seen, and I think this is an opportunity both for companies as well as some technology platforms and others, we haven’t seen enough of an infrastructure within companies to record complaints issues on a confidential basis in whatever format so that an insurance company can analyze some of that data and get comfortable to underwrite a rep and warranty policy. For example, in financial or legal diligence, the insurance company will send people in to review the documents in a similar way the buyer would, and then judge risk. The issue today is with #MeToo-related clauses and other elements across the employment spectrum that haven’t been tracked, or the confidential nature makes it harder to track. There are fewer data points for an insurer to evaluate. So one of the trends that we see, but it’s only the very beginning, is a rise in monitoring–evaluating and storing through technology platforms or otherwise–some of these complaints, issues, topics around the #MeToo-related and other clauses so that insurers can better understand it, but also buyers can better understand it. And I think that really moves things from opacity, from one person’s word against the other, to something that is easier to monitor. And to be clear, we’re at the early stages of that becoming commonplace within companies. Certainly small companies that have more limited budgets in terms of buying technology platforms aren’t subscribing to them. But that’s an interesting trend that we see and predict really evolving to address some of those needs between buyer and seller. If you think about how sexual harassment in the workplace will become less common, some of it is a story of shifting social norms, and some of it is a story of legal regimes, of lawsuits and enforcement actions against harassers and companies that enable them. But there is also this sort of third-order story of acquirers demanding representations and diligence and escrows, and insurers demanding tracking and documentation to underwrite risk, and companies building technology tools to track and respond to those demands. There is something creepy about this—about sexual harassment being just a diligence-checklist item that an insurer will underwrite—but also perhaps something effective about it. The way to solve a problem might not be to give it a lot of nuanced attention in a few high-profile cases, but to tame and domesticate it: Making its prevention a routine matter, putting it on a checklist, might actually work.

Is Larry Fink the president of the world? What if your model is that democratic political governance has just stopped working—not because you disagree with the particular policies that particular elected governments are carrying out, but because you have started to notice that elected governments in large developed nations are increasingly unable to carry out any policies at all? What if, meanwhile, corporations are actually good at doing stuff? Corporations, after all, are built to do stuff: They are hierarchical organizations with clear lines of authority that have to report on their accomplishments every three months. Democratic governments are built to be deliberative, with checks and balances to prevent rash unilateral action by any one person, but in some cases the effect of those safeguards is to prevent anything at all from happening. Obviously corporations are built to do different things from the things that democratic governments are built to deliberate. Corporations don’t wage war, though they do manufacture weapons; they don’t enforce a monopoly on violence, though they do run prisons; they don’t enact legislation, though they do help write legislation for understaffed and inexpert governments to enact; they don’t command patriotic allegiance or symbolically represent a community of people who identify primarily with the corporation, but they sure try. (What is Facebook Inc. up to, if not that? Or The We Company, for that matter?) But there is a lot of overlap. Retirement security and health-care coverage, at least in the U.S., are functions that can be the responsibility of government or corporations or both or neither. Job security and minimum wages and working conditions and income inequality can all be addressed by either power. Environmental concerns can be addressed by regulation, or by corporations—their executives and directors and shareholders—deciding that it is in their long-term interests to be good stewards of the environment. Discrimination and harassment in the workplace can be banned by law, or by corporate policy. People who care about these issues tend to distrust corporations—which tend to be run by rich people and focused on the bottom line—to get the answers right voluntarily, but that distrust might come from comparing actual corporations to hypothetical governments. If you are worried about global warming, you probably prefer a coordinated mandatory governmental or intergovernmental approach rather than relying on companies to self-regulate. But if there is no governmental approach , surely it’s better for corporations to address the problem than not. Anyway that seems to be roughly Larry Fink’s view: Unnerved by fundamental economic changes and the failure of government to provide lasting solutions, society is increasingly looking to companies, both public and private, to address pressing social and economic issues. These issues range from protecting the environment to retirement to gender and racial inequality, among others. Fueled in part by social media, public pressures on corporations build faster and reach further than ever before. … As divisions continue to deepen, companies must demonstrate their commitment to the countries, regions, and communities where they operate, particularly on issues central to the world’s future prosperity. Companies cannot solve every issue of public importance, but there are many – from retirement to infrastructure to preparing workers for the jobs of the future – that cannot be solved without corporate leadership. That’s from the letter that Fink, the chairman and chief executive officer of BlackRock Inc., sent to corporate CEOs this year. “The World Needs Your Leadership,” Fink tells the CEOs. He has some standing to lecture them like this, because for many of them he is their largest shareholder. (Or rather, BlackRock’s funds, which it manages as a fiduciary for outside clients, are collectively their largest shareholder.) The corporate chain of command tends to be very clear until it gets to the CEO, and fuzzier thereafter: Is the board the boss of the CEO, or does the CEO dominate the board? Are the shareholders the boss of the board, or does the board act independently on behalf of the corporate entity? But it would not be crazy to say that Fink, along with a handful of his fellow giant institutional money managers, is the ultimate boss of most public-company CEOs in America. So when he says, for instance, that “companies must embrace a greater responsibility to help workers navigate retirement, lending their expertise and capacity for innovation to solve this immense global challenge,” maybe they will? There is a certain amount of backlash to this sort of thing— Andrew Ross Sorkin quotes Sam Zell saying “I didn’t know Larry Fink had been made God,” and Warren Buffett saying “I don’t believe in imposing my political opinions on the activities of our businesses”—but the mechanisms of control are kind of straightforward. Larry Fink decides how a big block of stock is voted at every public company. Shareholders vote for the directors. Directors choose the managers. Managers carry out corporate policy. If Larry Fink really decided that, for instance, all companies had to provide ample pensions for their employees, he’d have some pretty powerful tools to make it happen. He is the boss of those companies, in a way that, for instance, the president of the United States is not the boss of Congress and cannot just order it to increase Social Security benefits. I am not the least bit convinced that Fink has decided any such thing, and it would cost a lot in effort and money and controversy (and perhaps client withdrawals) for Fink to actually use the tools available to him to boss around the companies (is he going to run a thousand proxy fights?), and in fact he explicitly disclaims that intent. (“We have no intention of telling companies what their purpose should be,” says the letter; “Rather, we seek to understand how a company’s purpose informs its strategy and culture to underpin sustainable financial performance.”) But his theoretical control rights at least obligate CEOs to pretend to listen to him. A theme that we talk about a lot around here is that public companies are increasingly owned by a small set of large and diversified institutional investors who have a novel and weird kind of power over corporate governance. John Coates calls this the “Problem of Twelve,” “the likelihood that in the near future roughly twelve individuals will have practical power over the majority of U.S. public companies.” Often this theme comes up in the form of academic worries that these diversified investors will discourage competition among public companies: If BlackRock owns all the companies in an industry, shouldn’t those companies focus on keeping prices high and maximizing the collective profits of the industry rather than on cutting prices to boost their own market share? I find that worry fascinating, but most people find it silly, in part because you almost never see BlackRock or Vanguard or State Street going around and telling companies to raise their prices and compete less aggressively. But you know what you do see? You see BlackRock going around and telling companies that they need to step up and address broad social problems that once might have been left to governments to figure out. As an approach to allocation of resources at an investment management firm, this makes sense: BlackRock owns securities of thousands of companies, many of them in passive portfolios, and it would take a lot of effort to understand the nuances of all of those companies and push them to increase or decrease or whatever their market share. Solving broad social problems, on the other hand, is good for the whole portfolio, probably. The thing is, though, that if you find the “Problem of Twelve” sort of creepy and unsettling when applied to issues of corporate governance and profitability, isn’t it even weirder when applied to, like, the environment, or the social contract for U.S. workers? “I didn’t know Larry Fink had been made God,” says Sam Zell, but what if he had and no one told you? What if large public companies are the most effective locus of political power in the world today, and what if Larry Fink is one of the most influential people at a lot of large public companies, and what if he decides to use his influence and those companies’ power to do things that would once have been the responsibility of governments? What if Larry Fink has been elected to a position of vast political power, not by the old-fashioned mechanism of people going to the polls and giving him their votes, but by the new, late-capitalist mechanism of people giving him their money to manage?

In general, you should be skeptical when someone tries to sell you a simple solution to a complicated problem. Complicated problems are complicated, and probably a lot of smart people have worked on them in good faith for a long time. Perhaps someone has come along with a new simple solution that they have all overlooked, and perhaps the solution works, but the odds are against it. What makes him so special? This is called “the efficient markets hypothesis.” On the other hand: index funds! The problem of maximizing your expected investment return is hard: There are a lot of stocks out there, and there is a lot of information about every company to assimilate, and even when you understand a company well and have a clear view of its business prospects, you have to worry about whether that understanding is already reflected in the market price. Picking the right stocks requires exceptional skill and endless difficult work and, even with all of that, a fair amount of luck. This is not really something that people want to hear, and so there is a deep market for simple solutions, most of which—Subscribe to My Penny-Stock Newsletter, etc.—are scams. And then there is the simplest solution, which is Just Buy All of the Stocks and Don’t Worry About It, and amazingly it works really well. You won’t outperform the market average, but you won’t underperform either, which—through the mystery of fees and trading costs— is better than most people will do. This, too, is a form of the efficient markets hypothesis, which tends to crop up everywhere. And this particular form is incredibly well supported both in theory and in practice: Most active managers usually underperform the index, and the ones who outperform one year tend not to outperform the next. And so now this approach—index investing—is enormously popular, and it works great and has saved ordinary investors billions of dollars in fees. John C. Bogle, who died yesterday, didn’t exactly invent indexing, but he might as well have. He founded what is now Vanguard Group, and in 1976 he “introduced the first index fund geared to individual investors.” Vanguard now has over $5 trillion of assets under management, much of it indexed, some of it—disclosure—belonging to me. It seems fair to say that this is a good thing. “I rank this Bogle invention along with the invention of the wheel, the alphabet, Gutenberg printing, and wine and cheese,” Paul Samuelson once said. We talk a lot around here—we just did it in the previous section—about the arcane and counterintuitive ways in which the rise of indexing might somehow be bad, but that is only because it would be too boring and obvious to constantly talk about how it is good. It is obviously good for me , and for a whole lot of individual (and institutional) investors who can get the benefits of market performance without the costs, or the effort, of deciding which stocks to buy or which stock-pickers to trust. But it also has an enormous aesthetic and intellectual appeal: It puts the findings of modern academic finance to work in the simplest and dumbest-sounding way, and—despite being both so simple and derived from financial academia—it really works. Anyway here are some obituaries of Bogle from my Bloomberg Opinion colleague Joe Nocera, from the New York Times, and from Vanguard. And here is a Bloomberg article rounding up other investment professionals’ remembrances of Bogle, which seems like the most appropriate way to commemorate a man whose great innovation was finding a way to aggregate the wisdom of the market and make it available to everyone.

A well-known problem in (some parts of) academic finance is that a researcher will come up with some factor or signal or indicator that might predict stock market returns, and will test that signal on a sample of data, and will find that it does in fact predict returns and that a strategy based on the factor outperforms the market and the results are statistically significant, and will write up the results, but oh by the way the strategy based on the factor outperforms the market by 0.12 percent a year and requires you to buy and sell lots of stocks that trade 100 shares a day, and so any hedge fund that reads the paper and tries to implement the strategy will actually lose far more money in trading costs than it will make in outperformance. This is a productive problem, by the way! It tells you something interesting about financial markets—that they are efficient at scale but inefficient in little pockets—and also something about how one can make money from that knowledge. One approach is to be small: There are some anomalies in the market that have predictable positive returns but not enough capacity for institutional investors, creating opportunities for small hedge funds or even for retail investors. The other approach is to be huge: If you run a large quantitative hedge fund that uses lots of different trading signals, adding one more signal to the mix can improve your performance even if that signal doesn’t have enough capacity to trade on its own. If stocks of companies whose CEOs have eight letters in their names outperform nine-letter-CEO stocks by 0.02 percent a year, a strategy of “buy eight-letter stocks and short nine-letter stocks and lever up” will cost too much to make any money, but if your more complex model is otherwise indifferent between an eight-letter stock and a nine-letter stock maybe that can be the tiebreaker. Anyway here is an early candidate for best financial journalism lede of 2019: A lot of fancy things can be built with Lego sets nowadays. Such as a diversifying portfolio that loads on the Fama-French size factor. Go on! In a paper titled “Lego -- The Toy of Smart Investors,” [Victoria] Dobrynskaya [of Russia’s Higher School of Economics] analyzed 2,300 sets sold from 1987 to 2015 to measure their price-return over time. She found that collections used for Hogwarts Castles and Jedi star fighters beat U.S. large-cap stocks and bonds, yielding 11 percent a year. Smaller kits rose more than medium-sized ones, similar to the size effect in the Fama-French model (though the relation isn’t exact). “The beta of the size factor is statistically significant and the dynamics of the Lego index we created for our research is similar to that of the size factor,” Dobrynskaya said by phone from Moscow. “Lego sets don’t show a significant correlation to the financial crises and can be seen as an attractive investment with a diversification potential.” Sounds great! So if I am running a $10 billion institutional portfolio how much of it should be in Legos? In one extreme case, a kit for Star Wars Darth Revan that retailed in 2014 for $3.99 went for $28.46 on eBay a year later -- a 613 percent premium. Uhhhhhhhhhhhhhhh. So the extreme case is making a profit of … $24.47 over a year? I mean, I guess you could buy … a million … of those Darth Revan sets … and … put them somewhere … but … no, I am going to say no, this is not a strategy with institutional capacity. (And you can’t use it as an additional signal in your multifactor general model of what stocks to buy, because they are Legos , not stocks.) I suppose if you are a perverse sort of finance professor though you should be using a factor model to trade Legos in your personal account; let me know—and, more importantly, brag to your students constantly about—how it goes. Also here is an extremely perfect quote from a markets practitioner about academic finance, about the Legos: “If you think about all the academics in the world, there are a lot of them, and all of them are looking for something interesting to say and it’s always going to be related to the Fama-French factor,” said Roberto Croce, Managing Director, senior portfolio manager at BNY Mellon. “Someone is going to find something that is correlated. Purely by randomness that’s going to happen. I’d take it with a grain of salt.”
