Here’s an insider trading hypothetical for you. It’s not a legal hypothetical but a trading one. The question is: If you got a company’s earnings release a day before it became public, what are the odds you could make money with it? You can trade any instruments you want—buy short-dated out-of-the-money options, whatever—and don’t worry (for now!) about the legal issues. You have all the normal public information (a Bloomberg terminal, analyst research reports, whatever) that you’d have anyway, plus a complete, accurate earnings release that no one else will see for 24 hours. Can you make money? How confident are you of that? You can’t be 100 percent confident, right? I mean, sure, there are some pretty obvious cases. If a company doubles Wall Street expectations on the top line, bottom line, margins, future guidance, everything, you can probably buy the stock and be confident it will go up. If the announcement says “we misplaced all our money and our factory blew up and we are going out of business, surprise,” you can probably short the stock and make money. But a lot of earnings releases are like “we beat analyst expectations by two cents but missed the whisper number, and top-line growth was a little soft but the CEO is really excited about a new product we’ll roll out next quarter,” and if you do not follow the company closely you might not know how the market will react. If you do follow the company closely you might not know how the market will react. In my former lives as a banker and a lawyer, I would often have to plan things for after an earnings release: The earnings release would go out on Tuesday, and we’d launch a deal on Wednesday, and it would be helpful to know in advance if the stock would be up or down. So on Monday I would ask the company’s CEO or CFO or the relationship banker—who had seen the draft earnings release, knew what it said, knew what Wall Street expectations were, knew the company well, had a good feel for the markets—whether the earnings release would be good or bad for the stock. They would invariably—invariably!—say “I have no idea, could go either way.” This is called “strong-form market efficiency,” I think, or it may just be evidence that investment bankers and corporate executives should not be stock traders. Still, the odds have to be better than 50 percent, right? Like if you got one random company’s earnings release one day early, you might have no idea what to do with it, or you might have a clear compelling idea that turned out to be wrong. But if you got 100 companies’ earnings releases one day early, you could probably make money on 70 of them and lose money on 30 of them, or even better, make money on 20 of them and leave the other 80 alone. Yesterday the Securities and Exchange Commission “announced charges against nine defendants for participating in a previously disclosed scheme to hack into the SEC’s EDGAR system and extract nonpublic information to use for illegal trading.” A company that plans to file an earnings release on Edgar will sometimes do a “test filing” beforehand to make sure that everything works; a 27-year-old Ukrainian hacker allegedly broke into the Edgar system and hacked it to send him copies of the test filings, then sent the filings to a network of traders who used them to trade and gave the hacker a cut of the profits. (The hacker, and some of the traders, were allegedly previously involved in the hacking of newswires to get advance access to press releases.) They allegedly “traded before at least 157 earnings releases from May to October 2016 and generated at least $4.1 million in illegal profits.” When we first talked about this case in 2017, I was skeptical that you could make much money on it: How many companies test file substantive draft earnings releases, with real numbers, hours before the actual filing? But the answer is apparently “a lot”—at least 157, anyway—and sometimes they test file days in advance. The SEC mentions one company that test filed its quarterly results on July 29, 2016, and actually filed them after the close on August 3, five days (and three trading days) later, which honestly seems a little unnecessary. But what is most delightful in the SEC’s complaint is the performance table tracking how the traders did with their allegedly stolen information. Here it is: Overall they made money about 77 percent of the time that they traded on stolen press releases, making $4.1 million of profits on their winners but also losing about half a million on their losers. Good, but not perfect; knowing a company’s earnings in advance does not, it turns out, guarantee that you can make money. The SEC notes: The Trader Defendants’ success rates when they had access to hacked earnings information are particularly notable because earnings announcements may reflect positive or negative news. The ability of these defendants to profit consistently, regardless of the direction of the price change, indicates that they had the benefit of deceptively-acquired, material nonpublic information. Despite this illegal advantage, it is not surprising that the Trading Defendants did not trade successfully based on this information 100% of the time. This is so because, unlike some other corporate announcements, it is not always predictable how the market will react to a given earnings announcement. For example, an earnings release may contain a combination of positive and negative news, may match analysts’ preexisting expectations, or the market may focus on a particular aspect of a release at the exclusion of other information that points to a contrary conclusion. By the way, you’ll notice that the table includes not only the traders’ win-loss record when allegedly trading on Edgar hacks, but also, brutally, their win-loss record the rest of the time. All of them, reports the SEC, were net losers when they traded without inside information, and their success rate was 45 percent. This is called “weak-form market efficiency.”

I dunno, as ways to end a banking career go, there are worse approaches than: Put on a big trade. Leave for a long, well-deserved Christmas vacation. Wake up one day on the slopes/beach/wherever to find the trade cratering and losing tens of millions of dollars. Ponder this ruefully for a minute, then turn to your family and say “good news everybody, we’re staying here forever!” I mean, there are better ways to go! After three decades of loyal service as a beloved and highly remunerated legend at the firm: fine, great. At 28, after making so much money that you never need to work again: even better. But if you’re going to blow yourself up on a trade, surely it is more relaxing to get the bad news when you’re already checked out of the office and in vacation mode. Plus you can tell yourself “it wouldn’t have blown up if I had been there to fix it” and not feel so bad about yourself. Plus—most importantly—you don’t have to leave the trading floor with everyone watching you to go sit in an office with your boss while she tells you how disappointed she is in you. You can just not be there, and then just continue not to be there, and let the disappointment go to voicemail. Anyway BNP Paribas SA apparently lost $80 million on equity index derivatives trades, oops: Antoine Lours, the New York-based head of U.S. index trading, has yet to return to the bank since going on his Christmas vacation after positions he took on the S&P 500 Index went awry, the people said, asking not to be identified because the details are private. The majority of the losses came over several days in the run-up to the holiday, the people said. Lours was on vacation when the trade began losing large amounts of money as the S&P 500 tumbled, the people said. High five, solid work. I wonder if this is a case of BNP calling him up and saying “hey don’t bother coming back yet,” or of him calling them up and saying “hey, just FYI, I’m going to extend my vacation for another month.” You wouldn’t want to come back to the office after losing $80 million either!

For instance, arguably a worse way to end a banking career is: Spend years developing a close relationship as a trusted adviser to a key client. Announce that you are leaving to become chief executive officer of that client. Proudly tell your bosses, expecting them to congratulate you and express best wishes for a continuing fruitful client relationship. Be surprised when your bosses say “get out and never darken our towels again, also we are enforcing your full 6-month gardening leave and taking away all your deferred compensation because you are leaving for a competitor.” Sheepishly tell your new employer about the setback. Have them rescind the CEO offer because they can’t make up all the deferred compensation you are losing. This is apparently how Andrea Orcel left UBS, oops: Banco Santander SA reversed course on installing Andrea Orcel as its next chief executive officer after a standoff over tens of millions of dollars in deferred pay. UBS Group AG held a hard line that Orcel, who led its investment bank until a few months ago, was defecting to a rival and wouldn’t receive bonuses he was owed from previous years. That meant Santander had to make it up to the Italian executive, who was poised to achieve his career ambition of leading one of the world’s biggest banks. It wouldn’t be unusual for UBS to take a tough stance to try to dissuade one of its top managers from leaving, but Santander executives wagered that once Orcel was gone, the Swiss bank would relent rather than risk losing it as a client. That backfired -- leaving a retail lender facing the prospect of telling its 200,000 employees it just spent as much as $60 million on their new boss. The Spanish bank chose not to. Orcel’s deferred compensation from UBS is somewhere between $40 million and $60 million, and “Santander was willing to pay 20 million euros ($23 million) of the total.” I am not sure what happens now: “Orcel doesn’t plan to return to a role at UBS,” but will he get to keep the deferred comp because it turns out he is not going to a competitor? If he loses the deferred comp anyway , just for quitting, then surely there is a trade here: He’s better off with $23 million and a job from Santander than no money and no job. But if he gets to keep the deferred comp as long as he doesn’t go to Santander then, yes, I can see how $60 million and no job is strictly better than $23 million and a job. It is all super weird though: “It feels to me like amateur hour,” said Ilana Weinstein, who runs Wall Street recruitment firm IDW Group LLC. “What I don’t understand is why Andrea and Santander didn’t see this coming. I think it was ambitious and potentially naïve to think UBS would just waive it.” High finance is conducted in the shadow of complex and carefully negotiated legal agreements, but it is rarely governed by those agreements, exactly. There are norms, customs, traditions, social pressures, relationships, personalities, expectations of future business, all of which feel more important than contracts most of the time. A great banker will have a feel for those norms and relationships and personalities and expectations, and will use them—rather than the blunt force of contractual rights—to get what he wants while leaving everyone happy. Sometimes I guess you read the room wrong though!

There is something a little odd about WeWork Cos.’ business model. WeWork rents office space to businesses. Other firms compete with WeWork to rent office space to businesses: They are called real estate companies, and they own office buildings, and they rent out slices of those buildings—some number of floors for some number of years—to businesses. WeWork is different, though: It rents buildings, or slices of buildings, itself, and then slices those slices further and rents the sub-slices—some number of desks for some number of months, or whatever—to businesses. Rather than owning buildings and renting them to tenants, WeWork is itself a tenant and rents to sub-tenants. It is a middleman. This is not especially odd; there are middlemen everywhere in the economy, and WeWork’s job is to be a value-added middleman. It can add value by doing good stuff with the space (renting some floors, making them really nice, installing beer taps, and then subletting them at a higher price), or by providing value-added not-quite-real-estate services to its subtenants (office management stuff, design, catering, the beer taps), or by a sort of term arbitrage where it can charge more renting desks by the month than it pays renting floors by the year, or by some combination of those things. It’s fine! It (maybe) works. Lots of hotels do not own their buildings and do a perfectly fine business; there is more to running a hotel than just renting out raw space, and I suppose the same is true of running a WeWork. Still it is just a little odd that WeWork is a commercial landlord that doesn’t own its buildings, and has to compete with other landlords who do. You’d think the other landlords might have better margins. You know what’s much weirder? Guess who does own some of WeWork’s buildings: One of the landlords behind the building was no ordinary owner: It was Adam Neumann, WeWork’s chief executive, who leased the property to WeWork after buying it, according to people familiar with the situation. Mr. Neumann has made millions of dollars by leasing multiple properties in which he has an ownership stake back to WeWork, one of the country’s most valuable startups. Multiple investors of the privately held company said the arrangement concerned them as a potential conflict of interest in which the CEO could benefit on rents or other terms with the company. Yes it really does seem like a conflict of interest! “A WeWork spokesman said all related-party deals are reviewed and approved by the board or an independent committee and disclosed to investors,” so that is good, but on the other hand, “Mr. Neumann, the 39-year-old executive who founded WeWork in 2010, is WeWork’s largest individual shareholder and has voting control over the company,” so it is not clear that the board can say no. (He got that control in 2014 with some super-voting stock; before that, he once tried to do a related-party deal and got turned down by the board.) One thing I will say, though, is that if you told me that a privately owned real estate company was engaging in transactions with its controlling shareholder and CEO that raised possible conflicts of interest, I would be like “ha, yeah, that’s the real estate industry for you.” Conflicts of interest are more common there, as everyone knows these days after years of stories about Donald Trump’s business dealings, and it is not surprising for a founder/controller/CEO to be involved in a deal with his company on multiple sides and in multiple ways. Private tech startups, on the other hand, tend to be a bit more pristine. They are not complex moneymaking structures for their founders but mission-driven enterprises where everyone’s incentives are ostentatiously and lavishly aligned: If the company gets big, the founder becomes a zillionaire; if not, he walks away with only his modest salary and a track record for failing ambitiously. WeWork is a weird company because it is a real estate company that thinks it’s a tech startup; it seems to have the culture and New-Age-y patter and grandiose ambition and valuation of a tech company. But what if, deep down in its heart, it really is a real estate company?

There are a lot of stories out there—they peaked in like 2010, but you still see them from time to time—about financial-services employees who quit the industry to start quirky artisanal food-related businesses. If the employee is young, he tends to start a food truck; if he is middle-aged and successful, it is more likely to be a winery. “Odey Hedge-Fund Partner Orlando Montagu Is Leaving to Run Sandwich Business,” this headline says, and my first reaction was, huh, hedge fund partners don’t usually leave for sandwich businesses, sandwiches are more of an analyst thing. But of course it’s not a sandwich business, it’s the Sandwich business (of sandwiches): Orlando Montagu, a partner at Crispin Odey’s hedge-fund firm, is leaving to focus on his family’s famous invention, the sandwich. Montagu is a direct descendant of the 4th Earl of Sandwich, who was credited with inventing the snack in the 18th century. He will leave Odey Asset Management at the end of March after more than 16 years at the firm. He’ll work at his family’s mostly U.S.-based business, also known as Earl of Sandwich, which has plans to open in London.

People sometimes buy stock in the wrong company, you know. There is some news about a company, and people go out and buy stock in a different company with a similar name. We talk about this around here occasionally, when it is silly and obvious—when Google announced that it was buying a private company called Nest, for instance, and the entirely unrelated stock of Nestor Inc. (ticker: NEST) was up 1,900 percent—but I bet it happens more often than that. I bet there was someone out there who bought stock in Time Warner Cable (TWC) because he really liked watching HBO, which was owned by Time Warner Inc. (TWX). Both companies have been acquired, eliminating this particular confusion, but it was confusing! Why should you have to read all the way to the third word of a company name to know what company it is? Really I imagine that there is a lot of this in every area of finance. People probably buy municipal bonds of Portland, Oregon, thinking they’re bonds of Portland, Maine, or vice versa, or whatever. There was an Uber driver who thought XIV was a high-performing company—“not sure whether it’s in biotech or a technology business, but they’re up 80 percent this year”—and was surprised to learn that it was actually an inverse exchange-traded note linked to volatility. Finance is complicated, and human stupidity is infinite, and a certain amount of inattention is surely rational, and most stocks are kind of correlated with each other. If, like, 1 percent of stock investments are in the wrong stocks, well, there are worse problems. On the other hand if you are a professional investor or trader—a hedge fund manager, a trader at a bank, etc.—you should really almost never buy the wrong thing. I am sure that I am going to get emails from markets professionals recounting the hilarious stories of the time they bought the wrong stock, so let me say: (1) yes please, I am looking forward to them and (2) that’s fine, you can do that, but, like, once . Once is a funny anecdote that your buddies can tease you about. More than that looks like carelessness. But credit default swaps! Man! They are traded exclusively by professionals, and they are nothing but trouble. The way credit default swaps work is that I write you a CDS contract on Company X, and you pay me some money, and then if Company X defaults on its debt I pay you some money. If I write you a CDS contract on Company X, and then Company Y defaults on its debt, I do not pay you any money. Those are different companies. On the other hand if I write you a CDS contract on Company Chi or Company Multiplication Sign, and then Company X defaults on its debt, then (1) I do not pay you any money but (2) you are pretty mad about it. It looked like an X! How were you supposed to know? Here is a weird story about how “an obscure quirk threatened to render contracts relating to telecoms company VodafoneZiggo completely worthless,” and it is a pleasingly onomatopoeic name: CDS buyer: There’s a default, you have to pay me money. CDS seller: No I don’t! Ziggo! I hope it becomes jargon, like “don’t litvak me.” “They got ziggoed.” To be clear, VodafoneZiggo has not actually defaulted, nor does it seem close to default. (“Market participants have belatedly spotted the potential flaw, people familiar with the matter said, sending the cost of the contracts falling to 164 basis points on Monday, after they began the month trading at 290bp,” but 290 is still pretty tight.) But here’s the problem: CDS contracts are written in highly legalistic terms and always relate to a specific entity within a company where the debt sits. If bonds are moved around in a corporate reorganisation or a merger, however, this can result in a phenomenon known as “orphaning”, where the CDS contracts end up referencing an entity that no longer has any debt. Normally, market participants spot that the debt has been moved and flag it to supervisors within 90 days. But in the case of VodafoneZiggo, the Netherlands’ largest cable operator that was formed in 2016, no one noticed that a unit previously backing the debt had been wound down in March 2018. The problem went undetected until the company filed a set of Dutch accounts last month. Oops! We have talked about orphan CDS before, but always when, you know, someone is doing something. Like: A hedge fund that has sold a lot of CDS on a company will go to that company and say “hey, if you reorganize your corporate structure to orphan your CDS, we will make a lot of money, and we will give some of it to you to make it worth your while.” Or: A company acquires another company and refinances its debt in a way that would ordinarily and unsurprisingly orphan its CDS, but hedge funds who bought a lot of that CDS will go to the acquirer and say “hey, if you don’t orphan that CDS, we will be a bit better off, and we will pay you something to make it worth your while.” Perhaps something like that happened here—perhaps a hedge fund that sold a lot of VodafoneZiggo CDS went to the company last year and said “hey if you quietly wind down your issuer subsidiary we will make a lot of money and give you some of it”—but there is no indication of that, and I doubt it. Instead this sounds like just a case of a company running its own business in the way it thinks best, without paying any attention at all to over-the-counter derivative contracts to which it is not a party, and the people buying and selling those derivatives not noticing. How much sympathy should you have for them? There is a lot of moaning about “a string of mishaps that have undermined confidence in the market” and “yet another example of why CDS is a broken product,” and I must say that when people buy Nestor stock on news about Nest, no one goes around saying that stocks are broken. Sometimes people just make mistakes! Still, I have some sympathy for them. There is nothing “highly legalistic,” really, about CDS contracts referencing the debt of a specific legal entity rather than some other entity. In a default, different subsidiaries of the same company can have different assets and different liabilities and different ultimate recoveries for creditors. If a company is sliding into default, it is important for investors to think about which subsidiaries have the money, and much of the skill of a distressed investor is in figuring that stuff out. If you are buying insurance against default by a company that you expect to default, you should give some careful thought to how the company might default, or not, and how the insurance actually works. But VodafoneZiggo CDS traded at 290 basis points, even before people noticed that it might be worthless. That is not a distressed level. That is not people making informed bets on the precise dynamics of an imminent default. That is people trading CDS on a normal healthy (though high-yield) company for the ordinary reasons: For far-out-of-the-money insurance against the hypothetical possibility of a default one day, or as a hedge to the price movements of VodafoneZiggo bonds (or other correlated bonds), or as part of an index bet on the price movements of European high-yield credit generally. These are not distressed-debt investors, and the mechanics of what would happen in a default are not top-of-mind for them, and for good reason: Those mechanics do not seem likely to play out any time soon and are not worth worrying about directly. They are, it turns out, worth worrying about indirectly: The specific mechanics of what would happen in a hypothetical default ramify back to the present prices; CDS that wouldn’t pay out when Bond X defaults really shouldn’t be a good hedge to the price movements of Bond X either. But that is often the sort of thing that you rely on the market to tell you: If CDS trades wider when Bond X trades wider, and tighter when Bond X trades tighter, and has a name that sounds a lot like “Bond X,” it is generally reasonable to assume that it is actually connected to Bond X. The problem is that, when everyone just assumes that the market works, there’s no one to make the market work , and sometimes everyone wakes up one day to find out that it doesn’t.

Most of the time, if someone has sold CDS on a company, and someone else has bought CDS on the company, and they cut a deal to tear up their trade in exchange for a final payment, the company shouldn’t care. The CDS doesn’t concern it; it’s not a party; it can just go about its business and not worry about some hedge funds’ side bets on its financial health. But Sears Holdings Inc. is not a particularly normal company, and as part of its convoluted bankruptcy proceedings it found some weird bonds that would affect payouts on its CDS, and auctioned those bonds so that CDS buyers and sellers could compete to own them. A CDS seller bought them, but some CDS buyers protested the auction and said that they would have paid more, and they all went to bankruptcy court, and the court indicated that there might be a partial do-over, and then over the holidays the CDS people all got together and agreed to a deal and told the court “never mind.” And now Sears—in the person of the committee of unsecured creditors to whom Sears owes money— is complaining, because it was hoping to get more money, and is asking the court to let it question the CDS parties and see if they got up to any illicit collusion. In general it is a nice windfall for a company to be able to play CDS buyers and CDS sellers against each other, because both sides will have incentives to give the company money, and then the company will have money. But if the CDS buyers and CDS sellers get together and decide to give each other money instead, the company will be a bit aggrieved. In other Sears news, “talks on the latest Sears takeover bid from Chairman Eddie Lampert are extending into Tuesday as stakeholders try to reach an agreement on whether Sears Holdings Corp. should live on.” And, while some people had asked for the settlement auction for Sears CDS to be delayed until those talks are concluded, the panel in charge said no yesterday.

If you invest money in a business, and the value of the business grows by 20 times, how much money do you get back? There are two main answers: If you invested in the business using a thing called “debt,” you get back as much money as you put in, though you also get paid interest along the way (and have a first claim to any money if the business doesn’t grow). If you invested in the business using a thing called “equity,” you get back 20 times as much money as you put in. There are good reasons why those are the two main answers. Those solutions—“you get back what you put in” and “your money grows as much as the business does”—are obvious, simple to understand, simple to document. But there is no reason why those should be the only answers. “You get back half the growth of the business,” or “you get back double the growth of the business,” or “you get back double the growth of the business up to a 200 percent return, then you participate one for one up to a 400 percent return, but you’re capped there”: These are all things that can be comprehended by the human mind and written down on paper by lawyers, and there is no theoretical obstacle to those things being the deal. What you actually get depends, as most things do, on your relative bargaining power and the background expectations of the market. And so in the case of venture capital investments in private tech companies, the norm is actually a little better for the investor (and worse for the company) than standard equity: It is convertible preferred equity , in which the investor’s return matches the company’s growth on the upside, but the investor gets some priority on the downside. Because, you know, the investor has the money, the entrepreneur needs the money, so the investor is able to invest on equity-but-better terms. One thing that we talk about from time to time around here, though, is that that power dynamic seems to be shifting. There is, to oversimplify, a lot of money, but only so many scalable world-transforming 100-times-payoff-for-venture-capitalists ideas. And so it seems like entrepreneurs are able to drive harder bargains and demand more “founder-friendly” terms—valuation or economic or governance terms—from venture capitalists. Meanwhile here is a story about companies that don’t want to provide scalable world-transforming 100-times payoffs for venture capitalists, and so are rejecting venture-capitalist money. Some of this is as simple as funding themselves out of operating profits and saying no when venture capitalists offer to invest, but some of it involves raising money from venture-capital-ish investors on non-quite-venture-capital terms: Indie.vc, based in Salt Lake City and part of the investment firm O’Reilly AlphaTech Ventures, offers start-ups the option to buy back the firm’s shares as a portion of their total sales. That caps the firm’s return at three times its investment. In the typical venture capital model, the earnings for a home-run deal are limitless. When Indie.vc started three years ago, it saw two or three applications a week, mostly from venture capital rejects. Now it gets as many as 10 applications a week, mostly from companies that could raise venture capital but don’t want to, said Bryce Roberts, the firm’s founder. Why not? The companies in this story seem to be mostly smaller, slower-growing, sustainable, lifestyle-ish companies that reject the venture-capital model of rapid growth followed by a near-term initial public offering or sale. But it is not unimaginable that larger, faster-growing, more-VC-appropriate companies might also want to break the normal VC mold: If you are confident that you will grow rapidly and achieve a 100x return in a triumphant IPO, why would you want to give up so much of that upside to your investors? Why not cap them at some reasonable multiple and keep the rest for yourself? They won’t like it, of course, but they’re the ones—now—clamoring to get into your deal. Also there is a stock buyback angle: Entrepreneurs are even finding ways to undo money they took from venture capital funds. Wistia, a video software company, used debt to buy out its investors last summer, declaring a desire to pursue sustainable, profitable growth. Buffer, a social media-focused software company, used its profits to do the same in August. Afterward, Joel Gascoigne, its co-founder and chief executive, received more than 100 emails from other founders who were inspired — or jealous. I look forward to a lot of hand-wringing about how our most innovative tech startups have stopped reinvesting in growth and are instead wasting their money buying back stock.

We talk a lot around here about the theory that common ownership of multiple firms in the same industry by diversified institutional shareholders reduces those firms’ incentives to compete with each other. Here is another paper about how, “When competing firms possess overlapping sets of investors, maximizing shareholder value may provide incentives that distort competitive behavior, affecting pricing, entry, contracting, and virtually all strategic interactions among firms.” This one is “Common Ownership in America: 1980-2017,” by Matthew Backus, Christoper Conlon and Michael Sinkinson, and it argues that “contrary to popular intuition, this is not primarily associated with the rise of BlackRock and Vanguard: instead, the trend in the time series is driven by a broader rise in diversified investment strategies, of which these firms are only the most recent incarnation.” When I talk to people about this theory, one argument that I sometimes hear is that index-fund managers like BlackRock and Vanguard probably aren’t doing anything to reduce competition. They are not really asset owners, after all, but just managers on behalf of clients, tools by which people can easily make diversified investments. Concentration of lots of stock in their hands does not really mean that public companies are becoming more closely held. Also BlackRock and Vanguard probably do not actually call up companies and say “hey please compete less”; in fact, arguably index fund managers do not have any real incentive to care about performance at all , since their promise to investors is that they will match the index’s performance, not that that performance will be good. But this seems to me to misunderstand the theory. It has nothing to do with BlackRock or Vanguard or indexing or, generally, the form in which companies are owned. It has to do with diversification versus not diversification. In a world in which individual investors—and investment managers—mostly pick a handful of stocks and bet on them, companies can assume that their investors are relatively undiversified and give little weight to the interests of their competitors. In a world in which individual investors—and investment managers—believe in the modern doctrine of diversification, it is simplest for corporate managers to assume that their investors own all the other stocks too. And if you assume that, and you want what is best for your shareholders, shouldn’t you want your competitors’ stocks to go up almost as much as your own? Elsewhere in indexing: State Street Global Advisors is calling on boards to review their companies’ cultures and explain its alignment with their strategy, in the latest example of large investors emphasising intangible factors as a means to create long-term value. There is a weird dynamic where index-fund investors have very little reason to care about most operational issues at the companies they own—they can’t overweight good performers or underweight bad ones, so there’s no reason to spend time researching or thinking about what factors lead to performance—but do feel the need to care about something , and to call it performance-related. If you own a lot of every stock, you will feel the urge to wade into the moral debates of the day that relate to stocks, and to have views on environmental stewardship or gun sales whatever. But you can’t just say that you are imposing your moral views on the companies that you own, since after all you don’t own them; you’re just working on behalf of your own investors. So you end up writing a lot of letters about very general social issues—“culture,” “ a positive contribution to society”—while also strenuously protesting that you only care about those issues because of their contribution to (long-term) profits. “The intangibles do drive the bottom line,” says State Street’s chief executive officer, but his letter to boards is about the intangibles, not the bottom line.

I’m a big fan of Slack Technologies Inc.’s approach to corporate finance. Near the peak of the unicorn boom, in 2015, Slack Chief Executive Officer Stewart Butterfield correctly noted that “it might be the best time for any kind of business, in any industry, to raise money for all of history, like since the time of the ancient Egyptians.” The relevance of that point to Slack was not obvious, though, because it happened to have all the money it needed. A less financially savvy tech unicorn might have taken that as a reason not to raise more money, but Slack decided that cheap money was cheap money and it was going to get some and worry about the rationale later. Top-ticking the market was its own reward. So Butterfield “said that his start-up had more than enough money in the bank—just before collecting $160 million more” and, when Slack’s bank accounts were totally stuffed, it started making its own venture capital investments: It had an easy time raising money, so why not put the money to work? A “meta-unicorn,” I called it. Also it kept raising money, including from the frankly pharaonic SoftBank Vision Fund. Is 2019 the best time in history for tech unicorns to raise money from the public markets? Ehh, not particularly. The S&P 500 is down more than 10 percent from its peak last year. Volatility is up. There is an overhang of several very large rumored unicorn initial public offerings, most notably one from Uber Technologies Inc., which might distract investors from other unicorns. Fortunately for Slack, it still doesn’t seem to need any money, perhaps because it did so very much top-ticking in the private markets. This gives it a certain amount of flexibility with respect to corporate finance. So: Slack Technologies Inc. is planning to go public through a direct listing, according to people familiar with the matter, potentially making it the second big technology company after Spotify Technology SA to bypass a traditional IPO. ... In a direct listing, a company bypasses the traditional underwriting process, which involves lining up investors ahead of time and selling shares at a set price, and instead lets the open market play a greater role in setting the price. No money is raised for the company and for that reason direct listings are rare. Spotify is the only large company that has done one, debuting last year on the New York Stock Exchange. If you are running a tech company in a decade in which private markets are lavishly generous about funding tech companies and public markets are sort of meh, a sensible approach is to raise a ton of money in the private market and then shrug your way public without raising any more. We talked a bunch about the Spotify direct listing when it happened, but it is hard to overstate the importance of the second big high-profile direct listing. There’s a reason that people still talk about Google’s Dutch auction IPO, 15 years later: because it didn’t inspire imitators. It didn’t become a standard tool of corporate finance, an option that is on the table for every company. It’s just a weird thing that Google did once. But if Slack follows Spotify’s lead in going public by direct listing, then it is much more likely to become a thing. Other tech companies considering going public won’t think “should we do that weird thing that Spotify did” but rather “what are the pros and cons of direct listings compared to initial public offerings?” Investment banks will—reluctantly!—put together pitchbook pages explaining direct listings and touting their own credentials at leading them. (“Haven’t only three banks ever led a big direct listing in the U.S.,” you might ask, but that just means that you don’t understand how pitchbook credentials work. Every bank is the market leader in everything, in the safety of their own pitchbooks.) But the impact of direct listings is not just the direct listings. Right now, the way you go public in the U.S. is with an IPO, and an IPO is a thing with a particular set of features. A direct listing is a different thing, with its own vague but developing set of features. But if they are both legitimate options, then there is no reason not to try to mix and match their features. Why not do a direct listing and then raise money a week later? (Why not do a direct listing and combine it with a buyback?) Or part of the reason that companies are interested in direct listings is that IPO bankers normally require a “lockup,” preventing the company and its major shareholders from selling shares for several months after the IPO. Why not just do an IPO without the lockup? The theory of the lockup is that investors won’t buy shares in a newly public company without protection against the overhang of more selling, but direct listings sort of prove that that isn’t true. Why not do an IPO without a greenshoe? Without a roadshow? The possibility of a direct listing just gives a company more leverage and flexibility to negotiate with its bankers, and with investors, about what is really necessary in an IPO. One theme that we talk about a lot around here is how large tech startups have broken down the normal categories of equity financing. It used to be that there were private markets, and there were public markets, and each category had well-defined features, and you’d have to choose one set of features or the other. You could stay private and raise money from venture capitalists: You’d keep a lot of control of your company (though those venture capitalists would demand board seats and some control rights), and you wouldn’t have the distractions of public financial reporting and activist shareholders, but you could raise only a limited amount of money and your employees and investors would eventually get impatient about their inability to sell their stock. Or you could go public and raise money from anyone, big mutual funds and retail investors alike: They have lots of money, so you could raise a lot of money, and your investors would have good liquidity, but you’d be giving up voting control of your company to strangers and you’d be subject to the whims of short sellers and high-frequency traders and Wall Street analysts focused on quarterly earnings. Now everything is mixed up. Private companies can raise limitless billions of dollars from mutual funds and retail(ish) investors, and can often have pretty good secondary liquidity, but they also sometimes suffer activist coups. And public companies can have non-voting stock, so that they don’t have to give up control to strangers and can perhaps focus on the long term. Companies no longer make a single choice—public or private—with a bunch of implied tradeoffs; they can make direct choices about each of the tradeoffs. It seems to me that the IPO process is going through something similar: It used to be that, if you wanted to go public, there was one way to do it. Now there are two. But the choice creates the possibility of more choice, of unlimited customization, of tweaking each feature to get exactly the tradeoffs you want. It sort of makes sense that this would be a project led by tech companies, no? The story is that there was a big old legacy business that comfortably sold a standard package of features for a lucrative price, and then a bunch of tech startups came in and questioned everything; they unbundled the service so customers could get what they wanted rather than what the legacy players wanted to sell. It’s just that the tech companies didn’t do it as competitors, by offering the disruptive unbundled product, but as customers, by demanding it.

Ah, the glamorous world of high finance! Brianna Wronko has an engineering degree from an Ivy League school and is the CEO of a health-care diagnostics company. Until this week, she never thought she’d be stuck holding business meetings in a San Francisco hotel bathroom. But with every restaurant, lobby, public park and cafe within walking distance of the J.P. Morgan Healthcare Conference’s headquarters packed by thousands of attendees, meeting space was at a premium. One hotel restaurant was charging a $300 an hour to sit at a bare wooden table. At the Westin St. Francis hotel, which hosts the investor meeting, the women’s bathroom didn’t have drink service, but it did have several marble vanities and plush leather chairs. “It’s quiet in here,’’ said Wronko, who founded and runs the startup Group K Diagnostics. That is, aside from all the flushing. Other great meeting spots include the furniture showroom at the local Macy’s, and imagine shopping for furniture at that Macy’s while this conference is going on. Salesperson: And here is our Executive Desk in imitation mahogany. You: Does it come with the health-care banker sitting at it? Banker: Shh I am holding a meeting here, the bathroom was full. You: Why are there six people in suits sitting on that bed. If you’re like me, you will read dozens of articles this year about how finance is becoming automated and investment bankers will all lose their jobs to algorithms, but none of them will be as good or informative as this one. Phones exist, you know? Email exists, and Slack; videoconferencing has gotten pretty good. But ten thousand bankers and clients and prospective clients and analysts and service providers and hangers-on left their comfortable well-equipped desks to get together in a space so crowded and inconvenient that they’re fighting to hold meetings in the bathrooms. There is something about a firm handshake and unmediated-by-technology eye contact that companies still seem to want, and that they are willing to go to stupid lengths to get. You can meet an algorithm anywhere, but sometimes you’d rather meet a human in a bathroom.

We have talked a bunch of times about the bankruptcy at Sears Holdings Inc. and the controversies involving its credit default swaps. Oversimplifying, a hedge fund called Cyrus Capital Partners is reported to have written a lot of CDS on Sears, which will pay out because Sears is bankrupt, but the specific amount of the payout will be based on the auction prices of a certain group of Sears bonds, and Cyrus has maybe cornered the market in those bonds. So the auction price will be high, and the CDS payout will be correspondingly low, and some broad group of people who own Sears CDS—to hedge other non-deliverable bonds, or to hedge other credit exposures, or because they are CDS index investors, or just because they wanted to bet against CDS—will not get a payout that reflects Sears’s actual (bad) financial situation. Or that’s the idea, though recently Cyrus seems to have settled its dispute with some of the big CDS buyers, and it’s not clear that any of this will actually happen. Still the controversy grinds on. For instance, the International Swaps and Derivatives Association’s Determinations Committee (which decides this stuff) has been asked “to delay an auction for CDS linked to a Sears Holdings unit until after Feb. 1,” because “a $525M deliverable second-lien loan held by Eddie Lampert’s hedge fund ESL could start trading after the company’s final sale hearing scheduled for Feb. 1.” The idea is that there are only so many debt instruments that are deliverable into the CDS auction, and Cyrus has maybe cornered the market on most of them. But there’s another one that is owned by Eddie Lampert, Sears’s boss, who has been trying to put together his own plan to take Sears out of bankruptcy. That plan would involve a credit bid—basically, Lampert would pay for Sears’s assets not in cash but by forgiving debt that he already owns—and so he is hanging on to that debt. But if the latest bid gets rejected then he will want to get rid of that debt, and the CDS auction would be a good place for him to sell it, and if he sold that debt in the auction then that would tend to bring down the auction price and, so, increase the payment on CDS. CDS holders want the auction to be delayed until this is resolved. Of course that is self-interested—adding Lampert’s bonds would increase their payout—but there is also a good general argument for it. If Sears can’t be saved, then sure, its bonds might be worth less than if it can be, and if CDS is going to pay off based on the actual value of Sears debt—if it is going to work as insurance against a Sears default—then it would be good to know what will happen before setting that payout. Whenever we talk about this stuff, someone emails me to say “why don’t they just make CDS pay out based on ____________.” Sometimes they will fill in the blank with something that reflects the “real” recovery of the debt—say, how much cash is distributed on the debt in bankruptcy. Other times they will fill in the blank with something that is easy to measure—for instance, a popular proposal is just to have CDS pay out 100 cents on the dollar in default, instead of messing around with auctions and recoveries. One thing to notice is that those things are in tension. If you want CDS to be good insurance for the actual risks that creditors take, then you will want it to pay out based closely on the actual recovery that lenders get at the end of a bankruptcy process. But you don’t only want accuracy, you also want convenience: Part of the benefit of buying insurance against default is that you don’t have to stick around through a lengthy bankruptcy process to figure out how much money you’ll get. CDS that paid out an arbitrary number at the instant of a bankruptcy filing would be very convenient but inaccurate; CDS that paid out based on the long-term value of whatever is distributed to creditors in bankruptcy would be more accurate but less convenient. (And here I am ignoring non-bankruptcy defaults and the various possibilities for gamesmanship in CDS and other complications.) But this is true of actually existing CDS too. Sears’s CDS will pay out based on the value of its bonds at some semi-arbitrary point in time after Sears filed for bankruptcy but before the case is finally resolved. Waiting longer might get you a value that more accurately reflects the real state of Sears’s finances, but it also requires Sears CDS holders to follow the details of the bankruptcy case, and fight to get their favored outcomes in that case, rather than just getting a payout quickly and moving on with their lives.

One of my favorite moments of the financial crisis was when Goldman Sachs Group Inc. put together a synthetic collateralized debt obligation that blew up on its clients, and the deal was so bad that a senior Goldman banker wrote an email calling it an expletive, and Senator Carl Levin, at a Senate hearing, read that email to then-Goldman Chief Financial Officer David Viniar and asked him if he thought that was okay, and Viniar, immortally, replied: “I don’t think it’s right to have that appear in an email.” (Disclosure: I worked at Goldman at the time.) This caused laughter in the Senate gallery, and people acted all shocked that Viniar criticized the email , as opposed to, for instance, the deal, or the fact that senior executives thought the deal was bad. But of course he had a point. Elsewhere in those hearings, Goldman executives argued eloquently that when they packaged risky securities and sold them to clients, they were giving those clients the exposures that they wanted; much of the work of a bank is subjective, giving customers what they want rather than what you think they should want, and there are not necessarily objectively right answers. Just because a deal blew up doesn’t mean that you put it together in bad faith. How can the Senate, or anyone, know that? And the answer is, well, if you were going around talking about how bad the deal was, boy, that sure seems like a sign of bad faith! Anyway here’s a story about how BNP Paribas SA converted a 130 million euro EuroMillions lottery jackpot into pounds and made rather a lot of money doing so—about 1 million pounds, or about 1 percent, which seems pretty rich on a fairly straightforward institutional-size foreign exchange transaction. But the story is not “BNP Paribas made too much money and that’s bad,” because everything is subjective and who knows how much money is too much. Instead the story is “BNP Paribas might have bragged about making too much money and that’s bad,” which, it is easy to see, would be bad: The lender has reviewed whether a salesperson made inappropriate comments about the fees it earned from working on the transaction, said people familiar with the matter. BNP Paribas earned about 1 million pounds from the EuroMillions transaction, the people said, declining to be identified as the details are private. It examined electronic communication on whether the employee bragged to others about how much it made on the deal, the person said, adding the fee is unusually high. The bank found no wrongdoing, one of the people said. Look, the thing is, in a lot of areas of banking, the whole job is figuring out how to charge people unusually high fees for transactions. Like your basic work is commoditized, and clients who know the deal can squeeze you down to the last basis point, and the only way you can make any money is by charging the more naive clients a lot. For the most part, if you got investigated every time you charged clients unusually high fees, the whole business model would break down. Go, charge unusually high fees! But do not brag about it. Elsewhere, here is a story about how the U.K. Financial Conduct Authority is investigating the “working culture” at Royal Bank of Canada in London. Usually the way people talk about “culture” in banking is that a bank does some bad stuff to its customers, or loses a bunch of money, and then people say “well this happened because the culture is bad,” and the bank commits to change its culture as part of its penance for the bad thing it did. Investigating the culture directly , without a triggering bad thing, seems unusually proactive.

I mean here is a simple model: They go to work every day, research companies, and think very hard about which stocks to buy. Based on that deep research and analysis, they buy the very best stocks they can find. Later, based on no research or analysis, but just sort of at random, they sell those stocks. It sounds dumb when you put it like that, but here (via Tyler Cowen) is a hilarious empirical paper by Klakow Akepanidtaworn, Rick Di Mascio, Alex Imas and Lawrence Schmidt, titled “Selling Fast and Buying Slow: Heuristics and Trading Performance of Institutional Investors,” that finds that it’s actually worse: We document a striking pattern: while the investors display clear skill in buying, their selling decisions underperform substantially. Positions added to the portfolio outperform both the benchmark and a strategy which randomly buys more shares of assets already held in the portfolio. This result holds both in terms of raw returns and adjusted for risk. In contrast, selling decisions not only fail to beat a no-skill strategy of selling another randomly chosen asset from the portfolio, they consistently underperform it by substantial amounts. PMs forgo between 50 and 100 basis points over a 1 year horizon relative to this random selling strategy, depending on the specification. As with buys, the selling result is robust when adjusting for systematic risk of the assets sold. We present evidence consistent with the discrepancy in performance between buy and sell decisions being driven by an asymmetric allocation of cognitive resources, particularly attention. When selling decisions coincide with exogenous releases of salient and portfolio-relevant information – company earnings announcements – sales also outperform the counterfactual. Buying and selling decisions are fairly similar in their underlying fundamentals: both require incorporating information to forecast the future performance of an asset. Forecasting returns with greater accuracy should improve the performance of purchases and sales. Skill in both decisions requires the investor to look for relevant information and integrate it into the forecast. Paying relatively little attention to selling would hinder the first step. But if the investor attends to the relevant information, then skill in buying should translate to skill in selling. Specifically, if decision-relevant information is salient and readily available, such as in the case of earnings announcements, differences in performance between buys and sells should be mitigated. Indeed, it does not appear that the investors lack fundamental skills for selling: selling decisions appear to capitalize on information during earnings announcements and outperform the counterfactual by between 90 and 120 basis points annually. This performance is in stark contrast to sales on non-announcement days, which consistently trail the random selling strategy by up to 200 basis points annually. On the other hand, the performance of purchases around announcement days does not meaningfully differ from those on non-announcement days. This is consistent with attention being generally allocated to buying decisions; in this case, the relevant information shock does not add much to the attention already devoted to making purchases. Okay, so the institutional investors (think: portfolio managers at asset-management companies who run portfolios for institutional clients) mostly pay attention to buying, not selling, but how do they sell stocks worse than randomly? Well, they just sell whatever has gone up a lot, or whatever has gone down a lot: PMs in our sample have substantially greater propensities to sell positions with extreme returns: both the worst and best performing assets in the portfolio are sold at rates more than 50% percent higher than assets that just under or over performed. Importantly, no such pattern is found on the buying side – unlike with selling, buying behavior correlates little with past returns and other observables “We conjecture that PMs in our sample focus primarily on finding the next great idea to add to their portfolio and view selling largely as a way to raise cash for purchases,” the authors write. “In order to quickly choose between alternatives to sell, PMs look for salient reasons to unload one asset over another,” and things that have gone up or down a lot are the ones that jump out at them. It is such a pleasing paper because, for one thing, it appears to be immediately actionable and in a ridiculous way. If you are a professional investment manager, you can go test your own past selling behavior, and if in fact your actual selling has underperformed random selling, you should replace it with random selling. Any time you need to sell a stock, just throw a dart at your portfolio and sell whatever it hits, and your performance will go up by 1 percentage point a year. For another thing it maps rather well onto the folk wisdom about investing. Anecdotally, if you hang around the financial markets you will get all sorts of generic process advice about how to decide which stocks to buy, and almost all of it—buy good companies with deep moats, buy good companies well below their intrinsic value, buy companies whose business you understand, buy companies that you’ve heard of, buy companies that your teenage children like, etc.—comes down to some sort of fundamental analysis of the underlying businesses. But you will also get—less, but some—advice about how to decide which stocks to sell, and it will often be pretty heuristic. “ Cut your losses and let your winners run,” is a thing that people say, which has nothing to do with the underlying businesses. “If you double your money, sell and take profits,” it says here, in Barron’s. The basic folksy rule-of-thumb wisdom for buying is about fundamentals, but for selling it’s usually about price action. Not always: One classic maxim is that you should dispassionately re-analyze each position each day, and if you wouldn’t buy it now you should sell it. But just typing it like that makes me suspect that it is an ideal that no one really lives up to. It sounds like a lot of work! And the paper is so psychologically plausible. The job is about analyzing companies and deciding which to buy; the fun is in starting relationships, not ending them; the glory is in finding the best stock that you don’t own and buying it, not finding the worst stock that you do own and selling it. The authors make much of the fact that “most research on heuristics and biases in financial decision-making has focused on non-experts, such as retail investors who hold modest portfolios,” while their study finds that professional investors also use inefficient heuristics. But of course they are professional investors . Just like retail investors are too busy doing their day jobs to make fully informed investment decisions, professional investors are too busy doing their day jobs—buying stocks—to make fully informed decisions about which stocks to sell.

One nice thing about Jeff Bezos is that he is just a regular shareholder of Amazon.com Inc. He’s a big shareholder—he owns about 16.1 percent of the stock, more than twice as much as the next-biggest holder—but he just owns ordinary common stock, with no special voting rights or agreements, and he has nowhere close to a majority. To the extent that he controls Amazon, it is because (1) he is the chief executive officer and (2) he is good at it. If a majority of the board of directors wanted to fire him, or if a disgruntled majority of the shareholders wanted to install a new board and management, they could, but this is not something that ever really comes up. Bezos’s situation is very different from that of Mark Zuckerberg, for instance; people do sometimes go around saying that Zuckerberg should not be CEO of Facebook Inc. anymore, but the only person who can do anything about that is Zuckerberg himself, since he is Facebook’s controlling shareholder by virtue of holding super-voting stock. Yesterday Bezos and his wife MacKenzie announced that they’ll be getting divorced. Here you can read an article with the headline “ Bezos Divorce Clouds His Stake in Amazon,” and, I guess, but only a little? Only the regular amount? Ms. Bezos, who was instrumental in helping to launch Amazon, could be entitled to half the couple’s wealth depending on where they divorce, attorneys said. If Ms. Bezos ends up with a chunk of Mr. Bezos’ stake, she could influence shareholder votes on resolutions and press for changes at the company. Sure. But she won’t, like, get a board seat. She won’t gain control of the company; she’ll just be a regular, large, but single-digit-percentage shareholder. And Bezos won’t lose control of the company; he is a large minority shareholder now and will be a large minority shareholder after the divorce. His control comes from being the founder and CEO, and from shareholders’ and directors’ trust in him, not from his voting rights. Amazon went public back when it wasn’t particularly fashionable for tech founder-CEOs to give themselves perpetual control rights through super-voting stock. Now it kind of is, though there has been a backlash. At the moment of going public, of course, directors and shareholders and the market tend to have a lot of confidence in the founder-CEO, but perpetual is a long time. The founder’s approach or personality might change, and the board’s and shareholders’ confidence in her might change, and also her personal situation might change. If you take your company public with dual-class stock so that the founder can retain control, I suppose you have to plan for divorce. What happens when a founder’s spouse takes half of her super-voting stock? Do the super votes go away on transfer in divorce, potentially eliminating the controlling block that kept the company safe from greedy activists or whatever? Do they stay with the stock, potentially giving a disgruntled ex-spouse power over the company? Do they go into a trust, reducing the ex-spouse’s control over the shares? There is a lot to think about, and no way to optimize in advance for every possible divorce dynamic. If the founder just has regular stock, it is all a bit simpler. One thing that I find a little weird about the Bezos divorce is that there are a lot of claims that it will make MacKenzie Bezos “the world’s richest woman.” I suppose there is a technical sense in which that is right, but it assumes not only that she will have a right to half of Jeff Bezos’s assets in divorce, but also that she has no such right in marriage. That strikes me as a strange way to think about marriage, and about the “community property” laws that might give her half the assets in divorce. (Surely those laws imply that she is in a sense a joint owner now?) I would have thought the more straightforward analysis is that she is the world’s richest woman now , because she is a member of a married couple that has more money than any other single person or married couple on the planet, but I guess that is not how the scorekeeping works. Still there is an obvious way in which divorce might make MacKenzie Bezos richer, or at least, more of a rich person. If you are the spouse of a gazillionaire founder-CEO, and you have a great idea to spend $5 billion on some investing or philanthropic or political endeavor, or on buying a newspaper or a sports team, and you talk it over with your spouse, then even in the most equal marriage your spouse might reasonably say “look we do not have $5 billion in cash; it’s all in company stock, and I (we) cannot sell my (our) shares because that would undermine shareholder confidence in the company and my leadership.” And so you can spend money like a very rich person, but not like a mega- rich person; you can buy a yacht, but not Manchester United. But once you get divorced and take half the stock, then even in the most amicable and supportive divorce you can probably just dump the stock and use the money for your own affairs. As a couple, there are some informal but real limits to the Bezoses’ diversification; once they split, some of those limits are relaxed.

Will the new Tesla Roadster “use SpaceX cold gas thruster system with ultra high pressure air in a composite over-wrapped pressure vessel in place of the 2 rear seats” in order to shoot flames out of its bottom and levitate above the street? [ Unfocuses eyes, stares blankly at a wall for 20 minutes. ] I don’t know. If it won’t, was it securities fraud for Elon Musk to tweet that it will? [ Unfocuses eyes, stares blankly at a wall for 20 minutes. ] I don’t know. Elon Musk has created an amazing sort of quantum superposition in which everything that he does is simultaneously a real revolution in automotive/rocket technology, a funny Twitter joke, and securities fraud. In honestly much weirder Tesla news, here is a securities filing from a Tesla Inc. director who on Monday apparently exercised stock options to buy 1,700 Tesla shares for $319.57 and then immediately turned around and sold those shares for $321.60, pocketing … [ unfocuses eyes, stares blankly at a wall for 20 minutes ] … $2.03 per share for herself. The options would have expired in 2024, making them theoretically worth something like $190 per share, which is more than $2.03. She exercised and sold under a pre-set Rule 10b5-1 trading plan. I do not know why you would do this!

Back when I worked in investment banking, it was considered bad form, except in an emergency, for a bank to fire people between, like, November and bonuses. You worked all year for a frankly below-market salary in the expectation that you’d get a big bonus at the end of the year; by Thanksgiving, that bonus felt pretty vested, and firing you before it was actually paid felt cruel. And everyone got a bonus; it was just part of the pay package rather than a special reward for exemplary performance. It feels a little like attitudes have changed: A portion of investment-bank pay has shifted from bonus to base salary, and if you have a bad year it is not as uncommon as it used to be to get a zero bonus. So firing poor performers just before bonuses isn’t so bad, since they wouldn’t be getting bonuses anyway. Here’s a story about how Morgan Stanley “is cutting dozens of jobs across sales and trading right before year-end bonuses” and, you know, fine. In other mean things that banks do, here is a story about how UBS AG is making Andrea Orcel sit out his entire six-month gardening leave before taking a job as chief executive officer at Banco Santander SA. I gather that he is sad about this and wanted to start sooner, but I have to say that I disagree. It seems to me that there are few better (though temporary) jobs in the world than high-level investment bank gardening leave. You get paid a lot of money not to work, what is not to like?

Here is a profile of Fahmi Quadir, who runs a tiny ($35 million) young (one-year-old) short-focused hedge fund called Safkhet Capital, which is named after the Egyptian goddess of, somehow, accounting; I have previously praised Quadir for coming up with the only good mythological hedge-fund name ever. As this profile demonstrates, she also has a certain way with investor letters: “This past quarter we were in a near constant battle against the faceless algorithms driving the ‘short squeeze’ bandwagon’s momentum,” she confessed. “Never did we expect that on such a compressed timetable, we would have such polarized performance.” And: “Knowing you’re right but that the market will always think you’re wrong at least until you become insolvent is the short-seller lesson everyone knows but few adhere to,” she wrote in the letter. “Knowing you’re wrong before the market knows you’re wrong is an adage I have yet to be told, perhaps reflective of an industry where the most common pitfall is a dearth of self-awareness and unwillingness to look inward.” I am not sure what that means but it sounds smart.

We talked the other day about achieving immortality through tax structuring. It was weird, you kind of had to be there. Anyway someone on Twitter referred me to this 2015 paper by Bret Bogenschneider of the University of Surrey titled “The Will to Tax Avoidence: Nietzsche and Libertarian Jurisprudence.” From the abstract: Libertarians also attempt to use money to “will” past physical death – to overcome death. In Nietzschean terms, this represents a psychological attempt to defeat Nihilism typically in the absence of a general belief in God or strong community values. Estate taxes in particular therefore represent permanent “death” since the Libertarian believes in the affirmation of “life” through tax avoidance. The idea of tax avoidance is therefore held as a fundamental right. The article describes the optimum design of tax systems as subject to a “minimum tax” threshold, thus preserving the Libertarian taxpayer an opportunity to affirm life through tax avoidance. I mean, sure. “Is death that which gives meaning to life,” the children ask in Barthelme’s “The School,” and the teacher replies “no, life is that which gives meaning to life,” but what about tax avoidance?
