Robin Wigglesworth has an article at the Financial Times about how algorithmic investing increases volatility, electronic trading leads to flash crashes, trend-following and volatility-targeting quantitative trading strategies are pro-cyclical, etc., the normal list of complaints. These complaints strike me as debatable—not that long ago people were worried that algorithmic trading created too little volatility—but plausible, and they are certainly the right category of complaints. Crowded pro-cyclical trading strategies really could increase systemic risk, electronic trading really does create the possibility of flash crashes, unmonitored computers really might rise up and enslave us, fine. But the article also quotes some hedge fund managers whose complaints are from the wrong category altogether. Here’s (former) hedge fund manager Philippe Jabre: “The last few years have become particularly difficult for active managers,” he said in his final letter to clients. “Financial markets have significantly evolved over the past decade, driven by new technologies, and the market itself is becoming more difficult to anticipate as traditional participants are imperceptibly replaced by computerised models. Mr Jabre is not alone. There has been recently a flurry of finger-pointing by humbled one-time masters of the universe, who argue that the swelling influence of computer-powered “quantitative”, or quant, investors and high-frequency traders is wreaking havoc on markets and rendering obsolete old-fashioned analysis and common sense. And here’s Stanley Druckenmiller: “These ‘algos’ have taken all the rhythm out of the market, and have become extremely confusing to me,” Stanley Druckenmiller, a famed investor and hedge fund manager, recently told an industry TV station. One issue here is that these are very narrow problems: The fact that some rich people personally find algorithms confusing is not something that I care about. Hedge fund managers don’t—or aren’t supposed to—get tenure; there is nothing unnatural about someone making a lot of money in the olden days and then being out-competed by the next generation. But the bigger issue is that these are not problems. If the market is “becoming more difficult to anticipate,” if algos “have taken all the rhythm out of the market,” those are good things . If markets are easy to anticipate, if they have a predictable rhythm, then that means that they are inefficient, that they do not incorporate all reasonably-easily-available information into prices. If Philippe Jabre and Stanley Druckenmiller are making money in rhythmic ways—if markets are predictable using “old-fashioned analysis and common sense” (“common sense”!)—then that means that other people are losing money in predictable ways, perhaps because they are stupid, or because they are driven by emotional factors, or because they have external constraints on their investing that Jabre and Druckenmiller can exploit. I have some aesthetic sympathy for the idea that smart ruthless people should make money at the expense of dumb emotional people, but one does not want to take that too far. The dumb emotional people are often retirement savers who are not deeply informed market experts because they have day jobs, or perhaps they are index funds whose trading is constrained by predictable rules. They buy too high and sell too low because the market has a rhythm and they don’t know how to clap to it; they are constantly coming in on the wrong beat, trading at the wrong price, and giving money to the smart hedge fund managers. When there’s no rhythm, when smart hedge fund managers can’t figure out what’s going on, that means the market is more efficient. That doesn’t mean that prices are right or whatever—who knows—but it does mean that prices aren’t wrong in ways that are easy to predict based on common sense. It means that regular people whose trading is driven by predictable emotions and errors are not getting the wrong price, because the wrongness of the price has been competed away. I mean they’re getting the wrong price, a little, because someone is doing that competing. The algorithms are taking advantage of the same human patterns that Jabre and Druckenmiller used to take advantage of, and—while it’s a mixed bag—they often do quite nicely out of it. (Bridgewater, Renaissance, Two Sigma and D.E. Shaw all had good years last year.) They just do it faster and cheaper, so that the price is less wrong and for a shorter time, so people like Druckenmiller can’t find any rhythm. The algorithms are providing the same service that the human managers used to provide: spotting human stupidity and correcting it to make markets more efficient. They’re just doing it more efficiently, and at scale. There are lots of stories like this, and they all read the same way. There were some people who worked in the widget factory in Widgetsville, and they made a good living and sent their kids to college on their widget earnings, and then someone invented a new widget machine that didn’t need so many workers, and now all the old widget workers are out of work, and the factory has shut down, and Widgetsville’s social fabric is crumbling, and reporters go to Widgetsville and write stories about the dire effects of technological change, which are concentrated and visible in Widgetsville, and meanwhile all the people who are getting their widgets 10 percent cheaper are pleased about it, in a vague abstract way, but there’s nothing particularly compelling about that story so no one writes about it. Similarly, the people who get more efficient, less predictable markets don’t have a particularly compelling story to tell. A lot of them are people like me, who invest as stupidly as possible: I buy index funds, so I don’t make any informed choice about what stocks to buy, and I buy those funds when I get money and sell them when I need money, so I don’t make any informed choice about timing. It is nice for me, in a vague abstract way, to think that rich fancy hedge fund managers have no more advantage than I do in picking stocks or in timing their purchases—that they can’t systematically profit from my stupidity—because the algorithms have robbed the markets of their rhythm. But honestly it is not something that I think about a lot, and it’s certainly not something that makes a material difference to my lifestyle. It makes a difference to the hedge fund managers’ lifestyle though! They used to make a good living, working in the artisanal workshops that produced market efficiency; they could send their kids to college with their earnings, and also get the college to name buildings after them. And now they can’t find their rhythm and they are confused. Of course they are complaining!

This is sort of a semantic point but if you go to an expensive college or trade school, and instead of taking out regular student loans to pay tuition you agree to pay the school back a percentage of your future earnings, meaning that if you make a lot of money then you will pay them a lot of money and if you are consistently unemployed then you will pay them nothing: Do you have any “student debt”? I say yes, you clearly do: You sign a contract agreeing to pay them money, and you have to pay them every month (that you have earnings), and if you don’t fulfill the contract—if you make a lot of money and don’t pay them any of it—then they can sue you and make you pay them. It is all fairly debt-like. It is not entirely debt-like. For one thing, you don’t have a fixed amount of debt; the amount you owe varies with your income. It’s like a structured note. The variance is also right-way: You owe more money when you have more money, and you owe no money when you have none, so the debt constrains your lifestyle less than regular fixed-amount debt might. (On the other hand it might cost you a lot more than regular debt, if all goes well.) These seem to me to be structural features of your debt, but they do not, I think, make it not debt. What makes it debt is the legal obligation to write a check every month. This is confusing, though, because the obvious analogy is to corporate equity: If you agree to pay the school 17 percent of your future earnings, then isn’t that like a company giving someone 17 percent of its stock? Aren’t the students who do stuff like this really selling stock in themselves , financing their education with equity rather than debt? No, not particularly, would be my view on the matter. Certainly a 17 percent shareholder of a public company isn’t entitled to receive 17 percent of its net income every month, though there are people who vaguely think that that’s how it works. And on the other hand a 17 percent shareholder of a public company will generally have some power to help elect the management of that company and decide its future strategy, while it would be very weird for an individual student to give a “shareholder” that kind of power. (It happens, but as performance art, not as a normal educational financing mechanism.) Anyway this concept of financing higher education through “equity” rather than “debt” has a long history where it gets some attention every couple of years and then fades away. I wrote a paper about it in law school once, and that was so long ago that I have paid off all of my (regular) law-school loans since then. We talk about it from time to time— we discussed it in 2016, for instance, when a financing- housing -through-“equity” startup got some attention—but here it is again from Andrew Ross Sorkin: What if there were a way to eliminate student debt? No, really. Ha, well, not really. The concept is deceptively simple: Instead of charging students tuition — which often requires them to take out thousands of dollars in loans — students go to school for free and are required to pay back a percentage of their income after graduation, but only if they get a job with a good salary. The idea, known as an Income Share Agreement, or I.S.A., has been experimented with and talked about for years. But what’s happening at Lambda School, an online learning start-up founded in 2017 with the backing of Y Combinator, has captivated venture capitalists. … At Lambda, students pay nothing upfront. But they are required to pay 17 percent of their salary to Lambda for two years if they get a job that pays more than $50,000. (Lambda says 83 percent of its students get a job with a median salary of $70,000 within six months of graduating.) If they don’t get a job, or their salary is lower, they pay nothing. Payments are capped at $30,000, so a highly paid student isn’t penalized for success, and if a student loses a job, the payments pause. It’s a coding school, of course; everything is a coding school. In the general case—funding college with “equity”—there are adverse-selection problems: The people most likely to take the deal will be the ones majoring in Classics or otherwise going into low-paying careers. (Or so theory would predict; in practice perhaps the ones most likely to take the deal are the financial engineers who are going to end up rich.) But perhaps that problem is more limited in a coding school where everyone is hoping to get similarly rich. You can, on Twitter, read criticisms of this that it is “ indentured servitude” or that Lambda has “ invented school taxes,” but those do not strike me as any more compelling than the claim that Lambda will “eliminate student debt.” It’s just a new (well, not that new) kind of student debt with a different structure; the question is whether the structural features are an improvement. I think there is a good argument that they are—that they reduce financial risk for students while giving the schools better incentives—but I guess I thought that 15 years ago too, so I’ve become a bit more skeptical about the practicality of this plan. In a society where everyone expects to become rich, it’s harder to get people to give up upside. Anyway here’s a funny quote from the founder guy: “There are no schools that are incentivized to make their students successful anywhere,” said Austen Allred, co-founder and chief executive of Lambda. “The schools get paid up front, they get paid in cash, whether that’s by the government or whether that’s by an individual doesn’t really matter. At the end of the day, the schools get paid no matter what.” This might come as a surprise to the good people at the Harvard College Fund who are currently standing behind my desk gently nudging me, but I suppose he is right that there are relatively few schools that are incentivized to make their students rich. Anyway I suppose I will write about this again when they, inevitably, put this program on the blockchain.

I dunno, if you are the chief executive officer of a gigantic multinational corporation, I would guess that at least every few weeks—maybe every day!—you are sitting down to meet with some of the people who use your product to talk with them about what they like and dislike about it, what new features and services they want, and so forth. Not every CEO, sure—there is the Steve Jobs/ Henry Ford approach of not talking to consumers about what they want because you don’t want to contaminate your pure vision of what to give them—but it does for the most part seem sort of normal to be interested in what your customers want and how to make your product serve them better. And then there is Mark Zuckerberg: Every year I take on a personal challenge to learn something new. I've built an AI for my home, run 365 miles, visited every US state, read 25 books, and learned Mandarin. … My challenge for 2019 is to host a series of public discussions about the future of technology in society -- the opportunities, the challenges, the hopes, and the anxieties. Every few weeks I'll talk with leaders, experts, and people in our community from different fields and I'll try different formats to keep it interesting. These will all be public, either on my Facebook or Instagram pages or on other media. This will be intellectually interesting, but there's a personal challenge for me here too. I'm an engineer, and I used to just build out my ideas and hope they'd mostly speak for themselves. But given the importance of what we do, that doesn't cut it anymore. So I'm going to put myself out there more than I've been comfortable with and engage more in some of these debates about the future, the tradeoffs we face, and where we want to go. “I’m also gonna complain publicly about Facebook every few weeks,” I joked on Twitter. It’s weird, right? I am tempted to say that, if you decide to start asking people about what they want out of your tech company 15 years after you start it , that’s a little late. But that would be far too glib. Zuckerberg had a sense of what people wanted out of his tech company when he started it, and the last 15 years have, for the most part, proved him totally correct in very straightforward ways: Everyone uses his product and he is very rich. It is good evidence for the Jobs/Ford approach, really: If Zuckerberg had started out by asking people “do you want a monolithic internet service that allows you to share baby pictures and also tracks your every move to give it to advertisers and law enforcement and Russian intelligence,” I think a lot of people would have said no, and he would not currently be a gazillionaire. There’s something stranger though. If an oil company CEO decided to meet with leaders and experts every few weeks to talk about the future of oil, your reaction would be: Well, yes, she sells oil, she needs to understand the future market and regulatory and scientific environment for oil so that she can prepare her company for the future. But with Zuckerberg it feels like the opposite: He is condescending to meet with leaders and experts to talk about their hopes and anxieties for the future of technology because he controls it , and he has decided it would be nice to get input from other people before deciding what the future of technology should be. It does not feel like the posture of a company founder seeking input from stakeholders to best position his company; it feels like the posture of a world leader seeking input from his subjects before deciding what to do with them. We I wrote yesterday about WeWork Cos. (sorry, “The We Company”) and its somewhat odd decision to sell some shares to SoftBank Group Corp. at a $47 billion valuation, at the same time that SoftBank will buy shares from existing investors at a $20 billion valuation. My takeaway was, huh, that’s weird, but I got a lot of pushback from readers who said: Well, no, that’s fine; the new shares will be preferred stock with a high ($47 billion-ish, one assumes) liquidation preference, while the old shares will be common stock or low-liquidation-preference preferred, and so the new shares really should be worth more. If WeWork was acquired for, say, $30 billion, SoftBank would normally get back all of the money that it put in at the $47 billion valuation, while the common stock would be paid out at a valuation of $30 billion or less. Fair! I sort of discount this argument for giant unicorns, where the most likely exit is usually an initial public offering that collapses the share classes, but it’s certainly true that a high-liquidation-preference preferred should be worth more than common stock. More than twice as much seems like a stretch here though. The famous recent paper from Will Gornall and Ilya Strebulaev arguing that big private tech-company valuations are too high—because headline valuations are based on preferred stocks with high liquidation preferences—finds that unicorn common stocks are on average 56 percent overvalued, meaning effectively that the latest round of preferred stock is worth on average 56 percent more than the common stock. But for stocks of $10-billion-plus unicorns the difference is much lower—10 percent for Airbnb, 16 percent for Dropbox, 11 percent for Palantir, 15 percent for Pinterest, 8 percent for Uber, and (based on earlier financing rounds) 14 percent for WeWork. SoftBank is apparently buying new WeWork preferred at a premium of … 135 percent? … to the common stock; I continue to think that’s a little weird.

In the olden days a stock exchange was a group of people who met in a big building to trade stocks. You had to be a member of the exchange to get into the building and trade the stocks, and the exchange was self-evidently a collective enterprise of the people who traded the stocks there. The people wanted to trade a lot of stocks, because their job was to trade stocks, and so they wanted the exchange to be a good place to trade stocks. If the building was comfortable and impressive, that was nice, but the building was not the fundamental element of the exchange. The fundamental element was the group of people who met there to trade. If they liked meeting in the building to trade then they’d keep meeting there. If the building got really drafty, or if it burned down, or if someone started standing at the door charging everyone $100 to go inside, then the people could just walk across the street and meet somewhere else to trade. This would not be simple and costless—you’d have to find everyone and get them all to agree on a new place, etc.—but it was certainly possible . The point of the exchange was to serve its members, and if a particular building or set of rules no longer met their needs then they could get together and agree on something else. These days a stock exchange is a big data center in New Jersey where algorithms meet to trade stocks. Also, in the U.S., 12 of the 13 exchanges are owned by one of three large for-profit public companies. The point of the exchange is to make money. This is a change! It leads to a certain amount of resentment: Basically, the exchanges charge the firms who trade there fees for data and access, and the trading firms complain about the fees and think they should be lower. The exchanges mostly have the upper hand, because each trading firm needs to be connected to every exchange more than each exchange needs to be connected to every trading firm. But not always. For instance, the Securities and Exchange Commission recently rejected proposed fee increases at some of the exchanges, after a lot of complaining from trading firms. Still it seems like there would be a more straightforward solution for trading firms who do not like the exchanges, which is to walk across the street and meet elsewhere to trade. The essence of a stock exchange is not the particular New Jersey data center that houses its matching engine, or the for-profit corporation that sets its rules and collects its fees; the essence is just a bunch of people (or algorithmic trading firms) who trade a lot of stocks and want to be able to trade with each other. They could do that anywhere! I mean, it’s more complicated than that—not only do you have the normal coordination problems of getting enough people to agree to meet elsewhere to trade, but also there is a complicated regulatory apparatus in the U.S. that controls how stock exchanges can operate—but it is still possible. Here’s a story about “Members Exchange or MEMX,” a new stock exchange that is being proposed by Morgan Stanley, Fidelity Investments, Citadel Securities LLC, Bank of America Merrill Lynch, Virtu Financial Inc., Charles Schwab Corp., E*Trade Financial Corp. and TD Ameritrade Holding Corp. While the last new stock exchange to launch in the U.S., the Investors Exchange or IEX, was self-consciously about protecting long-term fundamental investors from the ravages of high-frequency trading, MEMX seems to be self-consciously about protecting high-frequency traders from the ravages of stock-exchange fees: But brokers looking to save costs could be drawn to MEMX’s low fees. ICE, Nasdaq and Cboe have faced criticism for raising fees for services such as the data feeds that brokers use to monitor moves in stock prices. The three big exchange groups say their prices are fair. “We think with the right team we could run an exchange at a fraction of the cost of what the incumbents are offering,” said Virtu Chief Executive Officer Douglas Cifu. MEMX hasn’t yet said how much its fees will be. The involvement of Citadel Securities and Virtu could benefit the project if they become big buyers and sellers of shares on MEMX. The firms are the country’s two biggest stock traders, each handling around 20% of U.S. equities volume. It is not obvious what the right governance structure for a stock exchange is. An exchange run for the benefit of its members, rather than for the benefit of outside shareholders, clearly has some better incentives to maximize the volume, transparency, usefulness, etc. of the trading rather than the fees that it generates from that trading. On the other hand it probably also has some worse incentives, for instance to give its member firms advantages in trading against other traders. In any case these incentives are constrained—both because a fair efficient exchange will attract more business than an overpriced or sneaky one, and also because stock exchanges are pretty heavily regulated—but still, I am not sure that everything a stock exchange does for the benefit of its members will necessarily be for the benefit of markets. Elsewhere, here is a paper called “ Deviations from Time Priority on the NYSE,” by Robert Battalio, Robert Jennings and Bill McDonald, about the advantages that the New York Stock Exchange gives to its human floor traders: The New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) rule putting traders “on parity” is a vestige of the traditional floor-based trading model and favors floor-based traders. Parity requires that orders from floor brokers, the designated market maker, and the top of the electronic limit order book trade together. That is, floor trading interests can trade ahead of equally priced, previously arriving orders in the limit order book. The NYSE posits that floor traders provide valuable services to the investing public and one approach to remunerating them for these services is deviating from strict time priority. The cost of the potential benefits of the NYSE’s business model is not transparent. Our research is an initial attempt to quantify this cost. Their estimate of the cost is about $22.7 million to $61.1 million in 2017, which seems both (1) kind of small in the context of the U.S. equity market but also (2) quite a nice subsidy for floor traders.

An underrated sad aspect of aging is that a point comes in your life when you have bought most of the stocks you are going to buy. Before that point, you are—to be a bit pretentious—structurally short the stock market, so if the market drops that is good for you: You are a medium-term buyer of stocks, not a seller, so if stocks are cheap then you can buy more. “If you are a net eater of hamburger over the next ten years, you want hamburger to go down unless you are a cattle producer,” says Warren Buffett. Eventually, though, you have bought most of the stocks you are going to buy, and you become a net seller, as you slowly sell down your stocks to pay your living expenses. And then you just want the market to go up; when it goes down, you are sad, and have no consoling counterintuitive Warren-Buffett-y wisdom to rely on. When I was a lad I could enjoy a nice stock-market crash, but now it makes me nervous; that’s my retirement savings right there. This is a fact of human life but I suppose it is also a fact of the life cycle of investing firms, at least the kinds with long holding periods. If you run a venture capital or buyout fund, it is optimal to do all of your investing when investments are cheap, wait, and then sell all of your investments when they are expensive. This is made more difficult by the fact that it is generally much easier to raise money for your fund when investments are expensive, and more generally by the fact that modern workplace culture sort of expects you to do stuff every day. Still, you can dream, or I suppose just raise money in expensive times and then wait for cheap times. Anyway here is Erin Griffith on venture capitalists, such as Vini Letteri of KKR, who are waiting for a downturn: “When the market turns, we’re prepared to be more aggressive,” he said. He added that he had sketched out a “downturn list” of 150 targets — including financial tech, cybersecurity, and consumer internet companies — in case they become cheaper. Mr. Letteri is one of a growing number of venture capitalists rooting for a market dip to calm the overheated start-up scene. For the past few years, Silicon Valley tech start-ups have been awash in a stream of cash that has allowed them to expand quickly and sell or go public at high valuations. Yet that drove up the costs of deal making for venture capitalists, who often prefer to invest in young companies at lower prices in the hopes of making a bigger return later. I continue to be drawn to businesses where the optimal move is to do nothing. I should start a cyclical private equity fund whose gimmick is that we raise money during boom times and commit irrevocably to do nothing until the market crashes. “Here is evidence that I am being disciplined with your capital,” I would email limited partners every month, along with a snapshot of me sitting on a beach and an invoice for my management fee.

A stablecoin is a cryptocurrency that is supposed to always be worth a dollar. (Or some other fixed reference, but generally a dollar.) There are strange complicated ways to try to peg your stablecoin to the dollar, but the simplest way is also the most reliable: You issue your coins for a dollar, then you keep the dollars in a bank, and then when people want to redeem their coins you give them their dollars back. As long as you sell the coins for a dollar, and keep the dollars, and redeem the coins for a dollar on demand, then the coins should be worth a dollar. Ideally (for you) you’d have a bit of a bid-ask, so you’d sell the coins for $1.005 to people who really want a stable monetary instrument that is programmable and instantly transferable on the blockchain, and buy them back for $0.995 from people who really want dollars that they can use to buy a sandwich. Still there is a startup problem, which is that if you are trying to sell $1 coins for $1.005 to people who really want a stable monetary instrument that is programmable and instantly transferable on the blockchain, they might reasonably respond: Well, how do I know this is stable, and what kind of programming can I do with it, and whom can I transfer it to on the blockchain, and for what? In the future crypto utopia of smart contracts and seamless transfers, stablecoins will be super useful and the well-established trusted ones will have very stable values, I guess, but right now there is a certain novelty element to them. So if you are trying to get people to adopt your $1 stablecoin I guess you could … sell it to them for $0.99? That is one approach. Of course if you do that, and also agree to redeem your coin for $1, you’ve got a problem, which is that you’ve inverted your bid-ask spread. Still maybe it is fine if you just sell some coins at a discount, and use them to sort of seed the market, and—importantly— don’t redeem those coins for $1 immediately . Like, if you sell someone a coin for $0.99, you have to make them promise not to just come back to you a minute later and demand $1 for it. I gather that Gemini Trust Co., Cameron and Tyler Winklevoss’s cryptocurrency endeavor, did something like that when it issued its “ Gemini dollar” stablecoin. The Block reports: To spur adoption, Gemini offered their Gemini dollar to some over-the-counter trading desks at a discount – meaning each $1 token could be bought for less than a dollar. However, traders spotted an arbitrage opportunity in the deal where they could buy the discounted GUSD and then exchange it for Paxos Standard, Paxos’ stable coin, at the full dollar price – pocketing the difference. The point is that you can’t just buy a Gemini dollar for $0.99 and immediately turn around and sell it to the Winklevosses for $1; they will notice that. But you can buy a Gemini dollar for $0.99, trade it for a Paxos Standard (another stablecoin), and turn around and sell that to Paxos (another stablecoin issuer) for $1. Then presumably the person who bought your Gemini dollar for one Paxos Standard can turn around and redeem it from the Winklevosses for $1, so everyone wins, except the Winklevosses. It is a good arbitrage except that, in crypto, arbitrages never quite work: That caused headaches for Paxos. According to CEO Chad Cascarilla, traders exchanged vast sums of GUSD to PAX and then opened up dozens of accounts under relatives’ names to bypass Huobi, a fellow exchange’s, $10k transaction limit [for PAX withdrawals]. … “Some customers began structuring withdrawals to get around them; they were creating accounts under other people’s names who were not the owners of the funds to try to withdraw more PAX than the $10k limit — as many as 30 accounts in the same day,” Cascarilla said in a blog post after Paxos picked up on the conversion trick. The firm, which claims to scrupulously adhere to Wall Street’s KYC norms, responded by investigating those accounts and delaying redemptions. I feel like I am constantly reading about transaction limits for withdrawals of money from the crypto ecosystem, while I much less frequently read about transaction limits for putting money in . Similarly anti-money-laundering and know-your-customer procedures seem to constrain people from taking money out of cryptocurrencies more than they constrain people trying to put money in. It is an odd one-way ratchet. Elsewhere, Gemini is running an ad campaign with “slogans like ‘The Revolution Needs Rules,’” okay.

I wrote on Friday that “Companies don’t hire investment bankers to do big deals in the hopes that the bankers will buy them steak dinners afterwards; the bankers buy the steak dinners in the hopes that the companies will hire them to do big deals.” Honestly it did not occur to me that that statement might be controversial. But a reader pointed out that I’d forgotten about closing dinners, when bankers buy a fancy dinner for everyone on the client’s deal team after the transaction has closed. Closing dinners are standard and expected, and it is at least theoretically possible that a company’s executives might choose to do a big deal in the expectation that the bankers will buy them a fancy dinner afterwards. Also, closing dinners are big and traditional and expensive and found in almost every big deal, while buying fancy dinners for executives just to pitch them future business is common enough but not an essential feature of banking. I stand by my general point that bankers tend to do free work for clients mostly as a way to win future lucrative business, rather than as a way to thank the clients for past lucrative business, but on the specific issue of dinners I think I might have been wrong. The dinners might in fact be paid more in arrears than in advance.

If you are bribing government officials to give your firm lucrative construction contracts, an important question is: When do you pay the bribes? I am not an expert on bribes, but I had vaguely thought that the answer would be “before you are awarded the contracts.” It just seems like the government officials have more leverage than you do: They can award very large contracts, while you can only pay them somewhat smaller bribes; lots of people are competing to bribe them for the contracts, while there are relatively few corruptible governments that will give out lucrative contracts in exchange for bribes. Also of course this is, in different form, the normal approach in the gift economy of investment banking and big business generally: If you are a service provider trying to get a lucrative mandate from a company, you curry favor with the company by doing free work, taking executives out to dinner, etc., before they give you the mandate. Companies don’t hire investment bankers to do big deals in the hopes that the bankers will buy them steak dinners afterwards; the bankers buy the steak dinners in the hopes that the companies will hire them to do big deals. But the problem with bribes is that, if you pay a corrupt government official a large bribe before he awards you a lucrative contract, he can always not award you the contract. (Or he can hold out for more bribes.) It is hard to rely on his honesty and integrity, you know? And if he stiffs you it is not like you can sue. Plus, you might not have the money: You might need to get the contract payment first, so you can use some of it to pay the bribes. So here is an email that Jean Boustani, a salesman for Abu Dhabi-based shipbuilding company Privinvest Group, allegedly sent to an unnamed official of the government of Mozambique about the timing of alleged bribes (uh, “success fees”) connected to a contract that Mozambique awarded Privinvest to help build a “coastal monitoring system” to fight pirates: A very important issue which needs to be clear: we had various negative experiences in Africa. Especially related to the ‘success fees’ payments. Therefore, we have a strict policy in the Group consisting of not disbursing any ‘success fee’ before the signature of the Project Contract. Very fair! But look at it from the government official’s perspective. If he awards you the contract first, and then he doesn’t get his bribe, he still has leverage: He can cancel the contract or seize your assets in the country or whatever. But after the contract award he might be more constrained by institutions or publicity. Plus, in this particular case, the contract fee was paid at signing, so you’ve already got the money. Also, what if he loses an election? Here is how the Mozambican official allegedly responded to Boustani’s email: Fabulous, I agree with you in principle. Let us agree and look at project in two distinct moments. One moment is to massage the system and get the political will to go ahead with the project. The second moment is the project implementation/execution. I agree with you that any monies can only be paid after the project signing. This has to be treated separately from the project implementation … Because for the project implementation there will be other players whose interest will have to be looked after e.g. ministry of defense, ministry of interior, air force, etc. … in democratic governments like ours people come and go, and everyone involved will want to have his/her share of the deal while in office, because once out of the office it will be difficult. So, it is important that the contract signing success fee be agreed and paid in once-off, upon the signing of the contract. So the equilibrium is apparently that you pay the bribe at the same time the contract is signed. (Actually Privinvest allegedly wired its co-conspirators $10.2 million of bribes five days after signing, which is also when Mozambique wired Privinvest its $317 million fee under the contract.) Makes sense. Why would either party trust the other? Those emails are from this indictment that U.S. federal prosecutors in Brooklyn brought yesterday against Boustani, as well as Mozambique’s former Minister of Finance and three former Credit Suisse Group AG bankers who helped arrange the financing for the projects that Mozambique awarded to Privinvest. The indictment is full of instructive bribe-negotiation emails. For instance Boustani allegedly emailed the Mozambican official “requesting a bribe and kickback figure,” and the official replied: Fine brother. I have consulted and please put 50 million chickens. Whatever numbers you have on your poultry I will add 50 million of my breed. Look, again, I am not an expert on bribes, and nothing in this column is ever legal advice. But it does seem to me that, if you are looking for a code word for “bribes,” “success fees” is almost infinitely superior to “chickens.” Like if someone finds these emails and asks you “isn’t ‘success fee’ just a euphemism for ‘bribe,’” you can just tough it out and be like “oh no those are success fees, very standard, in every contract, you gotta pay a fee for success. Consulting! Local expertise!” But if someone finds these emails and asks you “isn’t ‘50 million chickens’ just a euphemism for ‘$50 million of bribes,’” what, are you going to be like “no no no we had a legitimate need for 50 million chickens for this coastal monitoring project, the chickens will be stationed on the seashore to look out for pirates”? Come on. If you are using “chickens” as a euphemism for “bribes,” you are not doing it to be sneaky; you are doing it to show off how ridiculously brazen you are. The charges against the three Credit Suisse bankers are in some ways stranger. A big part of them is: Credit Suisse originally demanded some stringent conditions for the loan, and in the course of negotiations the deal team replaced some of those conditions with less stringent but still perfectly reasonable conditions. For instance, Mozambique was receiving financing from the International Monetary Fund, which imposed limits on Mozambique’s borrowing from private sources, and Credit Suisse originally required Mozambique to inform the International Monetary Fund of the loan. This condition was replaced “with the less stringent requirement that Mozambique represent to investors ‘that they [were] in compliance with their IMF and World Bank obligations.’” That strikes me as a reasonable compromise: If the IMF required notice, then the compliance rep means that Mozambique would give the IMF notice; if the IMF didn’t require notice, then there’s no reason for Credit Suisse to. (Either way, the representation wasn’t true , but that’s a separate issue.) It is an unsettling read. Business deals are complicated, and there is a give and take in negotiating legal protections; a bank wants the strongest possible guarantee that its client is not doing anything legally risky, while the client wants as much flexibility as possible to run its affairs. The bank will generally start out by asking for a lot—copious representations and certifications and sign-offs and legal opinions and control rights for the bank—and the client will push back, and they will agree on a compromise. If it turns out that the client was doing enormously illegal stuff, then in hindsight that compromise will look suspicious: Why didn’t the bankers insist on ironclad guarantees? But that is just not generally how it works, even when there’s no bribery going on. Or there were some people involved in the deal—proposed deal partners and proposed directors of the entity formed by Privinvest and Mozambique—who were flagged by Credit Suisse executives or by an outside due diligence firm as bad actors. “A master of kickbacks,” is the phrase that a due diligence report used about one of them. The deal team “failed to relay” these concerns to Credit Suisse’s compliance department, alleges the indictment. But what they did instead was get rid of those people! “We need to structure him out of the picture,” the lead banker said about the kickback-master guy, and as far as I can tell they did. After seeing red flags about the proposed directors, the bankers got a different group of directors appointed, and then got compliance approval based on those directors “without revealing that two separate groups of directors had been researched.” I don’t know! That seems okay, no? Like, they considered doing a non-compliant transaction, and they researched it and decided that it would be non-compliant, so they decided to do a compliant one instead, and they took that one to the compliance department. In my former life as an investment banker, I tried to only go to compliance for approval of transactions that I thought were legal. Asking compliance to approve illegal transactions would have wasted their time and mine, and damaged my credibility. Occasionally people came to me—innocently enough, usually; the law is complicated—asking me to do transactions that were illegal, and I would say “no, that’s illegal, why don’t we do a legal transaction instead?” If they agreed, then I’d go get compliance approval for the legal one, not the other one.[1] The job of the deal banker is to structure a deal that works , that will get through compliance and committee approvals. Most deals start by not working, and the banker has to massage them to get them to work; you take the final one to compliance for approvals, not the bad rough draft. So I was sympathetic to the bankers up until I got to the part of the indictment alleging that “throughout 2013 and 2014, using loan proceeds, Privinvest made numerous kickback payments” to the Credit Suisse bankers! Specifically the lead banker allegedly got $45 million wired to a bank account that he set up in Abu Dhabi, characterized as “partial pymt on consultancy agreement” or “dividends payment,” some of which he allegedly shared with the other two bankers. These are much better euphemisms than “chickens,” but still, if you work at a bank you can’t have your banking client pay you millions of dollars personally for “consultancy”! Come on.[2]

A stylized story that you could tell about banking since, like, “It’s a Wonderful Life” is: In the olden days, each town had a local bank, and the local banker had a thick set of relationships with the people in the town that allowed him to make nuanced judgments of creditworthiness. If he saw you at church and knew your parents and was impressed by your firm handshake, he’d take a chance on giving you a loan; if he saw you at the pool hall and your parents were deadbeats and you had shifty eyes, he wouldn’t give you a loan no matter how good your collateral. The key determinant of creditworthiness was character, and the banker’s job was to evaluate character. Then banks became vast multinational entities and could no longer rely on those deep relationships to make credit judgments, and they were selling the loans anyway, so lending became a matter of crude judgments like FICO scores and debt-to-income ratios. This story is often told with an implication that the old methods were more accurate —that deep local knowledge and conservative banking led to better credit decisions than the crude numeric indicators—though I am not sure how true that is; I have never seen an empirical study on the relationship between firm handshakes and creditworthiness. And the old methods were susceptible to obvious biases; here is a recent study finding that (human-administered) auto loans tend to discriminate against minority borrowers more than (purely statistical) credit card originations. But in any case, the main point is that the new methods are faster, cheaper and much more scalable : If you are everywhere, it is hard to rely on local knowledge, and so you will rely on algorithms instead. But while not too long ago “algorithms” meant, like, “divide the loan amount by the customer’s income,” now the word “algorithms” carries the promise of infinite subtlety. Here’s a story about auto lenders who are using machine learning to evaluate borrowers, and the language can sound a little “It’s a Wonderful Life”-y: “What artificial intelligence and machine learning allow us to do is to get much broader perspective on consumers, and we’re going to be able to lend more to people who were invisible” thanks to additional data shedding light on their creditworthiness, she said. The computer doesn’t just look at crude signals, but probes deeply into the real story behind them, sort of: Instead of looking simply at whether a potential borrower has ever filed for bankruptcy, for example, the machine-learning system helped Prestige consider such factors as when the bankruptcy happened, and analyze that data with other variables, including previous car-payment records and time spent living in his or her current residence. (Amusingly, recent bankruptcies are better , for legal-risk rather than character-evaluation reasons.) If you are nostalgic for the old methods of individualized human evaluation, this is … good-ish? Lenders are making nuanced wholistic evaluations of a person’s life and character rather than just relying on crude scores. I tend to be an optimist about this sort of stuff, and I can easily believe that a machine-learning algorithm can end up making better lending decisions than both (1) local humans relying on their gut instinct for handshake quality and (2) simplistic numerical scoring mechanisms. And yet: creepy? The old-timey banker’s evaluation of your character was opaque and unpredictable and prone to bias, but at least there he was, sitting across the desk from you, shaking your hand. The algorithm’s evaluation of your character is opaque and unpredictable (at least to you), and perhaps prone to bias, and you have no human context to fit it into, no way to say “well I always thought that algorithm was a jerk.” It’s a story about lending but really it’s a story about postmodern life generally. In the olden days, people lived on a small human scale where they had deep connections to each other and all knew each other’s business. Then modernity occurred and people became more autonomous and anonymous, with weakening ties to their communities but, at the same time, with more freedom. Then, like, Facebook occurred, and now we somehow have the worst of everything; everyone knows everyone else’s business but in an inhuman, alienating, super-scale way.

If you’re buddies with New York Governor Andrew Cuomo, and he told you on Wednesday that he wasn’t going to shut down the L train, and you went and bought a bunch of real estate in Williamsburg before the official announcement on Thursday, and Williamsburg real estate prices shot up as soon as he made the announcement, would that be insider trading? Ugh I don’t know, who cares, though I will mention that a New York legislator is working on making it illegal. (Which maybe means that it isn’t now?) But what about if you’re friends with one of the engineers who worked on the alternative not-shutting-the-L proposal? Also seems like insider whatevering. But what if you’re friends with a tunnel engineer who didn’t work on the proposal, and has no connections to anything, but who nonetheless told you “you know there’s a way to repair the tunnel without shutting down the L and I bet they’ll figure that out”? That’s clearly legitimate research, right? It’s important for that engineering knowledge to be incorporated into the price of Williamsburg real estate, for market efficiency. I don’t know. Elsewhere, Sujeet Indap points to a “Social Q’s” column in the New York Times about material nonpublic information: My father is a big shot in finance. When I saw him recently, he asked about a friend and former roommate. I mentioned where he works. My father grimaced and said that my friend’s company will soon be sold. According to my dad, this will be terrible for my friend. Should I tell him to find a new job? If you did, and if he instead bought some stock in his company to profit from the sale, would that be insider trading? Ugh, I don’t know, who cares. My rough answer is: No, based on a theory of tipping from the big shot, but maybe yes, based on a theory of “come on, you work at the company, if you trade its stock knowing it’s going to be sold you will get in trouble.” But my real answer is that if a “big shot in finance” tells his son’s roommate that his company is going to be sold, he is half-remembering something he read in the newspaper about a different company, and the roommate should ignore him. This is not legal advice but, you know, the banker actually running the deal is not gossiping like that.

We talked a bit yesterday about flash crashes. “If humans just tried not to use market orders,” I said, a lot of trouble could be avoided: The problem is often that an exchange will only have so many orders lying around to buy a stock, so if someone comes in looking to sell a lot of that stock all at once, at whatever price she can get, the stock might briefly trade at a very low price before the buy orders are replenished. This prompted a reader, who is currently a leveraged loan trader at a bank, to email me this (lightly edited) reminiscence from his days at Wharton: Aug. ’03, MBA orientation: The bowels of Huntsman Hall housed a large ‘trading room’: ersatz Bloombergs, high ceilings, smug professor. Around 60-80 new students herded in to partake in a trading simulation with a bunch of stocks and commodities to trade off a fake news feed. After messing around for a few minutes I placed massively wide $0.01-$9,999 limits in a bunch of securities just to see what would happen. Started getting hit and lifted in size as people were putting in market orders against a really thin market. I could barely keep up with all the screens but knew every time it happened because I’d hear a “HEYYYYY… WHAT?!?” from somewhere in the room. Hardest part was replacing executed orders fast enough so I wouldn't miss the next one. Wound up +several $mm vs the field and decided “this trading thing is for me.” The bad news is that a lot of his classmates who got filled at $9,999 probably decided the same thing!

It’s worth spending a minute to talk about what a “flash crash” is. A “flash crash,” conventionally, means that some stock or bond or currency or whatever drops by a large amount very quickly, and then recovers a lot of that amount very quickly. (Colloquially it is also sometimes used to refer to when an asset goes up , and then back down, very quickly, but that’s kind of weird.) Sometimes the thing is worth just as much after the flash crash as it was before, and the flash crash is a pure glitch with no fundamental explanation, but often there is some fundamental shift, and the thing is worth less after the crash than before. It’s just that it’s worth a little less, whereas during the flash crash it was, briefly, trading for a whole lot less. And there is generally no fundamental explanation for that ; it’s not like terrible news occurred at 9:30 a.m. and then significantly mitigating news occurred at 9:30:05. The depth and rapidity of the crash is a pure artifact of market structure, not of fundamental value. So why does it happen? The popular answer is “ooh algorithms ooh” but that doesn’t really tell you much. But here is a very simple model: Lots of financial assets are traded using orders . Someone enters into a computer system a binding command to the effect of “I am willing to sell 100 things for $10 each,” and then they wait, and then someone else comes along and enters into the system “I am willing to buy 20 things for $10 each,” and then the computer says “aha, there’s a trade here,” and moves 20 things from the seller to the buyer and $200 from the buyer to the seller. Most of the time the computer systems have lots of orders sitting around. Some are very near to the market price: People are willing to buy a bunch of the thing for $9.99 and other people are willing to sell a bunch of the thing for $10.01. These people trade as prices move, or as other people come in who want to trade quickly and are willing to take whatever price is on offer. Other orders are farther from the market price: People are willing to buy some things for, like, $9.50, or $8, or sell them for like $10.50, or $12. Those people have to wait until the market moves a lot. (Other people are professional traders willing to buy a little at $9.99, sell a little at $10.01, and buy or sell a lot more for $9.50 or $10.50.) This mimics real life: In reality a lot of people think that, say, Bitcoin is worthless and wouldn’t pay anything for it, and a lot of people think that Bitcoin is the future of money and would pay $100,000 for it, and other people have views that are somewhere in between, and it happens to be that the price that balances those views is $3800 or whatever, and so there is a lot of trading at or near that price, but people who own Bitcoins and think they’re worth $20,000 have no desire to sell at that price, and people who don’t own Bitcoins and think they’re worth $20 have no desire to buy.[1] But it only loosely mimics real life. In the world , you can imagine a fairly complete demand schedule for a financial asset: Some people are high-frequency traders who want to buy it if the price drops a little or sell it if the price goes up a little, other people are deep-value investors who want to buy it if the price drops a lot but will otherwise stay away, other people are satisfied owners who will sell it if the price goes up a lot but will otherwise hold onto it, etc. But the computer system doesn’t capture all of that. Those people aren’t expressing those desires by putting far-away-from-market orders into the computer system. Lots of people who own, say, Tesla Inc. stock would sell it if the price doubled; lots of people who don’t own it would buy it if the price dropped by 50 percent; very few of those people have bothered to alert their brokers to those desires. There’s just no need, you know? If the price drops by 50 percent, then you can put in your buy order; if it doubles, then you can sell it; you don’t have to think about it now .[2] People are constantly coming to the market looking to buy or sell at whatever price is on offer. If they mostly balance each other out, then they’ll buy at $10.01 and sell at $9.99 and everything will bounce along. If more people are coming to buy than to sell, then the price will creep up; if more people are coming to sell then it will creep down. But if a lot of people want to sell all at once—or if one person wants to sell a lot all at once—then there will be a small, technical problem. The schedule of demand in the computer system will be sketchy and limited, reflecting not the actual demand for the thing in the world but just the orders that people bothered to put into the computer system based on the current price. And so if there are 100 orders sitting around to buy the thing at $9.99, and another 100 orders to buy at $9.95, and another 100 to buy at $9.90, and then 100 more to buy at $9.50, and then 50 more at $9, and then 100 more at $8, and someone sees the $9.99 bid price and puts in an order to sell 500 at whatever the market will bear, that person will buy all of the $9.99s and all of the $9.95s and so forth, and the price of the thing will fall all the way to $8, because that happens to be the highest bid sitting around that will fill the big sell order. And then the thing will print at $8 and all the people who were willing to buy at $9.50 or $9.90 or whatever but hadn’t bothered to put in an order to do that will be like “wait a minute this thing is on crazy sale” and will put in their own orders to buy, and the price will rebound up to $9.50 or $9.90 or whatever is justified by the actual schedule of fundamental demand in the world. And that’s a flash crash. This is probably not the whole story of any actual flash crash: There are more complicated algorithms, and stop-loss orders that get triggered, and fat fingers, and liquidity withdrawal, and whatever. But it does seem to be the basic intuition behind most of them. In a way, this really is a story about computers making markets less stable. If you couldn’t just leave your order in a computer system , this stuff mostly wouldn’t happen. Someone would come to the market and say “I want to sell 500 things” and the thing dealer would say “well I know there are people who want to buy 300 orders between $9.90 and $9.99, so you’re done on those, but after that it’s a little dodgy, let me call around and see if I can get you a decent price,” and she’d call a few more people and say “hey do you want to buy at $9.85” or whatever and get a price that actually reflects the real demand for the thing, rather than just mechanically relying on what is in the order book. And if she couldn’t—if she came back to you and said “yeah look the best I can do on your last 50 is $8, is that okay?”—you might just say no and not trade there, and the price would at least look more stable.[3] On the other hand, it is not a story about inscrutable computer algorithms behaving mysteriously in ways that humans can’t understand. It’s pretty easy to understand! Instead it is really a story about humans being inscrutable to the algorithms . If everyone just entered their entire schedule of demand into the computer—if everyone told the system exactly how much they’d be willing to buy or sell at every conceivable price, and updated that schedule as information changed—then the computer could cheerfully handle everything for everyone and there’d be no problem. That of course is unrealistic. Alternatively if humans just tried not to use market orders —if the people who wanted to sell a lot always told the computer “but not below $9.50, come on, that would be crazy”—then that would get most of the way there. The computer is a tool to allow the humans to express their views efficiently, but that efficiency comes at the cost of not capturing their views completely . Sometimes that leads to trouble. Anyway there was a currency flash whatever in Asia this morning. “Flash Crash” is in the Bloomberg News headline, but the main storyline is the sharp move up in the yen; currencies trade in pairs, of course, so one currency’s flash rally is another’s flash crash. (Here the crash was especially in the Australian dollar and Turkish lira.) The yen eventually gave up some of its gains, but not all of them, so presumably there is a fundamental view here; you can read various proposed fundamental explanations in the prior links but I will not discuss them here because this is not that kind of financial newsletter. Instead I will focus on vacations: With Japan on a four-day holiday this week, traders said they struggled to handle a flood of sell orders with pricing erratic. Once the yen strengthened past 105.50 against the dollar, others were forced to cover their short yen positions, said traders who asked not to be identified as they aren’t permitted to speak publicly. “It looks more like a liquidity event with the move happening in the gap between the New York handover to Asia,” said Damien Loh, chief investment officer of hedge fund Ensemble Capital Pte., in Singapore. “It was exacerbated by a Japan holiday and retail stops getting filled on the way down especially in yen crosses.” And time zones: There is a fragile spot in the $5.1 trillion currency market: early morning in Asia. This one- to two-hour period when U.S. traders are heading home— but market hubs in Singapore and Hong Kong aren’t yet fully up and running —has become known to traders as the twilight hour, a time when normally stable currencies can suddenly go haywire. What is the market structure problem here? Is it computers, or is it humans? Is it that the humans are lazy and stop paying attention for reasons like “holidays” and “sleep,” or is it that without human supervision the computers keep doing dumb stuff? It’s a little tempting to say that the problem is the combination of humans and computers. The problem is that humans expect to interact with humans who have a reasonable fundamental view of price, and computers expect to interact with computers (or humans) who have a rational approach to market structure, and there’s a brief period where most of the humans are asleep and the ones who are awake interact only with computers and get a nasty surprise.

I keep writing about fascinating convoluted machinations in the market for credit default swaps, and then they keep just going away at the last minute. We have talked a lot yesterday and before Christmas about Sears Holdings Inc., where, uh, some CDS stuff has been happening. Basically Cyrus Capital Partners seems to have sold a lot of CDS on a Sears subsidiary called Sears Roebuck Acceptance Corp., but it also seems to own most of the bonds of SRAC, and Sears is bankrupt, and the way CDS works is that there is an auction for the bonds to set the settlement price of the CDS, and if the auction price of the bonds is high (because Cyrus has them cornered) then the CDS will pay out little or nothing. Interesting! But then over the holidays Cyrus apparently cut a deal with some of the big owners of SRAC CDS to tear up their contracts, so never mind. It is not clear exactly how done this trade is—surely some people still own SRAC CDS, and some people (perhaps Cyrus) are still on the hook for SRAC CDS, and Cyrus still owns a bunch of SRAC bonds, and there will probably be a CDS auction and it might even be weird, but the stakes have gone way down. It is also not exactly clear what the deal was or how it was cut; lawyers for Sears’s creditors reported to the bankruptcy court that “the parties that appeared before the Court at the December 20 Hearing” (Cyrus and a couple of hedge funds that owned SRAC CDS) “have since engaged in private CDS-related transactions, purportedly through broker-dealers.” There is a pattern here. GSO Capital Partners had a clever idea to do weird stuff with CDS on Hovnanian Enterprises Inc., and we talked about it a bunch in this newsletter, and then U.S. regulators and the pope made scary noises about how GSO’s idea was bad, and ultimately GSO settled for, it seems fair to say, substantially less money than it could have made if it had fought to the death. The problem for GSO is that fighting to the death might have gotten it in trouble with regulators for “market manipulation,” definitely would have gotten it sued, might have pushed the International Swaps and Derivatives Association to change the rules of the CDS game, seemed likely to cause bad publicity and possibly ill will with investors, and also the pope was mad. And so, after staking out a pretty bold position, GSO retreated. Did that happen with Cyrus? I don’t know. In fact ISDA’s Determinations Committee had made some noises about changing the rules to blow up Cyrus’s trade, and that seems to have worried Cyrus. Unlike in Hovnanian, there have been no public statements from regulators about “market manipulation,” which in some ways is kind of odd. The Hovnanian trade—in which basically GSO offered Hovnanian some money to manufacture a default to make GSO’s CDS pay out—struck me as not at all like market manipulation. To me “market manipulation” means doing stuff to financial instruments to achieve an outcome that does not reflect the real world; the Hovnanian trade was intended to manipulate the real world . Seems fine! The Sears trade … I dunno, man, the basic idea is kind of cornering the market for some bonds, and then putting in a bid for those bonds that does not reflect their economic value but that creates a profit on an associated derivatives position. That … I mean … I feel like regulators pretty regularly decide that that is the core of market manipulation? That may not be quite fair: The bidding for these bonds is not in the “real” market, but in an auction that is expressly designed to settle derivatives; everyone involved in the auction is presumed to be interested in the derivatives price. Here is a fascinating memo to the ISDA Determinations Committee from Shearman & Stearling LLP, arguing that it should not change the rules to thwart Cyrus’s trade: It is clear that the Auction arrangements seek to establish a market price for the Deliverable Obligations. The market price is the market price within the confines of the Auction structure – it is not the market price more generally. While that market price may be informed by the wider creditor expectation of recovery in the insolvency/bankruptcy processes under way, that market price is also informed by other important factors, including critically the availability of and liquidity in the Deliverable Obligations. The principle of the Auction process is that the CDS market price is driven by market forces within the confines of the Auction structure. The CDS auction is a way of pricing bonds for CDS , not a way of determining the true value of the bonds. Manipulate it all you like I guess? One way to think about this is that there are some intuitive ways that CDS should work—it should pay out a lot if a company is bankrupt, and not if the company is fine, etc.—and a lot of CDS participants expect it to work that way. On the other hand, there are some non-intuitive ways that you might expect CDS to work, if you read the contracts very carefully and think very sneakily . And some smart sneaky careful hedge funds read the contracts like that and came up with clever trades that upended the reasonable expectations of the less-careful readers. But in fact there is a third level: CDS may not work exactly like your naïve expectations, but nor does it work exactly like your clever reading of the contract. What the contract says is only rarely the whole story of what the contract means; market expectations and public relations and regulatory pressures and, sometimes, the pope also matter. “This contract says we can do something crazy, let’s do it,” might be just as naïve a position as “meh this contract probably works the way we expect, let’s not read it.” The fact that the contract says you can do it doesn’t necessarily mean you can do it!

Yesterday on Twitter, Bloomberg’s Joe Weisenthal made a bit of fun of hedge fund managers “who start their letters with quotes from ancient philosophers,” the implications being (1) that’s annoying and (2) managers are more likely to wax philosophical when they are justifying losses than when they are reporting gains. Implication (1) is subjective (but not wrong!); implication (2), though, is an empirical question. If you had a good set of quarterly investor letters from a bunch of hedge funds over a long period, you could go read (or have an algorithm or a research assistant read) the letters and see what sorts of quotation habits correlate with what sorts of performance. Do managers actually quote ancient philosophers more after periods of bad performance? Is quoting ancient philosophers predictive of bad future performance? What about modern philosophers? Novelists? Movies? Popular songs? Poets? I would love to see a table correlating individual philosophers to future investment performance. I bet Wittgenstein has more alpha than Plato. Anyway I have enough readers who are professors or students of finance, and get asked enough for ideas for paper topics, that I’ve decided to start an occasional recurring Money Stuff section on “papers that someone should write.” Someone should write this paper! Get the quotes, categorize them in some interesting way, get the performance, run a regression, see if quoting philosophers predicts performance, etc. While you’re at it you could do other sorts of textual analysis on the letters. Are long letters good or bad? Long paragraphs, sentences, words? Is using the word “shall” a lot a negative sign? I feel like it would be. The problem is data collection; academics do not seem to have too much trouble getting decent data on hedge-fund returns, but investor letters are usually confidential, and gathering them seems like a labor-intensive and hit-or-miss process. (From my casual empirical experience, I’d bet that investor letters leaking correlates with negative performance.) There are tons of papers analyzing the language of public-company earnings calls and press releases, which are easy to get: Financial academics love language analysis, but they need a corpus. But if you could get this corpus, then you could find what sorts of linguistic markers correlate with what sorts of hedge-fund performance, and which ones are predictive of future performance. That would actually be kind of useful, and possibly hilarious.
