[1] This is conventional supply-and-demand economics but there is something off about it in financial markets: If financial markets are complete, if you think Bitcoin is worth $20,000 you should keep buying it until the price gets there, and if you think it’s worth $20 you should keep shorting it until the price gets there. There really shouldn’t be a normal demand schedule. However this description does seem to be … pretty accurate? Like there are a lot of value investors who go around saying that they buy stocks that they think are deeply underpriced, but none of them put 100 percent of their money on those bets. [2] More fundamentally, “ standing limit orders are options to trade,” and if you are really gung-ho to buy Tesla down 50 percent from today’s price you should be selling puts. That way you get paid some premium for the option. [3] This is how some markets work: Arguably it is part of the story of bond market liquidity (corporate bonds are mostly human-traded), and certainly it is the story of, like, mergers and acquisitions, or cars. Companies never accidentally sell themselves for a penny, and no one accidentally sells a car for a penny, because there is always a human there to say “wait a minute.” This is a popular argument among human stock traders not to cede control entirely to the computers, though of course stocks frequently have flash crashes; sometimes having a human around to say “wait a minute” does not seem to be sufficient to prevent flash crashes. In any case the obvious argument for the computers is that they are faster and cheaper, and in liquid products—stocks, currencies—this argument seems to have pretty completely carried the day.

Some stats for you. The last Money Stuff of 2018 was sent out in the morning of December 20; the previous day, the S&P 500 Index had closed at 2506.96. The first Money Stuff of 2019—this one—is going out in the morning of Wednesday, January 2; the previous trading day, Monday, December 31, the S&P closed at 2506.85. That’s a seven-trading-day move of 0.11 points, or about 0.004 percent. In the last ten years, there have been only six seven-trading-day periods with smaller stock-market moves. Basically my vacation was as quiet as the stock market ever gets, if you look only at the endpoints, which I did, because, remember, I was on vacation. In the middle, it was otherwise. The market went down a lot for a couple of days, and then it had an up 5 percent day last Wednesday, December 26, a day that was so good that it “was the first time ever, according to data compiled by Bloomberg that stretches back to 1990, in which more than 500 stocks in the S&P 500 finished positive.”[1] But it all ended up where it was when I left. Which is still not great; the market ended 2018 down about 6.2 percent for the year. The best stock market advice is of course Will Rogers’s—basically, buy the stocks that are going to go up—but let me also put in a plug for “if the markets are going to be wildly volatile for a week or so but end up where they started, maybe take the week off.” This is not good advice for everyone—if you’re a professional trader, volatile times are where you make your money, and I suppose there are like five retail investors for whom that is also true—but it is good advice for almost everyone.[2] But it is a particularly good approach if you are a financial columnist. Here I am, with the benefit of rest and hindsight, able to ignore the market gyrations of the last couple of weeks. But imagine if I’d come to work on Christmas Eve, with the market continuing its plunge, and felt the need to explain what had gone wrong. Feh! I am an efficient-markets purist, meaning that I believe not that markets are rational but just that I cannot explain or predict them. The market went down because it went down, and then later it went up because it went up, and fortunately you didn’t have to read that sage analysis from me at the time because I was on vacation. One analysis that you could have read last week, though, was this Wall Street Journal article about how the market drop was caused by algorithms: Behind the models employed by quants are algorithms, or investment recipes, that automatically buy and sell based on pre-set inputs. Lately, they’re dumping stocks, traders and investors say. “The speed and magnitude of the move probably are being exacerbated by the machines and model-driven trading,” says Neal Berger, who runs Eagle’s View Asset Management, which invests in hedge funds and other vehicles. “Human beings tend not to react this fast and violently.” Among the traders today are computers that buy and sell on models, and passive funds that seek only to hold the same securities as everyone else does. Meanwhile, bankers and brokers—once a ready source of buying and selling—have retreated. Today, when the computers start buying, everyone buys; when they sell, everyone sells. That was published on Christmas, and the next day saw a 5 percent rally, which I suppose was also due to algorithms? “It’s the algorithms” doesn’t have much power to explain or predict whether the market will go up or down. Nor does it have much power to explain or predict volatility; the last few months have been volatile, but “far from unheard of in terms of depth or velocity,” and lots of pre-algorithmic selloffs were more volatile. And as Allison Schrager points out, the “rise of algos and passive investing coincided with historically low volatility for years.” In general I am not especially moved by claims that algorithmic trading creates inscrutable volatility. Long before algorithmic trading, markets were volatile, and humans have always been notably terrible at explaining why markets move even when the humans were the only ones doing the moving. My general view is that market moves are emergent properties of many humans acting on their individual beliefs and desires, and that computers are tools that allow the markets to do what they were going to do anyway, but faster. Still there are perhaps interesting questions of computer cognition here. If the computers are just reflecting what the humans would do, then in a very loose sense the computers understand us better than we do: We don’t know what combination of geopolitical events and earnings surprises and animal spirits will cause the market to go up or down, but the computers do, or at least enact those moves up or down; our collective emotions are more legible to the computers than they are to us. On the other hand if the computers are adding something new—if they panic and sell everything when a human would remain calm, or coolly unplug themselves when a human would be frantically trading—then really that is weirder. Does that mean that the computers have developed emotions of their own? There is also the possibility that the current volatility is due to worries about bond market liquidity, or perhaps stock market liquidity.

We have talked a few times about goings-on involving credit default swaps on bankrupt retailer Sears Holdings Inc. and its subsidiary Sears Roebuck Acceptance Corp. The basic story is that there is a lot of CDS outstanding that references SRAC, but not a lot of actual SRAC bonds outstanding. The payout on CDS in bankruptcy is determined by an auction of the underlying bonds. If there aren’t many SRAC bonds, and if one seller has sold a lot of SRAC CDS, that one seller can just bid up the bonds in the auction and avoid paying out much on the CDS that it sold. But Sears discovered that it actually had some SRAC bonds lying around, and decided to sell them to raise some money in bankruptcy, which might have increased SRAC CDS payouts. But Sears ended up selling the bonds to Cyrus Capital Partners, which had reportedly sold a lot of SRAC CDS. And so now SRAC CDS seems unlikely to pay off much, and other hedge funds who own that CDS have tried various avenues—complaining to the bankruptcy court about the sale process, and to the International Swaps and Derivatives Association about the CDS auction—to try to change that. (A bankruptcy court hearing today on the sale process was scheduled for this morning, though the Sears unsecured creditors’ committee has declared the issue “resolved”; and the ISDA Determinations Committee meets tomorrow to consider the auction.) I have expressed both admiration for Cyrus’s and Sears’s work in making the best of a bad situation (Cyrus sold CDS on a bankrupt company and may not have to pay out! Sears found some intercompany notes in bankruptcy and was able to sell them for real money!), and also sympathy for the hedge funds on the other side who really will not get what they bargained for if their CDS doesn’t pay out. We talked about this in more detail before the break, and afterwards I got a number of emails to the effect of: What is the problem here? If you owned SRAC bonds and hedged them with SRAC CDS, this worked out fine for you. If the SRAC bonds go for 100 cents on the dollar in the CDS auction, then you can deliver the bonds in the auction, get 100 cents on the dollar on the bonds, and get zero on your CDS. You got the benefit of your hedge: You paid for protection in case your bonds weren’t repaid, and you’re getting fully repaid on your bonds. The only people who lost out here were people who owned SRAC CDS and weren’t using it to hedge SRAC bonds: They may get nothing on the CDS, and will get nothing on their bonds (because they have no bonds). But who cares about them? They were naked shorts, mere speculators who bet against the company to profit from its default, and the CDS market shouldn’t worry about them. Now this might in fact be true about some or all of the holders of SRAC CDS; I don’t know. But in general I think it has things exactly the wrong way round. The socially pointless CDS market is not people buying CDS without exactly offsetting bonds to hedge. The socially pointless CDS market is surely people buying CDS to exactly hedge their bonds . Who cares? Why does the world need an instrument that allows one person to buy a company’s bonds and not have credit exposure to the company, while another person has the credit exposure without owning the bonds? Just let the second guy buy the bonds! There is a widespread belief that the main socially useful purpose of CDS is to allow people to buy bonds and hedge out the credit risk, but that is weird: You can avoid the credit risk of bonds by just not buying the bonds! Buy Treasuries instead! I mean, buying CDS to hedge bonds is fine ; I don’t object to it, but I am not sure it makes the world a better place, or that there would be a big market for it if that was its only point.[3] No, the reason that CDS is valuable , that it expands the set of financial possibilities in the world, is that you can use CDS to hedge other things . If you are a Sears supplier who extends a lot of trade credit, you can buy CDS to hedge your risk. If you are a bank lender with an undrawn revolver commitment, you can buy CDS to hedge your contingent credit risk. If you are a counterparty selling interest-rate swaps to Sears, you can buy CDS to hedge your risk that Sears won’t pay you what it owes. If you are a bank lending money to a small private supplier to Sears, you can buy Sears CDS to hedge your risk that Sears will default and your borrower will have problems. If you are a bank lending money to small private companies that have nothing at all to do with Sears, you can buy index CDS to hedge your general risk that business credit will get worse generally, and that index CDS might include exposure to Sears CDS. If you are a holder of Sears Holdings bonds, you might buy SRAC CDS, if that CDS is more liquid and you figure that in a bankruptcy Sears Holdings and SRAC will both be about as bad. There are a lot of oblique, not-quite-perfect-hedge situations where you can combine Sears CDS with something else to create value , to make it possible to do something that you couldn’t do without that insurance. And you want at least some of them to work, to pay off in some intuitive way when your exposure to Sears goes bad. If none of them do—if the only thing that works is the perfect hedge—then that is bad, and CDS is a little pointless. This is a pretty general point. A lot of textbook descriptions of financial derivatives describe them as pure hedges: You buy a risky thing, and then you buy a perfectly matched derivative to eliminate the risk. A good question to ask is: Why would you do that? Why not just skip the risk, and the derivative, and watch TV instead? Sometimes the answer is “arbitrage”—buying the thing plus the derivative is somehow cheaper than doing neither—but that only pushes back the question (why are people selling the thing or the derivative so cheaply?). Usually the answer involves some set of people who have to buy the thing but don’t really want the risk, or who want the thing for reasons unrelated to the risk, or who can’t buy the thing and want to replicate the risk, or who have bought a slightly different thing and want a close enough hedge, or something. The case where the derivative perfectly offsets some other standard liquid financial instrument is easy to understand, but sort of trivial; what you want is a derivative that can do other things too.

s.h: Private markets are the new public markets
s.t: A pretty simple model of startup financing is: When you want to raise money from private markets, you go to venture capitalists. When you want to raise money from public markets, you go to investment bankers. Investment bankers, in this model, are specialists in public markets. If you’re a startup founder, you have no reason to have any expertise in how public markets work, but investment bankers do, so you hire them and pay them for their expertise (in structuring deals, pricing stocks, complying with securities laws, and marketing your stock to a long list of public investors). On the other hand if you want to raise venture-capital money you don’t hire investment bankers. Investment bankers aren’t specialists in private markets: They don’t know the “market” way to structure deals, they don’t necessarily have a good sense of how venture capitalists value startups, and they don’t have a long contact list of venture capitalists whom they can call up and get to buy private stock. And private investors don’t expect to do their investing through investment bankers: Venture capitalists expect to source their own deals rather than get pitches from bank salespeople, and to negotiate directly with founders rather than through bankers. But those are all just rough traditional generalizations and there is nothing essential about them. Here is a story from Bloomberg’s Sonali Basak and Olivia Zaleski about Morgan Stanley’s success in getting initial public offering mandates for tech companies. Part of this—which we have discussed before—is that Michael Grimes, the co-head of U.S. technology banking at Morgan Stanley, likes to do stunts: On the road, he relies on Airbnb Inc. to book accommodations and rent out his house, according to people familiar with his technique. Before leading Zynga Inc.’s IPO in 2011, he mastered its “CityVille” game on his phone. While pitching Ancestry.com, he showed the company an elaborate family tree he and his mother created together. For Uber, he moonlighted as a driver. (Tragically “Grimes became an avid reviewer on Yelp Inc. before its IPO in 2012” but did not end up leading the IPO, and imagine writing lots of Yelp reviews and not getting paid millions of dollars for your trouble.) But a more practical advantage is that Morgan Stanley is also good at raising money privately: Yet Grimes and his colleagues, many of whom have worked as bankers for 20 to 30 years, have another asset that’s even harder to mimic: The firm helps raise money for young companies in private markets, often tapping high-net-worth clients in its $2.5 trillion wealth management unit. This is good for Morgan Stanley because it is generally hard for an investment bank to prove its worth to pre-IPO companies: If those companies don’t need investment bankers until they are contemplating going public, they have no basis on which to evaluate different investment bankers, and the usual investment banking approach of winning big mandates by doing other investment-banking business for the company doesn’t work. (Thus, often, stunts.) But if Morgan Stanley can expand the category of investment-banking business—to advise not only on public-market financing but also on private financing—then it has an advantage in building pre-IPO relationships. It is also good for Morgan Stanley because private financing is lucrative: “The bank has earned about $60 million in fees arranging private funding for” Palantir Technologies Inc., “about equal to what it could earn handling an IPO.” And it’s good because it’s a nice selling point for the high-net-worth franchise: If Morgan Stanley can hand out Uber and Airbnb and Palantir shares before they go public, and other banks can’t, then customers who want those shares will choose Morgan Stanley. Still my basic model seems kind of correct? It is not like Morgan Stanley’s main approach here is calling up venture capitalists and getting them to invest in fledgling startups. It’s just that the work of a public-markets investment banker has expanded into markets that are, technically, private. Morgan Stanley is helping large established companies raise billions of dollars from institutional investors and high-net-worth individuals. Now it is doing that in private markets, but not too long ago, you would have called a deal like that an IPO.

Many complicated financial contracts contain a section that says something to the effect of “I have read this contract carefully, and I have had the opportunity to consult with my lawyer, and I am a sophisticated adult and understand what I am getting into.” The problem with that section is that, if you end up suing to get out of the contract because you didn’t understand it, that acknowledgment is a little self-defeating: You: I didn’t know what I was signing, the contract was so long and complicated, I am just an ordinary person, how could I know what it meant? Lawyer: But you acknowledged in section 14 of the contract that you are sophisticated and read the contract carefully! Was that a lie? You: Well I didn’t read that part either. One standard solution to this problem, and I am not kidding, is putting that section up front and printing it in big letters. Still that is imperfect, and what one really wants is a certification system where some objective third party validates the sophistication, literacy, competence, access-to-lawyers or whatever of a party to a contract. There are various rough forms of that in the U.S.—the “accredited investor” standard for private securities investments is a crude way of certifying sophistication—but nothing approaching how they do real estate transactions in Russia, where sellers “ need a certificate of sanity from a psychologist”: Sellers turn up at hospitals including Moscow’s Psychiatric Clinical Hospital No. 1, in the Clear Ponds neighborhood, home to some of the city’s most expensive real estate. Psychologists escort those who are planning real estate deals down a corridor to an examination room. The test lasts about 20 minutes. Antonina V. Parivova, a psychologist, said the test does not yield a medical diagnosis, but gauges whether a person is thinking rationally or has suffered brain damage. “A negative assessment results in a document saying, ‘Real estate trade is contraindicated.’” This is to prevent a form of fraud in which a seller agrees to sell her apartment, collects a down payment, and then voids the transaction claiming insanity. Presumably most real estate transactions are not done while insane, and this does seem like an inefficient equilibrium, but there might be some more general lessons here. I have argued in the past that the accredited-investor designation could be replaced by requiring a Certificate of Dumb Investment to invest in, um, dumb investments; I imagined the Securities and Exchange Commission supplying that certificate, but I’d be okay with a psychologist doing it instead. By the way the Moscow real estate market is very bad! Last year, state television reported that a gang of brokers kidnapped about 30 Moscow apartment sellers over eight years and then kept their properties. The former owners, mostly alcoholic single men, were put to work as slave laborers on a remote farm.
